Since there is often a time lag between the announcement of a policy and its implementation, an important question arises: when do rational actors incorporate new information into their market behavior, at the announcement or at the implementation of a policy? We investigate this question using the easing of trade tensions between China and the United States, marked by the "Phase One" trade deal announced in December 2019 and signed in January 2020, as a considerable positive trade shock. Focusing on two key events, the announcement of substantial tariff reductions on December 13, 2019, and the signing of the trade deal in January 2020, this study examines how both the announcement and the implementation of reduced trade barriers affected agricultural companies' stock prices. We employ an event study approach using data from the MSCI ACWI Select Agriculture Producers Investable Market Index to assess market reactions. The findings are consistent with the hypothesis derived from the conceptual framework, showing that rational market actors incorporate information at the announcement stage, not only at the implementation of a policy. However, sub-industry analyses indicate that a subset of sub-industries drives the aggregate effect, while additional heterogeneity analysis shows that the magnitude of the effects differs across continents. These findings are relevant for policymakers, businesses, and economists seeking to understand the broader economic implications of international trade agreements in general, and trade disputes in particular.
summary: An event study of the 2019–20 US–China Phase One trade deal finds agricultural firms' stock prices reacted at the announcement rather than the implementation, consistent with rational expectations.

title: The Cow or the Credit: Causal Relationship Between California Dairy Herd Consolidation and Anaerobic Digesters
authors: Michael McCullough; Jarrett Hart
abstract: The California dairy industry has experienced considerable consolidation over the past 30 years. During this period, there has also been substantial technological innovation, implementation of the state's Low Carbon Fuel Standard program, and rapid adoption of anaerobic digesters. This apparent correlation has fueled concerns that anaerobic digesters are causing consolidation. We test for a causal relationship between digesters and consolidation using synthetic differences-in-differences. Our findings dispute the theory that digesters are causing consolidation.
summary: Using synthetic difference-in-differences, disputes the theory that anaerobic digesters have driven the decades-long consolidation of California's dairy herd.

title: Complementary or Competitive? Emerging Interactions Between Restoration and Protection in the Conservation Reserve Program
authors: Wesley Zebrowski; Tyler Lark; Rich Iovanna
abstract: The USDA's Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) delivers environmental benefits to society by enrolling cropland and grasslands to reestablish or safeguard long-term vegetative cover. In recent years, the CRP has dramatically increased grassland enrollment while cropland enrollment has been in steady decline. This paper uses descriptive analysis, multivariate regression analysis, and a spatial comparison of participant incentives to assess the relationship between these two CRP signup types. We argue that while these two programs do not compete administratively under current trends, these enrollment patterns could tighten competition between the programs in future periods if total enrollment approaches a shared cap.
summary: Examines the shift from cropland to grassland enrollment in the USDA Conservation Reserve Program, arguing restoration and protection signups do not yet compete but could as total enrollment nears its cap.

title: Ex-Ante Assessment of Farm Resilience to Institutional Shocks: A Modeling Approach
authors: Nadja El Benni; Gabriele Mack
abstract: Using the agent-based model SWISSland, we simulate farm-level responses and interactions under two institutional shocks: tariff reductions and direct payment reductions. Using a framework we developed, we assess resilience capacities, resilience attributes, and the provision of private and public goods, following the shock. Results indicate that valley farms are vulnerable to tariff reductions and mountain farms to direct payment reductions. Payment cuts cause minor changes in private and public goods provision, while tariff reductions reduce provision levels. It shows that different shocks require different resilience attributes, underscoring the need for ex-ante resilience assessments to develop targeted measures strengthening farm resilience.
summary: Uses the agent-based model SWISSland to show Swiss valley farms are vulnerable to tariff cuts and mountain farms to direct-payment cuts, underscoring the need for ex-ante farm-resilience assessment.

title: Drought, Structural Breaks, and the Economics of Public Land Grazing: Evidence From the Intermountain West
authors: Zuyi Wang; Man-Keun Kim; Hernan A. Tejeda; Thomas R. Harris
abstract: This study investigates the decline in Bureau of Land Management (BLM) grazing allotments, authorized Animal Unit Months, across eight Intermountain states (Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming) from 1980 to 2022, examining the role of drought and structural change. Using outlier detection and structural break tests, we identify a concentrated regime shift in the early 2000s, with seven of eight states experiencing a statistically significant break between 2000 and 2003. Post-break allotments declined by 11% regionally, ranging from 8% in New Mexico to 27% in Colorado. Outlier analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity in the nature of shocks, with Idaho and Utah experiencing permanent level shifts, Colorado a temporary change, and Wyoming multiple shocks of all types. To quantify drought impacts, we estimate a fixed effects model with a lagged dependent variable and a state-specific structural break dummy. Results show that a one-unit decrease in the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) reduces allotments by 0.5% immediately and by 3.6% in the long run under sustained drought. The break dummy is negative and highly significant, indicating a permanent 6.5% reduction in allotments following the early 2000s drought that is not explained by drought or market variables alone. This suggests that factors beyond drought have reduced grazing capacity. A sustained severe drought (three-unit PDSI decrease) would permanently remove approximately 893,000 Animal Unit Months (AUMs) annually from the region, equivalent to 149,000–179,000 cow-calf pairs and representing between $9 million and $27 million in lost forage value at private lease rates. These findings support reforms to drought relief programs to account for lagged and permanent effects, flexible permitting mechanisms for temporary drought, and long-term adjustment assistance for permanent reductions. State-specific heterogeneity in drought impacts implies that, while BLM already administers grazing at state and district levels, further differentiation of drought relief and permit flexibility based on state-level vulnerabilities may improve effectiveness.
summary: Finds BLM grazing allotments across eight Intermountain states fell sharply after an early-2000s drought regime shift, with sustained drought permanently removing large amounts of authorized forage.

title: Expanded Farm Safety Net Payments Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act
authors: Oranuch Wongpiyabovorn; Tayatorn Pongspikul; Alejandro Plastina; Anup Paudel; Chandan Bhattarai; Jennifer Ifft
abstract: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) strengthens the agricultural risk coverage (ARC) and price loss coverage (PLC) programs by aligning program parameters more closely with recent market dynamics and allows for an expansion in program acres. This study projects the increases in ARC-County and PLC payments for corn, soybeans, and wheat under OBBBA, compared with those under the 2018 Farm Bill. Total projected program payments would increase by $4.65 billion for crop year 2025 and $1.30–$2.13 billion for crop year 2026 (depending on the relative enrollment rates), with high regional heterogeneity.
summary: Projects that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act sharply raises ARC and PLC farm safety-net payments for corn, soybeans, and wheat relative to the 2018 Farm Bill, with strong regional heterogeneity.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: FROM PAVEMENT TO PIXELS: Street Artists' and Urban Policy Responses to Generative AI in Bandung's Creative Economy
authors: Ardelia Indriani; Adiwan F. Aritenang
abstract: The rapid development of technology, particularly generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has brought significant transformation in the creative economy. GenAI has shown its capability to produce original artworks, presenting both opportunities and challenges for traditional artists. In this research we examine the perceptions of informal creative economy actors, particularly street painters in Braga Street, Bandung, and assess the local government's response to the emergence of GenAI. In this study, where we make use of stakeholder interviews and SWOT analysis, we found that artists' perceptions of AI are divided: some see AI as a tool, while others feel threatened by it. In the study we also highlight the absence of legal frameworks in Indonesia that regulate the ethical use of AI in the creative industry. Our findings reveal Bandung city as the leading art hub in Indonesia, responding to AI development through knowledge, artistic, and stakeholder networks. This study therefore contributes by highlighting the importance of artists' awareness and government policies to minimize risks and optimize the potential of GenAI in the arts sector.
summary: Through interviews and SWOT analysis of Bandung's street painters, finds artists are divided on generative AI and highlights Indonesia's absent legal framework for ethical AI use in the creative economy.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: POPULAR ENTREPRENEURSHIP: A Grammar of Moral Economy in Contemporary Urban Peripheries
authors: Henrique Costa
abstract: This article examines how popular entrepreneurship operates as a cultural grammar that disrupts established practices of wageless life in urban peripheries. Drawing on four years of ethnographic research conducted in São Paulo, it analyses entrepreneurial discourses not simply as ideological impositions, but as ambivalent mediations of everyday strategies of social reproduction. Rather than emerging solely from contemporary labour market transformations, entrepreneurship is shown to be rooted in longer-term trajectories shaped by family practices, moral values, and experiences of precarious work. The article situates the entrepreneurial ethos within broader processes of economic restructuring and the spreading of global trends of modernity, highlighting its entanglement with shifting expectations of mobility and autonomy. Empirical material from street-level commerce, entrepreneurship events, and in-depth interviews demonstrates how individuals navigate between survival and aspiration, mobilizing both residual practices and new normative frameworks. While entrepreneurship may provide access to resources, recognition and future-oriented projects, it also reorganizes existing tensions within the limits imposed by precarious conditions of life and work. In this sense, popular entrepreneurship is understood as a contradictory formation, through which longstanding ways of life are reworked rather than replaced, and where competing moralities, expectations and forms of economic action might converge.
summary: Drawing on São Paulo ethnography, argues 'popular entrepreneurship' reworks rather than replaces longstanding survival strategies in urban peripheries, mediating precarious social reproduction.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: NOCTURNAL INFORMALITY: Rethinking the Temporal Politics of Urban Informality
authors: Elmond Bandauko
abstract: Urban informality has long been theorized as a spatial condition of urban life—an expression of negotiation, improvisation, and survival within the uneven terrains of legality and governance. Yet this emphasis on space has obscured the temporalities through which informality is lived, governed, and contested. This essay develops the concept of 'nocturnal informality', drawing on experiences of street trading in Harare to foreground the night as a critical yet neglected temporal frontier of informal urbanism. Drawing on urban political theory and literature on the urban night, I argue that nocturnal informality reveals how the urban poor navigate shifting regimes of visibility, surveillance, and regulation across temporal rhythms. The night, I suggest, is not merely a temporal void but a socially and politically charged space–time in which informal practices unfold amid darkness, opacity, and affective intensity. Conceptually, nocturnal informality sharpens our understanding of how the local state is remade through the rhythmic and temporal dynamics of the urban night.
summary: Develops the concept of 'nocturnal informality' from Harare street trading to argue the urban night is a distinct temporal frontier where informal traders navigate shifting surveillance and regulation.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: DIFFERENTIATED INFRASTRUCTURAL CITIZENSHIP: Claims-Making and the Limits to Transformative Urbanization in a Fast-Growing Small City
authors: Nidhi Subramanyam
abstract: This article develops the concept of differentiated infrastructural citizenship (DIC) to explain how infrastructural citizenship is materially mediated, socially differentiated, and unevenly exercised in a rapidly urbanizing small city. It advances scholarship on infrastructural citizenship and everyday claims-making as political participation by arguing that the material-institutional terrain structuring infrastructural claims is not a neutral backdrop, but is produced through a hybrid waterscape that is itself an outcome of casteized land and housing tenures. By tracing DIC and its material and political outcomes in Tiruppur, a fast-growing small city in India, the article provincializes urban theory in two ways. First, it shifts analyses of infrastructural citizenship away from metrocentric accounts by theorizing how subaltern agrarian urbanization creates distinctive conditions for experiencing and exercising infrastructural citizenship. Second, it shows why critical theories on citizen participation must account for smallness: invented spaces of participation are unevenly accessible and difficult to sustain or scale in institutionally sparse contexts with fewer, segmented intermediaries. Findings from Tiruppur show that physical proximity to the state is insufficient for effective claims-making; DIC produces incremental, differentiated improvements without unsettling underlying structures of exclusion. It thus complicates normative claims about the potential of everyday claims-making to effect transformative urbanization.
summary: Introduces 'differentiated infrastructural citizenship' from Tiruppur, India, showing that proximity to the state yields only uneven, incremental infrastructure gains that leave underlying exclusion intact.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: MOBILIZING SUCCESS AND FAILURE: Strategic Ambivalence in Policy Mobility—Brasília and Argentina's Capital Relocation Debate
authors: Guillermo Jajamovich
abstract: Drawing on debates in policy mobility and relational urbanism, this article examines the proposal to relocate Argentina's federal capital from Buenos Aires to Viedma–Carmen de Patagones in the mid-1980s. It analyzes how external references were strategically mobilized across political and scalar arenas, focusing on the heterogeneous uses of Brasília during the debate. Rather than treating success and failure as opposing evaluations held by different actors, the article advances the concept of strategic ambivalence to capture the simultaneous mobilization of the same reference by the same politically powerful actors across different audiences, scales and moments of contestation. Brasília circulated at once as a successful model of territorial integration and as a cautionary example associated with urban, fiscal and planning failures—not as competing readings advanced by opponents, but as coexisting framings actively governed by proponents. This simultaneity, the article argues, is not inconsistency but a constitutive political practice. The article contributes to policy mobility scholarship by moving beyond accounts that locate divergent framings of success and failure in actors or coalitions and by showing how the politics of comparison itself—its connections, disconnections and deliberate instability—is strategically governed by state elites in contested territorial projects.
summary: Examines Argentina's 1980s capital-relocation debate to theorize 'strategic ambivalence'—how elites mobilized Brasília as both a success and a failure across different audiences.

title: Regime-Dependent Dynamics of Business and Financial Cycles: A Markov-Switching Framework for Morocco
authors: Marwan Rouahi; Abid Ihadiyan
abstract: This study aims to investigate the state-dependent interactions between business and financial cycles, challenging the linear assumptions prevalent in existing literature and arguing that these relationships are fundamentally regime-contingent. We employ a dual Markov-switching regression (MSR) framework to estimate two distinct models: one for the business cycle (output gap) and another for the financial cycle (private sector credit). This approach allows for the identification of distinct economic and financial regimes and an analysis of how drivers shift between them. Our results reveal an asymmetry. We identify distinct 'expansion' and 'recession' regimes for the real economy and 'credit boom' and 'credit crunch' regimes for finance. Crucially, credit contractions are significantly more persistent than expansions, and the fundamental drivers of each cycle shift dramatically across regimes, and in some cases decouple. We also document frequent desynchronization between cycles, signalling underlying vulnerabilities. The findings necessitate a paradigm shift towards pre-emptive, state-contingent and frequency-aware policy framework. For Morocco and similar emerging markets, this means macroprudential tools must be deployed aggressively during booms, while targeted interventions, rather than conventional monetary policy alone, are required to address persistent credit crunches. This research provides a template for policy design in economies navigating the complex interplay of financial integration and external volatility.
summary: Applies a dual Markov-switching framework to Morocco, finding business and financial cycles are regime-dependent, with credit contractions more persistent than expansions and cycles often desynchronized.

title: Local-Currency Sovereign Risk on South African Government Bonds: The Role of Sovereign and Exchange Rate Risk as Drivers of Changes in Nominal Bond Yields
authors: Mulalo Mamburu
abstract: While local-currency bond markets have become a dominant source of emerging-market financing and an integral component of the global financial system, market-observed measures of sovereign default risk are still based on foreign-currency denominated debt. This paper assesses the Du–Schreger credit risk spread on local-currency debt for South Africa for the period between January 2008 and October 2022, and shows that it is a good measure of local-currency credit risk for South Africa, in that it reflects developments in domestic sovereign risk while being less responsive to external developments than measures based on foreign-currency denominated debt. The credit spread is then used to examine the role of sovereign and exchange rate risk as drivers of changes in nominal bond yields. For the review period, global factors, particularly the US dollar, are shown to be significant drivers of changes in nominal yields relative to domestic factors, while sovereign risk became less significant over time.
summary: Assesses the Du–Schreger local-currency credit spread for South Africa, finding it a good measure of domestic sovereign risk and that global factors, especially the US dollar, drive nominal bond yields.

title: Clean Cooking in the Global South: A Critical Synthesis of Causal Evidence and a Future Research Agenda
authors: Yonas Alem
abstract: This paper synthesizes causal evidence on the transition from traditional biomass to improved cookstoves and modern fuels like LPG and electricity. Although literature identifies liquidity, gender and information as primary barriers to adoption, uncertainty remains regarding usage intensity and technological persistence. To address this welfare wedge, we propose a Clean Energy 2.0 research agenda centred on six critical frontiers: (i) financial innovations like Pay-As-You-Go models and labour-linked transfers; (ii) the objective measurement gap between self-reports and sensor data; (iii) increased methodological rigour and statistical power in randomized trials; (iv) the geographic imbalance favouring rural studies over urban charcoal hotspots; (v) a broader welfare lens encompassing general equilibrium effects on household time-use and agency; and (vi) the neglected energy behaviour of micro and small enterprises. We argue that accounting for the production sector is essential to prevent market leakage, where household-level gains are neutralized by industrial biomass consumption, decoupling productivity from environmental degradation.
summary: Synthesizes causal evidence on clean-cooking transitions in the Global South and proposes a 'Clean Energy 2.0' agenda spanning finance, measurement, trial rigor, and enterprise energy use.

title: Mathematics Skills in South Africa: Data Reliability, Quantifying the Undersupply, and Projecting the Future
authors: Martin Gustafsson
abstract: South Africa enjoys access to reliable data on mathematics skills among youths, skills which are vital for postschool opportunities and national development. But the data are underutilised and the available research could be communicated better. This article discusses several perceptions not supported by evidence. It presents new evidence confirming two things. Firstly, despite improvements in the schooling system, the supply of mathematics skills is still below present levels of university demand. Secondly, the supply of good mathematics skills is better in rural than urban parts of the country, which is counterintuitive and important for planning expansion to this supply.
summary: Argues South Africa's mathematics-skills data are underused, showing the supply of math skills remains below university demand and is counterintuitively stronger in rural than urban areas.

title: A Description and Critique of the Quarterly Labour Force Survey Public Earnings Data: 2010–2023
authors: Andrew Kerr
abstract: In this paper, I summarise research noting concerns with the quality of the QLFS earnings imputations, provide a description of the publicly available QLFS earnings data between 2010 and 2023 and describe how the structure of the earnings data that has been released publicly has changed over time. I explain why researchers and policymakers should not use the currently publicly available QLFS data to undertake comparisons of earnings over time or to undertake regression analysis at all.
summary: Critiques the publicly released Quarterly Labour Force Survey earnings data for 2010–2023, cautioning against using them for over-time comparisons or regression analysis.

title: The New Economics of Cape Slavery
authors: Johan Fourie
abstract: In this survey, I argue that the Cape Colony has become one of the most useful settings for studying the economics of unfree labour. The Cape offers a distinctive combination: a slavery regime linking the Indian Ocean and Atlantic worlds, an urban and agrarian economy, overlapping labour regimes and archives rich enough for linked micro-data. Recent work treats slavery as both a labour and an asset regime, reads the Cape against Atlantic plantation economies to separate slavery-as-capital from plantation scale and recovers enslaved people's agency as evidence on outside options. The paper sets out five research priorities.
summary: Surveys the economics of Cape Colony slavery, arguing its blended labor-and-asset regime and rich archives make it a valuable setting for studying unfree labour, and sets five research priorities.

title: Modelling spatial density: Data, methods, and R applications in statistics, econometrics, and machine learning
authors: Jean Dubé
summary: A methods paper presenting data, techniques, and R applications for modelling spatial density across statistics, econometrics, and machine learning.

title: Activating territorial circular ecosystems through intermediaries
authors: Thibaut Joltreau; Sebastien Bourdin; Christian Gnekpe
keywords: Circular economy; construction sector; material reuse; territorial circular ecosystems; territorial intermediation
abstract: This article examines how intermediary organisations activate territorial circular ecosystems. Drawing on 44 interviews in the construction material reuse sector in the Toulouse metropolitan area and the wider Occitanie region (France), it identifies four barriers to circular economy implementation: coordination failures, regulatory uncertainty, logistical and financial constraints, and skill gaps. The analysis shows that intermediaries address these barriers through regional matchmaking, regulatory translation, logistical orchestration, economic alignment and capability-building. These functions are shaped by organisational mandates, funding arrangements and governance positions. The article contributes to regional studies by conceptualising intermediation as a place-based coordination mechanism through which circular practices become operational, routinised and territorially stabilised.
summary: Examines how intermediaries activate territorial circular-economy ecosystems, contributing to regional circular-transition scholarship.

title: Territorial drivers of social innovations
authors: Filippo Berti Mecocci; Roberto Dellisanti; Amir Maghssudipour
keywords: agglomeration; density externalities; European regions; public funding; Social innovation; technological knowledge
abstract: What territorial conditions enable social innovation? This paper examines whether accumulated technological knowledge, density externalities and public funding help explain social innovation intensity across European regions. Relying on a regional dataset originally assembled from multiple sources and adopting different econometric specifications, findings suggest no significant role for accumulated technological knowledge, while population density is positively associated with social innovation intensity. Public funding also matters, but only in low-density areas.
summary: Investigates the territorial factors that drive social innovations across regions.

title: Lights, camera, coopetition: film and television production in a peripheral region
authors: Judith Woods; Frank Crowley; Rodney McAdam; Nola Hewitt-Dundas
keywords: antecedents; Coopetition; film and television production sector; peripherality
abstract: While ‘coopetition’ – the simultaneous competition and cooperation of firms in regional clusters – supports regional value creation, its dynamics in peripheral regions remain underexplored. This research addresses this gap by examining the antecedents of coopetition in the film and television production sector in the peripheral UK region of Northern Ireland (NI). The findings show that constraints linked to peripherality, firm size and age influence coopetition, while individual-level factors, particularly the owner-manager’s mindset, play a mediating role. Firms engage in coopetition as a relational response to spatial disadvantage. The study advances understanding of how coopetition functions in distinct regional and industrial contexts.
summary: Studies 'coopetition' in film and television production within a peripheral region, examining how firms cooperate and compete in creative industries.

title: The effect of polycentric urban spatial structure on individual housing affordability in China
authors: Wan Li; Qianqian Liu; Shuaishuai Han; Zhensheng Kuang
keywords: China; perceived housing affordability; polycentricity; Urban spatial structure
abstract: Polycentric development is increasingly promoted as a remedy for housing affordability challenges, yet systematic evidence on its effects remains limited and largely aggregate-level. Moving beyond this approach, this study examines the relationship between urban polycentricity and individual housing affordability across Chinese cities. Contrary to theoretical expectations, greater polycentricity is associated with lower affordability overall. This relationship is heterogeneous: residents in main centres and higher-income groups experience stronger affordability declines, while those in non-centre locations and lower-income households report relative improvements. City size does not significantly moderate these effects. These findings call for context-sensitive and socially attuned approaches to polycentric development.
summary: Examines how polycentric urban spatial structure affects individual housing affordability in China.

title: Intertwining scenario 'knowledges' in strategic spatial planning: a 'theories of truth' perspective
authors: Mikko Airikkala; Matti Sahlberg; Hanna Mattila; Raine Mäntysalo
keywords: case study; futures knowledge; scenario planning; spatial planning; theories of truth; Urban and regional development
abstract: The article introduces a theories of truth perspective to futures knowledge in spatial scenario planning. The theories advance existing typologies by making validity bases explicit: correspondence (empirical fit), coherence (narrative consistency) and pragmatic (usefulness). The theoretical analysis is illustrated with a scenario planning case, which studied the future of urban and regional structure of Finland and utilised different knowledge types integratively. The findings suggest that the constant intertwining of validity bases enhance the robustness of futures knowledge. The article recommends complementary use of knowledge types and proposes that pragmatic criteria–instrumentality and ability to generate planning action–should guide knowledge use.
summary: Applies a 'theories of truth' lens to how different scenario knowledges are intertwined in strategic spatial planning.

title: Spatial mobility network and influencing factors of digital talent in the Greater Bay Area
authors: Yuanfang Chen
keywords: complex network analysis; digital talent mobility; Online professional profile; spatial autoregressive interaction model
abstract: This study examines digital talent mobility in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area using online public professional profiles from 2015 to 2024. Combining complex network analysis with a spatial autoregressive interaction model, it reveals global hub-to-hub links, a national diamond structure and a regional hierarchy, with Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Hong Kong and Macau playing differentiated roles. Urban scale drives attraction and retention of digital talents, while salary effects are unstable. Education-related public investment attracts talent more strongly in central cities, and research and development capacity mainly supports local retention. Distance decay and negative origin-destination dependence reveal persistent spatial friction and corridor-level competition.
summary: Maps the spatial mobility network of digital talent across China's Greater Bay Area and its influencing factors.

title: The heterogeneous effects of South Korea's green belt policy
authors: Changro Lee
keywords: CATE; Green belt policy; land price; target transformation
abstract: South Korea's green belt policy aims to restrict development to control urban sprawl, but its economic burden on landowners varies substantially across locations. Using the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) framework, target transformation and machine learning models, this study estimates the policy's heterogeneous effects on land prices. Results reveal pronounced price declines in highly urbanised areas and minimal impacts in provincial townships. While the policy's negative effects diminish with distance from Seoul's core, townships with strong development potential still face significant price reductions despite their peripheral locations. By applying CATE, policymakers can identify sensitive areas and design targeted interventions.
summary: Estimates the heterogeneous effects of South Korea's green belt (development-restriction) policy.

title: Spatial spillovers in women's political empowerment
authors: Izaskun Barba Areso
keywords: gender equality; spatial diffusion; Spatial panel data; women's political empowerment
abstract: This paper investigates whether and how spillover effects shape the diffusion of women's political empowerment (WPE) across countries over time, using a dynamic spatial panel of 142 countries (1965–2023). Accounting for unobserved common factors avoids misattributing interdependence to global shocks or shared trends. A hybrid spatial weights matrix combines geographic proximity, cultural affinity, trade and migration. Spatial Bayesian model averaging selects the most suitable specification, and a heterogeneous dynamic spatial model assesses variation in spillovers. Results provide strong evidence of cross-country diffusion in WPE, with marked heterogeneity in spillovers and highlight the role of diverse proximity dimensions in shaping global transmission.
summary: Finds spatial spillovers in women's political empowerment across regions.

title: Regional innovation support and policy mixes: evidence from France
authors: Corinne Autant-Bernard; Paul Charruau; Frédéric Perrin
keywords: firm performance; policy mix; R&D subsidies; staggered event study
abstract: This paper evaluates the effects of research and development (R&D) place-based policies implemented by regional governments using a unique database covering collaborative R&D subsidies granted by the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes Region from 2009 to 2021. Using a staggered event study design, and controlling for non-regional supports, dynamic effects on employment, turnover, exports and financial performance are assessed. Regional support generates a gradual increase in turnover and employment, with a more pronounced effect emerging several years later, underscoring the need for long-term evaluations. Interaction effects reveal that regional policies particularly benefit companies that do not yet receive national aid, highlighting complementarities between policy levels.
summary: Examines regional innovation support and how policy mixes shape innovation outcomes, using evidence from France.

title: Spatial heterogeneity, efficiency and regulation in waste services: evidence from Italian regions
authors: Roberto Benedetti; Marialisa Mazzocchitti; Alessandro Sarra
keywords: Parametric frontier model; regulation; spatial regimes; waste services
abstract: This paper proposes an empirical strategy to measure the efficiency of local governments in organising waste services when unobserved spatial heterogeneity in production technology exists. The proposed strategy employed the SkaterF procedure for identifying spatial regimes–groups of adjacent local governments with homogeneous production technology–and the quantile regression for estimating a production function per regime (local production functions), which is used for efficiency measurements. An application for data from 926 Italian municipalities (2017–2020) is also presented. Results highlight that neglecting unobserved spatial heterogeneity in production technology (i.e., measuring efficiency with a global production function) leads to misguided regulatory interventions.
summary: Analyzes spatial heterogeneity, efficiency, and regulation in waste-management services across Italian regions.

title: A spatial-functional clustering algorithm for panel data with an application to Italian health tax detractions
authors: Mauro Marè; Francesco Porcelli; Francesco Vidoli
keywords: functional data analysis; health economics; Spatial clustering; tax expenditures
abstract: Regional socio-economic phenomena are shaped by both geography and time: where territories are located matters, but so does how they evolve. Yet existing clustering methods treat these two dimensions in isolation, capturing either spatial proximity or dynamic similarity, but rarely both. In this paper, we introduce a spatial-functional clustering algorithm, validated through simulated and real-world data, that achieves regional segmentation by simultaneously accounting for geographical coherence and similarity in temporal trends. Applied to health tax detractions at the municipal level in Italy, the algorithm uncovers five territorially coherent clusters with distinct per-capita levels and trajectories, revealing a marked North–South gradient in which fiscal capacity, rather than healthcare need, systematically drives tax benefit utilisation.
summary: Proposes a spatial-functional clustering algorithm for panel data, applied to Italian health-tax detractions.

title: Does fiscal decentralisation drive county economic convergence? Evidence from China
authors: Shuxin Deng; Zhe Xie; Mengxue Ji
keywords: county economic growth; Fiscal decentralisation; province-managing-county reform; regional convergence
abstract: This paper exploits a quasi-natural experiment of ‘Province-Managing-County’ (PMC) reform to investigate the impacts of the fiscal decentralisation on inter-county economic convergence in China. Using China’s county-level dataset from 2000–2020, we find that the PMC reform significantly increases the speed of convergence in per capita gross domestic product (GDP) across counties. Our finding survives under various robustness tests. Heterogeneity analyses show that the convergence effects differ for counties in terms of locations, economic status and institutional quality. Mechanism tests further indicate that promoting fiscal capacity and innovation are effective influencing paths through which the PMC reform facilitates the inter-county convergence.
summary: Tests whether fiscal decentralisation drives county-level economic convergence in China.

title: Pushed to the edges? Electivity patterns of urban stream homeless encampments in environmentally burdened areas
authors: Serena Alexander; Bennett Williamson; Jeff Wootton; Costanza Rampini; Gregory Brian Pasternack; Yufang Jin; Rune Storesund; Igor Lacan
keywords: disadvantaged communities; environmental justice; geospatial analysis; Homelessness; pollution burden
abstract: Urban stream corridors in the San Francisco Bay Area have increasingly become locations for homeless encampments, yet little is known about the environmental conditions of these spaces. This study uses a geospatial electivity index to examine whether urban stream encampments in Santa Clara and Contra Costa counties are disproportionately located in census tracts with high pollution burdens, as measured by CalEnviroScreen 4.0. Findings show a statistically significant overrepresentation of encampments in census tracts in the top 25% of pollution and vulnerability scores, and a significant underrepresentation in lower-pollution areas. These results suggest that homeless individuals are being pushed toward environmentally hazardous areas, likely due to enforcement pressures, lack of viable alternatives, and land use patterns that concentrate polluting infrastructure and activities in low-resource areas. The findings have implications for environmental justice, public health, and urban policy, especially as CalEnviroScreen plays a central role in allocating state resources to disadvantaged communities.
summary: Examines siting patterns of urban-stream homeless encampments, asking whether they are pushed into environmentally burdened areas.

title: Enclave encounters: Transient migrants as spatial mediators in Paya Lebar, Singapore
authors: Junjia Ye
keywords: Asia; co-ethnic; enclave; migrant; public space
abstract: This paper examines migrant placemaking through the production and maintenance of a weekend migrant enclave in Singapore. By highlighting migrants’ encounters with the state and co-migrants, I analyze how informal encounters are embedded with surveillance practices in the enclave. I contribute to the literature on urban encounters by arguing that encounters function as surveillance in these spaces, where low-waged migrants are actively engaging in boundary-making practices. Their encounters are not only with surveillance technology and actors of state agencies such as the police but also with other migrants in the community. Drawing upon qualitative data collected in Paya Lebar, a neighborhood in the east side of Singapore, I locate the sites of encounter at the levels of policy regulation and the everyday in shared spaces where branches of the state such as surveillance technologies, auxiliary police officers and new migrants encounter one another on weekends. Making and managing the enclave are marked by layered forms of surveillance that both subvert and reinforce dominant modes of belonging through encounters in place. The enclave is not an exceptional space, nor are migrants exceptional. Rather, the encounters in the enclave are a distillation of broader migrant surveillance in the city.
summary: Studies transient migrants as spatial mediators in the Paya Lebar enclave of Singapore.

title: Closing the 'outdoor living room': Investigating the impact of COVID-19 public green space closures on the housing experiences of low-income renters in Toronto
authors: Skye Roshan Collishaw
keywords: COVID-19; Housing; public space; rental housing; urban policy
abstract: The COVID-19 lockdowns in Toronto magnified the differentiated relationship between housing type and tenure, and inequitable access to outdoor green space. The design of many Canadian park-use restrictions had a policy preference toward single-family housing residents, yet little is still known about how citywide COVID-19 public park restrictions impacted the housing experiences of vulnerably housed renters. This is in part due to the siloed nature in which research and policy have traditionally approached housing—as a context separated from public outdoor space. This paper analyzes green space use of low-income renters within the context of Toronto’s housing system, arguing that park and green space use is reflective of, and not separate from, the functions of an increasingly inequitable financialized housing system. Rather than a stand-alone event, the COVID-19 park restrictions are emblematic of long-term (mis)understandings of the relationship between apartment housing and green spaces in Toronto. Ultimately, this paper calls for park restrictions and other green space policies to be reconceptualized in relationship to, and as extensions of, housing policy to more holistically account for how low-income tenants use neighborhood spaces.
summary: Investigates how COVID-19 closures of public green space affected the housing experiences of low-income renters in Toronto.

title: Mid-term rentals and the Airbnbification of housing
authors: Gianluca Bei; Barbara Brollo; Filippo Celata
keywords: housing crisis; Mid-term rentals; platform economy; student housing; temporary populations
abstract: This article critically examines the expansion of the mid-term rental market, situating it within broader debates on the platform economy and the housing crisis. It offers an empirical analysis and mapping of the main digital platforms operating in this segment across Italian cities, to explore their attractiveness for property owners, the ways in which they reshape access to housing for different tenant groups, their role in driving up rental prices and their potential impacts on the most affected cities and neighborhoods. Mid-term rentals, it is argued, constitute a strategic intermediate ground for extending the logics of platformization across the entire rental market. Their effects resemble those observed in the short-term rental segment, while also penetrating more peripheral residential areas, contributing to specific exclusionary and gentrification dynamics, and generating more complex regulatory challenges.
summary: Examines the rise of mid-term rentals and the 'Airbnbification' of housing markets.

title: She's a great lady and she works hard but I can't waive her rent: Residential rental property owner decision-making during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Jane Rongerude; Daniel Kuhlmann; Biswa Das
keywords: COVID-19 pandemic; Rental housing; residential rental property owner
abstract: Housing is a fundamental component of the physical environment of human communities, and in places dominated by rental housing of any kind, post-disaster stability requires that residential rental property owners (RRPOs) remain solvent. Despite popular conceptions of wealthy property owners with deep pockets, the majority of RRPOs in the U.S. own properties with a value of $200,000 or less and about 41% report having debt. The COVID-19 pandemic forced many to manage revenue shortfalls while trying to fulfill their obligations to provide tenants with safe housing at existing rents. Using qualitative data from 52 interviews in four cities with independent RRPOs who self-manage their residential rental properties, this study asks the question, “How did rental property owners respond to the tension between regulatory restrictions and their financial obligations during the COVID-19 pandemic?” Analysis reveals five key domains of RRPO stress: tenants, rental units, business operations, personal circumstances, and regulation. Weakened tenant relationships and a desire to leave the market emerge as key RRPO responses, suggesting that while disasters inhibit short term housing security for tenants, they also inhibit longer-term rental housing stability for communities.
summary: Explores how residential rental-property owners made decisions about rent during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Does unauthorized immigration drive community crime rates? Evidence from 11,500 U.S. neighborhoods
authors: Charis E. Kubrin; Derek Christopher; Cheyenne Hodgen; Xiaoshuang Iris Luo; John R. Hipp
keywords: crime; Immigration; neighborhoods; undocumented
abstract: Research on the immigration-crime nexus has grown substantially, yet few studies differentiate among immigrants of different legal statuses, including undocumented immigrants. Of those that do, analyses are conducted at state and metropolitan area levels, leaving unanswered the question of how the presence of undocumented immigrants is associated with neighborhood crime rates—our focus. To construct neighborhood-level estimates of the undocumented population, we access restricted-use individual-level Census data, where tract of residence can be identified, and apply an imputation procedure. We combine these estimates with a dataset containing crime information for roughly 11,500 neighborhoods across U.S. cities over a decade. Controlling for change in foreign-born citizens and lawful permanent residents as well as other correlates of community crime rates, we estimate neighborhood-level fixed effects models to determine how change in undocumented residents is associated with change in violent and property crime levels between 2010 and 2018. We find that neighborhoods that experienced greater increases in the share of undocumented residents saw greater reductions in property crime and no detectable change in violent crime. We also document distinct patterns in which increasing undocumented residents is associated with decreasing aggravated assaults but increasing robberies, consistent with a possible victimization explanation.
summary: Using 11,500 US neighborhoods, examines whether unauthorized immigration drives community crime rates.

title: Social network benefits for cluster firms: A co-worker mobility approach
authors: Balázs Lengyel; László Lőrincz; Guilherme Kenji Chihaya; Rikard Eriksson
keywords: co-worker networks; labor mobility; link prediction; administrative data; network simulation; firm growth; regional clusters
abstract: Regional clusters facilitate social interaction and learning across firms. Here, we assess how social networks of firms influence their competitiveness in relation to cluster- and firm-characteristics. Using survey and administrative data, we simulate co-worker networks that, following the mobility of employees, generate links across companies. Analyzing Sweden's ICT firms over 20 years, we find that inter-firm co-worker ties, even across companies not directly linked by mobility, predict firm performance. We document that small firms benefit more from inter-regional links and from having access to diverse networks, while local links assist firms to accumulate local knowledge in growing regional clusters.
summary: Simulating co-worker networks among Sweden's ICT firms over 20 years, finds inter-firm social ties predict firm performance, with small firms benefiting most from diverse, inter-regional links.

title: Numerical translations and labor conditions in China's honey supply chain
authors: Haohui Cai
keywords: translation; marketization; smallholder farmers; labor conditions; commodity chain; precarity
abstract: Building on Tsing's concept of salvage accumulation, which theorized capitalism as profiting without controlling commodity production, this paper takes Chinese apiculture – characterized by vertical integration – as a case study to examine how translation processes are performed and what labor conditions are (re)shaped within honey supply chains. In this system of merchant capitalism, smallholder beekeepers remain outside direct capitalist control during production; instead, they depend on middlemen to purchase their harvested honey for subsequent market exchange. These transactions are more than simple commercial exchanges. They operate as acts of translation that convert a non-capitalist, multispecies product into an abstract commodity value, measured through the Baumé scale. Yet, due to honey's lively materialities, such numerical indicators are inherently unstable, both ecologically contingent and technically modifiable. The interplay between translation mechanisms, material indeterminacy, and market pressure contributes to precarious livelihoods for beekeepers, who respond through forms of self-exploitation: intensifying labor, accelerating extraction cycles, and exerting metabolic pressure on honeybees to increase output. By unpacking these translation practices and labor dynamics in Chinese apiculture, this paper offers ethnographic and theoretical contributions on geographies of marketization and diverse economies, foregrounding the roles of friction politics, lively materialities, and localized capitalism.
summary: Uses Chinese apiculture to show how 'numerical translation' of honey into commodity value via the Baumé scale reshapes precarious smallholder-beekeeper labor and self-exploitation.

title: Pacifying attention-space: Marketization and the U.S. outdoor advertising industry, 1931–1941
authors: Jacob Saindon
keywords: attention; outdoor advertising; marketization; pacification; urban
abstract: This article examines the production of U.S. outdoor advertising markets in the 1930s through an analysis of the early procedures of the Traffic Audit Bureau (TAB). TAB was established in 1933 through the joint effort of three advertising industry professional organizations to standardize the measurement, auditing, and publication of outdoor advertisement circulation measures—estimates of addressable urban audiences in the U.S. and their "exposure" to outdoor advertisements. These measures served as the basis of exchange between sellers and buyers on the outdoor advertising market. I argue that TAB's procedures worked to stabilize the production of circulation measures, and thus the market for outdoor advertising, through the intertwining of (urban) space and (mobile) attention as attention-space. Specifically, I contend that the success of TAB's work hinged upon processes of pacification which abstracted and standardized urban attention-space to produce comparable circulation counts. I begin by introducing the concepts of pacification and diagrams before discussing the state of the U.S. outdoor advertising industry and markets circa 1933. The subsequent sections analyze several of TAB's foundational documents and procedures. I demonstrate how these procedures framed attention-space by analyzing how the Bureau (1) used circulation counts to establish the extents of urban retail areas; (2) determined appropriate coverage allotments of advertisements throughout an urban area; and (3) evaluated the relative visibility of poster panels.
summary: Traces how the 1930s Traffic Audit Bureau standardized outdoor-advertising circulation measures, 'pacifying' urban attention-space to stabilize the advertising market.

title: Online Reservation Systems, Buying Frenzies and Equitable Access to Public Lands
authors: Jonathan E. Hughes
abstract: Rationed access is an important tool to promote sustainable use of public lands. However, online reservation systems can lead to "buying frenzies" when low prices create excess demand. Using transaction-level data for river permits in the United States sold both by reservation-system buying frenzy and lottery, I show successful frenzy buyers reside in wealthier zip codes than those selected at random. This effect increases with congestion and leads to an unequal distribution of consumption benefits where high-income zip codes receive 25 percent more recreational trip value. These effects can undermine park managers' efforts to provide equitable access through low fees.
summary: Using US river-permit data, finds online reservation 'buying frenzies' favor wealthier zip codes, producing unequal access to public lands that low fees alone fail to remedy.

title: Mandatory Disclosure of Home Energy Efficiency: Price Premium Measurements from Portland
authors: Sharon Shewmake; Reid Dorsey-Palmateer
abstract: Providing home energy information to home buyers makes efficiency more salient in purchasing. We study the impact of disclosed energy efficiency information on housing prices in Portland, Oregon after the introduction of a Home Energy Score mandate for houses on the market. We find a $1 decrease in annual energy costs is associated with an approximate increase in housing value of $24 to $40. This effect is stronger for houses that are already energy efficient and for larger houses.
summary: After Portland's Home Energy Score mandate, finds a $1 reduction in annual energy costs raises home value by roughly $24–$40, with larger effects for already-efficient and bigger houses.

title: The Effect of Extreme Temperature Shocks on the Type of Firm Labor Hired: Empirical Evidence from the Philippines
authors: Kairon Shayne D. Garcia; Gregmar I. Galinato; Asif M. Islam
abstract: The article estimates the effect of extreme temperature on labor in the manufacturing and services sectors in the Philippines. We use firm-level survey and temperature data and exploit the exogenous annual variation of maximum temperature. We find a rise in the projected annual increase of extreme temperature from climate change by 0.08℃, reduces employment by 14 workers for a firm with 136 employees in export-focused industries in dry regions. Male, temporary, skilled workers in large, technology-dependent, non-food firms, are most affected by extreme temperature. The mechanism is the reduction in capital investment leading to a complementary reduction in labor hired.
summary: Using Philippine firm data, finds extreme-temperature shocks reduce employment—especially for skilled, temporary, male workers in export-focused dry-region firms—via cuts to capital investment.

title: Who Has the Upper HAND in a Hurricane? Flood Risk, Weather Shocks, and Property Prices
authors: Julian A. Plough; Sheila M. Olmstead; Douglas H. Wrenn
abstract: Flood risk is increasing in the United States, but how property markets respond to this hazard is unclear. Focusing on Houston, Texas, we analyze changes in flood risk capitalization in property prices after three major Gulf Coast hurricanes. We compare two measures of flood risk–floodplain designations from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and a hydrologically-imputed, continuous measure, Height Above the Nearest Drainage (HAND). HAND affects property prices after a storm in intuitive ways, while we observe counterintuitive post-storm price premiums within FEMA floodplains. Plausibly exogenous measures like HAND may be useful tools for characterizing flood risk in economic analyses.
summary: Comparing flood-risk measures in Houston after major hurricanes, finds the continuous HAND metric capitalizes intuitively into prices while FEMA floodplain designations show counterintuitive post-storm premiums.

title: Rural Electrification in the Brazilian Amazon: No Environment-Development Tradeoff
authors: Laura Villalobos; Jill Caviglia-Harris; Daniel Harris; Elaine Frey
keywords: Electrification; Brazilian Amazon; Light for All; Difference-in-Differences (DID); Rural Development
abstract: Rural electrification is widely promoted to improve livelihoods, yet its land-use consequences in forest frontiers remain unclear. Using longitudinal household surveys linked to property boundaries and satellite land cover in the Brazilian Amazon, we apply heterogeneity-robust staggered-adoption difference-in-differences. Electrification increases cattle income over the medium term but has no detectable effect on annual property-level deforestation. Income gains appear to reflect herd expansion on existing pasture and a modest refrigerated-milk price premium rather than higher per-animal productivity.
summary: Using staggered difference-in-differences in the Brazilian Amazon, finds rural electrification raises cattle income without detectably increasing property-level deforestation.

title: Toward a timber asset account for the United States: A pilot account for Georgia
authors: Sonia R. Bruck; Christopher Mihiar; Bin Mei; Thomas Brandeis; Matthew Chambers; Julie L. Hass; Scott Wentland; Travis Warziniack
abstract: This paper develops a pilot timber asset account for the United States, demonstrating how a novel discount price method can value timber stocks in Georgia. While valuing merchantable timber is straightforward, an important methodological challenge is valuing trees that are not yet harvestable. Our approach values young stands by discounting their expected harvest price until they reach merchantable size. This method requires standard forest inventory data and market prices currently available in the U.S., making it promising candidate for scaling nationally. For southern yellow pine in Georgia, we estimate timber assets of $5.9 billion, with pre-merchantable timber contributing $257.7 million.
summary: Develops a pilot US timber asset account for Georgia, using a discount-price method to value not-yet-harvestable stands and estimating $5.9 billion in southern yellow pine timber assets.

title: Species-specific wildlife recreation demand: Evidence from WTP and WTA estimates in Grand Teton National Park
authors: Peri M. Brimley; Todd L. Cherry; John Whitehead
abstract: The wildlife valuation literature largely focuses on eliciting willingness-to-pay for wildlife conservation, not recreation, and frequently groups species together under the banner of "wildlife". This study employs the contingent valuation method to value the likelihood of viewing specific wildlife in Grand Teton National Park (GTNP). We estimate willingness-to-pay (WTP) and willingness-to-accept (WTA) for species-specific recreation trips to explore substitutability between popular wildlife species. Estimates across species better equip wildlife managers to balance the inherent tradeoffs associated with climate impacts on habitats and populations as well as changing interests among recreationists.
summary: Uses contingent valuation to estimate species-specific willingness-to-pay and willingness-to-accept for wildlife viewing in Grand Teton National Park, informing management tradeoffs under climate change.

journal: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
title: Stimulating Climate Action through the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism
authors: Kenneth Bicol Dy; Han Yang
summary: Examines how the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism can stimulate climate action.

journal: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
title: Air Pollution during Religious Holidays: Evidence from Tomb-Sweeping Day
authors: Hung-Hao Chang; Yu-You Liou; Chad D. Meyerhoefer
summary: Uses China's Tomb-Sweeping Day to estimate air-pollution effects associated with religious-holiday activities.

journal: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
title: From simple to complex: A revealed preference test of discrete choice experiment designs
authors: Christian A. Vossler; Ewa Zawojska
summary: A revealed-preference test comparing simple versus complex discrete choice experiment designs in environmental valuation.

title: The determinants of declining internal migration
authors: William W. Olney; Owen Thompson
keywords: Internal migration; Wages; Housing prices; Mobility
abstract: Internal migration in the United States has declined substantially over the past several decades, which has important implications for individual welfare and macroeconomic adjustment. This paper studies the determinants of internal migration and how they have changed over time. We use administrative data from the IRS covering the universe of bilateral moves between every Commuting Zone (CZ) in the country over a 23 year period. This data is linked to information on local wage levels and home prices, and we estimate bilateral migration determinants in rich regression specifications that contain CZ-pair fixed effects. Consistent with theoretical predictions, we find that migration is decreasing with origin wages and destination home prices, and is increasing with destination wages and origin home prices. We then examine the contributions of earnings and home prices to the noted overall decline in internal migration. These analyses show that wages on their own would have led to an increase in migration rates, primarily because migrants are increasingly responsive to high earnings levels in potential destination CZs. However, these wage effects have been more than offset by housing related factors, which have increasingly impeded internal mobility. In particular, migration has become much less responsive to housing prices in the origin CZ, such that many households that would have left in response to high home prices several decades ago now choose to stay.
summary: Using IRS commuting-zone-pair data over 23 years, studies why US internal migration has declined and how its wage and housing-price determinants have changed over time.

title: The effects of comprehensive pay reform on achievement in urban schools
authors: Eric Hanushek; Jin Luo; Andrew Morgan; Minh Nguyen; Ben Ost; Steven Rivkin; Ayman Shakeel
keywords: Economics of education; Urban education; Teacher accountability; Pay for performance
abstract: Academic performance of disadvantaged students has been stubbornly hard to improve, particularly in urban schools. The Dallas Independent School District (Dallas ISD) addressed this problem in 2015 with a radical change in the structure of teacher compensation, basing it entirely on classroom effectiveness as determined by an evaluation system incorporating achievement growth, classroom observations and student surveys. We evaluate this institutional change with synthetic control methods that compare math and reading achievement in Dallas ISD schools with achievement for schools in other high-poverty Texas districts. We find large and significant positive effects on math achievement that increase steadily over time. For reading, there is no clear evidence of improvement in Dallas ISD relative to the synthetic control. A mechanism analysis shows that changes in teacher composition account for a majority of the math achievement increase.
summary: Using synthetic control, finds Dallas ISD's 2015 shift to effectiveness-based teacher pay produced large, significant gains in math achievement in high-poverty urban schools.

title: Selective migration and regional decline: Evidence from coal country
authors: Eleanor Krause
keywords: Labor-market adjustment; Population mobility; Regional inequality; Human capital; Energy transition
abstract: Why do regions decline? This paper explores how adverse shocks in one period affect regional adjustment to subsequent shocks, emphasizing the role of selective migration. I leverage differential exposure to coal's decline and variation in proximity to historical employment shifts to study this process of regional decline in Appalachia. The consequences of the 2007–2017 coal shock were more acute in counties that experienced larger declines in college-educated adults due to exogenous labor demand shifts in the 1980s. These findings indicate that the adverse effects of shocks can accumulate over time, leaving certain regions differentially vulnerable to new challenges.
summary: Shows Appalachian counties that lost college-educated adults to 1980s labor shocks suffered more acute effects from the 2007–2017 coal decline, evidence that adverse shocks compound through selective migration.

title: The air quality effects of Uber
authors: Luis Sarmiento; Yeong Jae Kim
keywords: Ride-hailing; Uber; Air quality; United States; Difference-in-differences
abstract: We estimate the causal effect of the entry of ride-sharing services, such as Uber, on air quality across US cities using the staggered introduction of these services across cities. We find that Uber improves air quality: the air quality index improoves by approximately 1%–2% in the year of entry, and the probability of unhealthy air quality episodes falls by 8%–18% following its introduction. We provide suggestive evidence that these improvements result from substituting trips in older, less efficient vehicles with Uber rides.
summary: Exploiting the staggered US rollout of ride-sharing, finds Uber's entry improves urban air quality by 1–2% and cuts unhealthy-air episodes, likely by displacing trips in older vehicles.

title: Judge for yourself? The impact of controls on the rental market in interwar New York
authors: Maximilian Günnewig-Mönert; Ronan C. Lyons
keywords: Rent control; New York City; 1920s
abstract: This paper examines the impact of early 20th-century rent control laws in New York City, exploiting judicial discretion as a source of variation. The 1920 regulations empowered municipal court judges to decide whether rent increases were "reasonable", with rulings shaped by partisan affiliation. We assemble a new dataset of over 20,000 rental listings from the New York Times (1918–1930) and more than 7000 archival building permits, linked to records on 125 district judges. Using a Regression Discontinuity Design at municipal court district boundaries, we find that market rents rose by nearly 10 percent when crossing from Democrat- to Republican-controlled districts after rent control. We examine supply effects using a difference-in-differences design. We show that judicially enforced rent control substantially reduced residential investment: total residential investment was about 76 percent higher in landlord-friendly districts during the rent-control period. Together, these findings demonstrate how judicial discretion shaped both prices and investment, leading to systematic differences in profits and construction activity across districts, which likely shaped the medium-run build environment.
summary: Using interwar New York rental listings and judicial partisan variation in a boundary RD design, finds market rents rose nearly 10% moving from Democrat- to Republican-controlled court districts under rent control.

title: Asian immigrants, school quality, and the U.S. housing market
authors: Amanda Ang; Eunjee Kwon; Siqi Zheng
keywords: Asian immigrants; Housing markets; Education amenities
abstract: This paper investigates how Asian immigrants affect U.S. housing prices and identifies the mechanisms underlying these effects. Using annual county-level data from 2009 to 2018 and a dual instrumental variable approach, we decompose the overall impact of Asian immigrants into education-related and non-education channels. We find that roughly 30%–40% of the housing price increase associated with Asian immigration is driven by the capitalization of improved educational amenities, while the remaining 60%–70% reflects non-education forces, such as home-biased foreign capital inflows and other neighborhood changes. The education-related capitalization effects are greater in counties with a higher share of Asian school-aged children, underscoring the key insight that immigrant composition — specifically, who arrives — matters for how immigration shapes local housing markets.
summary: Using county data and a dual-IV approach, finds 30–40% of the housing-price increase linked to Asian immigration reflects capitalized school-quality amenities, the rest non-education channels like foreign capital.

title: Property tax competition: A quantitative assessment
authors: Rainald Borck; Jun Oshiro; Yasuhiro Sato
keywords: Property taxes; Tax competition; Efficiency
abstract: We investigate which of four alternative taxation regimes often used in the public finance literature best approximates actual property taxation in Japan and Germany. To that end, we develop a model of property taxation and characterize equilibria under four alternative regimes: the Benthamite, rent-seeking, land-rent maximization, and tax harmonization regimes. We characterize possible sources of fiscal externalities in each regime. We then quantify the effects of switching from the observed tax system to each of the four regimes in Japan and Germany. We find that the Benthamite or rent-seeking regime best approximates the Japanese system, whereas the tax harmonization regime does so for Germany. We also quantify the welfare effects of switching to the different regimes.
summary: Develops a property-taxation model with four regimes and finds the Benthamite or rent-seeking regime best approximates Japan's system while tax harmonization best fits Germany's.

title: The impact of natural disasters on rental markets
authors: Katharine W.H. Harwood
keywords: Housing markets; Rental markets; Natural disasters; Rental subsidies; Affordable housing
abstract: This paper examines the effect of Hurricane Sandy on rental markets in New York City and how existing rental subsidies influenced post-disaster recovery. Using an event study design that exploits spatial variation in storm exposure, I document persistent heterogeneity in rent dynamics across neighborhoods. Specifically, flooded blocks in lower income neighborhoods experience rent declines for up to 7 years after the storm, while rents in higher income neighborhoods rebound, and increase further within two years of the storm. I provide evidence that these diverging effects reflect disparate neighborhood resources for recovery: market-rate landlords in lower income neighborhoods were constrained in their ability to renovate their properties until the distribution of the city's relief funds. In contrast, I show that voucher landlords in similar neighborhoods renovated much earlier, consistent with less binding capital constraints, and appear to have recouped the investment through increased tenant rents. Programmatic features shifted the incidence of these increases nearly entirely on the government, providing a sort of insurance for voucher landlords and tenants.
summary: Studying Hurricane Sandy in New York City, finds flooded blocks in low-income neighborhoods saw multi-year rent declines while high-income areas rebounded, reflecting unequal recovery resources.

title: Old but gold: Historical pathways and path dependence
authors: Diogo Baerlocher; Guilherme Lambais; Eustáquio Reis; Diego Firmino Costa da Silva; Henrique Veras
keywords: Historical roads; Geography; Multiple equilibria; Path dependence; Persistence; Population density
abstract: Following the discovery of gold in 1694 in Brazil, pathways were constructed to connect coastal settlements to mining regions in the unpopulated interior. While these pathways initially facilitated the creation of road towns, their influence faded by the late nineteenth century. With the mid-twentieth-century demographic and industrial transition, regions with higher historical road density experienced renewed population growth and greater migrant inflows. We argue that this resurgence reflects the role of road towns in supporting early urbanization and structural transformation. Using an extended Rosen–Roback–Glaeser framework, we estimate strong agglomeration spillovers, consistent with Brazil's spatial economy exhibiting multiple steady states and possible historical path dependence.
summary: Traces how colonial gold-rush road towns in Brazil left path-dependent agglomeration effects, with historically road-dense regions seeing renewed population and migrant growth in the twentieth century.

title: Extrapolative households and strategic firms
authors: Zhe Liu; Wei Shi; Yan Song; Weizeng Sun
keywords: Housing market; Land auctions; Developers' strategies
abstract: This paper examines households' extrapolative behaviors and developers' strategic responses in China's land and housing markets. Our stylized model predicts that when households extrapolate in the housing market, developers with nearby land holdings strategically bid higher, anticipating rising housing prices to boost the value of their existing stock. Using the exogenous timing of land auctions, we show that higher land premiums increase transaction prices and volumes of nearby houses. Furthermore, developers with nearby land stocks consistently pay higher premiums in the land auctions. We exploit a policy reform and implement various tests to support the hypothesis that developers strategically influence homebuyers' expectations.
summary: Models and tests how extrapolative households and strategic developers interact in China's land and housing markets, showing developers with nearby land bid higher land premiums anticipating price gains.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Do economic principles explain orbital use in space?
authors: Daniel Kaffine; Akhil Rao
keywords: Space debris; Open access; Low earth orbit; Integrated assessment models
abstract: While the global space economy continues to rapidly grow, and public policy challenges related to satellites and debris in orbit emerge, there is surprisingly little evidence connecting theoretical economic frameworks with observed orbital usage. Using a state-of-the-science integrated assessment model combining economic modeling with physical models of the space environment, we find the observed distribution of satellite orbits is well-explained by profit-maximizing satellite operator behavior. Furthermore, we find strong evidence that collision risk plays a key deterrent role. Finally, the observed location of the largest satellite constellation, Starlink, is consistent with a "sole owner" over particularly economically desirable altitudes.
summary: Using an integrated economic-physical model, finds the observed distribution of satellite orbits is well explained by profit-maximizing operator behavior, with collision risk acting as a key deterrent.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Protecting the environment: On the interplay between voluntary contributions and public policy
authors: Andrei Kalk
keywords: Environmental quality; Voluntary contributions; Warm glow; Environmental policy
abstract: We study the interplay between individuals’ voluntary contributions to environmental protection and public environmental policy in a dynamic general-equilibrium model. To capture the observed discrepancy between the willingness of individuals to contribute privately versus publicly to environmental protection, we treat the quality of the environment as a public good and assume that voluntary contributions are motivated by a ‘warm glow’ of giving. We show that in the laissez-faire scenario without government intervention, the strength of warm glow negatively affects aggregate output and positively affects environmental quality in the long run. However, when the government intervenes and decides on environmental policy in the interests of individuals, the warm-glow strength has a negative long-run effect on both variables. Thus, our results suggest that advocating for private actions to ensure a better environment in the future may be counterproductive in the presence of public environmental policies.
summary: Examines the interplay between voluntary private environmental contributions and public environmental policy.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: PFAS contamination disclosures and declining residential land prices in polluted areas of Japan
authors: Mingyao Wang
keywords: PFAS; Information disclosure; Land price; Japan
abstract: Residential land prices are highly sensitive to new information, particularly when pollution disclosures highlight potential health risks. Following the 2020 disclosure of nationwide government survey results, extensive contamination from per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, commonly known as 'forever chemicals,' was revealed, leading to intensified media coverage and heightened public awareness. This study applies a staggered difference-in-differences approach to quantify the impact of PFAS pollution disclosures on Japanese residential land prices. Using property-level panel data from the Land Market Value Publication, we compare treated properties to control properties within varying distance radii. In the 5 km radius analysis, statistically significant average post-treatment declines range from approximately 1.3% when Tokyo is excluded to 2.4% when Osaka and Okinawa, which had received PFAS-related disclosures earlier, are also excluded. Across the distance-buffer specifications, dynamic event-study effects reach approximately 4.4–6.4% by the fourth year after disclosure. Notably, significant price declines emerged only after media coverage intensified around 2023, highlighting the critical role of information salience in translating environmental disclosures into market responses.
summary: Using staggered difference-in-differences on Japanese land prices, finds the 2020 PFAS 'forever chemicals' contamination disclosures lowered residential land prices in polluted areas.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Quota regulation under corruption – Grand, petty and the cut-money culture
authors: Ayushi Choudhary; Rupayan Pal
