This effect operates through three mediating channels: reducing transportation costs, alleviating institutional barriers and enhancing technology diffusion, with the final channel dominating over traditional cost-driven motives as the primary driver. Moderation and heterogeneity analysis indicates that external environment, including intellectual property protection at institutional level as well as scientific talent distribution and digital infrastructure development at technological level, shows positive moderation effects. Furthermore, the impact of industrial intelligence exhibits substantial firm heterogeneity: Firms with stronger AI application capability, more optimized non-productive expenditure structures, and higher sustainable development ability are likely to achieve cross-regional investment elasticity. These findings extend beyond the unilateral cost-driven paradigm and establish a dual-pillar theoretical framework of institutional synergy and technology spillovers, revealing the renewed logic of firm boundary decisions in the digital era.
summary: Using Chinese manufacturing firm data, finds industrial intelligence significantly boosts cross-regional investment, with a one-standard-deviation rise raising dispersed subsidiary scale by 63%.

title: How does spatial expansion of higher education affect urban innovation? Regional evidence for Yangtze River Delta, China
authors: Xing Gao; Ying Zhang; Xingman Zhang
keywords: Higher education expansion; Urban innovation; Spatial spillovers; Metropolitan structure; Yangtze River Delta
abstract: In the context of the knowledge economy, higher education has increasingly functioned as a critical spatial infrastructure for regional innovation through human capital formation, knowledge production, and institutional coordination. While higher education expansion (HEE) has been widely implemented to enhance innovation capacity, existing studies have largely examined its average effects within administrative boundaries, paying limited attention to spatial spillovers, nonlinear effects, and metropolitan heterogeneity. Thus, this study aims to systematically investigate the spatial mechanism through which HEE affects urban innovation from a geospatial perspective. Focusing on 41 cities in China's Yangtze River Delta from 2001 to 2022, we construct a multidimensional urban innovation index based on a patent citation network and employ spatial econometric models to capture intercity interactions. We find: (1) HEE promotes urban innovation. Quantity shows linear positive effects, while quality exhibits an inverted U-shape relationship; institutional factors play critical roles. (2) Spatial spillovers are significant. Quantity expansion generates cross-regional positive spillovers, while quality improvement enhances local innovation. Spillover mechanisms gradually evolved from knowledge diffusion to institution-driven mobility. (3) Metropolitan structure shapes significant heterogeneity. These findings position higher education as a dynamic spatial infrastructure for innovation and offer theoretical and policy insights for fostering coordinated, cross-regional innovation under fragmented spatial governance.
summary: Studying 41 Yangtze River Delta cities, examines the spatial spillovers and nonlinear effects through which higher-education expansion affects urban innovation.

title: Expanding the 15-minute city through e-micromobility services
authors: Priyanka Verma; Dan Qiang; Grant McKenzie
keywords: Micromobility; 15-minute city; e-bike; e-scooter; active transport; connected communities
abstract: Urban planners are increasingly tasked with strengthening neighborhood economies and encouraging more connected communities. Central to this objective is ensuring equitable access to essential amenities such as grocery stores, parks, and hospitals. In recent years, shared e-micromobility services such as publicly available e-bikes and e-scooters have gained popularity as a means of local transport, offering potential to extend access. However, their contribution to the 15-Minute City framework across cities is not well understood. In this study, we assess if shared e-micromobility services expand access to essential amenities (i.e., supermarkets, schools, hospitals, parks, and entertainment venues), across five international cities. Observed e-micromobility trips are used to generate city-level travel time surfaces, which are compared with counterfactual walking times for the same trips. Results suggest access gains from e-micromobility are uneven, largely determined by urban form, distribution of amenities, and distance from city center. Cities and neighborhoods with less compact urban form and more dispersed land use tend to experience the largest gains in access with e-micromobility, increasing the proportion of the city reachable within 15 min by up to threefold in some cities. This work provides evidence to inform policies to better integrate new forms of local-scale transport (i.e., e-micromobility services), to improve access to essential services within the 15-Minute City framework.
summary: Assesses whether shared e-bikes and e-scooters extend access to essential amenities and thereby expand the '15-minute city' across cities.

title: Correction: Divergence-driven co-evolution between spatial regulation and urban development in complex urban systems
authors: Weixuan Fang; Wenbin Zhang
abstract: In the Original article, the authors have identified errors in references 1 and 2. The corrected references are given below. Incorrect reference 1: Raimbault, Juste. 2018. “Multi-Model Exploration of Urban Morphogenesis.” PLoS ONE 13(3): e0193646 Correct reference 1: Raimbault J (2018) Calibration of a density-based model of urban morphogenesis. PLoS ONE 13(9):e0203516 Incorrect reference 2: Raimbault, Juste. 2021. “An Evolutionary Theory of Urban Systems.” Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science 48(7): 1921–1937 Correct reference 2: Raimbault J, Pumain D (2021) Spatial dynamics of complex urban systems within an evolutionary theory frame. In: Handbook on entropy, complexity and spatial dynamics: a rebirth of theory? (Chap. 11, p. 175) This has been corrected in the Original article.
summary: A correction notice for a paper on the co-evolution of spatial regulation and urban development in complex urban systems.

title: Complex Network-Based Pre-disaster Protection Optimization of Integrated Energy System with EvoRein-Mixed Integer Linear Programming
authors: Chenwei Zhang; Ying Wang; Chen Wang; Yulong Jin; Tao Zheng; Kaifeng Zhang
keywords: Complex network theory; EvoRein-mixed integer linear programming; Protective decision optimization model; Weighted betweenness loss expectation
abstract: Nowadays, the integrated energy system (IES) faces significant security challenges from both natural occurrences and intentional disruptions, even minor disruptions can impact equipment operation and the system's energy supply. To mitigate such disruptions in IES, a protective decision optimization model (PDOM) has been proposed based on complex network theory, which combines three protective measures: backup protection, physical protection, and new lines connection to minimize the weighted betweenness loss expectation. The result of the calculation, i.e., an optimized pre-disaster protection scheme, aims to determine which nodes and lines need to be protected (and different-type protection) within the specified budget. Furthermore, EvoRein-mixed integer linear programming (EvoRein-MILP) algorithm is presented to optimize the proposed model's scheme. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility of the obtained scheme, as verified by three validation indicators (system fragmentation, energy transmission efficiency, and load losing rate). Finally, compared to the genetic algorithm (GA)-MILP algorithm and adaptive GA-MILP algorithm, the EvoRein-MILP algorithm exhibits superior optimization and operation time performance under identical conditions.
summary: Proposes a complex-network protective decision-optimization model combining backup, physical, and new-line protections to minimize disruption losses in integrated energy systems before disasters.

title: A Variational Inequality Framework for Multi-Echelon Supply Chains
authors: Gabriella Colajanni; Patrizia Daniele; Rebecca Fontanarosa
keywords: Multi-echelon supply chain; Variational inequality; Network optimization; EOQ
abstract: This paper proposes a profit-maximization model for a multi-echelon supply chain, integrating transportation and inventory decisions within a unified framework. The system is formulated as a Variational Inequality, ensuring equilibrium conditions under convex costs and network constraints. By incorporating the Economic Order Quantity policy, inventory variables are eliminated, reducing model complexity. A projection method is used for computation, and numerical results illustrate the effectiveness of the approach in capturing realistic logistics behaviors.
summary: Formulates a multi-echelon supply chain as a variational inequality integrating transportation and inventory decisions, using an EOQ policy and projection method to compute equilibrium.

title: Dynamic Correlation Between a Geopolitical Risk Index and Crude Oil Futures Prices: Evidence from a Mahalanobis Distance-Based Network Measures
authors: Linxi Wang; Sufang An; Zhiliang Dong
keywords: Crude oil price; Geopolitical risk index; Complex network; Dynamic correlation; Financial markets
abstract: This study presents a novel correlation network model that integrates the Mahalanobis distance and complex network theory to explain the dynamic relationship between geopolitical events and crude oil. The geopolitical risk index and three crude oil futures prices are selected as sample data, and a correlation network is established. The node represents a type of correlation pattern, which is a combination of symbolic correlations between a geopolitical risk index and any crude oil price on a given day. The frequency and direction between two nodes are expressed in terms of weighted edges. The evolutionary properties of correlations can be described by the network's topological structure. The results show that the correlation pattern in the network changes with time. The correlation between a geopolitical risk index and any crude oil price is strong and has long-term consistency. Furthermore, the correlation between China crude oil futures price and the geopolitical risk index slightly lags behind that between China crude oil futures price and the other two indices, and the influencing factors are discussed. This study explores the evolution of the dynamic mechanism of correlation, which can provide valuable implications for market investors and policymakers.
summary: Builds a Mahalanobis-distance correlation network to characterize the dynamic relationship between a geopolitical risk index and crude oil futures prices.

title: Forecasting Demand in Network System Methods: A Field-Based Evaluation of Nature-Inspired Optimization Models
authors: Weishun Zhong; Loke Kok Foong
keywords: Demand forecasting; Networked systems; Swarm intelligence; Daily demand; ANN
abstract: Accurate forecasting of daily demand in network systems is critical for efficient resource management, yet traditional forecasting methods often struggle to capture complex and dynamic demand patterns. Despite numerous studies on demand prediction, there remains a lack of systematic evaluation of nature-inspired optimization algorithms in field-based settings. This study addresses this gap by developing and assessing a daily demand forecasting model using four Swarm Intelligence algorithms: Black Hole Algorithm (BHA), Cuckoo Optimization Algorithm (COA), Shuffled Complex Evolution (SCE), and Stochastic Fractal Search (SFS). Historical demand data were collected through field surveys, and the forecasting model was constructed by integrating these algorithms with a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) network. The model's performance was evaluated using R² (Coefficient of Determination) and RMSE (Root Mean Square Error), benchmarked against traditional approaches. Results demonstrate that incorporating Swarm Intelligence significantly enhances forecasting accuracy. In particular, the SCE-optimized MLP achieved the highest R² values (0.99785 in testing, 0.99986 in training) and the lowest RMSE (0.01805 in testing, 0.00658 in training), indicating exceptional predictive reliability. Similarly, SFS yielded high R² (0.99554 in testing, 0.99995 in training) and low RMSE (0.02599 in testing, 0.00389 in training), confirming its effectiveness for daily demand prediction. These findings highlight the practical potential of SCE and SFS in improving network system forecasting accuracy and adaptability to dynamic demand patterns.
summary: Develops and field-evaluates a daily network-demand forecasting model using four swarm-intelligence optimization algorithms.

title: From Coal to Chlorophyll: Identifying Green Job Opportunities for Youth in the case of South Africa's Just Transition
authors: Robert Hill; Leigh Neethling; Morné Oosthuizen
abstract: In an attempt to mitigate their effect on climate change, a number of economies have already, or are in the process of shifting away from a reliance on coal-based power. This just energy transition means that many existing jobs in the coal industry will be lost in favour of so-called "green jobs", which aim to contribute positively and sustainably to the environment. South Africa is one such economy that is embarking on the process of a just transition, but given that the coal industry is predominantly represented by young people in the province of Mpumalanga, it is not clear how or if this vulnerable group will transition into newly created green jobs. Making use of occupational relatedness metrics, this research investigates the feasibility of green job opportunities to capture displaced youth in Mpumalanga, depending on their employment history. Results of this desktop study suggest that green jobs are relatively different to the existing experience and task competences of young people, and thus some form of reskilling programme is likely necessary for youth to access these opportunities.
summary: Using occupational relatedness, identifies green-job opportunities for coal-dependent youth in Mpumalanga as South Africa pursues its just energy transition.

title: Energy transition and ecological resilience in China: nonlinear distributional evidence from Quantile-on-Quantile and Kernel-Based Regularized Least Squares Models
authors: Busra Agan Celik
keywords: Ecological resilience; Load Capacity Factor; Energy transition; Environmental governance; Regional heterogeneity; Quantile-on-Quantile regression; KRLS
abstract: Understanding the regional dynamics of ecological resilience is central to achieving sustainable development in rapidly transforming economies. In the context of China's ongoing energy transition, this study investigated the nonlinear and distributional effects of nuclear energy consumption, economic growth, technological innovation and environmental governance on ecological resilience, proxied by the Load Capacity Factor (LCF). By employing a Quantile-on-Quantile Regression (QQR) framework, complemented by conventional Quantile Regression (QR) and Kernel-Based Regularized Least Squares (KRLS), the analysis captured heterogeneous relationships across different states of both explanatory variables and ecological conditions. The findings revealed pronounced distributional asymmetries in the energy–environment nexus. Nuclear energy presented heterogeneous and regime-dependent effects, displaying both positive and negative impacts across quantile combinations, while positive effects became more prevalent under higher levels of nuclear energy deployment and ecological resilience. In contrast, economic growth exerted a persistent negative influence across the distributions. Technological innovation showed predominantly negative and transitional effects across ecological regimes. Environmental governance emerged as a key regional driver, with stronger positive effects observed at higher institutional quality levels. These findings underscore the importance of region-specific and governance-driven policy frameworks in strengthening ecological resilience and facilitating low-carbon energy transitions, while contributing to the regional science literature by offering distribution-sensitive insights into the energy–environment nexus with policy-relevant implications for achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 7, SDG 12 and SDG 13.
summary: Using quantile-on-quantile methods for China, finds nonlinear, distributional effects of nuclear energy, growth, innovation, and governance on ecological resilience.

title: Farmer intentions to continuously use mobile apps for agrometeorological and agronomic advisory services: technology continuance theory model analysis on user feedback in Vietnam and Thailand
authors: Kathleen Mae Auxtero; Shubham Anil Gade; Marco Kemperman; Muhammad Yaseen; Malay Pramanik; Phantipa Plangklang; Long Hoang; Ly Quoc Dang; Spyridon Paparrizos; Uthpal Kumar; Avishek Datta; Sushil Kumar Himanshu
keywords: Agrometeorological advisories; Continuance intention; Greater Mekong Subregion; Mobile application; Technology continuance theory
abstract: This study examined user feedback from smallholder farmers in Nakhon Phanom, Thailand, and Can Tho, Vietnam, to identify factors that influence their intentions to continue using ClimaFarm, a mobile application providing agrometeorological forecasts and agronomic advisory services. Data were collected from 151 farmers with prior ClimaFarm usage and analyzed with an adapted Technology Continuance Theory framework and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling. The results revealed that continuance was significantly influenced by perceived usefulness (β = 0.261, p < 0.01), trust (β = 0.280, p < 0.01), satisfaction (β = 0.251, p < 0.05) and attitude (β = 0.247, p < 0.05), while household income showed a significant negative association (β = − 0.161, p < 0.05). Although most farmers remained active users, their reported challenges and reasons for discontinuing use included interface and language barriers, concerns about forecast accuracy and connectivity limitations, suggesting technological and usability barriers rather than a lack of perceived relevance of the advisory information. These findings contribute to post-adoption evaluation of digital agriculture initiatives. By quantitatively determining the factors influencing application usage and offering a relative comparison of their influence, these findings provide a pioneering empirical baseline for digital climate-smart agriculture solutions in Southeast Asia. Insights also offer a clear, evidence-based roadmap for designing and scaling digital advisory tools in climate-vulnerable regions.
summary: Using Technology Continuance Theory and PLS-SEM on smallholders in Thailand and Vietnam, finds usefulness, trust, satisfaction, and attitude drive intentions to keep using an agro-advisory mobile app.

title: Global shocks and food price dynamics in Bangladesh: application of interrupted time series analysis
authors: Mohammad Chhiddikur Rahman; Mohammad Ariful Islam
abstract: The COVID-19 lockdown and the subsequent Russia-Ukraine conflict deeply disrupted the economy of Bangladesh, especially agriculture. This study employed an interrupted time series analysis (ITSA) to examine how multiple policy shocks affect wholesale and retail prices, as well as price margins of major food commodities in Bangladesh. Using weekly price data, we analyzed the effects of lockdowns in 2020 and 2021, followed by the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Results showed heterogeneous price margin effects across commodities and intervention periods. While domestically produced items like rice, eggs, onions and potatoes remained relatively stable during the pandemic and the early stages of war, import-dependent commodities—including flour, maize, lentils (mosur) and edible oil—experienced significant price jumps. During lockdown, the increases in wholesale prices were well transmitted to the retail level. The coarse rice retail price rose by 49.9%, medium-grain by 38.8%, and fine-grain by 24.3%. Flour and maize saw hikes of 27.6% and 22.0%. Essential items like mosur, onion, edible oil, egg and potato rose up to 52.2%. In contrast, the Russia-Ukraine war had limited effects on self-sufficient goods (e.g., rice, onion, egg), but import-dependent items were hit hard: flour rose 36.8%, maize 25.5%, mosur 17.1%, and edible oil 31.2%. These trends underscore how domestic production shapes vulnerability to global shocks. In response, the Government of Bangladesh implemented welfare and incentive programs to mitigate the shocks. Overall, the 2021 lockdown was managed more efficiently than in 2020, allowing greater access to essential goods and services, transportation and other conveniences. Based on these insights, we recommend policies to strengthen supply chain resilience against future global crises. Furthermore, policies to enhance the supply chain responsiveness and resilience to future pandemics, global crisis and natural disasters are suggested, given the lessons learned from the COVID-19 lockdown and Russia-Ukraine war.
summary: Using interrupted time-series analysis, examines how COVID-19 lockdowns and the Russia–Ukraine war shifted wholesale and retail food prices and margins in Bangladesh, with domestic staples more stable.

title: Variations in Intergenerational Mobility Across Regions and Birth Cohorts in China: Patterns and Mechanisms
authors: Yanji Zhang; Liang Cai
keywords: Intergenerational social mobility; Blau-Duncan model; Market transition theory; Power persistence theory; Regional disparity
abstract: Using six waves of the Chinese General Social Survey (2010–2021) and cross-classified random effects modeling, this study investigates regional and cohort variations in intergenerational mobility and transmission processes in China. Results show that regional patterns in the levels of intergenerational mobility and in the effects of determinants of status attainment are relatively stable across birth cohorts from the 1940s to the 1990s. First-tier cities and eastern regions consistently exhibit higher absolute mobility and greater influence of socioeconomic achieved factors, while the influence of socioeconomic ascribed factors and institutional factors such as party membership and hukou is weaker. Fixed-effects panel analyses demonstrate that regional economic development is associated with greater absolute mobility and weaker institutional effects, while coinciding with strengthened roles of socioeconomic ascribed and achieved factors. Educational inequality aligns with heavier reliance on institutional factors and correlates positively with relative and absolute mobility. Higher public education expenditure is linked to greater absolute mobility and diminished ascriptive influences. The findings highlight that China's intergenerational mobility is shaped by intertwined economic, institutional, and policy dynamics, with enduring regional disparities despite overall progress towards a merit-based system.
summary: Using six waves of Chinese survey data, finds regional patterns of intergenerational mobility are stable across cohorts, with first-tier cities and eastern regions showing higher absolute mobility.

title: The Impact of Demonstration Zones for the Transfer and Transformation of Scientific and Technological Achievements on Urban Air Quality: Evidence from China
authors: Jicong Yang; Bo Li; Duohan Liang
keywords: Air pollution; DID; Mechanism analysis; Spillover effects
abstract: Can promoting the transfer and transformation of scientific and technological achievements open up new pathways for air pollution control? Based on data from Chinese cities and listed companies, this study employs a difference-in-differences (DID) model to examine the impacts and underlying mechanisms of National Demonstration Zones for the Transfer and Transformation of Scientific and Technological Achievements (NDZTTSTA) on urban air pollution. The findings show that NDZTTSTA can reduce air pollution. Mechanism analysis indicates that the demonstration zones curb air pollution through the scale effects of introducing emerging production factors, the technological effects of knowledge spillovers, and the structural effects of achievement transformation. Additional analysis reveals that the air pollution control effects of NDZTTSTA vary significantly across locational conditions and levels of resource dependence. Moreover, NDZTTSTA generate spillover effects on air pollution control both in regions with strong technological linkages and in neighboring cities.
summary: Using difference-in-differences, finds China's demonstration zones for scientific-achievement transfer reduce urban air pollution via scale, technology-spillover, and structural mechanisms.

title: Socioecological Trade-offs in the Yucatan Peninsula: Stakeholder Perceptions of How Urban and Tourism Development Reshape Nature's Contributions to People
authors: Paulina Vázquez-Martínez; Gabriela Mendoza-González; Blanca Vazquez; Carlos Esse
abstract: Tourism expansion and urban development in the Yucatan Peninsula have intensified pressures on ecosystems, altering the natural contributions to people (NCP) that sustain regional wellbeing. To better understand emerging socioecological conflicts, we applied a multi-criteria analysis to integrate and spatially represent the perspectives of key institutional stakeholders regarding: (1) the prioritization of NCP groups per ecosystem, (2) the NCP they consider most important, (3) the main ecosystem threats, and (4) the ecosystems most affected by tourism and urban development. To achieve these objectives, the following ecosystems were assessed: Coastal lagoon, Cultivated grasslands, Popal, Savanna, Tropical Forest, Tular, Coastal dunes, Halophytic-hydrophytic vegetation, Peten, Mangrove, Palm Forest, Cenotes. Regulatory contributions—such as water and air quality regulation and protection against extreme weather—were consistently identified as the most valuable across coastal ecosystems, whereas cultivated grasslands were primarily valued for their material contributions, particularly food production. Perceptions of threats and ecosystem vulnerability varied across states, reflecting distinct tourism and urbanization trajectories. Incorporating stakeholder perspectives allowed us to identify major socioecological trade-offs and land-use transformation patterns by state. Overall, current development dynamics appear to prioritize short-term socioeconomic gains at the expense of ecological functions, particularly regulatory NCP, underscoring growing concerns about the long-term integrity of the peninsula's socioecological systems.
summary: Uses multi-criteria analysis of stakeholder perceptions to map how tourism and urban development in Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula reshape nature's contributions to people.

title: Green Trade, Globalization and Ecological Sustainability in the Black Sea Basin
authors: Dilara Ayla; Kezban Ayran Cihan
keywords: Ecological deficit; Globalization; Environmental impacts
abstract: This study examines the factors affecting the ecological deficit levels of countries in the Black Sea basin within a spatial panel data framework. Using data covering the period 1996–2021, the General Nested Spatial (GNS) model is employed to simultaneously evaluate cross-country interactions and local determinants. The results show that trade in low-carbon technology products reduces the ecological deficit through channels such as clean technology transfer and structural transformation in production. Similarly, foreign direct investment improves environmental performance through technology diffusion and production efficiency, while political globalization limits environmental pressure through international environmental norms and institutional cooperation. In contrast, consumption expenditures and financial globalization expand the ecological deficit by increasing the use of natural resources, whereas information globalization increases environmental pressure through digitalization, information flows, and the diffusion of consumption patterns. The analysis of spatial effects indicates that increases in political globalization and foreign direct investment in neighboring countries generate positive spatial externalities that reduce the ecological deficit through regional policy coordination and production networks. Supported by robustness and sensitivity analyses, these findings suggest that environmental outcomes in the Black Sea basin are shaped not only by national dynamics but also by regional interactions, and they provide important implications for the design of sustainable development policies.
summary: Using a spatial-panel model for the Black Sea basin, finds low-carbon technology trade and FDI reduce ecological deficits through clean-technology transfer and efficiency.

title: Measurement and Explanatory Mechanisms of Urban-Rural Integrated Development From the Perspective of Rural Residence-Employment Coordination: Evidence From the Chengdu-Chongqing Metropolitan Area
authors: Zhiquan Tu; Lulu Qu; Yunxin Huang; Yuqiang Zhu; Lin Zhu
keywords: Rural residence-employment coordination; Spatio-temporal differentiation; Urban-rural integration; Explanatory mechanisms; Chengdu-Chongqing Metropolitan Area
abstract: Rural residence and employment spaces are key components of rural regional systems and are closely related to the coordination of rural living, production, and ecological functions. Taking the Chengdu-Chongqing Metropolitan Area (CCMA) as the study area and using county-level data for 2011, 2016, and 2020, this study examines the spatio-temporal differentiation and explanatory mechanisms of urban-rural integrated development from the perspective of rural residence-employment coordination. The results show that: (1) Rural residence-employment coordination (RREC) in the CCMA increased steadily from 2011 to 2020 and exhibited clear spatial heterogeneity and clustering characteristics. High-value areas were mainly distributed around Chengdu and central Chongqing, while low-value areas were concentrated in peripheral mountainous counties. (2) The Pearson correlation results indicate that RREC is not dominated by a single public-service variable, but is associated with rural employment structure, transportation accessibility, fiscal-economic conditions, and infrastructure-related factors. (3) The Geodetector results further show that the proportion of rural workers has the strongest and statistically significant explanatory power across all three years, while economic non-agriculturalization becomes a significant explanatory factor in 2020. Interaction detection shows that paired interactions involving rural employment structure consistently generate high explanatory power, suggesting that RREC differentiation is shaped by the combined mechanisms of local employment absorption, residential stability, and spatial connectivity. These findings suggest that rural residence-employment coordination in mountainous metropolitan regions should be promoted by strengthening local employment opportunities, improving spatial accessibility, and enhancing county-level public service and infrastructure capacity.
summary: Using county data for the Chengdu–Chongqing Metropolitan Area, measures rural residence-employment coordination and finds urban-rural integration rose steadily with clear spatial clustering.

title: Institutional Constraints and Excess School Commuting in Educational Living Spaces: Evidence from Central Urban Hangzhou
authors: Xuexiao Cheng; Zhanfu Luo; Jing Shi
keywords: Excess commuting; School district; Neighborhood enrollment; Educational accessibility; XGBoost regression; SHAP explainability model
abstract: Under the "neighborhood enrollment" policy, the spatial rationality of school district delineation is important for evaluating educational accessibility. Taking the main urban area of Hangzhou as a case study, this research introduces an excess commuting framework to measure the distance discrepancy between officially assigned public primary schools and geographically nearest public primary schools at the residential community scale. Based on GIS-based spatial analysis, XGBoost regression, and SHAP explainability methods, this study examines the spatial distribution of excess school commuting and its associated institutional, locational, and built-environment factors. The results show that: (1) around 21.1% of residential communities experience positive excess school commuting relative to the nearest-school baseline; (2) both assigned-school walking distance and nearest-school walking distance show a "low in the center, high in the periphery" spatial pattern; (3) high excess commuting values are mainly concentrated in transitional zones between urban cores and peripheral areas; and (4) excess school commuting is associated with residential location within school districts, proximity to school district boundaries, school facility dispersion, housing age, housing prices, and road and school density. This study provides a community-scale approach for identifying distance deviations under the public primary school districting system and offers empirical evidence for evaluating school district arrangements and optimizing the spatial allocation of public primary education resources.
summary: Using an excess-commuting framework in Hangzhou, finds neighborhood-enrollment school assignments create avoidable extra school commuting shaped by institutional and built-environment factors.

title: Geospatial Modelling of Stunting and Underweight Among Children Under Five Years: Insights from Sub-Saharan Africa
authors: Handan Wand; Azar Kariminia; Sarita Naidoo; Jayajothi Moodley; Vaneshree Govender
keywords: Geospatial assessment; Sub-Saharan Africa; Generalized additive models (GAM); Child malnutrition; Stunting; Underweight; Nutrition and health policy
abstract: Child malnutrition remains a major public health challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa, with persistent disparities in stunting and underweight among children under five. This study examined subnational spatial variation and structural determinants of child growth failure across the region using Demographic and Health Survey data from 24 Sub-Saharan African countries collected between 2015 and 2023 (n = 198,443). Generalized additive models with spatial smoothing were used to assess geospatial patterns of stunting and underweight. Stunting prevalence ranged from 16% to 55%, and underweight from 5% to 29%, with substantial within-country heterogeneity. Children in the highest cumulative disadvantage quartile, characterized by poor maternal education, low household wealth, limited healthcare access, and reduced access to information, had substantially higher odds of stunting and underweight compared with those in the lowest quartile. Population-attributable risk estimates suggested that 45% to 89% of the burden was statistically associated with the included structural and socioeconomic risk factors under model assumptions. Spatial interpolation and smoothed intensity maps revealed localized hotspots of malnutrition that were often obscured by national averages. Despite variation in overall prevalence across countries, similar structural and socioeconomic factors were consistently associated with poor growth outcomes. These findings highlight the value of integrating high-resolution geospatial analysis with population-level impact measures to inform targeted, equity-focused nutrition policies and resource allocation strategies across Sub-Saharan Africa.
summary: Using DHS data from 24 Sub-Saharan African countries, maps subnational spatial variation in child stunting and underweight, finding wide within-country disparities linked to cumulative disadvantage.

title: Effects of the Built Environment on Dockless Bike-sharing Usage Based on TabPFN-GWR: Evidence from Shenzhen
authors: Ying Chen; Jierong Long; Jiaxun Zhu; Lu Ou; Haoxiang Lin; Haoye Liu
keywords: Shared micromobility; Dockless bike sharing; Built environment; Spatial heterogeneity; Nonlinear relationship
abstract: Dockless bike sharing (DBS) is an important component of urban shared micromobility that helps bridge the last-mile gap to public transport, supporting short-distance daily travel, and advancing low-carbon urban mobility. Using four representative districts in Shenzhen as the study area, this paper defines 500 m × 500 m grid cells as spatial analysis units and integrates DBS orders with Baidu heatmap data, road networks, public transport facilities, buildings, and land-use data. A residual correction framework combining Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) and geographically weighted regression (GWR), hereafter TabPFN-GWR, is applied to examine how built-environment conditions are associated with weekday and weekend DBS usage and to diagnose local spatial deviations that may require planning responses. The findings show that TabPFN-GWR improves predictive performance over standalone TabPFN, with R2 values rising to 0.698 for weekdays and 0.716 for weekends. Local surrogate results indicate that Baidu heatmap density is the dominant local predictor in most grid cells, while road density, building count, metro station presence, industrial land-use share, and land-use mix further explain spatial differences in DBS usage. PDP results show that Baidu heatmap density, road density, building count, and land-use mix are positively associated with predicted DBS usage, whereas industrial land-use share exerts a persistent negative effect and metro station presence provides clear feeder benefits. The findings suggest that DBS planning should move beyond uniform fleet deployment toward area-based governance: improving non-motorized transport connectivity in poorly connected areas, organizing parking and transfers around transit nodes, adopting differentiated dispatching for commercial, residential, and industrial districts, and designating residual clusters as priority areas for field inspection and fine-grained spatial management.
summary: Using a TabPFN-GWR framework in Shenzhen, examines how built-environment conditions shape dockless bike-sharing usage to support last-mile, low-carbon urban mobility.

title: The Nexus of Creativity and Technology: A Spatial Analysis of Urban Firm Location
authors: Carles Méndez-Ortega
keywords: Spatial Analysis; Creative Industries; Urban Planning; Agglomeration Economics; High-Tech Amenities
abstract: Software and video game (SVE) firms are hybrid creative–tech activities that combine digital technologies with culturally embedded forms of production. However, existing research on firm location has largely focused on regional scales or treated creative and high-tech industries separately, providing limited evidence on the intra-urban distribution of hybrid sectors. This paper addresses this gap by analysing neighbourhood-level associations and cross-neighbourhood spatial patterns related to SVE firm entries in Barcelona. Using firm-level administrative data and neighbourhood indicators for the period 2017–2019, we estimate count-data models and spatial econometric specifications, including Spatial Lag of X (SLX) and Poisson Spatial Autoregressive (P-SAR) models, to examine local associations and inter-neighbourhood dependence. The results indicate that SVE firm entries are positively associated with pre-existing agglomeration, digitally active urban environments, creative diversity, and human-capital-related indicators, whereas higher reported crime levels are associated with fewer entries. The spatial estimations further indicate that some of these associations extend across adjacent neighbourhoods. These findings contribute to research on the micro-spatial distribution of hybrid creative–tech firms within urban environments and provide evidence relevant to place-based analyses of firm location.
summary: Using firm-level data for Barcelona, analyzes the intra-urban location patterns of hybrid software and video-game firms that blend creative and high-tech activity.

title: Digital Human Capital And Return Migrant Entrepreneurship: Unraveling The Serial Mediating Role of Information Acquisition And Opportunity Identification
authors: Yongsong Long; Ye Ma; Jianhong Fan; Da Liu
keywords: Migrants; Digital access; Return migrant entrepreneurship; Information acquisition capability; Opportunity identification capability; Rural revitalization
abstract: Digital access, as an alternative resource for human capital growth, exerts a profound influence on return migrant entrepreneurship in developing regions globally, empowering entrepreneurs to adapt and thrive digitally. Although digital human capital is recognized as pivotal for return migrant entrepreneurship, how return migrants leverage accumulated skills during entrepreneurship remains a pressing concern. Using China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) data (2018–2020), we examine the effect of digital access on entrepreneurship, incorporating mediating effects of entrepreneurial opportunity mechanisms. We find that digital access significantly enhances entrepreneurial behaviors in developing areas. Accumulated digital human capital significantly strengthens both the capability of entrepreneurial information acquisition and opportunity identification, which in turn independently boosts return migrants' entrepreneurial behaviors. Concurrently, digital access exerts an influence on return entrepreneurial behaviors through a sequential process-digital access first enhances information acquisition capability, then improves opportunity identification capability, and ultimately increases return entrepreneurial behaviors-that remains robust after conducting sensitivity tests. Furthermore, digital access demonstrate varying levels and manners of influence on necessity and opportunity return migrant entrepreneurship. While digital access significantly facilitates both, the former hinges predominantly on opportunity identification, and the latter relies on information acquisition. Our analysis reveals how return migrants harness digital democratization-particularly information access and opportunity recognition-to navigate evolving entrepreneurial landscapes. This study enriches theoretical understanding of digital access' impacts and provides policy-calibrated pathways for rural revitalization in the digital era.
summary: Using China Family Panel data, finds digital access boosts return-migrant entrepreneurship, mediated serially by information acquisition and entrepreneurial opportunity identification.

title: Temporal Regimes of Environmental Sustainability in G7 Countries: A Causal Decision Support Framework Based on MiniROCKET
authors: Fatih Keskinkılıç; Mücahit Ülger
keywords: Environmental sustainability; G7 countries; temporal regimes; machine learning; causal inference
abstract: This study examines the temporal dynamics of environmental sustainability in G7 countries and evaluates how dominant temporal transformation regimes are associated with different environmental sustainability indicators. Existing studies on environmental sustainability in advanced economies have largely focused on individual indicators, particularly CO₂ emissions, or on average relationships estimated through conventional empirical models. However, sustainability transformation is multidimensional and may differ across production-based emissions, consumption-based ecological pressure, and ecosystem carrying capacity. To address this gap, this study analyzes annual data for G7 countries over the 1997–2021 period using three complementary indicators: CO₂ emissions, Ecological Footprint, and Load Capacity Factor. The study develops an integrated decision-support framework that combines MiniROCKET-based temporal feature extraction, Principal Component Analysis, and Double Machine Learning. First, macroeconomic, demographic, technological, energy-related, and environmental variables are transformed into high-dimensional temporal features using MiniROCKET. Second, PCA is used to reduce these features into dominant temporal components. Third, DML is applied to estimate the average and country-specific heterogeneous associations between the dominant temporal regime and the three environmental indicators. In the main specification, PC1 is used as the treatment variable, while PC2–PC5 are included as control components. Robustness checks include an alternative PC1–PC2 treatment definition, alternative nuisance learners, bootstrap confidence intervals, and placebo treatment tests. The PCA results show that the first five components explain approximately 89.92% of the total MiniROCKET-based temporal feature variance, indicating that G7 sustainability dynamics can be summarized by a limited number of dominant temporal structures. The main DML results indicate negative directional associations between the dominant temporal regime and all three environmental indicators. The strongest association is observed for CO₂ emissions, followed by Ecological Footprint and Load Capacity Factor. However, bootstrap confidence intervals include zero; therefore, the findings should be interpreted as indicative and decision-support-oriented evidence rather than definitive causal proof. Country-specific CATE results reveal substantial heterogeneity across G7 countries. Italy displays the strongest negative CATE values for both CO₂ emissions and Ecological Footprint, while the United Kingdom shows positive CATE values for these indicators. LCF effects remain close to zero across countries. These findings suggest that G7 sustainability policies should be country-specific and indicator-sensitive, integrating emission reduction, responsible consumption, circular economy practices, supply-chain transparency, and ecosystem-capacity-enhancing measures.
summary: Using a MiniROCKET-based causal framework, examines how dominant temporal transformation regimes relate to multiple environmental-sustainability indicators across G7 countries.

title: Do Urban Greenway Soundscapes Influence Public Cycling Preferences? Evidence From Street View Imagery
authors: Congying Fang; Ming Gao
keywords: Urban Greenway; Cycling; Soundscape; Street View Images; Machine Learning
abstract: Urban greenways are increasingly promoted as key infrastructures for active mobility. However, the perceptual dimensions that shape cycling behavior along these corridors remain insufficiently understood. While prior research has predominantly focused on built environment attributes, the role of soundscape as an experiential and behavioral driver has received limited empirical attention. This study integrates crowdsourced trajectory data, street-level imagery, and machine learning techniques to examine the relationship between multidimensional soundscape features and cycling preferences along urban greenways, employing interpretable models to uncover underlying nonlinear mechanisms. The results indicate that soundscape attributes such as sound quality, eventfulness, and traffic noise exert significant yet nonlinear influences on cycling volume, suggesting that the relationship between acoustic conditions and cycling activity is more complex than a simple linear reduction in noise. By conceptualizing soundscape as an actionable perceptual resource rather than merely a noise-control issue, this study advances urban greenway research from physical performance evaluation toward experiential mobility planning. The findings provide quantitative evidence for integrating soundscape-oriented interventions into bicycle-friendly urban design, offering a cost-effective approach for promoting sustainable active travel.
summary: Combining trajectory data, street-view imagery, and machine learning, finds urban greenway soundscapes shape public cycling preferences through nonlinear mechanisms.

title: Behavior-Calibrated Spatial Accessibility and Hospital Choice: Evidence from Paired Tertiary Hospital Inpatient Data for Respiratory Conditions in Wuhan
authors: Jingjing Wang; Hao Wu; Yang Zhao
keywords: Hospital choice behavior; Distance threshold effects; Behavior-calibrated accessibility; Explainable machine learning; Two-step floating catchment area method
abstract: Amid China's ongoing urban transformation, the rational spatial distribution of hospitals as critical public service infrastructure is central to promoting equity and improving healthcare accessibility. However, empirical evidence on how accessibility contributes to predicting hospital choice at the individual level—particularly through nonlinear distance effects—remains limited. Adopting a behavior-oriented perspective, this study examines hospital choice within a constrained setting, specifically focusing on inpatient decisions for respiratory conditions between two tertiary (Class 3 A) hospitals in Wuhan that are geographically proximate and comparable in institutional attributes. Using inpatient records and a behavior-calibrated interpretation of spatial accessibility, we integrate explainable machine learning with geospatial and environmental data to identify distinct distance-response regimes governing patient decision-making, rather than assuming uniform distance decay. The results indicate that spatial distance shows the strongest association with hospital selection but operates through threshold-based behavioral switching, with marked transitions occurring at specific distance intervals. Embedding these behavior-derived distance thresholds into a Two-Step Floating Catchment Area (2SFCA) framework, the study refines conventional accessibility assessment by explicitly accounting for both population demand and hospital resource availability. Spatial analysis shows that greater medical resource abundance significantly attenuates distance sensitivity, highlighting the context-dependent nature of spatial friction in healthcare utilization. By linking individual choice behavior with accessibility modeling, this study advances a behavior-calibrated framework for assessing healthcare accessibility. The findings provide applied insights for optimizing medical facility planning and resource allocation, particularly in rapidly urbanizing contexts where conventional distance-based assumptions may misrepresent actual patterns of healthcare use.
summary: Using paired inpatient data for respiratory conditions in Wuhan, calibrates spatial accessibility to behavior and examines its nonlinear role in hospital choice between comparable tertiary hospitals.

title: Intra-urban Amenities and the Spatial Emergence of High-tech Employment: A Firm-centred Analysis of Guangzhou, China
authors: Jili Xu; Run Shi; Xingjian Liu; Teng Zhong
keywords: Urban amenities; High-tech employment; Emerging industries; Street-view image; Machine learning; Guangzhou
abstract: By developing a firm-centred framework that links the supply of employment opportunities with the demand for urban amenities, this study examines how surrounding intra-urban amenities shape emerging high-tech employment in Guangzhou, China. Drawing on original firm-level survey data, street-view imagery, and point-of-interest (POI) datasets, and combining interpretable machine learning with statistical and causal analyses, the study investigates the directionality and heterogeneity of amenity-employment relationships at the firm scale. The finding shows that urban amenities are important drivers of the spatial emergence of high-tech employment in Guangzhou, lending support to the "jobs follow people" argument in this context. However, these causal relationships are highly differentiated across amenity subcategories and firm groups. Constructed and green amenities exert positive causal influences, whereas commercial amenities negatively affect the emergence of high-tech employment; public service amenities show no significant causal effects. By foregrounding firm-centred supply-demand interactions and locally specific urban contexts, this research advances a more nuanced understanding of the spatial interplay between intra-urban amenities and emerging high-tech employment.
summary: Using firm survey data, street-view imagery, and POI data for Guangzhou, finds intra-urban amenities are important drivers of where high-tech employment emerges.

title: Multi-Source Enterprise Data for Fine-Grained Industrial Cluster Delineation: A Spatial–Network Analysis with Policy Implications in the GBA
authors: Youwei Tan; Jiayun Li; Zhihui Gu
keywords: Identifying industry cluster; Spatial co-location; Industrial chain; GBA
abstract: Identifying industrial clusters and tracing the evolution of their internal industrial chains are critical for both cluster theory and regional spatial planning. Existing cluster-identification studies have advanced from statistical classifications and input–output tables to interaction-based industrial networks. However, broad-coverage and cross-jurisdictionally comparable enterprise-level approaches remain limited, especially in metropolitan regions with heterogeneous data regimes. Focusing on the electronic information industry cluster in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), this study develops an enterprise-level, multi-source identification framework that combines semantic parsing of firm descriptions, neural-network-based industry classification, and industrial linkage network modeling. We dynamically delineate cluster boundaries and construct a cluster network knowledge graph. Comparative validation against prevailing cluster typologies indicates a high overall consistency, while the proposed framework further enriches the representation of value-chain segments and convergent industries that are insufficiently captured by existing classification systems. Empirically, the GBA cluster exhibits pronounced spatial–relational heterogeneity: some knowledge-intensive industry co-agglomerate geographically, whereas others maintain strong functional linkages despite spatial dispersion, suggesting functional complementarity beyond mere geographic proximity. The proposed approach provides a reusable pathway for fine-grained identification and dynamic monitoring of metropolitan clusters, and offers evidence to inform cross-jurisdictional coordination and pre-evaluation in industrial spatial governance.
summary: Develops a multi-source, enterprise-level framework to delineate the Greater Bay Area's electronic-information industrial cluster and trace its internal industrial chains for spatial planning.

title: The Limits of the Role of Economic Growth in Poverty Reduction: Spatial Evidence from Brazilian Municipalities
authors: Nícolas Volgarine Scaraboto; Luciano Nakabashi; Alexandre Nicolella
abstract: Poverty remains a relevant problem in Brazil, potentially hindering the economic development of its regions. Applying the poverty convergence approach developed by Ravallion (2012), we analyze the complex interactions between poverty and economic growth in Brazilian municipalities. Using a dataset from 1991 to 2010, our results reveal a pattern of absolute income convergence across Brazilian municipalities, implying that regions with lower initial income levels tend to experience higher subsequent per capita income growth (the advantage of backwardness effect). In addition, we find that per capita income growth reduces the incidence of poverty (the advantage of the growth effect). Therefore, poverty should converge across Brazilian municipalities. However, the initial incidence of poverty hampered poverty convergence by reducing the impact of backwardness and the growth effect. Furthermore, spatial spillovers matter, as income growth in neighboring municipalities contributes to local poverty reduction; however, high poverty levels in surrounding areas weaken this beneficial effect. Our results underscore the importance of public policies in addressing and reducing poverty incidence as a strategy to promote economic growth in Brazilian regions.
summary: Applying poverty-convergence analysis to Brazilian municipalities (1991–2010), finds absolute income convergence and that growth reduces poverty, while noting limits to growth's poverty-reducing role.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: The regional determinants of per-capita CO₂ emissions growth in Europe
authors: Daniel Schmidtner; Jesus Crespo Cuaresma
keywords: Greenhouse gas emissions; Bayesian model averaging; Spatial autoregressive models
abstract: We identify empirically the determinants of per-capita CO₂ emissions growth in 227 European NUTS-2 regions for the period 1995–2022. In order to account for geographical spillovers of unknown form, we employ Bayesian averaging of spatial autoregressive models, addressing uncertainty on the specification of spatial links across regions. Our results indicate that the initial level of emissions, the regional economic structure, population growth, the number of days requiring indoor cooling, as well as the number of cars per-capita, are robust determinants of per-capita emissions growth.
summary: Using Bayesian spatial model averaging across 227 European NUTS-2 regions (1995–2022), identifies initial emissions, economic structure, population growth, cooling days, and car ownership as robust drivers of per-capita CO2 emissions growth.

title: Online consumption and sustained air pollution exposure: Evidence from a quasi-experiment in China
authors: Sumit Agarwal; Long Wang; Yang Yang
keywords: Air pollution; Avoidance behavior; Online consumption; Winter heating policy
abstract: This study examines how air pollution affects household consumption in the digital economy. Using a proprietary dataset constructed from more than 500 million online transactions across 291 Chinese cities from 2017 to 2019, we study how online spending changes when pollution rises. To identify causal effects, we exploit quasi-exogenous variation in air quality generated by China's winter heating policy and implement a difference-in-differences design comparing northern and southern cities around the heating period. We find that pollution increases online spending on health-related products and necessities and reduces spending on non-essential goods. The response is concentrated in the heating period itself, with little evidence of stockpiling before or delayed adjustment afterward. Item-level evidence shows that the increase in spending operates mainly through higher quantities purchased rather than higher payment per item. Additional evidence from Baidu search activity suggests that the spending response is associated with greater attention to pollution risks and protective products, as well as worse mood.
summary: Uses a quasi-experiment in China to examine how the growth of online consumption relates to sustained air-pollution exposure.

title: Voting green, or not: what drives members of the European Parliament opposition to agri-environmental reform?
authors: Joaquin Villa-Garcia; Jeroen Candel; Nicolas W. Jager
keywords: Agri-environmental policy; Agri-food sector; European Union; Moonlighting; Post-exceptionalism; Voting behaviour
abstract: Substantive agri-environmental policy change has not materialized within EU agri-food governance despite emerging scientific consensus on the need for food system transformation. Agri-environmental legislative proposals often face strong resistance, resulting in their weakening or reversal. Although the challenges to adopting agri-environmental legislations are clear, existing analytical tools fall short in explaining why legislative rollbacks occur. This study addresses this gap by drawing on Rational Choice Theory to examine how individual-level motivations linked to the agri-food sector influence members of the European Parliament (MEP) voting behaviour on agri-environmental legislation. Roll-call vote data and a binomial generalized linear mixed model are used to test office-seeking, policy-seeking and vote-seeking motivations. Our analysis shows that MEPs with private financial interests in the agri-food sector were more likely to vote against environmental protection across the studied agri-environmental legislations, while MEPs with stronger environmental ideological affinity were more likely to support such measures. Institutional variables, mainly political group affiliation and COMAGRI leadership of legislative files, are also significant determinants of voting behaviour. These findings suggest that individual-level motivations and institutional structures help explain the lack of consistent legislative support for agri-environmental legislations between February 2022 and July 2024. Our findings raise normative questions about the need for stronger transparency and conflict-of-interest measures in EU agricultural governance.
summary: Examines what drives members of the European Parliament to oppose agri-environmental reform.

title: Quality-driven price dispersion: Implications for testing market efficiency
authors: Hisaki Kono; David Ernst; Tsilavo Ralandison; Yutaka Arimoto
keywords: Price dispersion; Quality; Reputation; Spatial integration
abstract: Spatial price differences in agricultural markets, after accounting for transport costs, are often interpreted as evidence of market inefficiency. However, price differences may also reflect product quality variation, especially where formal grading systems are absent. This study uses a novel transaction-level dataset on paddy rice sales from rural Madagascar in 2022–2023, including laboratory-assessed grain quality indicators. By employing hedonic regressions, we construct a composite quality index to quantify the extent to which observed price variation across locations can be explained by quality differences. We find that varietal identity commands substantial price premiums, but measured physical and post-harvest quality attributes beyond variety explain only a small share of the observed price dispersion. Controlling for the quality attributes has little effect on conventional measures of market integration. This result suggests that buyers face difficulties in accurately assessing physical quality at the point of sale. In such contexts, buyers may rely on location-specific reputation as a substitute. Consistent with this, transactions originating from villages with higher average quality are associated with higher prices even after controlling for observable quality attributes. We interpret this as descriptive evidence consistent with reputation or relationship-based sourcing in settings with limited quality observability.
summary: Analyzes quality-driven price dispersion in food markets and its implications for testing market efficiency.

title: Comparing carrots and sticks to create a more circular food system
authors: Junyoung Jeong; Yongyang Cai; Brian E. Roe
keywords: Circular food system; Computable general equilibrium; Food waste; Waste abatement cost; Waste tax
abstract: Circular economy solutions within the food system have prioritized prevention. Prevention policies can be formulated as carrots, e.g., waste abatement subsidies, or sticks, e.g., waste disposal taxes, and applied at one or more segments along the food supply chain. We develop a general equilibrium model of the U.S. Midwest that endogenizes food waste decisions and policy responses at key supply chain links. Existing models of circular food systems often fail to endogenize the amount of food waste and seldom apply multiple policies at different food supply chain stages. Our results identify how carrots and sticks differ across targeted supply chain stages. Waste abatement subsidies primarily result in a decrease in waste rates, while a food waste tax leads consumers to adjust both food purchases and waste rates equally. Subsidizing waste abatement can be five times more effective than a food waste tax in reducing food waste, despite both yielding comparable emissions reductions. 88% of emissions reduction caused by a tax derives from reduced food demand (and thus supply). With abatement subsidies, 28% of emissions reduction derives from decreased landfill deposits and 64% from reduced food supply. Our results also suggest that policies aimed at consumers can have four times greater impacts than those applied upstream. Lastly, as their combinations typically generate additive effects, carrots and sticks can complement one another, further informing an optimal policy suite that reduces food waste, while mitigating unintended consequences (e.g., rebound effects or consumption reduction).
summary: Compares incentive ('carrots') and penalty ('sticks') instruments for building a more circular food system.

title: Ozone pollution, cash crop production, and farmer adaptation: evidence from China
authors: Wanyu Ran; Xiaoguang Chen; Xiaoli Wang
keywords: Adaptation; Cash crops; China; Crop yields; Farm income; Surface ozone
abstract: Surface ozone pollution has emerged as a major threat to agricultural productivity, yet evidence on its impacts on high-value cash crops and farmers’ adaptive responses remains limited. Combining a household-level panel from the Chinese National Fixed-Point Survey with high-resolution pollution and weather data from 2003 to 2013, we find that rising ozone concentrations significantly reduced farm income of fruit growers, primarily driven by ozone-induced reductions in fruit yields, total production, and labor productivity. Sugar crops also experienced significant yield losses, while other cash crops exhibited negligible responses. Due to limited adaptive capacity, fruit growers responded by abandoning ozone-damaged plots, reducing input use, and reallocating labor towards off-farm employment, resulting in persistent income losses with little evidence of longer-run adjustment. In contrast, sugar producers offset yield losses by expanding cultivated area and increasing material inputs, maintaining output and income. These findings highlight the critical importance of ozone-control policies and targeted support to strengthen farmers’ adaptive capacity, particularly for fruit growers who are most vulnerable to rising ozone exposure.
summary: Examines how ozone pollution affects cash-crop production and how farmers adapt, using evidence from China.

title: Framing of ultra-processed foods in UK news media (2022-2023) and associations with quoted actors' interests
authors: Jennie C Parnham; Kiara Chang; Michael Essman; Deb Smith; Mike P Etkind; Maisie McKenzie; Prisha Shah; Milica Vasiljevic; Mark Petticrew; Martin White; Anthony A Laverty; Emma Boyland; Steven Cummins; Christopher Millett; Jean Adams; Eszter P Vamos
abstract: Increasing attention on “ultra-processed” foods (UPFs) and their health effects has sparked policy debate. News media influences public perceptions yet understanding of UPF framing and industry influence remains limited. This study analysed UPF framing in UK news media and trade press, exploring interests of quoted individuals and organisations. We systematically searched UK media for UPF articles in 2022–23, identifying 188 articles for mixed-methods content analysis. Articles were examined for their position towards classifying food by processing-level (accepted/contested/mixed). Framing Theory guided identification of UPF frames describing problem definitions, causes, and solutions. Actors’ interests were classified using academic journal guidelines. Half the articles (52%) accepted the UPF concept, 19% contested it, and 29% were mixed. Five frames were identified. The ‘Social Justice’, ‘Lifestyle Drift’, and ‘Science Report’ frames accepted the UPF concept, with the ‘Social Justice’ frame positioning UPF consumption as a structural public health problem requiring policy action such as taxes or front-of-package labelling. The ‘UPF Critique’ and ‘Market Justice’ frames contested the scientific basis of the UPF concept, proposing nutrient-based approaches instead. Among 116 named actors, 33% had UPF industry interests, with academics comprising 45% and industry spokespeople 11%. Actors with UPF industry interests were more commonly cited in contesting frames (e.g. ‘Market Justice’: 73%) than accepting frames (e.g. ‘Social Justice’: 10%). These findings highlight that industry influence on UPF media discourse is often obscured behind academic voices. Greater transparency around actor interests is urgently needed to ensure emerging UPF policies are shaped by independent evidence.
summary: Analyzes how UK news media framed ultra-processed foods in 2022–2023 and how framing related to the interests of quoted actors.

title: The new grain giants: the reliability of USDA's corn and soybean production forecasts for Brazil and Argentina
authors: Olga Isengildina Massa; Berna Karali; Scott H. Irwin
keywords: Accuracy; Argentina; Bias; Brazil; Corn; Efficiency; Forecast evaluation; Soybeans; USDA reports
abstract: While Brazil and Argentina emerged as major players in the world grain markets following a rapid expansion of corn and soybean production, little is known about their production forecasts. Our study demonstrates that the accuracy of USDA forecasts of Brazil and Argentina's corn and soybean production varies drastically over the extended forecasting cycle. Specifically, early forecasts are not directionally consistent and offer limited statistical advantage to a naïve alternative. After 8–10 months into the forecasting cycle, these forecasts begin to provide meaningful information to market participants and become more accurate, efficient and reliable for the remainder of the forecasting cycle. These forecasts support export estimates in the US WASDE balance sheets as well as USDA baseline forecasts that have implications for federal budget outlays and may result in misallocation of resources when early projections are used.
summary: Assesses the reliability of USDA corn and soybean production forecasts for the emerging grain exporters Brazil and Argentina.

title: Carbon food labels have limited effects on grocery shopping behavior: Evidence from a randomized experiment
authors: Maiken Maier; Lukas Paul Fesenfeld
keywords: Carbon food label; Demand-side policy change; Food consumption behavior; Food-related emissions; Plant-based diets; RCT
abstract: Demand-side food policies are increasingly recognized as important tools for aligning consumption patterns with climate change mitigation targets, and carbon food labels have attracted growing attention as a potential policy instrument. However, evidence on their effectiveness remains mixed, and causal evaluation results from assessing the effects of carbon food labels in real-world supermarket settings is scarce. This study presents evidence from pre-registered randomized field-embedded survey experiment with behavioral outcomes, combining a representative sample of 2,372 Swiss residents with transaction-level purchasing data covering more than five million daily food purchase decisions made by 1,601 consumers over several years. In collaboration with one of Switzerland's largest grocery retailers, we evaluate the causal impact of an information treatment designed to increase awareness of one of the world's first carbon food labels implemented in grocery stores on both stated preferences and revealed purchasing behavior. The results show that the information treatment significantly increases label awareness and leads to small but positive effects on attitudes, perceived behavioral control, and intentions to consider the climate compatibility of food purchases. When tracing these effects into revealed purchasing behavior, the treatment also affects actual food purchases, but effects are modest and heterogeneous across food categories. Rather than inducing broad shifts away from meat consumption, the information treatment primarily leads to a higher overall share of labeled products purchased, increased purchases of labeled convenience products, and a partial reallocation within meat consumption (e.g., lower beef and higher pork purchases). We find no evidence of substantial reductions in overall meat purchases or large cross-category substitutions toward plant-based foods. While heavy meat eaters do not react negatively to the treatment, men and more right-wing individuals show a modest behavioral backlash. Overall, the results suggest that carbon food labels capacity to substantially alter habitual food consumption patterns in stimulus-intensive retail environments is limited and should be thus complemented by additional demand-side measures.
summary: A randomized experiment finds carbon food labels have only limited effects on grocery-shopping behavior.

title: A business ecosystem approach to exploring local community collaboration in forest tourism: a systematic review
authors: Lingyun Tong; Anne Toppinen
keywords: Business ecosystem; Community involvement; Community participation; Nature tourism; Rural development
abstract: This study adopts a business ecosystem lens to examine actors and their collaborative dynamics in rural forest tourism. Drawing on a systematic review of case studies in emerging and developed countries, we identify five distinct business ecosystem models, each acting as a governance configuration that dictates actor collaboration, benefit-sharing, and conflict dynamics. Our findings reveal that rural community reliance on external support risks superficial engagement, while excessive state intervention may stifle organic collaboration. Comparably, state-led models with coordinating entities exhibit greater stability, by positioning governments as keystone players that integrate resources and utilizing dedicated coordinating entities to mitigate top-down conflicts and incentivize community participation. We clarify the dual role of governments and propose adaptive strategies for policymakers, including capacity building, cross-sector knowledge sharing, and inclusive platforms. Unresolved issues, such as institutional redundancy in the business ecosystem highlight priorities for future research. This work offers theoretical and practical insights for enhancing rural livelihoods, fostering high levels of local acceptance in the forest tourism destinations, and advancing more sustainable and resilient forest tourism.
summary: A systematic review applying a business-ecosystem lens to local community collaboration in forest tourism.

title: Villager emergency evacuation behavior in disaster response via rural on-site drill in plateau area
authors: Jianwu Xiong; Meijun Jin; Lingling Yong; Jing Wu; Qianru Yang; Yin Zhang; Gang Mao
keywords: Emergency evacuation; Experimental data fitting; High-altitude village; Human behavioural monitor; Rural disaster resilience
abstract: High-altitude rural settlements are particularly vulnerable to disasters because difficult terrain, limited infrastructure, and limited preparedness resources can constrain rapid evacuation. However, field-based evidence from these settings remains scarce. This study conducted an on-site evacuation experiment in a predominantly Tibetan village in western Sichuan, China. Seventy-seven residents aged 8–83 completed an approximately 300-m uphill or downhill route while GPS wristbands recorded location, instantaneous speed, heart rate, and elevation at 1-s intervals. Spatial trajectory analysis, age-group comparisons, interviews, and vector autoregression were used to examine environmental and physiological influences on evacuation. Participants slowed at sharp turns, intersections, and the later portions of uphill routes. Irregular branch roads and visually ambiguous shortcuts were also associated with hesitation and occasional route deviation. Young participants moved faster overall but showed larger within-route speed declines, whereas older participants maintained lower and more stable speeds. Short-term acceleration dynamics were dominated by their own lagged values, while lagged heart rate provided statistically detectable but limited additional predictive information. These findings suggest that route geometry, wayfinding complexity, and age-dependent fatigue should be considered when planning evacuation routes and shelter access in high-altitude rural settlements.
summary: Uses an on-site rural drill in a plateau area to study villagers' emergency evacuation behavior in disaster response.

title: Living a one planet life: Ongoing trials by space within Wales's sustainable rural development policy
authors: George Tonge; Keith Halfacree
keywords: Counterurbanisation; One planet development; Planning; Radical rural; Rural wales; Trial by space
abstract: A recent and still-emerging current within the well-noted phenomenon of counterurbanisation is what may be termed neo-rural back-to-the-land, involving especially new rural in-migrants seeking a land-production orientated sustainable life. Although apparent across the global North especially, living such a life is very challenging and, not least via its radical rural spatiality, is likely to be experiencing a tough ‘trial by space’ (Lefebvre, 1991). However, in rural Wales it has been encouraged via the Welsh Assembly Government's planning policy in support of One Planet Development (OPD) enterprises. Although subject to a very detailed range of extremely strict criteria, this policy allows construction of buildings in ‘open countryside’ that would not normally be seen as suitably placed. After setting up the global presence of neo-rural back-to-the-land counterurbanisation, the paper introduces the Welsh development of this policy, drawing on published sources and key informants, before its main focus examines how OPD is playing out for three case studies. The latter are all couples with children, rather than communal enterprises, seeking to combine a high degree of self-sufficiency from their smallholding with wider ways of living in tune with sustainability principles. A broadly positive, if qualified, sense that they are passing their trial by space is important in the context of assessing the contribution that radical forms of rural development can make to the huge global planetary sustainability challenge facing us all.
summary: Examines 'one planet living' trials by space within Wales's sustainable rural development policy.

title: Talking about fire: Attitudes, beliefs and discourses in an Australian rural community
authors: Sally Gardner; Danielle Couch; Paul Komesaroff
keywords: Australia; Bushfire; Community; Discourses; Meanings of fire
abstract: The 2019-2020 fire catastrophe in Australia has generated vigorous personal and public reflections about the nature and role of fire in Australian society and how to manage fire across the continent. Within local communities a variety of attitudes and perspectives has been debated, often with limited mutual understanding. To take advantage of this historical moment post-the catastrophic summer of 2019-20 and to contribute to more effective communication between the parties, we sought to examine the various ways in which inhabitants of a rural region experienced and understood fire, along with sources of agreement and disagreement. Semi-structured interviews about attitudes to different fire experiences were conducted with non-Indigenous people from a range of gender, age and professional backgrounds.
