Our results indicate that, in comparison to the baseline model without reinforcement strategy, the proposed model reduces the number of facilities that need to be opened by approximately 50% while maintaining the desired service level. These findings provide decision-makers with a practical and efficient strategy for enhancing disaster response capabilities under cascading uncertainty.
summary: A two-stage robust optimization model with decision-dependent uncertainty shows that pre-disaster reinforcement of emergency facilities substantially reduces the number needed and buffers cascading demand shocks in an Istanbul earthquake case.

title: Context-rich data sets for school operations models and methods
authors: Aysu Ozel; Karen Smilowitz
keywords: School operations; School districting problem; Education; Benchmarking data sets; Public sector operations research
abstract: In transportation and logistics problems, such as the traveling salesman problem or the vehicle routing problem, the geographic distribution of nodes can significantly impact both the solutions obtained and the performance of solution approaches. Therefore, it is common for researchers to share test instances for meaningful comparisons. In some contexts, this is more challenging when data are protected and cannot be shared. This is particularly true for transportation and logistics problems found in public school operations. Despite growing literature, proposed models and solution approaches are rarely compared across papers because data protection regulations prohibit sharing data. At the same time, randomly generated data can miss critical patterns existing in reality that may impact equitable access to education. In this paper, we introduce a framework to create context-rich data sets for school operations models and methods based on publicly available data that reflect public school district characteristics in the United States.
summary: The authors build a framework that turns publicly available US school district characteristics into realistic, shareable test instances for school transportation and operations research.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Tracks of equality: high-speed rail and its effects on intra-regional inequality—a quasi-experimental study based on China's district/county-level data
authors: Jiahao Lai; Fan Zhang; Ruilin Luo; Guo Chen
keywords: Inequality; High-speed Rail; Difference-in-Difference
abstract: The efficacy of high-speed rail (HSR) remains controversial, with critics contending that its welfare disproportionately accrues to affluent demographics, potentially exacerbating inequality. In this study, we employ nighttime light data at the district/county level in China from 2000 to 2019 to construct a nighttime light inequality index as a proxy for intra-regional inequality. Utilizing a quasi-experimental approach (Difference-in-Differences), we investigate the impact of HSR implementation on intra-regional inequality in China. We find that HSR significantly reduces inequality along its routes, with districts/counties experiencing mitigation of local disparities primarily through three channels: technological innovation, entrepreneurial activity, and urban expansion. HSR's inequality-reducing effects are most pronounced in megalopolis with multiple centers and balanced structural layouts. The presence of national-level tourist attractions enhances HSR's mitigating effect on local inequality. Notably, red tourism sites associated with Chinese Communist Party history exhibit a more substantial augmenting impact on HSR's inequality-reducing effects compared to conventional tourist attractions. Our research findings contribute to the ongoing discourse regarding the welfare effects of HSR and offer policy implications for developing nations contemplating HSR as a means to alleviate poverty and stimulate economic growth.
summary: Using nighttime light data as an inequality proxy, high-speed rail rollout in China lowered intra-county disparities along its routes via innovation, entrepreneurship, and urban expansion, especially in polycentric megalopolises with major tourist sites.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Comparing public investments across sectors with CBA-based impact information and participatory budget choices
authors: John M. Rose; Andrea Pellegrini
keywords: Cost benefit analysis; Participatory budgeting; Logit mixed logit model; Transport electrification
abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid decision-support framework that integrates cost–benefit analysis (CBA) with participatory budgeting (PB) to inform public-sector portfolio choices. To highlight the approach, we assume that CBA has been conducted to evaluate twelve independent infrastructure and service projects, establishing their economic viability. Subsequently, PB is employed to elicit community preferences regarding the same projects, ensuring alignment with public values. The combined framework aims to reconcile technical efficiency, understood here as welfare-economic appraisal implemented through standard modelling and valuation conventions, with democratic legitimacy, captured through direct, budget-constrained citizen prioritisation. Our findings show that respondents gave the strongest average support to health care and utilities projects, with education also performing relatively well, while public transportation and road infrastructure were preferred to transport-electrification initiatives. In contrast, public projects associated with private vehicle and freight vehicle electrification attracted comparatively weak support, and public transportation electrification was supported less strongly than conventional public transport investment. More broadly, respondents tended to favour projects that delivered larger consumer-surplus and environmental benefits and projects located in, or relevant to, their own area.
summary: Combining cost-benefit appraisal with participatory budgeting, citizens back health, utilities, and conventional public transport over vehicle-electrification projects, and favor investments delivering large local consumer-surplus and environmental gains.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Evaluating local-area transport interventions through mobile phone GPS data: a framework and case study of low traffic neighbourhoods
authors: Xianghui Zhang; Peter Jones; Andy Emmonds; Tao Cheng
keywords: Transport intervention; Evaluation framework; Travel behaviour; Mobile phone GPS data; Low traffic neighbourhoods
abstract: There is increasing adoption of local-area transport interventions worldwide, as part of a strategy to encourage more sustainable mobility. However, the impacts of such interventions are complex and wide-ranging and often difficult to monitor using conventional instruments, as they include various travel modes (e.g. car, bus, cycle, and walk), different population groups (e.g. residents, visitors, and non-local travellers), and multiple scales of influence (both social and spatial). This paper presents a new comprehensive evaluation framework to assess local-area scheme interventions that leverages the continuous, high-granularity spatial coverage of mobile phone GPS data to overcome these limitations. This framework is then applied to examine the impact of a set of Low Traffic Neighbourhood (LTN) Schemes in North-East London, in which through traffic is removed from predominantly residential areas, using road closures and traffic filters. Using Propensity Score Matching and a Difference-in-Differences model, it explores issues related to changes in mobility and activity patterns, at both individual and spatial levels. The findings reveal that, in this sample of LTNs, residents have reduced their driving outside LTNs and spend more time walking and engaging in other activities within their LTNs. It also enhances local attractiveness, as evidenced by increased footfall among non-residents during weekdays. Moreover, in this case the LTNs have reduced motor traffic flow on both internal and surrounding roads, challenging the notion that traffic is merely displaced to closely adjacent main roads. However, the LTNs have resulted in former pass-through drivers taking longer routes, potentially transferring motor traffic and increasing road usage in surrounding residential areas. This study demonstrates the value of using mobile phone GPS data and causal inference methods to provide a broader and richer evaluation of local-area transport interventions.
summary: GPS phone data reveal that London Low Traffic Neighbourhoods cut residents' driving, raise walking and non-resident weekday footfall inside the zones, and actually reduce motor traffic on surrounding roads rather than displacing it.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Environmental impact of a green tax on new vehicle sales in the presence of tax exemptions
authors: Andrés Gómez-Lobo; Juan José Price
keywords: Emissions; Environmental taxation; Registration taxes; Chile
abstract: At the end of 2014 a "Green" registration tax on new vehicle sales was introduced in Chile. In this paper we use a vehicle registration dataset to estimate the impact of this policy on average nitrogen oxide (NOx) emission rates of new vehicle purchases. We analyze two impact channels: substitution from diesel to gasoline vehicles and substitution from more to less polluting models within each fuel class. We rely on a difference-in-differences approach and focus our analysis on pickup trucks. Our identification strategy benefits from the fact that for this type of vehicle the policy defined a taxable and exempt group. In addition, the tax was increased on two occasions after its implementation, hence we can estimate its impact as a function of treatment intensity. Our findings suggest that an average tax that reached 7-8% of the sale price resulted in an overall increase of 4 to 8 percentage points in the probability of purchasing a gasoline over a diesel pickup truck for affected purchases, reducing the average emission rate for this class of vehicles. In addition, we find suggestive evidence that within the diesel pickup group the tax may have induced a substitution to a cleaner model once it became available in the market. The policy's aggregate environmental impact is small since a large fraction of the most polluting vehicles are exempt. Finally, we do not find evidence of an increase in CO2 emissions as a result of the tax. Policy recommendations are discussed.
summary: Chile's registration tax on high-emission new vehicles nudged pickup buyers from diesel to gasoline models and toward cleaner variants, but broad exemptions kept overall NOx and CO2 impacts small.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Penalties as prices? evaluating airline strategic responses to tarmac delay penalties in the US
authors: Hideki Fukui; Martin Dresner; Chikage Miyoshi
keywords: Tarmac delay penalties; Airline strategic responses; Counterfactual estimator; Synthetic difference-in-differences
abstract: We examine whether penalties for lengthy tarmac delays in the US aviation industry deter such incidents or are instead regarded by carriers as an acceptable cost of doing business. Exploiting penalties imposed on marketing carriers for severe-weather tarmac delays as a quasi-natural experiment, we compare changes in taxi-out and taxi-in times, the rate of lengthy tarmac-delay incidents, and cancellation rates between penalized and non-penalized carriers using difference-in-differences and synthetic difference-in-differences estimators. We find modest improvements in operational performance following penalties but also observe, in several cases, no improvements or even adverse changes. Specifically, the deterrent effect of these penalties seems to weaken when they are small relative to carriers' net incomes. Our results suggest that current penalties provide only limited deterrence and may be perceived by some carriers as an everyday cost of doing business, especially when financial conditions are favorable.
summary: US penalties for lengthy tarmac delays produced only modest and inconsistent improvements in airline taxi times and incident rates, suggesting carriers with healthy finances treat the fines as a routine cost of doing business.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Understanding the influence of public transport perceptions on the adoption of demand responsive transport services in the UK: A case study
authors: Shobhit Saxena; Chiara Calastri; Christine Currie; Julia Bennell; Rym M'Hallah
keywords: Demand-responsive transport; Adoption of DRT; Perceptions of reliability; Safety; Connectivity and affordability of public transport
abstract: This study investigates the adoption potential of demand-responsive transport (DRT) services in a large UK urban region, with particular emphasis on the role of perceptions toward existing public transport (PT) infrastructure. While DRT is often promoted as a sustainable alternative to conventional modes, its urban implementation in the UK has yielded mixed results, partly due to a limited understanding of behavioral factors that influence its uptake. We employ a hybrid modelling framework combining revealed and stated preference data from 1490 respondents in the Greater Leeds region, integrating latent perceptions of PT reliability, safety, connectivity, and affordability within a random utility maximisation structure. Unlike traditional integrated choice and latent variable (ICLV) models, we adopt a parsimonious specification using a single-indicator approach, facilitating better interpretability and policy simulation. Our analysis indicates that PT perceptions significantly influence modal preferences, with improvements in safety and connectivity increasing the likelihood of DRT adoption. Notably, these findings challenge the prevailing notion of DRT as a competitor to PT, instead emphasising the complementarity between the two modes. Our policy simulations demonstrate that a balanced "carrot-and-stick" approach–one that simultaneously improves PT infrastructure and service quality while discouraging private car use-can strengthen perceptions of PT, increase its ridership alongside DRT, and ultimately support a modal shift away from private vehicles.
summary: In a Leeds survey, perceptions that public transport is safe and well connected raise willingness to use demand-responsive services, positioning DRT as a complement rather than substitute for existing transit.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Hydrogen-powered aviation: What do we know and where do we go?
authors: Zahra Jaffary; Yahua Zhang; Zhifang Wu; Kun Wang; Xiaowen Fu; Yifei Cai
keywords: Hydrogen aviation; Airport hydrogen infrastructure; Decarbonization policy; Hydrogen supply chain
abstract: The transition to hydrogen-powered aviation is a critical step toward achieving net-zero emissions in the aviation industry. However, significant uncertainties and research gaps remain in understanding its feasibility, deployment and broader implications. This literature review analysed 138 hydrogen-related articles published between 2015 and 2025 to assess the current state of research. The synthesis included the lead authors and their affiliations, the citations, the status of the leading journals and highlighting key thematic areas. The key thematic areas identified include carbon reduction policies, hydrogen-powered aircraft, the hydrogen supply chain and infrastructure, safety and the environmental impacts of hydrogen fuel in aviation. An understanding of these thematic areas is essential for shaping future research priorities, particularly in areas such as airport hydrogen demand, supply chain and infrastructure planning, and policy frameworks. The findings of this literature review can offer valuable insights for airports, airlines, policy makers, decision makers and hydrogen industries in supporting the uptake and offtake of hydrogen fuel. Based on our findings, we call for (1) in-depth airport-specific case studies to assess hydrogen infrastructure needs, comparing onsite, offsite and hybrid supply chain models in particular; (2) an investigation of demand profiles at airports as well as spatial constraints and the feasibility of hydrogen development; and (3) the identification of the supportive policy frameworks and regulatory measures that will be required to enable a successful transition to hydrogen power at the airport level.
summary: A review of 138 studies on hydrogen aviation maps existing thematic clusters and highlights airport infrastructure, demand profiling, and supportive policy frameworks as the key knowledge gaps blocking net-zero flight.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Urban informal transportation and gentrification: empirical evidence from motorcycle taxis in Bangkok, Thailand
authors: Shota Emoto; Daniel del Barrio Alvarez; Prasongchai Setthasuravich; Saksith Chalermpong; Phathinan Thaithatkul; Muhammad Zudhy Irawan; Hironori Kato
keywords: Urban informal mobility; Gentrification; Developing city; Transit-oriented development; Propensity score matching
abstract: This study investigated the role of informal motorcycle taxi services in shaping residential and commercial gentrification patterns around rail stations in Bangkok. Although Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) has been widely associated with displacement and spatial inequality, limited research has examined how informal transportation systems intersect with these processes in the context of the Global South. Through propensity score and Mahalanobis distance matching with stratified analysis, this study estimates the average treatment effect of motorcycle taxi presence on gentrification outcomes across 250-m and 500-m rail station buffers. Although the baseline results revealed no significant citywide effects, the stratified analyses revealed geographical heterogeneity. First, in inner-city, transit-rich areas, motorcycle taxi presence is positively associated with both residential and commercial gentrification, suggesting that these services may reinforce accessibility-driven redevelopment. In contrast, in peripheral areas with limited transit coverage, motorcycle taxis mitigate residential gentrification by enhancing the mobility of low-income residents and supporting informal agglomerations. Second, in areas at medium distances from rail stations, motorcycle taxi presence was linked to increased commercial gentrification and decreased residential gentrification. Third, motorcycle taxis have significantly positive associations with commercial gentrification in areas of older rail stations but insignificant in those of younger rail stations. These patterns reveal the dual and context-sensitive role of informal transportation in urban transformation. This study contributes to debates on informality, accessibility, and gentrification in Global South contexts and calls for TOD frameworks to incorporate informal mobility systems as both infrastructural assets and tools for inclusive urban development.
summary: Motorcycle taxis around Bangkok rail stations amplify residential and commercial gentrification in inner-city areas but shield low-income households from displacement in transit-poor peripheries, revealing a dual role in transit-oriented development.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Impacts of transportation infrastructure on the stopping behavior of heavy commercial vehicles
authors: Jishi Wu; Tao Feng; Peng Jia; Gen Li; Junyi Zhang
keywords: Freight transportation; Heavy commercial vehicles stopping behavior; Stopping duration; Machine learning
abstract: Restricting heavy commercial vehicles (HCV) stopping behavior is essential for traffic management and efficient logistics organization. However, insights into HCV stopping behavior conditional on infrastructure remain limited. We utilize large GPS HCV trajectory data to investigate the spatial variability of stopping duration and its associated influential factors. Results show HCV stopping duration and pre-stop trip distance exhibit marked weekday-weekend heterogeneity, with longer stops and longer preceding trips being more likely to occur on weekdays. We further propose a spatial random forest model to predict HCV stopping duration. In addition to the superiority of the proposed model, we found parking distribution and land use collectively contribute to 76.76% of the predictive power, with trip distance identified as the most influential factor, followed by distance to the nearest freight rail station and to the nearest port, respectively. Furthermore, the analyses also exhibit complex non-linear associations between influential factors and stopping duration, and significant threshold effects. These findings offer valuable insights that can serve as a nuanced guide for planning HCV parking management.
summary: GPS trajectories show heavy commercial vehicles stop longer on weekdays after longer trips, with parking supply, land use, and distance to freight rail and ports jointly explaining over three-quarters of the variation in stop duration.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Public preferences for transport infrastructure improvements: An analysis of attitudinal drivers
authors: Friederike Beck; Michiel C.J. Bliemer; Allister Loder
keywords: Policy preferences; Attitudinal heterogeneity; Latent class modeling; Stated ranking experiment
abstract: Research has shown that public support for transport policy measures is one of the key factors affecting the successful implementation. But the heterogeneity in the population for broader policy objectives, namely the prioritisation of improvements across transport modes, had rarely been examined in detail. But understanding public preferences for transport policies is crucial for designing politically feasible pathways towards sustainable mobility. This study investigates how attitudes, socio-demographic/economic attributes, mobility behaviour, and built environment characteristics shape preferences for infrastructure improvements across modes. After administering an online stated ranking survey (N=2,011), we conducted an exploratory factor analysis to identify latent attitudinal dimensions and estimate a three-class latent class rank-ordered logit model. Results reveal five distinct attitudinal factors and three heterogeneous preference classes: environmental enthusiasts (18.82 %), car pragmatists (34.18 %) and moderates (47.00 %). Environmental attitudes emerge as a central cleavage that influences preferences for general infrastructure improvements across different modes. Furthermore, respondents' own mobility patterns strongly shape preferences, highlighting a pronounced self-interest bias. We find that moderates, representing almost half the sample and exhibiting a balanced attitudinal profile, could be a receptive group for targeted interventions, where increased exposure to sustainable modes may further strengthen their support for related policies. These findings suggest that reframing investments in sustainable transport to emphasise accessibility and service quality may enhance public support for policies aligned with decarbonisation goals.
summary: A latent-class analysis of 2,011 UK respondents identifies environmental enthusiasts, car pragmatists, and a large moderate group whose preferences for transport infrastructure investments hinge on attitudes and personal mobility habits.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: A welfare-based evaluation framework for UAVs in last-mile delivery: economic assessment and roadmap design
authors: Xing Yao; Yaru Li; Chunan Wang; Bowen Yi; Ying Fan
keywords: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs); Last-mile logistics delivery; Ground vehicles; Welfare impacts; Economic assessment
abstract: As a disruptive logistics delivery solution, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is now transitioning from conceptual model to practical application. Its large-scale deployment will influence social welfare across multiple dimensions, rendering it an issue that cannot be overlooked in policy formulation. This study establishes a welfare analysis framework for last-mile delivery, systematically comparing UAVs with traditional ground vehicles in terms of cost, efficiency, and externalities. By aggregating these components, the study evaluates net welfare impact resulting from the transition in last-mile delivery methods. The analysis identifies delivery distance, labor wages, and battery costs as major factors affecting welfare of utilizing UAVs in last-mile delivery. Based on an analysis of 31 provinces in China, regions with higher labor wages and short delivery distances are more suitable for prioritizing the promotion of UAV logistics. Applying a net welfare gain criterion for substituting traditional ground vehicles with UAVs in last-mile delivery, this study projects that 24 out of 31 provinces in China will be ready for large-scale adoption of UAV delivery by 2035. This highlights the 2030–2035 period as a strategic policy window for promoting UAV delivery. Based on estimates using 2024 express delivery volumes, this transition will bring China net welfare gains of 3.96 billion USD by 2030 and 26.30 billion USD by 2060. However, this transition is accompanied by increased energy consumption and emissions, which calls for close attention from policymakers.
summary: A welfare model finds that drone last-mile delivery becomes net beneficial across most Chinese provinces by 2035, offering large aggregate gains but rising energy use that policy will need to manage.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Impact of real-time crowding information on mass-transit passengers' platform placement choices
authors: Florian Leprévost; Arthur Portron; Kirusha Krishnakaran; Élise Grison; Simone Morgagni
keywords: Real-time Crowding Information; Passenger behavior; Experimental psychology; Crowd management
abstract: Crowding in public transport systems affects both passenger comfort and network efficiency. Besides operational solutions, interventions targeting passenger behaviour could address this issue efficiently. Real-Time Crowding Information (RTCI) systems, which display coach-level occupancy on platform screens, can help passengers avoid the most congested coaches or trains. However, existing research on RTCI's impact on passenger behaviour, relies predominantly on stated preference surveys, where respondents declare a single dominant strategy. Such designs cannot capture the trade-offs passengers make when competing cues – entrance proximity, exit knowledge, and crowding information – simultaneously influence their choice, nor can they reveal dynamic effects arising when passengers confront actual crowding after receiving RTCI.
summary: The study designs an experiment to examine how real-time coach-occupancy displays interact with entrance and exit cues in shaping where transit passengers choose to stand on the platform.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Unraveling systematic and unobserved heterogeneity in willingness-to-pay for traffic safety improvement: A hybrid decision tree and latent class Tobit approach with evidence from Pakistan
authors: Fazle Subhan; Hongmei Zhou; Muhammad Asif Khan; Shengchuan Zhao; Huanhuan Luo; Van Duy Tran
keywords: Latent class Tobit model; Decision tree; Heterogeneity; Willingness-to-pay; Risk reduction valuation
abstract: Evaluating traffic safety initiatives through cost-benefit analysis is essential for policymakers seeking effective resource allocation, and understanding individuals' willingness-to-pay (WTP) for improved traffic safety has therefore garnered increasing attention in recent years. However, important challenges remain in modeling WTP, namely, (i) the absence of systematic higher-order interactions in models, resulting in omitted variable bias and inaccurate model inferences, and (ii) the use of conventional models that presume a constant impact of explanatory variables on WTP, overlooking unobserved heterogeneity. This study addresses these gaps by integrating a decision tree with a latent class Tobit (LCT) model. The decision tree identifies potential systematic higher-order interactions that serve as inputs to the LCT model. The LCT model captures unobserved heterogeneity by partitioning individuals into distinct classes and identifying class-specific factors. The proposed modeling framework is tested on a sample of 653 car drivers from Peshawar, Pakistan. Results reveal two distinct classes in the population: "high" and "low" financial contributors. They further show that variables not significant in a conventional Tobit model become significant in different classes of the LCT model. Higher-order interactions identified through the decision tree are also incorporated in the model, capturing systematic heterogeneity in preferences. In addition, WTP for fatal and severe injury risk reductions is estimated and used to calculate the corresponding risk-reduction values. Overall, the proposed modeling framework enhances understanding of individuals' sensitivities toward WTP for improved traffic safety and provides actionable insights for policymakers seeking to target distinct population groups.
summary: Combining a decision tree with a latent-class Tobit model on Pakistani drivers uncovers two distinct willingness-to-pay classes for traffic safety and higher-order interactions that standard models overlook.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: How our values and means shape optimal transit fare policy
authors: Tianxing Dai; Yu (Marco) Nie
keywords: Fare-free transit; Utilitarian; Egalitarian; Fare policy; Transit design
abstract: This study examines how optimal fare policies are shaped by the need to balance moral values and financial means. Motivated by the growing interest in fare-free transit (FFT) and the lack of rigorous modeling frameworks to evaluate its impacts, we develop a joint transit design model that incorporates a means-based step-fare structure encompassing full-fare-free (FFF), partial-fare-free (PFF), and standard-discount-fare (SDF) policies. The model accounts for behavioral responses such as the zero-price effect, as well as operational and administrative savings from eliminating fare collection. It is then employed to identify optimal fare policies under both utilitarian and egalitarian objectives across a range of financial scenarios. Applied to the case of Chicago, our analysis yields several key findings. First, optimal policies depend critically on funding levels: FFF is both egalitarian and utilitarian only when robust financial support is available. Second, contrary to common belief, a utilitarian is more likely than an egalitarian to support FFF, as equity goals often require targeted benefits. Third, increasing financial flexibility does not always lead to more publicly acceptable designs. These findings offer guidance for transit agencies navigating the post-pandemic fiscal landscape and planners pursuing more sustainable and equitable urban mobility for their communities.
summary: A joint transit design model shows that fully fare-free transit is optimal on both utilitarian and egalitarian grounds only when funding is generous, and that utilitarian planners are surprisingly more likely to endorse it than egalitarians.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Two-region mixed autonomy network with park-and-ride: Macroscopic modeling, microscopic validation, and multi-scenario analysis
authors: Yifan Li; Ziyuan Gu; Nan Zheng; Wei Ma; Zhiyuan Liu
keywords: Park-and-ride; Mixed autonomy network; Parking dynamics; Macroscopic or network fundamental diagram; Autonomous vehicle
abstract: Urban transportation networks often face severe congestion and parking difficulties during peak periods due to demand–supply imbalances in traffic and parking. Park-and-ride (P&R) policies have been widely adopted to mitigate these issues by diverting vehicles to parking facilities near the boundary between central and outer regions of the city. However, the emergence of autonomous vehicles (AVs) fundamentally reshapes traffic dynamics and parking behaviors, thereby challenging the effectiveness of traditional transportation management polices. This study proposes a parsimonious two-region mixed autonomy network (MAN) model that incorporates self-driving-and-parking AVs and P&R dynamics to analyze their combined effects and mutual influences. The model is built upon an extended multi-pool representation tailored to MANs and employs an accumulation-based approach to capture the dynamic evolution of different vehicle families within the system. Discrete choice models and Monte Carlo simulation are further integrated to characterize the distinct parking behaviors of AVs and human-driven vehicles (HVs). The consistency analysis against a microscopic model confirms that the proposed macroscopic model accurately captures the temporal evolution of traffic network conditions. Additionally, experimental results demonstrate that while P&R remains effective for regulating HV inflow to central regions, its impact diminishes as AV penetration increases, owing to AVs' ability to self-park. These findings suggest that AV-specific management policies may be required to complement traditional HV-oriented P&R strategies. Overall, the proposed model offers a structured approach to inform decision-making on various urban parking policies and services for better traffic management in the era of AVs.
summary: A two-region macroscopic traffic model, validated microscopically, shows that park-and-ride effectively regulates human-driven vehicle inflows to city centers but loses bite as self-parking autonomous vehicles enter the fleet.

title: What shapes tourism flow networks in China? unraveling spatial characteristics and proximity mechanisms with group tour data
authors: Wentian Shi; Chenyang Zhai; Wenlong Yang
keywords: Complex Networks; Economic Geography; Ecological Network; Network topology; Regional Geography; Transport Geography
abstract: Tourism flow carries production factors such as culture, economy, information, and knowledge, having a profound impact on regional economy and sociocultural development. This study based on group tourist flow data, reveals spatial characteristics and proximity mechanisms of tourism flow networks within China by integrating spatial analysis, social network analysis, and econometric methods. The results indicate significant spatial imbalances in tourism flow distribution, showing a trend of "southward, eastward, and westward," with Hainan Island, the Yangtze River Delta, and the Southwest region being popular tourist destinations. Network nodes exhibit high clustering, with high values of degree centrality, weighted degree centrality, and betweenness centrality dispersed spatially, with cities like Sanya, Hangzhou, and Lijiang standing out. The network exhibits a clear core–periphery structure, with 16 cities located in the core and the majority of cities situated in the peripheral regions. Hierarchical analysis of the network structure shows that Sanya as the national dominant node, and 17 cities including Hangzhou, Kunming, Chengdu, Chongqing, Xi'an, and Yinchuan as subdominant nodes, while most cities serve as affiliated nodes. Regarding driving mechanisms, geographical, social, economic, and cultural proximities all promote tourism flow, while institutional proximity shows a negative correlation.
summary: Group-tour data reveal that Chinese tourism flows form a core-periphery network dominated by Sanya and eastern-southwestern hubs, with geographic, economic, and cultural proximity all boosting flows while institutional proximity dampens them.

title: Global value chains and top income inequality: evidence from European regions
authors: Martina Pardy; Eduardo Hernández-Rodríguez
keywords: Global value chains; income inequality; European regions; forward participation; institutional quality
abstract: This paper analyses the link between global value chain participation and intra-regional income inequality across European regions from 2003 to 2010. It combines regional input–output data to construct different indicators of global value chain participation and income data for regions at NUTS-2 level. Using fixed effects and instrumental variable estimations, we show that it matters how regions participate in global value chains: forward participation is on average linked to higher inequality at the top of the income distribution, while backward participation, in contrast, is not significantly associated with inequality. This relationship varies across industries: sectors such as manufacturing, transport and communication, and business activities are among the main drivers of this relationship. Moreover, the effect of forward participation on top income inequality varies by development level and institutional quality, showing that it is more pronounced for less developed regions and regions with lower institutional quality. These findings offer a new perspective on the link between regional global value chain integration and increased top income inequality.
summary: Across European NUTS-2 regions, forward participation in global value chains raises top income inequality, especially in less developed regions and those with weaker institutions, while backward participation shows no comparable effect.

title: How agricultural subsidies shape local employment: evidence from the French support policies for mountain areas
authors: Yrabo Dabou; Julie Le Gallo; Lionel Védrine
keywords: Agricultural subsidies; rural employment; regional policy; France; difference-in-differences; spatial spillovers
abstract: Do place-based farm subsidies reshape rural labour markets beyond agriculture? We estimate the causal impact of France's mountain-area support (MA) scheme within the Less Favoured Areas (LFA) framework on municipal employment over 1962–1990, combining entropy balancing with an extended two-way fixed-effects estimator on 23,651 municipalities. We find that MA classification reduces total agricultural employment by roughly 15%, driven by an 18% decline in self-employment as farms consolidate and expand. Salaried farm jobs rise by about 16%, but this increase falls well short of offsetting the contraction of family labour. We also document positive spillovers to neighbouring municipalities and inter-sectoral linkages beyond agriculture: trade and services expand within treated municipalities, while agri-food and construction employment rises in nearby untreated areas. Treatment heterogeneity indicates stronger effects where farms are mid-sized and market access is limited, suggesting the programme compensates for labor market thinness in remote areas rather than complementing pre-existing urban advantages. Overall, a policy designed to sustain farming in disadvantaged areas appears to have reconfigured both the composition and the spatial distribution of rural employment.
summary: France's Less Favoured Areas mountain support cut total farm employment by fifteen percent as self-employed farmers consolidated, but generated spillovers into local trade and services and neighboring agri-food and construction jobs.

title: Land conservation policy and rental markets: evaluating unintended housing price effects
authors: Corey Lang; Jarron VanCeylon
abstract: Environmental policies can generate distributional impacts through the housing market, impacting homeowners and renters in unequal ways. While environmental improvements often benefit disadvantaged groups, one concern is that these improvements can increase the desirability of neighborhoods, which in turn can increase housing costs for renters and leaves the overall welfare effect ambiguous. In contrast, homeowners benefit from the additional amenities and the equity gain. This paper seeks to evaluate how rental prices respond to gains in nearby land conservation relative to owner-occupied home values using a panel of census and conservation data for the whole USA. We employ a first-difference regression model and use propensity score matching as a pre-processing method to improve the comparability of areas with and without new conservation. Our results suggest that local gains in conservation do not capitalize into rental prices but do capitalize into home values. Overall, our findings indicate that concerns for renters' welfare and unintended consequences of land conservation are unsupported.
summary: Across the US, new nearby land conservation raises owner-occupied home values but does not spill into rental prices, easing concerns that conservation-driven amenities systematically hurt renters.

title: How inter-city differences affect cross-city crime spatiotemporal prediction performance under few-shot scenarios: evidence from 12 U.S. cities
authors: Miaoxuan Shan; Jinguang Sui; Peng Chen
keywords: Cross-city crime prediction; Transfer learning; Urban heterogeneity; Spatiotemporal modeling; Few-shot scenarios
abstract: Transfer learning has been recognized as an effective approach to enhance model performance in urban spatiotemporal prediction under few-shot conditions. However, how inter-city structural characteristics influence its effectiveness in cross-city crime prediction remains underexplored. To address this issue, we conducted a systematic evaluation across 12 major U.S. cities at two spatial resolutions, covering property and violent crime types over multiple time periods. The results were interpreted from the perspectives of Routine Activity Theory and Crime Pattern Theory to understand cross-city transferability. Findings suggest substantial heterogeneity in cross-city crime spatiotemporal prediction performance across crime types and spatial scales. Overall, transfer learning consistently improves predictive performance for both property and violent crime, with significant improvements observed in most evaluated scenarios. However, the magnitude of improvement varies considerably across cities and spatial resolutions. For property crime, transfer performance is relatively stable across scales and is associated with urban functional organization and spatial opportunity structures in the source city. This pattern is broadly consistent with the opportunity-based mechanisms and stable routine activity patterns described by these theoretical frameworks. In contrast, violent crime prediction exhibits scale dependency, with transfer performance more strongly associated with local urban characteristics at the 1 km scale, while exhibiting different association patterns at the 2 km scale. In summary, this research uncovers the complex interactions among urban environments, spatial scales, and the transferability of crime spatiotemporal prediction models, highlighting the roles of spatial scale and urban structural heterogeneity in shaping the generalizability of crime spatiotemporal patterns across cities.
summary: Transfer learning improves cross-city crime prediction across twelve US cities but with heterogeneity that depends on crime type and spatial scale, aligning with routine activity and crime pattern theories.

title: Radial variability in assessing shape compactness
authors: Alan T. Murray
abstract: The shape of an area is an important geographical concept that is largely defined by its degree of being compact. As a result, much attention and focus has been on the best approach(es) to measure compactness in order to assess the relative characteristics of an area. Geographers have made important contributions to the specification of measures and metrics associated with compactness. In fact, the radial deviation approach proposed by Boyce and Clark (Geogr Rev 54(4):561–572, 1964) remains particularly popular and broadly applied. This paper investigates this measure with respect to properties and theoretical relationships. A GIScience based generalization is possible that extends the radial sampling and approximation notion to a closed form exact approach. Empirical assessment explores the merits of this generalization with respect to implementation and application in GIS. The findings highlight that existing approaches do not accurately estimate average radial distance from a center to shape boundaries, creating bias and misleading compactness measurement. Further, the findings demonstrate that this can be overcome through the proposed generalization and extension relying on the actual average radial distance.
summary: A closed-form generalization of the Boyce-Clark radial deviation measure removes systematic bias in estimating average radial distance, yielding more accurate shape compactness metrics for GIS applications.

title: Assessing the seasonal mitigation of urban heat exposure risks raised by urbanization through greening strategies in eight US cities
authors: Xinyue Gu; Liyue Zhang
keywords: Urban heat mitigation; Heat exposure risk; Urban greening; Urbanization; Interpretable machine learning model
abstract: The intensification of the urban heat island effect as a consequence of global warming represents a considerable threat to urban populations, elevating the risk of heat exposure. Studies have investigated the effects of urbanization or greening on heat exposure, while the mitigation of seasonal greening and its interactions with urban typologies at the community level is still understudied. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the variation in urban heat island effect and heat exposure risk across cities, and how urban greening mitigates the adverse effects of urbanization. Using interpretable machine learning models and remote sensing data from eight different US cities in 2020, the study found that urban heat exposure risk is strongly related to the urban heat island effect and is significantly pronounced in summer and fall. There are seasonal differences in the risk reduction associated with urban greening, suggesting that it should take into account the seasonality of vegetation growth. Particular attention should be paid to green spaces and tree canopy height, as these have the best mitigation effects. Taken together, the study examines the impact of urbanization on heat exposure and its interaction with green spaces, with the aim of providing actionable insights for effective landscape strategies that can mitigate urban heat exposure.
summary: Machine learning on remote sensing from eight US cities finds urban greening mitigates heat exposure risk most in summer and fall, with tree canopy height and green space quality driving the seasonal benefits.

title: Measuring the Resilience of Renewable Energy Communities: A Scenario Analysis of the Regenerative Capacity
authors: Natalia Selini Hadjidimitriou; Maria Angela Butturi; Alessandro Neri; Rita Gamberini; Marco Mamei; Raffaele Nastro
keywords: Renewable energy communities; Resilience; Regenerative capacity
abstract: The growing adoption of decentralized renewable energy systems highlights the need to assess their resilience to disruptions. Renewable Energy Communities (RECs), composed of consumers and prosumers, rely on rooftop photovoltaic generation and peer-to-peer (P2P) energy sharing to meet local demand. Although previous studies have evaluated RECs from energy and economic perspectives, the influence of P2P network topology on resilience remains largely unexplored. This study proposes a framework that combines energy performance assessment with graph-based network vulnerability analysis to evaluate REC resilience under targeted disruption scenarios. P2P energy exchanges are simulated to construct directed, weighted energy-sharing networks, and graph-theoretic centrality measures are used to identify critical nodes whose sequential removal mimics targeted attacks. Results show that RECs provide substantial environmental and economic benefits, reducing greenhouse gas emissions to 61% of the baseline and achieving an average energy bill reduction of 22.5%. The self-consumption rate (SCR) indicates that 39.6% of locally generated renewable energy is consumed within the community, while the self-sufficiency rate (SSR) shows that local generation and P2P sharing satisfy 39.2% of total electricity demand. However, removing a small number of highly connected users significantly decreases network efficiency, highlighting the importance of increasing participation and redundancy to enhance REC robustness.
summary: Renewable energy communities cut emissions and bills substantially, but their peer-to-peer sharing networks are fragile because removing a few highly connected participants sharply degrades system efficiency.

title: Connectivity, Redundancy, and Resilience in Freight Transport Networks under Disruptive Shocks
authors: Tomoo Noguchi
abstract: Freight transport networks are vulnerable not only because links or nodes may be physically disconnected, but also because residual capacity may become insufficient even when origins and destinations remain topologically connected. This paper develops an analytically tractable framework for freight network resilience that treats connectivity and redundancy as explicit structural economic variables. We represent a multimodal freight system as an attributed spatial graph whose links and nodes may differ by mode, capacity, generalized cost, and transfer function. Connectivity is defined in two complementary ways: topological connectivity through edge-disjoint paths and capacity-mediated connectivity through max-flow/min-cut capacity and cut slack. Disruptive shocks are modeled as link or node removal, capacity degradation, and cost jumps, capturing freight-specific disruptions such as port closures, bridge and rail-corridor failures, border delays, canal blockages, and intermodal terminal disruptions. The analysis derives cut-based vulnerability conditions, regime boundaries between smooth degradation, capacity infeasibility, and disconnection, and spatial incidence results governed by binding cuts and corridor shadow prices. A computational experiment on a synthetic bottleneck-corridor freight network illustrates the operability of the proposed measures and shows that binary connectivity can substantially overstate resilience when residual capacity is depleted. The framework bridges network theory and spatial economics by clarifying when redundancy yields systemic resilience benefits rather than marginal capacity improvements.
summary: A cut-based analytical framework shows that assessing freight network resilience by topological connectivity alone overstates robustness once residual link capacity is exhausted.

title: Community De-gating, Streetscape Environment, and Governance: Impacts on Residents' Perception of Safety in Beijing, China
authors: Ju He; Jingcheng Cai; Li Chen; Meng Yang; Yunxiao Dang; Wenzhong Zhang
keywords: Residents' perception of safety; Gated communities; Community governance; Moderating effect
abstract: Gated communities are widespread in Chinese cities. With the promotion of community de-gating in urban renewal, it is important to examine how different forms of community enclosure affect residents' perception of safety (RPS). This study leverages data from 1,188 valid questionnaires and community street-view imagery, collected across eight communities in Beijing in 2021, to explore the influence of the community streetscape environment on RPS and to identify the moderating impact of community governance on RPS within communities undergoing de-gating. The findings indicate that: (1) The RPS among residents of gated communities is markedly higher than that of those in communities that have undergone de-gating, with a pronounced divergence in the streetscape environments between de-gated and gated configurations. (2) The flow of vehicles and pedestrians, architectural structures, and road intersections are identified as pivotal environmental factors that tend to erode RPS. (3) The level of community governance exerts a significant moderating influence on RPS when a community transitions to an open state, notably augmenting the perception of safety. This study provides empirical evidence for community de-gating policies and highlights the need to integrate spatial design with community governance to maintain RPS.
summary: Beijing residents in de-gated communities feel less safe than those in gated ones, but strong local governance meaningfully offsets that loss during the transition to openness.

title: Spatial Inequality in Access to Publicly Subsidized Sports Infrastructure: A National Analysis of NFL Stadium Accessibility Across U.S. Counties
authors: Ali Akram
keywords: Spatial accessibility; Spatial equity; Sports infrastructure; Regional inequality; Public subsidy
abstract: Major sports venues in the United States are frequently financed in part through public subsidy, yet how the resulting infrastructure is distributed across the population has received little systematic attention. This study quantifies the spatial accessibility of all thirty National Football League (NFL) stadiums for the 339.6 million residents of the contiguous United States, using county-level 2025 population estimates and transparent distance-based measures. The analysis is descriptive: it characterizes how far residents live from subsidized venues and how that distance varies across regions and population-density classes, rather than asserting that distant residents are deprived of a necessity. Half the population lives within 100 km of a stadium and three quarters within 200 km, but access is geographically concentrated: the population-weighted mean distance to the nearest venue is 140 km against an unweighted county mean of 250 km, and one quarter of the population (25.5%) lives beyond 200 km of any venue. The population-weighted mean distance ranges from 76 km in the Northeast to 174 km in the West. The distance gradient is patterned by population density: 61.0% of residents in lower-density counties live beyond 200 km of a venue, against 18.8% in higher-density counties, a more than threefold difference that is stable across distance thresholds and robust to road-circuity adjustments. The pattern is not purely rural; fifty-three higher-density counties containing 24.1 million residents, including San Antonio, Austin, Raleigh, and Salt Lake City, also lie beyond 200 km, reflecting the location of teams rather than the dispersion of population. Facility attributes such as seating capacity and age show no detectable association with catchment population. Because a meaningful share of stadium financing flows through federally tax-exempt municipal bonds, whose cost is borne by taxpayers nationally, the national distribution of physical access is a relevant descriptive complement to the predominantly economic literature on stadium subsidy. The analysis provides a reproducible national baseline for describing the distribution of physical access to publicly subsidized infrastructure.
summary: Publicly subsidized NFL stadiums serve a spatially concentrated share of Americans, with residents of lower-density counties more than three times as likely as urban residents to live over 200 km from any venue.

title: Modelling Internal Migrations in Poland at the Municipality Level and Their Relationship to Unemployment (2004–2023): Results, Implications and Potential Use
authors: Jarosław Tomasz Stańczak; Jan W. Owsiński; Przemysław Śleszyński; Rafał Wiśniewski
abstract: The paper presents the results from a study, devoted to modelling internal migrations in Poland at the municipality level. Thus, data concerns some 2,500 units across 20 years from the first two decades of the 21st century. The basic model studied assumes the dependence of migration flows on the unemployment rate. Then, the results of this model (identified for each of 20 years, i.e. actually 20 models) are compared with several of its extensions. The main conclusion is that the basic hypothesis of migration dependence upon unemployment is strongly confirmed. What is, however, even more important, is that the analysis of model errors, both of the basic model and its extensions, provides essential and quite specific information on the spatial character of the phenomena and processes analysed. These can be directly used for further, more detailed studies, but also for development policy purposes. While the results do not categorically state that this relationship must be positive for all units considered, they provide strong evidence that this may be the case to a much greater extent than we previously thought. On the top of this, the very clear spatial pattern constitutes an important value added.
summary: Municipal internal migration in Poland tracks unemployment more strongly than previously believed, and the spatial pattern of model residuals itself carries useful information for regional development policy.

title: Relationship Between the Employment Spatial Form and Commuting Distance of Residents in Different Communities: Evidence From Beijing, China
authors: Bo Liu; Hong Liang; Xiaodong Zhang
keywords: Employment spatial form; Community; Commuting distance; Agglomeration; Polycentricity
abstract: This study examines the relationship between employment spatial form and commuting distance at the community-scale using mobile phone signaling data for Beijing, China. We identified employment locations for 535 communities, classified them into eight distinct types based on commuting distance distributions, and delineated employment centers for each community using the contour tree method. Six indicators, including employment density, primacy, and polycentricity index, were calculated to quantify agglomeration and polycentricity characteristics of employment spatial forms. The results reveal a non-monotonic relationship. Communities with nearly identical average commuting distances can exhibit markedly different employment spatial forms, ranging from highly concentrated monocentric structures to low-density dispersed patterns. Two interpretations help to understand these patterns. The location factor drives short commutes and concentrated employment in communities close to major employment centers, while the transit factor enables longer commutes and dispersed polycentric employment patterns in peripheral communities by offsetting locational disadvantages via rail transit. This finding suggests that jobs-housing balance should not be measured solely by geographical proximity. Based on these results, three differentiated policy interventions are proposed for targeted transportation planning. This study provides empirical evidence for community-scale jobs-housing relationships and offers a basis for differentiated policy making.
summary: In Beijing, similar average commute distances hide very different employment spatial forms, since good rail transit lets peripheral communities sustain longer commutes to dispersed polycentric jobs.

title: Integrating Geospatial and Community-Based Insights to Unveil the Interaction of Road Infrastructure and Land Dynamics: Evidence from Bangalore-Mysore Urban Corridor in India
authors: Ali Younes; Asima Nusrath
keywords: LULC; Infrastructure; Land-Use Transport Interaction
abstract: This study examines infrastructure-induced land transformation across Bangalore–Mysore Urban Corridor (BMUC), a rapidly evolving region between two major urban centres in southern India. Employing an integrated geospatial approach supplemented by qualitative insights from local communities, the study captures the multifaceted spatial and social dimensions of change. Findings reveal that Bangalore–Mysore Expressway (NH275) functions as a spatial catalyst, driving accelerated urban expansion and a marked decline in agricultural land and natural vegetation. The intensity of land use and land cover change exhibits a strong spatial gradient, strongly correlated with expressway proximity—underscoring the transformative influence of transport infrastructure on adjacent landscapes. Predictive modelling projects a continuous intensification of these trends through the late 2030s, particularly along Bangalore fringe. Concurrently, socioeconomic analysis uncovers emerging spatial inequities, characterized by divergent development trajectories and a deepening urban–rural divide. By synthesizing spatial modelling with grounded community narratives, this study advances a novel framework for interpreting infrastructure-led land dynamics in the Global South. It critiques dominant top-down planning paradigms, illustrating not only the persistent marginalization of local communities in accessibility outcomes but also their agency in moderating land change trajectories. The findings offer actionable insights for regional policymakers, emphasizing the strategic importance of participatory governance as a cornerstone of inclusive and spatially just development.
summary: The Bangalore–Mysore expressway drives urban expansion and farmland loss in a strong distance-decay pattern, deepening the urban–rural divide and marginalizing local communities in accessibility gains.

title: One region, three universities: complementary differentiation in regional sustainability transitions
authors: Ridvan Cinar; Lars Coenen
abstract: An increasing number of stakeholders demand that higher education institutions contribute to sustainability transitions in places where they operate. Concurrently, policymakers encourage universities to differentiate themselves from each other. On the one hand, universities' sustainability contributions through third mission must complement those of other institutions in the same region to prevent resource fragmentation. On the other hand, they must also distinguish themselves to ensure that their sustainability efforts do not overlap excessively and become too similar. This article reports on the findings from a study of three higher education institutions in Vestland, Norway, exploring how external pressures and internal organizational dynamics influence their third mission positioning in relation to local sustainability transitions. The findings suggest that multiple coercive isomorphic pressures have played a key role in making these otherwise distinct institutions moderately similar over time. This convergence has, in turn, laid the foundation for closer coordination and collaboration in addressing regional sustainability challenges. Furthermore, we identify specific institutional carriers—symbolic systems, relational systems and routines—that have been instrumental in fostering complementary differentiation in third mission activities of the three universities. The article concludes with proposition of complementary differentiation as a conceptual lens to explore universities' positioning in regional sustainability transitions, followed by policy recommendations and avenues for future research.
summary: Three universities in a Norwegian region converged under external pressure yet still carved out complementary roles in regional sustainability transitions, illustrating a distinct pattern the authors call complementary differentiation.

title: Are we all Cistercians now?
authors: Nico Sonntag
abstract: This study revisits the hypothesis that the Cistercian monastic order has had a persistent and still measurable influence on contemporary European work values, specifically the claim that there are "pre-Reformation roots" to a strong ('Protestant') work ethic. Theoretically, this claim faces historical objections regarding the function of work within Cistercian monastic thought and the resulting ambiguous doctrinal stance, especially concerning the work ethic of the lay population. Drawing on data from the European Values Study (EVS 2008) and an expanded dataset of medieval monastic communities, the analysis tests the relationship between the historical regional presence of Cistercians and modern work-related values of respondents. The study improves upon previous research, inter alia, by considering a broader range of measures of work ethic and by incorporating data on three other religious orders. The results cast doubt on the existence of a persistent Cistercian effect on European work ethic. Most indicators of a strong work ethic show no or theoretically unexpected associations with past Cistercian presence. Likewise, placebo outcomes and associations between other orders and work-ethic indicators suggest that the research design may be vulnerable to spurious results, which may explain the few positive findings in this as well as in previous studies.
summary: Reanalyzing European Values Study data with a broader set of measures and monastic orders finds no robust evidence that historical Cistercian presence still shapes contemporary work ethic.

title: Public investment and tourism development: short-term evidence from French and Spanish regions
authors: Marta L. Suárez-Tostado; Yvan Tegui; Ana Belén Ramón Rodríguez
abstract: Tourism constitutes a key driver of regional economic development, integrating diverse industries and fostering socio-economic growth. Acknowledging the strategic importance of public intervention in enhancing tourism development and competitiveness, this paper employs a disaggregated, dynamic panel analysis across two major EU tourism economies to isolate the effects of thematically classified public investments, according to the objectives of the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) 2014–2020 programming period, on tourism performance. This study provides evidence on the short-term associations between finalized ERDF investments and regional tourism development, as measured by the Gross Value Added (GVA). The findings reveal that investments in connectivity infrastructure have a significant and positive influence on regional tourism outcomes. In contrast, other ERDF-funded initiatives did not exhibit immediate measurable effects, likely due to their broader or longer-term objectives. The results provide a nuanced understanding of the relationship between specific types of public investment and tourism dynamics, offering actionable insights for policymakers seeking to optimize resource allocation and promote sustainable regional development.
summary: Among finalized ERDF investments in France and Spain, only spending on connectivity infrastructure shows measurable short-run gains for regional tourism value added.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Spatial spillovers of US tariff policy
authors: Purba Mukerji; Yevgeny Yuzefovich
keywords: Trade contagion; US trade policy; Tariffs; Global supply chains
abstract: Given the growing importance and deeply interrelated nature of international supply chains, we investigate whether spatial spillover effects arise from trade relationships between countries following the substantial U.S. tariff changes announced by the new U.S. administration in early 2025. In doing so, we contribute to a literature that uses crises and other unexpected economic shocks to examine how effects propagate across countries. Our findings indicate robust spatial spillovers through trade linkages. Given the timing and evolution of spillovers, we interpret this as evidence of the importance of supply-chain connections that increasingly shape international commerce. Using data from April 2025, in the week immediately preceding and three weeks following the major U.S. tariff announcements, we estimate spillovers in stock market returns for 45 countries with the highest GDP in 2024, while controlling for U.S. tariff announcements and export exposure to the United States, China, and the rest of the world (ROW). The estimation is based on a spatial error model to account for spillovers arising from omitted supply-chain networks. The results indicate a strong spatial spillover effect via the trade-based weighting matrix, which rises initially through the spillovers via direct exposure to US trade, evolving into a rise in error spillovers, and finally, the spillovers fall as more information becomes available regarding the tariffs, reducing uncertainty and allowing potential supply chain adjustments to be considered.
summary: Stock returns across 45 major economies show strong spatial spillovers via trade linkages after the 2025 US tariff announcements, spiking with tariff uncertainty and fading as supply-chain information improves.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Modeling commuter mobility in Stockholm: a spatial panel approach using mobile phone data
authors: Marina Toger; Umut Türk; John Östh; Manfred M. Fischer
keywords: Spatial econometrics; Bayesian estimation; heteroscedastic spatial Durbin panel data model; GSM-based mobility flow data; spatial spillover effects; Greater Stockholm area
abstract: This paper examines the sociodemographic and socioeconomic determinants of regional commuter mobility in the Greater Stockholm Area using a heteroscedastic spatial Durbin panel data model estimated via Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Drawing on mobile phone–derived origin–destination flows from the MIND database, the analysis exploits unusually fine spatial and temporal granularity across a balanced panel of 675 regions over the period 2018–2023. A k-nearest neighbor spatial weight matrix (k = 18), selected via Bayesian model comparison, captures the topological structure of interregional connectivity. By modeling spatial lags in both the dependent and independent variables, the framework enables explicit recovery of direct (own-region) and indirect (spillover) effects from scalar summary measures of the matrix of partial derivatives — providing robust posterior inference on how sociodemographic and socioeconomic conditions propagate through space. This approach addresses a key limitation of conventional non-spatial methods, which risk producing biased estimates by ignoring spatial interdependence. Empirical results confirm that spatial spillovers predominate over direct effects, with educational attainment and car ownership emerging as the principal determinants of commuter mobility, while age composition plays a comparatively modest role. These findings underscore that evaluating direct effects in isolation systematically underestimates the broader societal returns to mobility-enhancing regional policies.
summary: In Greater Stockholm, spatial spillovers dominate direct effects on commuter mobility, and education and car ownership stand out as the main drivers across 675 regions.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Territorial development thresholds and the spatial effectiveness of sustainability investment: evidence from Colombian regions
authors: Mario de la Puente; Jose Torres; Hernan Guzman; Anderson Dominguez; Juan Lamby
keywords: Sustainability investment; Threshold effects; Colombia; Resilience; Institutional capacity
abstract: This study examines how territorial development levels condition the effectiveness of public sustainability investment across Colombian regions (2014–2024). Using panel threshold models and spatial analysis of 32 departments, we identify two development thresholds creating distinct investment–outcome regimes. Medium-development territories show the highest investment returns (β = 0.487), while low-development areas exhibit limited effectiveness (β = 0.132) and high-development regions show diminishing returns (β = 0.283). Mediation analysis reveals that institutional capacity and infrastructure quality are the primary mediating channels through which investment affects socio-environmental resilience. These findings suggest that spatially differentiated investment strategies outperform uniform allocation models in heterogeneous territorial contexts.
summary: Sustainability investment in Colombian departments pays off most at middle levels of territorial development, mediated by institutional capacity and infrastructure quality, favoring spatially differentiated allocation.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Special economic zones, COVID-19 pandemic, and interprovincial income inequality in the Indonesian manufacturing industry
authors: Takahiro Akita; Armida Salsiah Alisjahbana
keywords: Special economic zone; COVID-19 pandemic; Interprovincial inequality; Manufacturing industry; Indonesia
abstract: Using provincial manufacturing GDP data from Gross Regional Domestic Product of Provinces in Indonesia by Industrial Origin, this study examines how structural changes have affected interprovincial inequality in manufacturing GDP in Indonesia, employing several inequality decomposition methods. Particularly, it investigates the impact of structural changes associated with the establishment of special economic zones (SEZs) and the COVID-19 pandemic. The center of manufacturing growth appears to have shifted from labor-intensive to capital-intensive sectors. Interprovincial inequality in manufacturing GDP declined slightly prior to the pandemic and stabilized afterward. However, disparity among the five regions — Sumatra, Java–Bali, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, and Eastern Indonesia — declined markedly, reducing its contribution to overall interprovincial inequality. This reduction became particularly pronounced in the late 2010s, when several SEZs became operational. However, it was accompanied by rising interprovincial inequality within Sumatra and Sulawesi, likely driven by the establishment of SEZs. Most manufacturing sectors were severely affected by the pandemic. The transport equipment sector was hit hardest. However, overall interprovincial inequality remained largely unaffected. The manufacturing industry exhibits very high interprovincial inequality. With further development in the eastern parts of Indonesia, particularly Sulawesi and Eastern Indonesia, disparities among the five regions are likely to decline. However, if such development is enclave-type, concentrated in a few SEZs, it may lead to rising interprovincial inequality. To alleviate rising interprovincial inequality, it is imperative to promote labor-intensive sectors, as they are inequality-reducing.
summary: Indonesia's special economic zones coincided with narrowing gaps between its five macro-regions but widening manufacturing inequality within Sumatra and Sulawesi, while the pandemic left overall dispersion largely unchanged.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Industrial specialization and employment growth in Mexico: evidence from a spatial panel data model
authors: Rafael Garduño Rivera; Neil Reid; Haoying Wang
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between industrial specialization and employment growth across Mexican municipalities over the period 1986–2019. The analysis is framed within the debate on Marshall–Arrow–Romer (MAR), Porter, and Jacobs externalities. Using the Krugman Specialization Index (KSI) and a spatial autoregressive (SAR) panel data model with municipality and time fixed effects, we estimate the impact of specialization on total and sectoral employment. The results indicate that higher specialization is generally associated with lower employment growth at the municipal level. However, this relationship varies across sectors: the negative effect is strongest in commerce and services, not statistically significant in manufacturing, and positive in mining. In addition, we find strong evidence of positive spatial spillovers, suggesting that interactions across neighboring municipalities shape employment dynamics. These findings suggest that specialization may enhance productivity without necessarily generating employment gains. More broadly, the results highlight the role of productive structure, sectoral heterogeneity, and spatial interdependence in shaping regional labor outcomes. Policy should therefore emphasize balanced and context-specific development strategies rather than relying on specialization alone.
summary: Across Mexican municipalities, industrial specialization is generally linked to slower employment growth—strongest in commerce and services—suggesting productivity gains that do not translate into more jobs.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Spatial Durbin meets Tobler
authors: Luc Anselin; Renan Serenini; Pedro Amaral
keywords: Spatial econometrics; Spatial Durbin model; Tobler's law; Distance decay; Parameter constraints
abstract: An important practical use of coefficient estimates in a spatial regression model is to interpret the strength and range of implied spatial spillovers. In the classic spatial lag model, the structure of the reduced form ensures a smooth distance decay of neighboring multiplier effects. This can be viewed as following Tobler's First Law of Geography. However, in the linear SLX and spatial Durbin models, this is no longer guaranteed. In this paper, we investigate the interplay between parameter space for the spatial coefficients and Tobler's law, with a particular focus on the spatial Durbin model. We carry out a series of numerical illustrations and complement this with a small meta-analysis of empirical results reported in the literature. We provide a taxonomy of parameter values that yield different multiplier effects and the implied Tobler constraint. We close with some recommendations for practice.
summary: Spatial Durbin and SLX models do not automatically satisfy Tobler's distance-decay logic, and the paper maps which parameter regions produce sensible neighboring-multiplier patterns.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: How urban vehicle composition influences population concentrations in Indian cities?: a panel data analysis
authors: Sabyasachi Tripathi; Stuti Kabra
abstract: Cities become more productive and enjoyable places to live with improved transportation management. However, most cities in developing countries still lack it. In this context, the present study examines the relationship between the different types of vehicles (measured by passenger and freight vehicles) and urbanization (measured by city population size and density) in India. We also assess whether the relationship is linear or nonlinear. We consider data from 45 cities in India with populations of 1 million or more from 2011 to 2020. The study employs Fixed Effects and Feasible Generalized Least Squares panel data model. The results show that urban population and density are positively associated with private passenger vehicles, particularly two-wheelers, light passenger motor vehicles, and cars. Public and shared transport modes such as buses and omnibuses show negative associations with urban population concentration. Urban population has a negative relationship with freight-related vehicles, especially light motor vehicles for commodities and multi-axled trucks. The results also reveal that, while larger cities have greater transportation infrastructure, the expansion of private vehicles remains more closely associated with within-city population growth over time. Finally, the U-tests show no statistically significant inverse U-shaped relationship between urbanization and vehicle numbers. This indicates that congestion does not decrease or is not mitigated with the availability of inadequate infrastructure. Finally, we suggest several policy options to make Indian cities more compact, inclusive and sustainable through an efficient transport system.
