summary: Larger and denser Indian cities are associated with more private cars and two-wheelers rather than more buses, with no evidence of the inverse-U pattern that would signal congestion relief.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Examining the impact of air transportation, tourism, and economic growth on PM2.5 pollution: a comparative analysis of EUROCONTROL member nations
authors: Hicran Ergen; Alper Aslan
abstract: This study utilizes the PM2.5 variable, which is recognized as a significant determinant of contemporary climate change. This research examines the impact of air cargo, tourism income, and GDP on PM2.5 levels in the 16 member countries of EUROCONTROL. EUROCONTROL is an organization that was created to facilitate the development of a pan-European Air Traffic Management (ATM) system by coordinating the efforts of all aviation stakeholders in Europe. The analysis covers the period from 1990 to 2019 and employs ARDL coefficient estimation and Granger Causality testing methods. Based on the findings of the ARDL coefficient estimation, it was seen that a 1% rise in air cargo volume, tourism income, and GDP corresponded to a concomitant increase of 0.15%, 0.09%, and 0.11% in the concentration of PM2.5. Based on the findings of the Granger Causality Test, it can be concluded that there exists a unidirectional relationship between the long-term levels of PM2.5 and GDP. Additionally, the analysis reveals that there is a unidirectional causal link from GDP to tourism revenues. Thus, it can be observed that there exists an indirect causal relationship between the quantity of PM2.5 and the earnings generated from tourism. Based on the findings, this study proposes measures aimed at mitigating air pollution in the tourism and air transportation sectors of EUROCONTROL member nations.
summary: In EUROCONTROL member countries between 1990 and 2019, growth in air cargo, tourism income, and GDP each raised PM2.5 concentrations, with GDP driving pollution both directly and indirectly through tourism.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Can the digital economy reduce regional inequality in China's higher education? Evidence from spatial analysis
authors: Feifei Tan; Yao Ma; Zhiyuan Niu
keywords: Digital economy; Higher education quality; Regional inequality; Spatial spillovers; Policy intervention; China
abstract: Can the digital economy narrow regional disparities in higher education? This study examines the impact of China's digital economy on higher education quality and spatial distribution, focusing on its spillover effects and links to regional inequality. Using provincial panel data, we construct a multidimensional higher education quality index via the entropy-weighted TOPSIS method and assess cross-regional spillover effects with spatial econometric models. The results reveal two key findings: (1) A 1% increase in the digital economy index drives a 0.457% rise in local higher education quality, with more pronounced effects in central-western regions and areas with scattered Double First-Class universities; (2) Positive spatial spillovers exist: a province's digital economy development benefits neighboring regions' higher education systems. We outline policy levers—such as digital integration, cross-regional resource sharing, and differentiated resource tilt—to unlock the digital economy's potential in narrowing regional higher education gaps. These insights offer lessons for economies tackling educational inequality in the digital era.
summary: A stronger provincial digital economy in China raises local higher-education quality and spills over to neighboring provinces, with the largest gains in central-western regions with dispersed elite universities.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Navigating financial and governance barriers to renewable energy in LMICs: insights from machine learning and econometrics
authors: Abbas Khan; Li Shuangjie; Ai Xiaoqing; Muhammad Farrukh Shahzad; Abdul Razzaq
keywords: Renewable Energy; Financial barriers; Governance; LMICs; Hybrid modelling
abstract: This study investigates how financial and governance factors influence renewable energy (RE) adoption in five LMICs: Honduras, Jamaica, Kenya, Nicaragua, and the Dominican Republic, using data from 1996 to 2023. A hybrid approach that combines Random Forests (RF) and Fixed Effects Modelling (FEM) is used to evaluate how domestic credit, foreign direct investment (FDI), interest rates, and governance quality affect RE adoption. The findings suggest that domestic credit is essential for RE development in Honduras and Jamaica, whereas high interest rates negatively affect RE development in Dominican Republic. FDI encourages RE in Honduras, and the quality of the governance is important in attracting investment in Jamaica and Kenya. Energy imports affect RE adoption differently across countries. Policy recommendations include designing tailored financial strategies to improve access to domestic credit, adjusting interest rates to support RE growth, fostering a conducive governance environment to attract FDI, and encouraging domestic RE projects.
summary: In five low- and middle-income countries, domestic credit, FDI, interest rates, and governance quality shape renewable-energy adoption in country-specific ways rather than through a single common channel.

title: Regional foresight and scenario modeling of socio-economic transformation: The case of the Kostanay Region, Kazakhstan
authors: Aigul Sergeyeva; Murat Makhambetov; Gaukhar Keubasova; Shynar Mendaliyeva; Raibek Sagadatov; Anatoly Stepanov; Miroslava Omirzakova
abstract: This study investigates the spatial and socio-economic transformation of the labour market in the Kostanay Region of Kazakhstan through the application of foresight and scenario modelling. The research aims to construct a conceptual and predictive framework of regional employment transformation that integrates statistical indicators, expert judgments, and technological trajectories within a spatial foresight perspective. A mixed quantitative–qualitative design was employed, combining regression modelling, SWOT analysis, and expert foresight sessions. Empirical data were derived from official statistics for 2018–2023 and complemented by ILO, OECD, and WEF reports. Expert panels (n = 42) from academia, business, and public administration contributed to validating the scenario assumptions. Multiple regression analysis revealed that Gross Regional Product, investment in fixed assets, and digitalization exert positive effects on employment, whereas migration balance negatively influences labour potential. Three alternative development scenarios were modelled up to 2039: Baseline, Innovation-Driven, and Green Growth. The innovation-driven trajectory ensures the highest productivity and export potential through technological modernization, while the green scenario emphasizes ecological efficiency and sustainability. The findings underscore that the integration of investment, technological, and human capital policies is critical for enhancing regional competitiveness and achieving sustainable socio-economic development under demographic constraints.
summary: Regression and expert-panel scenarios for Kazakhstan's Kostanay Region show that regional output, investment, and digitalization lift employment while out-migration erodes labor potential, favoring an innovation-led development path.

title: Neighborhood assets as enablers of urban-suburban innovation capacities: Uncovering patterns and divides in Massachusetts and New York using traditional and API-mined data
authors: Eleni Oikonomaki
abstract: Large, open-source, and API-mined data have revolutionized the analysis of urban and suburban city neighborhoods with respect to their innovation capacities. Such data complements traditional census and government data collection methods and sources to help explain significant variations in invention activity across neighborhoods within a city. This paper combines diverse data sources to assess urban-suburban capacities and divides in the generation of patent-based innovation. First, it identifies patterns in innovation outcomes using USPTO patent records and illustrates spillovers across all ZIP codes in New York and Massachusetts and compares them with data from Google Maps to obtain a more granular and broader understanding of the concentration of innovation spaces. The findings reveal variations in the distribution of activity when comparing traditional patent records and API-mined data. Second, the study examines how economic, social, and spatial characteristics are associated with high levels of granted patents across neighborhoods in New York and Massachusetts. Drawing on a composite dataset assembled from multiple sources, the research interrogates the density of correlations between neighborhood variables and patent activity. Third, a comparative design spanning the two US states with distinct urban contexts deploys difference-in-means testing to systematically identify both shared patterns and divergences in how place-level conditions relate to high patent performance. Beyond the empirical findings, the study contributes a replicable methodology for assembling neighborhood asset indicators from heterogeneous data sources and offers a grounded interpretation of results for planning practice and innovation policy. The findings suggest that while traditional datasets provide long-term insights for formal study, alternative data-driven approaches reveal dynamic information that is important for understanding the evolving nature of innovation landscapes and informal innovation activities. Ultimately, this study advocates for a hybrid model that integrates both traditional and API-mined data paradigms to promote urban intelligence and equity. It advocates considering alternative innovation measures when designing innovation policies.
summary: Combining USPTO patents with Google Maps data across ZIP codes in Massachusetts and New York reveals urban–suburban innovation divides that traditional census sources alone underestimate.

title: Spatiotemporal Assessment of Expressway-Induced Land Cover and Landscape Transformation in Sri Lanka
authors: Piyoda Wijesekara; Amila Jayasinghe
abstract: Since the twentieth century, the sustainable use of land has emerged as a critical concern, with land use patterns shifting rapidly from agricultural and settlement expansions to infrastructure and urban development. Transport infrastructures are tightly connected in urban expansions, while exerting positive and negative impacts on land, society, economy and biodiversity. In addressing the need for sustainable land management, land cover change detection studies offer valuable insights that help scholars and policymakers overcome contemporary challenges in environmental conservation. This study focuses on the Southern Expressway Development Project (STDP) of Sri Lanka, where large-scale linear development projects represent a relatively new phenomenon. The study detects the change within a 5km buffer zone of the first phase of the STDP between the period 2001-2021, utilizing Geographic Information System (GIS) and Remote Sensing (RS) techniques. ArcGIS 10.8 and FRAGSTATS 4.2 were mainly used while the Landsat 8 images (path-141 and row-055 and row-056, with less than 10% cloud cover and of 30m-by-30m spatial resolution) were obtained from US Geological Survey's Natural Resources Observation Terminal Database website (https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov) for both years. Seven land classes were identified using supervised image classification. The overall accuracy of the images were 84% in 2001 and 85% in 2021. Analysis depicted that natural vegetation and built-up land cover have increased significantly, while cultivated lands, paddy and homesteads decreased by 5%, 7.73% and 6.44%. Water areas do not depict a considerable change. The Transfer Matrix depicted that 11066.14 ha of cultivated lands were transferred to natural vegetation. While a large amount of paddy lands was converted into cultivated lands (8530.64 ha) and natural vegetation (7218.78 ha). Results obtained through FRAGSTATS analysis revealed that the patch density of the area was increased from 112.57 to 169.42 and the number of patches of the overall landscape was increased by 58459. Class level analysis revealed though the natural vegetation and urban lands increased in total area, both land uses were highly fragmented. The area means of all the land uses were also reduced. Accordingly, the study concludes that the findings of the study are valuable for urban planners in two fronts. On one hand, the study provides a quantitative analysis of the impact of STDP on land use and land cover changes. On the other hand, the GIS & RS based method and technical process adopted in the study would be effective and useful for urban and regional planners to evaluate the land use changes and fragmentation.
summary: Along Sri Lanka's Southern Expressway corridor from 2001 to 2021, built-up land and secondary vegetation expanded sharply while paddy, homesteads, and cultivated land contracted within the 5 km buffer.

title: Housing Affordability and Migration Choice Among US Urban Areas
authors: Timothy R. Hodge; Jonathan Silberman
keywords: Migration; Relative Economic Conditions; Housing Affordability
abstract: Our study examines several factors affecting migration choice among US urban areas, with emphasis on a factor currently at the center of policy discussions: housing affordability. Aggregating county-to-county IRS migration data for core-based statistical areas in each of the 48 continental US states from 2014 through 2020, we implement a zero-inflated negative binomial model to estimate the effect of house price and rent differentials on migration choice. Our findings confirm that housing affordability is a relocation barrier that results in a loss of productivity and economic growth for the US economy. We also show that using an average measure of housing affordability masks important effects and reveal that differences in house prices greater than $50,000 and rents greater than $250 are thresholds for negatively impacting migration choice.
summary: House-price gaps above roughly $50,000 and rent gaps above $250 measurably deter migration between US metros, so housing affordability functions as a real barrier to reallocating workers.

title: Model selection strategies in a spatial setting: Some additional results
authors: Jesús Mur; Ana Angulo
keywords: Spatial econometrics; specification strategy; model selection techniques
abstract: This paper continues from the discussion of Florax et al. (Florax, R., H. Folmer and S. Rey, 2003. Specification searches in spatial econometrics: the relevance of Hendry's methodology. Regional Science and Urban Economics, 33, 557–579.), regarding the properties of various specification strategies for spatial econometric models. Habitual practise has popularised a technique based on the well-known Lagrange Multipliers, characterized as a Specific-to-General approach, and which seems to give good results. In our work, we contemplate other alternatives, some of which may be seen as slight variations of this proposal, including the selection tests of Vuong (Vuong, Q., 1989. Likelihood ratio-tests for model selection and non-nested hypotheses. Econometrica, 57, 307–333.) and of Clarke (Clarke, K., 2003. Nonparametric model discrimination in international relations. Journal of Conflict Resolutions, 47, 72–93.). We also examine an approach of the General-to-Specific type, as clearly opposite to the others. The comparison of the two strategies is carried out through a Monte Carlo experiment, the results of which are quite diffuse, in the sense that we do not find conclusive evidence in favour of either of these two approaches. However, it should be recognized that the General-to-Specific strategy seems to be more robust to the existence of anomalies in the Data Generating Process.
summary: Monte Carlo comparison of spatial model-selection strategies finds no clear winner between the popular Lagrange-multiplier specific-to-general approach and general-to-specific searches, though the latter is more robust to misspecification.

title: Automating the Transfer of Data between Census Sections and Postal Codes Areas Over Time. An application to Spain
authors: Virgilio Pérez; Jose M. Pavía
keywords: Spatial statistics; longitudinal data; census sections; R-stats; sc2sc; geospatial analysis
abstract: Cross-section and longitudinal spatial statistics and econometric models rely on spatially and temporally referenced data. Administrative units like cities, counties, and provinces provide stable data sources, enabling models to combine statistics collected at different times. In Spain, census sections serve as the smallest territorial units in which official statistics are delivered. These areas offer valuable statistics, such as population and housing censuses. Providing these statistics at the postcode level is also pertinent for conducting local analyses and surveys. The issue is that boundaries of census sections undergo regular updates, sometimes involving significant reorganization. The R-package sc2sc automates the transfer of variables between different census sections and postal codes. This paper introduces the package and outlines its methodology, which employs areal weighting to transfer counts and rates.
summary: The R package sc2sc uses areal weighting to harmonize Spanish statistics across changing census-section and postcode boundaries, letting analysts build consistent longitudinal small-area datasets.

title: Unveiling the pandemic's impact: Did COVID-19 drive business failures? A Cutting-Edge Analysis with Spatial Autoregressive Modelling
authors: David Garnés-Galindo; Manuel Ruiz-Marín; María Luz Maté-Sánchez-Val
keywords: Business failure; covid; Differences-in-Differences; current ratio; debt ratio; profitability; efficiency; spatial dependence
abstract: The objective of this study is to estimate the impact of Covid-19 on business behavior and its spatial effect among companies. Four specifications have been developed to analyze the pandemic's influence on key variables determining business behavior: liquidity, indebtedness, profitability, and efficiency. This study has focused on the province of Barcelona, Spain, from which a database of failed and non-failed companies has been compiled, both before and after the pandemic. The models have been estimated using the spatial Seemingly Unrelated Regressions (SUR) methodology, and each equation was estimated following a spatial Differences-in-Differences model. The results confirm that the emergence of Covid-19 has had a significant impact on companies' financial ratios, worsening their positions in terms of liquidity, indebtedness, and efficiency, with the existence of a spatial contagion pattern.
summary: In Barcelona, COVID-19 significantly worsened firms' liquidity, indebtedness, and efficiency, and spatial models detect a contagion pattern in these effects across neighboring companies.

title: Spatio-temporal dynamics of regional economic growth: An empirical model for the Spanish Autonomous Communities
authors: Julián Ramajo; Alejandro Ricci-Risquete; Geoffrey J.D. Hewings
keywords: Temporal dynamics; spatial dependence; spatio-temporal models; regional production; Spain
summary: A spatio-temporal econometric model of Spain's autonomous communities characterizes regional growth dynamics (the abstract is empty in the provided record).

title: Defining daily space use patterns in Hungary: mapping functional catchment areas
authors: Kristóf Bertalan Orbán; Gábor Mayer; Katalin Mezei; Judit Berkes; Tibor Navracsics
keywords: functional urban area; use of space; functional catchment area (FCA); accessibility; spatial planning; small and medium-sized towns; commuting
abstract: The prevailing methodology for delineating functional urban areas relies predominantly on labour market commuting data related to urban centres with more than 50 thousand inhabitants. However, this approach does not account for other functional relationships arising from residents' daily needs. In the development policy of the European Union, the widely used functional urban area delineation method (Dijkstra et al. 2019) maps connections between settlements by analysing a specific segment of the population on the basis of their location, jobs, and activities. A notable shortcoming of this method is that it neglects the role of small and medium-sized towns – places of unquestionable importance from a regional development perspective. To obtain a more accurate and comprehensive picture of society's spatial usage, extending these studies to a broader range of spatial and temporal characteristics of residents' activities is necessary. This multidimensional analysis allows for more accurate mapping of Hungary's functional catchment areas (FCAs) than the widely used EU–OECD functional urban areas (FUA) framework does. The methodology used is also capable of identifying smaller functional urban areas that are organised around less attractive peripheral, rural towns or suburban subcentres in a more fragmented and complex system of inter-settlement relationships. The resulting primary FCAs, with few exceptions, have an average spatial extent of approximately 468 km² (73% are between 100 and 1,000 km²). However, in terms of population, they exhibit significant variation, with an average of 43,776 residents, ranging from 6,093 to 321,953 inhabitants. As a result, the spatial structure of the mapped catchment areas can provide forwards-looking guidance for a more territorially balanced organisation of services. However, there is a need for further development of the methodology, considering the principle of population proportionality more strongly. This can play an important role in mapping the internal, partly intraurban daily spatial use subsystems of agglomeration areas.
summary: Adding non-commuting daily activities to the standard functional-urban-area method uncovers finer, smaller catchment areas around Hungary's peripheral and suburban towns that the EU–OECD framework misses.

title: Analysing economic and environmental sustainability in Kazakhstan: how cities perform in SDGs?
authors: Aigul Meirmanova; Tamás Sikos T.; Dóra Szendi
keywords: sustainable development goal; Kazakhstani cities; complex sustainability index; sustainable smart city; urban management
abstract: Sustainable Urban Development necessitates optimizing multidimensional targets across social, economic, and environmental pillars of development. These multidimensional targets are largely explained by 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) set by the United Nations (UN). However, knowledge gaps exist in quantitatively assessing progress towards SDGs for under-researched context, such as Kazakhstani cities. This empirical study assesses the performance of Kazakhstani cities, focusing on 3 dimensions of the 17 UN SDGs: SDG 8 (decent work and economic growth); SDG 9 (industry, innovation and infrastructure); and SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities), by using normalization method and average calculation to construct the SDG pillar and a complex sustainability index. The performance of SDG indicators for each city was visually represented using a monochromatic colour-coding scheme on a defined scale (five colour bands ranging from white (worst – 0%) to black (best – 100%) with a threshold of 20%). We further analysed the cities using a logical clustering to create three cluster groups. Almaty (complex sustainability index (CSI) score is 72.36) indicated high sustainability performance, significantly outperforming other cities. This implies well-balanced infrastructure, innovation, services and governance quality, consistent with Almaty's role as Kazakhstan's economic hub. Shymkent, Aktobe, Karaganda, Taraz, Oral, Oskemen, Pavlodar, Taldykorgan, and Turkestan (CSI 45–59.99) demonstrated moderate sustainability but unremarkable performance. This implies these cities have a stable infrastructure base and effective urban management, however, there is room for growth through boosting innovation ecosystems. Aktau, Petropavl, Semey, Kostanay, Kokshetau, Atyrau, and Kyzylorda (CSI < 45) demonstrated lower CSI scores indicating systemic issues. This implies economic stagnation and urban planning deficits. These lagging cities need actionable but not siloed approaches and roadmaps in favour of systemic change. The resulting CSI clusters reflect the spatial characteristics of the Kazakhstani urban network in terms of sustainability performance, and serve as an indicator to rank Kazakhstani cities and track changes in the rankings, providing useful information for policymakers and scholars.
summary: A composite SDG index across Kazakhstani cities places Almaty far ahead, groups most regional centers as middling, and highlights weaker performers where infrastructure, innovation, and services lag.

title: Business students' perceptions of labour market soft skills expectations and characteristics in light of Hofstede's cultural dimensions
authors: Tímea Juhász; Tamás Gáspár; Agneš Slavić; Maja Strugar Jelača; Alena Čarvašová; Petr Řehoř; Wioleta Gałat; Norbert Laurisz; Aidana Kusmangazynova
keywords: soft skill; Hofstede dimensions; labour market placement; skill development; university students; future expectations
abstract: Soft skills have gained significant attention in the domains of business and education. The past few decades have witnessed dynamic technological advancements, as well as serious climate, economic and social crises, which have collectively challenged the existing global system, human lifestyles and mindsets. It is no coincidence that soft skills have simultaneously become a key focus area for employers. Now, students seeking jobs after completing their degree courses are expected to possess these skills. This paper presents the results of a questionnaire survey of business students from five countries. It aims to explore how students evaluate their own soft skills in light of labour market expectations. The survey analyses this matter from the perspective of Hofstede's cultural typology based on the students' responses. The analysis uses univariate and multivariate statistical methods, employing SPSS version 28. The results demonstrate that countries differ in their perceptions of the research question based on their individual–collectivist characteristics and their power distance index. However, this study exhibits no clear evidence of a positive relationship between students' perceptions of their employers' expectations of soft skills and Hofstede's cultural dimensions.
summary: Business students across five countries diverge in how they judge their own soft skills against employer expectations, but the differences map only weakly onto Hofstede's cultural dimensions.

title: Unveiling indirect greenhouse gas emissions: an environmentally extended input–output analysis of the carbon footprint in the Visegrad countries
authors: Mária Csutora; Imre Dobos; Zsófia Vetőné Mózner
keywords: carbon footprint; Visegrad countries; indirect emissions; environmentally extended input–output model; climate policy
abstract: In a globalised world economy, direct emissions account for an increasingly smaller proportion of the total greenhouse gas emissions of countries. Thus, greenhouse gas emissions embodied in traded goods must also be calculated to identify the drivers of total greenhouse gas emissions. This study presents an environmentally extended input–output (EEIO) analysis of the embodied greenhouse gas emissions in the Visegrad countries (V4) – the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia – from 2015 to 2023. Grounded in Leontief's input–output model, the EEIO model enables the emissions to be allocated to final demand categories, such as household consumption, government spending, gross capital formation, and exports. This approach reveals the full carbon footprint of economic activities, including upstream and downstream interdependencies. The cross-country analysis includes the input–output tables of Eurostat and emissions data of 63 economic sectors. Across all V4 countries, embodied greenhouse gas emissions are, on average, more than three times higher than direct emissions. Sectoral analysis reveals that industries such as motor vehicles and electrical equipment exhibit high embodied emissions despite having relatively low direct emissions. Furthermore, the drivers of greenhouse gas emissions in the V4 countries are revealed by decomposing the final demand categories. Results indicate that household consumption primarily drives Poland's emissions, whereas exports account for nearly half of Hungary and Slovakia's embodied emissions because of their greater integration in global value chains. These differences reflect structural economic variations and differing energy profiles across the V4 countries. The study underscores the importance of EEIO analysis in identifying high-impact sectors and informing targeted mitigation strategies. It argues for the inclusion of embodied emissions into national climate policies to help the European Union (EU) achieve its decarbonisation goals. This research contributes to the discourse on carbon responsibility, trade-related emission transfers, and policy effectiveness in the EU.
summary: In the Visegrad countries, embodied greenhouse-gas emissions run more than triple direct emissions, with household consumption dominating Poland's footprint and exports driving Hungary's and Slovakia's.

title: Primary, secondary, and tertiary economic activities and state revenue
authors: Luis Miguel Cruz-Lázaro; Humberto Banda-Ortiz; Omar Bautista-Hernández
keywords: local public spending; economic growth; industrial sectors
abstract: This study examines the impact of federal contributions, federal revenue, and state revenue on economic sectors in Mexico. We construct six data panels using quarterly state economic activity (ITAEE) indices for primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors as dependent variables, and state revenue, federal revenue, and federal contributions as independent variables. The results reveal that federal contributions, federal revenue and state revenue do not have a statistically significant impact on primary, secondary, and tertiary industrial sectors' ITAEE (tax expenditure) in the Mexican states. The findings demonstrate that the revenue received by the Mexican states does not have a statistically significant impact on primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors' growth. This does not imply that the Mexican states do not spend revenue, but that this spending does not have a statistically significant impact. One limitation of this research is that the sample does not include all of the 32 states in Mexico.
summary: Panel estimates find that federal transfers and state revenue have no statistically significant effect on the growth of primary, secondary, or tertiary sectors across Mexican states.

title: Prosumer behaviour in online communities: national and regional features in Hungary
authors: Gyula Zilahy; Noémi Csigéné Nagypál; Ágnes Zsóka
keywords: online community; extrinsic and intrinsic motivation; prosumption; sustainable development; regional differences
abstract: Online communities have transformed patterns of communication and now constitute an important part of the everyday life of many individuals. Such communities enable individuals to produce and consume information at the same time, becoming prosumers, which has potential implications for sustainable lifestyles and sufficiency-oriented consumer behaviour. The motivations and behaviours of online community members have received widespread scholarly attention internationally, however, there is limited evidence from Hungary and little understanding of the ways that motivations relate to sustainability-oriented impacts at the regional level. This study explores the characteristics, motivations, and perceived impacts of participation in online communities in Hungary, with attention paid to regional variation. Building on established typologies of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and on the concept of peer-to-peer prosumption, a two-stage quantitative survey was conducted in 2022–2023. A nationally representative sample of 2,511 respondents reported on general prosumption activities, and a subsample of 540 regular online community members completed a detailed questionnaire on their activities, their motivations, and the perceived behavioural impacts. A factor analysis of 13 motivational variables identified three underlying dimensions: (1) getting useful ideas (e.g., time- and cost-savings and quality-of-life improvements), (2) recognition and contribution (status, belonging, and usefulness), and (3) entertainment and pleasure (enjoyment, relaxation). The first two dimensions combined intrinsic and extrinsic drivers, confirming recent findings that these motives often operate together. Cluster analysis of these factors yielded four participant types: pleasure-driven (15.2%), motivated by enjoyment; uninterested (15.0%), having low scores across all factors; prosumption-driven (46.3%), motivated by contribution, recognition, and belonging; and utilitarian (23.5%), focused on practical benefits. Engagement intensity and activity diversity did not vary significantly by region, but cluster membership did: Eastern Hungarian respondents were more often pleasure- or prosumption-driven, and Central and Western Hungarian respondents were more frequently utilitarian or uninterested. Perceived impacts on prosocial and pro-environmental behaviour differed by motivation type. Pleasure-driven members showed the strongest positive changes, including increased openness to others, environmental awareness, and sense of societal usefulness. Prosumption-driven members had the highest awareness of their producer-consumer role and exhibited strong intention to remain active. Utilitarian members valued the information that they received, but they showed a lower willingness to contribute, whereas uninterested members perceived little change. Eastern Hungarian participants had greater environmental awareness and more conscious information consumption; they were more motivated by positive feedback than those from other regions. These results confirm that the motivation for participation in online communities is multifaceted and linked to behavioural outcomes, with intrinsic drivers that are strongly associated with sustainable and prosocial impacts. They extend the literature by showing the coexistence of intrinsic and extrinsic motives, identifying pragmatic utilitarian prosumers, and highlighting subnational variation in culture.
summary: A survey of Hungarian online-community members identifies three motivational dimensions—useful ideas, recognition, and enjoyment—shaping prosumer behavior with regional variation in sustainability-related impacts.

title: Assessing EU member states' circular economy transition
authors: Ahmad Alaraj; Imre Dobos; Mariann Szabó
keywords: EU CE monitoring framework; environmental pressure indicators; PCA; hierarchical clustering; circular indicators
abstract: This study explores the European Union's (EU) transition to a circular economy (CE) using macro-level indicators from the year 2020. Motivated by the urgency to reverse resource depletion, waste generation and environmental deterioration resulting from the linear 'take-make-dispose' model, the EU has embraced the CE in action plans since 2015 with the objective of advancing sustainability, resource efficiency and climate neutrality. However, the actual environmental and socio-economic benefits and performance variations across EU member states remain points of investigation. Using Eurostat data from 2020 for 27 EU countries, we employ principal component analysis (PCA) and cluster analysis to eight key CE indicators covering environmental impact, resource efficiency and socio-economic factors. Three statistically significant clusters of EU member states are identified by the CE performance profile analysis. In 2020, differences in environmental impact intensity – most notably greenhouse gas emissions and municipal waste generation – are the key drivers separating these clusters ahead of resource efficiency effects or labour metrics. The results demonstrate that although the EU established a macro-level tracking framework, the CE transition did not equally decrease environmentally relevant pressure throughout the EU in 2020. Furthermore, the socioeconomic gains of employment in the CE did not positively correlate with the use of circular materials. By pairing PCA-derived factors with hierarchical clustering and one-way of analysis of variance and explicitly examining the influence of material import dependency and CE employment, this EU27 (2020) analysis addresses a key gap in macroassessments by verifying whether circularity proxies align with environmental pressure indicators.
summary: PCA and clustering of 2020 circular-economy indicators split the EU-27 into three groups differentiated mainly by emissions and waste intensity rather than by resource efficiency or circular-sector employment.

title: Local economic resilience in urban–rural context: the case of districts in Turkey
authors: Berfin Karabakan Gökhan; Hasan Engin Duran
keywords: economic resilience; economic crises; Covid-19; urban–rural context; spatial regressions
abstract: Regional economic resilience (RER) is a specific term to define the set of abilities that a region can resist disruptions, display a prompt rebound and re-configure its structure to adapt to a (new) superior long-term equilibrium. Many empirical studies have quantified the degree of resilience of regions, and the underlying determinants. From another perspective, the urban–rural distinction is a pivotal phenomenon in spatial studies. It is noteworthy that the differences between urban and rural areas have not yet been sufficiently examined in a resilience context, which may include far different dynamics and policy implications. The aim of this study is to explore the differential resilience behaviours and determinants across urban, rural, and mixed areas. The dataset covers 973 districts of Turkey and the 2018–2023 period that includes both the currency crisis (in 2018) and the Covid-19 pandemic (2020-onwards). Having applied a wide range of empirical methods (spatial and non-spatial regressions), we reach two main conclusions. First, semi-urban districts are observed to be the most resilient type whereas the mega-urban districts are observed to be the most fragile. Urban and rural areas exhibit similar behaviour. Second, the resilience drivers are group specific rather than common. At the same time industrial diversity and structure are crucial for rural and semi-urban areas. Demographic structure and human capital are significant for urban districts, and trade openness is critical for the mega-urban areas. Therefore, each urbanization group has different dynamics that require local and place specific policies.
summary: Across 973 Turkish districts, semi-urban areas prove most economically resilient and mega-urban areas most fragile, with the drivers of resilience differing markedly between rural, urban, and metropolitan groups.

journal: The Canadian Journal of Regional Science
title: Effet des transferts de l'État sur le développement local (Bénin)
authors: Arnaud Modeste Dèdèhouanou; Bernard Hounmenou; Louis Tchonkloe
keywords: Municipal investment; Decentralization; own resources; State transfers; health; Education
abstract: In Benin, decentralization is implemented through the transfer of financial resources from the central government to local governments (LGs). However, the relationship between these transfers and local development remains underexplored in the empirical literature. This study seeks to fill this gap by examining the effect of central government transfers on local development in Beninese local governments. It highlights the differentiated impact of both conditional and unconditional transfers on local development. Methodologically, the study relies on an econometric panel data analysis covering 77 local governments over the period 2003–2022, using the Fully Modified Ordinary Least Squares (FMOLS) estimation technique. The empirical results show that health-sector conditional transfers (FADeC earmarked for health) are positively associated with local development. In contrast, other transfers, particularly those earmarked for education (FADeC earmarked for education), are negatively correlated with local development. These findings reveal several important policy implications for the design and implementation of decentralization and local development policies in Benin, particularly with regard to the sectoral targeting and efficiency of resource allocation to local governments.
summary: Panel evidence from 77 Beninese local governments shows conditional health-sector transfers boost local development, whereas earmarked education transfers are negatively associated with it.

journal: The Canadian Journal of Regional Science
title: Le domaine culturel face aux crises financières, sanitaire et climatique en France et au Québec
authors: Fabrice Thuriot
keywords: culture; crises; Covid; financement; transition écologique
abstract: The cultural sector has been affected by several crises in recent years and has been hit again recently: financial crises (2007-2008, 2014-2015, 2020, 2024–2025 in part), the COVID-19 health crisis (2020–22), and climate crises (for several years with preventive measures, but only recently with corrective measures). Like other sectors, it is affected nationally and regionally, but with particular severity due to its fragile and optional nature. It is often considered first in budgetary choices, as well as nonessential and even dangerous in the fight against the pandemic due to its activities requiring people to be outside their homes and negatively impacting the climate in ecological terms (travel, energy, materials, etc.). The aim of this contribution is to clarify the logic behind the cultural sector's responses to these crises in France and Quebec.
summary: The cultural sector in France and Quebec responded to successive financial, health, and climate crises with distinctive but similarly fragile logics reflecting its treatment as budget-optional and pandemic-risky.

journal: The Canadian Journal of Regional Science
title: Gouvernance Partenariale Entre État, Compagnie Minière et Communautés Locales en Guinée: Systémique des Politiques Publiques dans la Région Bauxitique de Boké
authors: Idiatou Bah; Mario Carrier
keywords: Partnership governance; systemic public policy approach; Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR); mining; Guinea-Boké
abstract: Using Vincent Lemieux's (2009) systemic public policy model combined with the concept of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), this article seeks to understand the reasons and factors explaining the difficulties faced by the Compagnie de Bauxite de Guinée (CBG) in developing a partnership-based governance system capable of generating sustainable local benefits in Boké. Based on a qualitative and empirical approach, the study highlights the evolution of the multinational company's partnership governance in response to a changing and evolving environment. It also reveals the ambiguity of CBG's behavior toward emerging public policies related to corporate social responsibility and local content requirements. Finally, the article emphasizes the need to assess the company's capacity to adapt to this evolving environment through a reassessment of its activities, its collaboration with stakeholders, and the sustainability of its development objectives. Situated within the field of public policy in regional and development studies, the article ultimately sheds light on the dynamics of State–company–community relations within Guinea's bauxite sector in the context of extractive industry reforms aimed at promoting sustainable development.
summary: Applying Lemieux's public-policy model and a CSR lens to Guinea's Boké bauxite region shows how the mining company's partnership governance struggles to adapt to emerging local-content and CSR rules.

journal: The Canadian Journal of Regional Science
title: La précarité énergétique au Québec : une problématique à reconnaître pour une transition juste et équitable
authors: Sophie Kutuka; Mylène Riva; Laurianne Debanné; Sébastien Breau; Caroline Adam; Runa R. Das
keywords: energy poverty; housing; vulnerability; well-being; Québec
abstract: In Québec, despite having some of the lowest electricity rates in North America, many households experience energy poverty, meaning they struggle to afford or access the residential energy services required to meet their needs. To enhance understanding of energy poverty and to inform a just and equitable energy and climate transition, this study pursues three objectives: (1) to quantify the extent of energy poverty in Québec; (2) to identify factors associated with energy poverty; and (3) to examine its association with health and well-being among the adult Québec population. Pooled and weighted data from the 2018 and 2021 cycles of the Canadian Housing Survey were analyzed. Depending on the measurement approach, between 9% and 16% of Québec households experience energy poverty. Energy poverty is more prevalent among renters, older adults, individuals living alone, those with lower income and education levels, and those residing in housing requiring major repairs. Results from regression models adjusted for potential confounders indicate that energy poverty is significantly associated with poorer general and mental health, and with lower life satisfaction. Addressing the energy needs of households whose well-being is compromised by inadequate access to energy services is essential to support the development and implementation of policies and programs that effectively reach those most in need.
summary: Despite Quebec's cheap electricity, 9–16% of households face energy poverty—concentrated among renters, older, poorer, and single-person households—and it is linked to poorer physical and mental health.

journal: The Canadian Journal of Regional Science
title: Examining the Relationship Between Rental Housing Assistance Type and Characteristics of Neighbourhood Satisfaction in Canada
authors: Laurence Simard; Xavier Leloup; Catherine Leviten-Reid; Kristen Desjarlais-deKlerk; Nazeem Muhajarine; Pablo Mendez
keywords: Canadian housing policies; Canada Housing Survey; rental housing types; social and community housing; neighbourhood quality
abstract: This paper analyzes the Canada Housing Survey (CHS) first-wave data (2018) to examine the relationship between various aspects of neighbourhood satisfaction and rental housing type (e.g., government, co-operative, not-for-profit [NFP], and private) inherited from past Canadian housing policies. Using partial proportional odds models, we consider feeling of safety, resource accessibility, and community/neighbourhood satisfaction. This approach allows for nuanced interpretations beyond purely objective measures, encompassing factors like service adequacy, personal characteristics, and neighbourhood issues. CHS data reveal lower neighbourhood satisfaction among renters, with public housing showing lower satisfaction and lower feelings of safety compared to other housing types. Co-operative and NFP housing appear to offer less favourable options for tenants occupying a subsidized unit in terms of access to services responding to their needs. Finally, a predominance of personal characteristics appeared in the modelling, which we believe demonstrates persistent inequality in Canada linked with urban design and housing access for historically marginalized groups.
summary: Canadian renters report lower neighborhood satisfaction than owners, with public-housing tenants feeling least safe and cooperative or nonprofit tenants reporting weaker access to services they need.

title: Invisible chains of conflict: economy-wide spillovers from an agricultural shock in Ukraine – mixed input–output evidence
authors: Jérôme Verny; Youssef Bouazizi; Ouail Oulmakki; Luc Savard
abstract: This article quantifies how a conflict-related agricultural supply shock propagates through Ukraine's economy. Instead of the conventional demand-driven Leontief model, we use a mixed input – output model that introduces the shock directly as a capacity constraint in agriculture. In our central scenario, a 25% reduction in the agricultural workforce leads to a 4.6% decline in GDP, and impacts spread rapidly beyond farming. Sectors highly dependent on agricultural inputs are hit hardest, with chemicals (−30%) and motor vehicles (−28.8%) showing the largest losses, while public services remain comparatively stable. Sensitivity and robustness checks indicate near proportional effects, consistent with fixed-coefficient technologies and short-run rigidities. The results reveal a hierarchy of vulnerabilities and provide policy-relevant benchmarks to help secure critical supply chains and strengthen economic resilience against cascading shocks.
summary: A mixed input–output model finds that a 25% drop in Ukraine's farm workforce would cut GDP by 4.6%, hitting agriculture-dependent sectors like chemicals and motor vehicles hardest.

title: Supply-chain propagation of local economic shocks: an interregional general equilibrium analysis of the ISIS conflict in Iraq
authors: Inácio F. Araújo; Kieran P. Donaghy; Eduardo A. Haddad; Geoffrey J.D. Hewings
abstract: Extreme events, particularly human-induced conflicts, pose complex challenges for measuring higher-order effects and their geographical propagation through supply chains. This study develops an interregional computable general equilibrium model to evaluate conflict-related disruptions, integrating input–output linkages and resilience modeling to capture higher-order effects across regions and sectors. We apply the model to the ISIS conflict in Iraq (2014–2017), using an interregional input–output table for 18 Iraqi governorates. The analysis estimates GDP and gross regional product losses, identifies vulnerable sectors, and quantifies regional spillovers from conflict-induced shocks in capital stock, labor markets, and household income. The results reveal significant economic losses in directly affected governorates, offset by modest gains in indirectly affected regions due to spatial substitution in supply chains. This methodology provides a practical tool for post-conflict economic assessment, adaptable to other extreme events, such as natural disasters or climate-related shocks, and supports policymakers in prioritizing recovery and resilience strategies.
summary: An interregional CGE model of the 2014–2017 ISIS conflict shows large GDP losses in occupied Iraqi governorates partly offset by gains elsewhere as supply chains substitute across regions.

title: Generalized Cross Entropy estimators and the estimation of interregional trade flows
authors: Esteban Fernández Vázquez; Bartlomiej Rokicki
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of estimating interregional trade flows, a crucial concern for subnational input–output and Computable General Equilibrium models. A commonly used solution is the gravity approach; however, entropy maximization can serve the same purpose. We examine two distinct entropy specifications: the data-constrained Generalized Cross Entropy (GCE) estimator and the moment-constrained GCE estimator. The performance of each estimator is evaluated through numerical simulations. Our results show that entropy-based estimators yield more accurate results than the gravity model, once the possibility of potential errors in row or column totals is taken into account. The larger the potential error and the higher the number of regions, the greater the difference in accuracy between the gravity model and GCE estimators. Additionally, we find that the moment-constrained GCE estimator appears to be more accurate than the data-constrained GCE estimator under specific conditions.
summary: In simulations, generalized cross-entropy estimators recover interregional trade flows more accurately than gravity models, especially when regional row or column totals contain errors.

title: The impact of market concentration and economies of scale on production networks: a new nonlinear input–output framework
authors: Michel Eduardo Betancourt-Gómez
abstract: The traditional Leontief input–output model analyzes an economy's productive structure under the assumption of perfect competition. However, this limits its ability to capture the impact of market concentration and economies of scale in production networks. This article proposes a new methodological framework that explicitly incorporates these elements via a nonlinear reformulation of the model. The strategy has two stages: first, a theoretical reformulation that incorporates concentration and scale indicators, and second, econometric estimation of those parameters. The methodology is applied to Mexico using the most recent available input–output table. The results suggest that concentrated industries significantly influence intersectoral relationships. This proposed method opens a new line of research with promising potential for investigating how market concentration shapes the demand for intermediate inputs and influences economic development.
summary: Reformulating Leontief's input–output model to embed market-concentration and scale parameters and estimating them for Mexico shows concentrated industries substantially reshape intermediate demand across sectors.

title: Modelling the impact of the clean environment cess on India: an environmentally-extended input–output approach
authors: Rajat Verma; Ganesh Sivamani
abstract: The Clean Environment Cess (CEC) was a tax levied in India on the total sales of all types of coal to reduce emissions and tackle climate change. This paper seeks to simulate the impact of this cess on greenhouse gas emissions and GDP, using an environmentally extended input–output table. The Rs 180/tonne ($2.7) increase to the actual tax rate of CEC in 2016 resulted in a 0.09% reduction in GDP, a 0.90% reduction in emissions from burning coal and petroleum products, and a 0.80% reduction in the emissions intensity. According to our estimates, the coal electricity sector would be most affected by the cess, with a 1.5% reduction in Gross Value Added (GVA). A study found that the cess leads to a 0.47–1.2% reduction in the GVAs of the coal and lignite, cement, crude petroleum, and iron and steel sectors, with emissions reducing across sectors in the same order.
summary: Simulating India's 2016 Rs 180/tonne Clean Environment Cess suggests a small GDP loss alongside meaningful cuts to coal- and petroleum-related emissions, concentrated in the coal-electricity, cement, and iron and steel sectors.

title: Assessing the development impacts of bio-innovations: the case of genetically modified maize and cassava in Tanzania
authors: Rui Benfica; Patricia Zambrano; Judy Chambers; Jose Falck-Zepeda
abstract: Tanzania's agriculture is characterized by low productivity due to unpredictable rainfall and the prevalence of pests and diseases. Genetically modified (GM) maize offering protection against drought and insects are being developed. Likewise, GM varieties resistant to cassava brown streak disease were developed. Building on prior crop-based analyses, we use the Rural Investment and Policy Analysis (RIAPA) CGE model to assess the impacts of the adoption of those GM crops. GM maize and cassava have positive effects on the economy, the Agri-Food System (AFS), and poverty. Given its stronger linkages in the AFS, the effects of the GM maize are stronger, especially in higher adoption and high yield scenarios. Likewise, the effects on the poorest and rural households are greater. The high variation across scenarios, and the significant effect of the high adoption/high yield scenarios, suggests a high return to investments and policies that realize these adoption rates and yield potential.
summary: CGE simulations for Tanzania indicate that adopting drought- and disease-resistant GM maize and cassava would raise incomes and cut poverty, with maize delivering the larger effects because of its stronger agri-food-system linkages.

title: Why do trade statistics and national accounts' trade values differ? The role of misclassification of products
authors: Juan M. Valderas-Jaramillo; José M. Rueda-Cantuche; Nadim Ahmad
abstract: International trade statistics rarely align with the corresponding trade values in national accounts due to trade asymmetries, the national accounts' ownership principle (compared to the cross-border principle applied in trade statistics), international transport and insurance costs, and the possible misclassification of products, among other factors. This paper presents a novel method to resolve discrepancies related to the potential product misclassification. Unlike automatic balancing processes, this approach is designed to be transparent, allowing users to understand how national data can be adjusted to fit within globally balanced trade datasets and inter-country input–output tables. It also aims to improve consistency across various international initiatives such as those of Eurostat (FIGARO), OECD, UN-ECLAC and ADB, among others. The proposed method enables users to develop balanced international trade datasets, thereby substantially reducing discrepancies in national accounts' trade values arising from product misclassification.
summary: The paper proposes a transparent method for reconciling international trade statistics with national-accounts trade values by explicitly correcting product misclassification instead of relying on opaque automatic balancing.

title: Second-hand gentrification: Theory and evidence from high-speed rail extensions
authors: Gabriel Loumeau; Antonio Russo
keywords: Gentrification; High-speed rail; Housing market; Intercity travel
abstract: Does gentrification spread along intercity transport connections? We study the 2017 French high-speed rail (HSR) extensions from Paris to Bordeaux and Rennes. We build a model where HSR reduces the cost of accessing a primary city from a secondary one, enabling skilled workers to enjoy the primary city's labor market while living in the more affordable secondary city. This induces migration from the primary to the secondary city, raising housing prices there. Empirically, the HSR connection raised housing prices in Bordeaux and Rennes by 12%, central-neighborhood median income by 2%, and within-neighborhood inequality by 2%. Near Montparnasse, the connecting Paris terminal, prices fell 4% relative to the rest of Paris.
summary: French high-speed rail extensions raised housing prices ~12% and incomes in secondary cities while depressing prices near the Paris terminal, spreading gentrification along intercity rail.

title: Can rapid rental assistance avert evictions? Evidence from administrative delays
authors: Mason Alexander; Matthew Freedman; Stephanie Casey Pierce
keywords: Rental assistance; Evictions; Administrative burden; Compliance costs
abstract: Many communities in the U.S. have programs that make financial assistance available to families with low incomes who are struggling to pay rent. In this paper, we examine the average and distributional impacts of reducing wait times for emergency housing assistance on evictions. Taking advantage of administrative data from Franklin County, Ohio and exploiting exogenous changes in application processing times in two complementary empirical approaches, we find that each additional week of delay in receiving assistance increases the probability of an eviction filing within 12 months by 19–29%. A substantial share of the additional filings result in judgments against tenants. Our results have important implications for the design and implementation of emergency rental assistance programs. More broadly, our findings speak to the downstream impacts of passive compliance costs in social safety net programs.
summary: Each additional week of delay in receiving emergency rental assistance raises the probability of an eviction filing within 12 months by 19-29%.

title: Gender, land rights and climate change adaptation in Ghana: Implications for land tenure, agriculture and rural development
authors: Peter Asare-Nuamah; David Anaafo; Tina Beuchelt
keywords: Gender inequality; Land rights; Tenure security; Adaptation; Smallholder agriculture
abstract: Land rights, important dimensions of land tenure, are crucial for smallholder farmers' land tenure security and climate change adaptation. However, there are knowledge gaps on the nexus between land rights and climate adaptation in Ghana, particularly from a gendered perspective. This study draws on land right frameworks to explore the nexus between gender, land rights and climate change adaptation among men and women smallholder farmers in rural Ghana. Data were collected through a randomized survey administered to 510 smallholder farmers from four purposively selected communities in the Adansi Asokwa District, and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. The results showed that compared to women, more men own more farmlands (averagely 6.8 vs. 5.4 acres for women), have formal land title deeds, and exercise more land rights, particularly exclusion and alienation rights, enhancing their tenure security. Besides frequency of pest invasion, there is no significant differences in men's and women's climate change perceptions and experiences. Farmers used multiple climate adaptation strategies, including planting improved crop varieties, changing planting season, climate information services and agrochemical application. We found a significant difference between men's and women's adoption of crop diversification, crop-livestock integration and seed storage. Unlike men's adaptation strategies, those of women are influenced by the number of rights they exercise and farmland size. Also, perceptions about the raining season and temperature intensity as well as marital status, locality, years of farming experience, access to non-farm livelihood activities and credit significantly influence farmers' climate change adaptation. Gender differentiated policies and incentives for farmers are needed to enhance tenure security and climate change adaptation.
summary: In rural Ghana men hold more land and stronger land rights than women, and women's climate-adaptation choices depend on the rights they exercise and farm size, calling for gender-differentiated policy.

title: Payment for environmental services in Brazil: A systematic scoping review of policy design, governance, and territorial patterns
authors: Manoel Martins da Costa Junior; Vanessa Batista Schramm; Fernando Schramm
keywords: Payment for environmental services; Ecosystem services; Environmental governance; Policy evaluation; Brazil
abstract: Brazil established its National Policy of Payment for Environmental Services (PES) to promote maintenance, recovery, and enhancement of ecosystems. Yet the diversity, spatial distribution, and effectiveness of existing initiatives remain poorly understood. This study provides the first nationwide synthesis of all PES programs implemented in Brazil since 2000, based on a systematic scoping review of 80 peer-reviewed papers documenting 138 distinct programs. We apply an analytical framework with 11 dimensions to classify and compare programs by ecosystem type, service category, funding source, objectives, and governance mechanisms. Results show initiatives concentrate in the Atlantic Forest (49.3%) and Cerrado (23.2%) biomes, largely targeting regulation services (93.2%) via forest conservation (65.2%) and restoration (61.6%) actions. Watershed (73.9%) and Forest & Carbon (14.8%) programs predominate; 59.4% of initiatives are in Southeast and 17.4% in North. Most programs rely on public funding (94%), while private and market-based mechanisms remain rare. Despite frequent social objectives (65%) and non-monetary benefits (35%), fiscal dependence and regional imbalance constrain scalability and policy sustainability. By comparing Brazil's experience with international trends in PES governance, we identify structural challenges to design more adaptive, inclusive, and financially diversified mechanisms that strengthen ecosystem protection and social equity across biomes.
summary: A first nationwide review finds Brazil's payment-for-environmental-services programs concentrated in the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado and heavily reliant on public funds, leaving them regionally imbalanced and fiscally fragile.

title: Informal coastal reclamation driven by monitoring and enforcement gaps: from plans to practice in a protected lagoon
authors: Patryk Sitkiewicz; Bartosz Płóciennik; Monika Michałek; Anastazja Mastylak; Shasha Liu; Łukasz Janowski; Damian Moskalewicz; Radosław Opioła
keywords: Informal coastal reclamation; Tourism-driven campground expansion; Regulatory loopholes; Enforcement gaps; Governance paradox; Coastal zone management; Protected lagoon systems
abstract: Coastal zones increasingly face conflicts as societal demands, economic development, including tourism, and nature conservation compete for limited coastal space. Although lagoon coasts are ecologically valuable and morphologically stable, these remain especially vulnerable to incremental, tourism-driven land-use changes. Fragmented spatial monitoring allows many of these small-scale alterations to escape detection, undermining enforcement and the implementation of coastal plans.
summary: Fragmented spatial monitoring lets incremental, tourism-driven coastal reclamation escape detection and enforcement in a protected lagoon, exposing a coastal-governance gap.

title: Human climate niche, habitability range, and economic growth
authors: Jean-François Gajewski; Paul-Oliver Klein; Fatima Ezzahrae Tahri
keywords: Climate Change; Global Warming; Population; Temperature; Humidity
abstract: This study develops a contemporaneous measure of the human habitability of geographic areas, the Habitability Range that builds upon the work of Xu et al. (2020) on pretechnological human density in a temperature-precipitation climatic space. Using this measure with climatic data from 1901 to 2022, we document a 32.98% (−8.40 pp) global decline in human habitability over the past century. Using economic data from 181 countries (1950–2022), we find that a one standard deviation loss in habitability reduced GDP per capita by 4.24% at country level and by 2.46% at subnational level. While high Total Factor Productivity (TFP) reduces dependence on the climate niche, declines in habitability can lower TFP, thereby limiting adaptation capacities.
summary: Global human habitability fell about 33% over the past century, and habitability losses significantly reduced GDP per capita, with high productivity only partly buffering the effect.

title: Farmers' preferences and attitudes in conversion to organic farming: A lab-in-the-field experiment
authors: Tuan Nguyen-Anh; Phu Nguyen-Van; Nguyen To-The
keywords: Risk; Ambiguity; Time preference; Social value orientation; Organic farming; Lab-in-the-field
abstract: Despite rising organic food consumption, the transition to organic farming lags, particularly in developing countries, where only 2% of agricultural land was organic in 2022. To address this, we investigate how farmers' elicited preferences (risk tolerance, ambiguity tolerance, and time preferences), social factors, and environmental attitudes shape their intention to convert land to organic farming. Using a lab-in-the-field experiment with 311 Vietnamese farmers, we apply a fractional regression model to analyze the intended percentage of land conversion. Results show that higher risk tolerance, higher ambiguity tolerance, future bias, pro-social preferences, perceived behavioral control, and social norms are positively associated with conversion intent, while environmental attitude lacks statistical significance. The revised robustness analysis shows that these patterns are stable when we account for outcome spikes and focal-point responses.
summary: Among Vietnamese farmers, risk and ambiguity tolerance, pro-social preferences and social norms raise intended organic-conversion, whereas environmental attitude has no significant effect.

title: Willingness to pay for birdsong
authors: Anthony Higney; Charlotte Gerling; Claire Buchan; Simon Butler; Liam Crowther; Melissa Marselle; Eleanor Ratcliffe; Konrad Uebel; Nick Hanley
keywords: Birdsong; Non-market valuation; Discrete choice experiments; Willingness to Pay (WTP); Ecosystem services; Eco-acoustics
abstract: We present the first estimate of the causal effect of auditory sensation on willingness to pay and the first estimate of the marginal value of bird song, using constructed soundscapes. We compare willingness to pay values for increases in bird wildlife habitat quality and quantity between samples where respondents are played recordings of soundscapes compared to respondents who do not get to listen to these simulated soundscapes. Willingness to pay for habitat quality enhancements were found to be significantly larger in the treated "with soundscapes" sample, mainly due to treatment reducing cost sensitivity. Methodologically, this paper reports on the use of simulated soundscapes in choice experiments as a means of increasing the information respondents have before making their choices.
summary: Playing simulated birdsong soundscapes in a choice experiment significantly raises willingness to pay for bird-habitat improvements, mainly by lowering cost sensitivity.

title: From utopian impulse to urban engagement: The role of doughnut economics in shaping residents' participation in smart cities
authors: Frédéric Basso; Norbert Lebrument; Corinne Rochette
keywords: Transformative Utopian Impulse; Doughnut Economics; Smart Cities; Citizenship Participation
abstract: Smart cities are often framed through techno-utopian narratives, yet their capacity to support sustainable transitions depends on residents' engagement. This article examines how the transformative utopian impulse and support for the principles of Doughnut Economics shape residents' intention to participate in smart city projects. Drawing on a survey of 645 residents in five French cities (Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Lille and Toulouse), we estimate a model using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) combined with Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) to distinguish sufficient from necessary causal relations. PLS-SEM results show that the transformative utopian impulse significantly influences participatory intention, both directly and indirectly through support for Doughnut Economics principles. NCA complements these findings by revealing that both constructs operate as necessary conditions for high levels of participatory intention, with support for Doughnut Economics emerging as the most critical precondition for high levels of participatory intention: while it contributes relatively little as a direct average driver of participation, its absence effectively prevents residents from reaching the highest levels of engagement. This "axiological" threshold effect indicates that commitment to post-growth principles shifts from secondary to indispensable as participation intensifies. The study advances urban governance research by moving beyond the opposition between technology-centric smart city agendas and post-growth urbanism: Doughnut Economics functions as an intermediary normative framework translating utopian aspirations into more concrete forms of urban engagement. For practitioners, the results highlight that participatory mechanisms must be coupled with coherent value frameworks if smart city programmes are to mobilise residents for transformative and sustainability-oriented projects.
summary: A survey of French city residents finds that a transformative utopian impulse and support for Doughnut Economics principles are necessary drivers of high participation in smart-city projects.

title: How justice shapes local support for grassland conservation program: A mixed-methods research
authors: Ruxin Zhang; Zhuohui Ye
keywords: Justice; Conservation outcomes; Mixed-methods; Grassland; Chinese herders
abstract: Justice is widely theorized as foundational to conservation success, yet rigorous empirical evidence remains limited. This study addresses this gap by investigating the influence of justice on herders' support for China's Grassland Ecosystem Conservation Program (GECP). Employing a sequential mixed-methods design, we first conducted in-depth interviews to develop context-specific indicators of distributive, procedural, and recognition justice. We then applied a Double-Hurdle Model to survey data, complemented by semi-structured interviews, to examine how these justice dimensions shape herders' behavioral compliance—a key observable manifestation of local support. The integrated analysis reveals three main findings. First, all three justice dimensions exert significant positive effects on compliance, yet their relative importance differs markedly: distributive justice has the strongest effect, followed by procedural justice, and then recognition justice. Second, the interactions among these dimensions are consistently negative and significant, indicating that they function as partial substitutes rather than mutually reinforcing complements. Third, the substitution pattern between distributive and recognition justice varies with herders' socio-economic characteristics. These findings place calls to embed justice in conservation on firmer empirical ground and underscore the need for a sequential, context-sensitive approach to justice-enhancing interventions.
summary: Distributive justice most strongly raises Chinese herders' compliance with a grassland conservation program, and the three justice dimensions act as partial substitutes rather than complements.

title: Limited and unintended effects of climate, health, and animal welfare labels
authors: Amelie Griesoph; Thomas Schreiner; Christine Merk; Stefan Hoffmann; Katrin Rehdanz; Ulrich Schmidt
keywords: Labels; Climate change; Health; Animal welfare; Field experiment; Consumer behavior
abstract: Policymakers and practitioners widely introduce food labels to promote more sustainable consumption. However, evidence on their effectiveness in real-world settings remains limited. We analyze transaction data from three large-scale field studies in university canteens, comprising more than 1.7 million individual purchases aggregated to daily dish-level market shares. Using market share attraction models, we examine the association between climate, health, and animal welfare labels and consumer demand. Across specifications, labels are associated with either unintended or statistically nonsignificant changes in market shares. These patterns remain consistent across robustness checks, including specifications incorporating interaction effects and propensity-score weighting to address comparability concerns. Our findings suggest that menu labels, as currently implemented, may not effectively shift consumer choices toward more sustainable options. By providing large-scale field evidence, this study contributes to the literature on informational instruments and highlights the need for context-sensitive label design and research leveraging exogenous variation to establish causal effects.
summary: Across 1.7 million university-canteen purchases, climate, health and animal-welfare menu labels produced only unintended or statistically insignificant shifts in dish choices.

title: The costs of social and environmental degradation in affluent economies
authors: Giulia Slater; Francesco Sarracino
keywords: Subjective well-being; Quality of life; Defensive consumption; Defensive growth; Compensating differentials; Shadow value; Willingness to accept
abstract: Individuals' attempts to defend from the deterioration of common goods, such as natural and social capital, are a source of defensive growth, that is new economic activity driven by private and public consumption in response to collective problems. We use a compensating differential approach to compute the value of social and environmental degradation. To do so, we conduct a regression analysis of life satisfaction on aggregate consumption levels and various social and environmental externalities (which we refer to as "bads"). Our findings indicate that the welfare equivalent consumption to defend against collective problems is substantial. One standard deviation increase in each bad is worth about $21,800 per capita, which corresponds to 65% of the observed yearly consumption per capita in our sample. Ceteris paribus, if bads could be avoided, consumption would be smaller, the economy would grow less, and individuals would be better-off. In so far as part of economic growth is defensive, only a portion of its expansion reflects true progress.
summary: Using life-satisfaction data, defending against social and environmental 'bads' is worth about $21,800 per capita, implying much measured economic growth is merely defensive.

title: Scenario discovery for a just low-carbon transition
authors: Nicola Campigotto; Marco Catola; André Cieplinski; Simone D'Alessandro; Tiziano Distefano; Pietro Guarnieri; Till Heydenreich
keywords: Ecological macroeconomics; Just transition; Inequality; Scenario discovery
abstract: There is currently no consensus among scholars on how to achieve a just low-carbon transition. To address this issue, this paper subjects a macrosimulation model to an extensive sensitivity analysis and then fits random forests to the simulation results to identify policy combinations that can reduce carbon emissions while promoting income equality. Our findings indicate that interventions aimed at supporting low-income groups result in an increase in these groups' energy demand and emissions, and that this negative effect should be offset through a faster deployment of renewable energy sources and measures that redistribute income away from top earners.
summary: Supporting low-income groups raises their energy use and emissions, so a just low-carbon transition also requires faster renewables deployment and redistribution away from top earners.

title: Wealth taxes for an eco-social transition: How different tax designs align with post-growth goals
authors: Thomas Webb; Arthur Apostel; Milena Büchs; Richard Bärnthaler
keywords: Post-growth; Redistribution; Rent-seeking; Sustainable welfare; Wealth inequality; Welfare states; Eco-social policy
abstract: Wealth taxes are frequently proposed within the post-growth policy literature, but evaluations of their alignment with post-growth goals, and empirical estimates of their potential effects, are lacking. We contribute to this literature by examining the extent to which different wealth tax designs can contribute to four goals of a post-growth transition: redistributing wealth; eradicating extreme wealth; curbing rent-seeking; and reducing CO2 emissions. The analysis is based on microsimulation modelling, using household-level data from 18 countries of the 2017 EU Household Finance and Consumption Survey.
