It shows that broad-based net wealth taxes with lower thresholds and higher rates are most effective for maximising revenue, reducing top 10% wealth shares, limiting extreme wealth, and lowering inequality-related CO₂ emissions; more targeted net wealth taxes with higher thresholds and rates maximise progressivity and reduce top 1% wealth concentration; while taxes on financial and investment property wealth tend to be most effective at curbing rent extraction (all else equal). However, we also identify trade-offs and conflicts between different tax designs and goals. As a result, a broader package of policies will be necessary to navigate these conflicts and mitigate the limitations inherent in any single wealth tax design.
summary: Microsimulations across 18 EU countries show broad-based low-threshold net wealth taxes best cut wealth concentration and inequality-related CO2, but no single design meets all post-growth goals.

title: Water justice: Empirical analysis of U.S. patterns and regional heterogeneity
authors: Zoey Reed-Spitzer; Bonnie G. Colby
keywords: Water; Justice; Green space; Disproportionate exposure; Environmental burdens; Water access; Water quality
abstract: Water quality, water access and competition among competing water uses are a concern around the globe. In many areas of the U.S., water availability is constrained by pollution and lack of water delivery and treatment infrastructure. These constraints have disproportionate effects on low-income areas and communities of color. In this article, we analyze differential exposure among racial and ethnic groups to specific environmental burdens linked to how water is used and managed. We examine differential exposure by analyzing data from the U.S Council on Environmental Quality, combined with U.S. census data for 73,225 census tracts covering the entire U.S. We find that Hispanic and Black populations are disproportionately exposed to three of the environmental burdens examined in this study: dust pollution, leaky underground storage tanks and lack of green space. Black and American Indian populations are more likely to be in census tracts with higher proportions of inadequate household water access. We also document substantial regional heterogeneity in these patterns, with disparities among groups varying significantly in magnitude across U.S. regions. Identifying systemic patterns of differential exposure is a first step in motivating and shaping policy measures to mitigate disproportional adverse effects on vulnerable populations.
summary: US Hispanic, Black and American Indian populations face disproportionate exposure to water-related environmental burdens, with disparities varying substantially across regions.

title: The impact of climate on Indian households' living costs
authors: Yuhang Qu; David J. Maddison; Robert J.R. Elliott; Eric Strobl
keywords: Climate; India; Household expenditures; Equivalence scales
abstract: We exploit the geographical variation in climate across India, along with the availability of district-level household expenditure data, to estimate the equilibrium impact of climate on Indian households' living costs. Using a methodology more commonly employed to calculate demographic equivalence scales, we find that households' cost of living decreases by about 0.2% with 100 mm increase in annual precipitation; for every 100 units increases in annual heating degree days and cooling degree days, Indian households would experience an increase by 0.4% and 0.6% in living costs, respectively, and an increase of 1% in annual humidity will raise households' cost of living by 1.3%. Based on these results, we calculate climate equivalence scales for households in major Indian cities.
summary: Hotter and more humid climates raise Indian households' cost of living, allowing the authors to construct climate equivalence scales for major cities.

title: Why would you move to a polluted area? Green compromise in Coastal Sydney and Illawarra
authors: Marta Conde; Isabelle Anguelovski
keywords: Pollution; Environmental justice; Green compromise; Environmental privilege; Cognitive psychology; Green gentrification; Industrial transitions
abstract: In pursuit of greener and more affordable lifestyles, residents from Sydney are increasingly relocating to the scenic Illawarra coastal region. However, this shift is complicated by the area's legacy of soil and air pollution from historical and ongoing industrial activities and coal mines. Drawing on environmental justice and privilege literature, this study integrates insights of cultural and cognitive psychology to examine how residents rationalise their decisions. We conceptualise these dynamics as a green compromise, through which residents exhibit a series of cognitive biases where pollution is made invisible through limited information (availability bias), relativised compared to past experiences (anchoring bias), and normalised or minimised by integrating it into a mining-industrial identity. By adapting to and setting aside pollution, these "environmentally privileged" middle-income residents further reduce the pressure for monitoring and remediation, thereby contributing to the perpetuation of structural -socioeconomic and environmental- injustices. By linking cognitive biases with affordability and environmental risk perception, the study deepens our understanding of green gentrification in transitioning regions. It shows how cognitive processes shape environmental decision-making among relatively advantaged residents, highlighting their relevance for policymaking in industrial and energy transitions.
summary: Middle-income migrants to a scenic but polluted Australian coastal region rationalize pollution through cognitive biases ('green compromise'), easing pressure for monitoring and remediation.

title: Spatial-temporal impacts of climate change on coral reef recreation values in the main Hawaiian Islands
authors: Ashley Lowe Mackenzie; Anders Dugstad; Carlo Fezzi; Lansing Perng; Kirsten L.L. Oleson
keywords: Coral reefs; Climate change; Integrated ecosystem modeling; Economic valuation
abstract: Coral reefs are highly diverse and productive ecosystems that provide a wide range of ecosystem services, including recreation, coastal protection, and marine biodiversity. Climate change impacts, including ocean warming and acidification, pose a significant threat to coral reefs and the ecosystem services they provide. The variability of these impacts highlight the need to develop more spatially explicit tools in coastal ecosystem management that integrate and assess potential ecological and socio-economic outcomes. To address this, we use a spatially explicit predictive ecological model to project changes in coral reef cover using downscaled data from Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) climate scenarios. By coupling the projections to a recreational demand model we downscale impacts to 1 km squared grids and calculate net present value (NVP) across landscapes and islands. Our findings indicate cumulative NPV welfare losses by 2100 for Hawaiʻi residents range from $1.8 to $3.0 billion in 2024$. We examine per-capita loses and use EJScreen tool to assess variation in welfare impacts by identifying disadvantaged communities based on demographic and environmental indicators. The findings provide spatially explicit evidence linking projected ecological decline to distributed welfare losses, informing resource allocation and conservation prioritization across the Hawaiian Islands.
summary: Climate-driven coral-reef decline could impose $1.8-3.0 billion in cumulative recreation-value losses on Hawai'i residents by 2100, distributed unevenly across communities.

title: Humanity does not play DICE: A sensitivity analysis of technical progress
authors: Antoine Ronsain; Alexandre Gondran; Estelle Malavolti
keywords: DICE; Backstop technology; Climate damage; Uncertainty; Sufficiency; IAM
abstract: The DICE model claims that technological progress can prevent global warming at low cost. However, its conclusions are predicated on highly optimistic and contested assumptions regarding the costs and effectiveness of backstop technologies, as well as the magnitude of climate damages. This study assesses the robustness of the DICE model's recommendations by exploring their sensitivity to these core assumptions. We investigate scenarios where assumptions prove to be more pessimistic than DICE standard baseline. We employ a large-scale scenario-based analysis to account for the possible range of the climate damage function and the level of efficiency of future backstop technologies, as well as their financial costs. Our results demonstrate that relying on technology alone is a very risky bet; under a wide spectrum of plausible, less optimistic assumptions, 84 % of scenarios lead to a climate-induced economic collapse. To address this fragility, we introduce a social lever into the model: economic sufficiency, defined as the policy option to produce less than the maximum production capacity. The inclusion of this lever dramatically alters the outcomes if the social-planner is enough forward looking. Our study concludes that relying on purely technological solutions is a hazardous strategy under uncertainty and that a dual strategy, combining both technological and social levers, is required to reduce the risk of climate collapse.
summary: Under less optimistic assumptions, 84% of DICE model scenarios lead to climate-induced economic collapse unless an economic-'sufficiency' lever is combined with technological progress.

title: Is the garden green? The paradox of consumer motivations for gardening and substrate preferences
authors: Holger Braun; Terese Venus; Benedikt Rilling; Carsten Herbes
keywords: Q-methodology; Sustainable consumption; Gardening; (Peat-free) gardening substrates; Consumer preferences; Carbon sink; Sustainability marketing
abstract: Peatlands are crucial natural carbon sinks and reducing the peat usage in gardening substrates is vital for their preservation. As attitudes and values are important in gardeners' decision-making, we analyze the discourse around environmental and climate impacts of hobby gardening using the Q-methodology. We uniquely compare the results of two Q-sorts related to motivations and actions. Based on our participants' motivations for gardening, we identify three perspectives: (i) egoistic food-producers; (ii) altruistic-conservationists, and (ii) relaxed-horticulturists. Based on actions, i.e. substrate use, we identify four perspectives: (i) competent climate-gardeners; (ii) climate-gardeners with limited substrate awareness; (iii) consumption-relativists and (iv) overwhelmed consumers. We find a weak relationship between sustainability motivations for gardening and actions, revealing a paradox: gardeners may harm the environment through substrate use despite intending to garden sustainably. Gardeners particularly often relativize their personal impact because of their minimal substrate need. Regarding the elimination of peat, our research demonstrates the importance of bridging the disconnect between consumer motivations and actions, for example, through various marketing tools. Policy-makers should consider mandatory and progressively increasing minimum levels of peat alternatives in substrates. This would gradually introduce and accustom consumers to peat alternatives, making it easier to adapt their purchase and application behavior.
summary: Hobby gardeners' sustainability motivations translate only weakly into peat-free substrate use, revealing a motivation-action paradox relevant to peatland carbon-sink protection.

title: Philanthropic food assistance in high-income countries: Lessons from Israel's food-aid network
authors: Moran Accos; Orly Tamir; Aron M. Troen
keywords: Food insecurity; Food-aid; Food banks; Welfare state; NGO; Philanthropy
abstract: Food insecurity (FI) in high-income countries (HICs) is increasingly addressed by philanthropic food-aid organizations that operate with limited state oversight. Such is the case in Israel, a high-income country that faces persistent FI and social inequality, but has never conducted a comprehensive mapping of its philanthropic food-aid network. This study is the first national-level analysis of food-aid NGOs in Israel. We evaluated their distribution, purpose, scale, and alignment with need, using administrative data from Guidestar, Israel's official NGO database, and from the country's two largest food banks. We analyze the system through the lenses of effectiveness, equity, and efficiency – the three key dimensions used globally to assess food-aid systems.
summary: A first national mapping of Israel's philanthropic food-aid NGOs assesses the loosely regulated network through the lenses of effectiveness, equity and efficiency.

title: The effects of U.S. poultry industry consolidation on employee productivity and labor costs
authors: Tina L. Saitone; K. Aleks Schaefer; Daniel P. Scheitrum; Shawn Arita; Vince Breneman; Rebecca Nemec Boehm
keywords: Poultry industry; Consolidation; Employee productivity; Labor costs
abstract: In this paper, we consider the relationship between poultry processing industry concentration and labor costs at the industry level using plant-level data for all poultry processing facilities in the U.S. We find that plant acquisition by an industry leader firm generates an increase in future sales-per-employee at the plant in subsequent periods. Increased ownership concentration at both the national and state-level leads to a reduction in poultry processing worker renumeration, relative to the compensation for comparable jobs in other sectors. Relative to concentration and consolidation levels 25 years ago, these developments have led to between $37 and $710 million in additional revenues per year and between $27 and $218 million savings in the aggregate wage bill for the four largest poultry firms, implying a 2.6–12.0% increase in the gross labor margin for these firms.
summary: US poultry-processing consolidation raised sales-per-employee but lowered worker pay, boosting the four largest firms' gross labor margin by 2.6-12%.

title: Shrinkflation, unit price disclosure, and consumer welfare: Evidence from canned tuna
authors: Xibo Wan; Katherine Harris-Lagoudakis; John M. Crespi
keywords: Attribute disclosure; Collusion; Greedflation; Scanner data; Shrinkflation
abstract: Shrinkflation, the downsizing of packages without proportional price cuts, raises effective prices in ways that are often difficult for consumers to detect under bounded attention. We exploit a documented episode of product downsizing, combined with preexisting state-level variation in unit price disclosure rules, to identify how information design affects consumer behavior and welfare. Using a matched sample of scanner data and a control function approach, we show that consumers in regulated states are three times more responsive to unit price changes, consistent with disclosure increasing the salience of the relevant price metric. Counterfactual simulations indicate that nationwide disclosure would raise annual consumer surplus by $3.03 million in the short term and $8.33 million in the long term once retailers adjust prices strategically. At present, only 16 states regulate unit price labeling on food items. Our findings demonstrate that such labeling improves consumer decision-making under shrinkflation.
summary: Unit-price disclosure rules make consumers three times more responsive to shrinkflation, and nationwide disclosure would raise consumer surplus by up to $8.33 million long-run.

title: Welfare program participation among US farmworkers
authors: Alexandra E. Hill; Sarah C. Whitnall; Elizabeth C.A. Saunders; Timothy K.M. Beatty
keywords: Agricultural workers; SNAP; WIC; Medicaid; Undocumented eligibility
abstract: This study examines US farmworker participation in social safety net programs, providing the first comprehensive comparison across the National Agricultural Workers Survey, the American Community Survey, and the Current Population Survey. We measure levels, trends, and predictors of farmworker participation rates in six programs: the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), Medicaid, Unemployment Insurance (UI), the National School Lunch and Breakfast Program (NSLP), and the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC). Across surveys, we find that participation rates among income-eligible farmworker households are consistently highest for Medicaid (71%–79%) and the EITC (75%) and lowest for UI (21%). We evaluate how survey design and data collection methodologies shape these estimates through question wording, farmworker coverage, nonresponse, and measurement error. Comparing across surveys, we identify multiple persistent predictors of participation, including citizenship, gender, age, and educational attainment. These findings inform targeted outreach and policy interventions to enhance participation among US farmworkers and mitigate health and economic disparities.
summary: US farmworker safety-net participation is highest for Medicaid and the EITC and lowest for unemployment insurance, with survey design strongly shaping the estimates.

title: Is newer better? The effect of varietal age on real-world maize yield in Kenya
authors: Michael K. Ndegwa; Paul N. Nyangáu; Sarah Kariuki; Moti Jaleta; Hope Michelson; Jill Cairns
keywords: Varietal turnover; Smallholder; Maize yield gaps; Newer is better; Beliefs; Fertilizer response
abstract: Replacing old maize varieties with new ones is central to agricultural policy across Sub-Saharan Africa, widely promoted as a pathway to boosting productivity and strengthening food security. Yet the extent to which varietal turnover translates into higher yields on farmer-managed plots remains uncertain. We provide new evidence from Kenya, quantifying the yield effects of maize varietal age. We use a three-visit, multi-season panel survey of 4160 smallholder households across Kenya to estimate the effect of varietal age on maize yield, employing entropy balancing and weighted regression models to address endogeneity. Our results establish a strong negative relationship between varietal age and yield. New varieties yield 147 kg/ha more than old in the long rains and 91 kg/ha more in the short rains. More granular age categorization shows that switching to varieties released within the past five years delivers the highest gains – 360 kg/ha in the long rains and 269 kg/ha in the short rains – over varieties that have been in the market more than 20 years. These findings suggest that slow varietal turnover lowers yields and crop production. We show that while farmers generally perceive new varieties favorably in terms of yield potential, early maturity and grain quality, their concerns that new varieties require more labor may delay adoption. Providing farmers with clear, locally-relevant performance data and opportunities for on-farm experimentation may help shift perceptions and drive wider and faster adoption.
summary: Newer maize varieties yield substantially more on Kenyan smallholder plots, so slow varietal turnover lowers yields, while labor concerns delay adoption.

title: Food systems policy coherence: A ten-country assessment
authors: Stella Nordhagen; Mahamadou Tankari; Jamie Morrison; Julie Collins; Kelly Parsons; Danielle Resnick; José Valls Bedeau
keywords: Policy integration; Policy coordination; Food system transformation; Policy analysis methods
abstract: Policy coherence is widely recognised as essential for achieving food systems transformation, but attempts to assess food systems policy coherence have been limited to date in terms of their scope of topics and geographies and lack of comparable methods. This paper introduces the Food Systems Policy Coherence (FSPC) Diagnostic Tool and uses it to analyse food systems policy coherence across 10 low- and middle-income countries in Africa and Asia through key informant interviews (n = 189) and review of policy documents (n = 808). The FSPC Diagnostic Tool considers two aspects of policy coherence: (1) the structures and mechanisms that may contribute to achieving stronger policy process coherence and (2) coherence between policies from six sectors and ten common food systems goals. Regarding the former, all countries analysed had strong framework documents for cross-sectoral food policy, backed by high-level political commitment, but they tended to be much weaker when it came to capacity for implementation and especially monitoring and accountability. Policy coherence across sectors was generally strong for the goals of climate change adaptation and social protection but weaker for goals of healthy diets for all, adequate wages for food system workers, and climate change mitigation through food systems. Trade policy was the policy area with the greatest incoherence with a diverse range of food systems goals. The results offer the most comprehensive analysis of food systems policy coherence to date. The tool makes a useful contribution to measuring policy coherence and can serve as both a foundation for future research and enhance accountability for achieving coherent policy outcomes.
summary: A new diagnostic tool applied to 10 low- and middle-income countries finds strong food-policy frameworks but weak implementation and monitoring, with trade policy the most incoherent area.

title: Food price inflation forecasting: Insights from a Macroeconomic Auto-Regressive Random Forest approach
authors: William McWilliams; Shamar L. Stewart; Olga Isengildina Massa
keywords: Food price inflation; Forecasting; Random forests; Generalized Time-Varying Parameters; High-dimensional macroeconomic data; Factor models
abstract: This study proposes a Macroeconomic Auto-Regressive Random Forest (MARRF) model to complement existing methods for forecasting annual U.S. food price inflation. Leveraging the flexibility of ensemble machine learning and the interpretability of Generalized Time-Varying Parameters (GTVPs), the MARRF model integrates high-dimensional macroeconomic information extracted from the FRED-MD database to produce forecasts that are both accurate and economically informative. Out-of-sample evaluation over 2003–2024 reveals that despite informational inefficiencies, the MARRF and SARIMA exhibit complementary strengths. Forecast encompassing tests confirm that each model captures distinct information, and simple averaging of the two yields both bias reduction and accuracy improvement across the full forecast cycle—outcomes neither model achieves on its own. Furthermore, variable importance metrics and time-varying parameters reveal shifting macroeconomic drivers of food price inflation across time and forecast horizons.
summary: A machine-learning MARRF model and SARIMA capture complementary information, and averaging the two improves US food-price-inflation forecasts.

title: Strait of Hormuz disruption, fertilizer market transmission, and food policy response
authors: Sandro Steinbach; Shawn Arita; Rwit Chakravorty; Jiyeon Kim; Ming Wang
keywords: Strait of Hormuz; Fertilizer markets; Food Security; Input-cost shocks; Market transmission; Trade Policy
summary: The authors argue a Strait of Hormuz disruption would transmit to agriculture as a fertilizer, fuel and shipping input-cost shock, hitting import-dependent producers hardest (IDEAS lists only article highlights, no prose abstract).

title: Do Producer organizations Promote Climate-Smart Agriculture? assessing direct and spillover effects in Nigeria
authors: Abebayehu Girma Geffersa; Martin Paul Tabe-Ojong Jr.
keywords: Adoption; Spillovers; Climate change; Climate-smart agriculture; Nigeria
abstract: Climate change threatens the livelihoods of millions of smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa and beyond, yet the adoption of Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) remains low. In this paper, we examine the role of producer organizations (POs) in promoting CSA adoption among their members and non-members through spillover effects. We rely on a three-wave panel dataset of over 1,500 farm households fielded between 2017 and 2019 and estimated the multivariate probit model to capture interdependencies in adopting four key CSA practices: climate-resilient groundnut varieties (CRVs), organic fertilizers, crop rotation, and intercropping. We also examine the association between POs and the adoption intensity of CSA practices, including number of CSA practices used and area under CRVs. Employing the Mundlak–Chamberlain device to address time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity, we find that PO membership is positively associated with the adoption of CSA practices. Beyond the independent use of these CSA practices, we also highlight a positive association between POs and both the adoption intensity and the joint use of these practices which indicates bundling. Importantly, positive spillover effects are observed among non-members, especially for low-cost, easily observable practices such as intercropping and crop rotation, indicating the role of peer learning and informal networks. Conversely, spillovers are less evident for input-intensive practices such as CRVs and organic fertilizers, highlighting the need for targeted support. The results point to two distinct adaptation pathways: a technology-driven strategy reliant on financial and institutional resources, and a diversification-driven strategy based on cost-effective, observable practices. Overall, the study demonstrates the critical role of POs in fostering resilient and sustainable agricultural systems through both direct engagement and community-wide spillovers.
summary: Nigerian producer-organization membership raises adoption and bundling of climate-smart practices, with positive spillovers to non-members for low-cost, observable practices.

title: Healthier diets: a global economic modelling study of income and employment impacts across regions
authors: Adam M. Komarek; Dirk Willenbockel; Shahnila Dunston; Nicola Cenacchi; H. Charles J. Godfray; Daniel Mason-D'Croz; Timothy B. Sulser; Keith Wiebe
keywords: Economic modelling; Food affordability; Healthier diets
abstract: Interest has grown in how to achieve healthy, sustainable, and affordable human diets. The potential income and employment effects of a transition towards healthier diets have received much less attention. We simulate aggregate and sectoral income and employment for business-as-usual and healthier diets for all geographic regions up to 2050 using scenario-based modelling. These healthier diets can increase food's share of household expenditure in some regions, for example from 18% to 25% in East and Central Africa in 2050. Our results suggest that a global shift towards healthier diets leads to a reallocation of primary factors of production, especially low-skilled labour and capital, from non-agricultural sectors to crop agriculture in parts of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Notably, in 2050, with healthier diets, agriculture's share of low-skilled labour increases by 3.2 percentage points in East and Central Africa and 1.5 percentage points in South Asia excluding India. Although Gross Domestic Product increases in these regions relative to business-as-usual, this reallocation raises agriculture's share of Gross Domestic Product, consistent with a slower pace of long-run structural transformation. The reallocation leads to a mild increase in wages for low-skilled workers relative to high-skilled workers in most of these regions, compared to business-as-usual. However, in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, food price increases outweigh wage gains for low-skilled labour, reducing real purchasing power. Policies that encourage healthier diets may also alter income and employment and reduce economic welfare of poor populations in some regions, so care is needed in policy design to avoid adverse unintended consequences.
summary: Global modelling finds a shift to healthier diets reallocates labor toward agriculture in parts of Africa and South Asia and can cut poor populations' real purchasing power despite GDP gains.

title: Estimating plant-based milk impacts on U.S. fluid milk prices and quantities
authors: Sangwon Lee; Daniel A. Sumner
keywords: Plant-based milk; Milk demand; Dairy markets; Food demand estimation; Simulating demand impacts
abstract: Per capita consumption of fluid cow's milk has declined steadily in North America and Europe. In the United States, that well-known decline accelerated in percentage terms in the past two decades as the market for plant-based substitutes surged. This paper documents and explains significant impacts of plant-based products on the retail prices and quantities of fluid cow's milk products in the United States, using a discrete-choice model of milk product demand with random coefficients. Demand estimates based on household purchase and store scanner data from 2018 to 2020 show that plant-based milk is more substitutable for organic and lactose-free cow's milk products than for conventional cow's milk. Based on our demand estimates, if plant-based milk products had not been available in the consumer choice set, the retail quantity of organic cow's milk would have been 14.5%, lactose-free cow's milk 10.2% higher, and conventional cow's milk by 7.7% higher. The absence of plant-based alternatives would increase annual retail purchases of fluid cow's milk by 1.46 gallons for a representative survey of households. In these data, each gallon of plant-based milk displaced 0.68 gallons of cow's milk. While plant-based milk continues to affect the demand for fluid cow's milk products, especially the higher-priced organic and lactose-free products, evidence shows that it has not been the primary driver in the recent accelerated decline in the consumption of fluid cow's milk.
summary: Plant-based milk substitutes mainly for organic and lactose-free cow's milk and, though it displaces some cow's milk, was not the primary driver of the recent accelerated fluid-milk decline.

title: Understanding Nutrient - Contaminant Tradeoffs in fish consumer preferences: Evidence from Kenya
authors: Kira Lancker; Christopher B. Barrett; Kathryn J. Fiorella; Christopher M. Aura; Hezron Awandu; Fonda J. Awuor; Patrick Otuo
keywords: Food labels; Fish consumer behavior; Interdependent preferences; Choice experiment; Polyunsaturated fatty acids; Algal blooms; Lake Victoria
abstract: Fish consumers are often challenged by tradeoffs between nutritional benefits and contaminant risks, which increase due to environmental pollution. Health campaigns and labeling initiatives can guide decision-making by providing information both on contaminant risk and nutritional value of a product, but it is not well understood how consumers react to such complex dual labels. We use data from a stated choice experiment in Kenya's Lake Victoria region to study how consumers respond to dual labels on fish products, and how their responses to each label interact. We focus on the tradeoff between polyunsaturated fatty acids and contamination with microcystins, a class of toxins produced by harmful algae blooms that can accumulate in fish tissue. Our findings suggest that, faced with a dual information policy, consumers react rationally to dual health attribute labeling, and that nutrient labels and contaminant warnings can function concurrently, indeed even be mutually reinforcing, but pose a risk of inadvertently concentrating unhealthful consumption in less responsive subpopulations.
summary: Kenyan fish consumers respond rationally to dual nutrient-and-contaminant labels, which can be mutually reinforcing but may concentrate unhealthful consumption in less responsive groups.

title: Diverse leadership, sustainable futures: unveiling the role of gender diversity in enhancing financial performance and achieving SDGs in Bangladesh's banking sector
authors: Sayna Islam Diba; Anup Karmakar; Mohammad Abu Shahriar Hossain; Md Kamruzzaman
keywords: Gender diversity; Corporate governance; Financial sustainability; Sustainable development goals (SDGs); Bangladesh banking sector; Two-step system GMM; Board gender diversity (BGD)
abstract: This study examines the influence of corporate board gender diversity on the financial performance and sustainability of banks in Bangladesh within the context of the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Using panel data from 30 banks listed on the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) over 2016–2023, the research demonstrates that greater female representation on corporate boards supports SDG 5 and SDG 8, while stronger governance practices contribute to SDG 16. The Two-Step System Generalized Method of Moments (System GMM) estimator addresses potential endogeneity. Results reveal that board gender diversity is positively associated with financial performance and sustainability metrics including Tobin's Q, Return on Assets, Return on Equity, Operational Self-Sufficiency (OSS), and Financial Self-Sufficiency (FSS). A one-percentage point increase in female board representation correlates with a 3.05% increase in OSS. The Blau Gender Index is associated with lower governance risk and stronger organizational resilience. Greater gender diversity shows increases of 3.56% and 2.75% in Tobin's Q and Return on Equity respectively. The robustness of findings is confirmed using Two-Step Difference GMM estimator, highlighting the strategic importance of gender-diverse boards in strengthening corporate governance and supporting sustainable economic development in emerging economies.
summary: Greater female board representation is positively associated with financial performance and SDG-aligned sustainability in Bangladeshi banks.

title: Life expectancy and its determinants: A machine learning analysis with implications for policy interventions
authors: Milena Lopreite; Michelangelo Misuraca; Michelangelo Puliga
keywords: Longevity; Socioeconomic factors; Air quality; Machine learning model
abstract: Life expectancy at birth is a key indicator of national health and socioeconomic development. Identifying the main factors associated with its variation is essential for policymakers seeking to improve population well-being. This study employs a range of machine learning techniques to analyse the relationship between life expectancy and a set of macro-level indicators across 49 OECD countries over time. Multiple predictive models are implemented and compared, and the best-performing specification is used to assess the relative importance of the considered variables. In addition, controlled perturbations of key variables are introduced to examine the model-implied response of life expectancy predictions. The results consistently identify GDP per capita, healthcare expenditure, and PM2.5 concentrations as the variables most strongly associated with life expectancy. In particular, lower levels of air pollution are systematically linked to higher predicted longevity, consistent with the potential public health relevance of environmental improvements. Overall, the findings provide a comparative and data-driven assessment of the factors most closely related to life expectancy, suggesting that aligning environmental policies with economic and health investments can significantly improve population well-being.
summary: Across OECD countries, machine-learning analysis identifies GDP per capita, healthcare spending and PM2.5 air pollution as the strongest determinants of life expectancy.

title: Optimizing facility locations and shuttle routes for senior welfare centers in aging societies: A priority-based approach
authors: Jiyeong Min; Seokho Yoon; Hyeong Suk Na; Sang Jin Kweon
keywords: Location routing problem; Decomposition-based matheuristic; Socio-economic vulnerability; Social equity; Residence-based priority
abstract: With the rapid growth of the elderly population, senior welfare centers play an increasingly important role in meeting rising care needs and improving well-being. Optimizing the locations of these centers and their shuttle routes is crucial for enhancing accessibility and ensuring equitable resource distribution. However, few studies have simultaneously addressed facility location-allocation and shuttle route optimization for elderly welfare while incorporating floating population data and residence-based priority scores. To bridge this gap, this study proposes a decomposition-based matheuristic for the extended location routing problem, integrating the optimization of senior welfare facility locations with shuttle route planning. This integrated framework explicitly incorporates floating population data and priority scores to enhance elderly accessibility. Compared with conventional optimization solvers, the proposed algorithm demonstrates greater scalability and computational efficiency, enabling the solution of problems with a size that is otherwise intractable due to the NP-hard nature of the problem. We validate our algorithm through a case study in Ulsan, Republic of Korea. Results demonstrate its effectiveness and applicability in optimizing the location of senior welfare centers and routes of their shuttle to better serve vulnerable elderly residents. Additional analyses examine cost efficiency and the consideration of high-priority demands to investigate the impact of population size on each demand node and the distribution of demand nodes on route efficiency. Lastly, a sensitivity analysis on shuttle capacity further demonstrates the model's adaptability across operational scenarios. This study contributes to efficient resource allocation by prioritizing areas with the greatest need and addressing social equity in aging societies.
summary: A decomposition-based matheuristic jointly optimizes senior-welfare-center locations and shuttle routes to improve elderly accessibility and equity, demonstrated in Ulsan, South Korea.

title: Assessment of primary healthcare accessibility in rural areas considering vulnerability
authors: Valentina Castañeda-Torres; Sofía Pérez-Guzmán; Elena Valentina Gutiérrez-Gutiérrez
keywords: Rural primary healthcare; Accessibility; Vulnerability; Deprivation costs
abstract: Providing primary healthcare (PHC) is a global challenge, particularly in rural areas where nearly half of the global population lives and lacks adequate access to essential healthcare services. This research addresses the assessment of accessibility to PHC in rural areas, where multiple socioeconomic, geographic, and infrastructure factors limit service accessibility and exacerbate populations' vulnerability. We propose a p-median facility location problem and explicitly model vulnerability by employing deprivation cost functions. We conduct a case study in a rural region in Colombia, and a series of sensitivity analyses of the impact of deprivation and terminal costs on PHC access. The findings show that 22% of the municipalities lacks access to PHC service points, and among those with access, 20% shared PHC service points and ranked highest in deprivation costs. This research also shows that terminal costs highly influence the optimal allocation of PHC service points to populations, conditioning the prioritization of more vulnerable populations when allocating essential resources.
summary: A p-median model with deprivation costs finds 22% of a rural Colombian region's municipalities lack primary-healthcare access, with terminal costs shaping equitable allocation.

title: Is last-mile delivery by autonomous robots a reality?: A multi-criteria decision-making approach for prioritization of autonomous vehicle modes
authors: Đorđije Dupljanin; Sara Jovčić; Slaviša Dumnić; Libor Švadlenka; Vladimir Simic; Momčilo Dobrodolac
keywords: Smart cities; Autonomous vehicles; Last-mile delivery; AROMAN; FullEx; Decision-making
abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce and the resulting surge in last-mile deliveries have intensified urban congestion and logistical inefficiencies. Although recent studies highlight the potential of autonomous vehicles and delivery robots to improve delivery efficiency and sustainability, the practical realization of these systems remains limited. Most existing research focuses on technological development or simulation-based optimization, while comprehensive decision frameworks for prioritizing different autonomous delivery modes under real urban conditions are largely absent. Addressing this gap, this study investigates whether last-mile delivery by autonomous robots is a viable and implementable reality. We propose a multi-criteria decision-making framework that integrates the AROMAN and FullEx techniques to systematically evaluate and prioritize various autonomous vehicle modes for last-mile logistics. The proposed approach incorporates multiple evaluation dimensions – economic, technical, environmental, and operational, to support evidence-based decision-making. The methodology is demonstrated through a case study in the city of Novi Sad, which illustrates the framework's applicability in assessing the readiness and suitability of autonomous delivery solutions in a real-world urban context. Findings from the study contribute to both academic discourse and practical logistics management by offering a structured approach to determine when and how autonomous delivery systems can transition from concept to reality.
summary: An AROMAN+FullEx multi-criteria framework evaluates and prioritizes autonomous last-mile delivery modes under real urban conditions, applied to Novi Sad.

title: Territorial disparities in organic food markets: Evidence from scanner data in Italy
authors: Ilaria Benedetti; Tiziana Laureti; Luigi Palumbo
keywords: Organic food; Scanner data; Organic-conventional price differential; Hedonic pricing; Market structure; Sustainable consumption
abstract: Ensuring equitable access to sustainable diets remains a critical challenge for food systems. This study examines territorial inequalities in the Italian organic food market by leveraging nationally representative retail scanner data covering 103 provinces. Focusing on a set of key staple product categories (eggs, rice, flour, and yogurt) within the modern retail sector, we develop novel indicators of organic product availability and market diffusion and, applying hedonic price models, we estimate provincial-level organic–conventional price gaps, highlighting their implications for affordability. Results reveal marked North–South disparities: organic products are consistently more available and sold at lower price gaps in central and northern Italy than in southern regions, even after controlling for packaging and product characteristics. These findings suggest that territorial inequalities in organic food access are not only demand-driven but also structurally linked to retail market organisation. Beyond the Italian case, the proposed framework demonstrates the potential of scanner data for monitoring spatial disparities in sustainable food access and supporting evidence-based policies to promote a more inclusive transition toward sustainable consumption.
summary: Italian organic staples are more available and carry smaller price gaps in the North than the South, reflecting retail-market structure rather than demand alone.

title: Strategic planning of polycentric urban regions: a modeling approach for practical applications
authors: Joao F. Bigotte; Susana Freiria; Antonio P. Antunes
keywords: Regional planning; Polycentric urban systems; Accessibility planning; Facility location; Network design; Spatial optimization; Decision support
abstract: Developing polycentric urban regions is increasingly seen as a sustainable and equitable planning goal. However, operationalizing polycentrism has proved to be challenging. While there is ample literature on assessing polycentrism from morphological and functional perspectives, prescriptive models for planning purposes remain scarce. Additionally, spatial planners and transport engineers have typically approached urban systems and transport network design separately.
summary: Proposes a prescriptive optimization modeling approach that integrates polycentric urban-system planning with transport-network design.

title: Utility effectiveness, composite indicators and 'benefit of the doubt' models: How important are preferences when evaluating the performance of innovation systems?
authors: José Luis Zofío; Juan Aparicio; Javier Barbero; Jon Mikel Zabala-Iturriagagoitia
keywords: Utility effectiveness; Composite indicators; Benefit-of-the-doubt evaluation; Innovation systems; Innovation performance
abstract: This study introduces a methodology that embeds 'Benefit of the Doubt' evaluations of performance of innovation systems, based on objective measures of technical effectiveness—that compare the values of a set of indicators across countries—into the literature of composite indicators, which rank countries relying on utility functions and whose aggregating structure and weights are subjectively chosen by the decision makers. Considering the general case of the constant elasticity of substitution utility function, whose power mean formulation nests popular specifications such as the weighted (linear) arithmetic mean, weighted geometric mean (Cobb-Douglas), and fixed-proportions (Leontief), we define the concept of utility effectiveness of an alternative as the ratio of its observed utility to the maximum utility observed across countries. We show that the utility loss resulting from an ineffective performance can be consistently decomposed into two mutually exclusive factors: first, grounded in the objective criterion of Pareto-dominance, the mentioned technical effectiveness is represented by a technical (radial) measure depending only on quantities, which gauges the distance to the utility frontier; second, a measure of allocative effectiveness, determining the additional utility loss resulting from an unbalanced composition of indicators given the preferences of the decision maker. Using data from the European Innovation Scoreboard, our results show high levels of utility ineffectiveness in Southern and Eastern European countries. On average, these countries' performance is half of the maximum utility reached by the best performing innovation systems. Objective technical ineffectiveness generally dominates over subjective allocative ineffectiveness (except for the fixed proportion specification), showing that the practical impact of choosing one utility specification over another, although sizable, is limited. Consequently, main performance deficits are often not due to substitutability or compensatory issues, but rather to real shortfalls in indicator levels, while preference-driven differences tend to be second-order and comparatively robust.
summary: Decomposing innovation-system performance into technical and allocative effectiveness, the study finds real shortfalls in indicators dominate over preference-driven differences in EU data.

title: Structural patterns and energy productivity in the EU-27 decarbonization process
authors: C.H. Siemens; J.M. Guaita-Martinez; R. Puertas; L. Gallego-Martín
keywords: Decarbonization; EU-27; Energy productivity; Technical efficiency; Random forest; Energy policy
abstract: Decarbonization is one of the defining challenges of the twenty-first century for the European Union, crucial to ensuring long-term sustainability, competitiveness, and energy security. This study pursues three objectives: (1) to identify homogeneous groups of EU countries according to their energy structure and dynamics; (2) to assess technical efficiency in decarbonization processes; and (3) to analyse the drivers of energy productivity changes within the EU-27 over the period 2015–2023. A multi-method approach is applied, combining Ward.D2 clustering, a non-convex metafrontier, and a sequential Malmquist index to estimate efficiency and productivity, complemented by a Random Forest algorithm to determine structural and technological factors. Results show that technological change has been the main source of convergence, while technical efficiency improvements have been more moderate. Public R&D expenditure in energy, green patents, and tertiary education emerge as the most influential drivers of energy productivity, underscoring the central role of innovation and human capital in modernizing the European energy system.
summary: In the EU-27, technological change rather than efficiency gains drove decarbonization convergence, with public energy R&D, green patents and tertiary education the key productivity drivers.

title: What really drives food waste? Advancing food waste prevention through behavioral evidence
authors: Lucas Rodrigues Deliberador; Mário Otávio Batalha; Aldara da Silva César
keywords: Food surplus; Sustainability; Multivariate analysis; Emerging country; Food insecurity
abstract: Food waste accounts for nearly one-third of global food production, and Brazil is among the countries with the highest levels of household food waste, exacerbating national food insecurity that affects approximately 52 million people. Addressing this challenge is crucial for advancing cleaner production and more sustainable consumption patterns. This study examines the behavioral determinants of food waste in Brazilian households to support the development of prevention-oriented strategies. A literature review identified key behavioral drivers, informing an analytical framework grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). Survey data collected from 2047 consumers were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The results confirmed eleven of the eighteen proposed hypotheses. Environmental and economic concerns, feelings of guilt, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control significantly increased consumers' intention to reduce food waste. Conversely, actual food waste behavior was primarily explained by perceived behavioral control, household planning practices, consumption of convenience foods, and the identity associated with being a good provider. By highlighting how behavioral factors shape household food waste in an emerging economy, this study contributes to the literature on sustainable consumption, offers insights for designing effective food waste prevention policies, and supports broader efforts to promote cleaner production and reduce resource inefficiencies and environmental impacts.
summary: In Brazilian households, actual food-waste behavior is driven mainly by perceived control, planning, convenience-food use and provider identity rather than by intentions.

title: Performance evaluation of Natural Science Foundation projects based on hierarchical causal relationships
authors: Qiuhong Zhao; Yanchun Ma; Xunzhuo Xi; Guoliang Yang
keywords: Performance evaluation; DEMATEL; AHDT; Hierarchical causal relationship
abstract: To evaluate the performance of Natural Science Foundation projects more rigorously and transparently and to address the limitations of traditional evaluation methods, which often struggle to capture complex inter-indicator relationships and tend to produce "black box" scores, this study develops a comprehensive evaluation framework that makes explicit the internal logic and value transmission pathways of performance outputs.
summary: Develops a transparent DEMATEL/AHDT evaluation framework that makes explicit the causal pathways behind research-foundation project performance.

title: Agricultural production risks, crop losses, and the role of extension services: Insights from India
authors: Ph Romen Sharma; Subhashree Sahu; Laishram Priscilla; Shridhar Patil; Renu Balakrishnan; Sumanta Chatterjee; Alok Kumar Sahoo; Priyajoy Kar; S.L. Jat
keywords: Crop loss; Agricultural production risks; Agricultural extension services; Propensity score matching; Farm household welfare
abstract: This paper examines the economic impacts of agricultural production shocks and the role of Agricultural Extension Service Providers (AESPs) in mitigating welfare losses among farm households in India. Three interrelated questions are addressed: how production shocks affect crop income; whether crop-loss experience motivates AESP engagement; and to what extent extension access improves welfare outcomes. Using nationally representative data from the 77th round of India's National Sample Survey Office (2018–19), covering 41,794 households across 657 districts, the study employs Propensity Score Matching to estimate income losses alongside probit and multivariate probit models to analyse determinants of access across four provider categories: public extension, private providers, mass media, and progressive farmer networks. Results indicate that 51.9% of agricultural households experienced crop losses, with drought causing the severest income decline at 35.78%, followed by floods at 29.91% and pests and diseases at 14.77%, yielding an overall average reduction of 27.69% in net crop income per hectare. Crop-loss exposure significantly increased AESP engagement across all provider categories, yet access remained constrained by landholding size, caste identity, and household resource endowments. Among crop-loss-affected households, AESP access was associated with significant multi-dimensional welfare improvements, encompassing higher net crop income, enhanced crop and income diversification, substantially higher crop insurance uptake, and improved per capita consumption expenditure. These findings establish extension access as a high-return resilience mechanism, underscoring the need for inclusive, equity-sensitive extension systems capable of reaching the most vulnerable farm households in India and analogous developing-country settings.
summary: Indian crop losses cut net crop income about 28%, and access to agricultural extension services significantly improves affected households' income, diversification and insurance uptake.

title: Designing a resilient humanitarian supply chain with intermodal transportation: A two-stage stochastic programming approach
authors: Dorsa Taghvaei; Masoud Rabbani
keywords: Humanitarian logistics; Resilience; Intermodal transportation; Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS); Simulated Annealing (SA)
abstract: This study proposes a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer nonlinear programming model to design a resilient and centralized humanitarian relief network based on a hub-and-spoke structure. Unlike most prior studies, which have focused on unimodal or multimodal contexts, the model explicitly includes intermodal transportation as well as resilience strategies, including hub fortification and post-disaster arc restoration. It also captures multiple sources of disaster-induced uncertainty, including fluctuating demand and disruptions to hubs and transport arcs. To ensure fair relief distribution, the problem is defined as a p-hub center model. To address the computational complexity, two tailored metaheuristics—Simulated Annealing (SA) and Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS)—are implemented. A real-world case study of Tehran under three seismic scenarios, using Red Crescent warehouses as candidate hubs and the 22 municipal districts as demand locations, verifies the approach. The findings reveal that resilience strategies considerably reduce response time and network vulnerability, whereas intermodal transportation serves as a critical backup when road access is impeded. Comparative analysis reveals that although both metaheuristics generate efficient solutions, ALNS consistently achieves superior quality and stability. Overall, the suggested framework offers humanitarian organizations with actionable insights into designing fair, resilient, and efficient relief distribution networks under uncertainty.
summary: A two-stage stochastic model adding intermodal transport and resilience strategies reduces humanitarian-relief response time and network vulnerability in a Tehran earthquake case.

title: Resilient and sustainable closed-loop pharmaceutical supply chain network: A smart contract application in the presence of quality disruptions
authors: Saeed Nikounia; Mohammad Yavari
keywords: Pharmaceutical closed-loop supply chain; Quality disruption; Resilience; Sustainability; Smart coalition; Smart contract
abstract: Quality disruption not only affects the flow of pharmaceuticals but also can undermine environmental and social dimensions of sustainability. In addition to the likelihood of occurrence, rapid detection of such a disruption is also important neglected by previous studies. This research investigates the development of a smart coalition in the downstream pharmaceutical supply chain (PSC), using smart contracts to deal with quality disruptions. This proposed resilient strategy is included in a novel multi-objective mathematical programming model for a pharmaceutical closed-loop supply chain (CLSC) network that aims to enhance sustainability by simultaneously optimizing three objectives: maximizing net profit to support economic viability, minimizing water pollution from improper pharmaceutical disposal, and reducing the distribution of tainted drugs to uphold social responsibility. This model evaluates the deployment level of smart contracts and integrated decisions for inventory management, network design, and recycled products pricing. The proposed smart coalition and designed model are validated through implementation in a real case study of the 500 mg naproxen tablet CLSC in Tehran, Iran. The Results revealed that the CLSC structure led to supply chain profitability, a 31% reduction in water pollution and a 51% decrease in tainted drug distribution compared to a forward supply chain. With the integration of the smart coalition, further improvements were observed across all sustainability dimensions, including a significant 28% reduction in tainted drug delivery and a 59% increase in net profit. These results demonstrate the practical effectiveness of CLSC design, integrated decision making, and smart coalition strategy in enhancing sustainability and resilience.
summary: A closed-loop pharmaceutical supply-chain design using smart contracts cuts water pollution and tainted-drug distribution while raising profit, shown for a naproxen case in Tehran.

title: Fundraising and competition of NGOs in three tiers non-profit supply chain with leverages of investment and donation
authors: Ata Allah Taleizadeh; Salar Shams-Azar
keywords: Non-governmental organization; Supply chain; Competition; Fundraising; Donation
abstract: In recent years, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) have faced increasing challenges, including unstable financial resources, intensified competition for funds, government regulations, and issues related to public perception and trust. As a result, improving the efficiency and decision-making mechanisms of NGOs has become an important and widely discussed research topic. To address these challenges, NGOs must adopt effective strategies for resource acquisition and allocation. Among these strategies, fundraising operations play a critical role in securing financial resources. The financial resources of NGOs are typically allocated to two major types of activities: operational and campaigning activities, referred to in this study as leverage donation and leverage investment, respectively. Leverage investment includes activities such as organizing advocacy and protest campaigns to influence government policies, increasing public awareness of NGO missions, enhancing fundraising capacity, and investing in infrastructure to improve societal welfare. In contrast, leverage donation focuses on direct support activities, including identifying disadvantaged individuals and providing immediate financial and humanitarian assistance. Achieving an appropriate balance between leverage investment and leverage donation is essential for optimizing NGO decision-making and enhancing societal satisfaction. This paper investigates a non-profit supply chain consisting of two competing NGOs operating across two distinct segments, each supported by heterogeneous donor groups. To address the aforementioned challenges, each NGO develops two internal leverages corresponding to public-sector and private-sector activities. We model the interaction among NGOs, donors, and internal levers through a game-theoretic framework, in which NGOs compete under Nash equilibrium to determine optimal fundraising efforts and societal satisfaction levels. The proposed model determines the optimal allocation of resources between the two levers, the optimal fundraising effort, and the resulting equilibrium outcomes. Competition among NGOs is driven by activities that generate societal satisfaction, which in turn influences donor utility and willingness to contribute. Each NGO strategically adjusts its fundraising and satisfaction efforts to attract donors across segments, aiming to enhance financial sustainability while serving disadvantaged communities. The results show that increased fundraising intensity across segments is positively correlated with societal satisfaction in both channels. However, beyond certain levels, the effectiveness of leveraged donations slightly decreases, while the utility of competing levers increases. This outcome is primarily driven by the prioritization of meeting fundamental societal needs. Overall, the findings provide valuable insights into NGO financial decision-making and highlight the complex interrelationships among donors, NGOs, internal levers, and society within a non-profit supply chain context.
summary: A game-theoretic model shows how competing NGOs should balance 'leverage investment' and 'leverage donation' to maximize fundraising and societal satisfaction.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: A quantitative framework for assessing rail station operational resilience under infrastructural modifications
authors: Md Tabish Haque; Jan Eisold; Nikola Bešinović
keywords: Resilience; Capacity management; Railway; Disruption
abstract: Rail stations are essential components in rail networks, influencing operational continuity and urban connectivity. The track and signalling configuration around a station area, where trains arrive and depart, is highly vulnerable to disruptions. Prior research has largely assessed resilience at the network level or the impact of station design on passenger flow; less attention has been paid to the impact of physical track and signalling configurations within the station area on train operations. This study presents an optimisation-based framework that examines the impact of targeted station area infrastructure upgrades on train routing and scheduling during disruptions. The framework evaluates two key performance metrics: the ability to adapt train movements and the stability of scheduled service during disruption. A real-world case study from the German rail network demonstrates the framework's applicability, supported by sensitivity analysis across disruption and varying operational measure configurations. Results indicate that although resilience is highly sensitive to disruption type and traffic levels, targeted infrastructure modifications can significantly reduce overall impact, operational changes and support faster recovery across diverse disruption scenarios. Further, the study highlights that during severe disruptions involving multiple simultaneous failures, targeted infrastructure modifications continue to have better performance, supporting service continuity. Overall, the findings provide infrastructure managers with a practical basis to strategically prioritise station area upgrades and make resilience-oriented informed decisions.
summary: An optimization framework shows targeted station-area track and signalling upgrades significantly improve rail operational resilience during disruptions, demonstrated on the German network.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Digital twin federation for urban mobility assessment: Definition, pillars, and a human-in-the-loop functional architecture
authors: Jingjun Li; Jascha Grübel; Ali Nadi; Maaike Snelder; Bart van Arem; Jie Gao
keywords: Digital twin; Federation; Human in the loop; Urban mobility; Multilevel modelling; Low-car cities
abstract: Urban mobility systems face growing challenges. While various smart mobility solutions have been proposed, there is still a lack of comprehensive tools for assessing the impact of these solutions in a dynamic and iterative manner. Recent literature increasingly adopts the Digital Twin (DT) concept. However, DTs have conventionally been framed around automating solutions, which often conflict with the requirements of human-driven planning in socio-technical systems, leading to ambiguities in how DTs should be defined and operationalised for mobility planning. To fill this gap, this paper presents the concept of a Digital Twin Federation (FedDT) designed for comprehensive urban mobility assessments. Firstly, a definition of the FedDT concept is established based on four conceptual pillars, including physical & digital system exchange, system monitoring & planning, outcome evaluation & immersive experience, and human-in-the-loop control. Building on the concept and 5 stakeholder co-design sessions, we present a functional FedDT architecture that enables iterative, bidirectional data exchange between the physical and digital mobility systems, thereby supporting a data-driven decision-making process while ensuring the interests of stakeholders are continuously integrated. Finally, we demonstrate how the FedDT architecture can be instantiated through a proof-of-concept application framework. This framework serves as a research agenda that guides and links the development of separate modules to reduce private vehicle dependency in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Overall, this work lays a conceptual and architectural foundation for FedDT, advancing the implementation of integrated digital twin solutions for sustainable mobility systems.
summary: Introduces a human-in-the-loop 'Digital Twin Federation' concept and architecture for iterative, stakeholder-integrated urban-mobility assessment, with an Amsterdam proof-of-concept.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Consumer involvement in last-mile e-commerce transport and impact on travel Patterns: A case study in Sweden
authors: Lena Winslott Hiselius; Emeli Adell; Ulrik Berggren; Lena Smidfelt Rosqvist
keywords: Longitudinal travel survey; Travel behaviour; E-commerce; Last-mile transport; Delivery options
abstract: The growth of e-commerce has transformed consumer shopping patterns and reshaped travel behaviour, yet knowledge is limited regarding how different delivery options interact with individual mobility in everyday life. This study analysed how delivery options, trip characteristics, and socio-demographic and spatial factors relate to e-commerce activity travel and the degree of consumer involvement in last-mile transport. Using a longitudinal, smartphone-based travel survey combined with daily reporting of e-commerce activities, data were collected. The dataset prepared for analysis included 238 respondents, validating 11,221 days and 48,145 trips. Of these, 197 respondents engaged in an e-commerce activity at least once in a 28-day period. The results showed that nearly 60% of e-commerce activities required out-of-home travel, indicating substantial consumer involvement in last-mile logistics. Many of these trips were conducted as standalone errands, particularly for deliveries collected from agents and delivery boxes. Delivery boxes and in-store pickups were associated with car usage for e-commerce travel, while trip chaining facilitated integration of the pickup into broader activity patterns and mode use. Socio-demographic characteristics (including age and car access) and frequency of e-commerce use significantly shaped travel mode and delivery choices, with frequent users of e-commerce showing lower car dependence. Spatial context further moderated behaviour: urban residents displayed greater use of in-store pickups and other modes than cars, whereas rural residents depended more on cars. Overall, the findings demonstrate that e-commerce does not replace physical mobility, but reshapes it in ways dependent on delivery design, trip context, and local setting.
summary: In a Swedish sample nearly 60% of e-commerce deliveries required out-of-home travel, showing e-commerce reshapes rather than replaces physical mobility depending on delivery design and setting.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: The distributional effects of high-speed rail investment in China: fast tracks to inequality?
authors: Xutao Yang; Erik Verhoef; Mark Lijesen; Jianhong Wu
keywords: High-speed rail; Conventional rail; Distributional effects
abstract: High-speed rail (HSR) has become one of China's most ambitious infrastructure projects, redefining accessibility and connectivity across vast regions. However, rigorous empirical investigations on the impact of HSR on the conventional rail (CR) operation and the following effects on CR passengers remain scarce. Therefore, we investigate how CR trips, often made by low-income groups, are impacted by the operation of HSR using a comprehensive rail operation dataset. Our regression discontinuity design (RDD) results reveal that the operation of HSR leads to a significant decrease in CR trains (CT) frequency with both immediate and sustained declines observed, and slows down the increase of travel speed over the years. Heterogeneous impacts are found in different travel station types, different types of CT, and HSR operation intensity. Our imputed effects indicate that aside from construction and operation cost by using the public investment, the distribution of benefits and costs on CR passengers is overall regressive, since the generalised cost changes appear to benefit high-income groups, but disadvantage low-income groups.
summary: High-speed rail operation in China cut the frequency of conventional-rail service used by low-income riders, making the distribution of benefits and costs overall regressive.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Household life-cycle heterogeneity in commuting to emerging subcenters: An excess commuting-based study of the Seoul metropolitan Area, South Korea
authors: Hyunseong Yun; Seung-Nam Kim
keywords: Excess commuting; Heterogeneity; Family life cycle; Metropolitan area; Emerging subcenter
abstract: New employment subcenters are continuously emerging in global metropolitan areas. The growth of employment in emerging subcenters attracts workers from a wide range of areas, potentially leading to extremely long commuting distances. Many emerging subcenters primarily comprise high-tech industries, which are more favorable to workers in younger life cycles. Subcenter studies encourage planners to supply an adequate quantity of housing to keep jobs and housing balanced in order to mitigate attracted commutes. However, the effects of the job-housing balance on attracted commutes to emerging subcenters require investigation, because the heterogeneity of emerging subcenters raises concerns regarding spatial mismatch across household life cycles. This study aims to provide evidence that a quantitative job-housing balance may contribute to mitigating attracted commutes by examining commuting behavior in the Seoul Metropolitan Area, South Korea, across household life cycles. Utilizing Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP)-minimized employment data from 2006 and 2016, seven Traffic Analysis Zones are identified as emerging subcenters. Excess commuting indices are measured to demonstrate inter-life-cycle heterogeneity in the relationship between the job-housing balance and observed commuting behavior. Cross-classified multilevel analysis indicates that commuting distance is shorter when commuters live in locations with greater nearby job opportunities and work in locations with greater nearby residential opportunities. Together with observed commute comparisons and multilevel model results, the findings suggest that quantitative job-housing balance may help moderate attracted commutes to emerging subcenters.
summary: In the Seoul metropolitan area, a quantitative job-housing balance helps moderate long 'attracted' commutes to emerging subcenters, with effects varying across household life cycles.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: A two-level collaborative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for variable speed limit control of freeway tunnel groups
authors: Jieling Jin; Hui Zhang; Lu Xing; Helai Huang; Yansheng Chen
keywords: Freeway tunnel groups; Variable speed limit; Multi-agent reinforcement learning; Two-level collaboration; Spatial graph model; Importance weight
abstract: Compared to freeway mainline sections, freeway tunnels present a higher risk of collisions and pose greater challenges for rescue operations, owing to the distinctive features of tunnel lighting and structures. Moreover, the safety demands for tunnel groups, which consist of multiple tunnels, are more pronounced. Recent studies have demonstrated the promising application of reinforcement learning in implementing variable speed limit (VSL) control on freeways to enhance safety and efficiency. However, existing approaches cannot adequately capture the interaction of traffic flows across different tunnels in group scenarios, nor can they efficiently train policies under highly complex environments. This study proposes a VSL strategy based on a two-level collaborative multi-agent reinforcement learning (TCMARL) framework to improve the safety and efficiency of freeway tunnel groups. The framework realizes coordinated control at two levels: (1) capturing potential spatial dependencies among tunnel agents through a spatial graph model, thereby achieving synergy at the information input level; and (2) constructing a mixing network that fuses features of different tunnel agents and introducing an importance weight vector to optimize the global Q-value output, achieving synergy at the action output level. To improve training efficiency and policy generalization, a model-based reinforcement learning mechanism is further incorporated to generate short-horizon virtual rollouts. Simulation experiments are conducted in four tunnel-group scenarios, including two-, three-, four-, and five-tunnel configurations. Comparative results show that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and better safety and efficiency performance than benchmark methods. Additional ablation and sensitivity analyses confirm the complementary roles of the two-level collaboration design and the model-based planning mechanism, while out-of-training testing under unseen demand profiles demonstrates robust transferability. Beyond algorithmic performance, the findings provide policy relevant evidence for corridor level speed management in smart freeway tunnel systems, informing practical guidelines on coordinated VSL deployment and operational governance.
summary: A two-level collaborative multi-agent reinforcement-learning framework for variable speed limits improves safety and efficiency across freeway tunnel groups.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: A multi-source, multi-stage framework for ride-hailing safety management
authors: Jiayu Yang; Jaeyoung Jay Lee; Suyi Mao; Constantinos Antoniou
keywords: Ride-hailing driver; Risky driving identification; Real-time risk prediction; Safety policy
abstract: The rapid growth of ride-hailing services has transformed urban mobility, but the predominance of non-professional drivers raises pressing safety concerns. Existing research often lacks a comprehensive framework that integrates trajectory, environmental, and driver-related data to thoroughly examine risky driving behaviors. To address this gap, this research proposes a framework to analyze, predict, and intervene in speeding and jerky driving among ride-hailing drivers. It also explores the underlying factors contributing to such behaviors and offers targeted improvement strategies. The analysis uses a rich multi-source dataset, including over six million GPS trajectories, OpenStreetMap road network, and real-time weather data, along with 450 self-reported questionnaires from ride-hailing drivers. A multi-stage framework is employed, consisting of three components: (i) a bivariate random parameter model with heterogeneity in means to identify contributing factors to risky driving behavior; (ii) a Dual-Task Gated Cross-Attention Network for real-time risk prediction and proactive safety monitoring; (iii) a Gradient Boosting Classifier model to investigate factors influencing drivers' willingness to reduce risky behaviors. The analysis illustrates that, while speeding and jerky driving share common risk factors, such as trip distance and acceleration, they diverge substantially in their sensitivity to infrastructure and geometric conditions. The questionnaire survey analysis reveals several factors that influence a driver's willingness to improve their behavior: driving experience, driver ratings, risk perception, income level, and crash history. Overall, the proposed framework offers a robust, data-driven approach for managing risky driving in ride-hailing services, supporting real-time supervision and targeted policy development to enhance urban road safety.
summary: Combining six million GPS trajectories with road, weather and driver-survey data, the framework identifies, predicts and targets risky driving among ride-hailing drivers.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Bridging land use and transport planning: An AI-enabled decision support system for new urban developments
authors: Jiawei Tong; Guangyu Wang; Ruoxi Liao; Shuihua Wang; John Moraros
keywords: Land use-transport integration; Explainable artificial intelligence; Urban expansion planning; Evidence-based decision-making; Online learning; Uncertainty quantification
abstract: Rapid urban expansion demands immediate land use decisions whose transport implications shape accessibility for decades. Yet traditional approaches lack transparent mechanisms to link controllable planning features (density regulations, network design standards, zoning policies) to observable mobility consequences, breaking the connection between what planners can control and what they need to predict. To address this fundamental challenge, we introduce Adaptive Dynamic Analysis for Predictive Transport (ADAPT), an explainable AI framework employing a two-stage architecture: Stage One learns categorical traffic patterns from 4397 established scenarios using conditional variational autoencoders, revealing that functional classification explains 38% of variance while density and spatial context contribute 28%. Stage Two transfers learned patterns to new developments through intelligent initialization and online adaptive learning. ADAPT advances land use-transport integration by linking planning features to observable mobility patterns through interpretable prediction. It provides three capabilities: feature importance estimates that show which planning characteristics predict traffic generation, context-dependent mechanisms that identify nonlinear thresholds across urban forms, and uncertainty-aware protocols that align infrastructure commitment with prediction confidence.
