Within “objectivist orthodoxies,” motorways are treated as delineable technical systems serving a pre-defined economic logic. Conversely, “ethnographic subjectivisms” challenge these orthodoxies by focusing on everyday practices. Yet both approaches isolate the motorway either as a static entity or as a mere matter of individual perception, thereby obscuring the internal relations between state and capital. To offer a more comprehensive conceptualization, I draw on a dialectical methodology. I argue that motorways must be understood as a concrete universal, a socio-material system practically produced within capitalist social relations and a global network of nation-states. Accordingly, local practices are neither independent of these structures nor strict reflections of them; instead, they constitute a field of metabolic struggle where the violence of capital and statehood can be revealed and challenged.
summary: Uses a dialectical framework to argue motorways are a 'concrete universal' produced within capitalist and inter-state relations, transcending objectivist and ethnographic binaries.

title: Holding open the urban imagination
authors: Michele Acuto
keywords: Urban imagination; urban futures; urban resilience; urban sciences; global urbanism; fragments
abstract: Urban studies has repeatedly depended on imaginative acts, even if its imaginative capacities have often remained implicit, unevenly distributed, or overshadowed by explanatory commitments to understanding cities as they are rather than as they might become. Can urban imagination still sustain urban futures in a time of geopolitical fragmentation, democratic uncertainty, and academic precarity? This debate paper introduces the special issue on Urban Imaginations and Urban Futures by proposing a conceptual and methodological reorientation of urban studies around the relationship between imagination and futures thinking. It argues that urban imagination should be understood not simply as a representational domain but as an enabling infrastructure through which urban futures are made thinkable, actionable, and contestable. Drawing on recent debates on crisis, infrastructure, urban uncertainty, southern praxis, and computational urbanism, the paper advances three propositions. First, imagination is conceptualized as a distributed capacity embedded across diverse urban sciences and practices, from everyday urbanism and architectural design to engineering and computational modelling. Second, fragments are proposed as methodological resources that enable interdisciplinary dialogue while sustaining epistemic plurality and critical engagement. Third, imagination is positioned as a critical means of reclaiming resilience from its technocratic uses by expanding the generative capacity of urban scholarship to engage uncertainty, plurality, and transformation, thereby helping keep urban futures open.
summary: A debate paper introducing a special issue that reframes urban imagination as an enabling infrastructure for making urban futures thinkable, actionable and contestable.

title: The military spatial complex: A framework of neoliberal urban power relations
authors: Gabriel Schwake
keywords: urban development; conflict; re-militarization; neoliberalism; planning
abstract: This paper develops the concept of the military–spatial complex (MSC) to analyze how armed forces increasingly shape neoliberal urban development. While military urbanism has often been studied through the visible apparatus of surveillance and security, the MSC highlights subtler forms of militarization: the embedding of martial authority into civilian urban life through planning, land governance, and property development. Correspondingly, this paper argues that militaries today operate as hybrid actors, part sovereign apparatus, part market developer, transforming their privileged access to land and resources into mechanisms of accumulation and control. Drawing on Israel, Egypt, and Serbia, the paper demonstrates how the MSC operates across different political economies and institutional configurations. Whether the relocation of Israel Defense Forces (IDF) bases and the militarization of the Israeli south, the development of the new administrative capital in Cairo and the military-led slum clearance programs, or the housing projects for military personnel alongside the rearrangement of military sites in Serbia, these cases reflect a broader reconfiguration of state power under neoliberalism, in which rather than retreating, states restructure authority through military-led urbanism.
summary: Introduces the 'military-spatial complex' to show how armed forces act as hybrid sovereign-developer actors shaping neoliberal urban land and property in Israel, Egypt and Serbia.

title: Building a circular construction economy in New York State: A multi-level perspective study of prospects for circular cities and statewide socio-technological transition
authors: Jennifer S. Minner; Courtney Bower; Felix Heisel; Wyeth Augustine-Marceil
keywords: circular cities; circular economy; construction and demolition debris; multi-level perspective; deconstruction; building material reuse; circular transition
abstract: Globally, construction and demolition of the built environment contribute significantly to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and generate vast amounts of waste. In New York State, buildings and waste management rank as the first and fourth largest GHG emitters, collectively responsible for 43% of annual emissions. To address this, a network of academic labs and community leaders developed a vision for deconstruction and building material reuse, aiming to foster a circular construction economy. The network and the vision it promotes represent growing niches of innovation against a backdrop of COVID-19 and pandemic recovery, uneven urban development pressures, and climate and political change. Using the multi-level perspective (MLP) framework, this article explores how micro-level innovations in New York State can be scaled and institutionalized, and identifies actionable pathways and policy recommendations for advancing a circular construction economy. The result is a study of the roles of state and local governments, private industry, nonprofits, and citizens in creating a new socio-technological configuration. The authors argue that New York's circular construction initiatives, viewed through the MLP lens, are transitioning from experimentation to early stabilization, with the potential for wider diffusion. The article further examines the implications of scale and multi-level governance in advancing these innovations.
summary: Applies the multi-level perspective to trace how deconstruction and building-material-reuse niches in New York State are scaling toward a circular construction economy.

title: Only for the big players? How small and medium-sized cities seek recognition and agency in the European Union
authors: Dorothee Riese; Simon Lenhart; Benjamin Gröbe; Renate Reiter; Stephan Grohs
keywords: European Union; cities; agency; uploading; networking
abstract: Cities are affected by the European Union (EU) in multiple ways, for example when using funding or implementing EU legislation. However, they need not be just passive recipients of rules or money: cities are increasingly recognised as an integral part of the EU as illustrated by the Lisbon Treaty's new provisions on local government or programmatic developments like the Urban Agenda for the EU. But while research has focused on large cities in the EU, showing how they develop agency, for example, through lobbying for their interests, we know much less about small and medium-sized cities. Therefore, this paper asks how and under what conditions smaller cities, too, develop agency, despite less favourable conditions compared to their large counterparts. To answer these questions, the paper relies on a concept of agency that includes agency claims on the one hand and recognition of these claims on the other. Furthermore, it takes the concepts of uploading and horizontal networking from Europeanisation literature to distinguish who is addressed by agency claims. Empirically, the paper focuses on German cities, drawing on a quantitative survey and eight qualitative case studies (cities). The analysis shows that small and medium-sized cities are only partly engaged in uploading activities, but very active in horizontal networking. Through our theoretical lens, horizontal networking can be interpreted as a source of recognition that is often considered missing in uploading activities. By linking Europeanisation and city agency literatures, we also contribute to the broader literature on cities' international agency.
summary: Survey and case studies of German cities show small and medium-sized cities build EU agency mainly through horizontal networking rather than 'uploading' to Brussels.

title: Localizing challenges: Perception and localization of societal threats in two bay areas
authors: Yuhao Zhuang; Wei Luo; Axelle Miel; Christof Brandtner
keywords: community; neighborhood; inequality; diversity/cohesion/segregation; civil society organizations; managerialism
abstract: Civil society organizations (CSOs) are often portrayed as “agents” of urban change that respond to large-scale societal threats such as economic downturns, urban inequality, or environmental risks. Yet even within the same locality, CSOs differ markedly in how they perceive and localize threats. While some turn broader societal threats into actionable organizational mandates, others fail to do so. Our study proposes that managerialism, understood as the adoption of formal organizational practices, facilitates this localization by equipping CSOs with the reasoning and resources to bridge macro-level threats with organizational concerns. We test this proposition by drawing on qualitative and quantitative data from a comparative survey of randomly sampled CSOs in the two “Bay Areas” of Shenzhen, China, and San Francisco, United States—two tech-centered regions that exemplify contrasting urban regimes in the Global South and North. Adopting a two-stage selection model, we demonstrate that organizations geographically embedded in neighborhoods or cities are more likely to perceive societal threats and that managerial CSOs are subsequently more likely to localize them. Our findings highlight threat perception and localization as important precursors to organizations' involvement in urban change, contributing to the literature on organizational dimensions of urban inequality, opportunity recognition in CSOs, and the role of managerialism in sustaining urban civil society.
summary: Comparing civil-society organisations in Shenzhen and San Francisco, finds geographic embeddedness and managerialism drive whether groups perceive and localise societal threats.

title: The real estate turn in the slum: India's urban land monetization in comparative perspective
authors: Anitra Baliga; Liza Weinstein
keywords: Delhi; Mumbai; policy mobility; real estate turn; slum redevelopment; subnational comparison
abstract: This article contributes to scholarship on Asia's 'real estate turn' through a comparison of in situ 'slum redevelopment' programs underway in Delhi and Mumbai that reveals the institutional underpinnings and character of state involvement in each city. Comparative research on state-led financialization in Asia, has typically tended to treat China as the paradigmatic case, with its centralized land regimes and relatively autonomous state land managers, while India's more fragmented regimes and diffuse authority have been viewed as structural liabilities for a successful real estate turn. Drawing on a multi-method comparison of city-level programs of urban land monetization in Delhi and Mumbai, the article seeks to disaggregate national types, by highlighting subnational variation and unexpected implications of India-specific state structures. Finding more extensive land conversion and a smoother real estate turn underway in Mumbai than in Delhi, our analysis suggests that, counter to expectations from the literature, Mumbai's more agile institutional structures and opportunities for negotiation have helped ease land clearance efforts. By contrast, Delhi's more centralized control has led to diminished developer interest and heightened conflicts with residents. Unsettling prevailing understandings of the institutional conditions facilitating Asia's real estate turn, the paper argues that China-style state control can pose a liability in Indian cities, where resident demands and complex land tenure produce more contentious development politics requiring distinct state strategies.
summary: Comparing slum-redevelopment land monetization in Delhi and Mumbai, argues Mumbai's more negotiable institutions ease the 'real estate turn' while Delhi's centralized control breeds conflict.

title: Reconstruction as enclosure: The making of a propertied place in post-conflict Diyarbakır
authors: Fırat Genç
keywords: post-conflict urbanism; enclosure; property; commons; place-making
abstract: Despite the technical and humanitarian rhetoric surrounding post-conflict reconstruction, such processes frequently produce more commodified, securitized, and fragmented urban formations, generating novel configurations of power. Recent scholarship on post-conflict cities has increasingly emphasized transformations in everyday practices and lived experience in order to understand these dynamics. This article engages these debates through the case of Diyarbakır, the principal urban center of Turkey's Kurdish-populated southeast, focusing on the reconstruction of its historic core, Suriçi, following the urban clashes of 2015–2016. While existing scholarship has primarily examined how the Turkish state deployed coercion to demobilize Kurdish contentious politics, less attention has been paid to how reconstruction generated new sociabilities through more diffuse spatial practices and imaginaries. Addressing this gap, I conceptualize Suriçi's reconstruction as a process of enclosure that operated not only through authoritarian imposition from above but also through the quieter neutralization of collective praxis from within. Based on fieldwork conducted between December 2022 and February 2025, the article examines how reconstruction instituted a novel regime that transformed Suriçi into a propertied place while dismantling the infrastructures of commoning and the contingent forms of place-making through which Kurdish urban poor had sustained social and political capacities. In doing so, the article argues that reconstruction extended violence beyond destruction and displacement by reorganizing the material, social, and affective conditions of urban life. Conceptualizing reconstruction as enclosure thus offers a framework for analyzing the everyday modalities of power shaping post-conflict urbanities.
summary: Fieldwork in post-conflict Diyarbakır frames the reconstruction of Suriçi as enclosure that produced a propertied place while dismantling Kurdish commoning and place-making.

title: Residents Welfare Associations and the economic territorialization of recyclables collection markets in the Delhi metropolitan area
authors: Aman Luthra
keywords: informal recycling; neighborhood associations; urban India; spatial monopoly; competition
abstract: Resident Welfare Associations (RWAs) in urban India act like states, exercising their sovereign power over the territories they control. While a rich literature has provided a deep understanding of the social regulation of neighborhood spaces by RWAs, their role in the economic regulation of informal labor remains underexplored, even though neighborhoods are vibrant sites of a range of informal economic activities that residents depend upon. Drawing on interviews with 33 kabariwalas (informal workers who buy recyclables from households) and 17 dealers (to whom kabariwalas sell those recyclables), and an analysis of balance sheets of 16 RWAs in the Delhi metropolitan area, this article shows how territorial control over neighborhood space allows RWAs to expand and exercise their state-like powers. By virtue of having monopoly rights over the neighborhood space, RWAs regulate: (a) the labor of kabariwalas by requiring permits; (b) the flows of the commodity (recyclable materials) by only allowing permitted kabariwalas to enter the neighborhood; and (c) the firms (dealers) whom some RWAs contract to provide collection services. Increasing competition in this sector because of macroeconomic shifts makes permits and contracts desirable for kabariwalas and dealers, and also allows some RWAs to capture monopoly rents. In making these contributions, this article not only adds to our knowledge about a hitherto underexamined sector of the informal economy of waste in urban India, but it also provides insight into the processes of economic territorialization of neighborhoods as a crucial part of the process of neighborhood state formation.
summary: Shows how Delhi Resident Welfare Associations act as neighborhood 'states', using territorial control to regulate informal recyclables collectors and capture monopoly rents.

title: Echoes of growth: Demographic decoupling and path-dependent legacies in urban expansion across Europe
authors: Alexandra Sandu
keywords: urban expansion; demographic decoupling; European cities; path-dependent development; echo urbanisation
abstract: Urban expansion across Europe increasingly unfolds under heterogeneous demographic conditions. While population change has long structured interpretations of urban growth, recent evidence suggests urban expansion no longer adjusts to contemporary demographic dynamics as it once did. This article examines urban expansion across 181 European Functional Urban Areas between 2000 and 2025, with particular attention to changes after 2015. Using stacked regression models, it identifies an acceleration in urban expansion after 2015 alongside evidence of demographic decoupling. A complementary cross-sectional analysis conditions post-2015 urban expansion on earlier development trajectories, allowing deviations from historically expected patterns to be identified. The article refers to this pattern as echo urbanisation, a benchmark-relative diagnostic that captures urban expansion exceeding what prior development paths and demographic change would predict. The results show that echo urbanisation cuts across population growth and decline and is not confined to post-socialist Europe, pointing to a broader European regime of demographically decoupled urban expansion, within which echo-driven expansion is widespread. It complements existing expansion indicators by flagging cities accelerating beyond expected paths that conventional density, sprawl or demographic-mismatch measures may miss.
summary: Analysing 181 European functional urban areas, identifies post-2015 'echo urbanisation' where built-up expansion accelerates and decouples from underlying demographic change.

title: Gender quotas and female entrepreneurship: evidence from Italian municipalities
authors: Enrique Carreras; Elena Grinza; Alessandro Manello; Noemi Oggero
abstract: This article estimates the effect of gender quotas in local politics on female entrepreneurship. We exploit the introduction of a 2012 Italian reform mandating female candidate representation in municipal elections for municipalities above 5,000 inhabitants, and implement a difference-in-differences event-study design comparing municipalities first exposed to the reform with never-treated municipalities, restricting attention to a narrow population window around the binding threshold. Using a balanced panel of 607 municipalities observed from 2007 to 2022, we find that quota exposure increases female entrepreneurship by approximately 2–3 per cent. The effect is concentrated in regions with lower baseline gender equality, consistent with a catch-up mechanism whereby female political visibility matters most where it is most novel. We find no evidence that the effect operates through increased municipal spending on childcare or social-care services, providing no support for the most natural policy channels. The evidence is instead broadly consistent with a role-model interpretation: the increased visibility of women in local political leadership appears to shift the perceived feasibility of entrepreneurial entry among women in gender-unequal environments.
summary: A diff-in-diff study of Italy's 2012 municipal gender-quota reform finds it raised female entrepreneurship by 2-3%, especially in less gender-equal regions, via a role-model channel.

title: Transport mode and the geography of exchange rate pass-through
authors: Davide Del Prete; Aminur Rahman; Edoardo Tolva
abstract: This article examines how transport mode shapes the geography of exchange rate pass-through (ERPT) within Global Value Chains. Using transaction-level customs data from the Bangladeshi garment sector (2018–24), we exploit the sharp depreciation of the Bangladeshi Taka in 2022 to compare maritime and air-based trade corridors through Chittagong seaport and Dhaka airport. We show that ERPT to exporter prices is incomplete on average and systematically lower in buyer–seller relationships that rely more intensively on air transport. This differential is concentrated in destinations and products where delivery speed is especially valuable, notably European fast-fashion markets.
summary: Using Bangladeshi garment customs data around the 2022 Taka depreciation, shows exchange-rate pass-through is lower on air-transport trade corridors where delivery speed matters.

title: How evolving institutions shaped China's economic geography
authors: Wen-Tai Hsu; Jing Li; Lin Ma
abstract: This article reviews how evolving institutions shaped China's economic geography since the reform era. The review covers three areas. First, we examine reductions in spatial frictions through hukou reform and transportation expansion, and their effects on migration, productivity, welfare, and spatial inequality. Second, we review urban and rural land reforms, housing reform, land-based public finance, and the promotion tournament, which improved allocation but distorted land use, infrastructure, and local debt. Third, we discuss place-based policies and agglomeration, including special economic zones as bundled institutions combining economic incentives with political support. We highlight China's contribution to core questions in economic geography.
summary: A review of how post-reform institutions - hukou and transport, land and housing reforms, and place-based policies - shaped China's economic geography.

title: The economic footprint of short-term rentals on local businesses: evidence from Portugal
authors: Ronize Cruz; Francisco Nobre; João Pereira dos Santos
abstract: We analyze how the proliferation of short-term rentals (STRs) affects firm survival, performance, and entry in two European cities with high STR density. Using administrative firm-level accounting data, a shift-share instrument, and an event-study design, we find that STR growth increases exit rates among underperforming firms, while surviving firms experience relative gains in sales and profits, with no effects on employment or investment. Corporate tax revenues accruing to the central government also rise, pointing to broader fiscal spillovers. STR expansion stimulates entrepreneurship, though new entrants face higher costs and lower initial profitability. These findings underscore the nuanced impacts of tourism-driven demand shocks on urban economic ecosystems.
summary: Firm-level evidence from two high-density Portuguese cities shows short-term-rental growth raises exit among weak firms while boosting surviving firms' sales, profits and entrepreneurship.

title: The local economic and innovation spillover effects of mega firm subsidiaries
authors: Fanghua Li
abstract: This article studies the local economic and innovation spillovers from subsidiaries of domestically large firms in China. I construct a geo-referenced dataset linking subsidiaries of publicly listed firms (PLFSs) to the universe of patent applications and nighttime lights (NTL), and iteratively select newly established PLFSs in areas without pre-existing nearby listed-firm subsidiaries. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design that compares earlier- and later-entry locations, I estimate the local effect of a single PLFS at a granular spatial scale. PLFS entry increases local economic activity and innovation, raising NTL by 26.4 per cent and local patenting by 95 per cent within 2.5 km. Firm-level decomposition shows both incumbent innovation gains and more innovative entry, suggesting localized innovation growth rather than pure relocation. Further inventor-level analysis provides evidence of creative destruction, as local innovation paths shift, with pre-existing inventors being replaced by new ones. These findings highlight the role of mega-firm subsidiaries in driving local economies and inform the design of firm-specific place-based policies.
summary: Geo-referenced Chinese data show that entry of a large-firm subsidiary sharply raises nearby economic activity and patenting within 2.5 km, with evidence of local creative destruction.

title: Geopolitical Integration vs. fragmentation: the economic geography of disparities in Europe
authors: Roberta Capello; Andrea Caragliu; Roberto Dellisanti
abstract: Rising geopolitical tensions and emerging skepticism against globalization cast doubt on the future evolution of European regional economic growth. We simulate regional GDP growth rates for all NUTS2 regions in the EU27+UK for the period 2021–2035, using the MASST5 model, in two extreme scenarios; the first, termed “Cohesive EU in an Integrated World”; the second, labeled “Nationalistic EU in a Fragmented World”. Results document substantial spatial heterogeneity in the outcomes of the two scenarios, with Integration leading to superior economic performance but at the cost of increasing regional disparities triggered by higher growth opportunities for national champions.
summary: MASST5 simulations of EU27+UK NUTS2 growth to 2035 show geopolitical integration outperforms fragmentation but widens regional disparities favouring national champions.

title: Contested clocks: uniformity and resistance in global time zone standardization
authors: Thomas Sigler; Matthew Zook
abstract: This paper analyzes the political processes by which time zones are locally managed and changed, and how these are converted into global standards in the absence of an international time zone standardization body. We argue that the persistence of a singular global time zone standard depends on technical infrastructures operating largely independently of state and non-state actors. The apparent neutrality of time zones as technical artifacts supporting international coordination required for economic globalization obscures locally negotiated practices shaped by social, biological, political, and economic rationales. The study highlights how globally uniform technical systems can coexist with locally differentiated yet politically contested practices.
summary: Analyses how locally negotiated, politically contested time-zone practices are converted into a uniform global standard sustained by technical infrastructures.

title: The impacts of high-speed Internet access on monopsony power
authors: Li Yu; Yurou Wang; Jingxiang Song; Mengjun Yang
abstract: While the literature on the Internet's economic impact often focuses on skill-biased technological change, less is known about its effect on employer market power. This article asks whether the arrival of high-speed Internet can weaken firms' monopsony power, particularly in a developing country context. Using firm-level data from China and leveraging the quasi-exogenous expansion of broadband Internet around the year 2000 in a difference-in-differences design, we find that broadband access leads to a significant reduction in firm-level wage markdowns. This effect is driven by four channels: reduced search frictions, increased labor mobility, enhanced firm entry, and stronger worker bargaining power. The resulting decline in labor market power is associated with a higher labor share of income and an increased pass-through of productivity gains to wages. Our findings challenge the conventional view that information and communications technology exacerbates inequality, demonstrating that by promoting labor market competition, it can also have a significant pro-labor equalizing effect.
summary: Chinese firm-level evidence shows broadband Internet expansion reduced employers' wage markdowns and monopsony power, raising the labour share via lower search frictions and mobility.

title: Europe's two towers: the uneven regional geography of telecommunication standard essential patents
authors: Bernardo S Buarque; Ronald B Davies; Ryan M Hynes; Gianluca Tarasconi; Dieter F Kogler
abstract: This paper explores the role of Standard Essential Patents (SEPs) in shaping technological development and regional innovation in Europe's telecommunications sector. Results reveal strong geographic concentration: Helsinki and Stockholm account for one-third of all cellular SEPs. Unlike other technologies, SEP distribution does not scale with population or prior technological expertise. Findings suggest a “rich-get-richer” dynamic where early leadership reinforces future dominance; however, this advantage weakens across technological generations. This study offers new insights into standardization's spatial dynamics and underscores the need for long-term perspectives when modeling technological competition and diffusion.
summary: Maps Europe's cellular standard-essential patents, finding Helsinki and Stockholm hold a third and a 'rich-get-richer' concentration that weakens across technology generations.

title: Intellectual property rights and the efficiency of international production networks: evidence from the automotive industry
authors: Giuseppe Cavaliere; Graziano Moramarco; Alireza Naghavi
abstract: This study investigates the potential benefits of intellectual property rights (IPR) institutions for international production networks. Using unique data on manufacturer-supplier linkages in the automotive industry, we establish a positive empirical relationship between the efficiency of vehicle producers and IPR protection in their suppliers' locations. Notably, IPR do not have the same impact on ownership networks as knowledge is internalized within the boundaries of the firm. We confirm that the results are not driven by other firm- or country-level characteristics, and address potential endogeneity concerns by employing a novel gravity-based IV approach using geographical distance and language proximity.
summary: Automotive manufacturer-supplier data show stronger IPR protection in suppliers' locations improves vehicle producers' efficiency, except within firm-owned networks.

title: Power and governance in global value chains: upgrading of Pakistani mobile application vendors in an era of platforms
authors: Umair S Choksy; Mark P Dallas; Matthew Alford; Yusuf Kurt
abstract: This study integrates Gereffi et al.'s governance framework with Dallas et al.'s power typology to explain the functional upgrading of low-capability suppliers under increasing industry complexity. We argue that governance alone cannot account for upgrading in platform-mediated global value chains, without accounting for how institutional and constitutive power interact. By examining Pakistani mobile application vendors in Apple's iOS and Google's Android ecosystems, we demonstrate that while platform codification facilitates initial learning, it does not by itself lead to functional upgrading. Instead, upgrading depends on both platform codification and suppliers' ability to gain legitimacy, enabling shifts from captive to modular governance.
summary: Case study of Pakistani mobile-app vendors in the iOS and Android ecosystems shows functional upgrading requires both platform codification and suppliers gaining legitimacy.

title: The effect of transaction partners' location on firms' relocation choice: a natural experiment using a massive earthquake in Japan
authors: Arito Ono; Daisuke Miyakawa; Kaoru Hosono; Hirofumi Uchida; Iichiro Uesugi
abstract: This study examines the role that the location of transaction partners plays in firms' location choice. To alleviate endogeneity concerns, we use data of Japanese firms that were forced to relocate due to the massive Tohoku earthquake in 2011. We find that firms tended to relocate to cities where their customers were located rather than where their suppliers were located. Firms also tended to relocate to cities where their banks were located. The positive role that the presence of customers and banks played in firms' relocation choice was weaker if their customers and banks were also damaged by the earthquake.
summary: Using firms displaced by Japan's 2011 Tohoku earthquake, shows relocation choices gravitate toward the cities of customers and banks rather than suppliers.

title: The making of sustainability standards in the Global South: power, contestation, and global value chain governance
authors: Natalie J Langford; Matthew Alford; Khalid Nadvi
abstract: Sustainability standards are central to the governance of global value chains, shaping labour conditions and environmental practices. Yet established scholarship privileges standards originating in the Global North, creating a significant gap in understanding how sustainability governance is shaped for and within the Global South. Through a comparative analysis of standards in South African wine and Indian tea, this article shows that Southern standards are produced through relational and trans-scalar struggles embedded in uneven material power relations within and across value chains. By tracing their interaction with established Northern regimes, the article reconceptualises sustainability governance as a contested and polycentric field.
summary: Comparing South African wine and Indian tea standards, reframes Global South sustainability governance as a contested, polycentric field shaped by trans-scalar power struggles.

title: Smartphones, information, and bargaining power: Evidence from pastoral areas in China
authors: Min Liu; Kaixing Huang; Jianyu Yu; Shukun Wang; Weidong Wang; Xiaohua Yu; David Wuepper
abstract: This study examines the impact of smartphone adoption on livestock trading in pastoral China. We develop a bargaining and search model with two mechanisms: information discovery, which reduces herders' search costs, and information posting, which expands market access. Using household survey data, we find that smartphone adoption increases selling prices. Mechanism analysis shows that traditional phone functions improve information access, while smartphone-specific features, especially information posting, enhance bargaining power by expanding selling channels and trader access. These findings demonstrate that digital technologies affect market outcomes not only through improved information access but also by reshaping bargaining structures and market participation.
summary: Household survey evidence from pastoral China shows smartphone adoption raises livestock selling prices by improving information access and, via posting features, herders' bargaining power.

title: Commodity price risk in phosphorus recycling investments
authors: Jan-Philip R Uhlemann; Alfons Oude Lansink; James J Leahy; Jean-Paul Chavas; Tobias Dalhaus
abstract: There are optimistic targets for phosphorus recycling from waste streams to solve environmental and supply issues simultaneously. The recycling process requires high energy inputs, thus the joint distribution of (input) energy and (output) fertilizer commodity prices is a crucial determinant of the profitability of investing. We propose a methodology to model the investment risk and price dependencies using quantile vector autoregression and copulas. Moreover, we show that standard approaches overestimate the variance of investment returns. Finally, we find that phosphorus recycling investments are only profitable with substantial subsidies or savings on disposal expenditures.
summary: Models energy-and-fertilizer price dependencies with quantile VAR and copulas, finding phosphorus-recycling investments are profitable only with substantial subsidies or disposal savings.

title: Deep pockets needed? Financial health and organic certification adoption in the European Union
authors: Lina M Tennhardt; Martina Bozzola; Christian Grovermann
abstract: Adoption of organic certification across the EU remains lower than anticipated, with financial risks during and after conversion often cited as barriers. We examine whether farms with stronger financial health (FH) are associated with a higher likelihood of adopting organic certification. Using Farm Accountancy Data Network panel data from 2014 to 2018 covering 24,797 EU farms, we classify farms by FH and apply matching and logit regression to analyse the relationship between preconversion FH and organic certification adoption. Results show no clear association between FH and adoption, while preconversion land-use intensity consistently correlates with organic certification uptake, suggesting relevance for EU policy design efforts.
summary: FADN panel data on 24,797 EU farms find preconversion financial health is not clearly linked to organic certification adoption, whereas lower land-use intensity is.

title: Alternative Agricultural Carbon Border Adjustment and Climate Club Designs: a Quantitative Assessment
authors: Lærke Jensbye; Wusheng Yu; Francesco Clora
abstract: We analyze alternative agricultural carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) designs across three dimensions (participating countries, emission intensity, and carbon price). We find that an agricultural CBAM by the European Union (or an expanded climate club consisting of the EU and other countries) has minor global agricultural GHG emission implications but protects the most emission intensive domestic production. Nevertheless, having a larger climate club imposing CBAM tariffs and applying exporters' emission intensities are more effective in lowering global emissions. Compared to national carbon prices, harmonized carbon prices at climate club level can reduce trade disruptions while attaining similar emission reduction outcomes.
summary: Quantitative assessment of agricultural carbon border adjustment designs finds larger climate clubs and harmonized carbon prices cut global emissions more effectively with fewer trade disruptions.

title: The role of specialized knowledge and 'know-how' for firm productivity: Evidence from the equine sector
authors: Pia Nilsson; Hans Andersson; Tobias Heldt
abstract: Using matched employer–employee data, we examine how workforce knowledge characteristics relate to firm productivity in the equine sector. Using panel data on Swedish equine firms from 2010 to 2022, we construct measures of workforce composition, including occupation-specific education, accumulated work experience and knowledge diversity. The results show that access to occupation-specific human capital is positively associated with productivity, with substantial heterogeneity across firms. Knowledge effects are stronger among firms specializing in horse racing than in breeding, highlighting differences in the role of human capital across production orientations. The findings have implications for policy and firms' investment decisions.
summary: Matched employer-employee panel data on Swedish equine firms show occupation-specific human capital raises productivity, more strongly in horse racing than breeding.

title: The relationship between pesticides and risk in apple production
authors: M Casati; L Arata; A Varacca; P Sckokai
abstract: We examine how pesticide expenditure relates to the probability distribution of yield and revenue per hectare in apple production in northern Italy. Using a flexible moment-based approach, we find that pesticide expenditure is negatively associated with downside risk in yield and revenue, whereas late frosts are positively associated with downside risk in yield. Sensitivity analyses show that mean-equation estimates are robust to unobserved confounders, while negative semi-variance models are less robust overall. Only the pesticide–expected outcome relationship appears plausibly causal. Therefore, conclusions about pesticides as risk-increasing or risk-decreasing inputs should be made with caution.
summary: A moment-based analysis of northern Italian apple farms finds pesticide expenditure reduces downside yield and revenue risk while late frosts increase it, urging caution on causal claims.

title: Beyond determinism: Accounting for weather variability in the carbon pricing debate for EU agriculture
authors: Davit Stepanyan; Sebastian Neuenfeldt; Alisa Spiegel; Mareike Söder; Julio G Fournier Gabela; Florian Freund; Claudia Heidecke; Bernhard Osterburg; Alexander Gocht
abstract: Agriculture accounts for 11 per cent of EU greenhouse gas emissions, yet sectoral emissions have stagnated over the past two decades. This paper evaluates carbon pricing in EU agriculture by integrating stochastic yield variability into the CAPRI model. We assess how different carbon price levels affect emissions and outcome uncertainty. Results show that carbon pricing reduces emissions, and higher price levels are associated with lower uncertainty in policy outcomes. While expected results remain similar to deterministic simulations, stochastic modeling reveals greater regional and sectoral heterogeneity. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for production risk when designing agricultural climate policies.
summary: Integrating stochastic yield variability into the CAPRI model shows carbon pricing cuts EU agricultural emissions, with higher prices reducing outcome uncertainty but revealing regional heterogeneity.

title: Market integration and the impact of violence on trade networks: Evidence from Nigeria
authors: Jiawen Liu; Michael Olabisi; Mywish K Maredia
abstract: Market integration is critical for food security in developing economies facing socio-political instability. Using weekly price data from ninety-seven Nigerian markets, this study investigates how violent conflict influences price dynamics between market pairs. Results reveal that frequent violent events have limited short-term effects on price transmission, and changes in conflict intensity do not significantly disrupt price adjustments. Markets with stronger trade connections demonstrate greater resilience by leveraging alternative trade routes. These findings highlight the role of market connectivity in maintaining trade efficiency, suggesting that policies that enhance market networks can strengthen resilience and improve food security.
summary: Weekly price data from 97 Nigerian markets show violent conflict has limited effect on price transmission and that better-connected markets are more resilient via alternative trade routes.

title: Combining stated and revealed preferences for valuing attributes associated with organic chicken meat
authors: Jose Eduardo Ribeiro; Adelina Gschwandtner; Cesar Revoredo-Giha
abstract: This paper examines consumer willingness to pay (WTP) for attributes of organic chicken meat in the UK, a product experiencing increasing popularity both domestically and internationally. We combine stated preference (SP) data from a discrete choice experiment with revealed preference (RP) data from supermarket scanner transactions in a joint estimation framework. This approach mitigates common limitations of analysing SP and RP data separately, such as hypothetical bias in SP and multicollinearity in RP. Using a heteroskedastic conditional logit model with interaction terms, we estimate WTP values that account for both preference heterogeneity and scale differences across datasets. Results indicate that consumers assign a substantial premium to the organic attribute, with joint estimates approximately 9 per cent higher than those based solely on SP data and more than double those from RP. These findings underscore the importance of integrating SP and RP data to inform evidence-based food policy.
summary: Jointly estimating stated and revealed preferences for UK organic chicken finds a substantial organic premium, with combined estimates well above single-source approaches.

title: Conservation auctions: An online double constraint reverse auction experiment
authors: Adrien Coiffard; Raphaèle Préget; Mabel Tidball
abstract: Conservation auctions are designed to allocate payments for environmental services to voluntary farmers. The auctioneer may announce either the maximum number of contracts (target-constrained auction) or, more commonly, the total budget available (budget-constrained auction). Building on previous work that compared these two formats, we introduce a new double-constraint auction, where both constraints—set at the same levels as in the benchmarks—are simultaneously disclosed to participants. Using the same experimental methodology, we assess performance consistent with a generic policy objective: maximizing environmental benefits while minimizing expenditures. On average, the double-constraint auction outperforms both target- and budget-constrained formats.
summary: An online reverse-auction experiment shows a new 'double-constraint' conservation auction, disclosing both budget and contract caps, outperforms target- and budget-constrained formats.

title: Time preferences in rural economies: A systematic global review
authors: Vanessa Berghoff; Daniel Hermann
abstract: Time preferences shape decisions about resource use, investment and sustainability, yet evidence on how they are measured in rural field settings remains fragmented. This systematic literature review covers 67 studies eliciting time preferences among rural populations, focusing on farmers and fishers. We map the theoretical models used, compare elicitation methods and experimental designs, and synthesise reported patterns. The review documents substantial heterogeneity in how time preferences are conceptualised and measured, and highlights recurring methodological and reporting challenges that limit comparability across contexts. For more reliable, replicable and policy-relevant research, we propose a structured reporting guide.
summary: A systematic review of 67 studies eliciting time preferences among farmers and fishers documents wide methodological heterogeneity and proposes a structured reporting guide.

title: Can reducing technical inefficiencies of pesticides achieve environmental impact targets? The case of Dutch arable farms
authors: Emmanuel Ahovi; Jaap Sok; Alfons Oude Lansink
abstract: Farmers manage each type of pesticide differently, given the varying risks they address. As both damage-abating and polluting inputs, we have incorporated their negative impacts into a non-parametric framework to estimate the technical inefficiency of different pesticides and environmental inefficiency of Dutch arable farms from 2011 to 2021. Results suggest that farmers are more efficient in using insecticides rather than fungicides, herbicides and other pesticides, and have a higher potential to reduce negative pesticide impacts on aquatic organisms compared to soil organisms. However, even with full efficiency, the vast majority of farmers would not meet acceptable pesticide impact levels that are seen as sustainable in the long run.
summary: A non-parametric efficiency analysis of Dutch arable farms finds that even fully efficient pesticide use would leave most farms short of long-run sustainable impact targets.

title: Firm-level innovation, productivity, and efficiency in riskful business environments: A case study of agribusiness in El Salvador
authors: Gabriel Rosero; José Salguero; Bernhard Brümmer
abstract: Agribusinesses contribute 40–70 percent of the total value added in the food value chain of developing countries; however, they remain under-researched. We investigate whether firm-level innovation improves economic performance using World Bank Enterprise Surveys for El Salvador. We extend the Crépon–Duguet–Mairesse model with a selectivity-corrected stochastic frontier and a metafrontier framework. We find that innovation increases potential total sales and reduces the technology gap, but does not improve technical efficiency. This suggests that, without complementary managerial and institutional support—particularly in contexts where insecurity imposes high operational and opportunity costs—the benefits of innovation do not necessarily lead to productivity gains.
summary: Using World Bank Enterprise Survey data for El Salvador, finds agribusiness innovation raises potential sales and narrows the technology gap but does not improve technical efficiency.

title: A Spatial Clustering Approach of Economic Activities: An Application to the Agribusiness Sector in Brazil's Midwest Region
authors: Rosario Junior
abstract: The spatial distribution of economic activities is central to regional economics. However, empirical tools for comparing industries based on the similarity of their spatial distributions remain limited. Traditional cluster analysis typically ignores geographical distance and connectivity, while spatial methods focus on clustering places rather than economic activities. This paper addresses this methodological gap by proposing a framework for clustering economic activities based on the similarity of their spatial distributions, explicitly incorporating geographical space. The Wasserstein distance is employed with a geographically informed cost matrix, that is, the Shimbel matrix, to measure the effort required to transform one activity's spatial distribution into another. This approach is compared with traditional non-spatial distance metrics through an illustrative example and then applied to 272 agribusiness activities across 466 municipalities in Brazil's Midwest region from 2013 to 2021. The results reveal four main clusters: one spread throughout the region and others concentrated in northern, southern, or eastern areas, consistent with regional endowments, historical trajectories, and agro-industrial linkages. The case study suggests that the approach offers a useful complementary tool for identifying co-distributed activities and spatially similar industrial patterns, with implications for regional development analysis, place-based policy design and future studies of economic linkages and shock exposure.
summary: A spatial clustering method is applied to identify agglomerations of agribusiness economic activity across Brazil's Midwest region.

title: Higher Education Expansion and the Pattern of Regional Specialization: Evidence From China
authors: Ma
keywords: college expansion; comparative advantage; factor endowment; human capital; regional specialization
abstract: This paper investigates how the expansion of higher education influences regional patterns of regional specialization. Exploiting a natural experiment arising from the large-scale college expansion in China, we apply a triple-difference (DDD) approach to identify the causal impact. Our findings reveal that industries with greater demands for human capital tend to account for a larger output share in cities that experienced more significant college expansion. This effect is primarily driven by the growth of existing firms, rather than the entry or exit of firms. Sub-group analyses further indicate that firms with educated and skilled workforces, and those investing in staff training and R&D, were more affected. Strong evidence highlights labor productivity improvements and R&D-driven TFP gains as key mechanisms, with no support for the technology adoption channel.
summary: Examines how China's expansion of higher education has reshaped patterns of regional economic specialization.

title: Bridging the Regional Innovation Gap: The Driving Role of Digital Governance in China
authors: Li
keywords: cross-regional capital flow; digital governance; institutional transaction cost; market integration; regional innovation gap
abstract: Digital governance (DG), functioning as a critical driver in regional innovation ecosystems, effectively promotes spatial equity and innovation equilibrium. Based on a panel of Chinese cities from 2010 to 2023, we treat the Internet + Government Services policy as a quasi-natural experiment of DG and apply a difference-in-differences model to analyze the impact of the DG on the regional innovation gaps (RIG). Results indicate that DG significantly narrows RIG, particularly in cities with advanced digital infrastructure, non-shrinking population, large-scale cities and abundant human capital. The mechanism analysis demonstrates that DG narrows RIG by eliminating disparities in the innovation environment and facilitating the cross-regional flow of innovation factors. This convergence effect predominantly originates from reducing RIG between developed and less-developed regions. Additionally, DG exerts a more pronounced promotional effect on innovation development in central municipal districts, while its effect on county-level areas remains relatively limited, thereby exacerbating the RIG within cities. These findings offer substantial implications for formulating targeted DG strategies to foster spatially balanced regional innovation development.
summary: Assesses how digital governance narrows regional innovation gaps across Chinese regions.

title: The Conditional Impact of Recent Economic, Global, and Technological Challenges on Productivity Growth in EU Regions
authors: Tsiapa
keywords: EU regions; fourth industrial revolution; global value chains; regional productivity growth; resilience
abstract: The global landscape is marked by ongoing transformations and abrupt shifts driven by new forms of globalisation through the expansion of Global Value Chains, the Fourth Industrial Revolution, and recurring crises. This paper examines the role of these key economic, global, and technological challenges in shaping productivity growth across EU regions, assessing both the nature and variability of their impacts at the sub-national level. The novelty of the paper lies in its ability to uncover the complex dynamics and pronounced spatial variations often masked by national aggregates, many of which remain underexplored. The results show that productivity imbalances stem from economic challenges, where resilience depends on the adaptation and adaptability of regions anchored in the secondary sector; from global challenges, as integration imposes limits and leads to losses through overexposure and dependence on Global Value Chains via backward linkages; and from technological challenges, as the new industrial revolution drives higher productivity gains in the most digitally intensive sectors of manufacturing. By demonstrating that regions differ not only in their exposure to these challenges but also in their capacity to adapt and thrive, the paper provides valuable insights for policymakers aiming to address regional disparities and foster more balanced, sustainable productivity growth across the EU.
summary: Analyzes how recent economic, global, and technological shocks conditionally affect productivity growth in EU regions.

title: Challenging the Pollution Haven Effect: Insights From the Yangtze River Delta's Regional Integration
authors: Sun
keywords: environmental regulation; pollution haven hypothesis; pollution transfer; regional integration; Yangtze River Delta
abstract: This study critically revisits the Pollution Haven Hypothesis (PHH), which suggests that stringent environmental regulations drive polluting industries to relocate to areas with laxer standards. Focusing on the context of China's national strategy for Yangtze River Delta (YRD) regional integration, we employ a difference-in-differences-in-differences (DDD) estimation approach alongside multi-level panel data from 2003 to 2013 that exploits spatial and temporal variations in YRD expansion. We investigate whether regional integration facilitates the relocation of pollution-intensive industries (PII) to less-developed areas within the YRD. The analysis reveals that the integration boundary of YRD actually inhibits the transfer of polluting industries to peripheral cities in the region, though the trend of polluting industries shifting toward regional boundaries has strengthened. Thus the integration contributes to reducing the risk of becoming pollution havens for peripheral cities. These findings challenge the conventional PHH framework, indicating that regional integration can mitigate the PHH effects and limit the internal dispersion of pollution. Our results offer new insights into the influence of regional integration on the geographic distribution of polluting industries, highlighting the potential of coordinated regional governance to achieve both economic and environmental objectives.
summary: Tests the pollution-haven hypothesis in the context of regional economic integration in China's Yangtze River Delta.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: PLANET AT THE END OF THE CITY: How Climate Changes the Nature of Urban Theory
authors: Goh
keywords: cities; climate change; critical urban theory; rural-urban entanglements; the planetary; urban politics
abstract: Is the city good or bad for climate? You would think we would know. Stories abound in newspaper op-eds, policymaker commentaries and climate reports about the presumed environmental benefits of cities. For critical urban theorists the goodness and greenness of the city is not always so evident, but so far critical urban theory seems unable to shift the emerging consensus about the state of the city at the possible end of the planet. I examine urban theory in a space and time of planetary boundaries. Bringing critical urban theory into dialog with ideas from ecological economics and land change science about urbanization and a not-boundless planet, I show that foundational ideas about cities have been externalizing, not only as processes but also as concepts. Paying closer attention to the nature of socionatural change and critical urban theorists’ own theoretical precepts, I probe the limitations and possibilities of particular urban theoretical frameworks to take on problems of planetary nature. I end with a proposition for a meshwork of urban frameworks—interfaces between urban frameworks and other ways of seeing processes of planetary significance—and a view on the political stakes of a better way to see city and planet.
summary: Argues that climate change fundamentally reshapes the conceptual basis of urban theory.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: INFRASTRUCTURAL EXTENSIONS: Rethinking Infrastructure in Urban Studies
authors: Marvin
keywords: care; cyber-physical; elemental; extended infrastructure; infrastructural modulation; multispecies; neurotechnology
abstract: This essay explores how contemporary urban infrastructure is being conceptually and operationally extended into new domains. Across five key arenas—elemental, care, more-than-human, cyber-physical and the neurotechnical—we trace how infrastructures are no longer confined to traditional networked systems but instead permeate and co-compose atmospheres, bodies, ecologies and cognition. These extensions reconfigure what infrastructure is and does, operating as agents of socio-technical modulation under conditions of planetary crisis. We argue that these emergent infrastructural forms constitute a significant shift, where the capacity to live, sense, feel and adapt is increasingly subject to infrastructural capture, stratification and control. The essay reflects on the risks of conceptual overreach while asserting that a more expansive understanding of infrastructure is necessary to grasp contemporary urban governance. We conclude by proposing a renewed research agenda for urban infrastructure studies that is interdisciplinary, ethically attuned and responsive to the operationalization of life itself under conditions of turbulence and inequality.
summary: Proposes a rethinking of how infrastructure is conceptualized within urban studies.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: THE URBANOLOGISTS COME TO TOWN: Professional Life and Work in the Urban Solutions Industry
authors: Bok
keywords: critical urban theory; global ethnography; professionals; technology; urban governance; urbanology
abstract: This article charts the upsurge of an eclectic global community of professionals new to the field of urban policy and governance, animated by playful and celebratory attitudes towards cities and urbanization: the urbanologists. It contributes to debates in critical urban theory and critical ethnographies of technology to problematize innovation in contemporary society and economy. Exceeding the strictures of technocratic and technical practice, urbanological approaches are evocative of a distinctive context of global urban governance. Drawing on twenty-three months of multi-sited ethnographic data, the analysis explores urbanology as the dominant ideology of mainstream urban governance across the global North and South. Doing so discloses four dimensions of urbanology: a performative fetishization of urbanization; a motivation to break down institutional and sectoral barriers in urban governance; a projectification of urban space; and a persistent obfuscation of questions of inequality, politics and history. It explains, ultimately, the prevalence of scattershot solutions, short-termism and the strategic avoidance of accountability as power is exercised over cities from afar to systemically circumvent transformative possibilities. Such an approach to global urban governance amounts to a form of crisis-management that is motivated, above all, to contain and displace difficult global challenges onto the spatial scales of the urban.
summary: Investigates the professional practices and labor of consultants in the urban solutions industry.

title: Online platform entry and food safety risk: Evidence from the Chinese restaurant industry
authors: Ma
keywords: food safety; machine learning; online food delivery; restaurant
abstract: The online food delivery (OFD) industry has witnessed substantial global expansion. In this study, we examine how OFD platforms in China affect the food safety conditions of restaurants. Given the difficulty quantifying food safety, we first propose a machine learning approach to construct a restaurant-specific food safety risk indicator based on online customer reviews. The approach features high-frequency continuous measurements with complete geographic coverage. We also conducted an event study and found that the food safety risk in restaurants decreased significantly in response to OFD platforms, with the effects concentrated in the five quarters including the entry period. Our mechanism analysis suggests that this improvement might come from extended market information, strengthened market competition, and heightened supervision and regulation. The impact is also more pronounced for chain restaurants, restaurants that are relatively popular and expensive, and restaurants offering low-risk food items.
summary: Estimates how entry of online food-delivery platforms affects food safety risk among Chinese restaurants.

title: How cold is too cold? A theoretical analysis of the optimal trigger for index insurance for frost damage to crops
authors: Prakasha Kumar
keywords: agricultural economics; crop insurance; index insurance
abstract: Crop insurance is undoubtedly an extremely valuable element in protecting agricultural businesses, but in many cases standard indemnity-based products have had very low uptake due to high transaction costs elevating premiums to unaffordable levels. Index insurance options in which coverage is written on a publicly observable “trigger” (involving much lower transaction costs) have begun to fill the void. In almost all of the previous economics literature on index insurance, the only variable that the insurance demander is permitted to choose is the payment to be received should the index trigger value be verified. However, it is clear that the trigger value itself is an integral element in the contract, and it is an element about which the insurance demander has clear preferences. In this article, we analyze the optimal demand for index insurance under the assumption that the demander can choose both the payment to be received if the index trigger is satisfied and the trigger value itself. We find that there is always an interior solution to this problem. We also consider the market equilibria that emerge under a variety of settings in regard to the position of the insurer. The article is cast within the scope of insurance for frost damage to a crop, but all of the results are directly applicable to any peril for which a publicly observable signal exists. The article shows that allowing the demander to choose both indemnity and trigger value should increase uptake of index insurance products.
summary: Develops a theoretical framework for setting the optimal temperature trigger of index insurance against crop frost damage.

title: Unemployment-Linked Food Hardships in Medicaid Expansion and Nonexpansion States During the COVID-19 Pandemic
authors: Benitez
abstract: Job losses (e.g., layoffs, furloughs) during the COVID-19 pandemic were associated with higher levels of food hardship including food insufficiency, marginal food insufficiency, and difficulty affording food. However, we find the association between pandemic-related job loss and food hardship was smaller in states with expanded Medicaid eligibility compared against job losses in states that did not expand Medicaid. Our key findings are larger among higher-income households and childless adults–groups generally beyond Medicaid's core low-income population, and they suggest that Medicaid's value as an antipoverty program complements other safety net programs during periods of unexpected material hardship.
summary: Compares unemployment-related food hardship across Medicaid expansion and nonexpansion states during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Networked Regional Resilience: Diffusion of Risk and Adaptation Across Interconnected Regions
authors: Han
keywords: endogenous networks; network-aware interventions; peer effects; regional resilience; socio-spatial networks; spatial diffusion; spatial dynamic panel data (SDPD) models
abstract: Regions face not only direct exposure to economic and physical shocks but also indirect consequences of actions in interconnected regions. This paper examines how socio-spatial networks shape regional resilience to contagious shocks through dynamic feedback between risk diffusion and adaptation diffusion. In our framework, peer effects generate positive spillovers in risk-mitigating adaptation across social networks, while evolving cross-regional physical connections mediate the spatial spread of risks. Calibrated to U.S. regional data, we simulate and compare network-aware intervention strategies that prioritize regions based on social centrality, spatial centrality, and population scale. The results show that the cost-effectiveness of interventions depends critically on the population scale of socially or spatially central regions. Strategies that maximize aggregate risk reduction do not always align with those that are the most cost-effective, revealing fundamental trade-offs that call for hybrid, model-informed intervention design. Our findings underscore the importance of interregional linkages and network-aware policy design in shaping regional resilience to systemic shocks, with broader implications for economic contagion, climate adaptation, and public health.
summary: Models how risk and adaptation diffuse across networks of interconnected regions to shape regional resilience.

title: From smile curve to wicked smile? The role of e-commerce platforms in reshaping industry value chains and empowering clusters
keywords: China; clusters; Digital platforms; furniture industry; smile curve; wicked smile
abstract: This study examines how e-commerce platforms reshape traditional value chains by analysing China’s furniture industry and three representative clusters. Conceptually, we introduce the ‘wicked smile’ hypothesis to postulate how platformisation transforms value creation and distribution at the industry level. Empirically, our comparative cluster-level analysis reveals that platforms exert uneven impacts across regions. While emerging clusters can enter higher value activities via platforms, their long-term competitiveness is constrained by their initial limitations. Furthermore, platforms disproportionately capture value, limiting latecomer clusters to achieve true catch-up. These findings highlight the complex and paradoxical role of platforms in cluster development and related regional industrial transformation.
summary: Examines how e-commerce platforms reshape industry value chains and empower regional clusters.

title: The rider as an agent of urban assemblage: The case of Seville (Spain)
keywords: assemblage; glitch; platform urbanism; Riders; spatial fix
abstract: The development of platform urbanism gives strategic value to riders or home delivery drivers as necessary actors in the spatial connection of supply with demand. In this paper, we examine the role of these workers in the assemblage of urban space, using the city of Seville (Spain) as a case study. We provide an ethnographic description of various situations in which the spatial configuration of urban space envisaged by the platform is incomplete, insufficient, or directly contradictory to the socio-spatial solutions required by riders in their daily work. The main contribution of this paper is to ethnographically document the socio-spatial practices through which workers complement and make effective the “spatial-fix” provided by the delivery platforms. The results suggest that applying the ethnographic method to the study of the platform/city interface highlights the limits of the “spatial fix” projected by such platforms and the crucial role of riders in implementing responses to glitches as situations of failure or mismatch.
summary: Studies delivery riders as agents shaping the urban assemblage in Seville, Spain.

title: Fortunate people in a fortunate land: At home in Santa Monica's rent-controlled housing, by Lauren E. M. Everett
summary: A book review of Lauren E. M. Everett's study of life in Santa Monica's rent-controlled housing.

title: Mundane Geopolitics, Strategic (De)Coupling, and Chinese Infrastructure Investment in Europe
authors: Mohan; Chen
abstract: Geopolitical rivalry between China and the US is profoundly affecting transnational investments. We develop an analytical framework that augments the notion of strategic coupling to capture whether and how transnational investment projects can cohere in a geopolitically charged world. Two cases—Duisburg in Germany and the Royal Albert Dock in London, UK—are used to analyze why local development efforts hinging on Chinese capital failed to materialize. Our cases demonstrate that rather than high-profile ruptures in the coupling process the (re-)emergence of geopolitics is driving a process of dealignment between national-level priorities, such as de-risking, and the developmental aims of city-regions. This dealignment reflects more mundane geopolitical influences that need integrating into our understanding of strategic coupling. We also find that geopolitical factors alone do not determine the success or failure of such transnational investments, and analysis must include the interests of key stakeholders and the possibility of miscalculation. Our findings challenge state-centric narratives and underscore the need to account for contingent, multiscalar coalitions that shape development outcomes in the era of geopolitics.
summary: Analyzes how everyday geopolitics and strategic decoupling shape Chinese infrastructure investment across Europe.

title: Inequality in Brazil seen through consumption behavior: toward better economic modeling with utility function estimation
keywords: computable general equilibrium; Consumer behavior; demand elasticity; linear expenditure system
abstract: Household consumption accounts for approximately 60 percent of Brazil's GDP. Accurate representation of this component in applied economic models requires accounting for household preferences to capture spending heterogeneity across income groups. This paper is the first to estimate parameters of a Stone-Geary utility function for Brazil, covering 31 productive sectors and ten household income deciles. Results reveal a negative relationship between income and subsistence spending share in total expenditure, especially for food and housing. Higher-income households allocate a greater proportion of their income to services, such as private education, healthcare, tourism, culture, and recreation. The estimated parameters are applied in Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) simulations to evaluate their importance. Compared to a non-parameterized scenario, the estimated model yields 30% smaller GDP impacts, 40% smaller sectoral output effects, and heterogeneous shifts in consumption patterns, including 15 times higher impacts on imports and 6 times greater impacts on insurance by top-income households.
summary: Uses estimated utility functions and consumption behavior to model economic inequality in Brazil.

journal: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
title: Noise and Learning: Evidence from India
authors: Arzi Adbi; Sumit Agarwal; Pulak Ghosh
keywords: noise pollution; developing economies; learning; academic performance
abstract: Despite high noise pollution, empirical research on the impact of noise on learning in developing economies has been sparse. We investigate this question by analyzing spatial and temporal variation in noise pollution recorded by monitoring stations in India and academic performance in high-stakes Class 12 examinations across schools. We find that a 10-percentage-point increase in noisy days during the exam quarter is associated with a 2.3% increase in the failure rate of Class 12 boys. This pattern is not gender neutral, as no association between noise pollution and failure rate is observed for girls. We do not find any effect of noise pollution recorded during non-exam months. By documenting how noise pollution hinders learning in India and shedding light on cognitive burden explanation, our study highlights an overlooked threat to human capital accumulation in developing economies and underscores the importance of integrating noise pollution mitigation strategies into education and urban policies.
summary: Noise pollution near Indian schools raises Class 12 exam failure rates for boys but not girls, pointing to an overlooked threat to human capital.

journal: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
title: Increasing Household Waste Segregation Rates in the Presence of a Segregated Collection Service: A Randomized Controlled Trial in India
authors: Shivani Wadehra; Zihan Nie; Francisco Alpizar
keywords: collection service; household campaign; information; waste segregation; reminders
abstract: Proper waste management is an increasingly important challenge in developing countries, and waste segregation at source is a critical step toward greater efficiency and smaller environmental impacts. This study presents the results of a field experiment in India, examining whether and how a household campaign can change households' waste segregation behavior in the presence of a reliable segregated collection service. The campaign has two variants: (1) a one-shot household campaign providing an information brochure and a bucket and (2) the same one-shot campaign enhanced by weekly reminders. We find that, with a reliable collection service in place, a household campaign providing information brochures and buckets increases the waste segregation rate by 45 percentage points, and the "campaign plus reminders" treatment increases the segregation rate by 60 percentage points. We show that a low-cost, soft-touch household campaign can quickly and significantly increase waste segregation when a reliable segregated collection service exists.
summary: An Indian RCT shows a low-cost household campaign, especially with weekly reminders, sharply raises waste segregation where reliable collection exists.

journal: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
title: The Impact of Offshoring and Import Competition on Carbon Emissions
authors: Jonathan Leisner; Jakob R. Munch; August Twile Nielsen; Georg Schaur
keywords: environmental economics; international trade; climate policy; emissions
abstract: We use Danish firm-level data to jointly examine the causal effects of offshoring and Chinese import competition on carbon emissions, output, and the emission intensity of output. Offshoring reduces firms' emission intensity but also increases their production such that firm-level emissions do not change. Chinese import competition reduces firms' production and their emission intensity. Next, we apply our firm-level estimates in counterfactual decompositions and in the computation of emission-leakage rates. The resulting evidence shows that offshoring leads to cleaner production in the manufacturing sector while import competition from China mostly leads to more emissions abroad.
summary: Danish firm data show offshoring lowers emission intensity without cutting firm emissions, while Chinese import competition shifts emissions abroad.

journal: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
title: Energy Efficiency Dynamics and Climate Policy
authors: Gregory Casey; Yang Gao; Peter K. Kruse-Andersen
abstract: We study the effectiveness of climate change mitigation policies in reducing carbon emissions, focusing on the channel of economy-wide energy efficiency. Using US data, we estimate an impulse response function (IRF) that characterizes how energy efficiency responds to energy price shocks. Standard climate-economy models cannot replicate the slow transition dynamics observed in the data. We build a tractable model that nests the existing literature and can closely replicate the empirical IRF. The slow dynamics in our model imply that carbon taxes reduce short-run and cumulative emissions less than predicted by standard models. The slow dynamics also imply that higher carbon taxes and greater reductions in output are needed to achieve a given environmental target.
summary: Slow energy-efficiency adjustment to price shocks means carbon taxes cut emissions less than standard models predict, requiring higher taxes to hit targets.

journal: Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists
title: The Potential of Carbon Border Adjustments to Foster Climate Cooperation
authors: Timothe Beaufils; Joschka Wanner; Leonie Wenz
keywords: carbon border adjustment; climate policy; trade policy; climate clubs
abstract: We evaluate the potential of the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (EU CBAM) to foster a climate coalition.
