Using a general equilibrium quantitative trade model to evaluate the payoffs of a coalition formation game, we find that the EU CBAM motivates the adoption of carbon pricing in four countries. This results in a 73% greater reduction in global emissions compared to a scenario in which only the EU prices carbon, with the coalition-building effect outweighing the direct anti-leakage effect of the CBAM. This effect holds across a broad range of policy designs and modeling assumptions. The size of the induced climate coalition varies strongly with trade elasticities and marginally with input substitutability. Next to the carbon price level, the CBAM implementation plays a decisive role: a CBAM that covers more products or indirect emissions leads to larger coalitions. By contrast, introducing export rebates renders the coalition unattractive.
summary: A trade-model coalition game finds the EU CBAM can induce carbon pricing in four countries, cutting global emissions far more than EU-only pricing.

title: Assessment of individualised dynamic environmental exposures within The World Avatar
keywords: Dynamic environmental exposure; Scalability; Semantic interoperability; Temporal and spatial context-aware
abstract: The environment in which people spend their lives influences their health behaviours and health outcomes. Traditional studies often use fixed descriptions and ad hoc analyses to characterise environmental exposures at static locations, relating a single environmental factor to one health aspect, even though both the environment and the exposures of people who move through it are dynamic. We introduce a digital twinning approach that semantically integrates ontological concepts and data across environmental features into machine-readable knowledge, enabling scalable and context-aware assessment of individual exposures. This work is built on The World Avatar project, which aims to create an all-encompassing digital twin based on a dynamic knowledge graph. The proposed approach deploys a computational agent to calculate exposures based on semantic representations of environmental features in time and space. The time-specific part of the exposure calculation considers both the historical context (i.e. whether features of the environment had been built) and current context (i.e., whether something was open or accessible) of the exposure. The scalability of the approach is illustrated through the construction of interoperable digital twins and the analysis of smartphone data describing movements in both the UK and Singapore. The resulting exposures capture historic year-specific changes in greenspace and time-specific accessibility based on opening hours of the food retail environment. This approach could facilitate large-scale digital studies, yielding critical insights that help create healthy cities.
summary: Uses The World Avatar knowledge-graph framework to assess individualised, dynamic environmental exposures.

authors: Krisztian Ritter; Orsolya Varga
summary: Identifies drivers of and pathways toward local sustainable development.

title: The effect of fiscal decentralization on corruption

summary: Examines how fiscal decentralization affects corruption.

title: Les determinants de l'innovation regionale en France suite a la reforme territoriale : une analyse QCA
summary: QCA analysis of the determinants of regional innovation in France after territorial reform.

title: Subsidize rent or subsidize homeownership? Evidence from a Hong Kong experiment
authors: Michael B. Wong
keywords: Subsidized rent; Subsidized ownership; Public housing
abstract: Governments often provide homeownership subsidies, but their effects may depend critically on institutional context. This paper estimates the impacts of Hong Kong's Tenants Purchase Scheme, an unusual program that allowed 183,700 regularly income-tested public housing tenants to buy restricted ownership rights. Leveraging its incomplete roll-out between 1998 and 2006, I find that the program increased the share of "well-off" households in treated housing estates by 44 percent from 11 p.p. Further evidence suggests that incumbent households purchased units to avoid regular income tests and reconfigured co-residence among family members to obtain additional public housing units. The unintended consequence was to exacerbate hardship for excluded low-income populations.
summary: Hong Kong's Tenants Purchase Scheme, which let public-housing tenants buy restricted ownership, raised the share of well-off households in treated estates by 44% as incumbents bought to escape income tests, worsening hardship for excluded low-income groups.

title: What are the benefits of metro rail in Mumbai, India?
authors: Palak Suri; Maureen L. Cropper
keywords: Benefits of metro rail; Metro rail and property prices; Public transit in developing countries
abstract: We estimate the effects of the first metro rail line in Mumbai using administrative data on assessed property prices from 2011–18 for 723 subzones in the city. Comparing areas within 1 km of the metro with those beyond 1 km but within 3 km, we estimate the effects on property values for commercial, industrial, and residential properties. We find a significant and persistent increase in prices of 6%–8% for residential and commercial land use categories in treated areas relative to control areas after Metro Line 1 opens. We show that commute time savings and improvements in employment accessibility are plausible mechanisms underlying these effects.
summary: Mumbai's first metro line raised residential and commercial property prices within 1 km by a persistent 6–8%, driven plausibly by commute time savings and better job accessibility.

title: Sponge city and impermeable housing value: Evidence from London
authors: Yihao Wu
keywords: Urban flooding; Green stormwater infrastructure; Property values; Housing market; Difference-in-differences; Sustainable Drainage Systems
abstract: Climate change has intensified flash flooding, prompting cities worldwide to implement green stormwater infrastructure as a scalable adaptation strategy. This paper evaluates the economic consequences of London's Sustainable Drainage Systems (SuDS) program on the local housing market. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design and an LSOA-by-year panel dataset from 2010 to 2024, I find that neighborhoods receiving green infrastructure record 3.2–3.7% increases in housing prices on average but no discernible rise in transaction volumes. Event study estimates reveal a hump-shaped temporal profile, with effects peaking around the fifth year before partially attenuating. The price responses exhibit a non-monotonic pattern across flood risk categories, largely because infrastructure salience drives value creation more than hydraulic performance. My findings suggest that successful climate adaptation requires balancing engineering effectiveness with public perception, and that green infrastructure can generate sufficient returns to self-finance through property tax revenue.
summary: London's Sustainable Drainage Systems green-infrastructure program raised neighborhood house prices by 3.2–3.7%, with effects driven more by infrastructure salience than hydraulic performance, suggesting it could self-finance via property taxes.

title: The effects of neighborhood redevelopment on housing markets and beyond: Evidence from HOPE VI Revitalization Program
authors: Lizhong Liu
keywords: Neighborhood redevelopment; Place-based housing policy; Public housing; Housing values and rents
abstract: Many advocates highlighted place-based housing policies as a remedy for urban decay despite mixed evidence on their long-term effects. This paper presents a national-level study investigating changes in the trajectory of local housing markets caused by the Housing Opportunities for People Everywhere (HOPE VI) Revitalization Program, the largest federal investment in public housing redevelopment. I combine a stratified version of the synthetic difference-in-difference method with a stacked event study model to identify the effects of HOPE VI redevelopment and the underlying mechanisms. The analysis finds that HOPE VI led to long-lasting changes of housing markets and socioeconomic conditions in target neighborhoods. Housing values and rents increased by 8 and 11 percent, respectively, more than 20 years after redevelopment. These effects varied systematically with both the scale of redevelopment and baseline neighborhood characteristics. Distinguishing mechanical from non-mechanical channels reveals that only a portion of the rent increase reflects compositional replacement, while the majority is associated with improvements in housing quality and positive spillovers to nearby neighborhoods.
summary: HOPE VI public-housing redevelopment raised neighborhood housing values by 8% and rents by 11% even 20+ years later, mostly through quality improvements and spillovers rather than compositional change.

title: Can credit collections on traffic violations save lives? Evidence from Chinese vehicle insurance market
authors: Ying Liu; Congrong Pan; Lihua Qin; Fangjie Zhang
keywords: Credit collections; Traffic violations; Deterrence; Non-monetary sanctions; Moral hazard
abstract: This paper estimates the effects on road safety of a regulation that imposed credit collections on traffic violations, thereby establishing a non-monetary sanction in addition to the penalty-point system. Using individual underwriting and claims data in the vehicle insurance industry in china and employing a quasi-experimental approach, we show that this regulation was effective in reducing fatalities and minor injuries by 22.9% and 87.1%, respectively. This result is robust to various checks including the propensity score matching approach. We compare this effect with that of monetary sanctions and find that it is uniform across wealth groups, whereas drivers with higher risk profiles are more responsive. This is in sharp contrast to the impact of monetary sanctions. We attribute the road safety effect of this regulation to the general deterrent effect exclusively.
summary: A Chinese regulation attaching credit-record sanctions to traffic violations cut fatalities by 22.9% and minor injuries by 87.1%, with deterrence uniform across wealth groups unlike monetary fines.

title: Housing market pressures and post-earthquake displacement: Evidence from the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes
authors: Muhammed Hamza Kayrıcı; Yusuf Emre Akgündüz
keywords: Natural disaster; Housing market; Population displacement; Migration patterns
abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the February 2023 Türkiye earthquakes on housing markets in unaffected regions using online real estate listings and a time-based Regression Discontinuity Design. We document a sharp post-disaster demand shock driven by large-scale population displacement, with effects concentrated in the residential rental market. Consistent with a residential displacement shock, no significant effects are detected in commercial property markets. Price increases were highly segmented: pressures were strongest for multi-room units, reflecting the larger family structures of displaced households, and for newly constructed units, indicating a post-disaster flight-to-safety. Cross-sectional province-level and difference-in-differences estimates show that pre-existing migration networks and geographic distance are the primary determinants of rental price pressures.
summary: Displacement from the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes created sharp rental-price pressures in unaffected regions, concentrated in multi-room and new units and shaped by prior migration networks and distance.

title: Cropland abandonment threatens food security in rural Nepal: Understanding the role of long-term and seasonal migration
authors: Qi Zhang; Conghe Song; Sophia A. Graybill; Erin O. Sills; Rajan Parajuli; Richard E. Bilsborrow
keywords: Cropland Abandonment; Rural Outmigration; Seasonal Migration; Remittances; Food Security
abstract: Cropland abandonment is a growing concern in rural Nepal, with critical implications for food security, land management, and the future of community forestry. This study investigates how different forms of labor outmigration, including long-term and seasonal migration, along with remittances, are associated with household land-use decisions on cropland abandonment. Drawing on household survey data from community forest user groups in two watersheds in Pyuthan and Salyan districts, we apply statistical models to examine cropland abandonment decisions, area, and parcel numbers. Our findings reveal that long-term migrant counts are consistently associated with cropland abandonment, while remittances show weaker, less consistent associations. In contrast, seasonal migration tends to have limited or even countervailing effects. Among abandonment measures, the number of abandoned parcels shows the clearest association with long-term migrant count, suggesting that parcel-level outcomes may better capture management burdens in fragmented smallholder landscapes. Households report labor shortage due to migration, alongside other factors, as one of the leading reasons for cropland abandonment. These results highlight the need for integrated policy responses that consider migration patterns, reduce labor and management burdens in fragmented landscapes, and support context-specific strategies for maintaining cultivation where feasible. Addressing cropland abandonment is essential not only for enhancing rural food security but also for maintaining the ecological and social sustainability of Nepal's community forestry.
summary: In rural Nepal, long-term labor outmigration is consistently associated with cropland abandonment (especially the number of abandoned parcels), while remittances and seasonal migration show weaker or countervailing links.

title: Does industrial land bias crowd out social public services? Evidence from China
authors: Zekun Fan; Zhihao He; Weidong Qu
keywords: Industrial land policy; Public service provision; Land use allocation; Land pricing; China
abstract: This paper examines whether industrial land bias in China's land-supply policy crowds out social public services. Using prefecture-level panel data spanning 2002–2022, we construct an Industrial Land Bias Index (ILBI) and a City Public Service Index (CPSI) to analyze the relationship between growth-oriented land allocation and public service composition. We document a robust structural crowding-out effect: a one-standard-deviation increase in industrial land bias corresponds to a 0.32 %age-point decline in the share of social services (education, healthcare, social security and welfare, and culture and sports) within total public service capacity. Decomposition analysis reveals that this effect operates primarily through price concessions rather than quantity allocation. The crowding-out relationship is stronger in more market-oriented land-transfer environments, consistent with price discounts providing clearer signals of pro-industry commitment. The effect is most pronounced among cities with high fiscal self-sufficiency and among those with more service-oriented economies. These findings expose hidden opportunity costs of China's "land-for-growth" model and offer policy implications for rebalancing urban public service provision.
summary: Chinese cities that bias land supply toward industry, mainly via price concessions, shift public service capacity away from social services such as education and healthcare, revealing hidden costs of the land-for-growth model.

title: Impact of reverse rural-urban migration on farmland transfer: Empirical evidence from the China Family Panel Studies
authors: Qianlong Yang; Yuanyuan Zhu; Yilin Gan; Zhenfa Tu; Jiaxing Cui
keywords: Reverse rural-urban migration (RRUM); Farmland transfer; Probit model; Propensity score matching (PSM); Rural revitalization; China
abstract: The mobility of rural agricultural labor is critical for the efficient allocation of farmland resources. Earlier studies have primarily focused on the impact of rural out-migration on farmland transfer. However, reverse rural-urban migration (RRUM), as an integral component of bidirectional urban-rural factor flows, has received comparatively limited scholarly attention. Therefore, this study draws on data from four waves of the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) and employs Probit models to examine the effects of RRUM on farmland transfer. It also investigates whether household income and regional consumption moderate these effects. The results indicate that RRUM significantly promotes farmland transfer-in but does not exert a statistically significant impact on farmland transfer-out. The observed spatial heterogeneity indicates that RRUM has a stronger positive effect on farmland transfer-in in Eastern and Central China, while its impact on promoting farmland transfer-out is more pronounced in Northeastern and Western China. Moreover, households headed by older farmers are more inclined to transfer-in farmland. Moderation analysis further shows that household economic status negatively moderates the effect of RRUM on farmland transfer-in, whereas regional consumption expenditure negatively moderates its impact on both farmland transfer-in and transfer-out. RRUM has a significant positive effect on whether farmers pay rent after farmland transfer-in, but no significant impact on their likelihood of collecting rent after farmland transfer-out. The generalized linear model (GLM) results further suggest that RRUM has no significant effect on either rent payment or rent collection by farmers. These findings provide empirical evidence of the dynamics of farmland transfer in China under bidirectional urban-rural factor flows and offer guidance for designing region-specific farmland-transfer policies that promote global sustainable agricultural development.
summary: Return migration from cities to rural China significantly increases households' farmland transfer-in but not transfer-out, with effects varying by region, household income and local consumption.

title: Behavioral drivers of the adoption of sustainable agricultural practices: A best-worst scaling experiment among Italian winegrowers
authors: Claudia Stefania Gondos; Mirta Casati; Margherita Muzzillo; Vincenzina Caputo; Elena Castellari
keywords: Voluntary measures; Behavioral factors; Best-worst scaling; Common Agricultural Policy; Italy; Winegrowers
abstract: The European Union's increasing focus on voluntary approaches to the adoption of sustainability practices calls for a deeper understanding of farmers' decision-making and the behavioral mechanisms underlying the uptake. We conducted a best-worst scaling experiment among Italian winegrowers investigating the most and least relevant among 11 behavioral factors—encompassing dispositional, social, and cognitive dimensions—associated with the decision to adopt sustainable farming practices. Moreover, we also evaluated how contextual and farm structural characteristics relate to the relative importance attributed to each behavioral factor. Results indicate that expected environmental benefits and sensitivity to environmental issues are the most important factors, followed by expected economic benefits and expected costs, whereas social approval and the behavior of other farmers are the least important. The relative importance attributed to behavioral factors is significantly associated with farm size, farm type, and perception of barriers to adoption. The perception of economic barriers is significantly associated with a lower importance attributed to most factors. From a policy perspective, our findings suggest that providing information on the costs and benefits of sustainable farming practices should be prioritized; however, this alone is likely to be insufficient without accompanying economic support for adoption.
summary: A best-worst scaling experiment with Italian winegrowers finds expected environmental benefits and environmental sensitivity matter most for adopting sustainable practices, while social approval and peer behavior matter least.

title: Grey fields in rural China: Industrial pollution and agricultural productivity losses
authors: Luo, Sixuan
keywords: Rural industrial pollution; Highly polluting industry; Agricultural total factor productivity; Labor quality; Land-use governance
abstract: Rural industrial transfer has increasingly reshaped land-use patterns and environmental burdens in China's countryside, yet its implications for agricultural productivity remain insufficiently understood. Guided by an extended agricultural household framework, this study examines whether the presence of highly polluting industries near rural villages is associated with changes in agricultural total factor productivity (TFP). Using panel data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), we employ a difference-in-differences framework based on the reported presence of highly polluting industries within 5 km of villages. The results indicate that the emergence of nearby highly polluting industries is associated with an approximately 23% decline in agricultural household TFP. A series of robustness checks, matching analyses, and placebo exercises suggest that the negative association remains relatively stable across alternative empirical specifications. Additional analyses provide supplementary evidence broadly consistent with pollution-related channels, partly through reduced labor quality, although the available data do not allow direct observation of pollutant exposure or definitive identification of specific mechanisms. We further find substantial heterogeneity across locations and village structures: the negative association is stronger in villages located farther from provincial or county capitals and weaker in villages with higher concentrations of large surnames. These findings highlight the potentially uneven environmental costs of rural industrialization and underscore the importance of land-use governance, industrial siting regulation, and rural environmental protection for sustainable agricultural development.
summary: Using China Family Panel Studies data, the paper links highly polluting industries located near rural villages to roughly 23% lower agricultural household total factor productivity.

title: Is Transfer of Development Rights (TDR) feasible? The impact of land use and market-based tools on carbon storage
authors: Han Wang; Qing Kang; Zhoupeng Chen; Fengqin Li; Xin Nie
keywords: Market-based instruments; Land use management; Transfer of Development Rights; Carbon storage; Scenario simulation
abstract: Market-based instruments and land-use management are key mechanisms for emission reduction, directly influencing regional carbon storage and constituting critical considerations for achieving the 'dual-carbon' goals. Previous studies have primarily assessed the response of regional carbon storage to land-use management, while largely overlooking the role of market-based instruments. As an integration of market mechanisms and land-use management, whether Transfer of Development Rights (TDR) can effectively improve regional carbon storage remains unclear. Therefore, it is necessary to explore the impact of TDR on regional carbon storage. This study employs the PLUS model to simulate four land-use scenarios in Guangxi for 2030: Baseline Scenario (BS), Development Scenario (DS), Protection Scenario (PS), and TDR scenarios (TDR). On this basis, the InVEST model is used to quantify carbon storage under each scenario. Through scenario comparison, the impact of TDR on regional carbon storage is identified. The results indicate that TDR improves regional carbon storage by optimizing land-use structure and reallocating development rights across zones. With a total carbon storage of 3269,444.5 × 10⁴t, the TDR represents an optimal solution that balances regional development and ecological protection, aligning with China's territorial spatial governance and green low-carbon development policies. Therefore, this study provides an effective pathway for promoting low-carbon land use.
summary: Land-use scenario simulations for Guangxi in 2030 show a Transfer of Development Rights scheme yields the highest carbon storage while balancing development and ecological protection.

title: Measuring adaptation in action: Uncovering agricultural land-use responses to changing yields and prices
authors: Mansi Nagpal; Christian Klassert; Jasmin Heilemann; Bernd Klauer; Erik Gawel
keywords: Multi-agent model; Cropping decisions; Economic factors; Drought; Climate change; Adaptation costs
abstract: Climate change affects agriculture directly through crop yield losses and indirectly through changes in crop prices. Farmers need to adapt their land-use decisions to these changing conditions. These decisions are made in advance and under considerable uncertainty. The extent to which farmers adapt their crop area allocations to changing yields and prices remains unclear, particularly at the national scale. We present an approach for measuring the adaptedness of observed crop area allocations to changing yields and prices in terms of the number of hectares differing from an economically optimal cropping pattern. We demonstrate the approach in a case study in Germany (1999–2020). To identify economically optimal crop area allocations under changing yields and prices, we employ an econometric mathematical programming (EMP) approach within a multi-agent system modeling framework. Over the 20 years, we find persistent changes in crop area allocations averaging 36% ±4% of each district's agricultural area. Of these changes, 43% improved the adaptedness to today's yields and prices. We observe a trend of increasing adaptedness over time, though significantly lower in districts facing drought conditions. Adaptation, however, prevails both under drought and non-drought conditions. Our results suggest that the economic impacts of changing yields and prices play a significant role in shaping observed land-use patterns, with important implications for land-use dynamics under climate change. Our approach opens promising avenues for further research seeking to disentangle the drivers of land-use adaptation over time and to inform future policies aimed at supporting agricultural adaptation to increasing weather extremes and changing climatic conditions.
summary: Measuring German districts' crop allocations against an economically optimal benchmark (1999–2020), the study finds 43% of observed changes improved adaptedness to yields and prices, with adaptation rising over time but weaker under drought.

title: Customary property rights and urban property values: Insights from Ingonyama Trust lands in Durban, South Africa
authors: A. Panman; C. Marx; G.M. Lincoln; N. Lozano-Gracia; R.J. Hansmann; J. Houghton
keywords: Customary tenure; Urban land use; Housing values; South Africa; Africa
abstract: Africa is urbanizing rapidly. In many cases, cities are expanding into areas where land is held under customary tenure, which differ in important ways from the 'transparent, secure, and alienable' private rights that underpin most models of cities in urban economic theory. This paper therefore asks: how does customary tenure shape the development, use, and value of land in urbanizing areas? Drawing on a unique data set of 1400 households in eThekwini Municipality, Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition analysis is used to examine observable differences in characteristics and values of housing located in legally recognized customary areas with those that are not. The results provide a rare empirical snapshot on urban development patterns in this context, revealing variation in housing values across these two areas that is largely attributed to differences in public services rather than factors that are widely linked to individual investment decisions and tenure security, such as housing size and quality of building materials. We also find tentative evidence of a price discount for housing on customary land in densely urbanized areas and a price premium in more rural locations, raising questions for further research on the interaction between property rights and spatial transformation.
summary: In Durban, housing value gaps between customary Ingonyama Trust land and other areas are explained mainly by differences in public services rather than tenure-linked investment, with a tentative customary-land discount in dense areas and premium in rural ones.

title: Land tenure security and soil health: Evidence from Uganda
authors: Richard Alioma; Denis Gobo; Zac Gidongo Halasi
keywords: Land tenure; Soil health; Certification; Uganda; Sustainable land management; Property rights
abstract: Land tenure security plays a vital role in promoting sustainable land management, but its impact on soil health remains poorly understood within Uganda's complex tenure systems. This study examines how formal land certification and tenure systems influence soil health outcomes using data from the Uganda National Panel Survey (2020/2021) and robust econometric methods, including ordinary least squares, instrumental variables, and propensity score matching. We constructed the soil health index by combining five key variables, namely organic matter, biodiversity, erosion control, fertilizer use, and fallow practices, with each factor weighted based on its importance. To reduce endogeneity, we used instrumental variables like historical land reform and distance to land registry offices. The results indicate that formal land certification enhances soil health, with leasehold and freehold land systems demonstrating the most substantial positive effects. Nonetheless, the impacts of land certification differ by tenure system. Certification of land combined with customary tenure has a significant impact on soil health, whereas certification within customary systems proves ineffective, underscoring the need for supplementary interventions. Conversely, inherited land and households led by widows are associated with negative outcomes for soil health, which may reflect issues of land fragmentation and resource limitations. Analysis of heterogeneity of the impact of land certification reveals that Mailo and Leasehold land tenure systems benefit from land certification. In contrast, Freehold systems exhibit negative returns, potentially due to existing security arrangements. We recommend including scaling up Uganda's Certificates of Customary Ownership while integrating gender-sensitive support, education, and credit access to maximize the benefits of soil health.
summary: Formal land certification in Uganda improves a composite soil-health index, but effects vary by tenure system, with Mailo and leasehold land benefiting most.

title: Layered land rights under government-led decentralization: Implications for land value capture implementation in Jakarta, Indonesia
authors: Yescha Nuradisa Ekarachmi Danandjojo; Samira Ramezani; Johan Woltjer
keywords: Decentralized governance; Land value capture; Multiple land rights; Transport infrastructure finance
abstract: Multiple land rights holders and layered land rights structures create fundamental challenges for implementing land-based financing methods such as land value capture (LVC). In a decentralized governance system, overlapping land rights and fragmented planning complicate coordination and limit the effectiveness of LVC for financing transport infrastructure development. This study examines how different rights holders contribute to implementing land value capture within a layered land rights and multi-level governance system in Indonesia, using the Jakarta Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) project as a case study. In Indonesia's decentralized system, multiple levels of government apply different planning tools to regulate land use and development, complicating coordination between planning, land rights, and LVC mechanisms. Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews and policy analysis show that overlapping land rights and fragmented regulations create legal and administrative uncertainty. This uncertainty acts as a barrier to cross-governmental coordination and private stakeholder engagement, both of which are necessary for a workable LVC framework. Although a formal LVC framework exists, unclear rules on which rights holders should contribute, combined with complex administrative procedures, limit its practical use. This study contributes to the LVC literature by linking instruments to specific land rights holders and by extending the bundle-of-rights perspective. It explains why LVC remains underutilized in contexts with layered land rights and decentralized governance. The findings highlight the need for policy reforms to clarify contribution obligations, improve coordination across governance levels, and simplify the administrative process.
summary: The Jakarta MRT case shows that overlapping land rights and fragmented regulation under decentralization create legal uncertainty that keeps land value capture underused for financing transit.

title: Can the ecological transition of cropland use narrow rural-urban income inequality? Evidence from China's Huang-Huai-Hai Region
authors: Linpeng Yang; Yansui Liu; Cong Ou; Yurui Li
keywords: Ecological transition of cropland use; Rural-urban income inequality; Agricultural multifunctionality; Huang-Huai-Hai Region; Agricultural regional system
abstract: Rural-urban income inequality (RUIE) remains a persistent challenge across many rapidly developing regions, undermining socio-economic welfare and hindering sustainable development. The ecological transition of cropland use (ETCU), a management paradigm rooted in the principles of sustainable intensification, is widely advocated to enhance agricultural sustainability. While localized case studies suggest that such practices can bolster rural incomes through improved resource efficiency or product diversification, robust empirical evidence on whether large‑scale ETCU adoption mitigates regional RUIE remains scarce, and the underlying systemic mechanisms are poorly understood. This study develops a multi-scale "cropland-agriculture-rural" framework to analyze how ETCU influences RUIE in China's intensively cultivated Huang-Huai-Hai Region. By integrating plot-scale biogeochemical modeling (PEST-DNDC), county-level panel data (2000–2020), and Structural Equation Modeling, we systematically quantify the spatiotemporal patterns and causal pathways of this transition. The results demonstrate that: (1) ETCU and RUIE exhibit spatially heterogeneous co-evolution; improvements in ETCU are not consistently associated with reduced inequality, and in some coastal counties, they even coincide with widening gaps. (2) ETCU affects RUIE primarily by restructuring agricultural multifunctionality, which serves as the core mediator. (3) The effects are highly dimension-specific. Enhancing resource-use efficiency exerts a modest yet significant direct mitigating effect on RUIE. Conversely, improvements in productivity and environmental performance exhibit no direct effect; instead, they indirectly exacerbate inequality by weakening the agricultural product supply function—which our model identifies as a strong and direct suppressor of RUIE. The economic value-added and ecological conservation functions do not exhibit significant direct equalizing effects. These findings indicate that the equity outcomes of ETCU are not automatic but depend critically on how it reshapes the multifunctional structure of agriculture. Policy interventions must therefore adopt an integrated approach that strategically guides the agricultural transition toward balanced multifunctionality, safeguards diversified production, and ensures that efficiency gains translate into broadly shared benefits for both rural and urban households.
summary: In China's Huang-Huai-Hai Region, the ecological transition of cropland use does not automatically narrow rural-urban income gaps; only resource-efficiency gains reduce inequality, while productivity and environmental gains can widen it via weaker product supply.

title: Emergency land take, road-network centrality and post-disaster land-use policy: Evidence from the post-earthquake reconstruction of L'Aquila, Italy
authors: Federico Mara; Cristina Montaldi; Francesco Zullo; Valerio Cutini
keywords: Emergency land take; Post-disaster governance; Road-network centrality; Emergency siting; Space Syntax; Post-earthquake reconstruction
abstract: Land-use policy increasingly operates under conditions of shock and uncertainty, yet the mechanisms through which emergency measures produce persistent land take remain underexplored. In this paper, land take refers to land development involving the conversion of natural, semi-natural or agricultural land to artificial uses, often associated with impervious soil cover. The paper examines how post-earthquake road-access restrictions, safety cordons, and infrastructure-and-amenity siting choices interacted with road-network centrality and land-use change in L'Aquila, Italy. Using a configurational approach, namely Space Syntax, on reconstructed pre-earthquake and post-earthquake road networks, we compute segment-based Integration (NAIN) and Choice (NACH) at multiple radii and relate centrality deciles to a 2014 post-event census of commercial and public amenities through nearest-segment association and buffer-based sensitivity tests. Results show a strong spatial alignment between road closures in and around the historic centre, the emergence of high-centrality road corridors, notably Viale della Croce Rossa and the SS17, and the concentration of post-disaster amenities along those corridors and their immediate surroundings. Two peripheral district centres, Torrione and Torretta, also consolidated as locally autonomous service nuclei, reinforcing a more polycentric pattern that only partly aligned with statutory planning objectives. Rather than proposing a formal predictive model, the paper uses single-case evidence to show how road-network diagnostics can help identify corridors where temporary land uses and emergency-related land take are most likely to persist; support decisions on the reopening of strategic road links; and inform time-bound rules for de-commissioning, reuse, regularisation, and development caps on floor area and intensity. The workflow is low-cost, open-data based and transferable to other hazards and city sizes, providing actionable evidence for planners and governments seeking to align post-disaster responses with land-take control objectives.
summary: After the L'Aquila earthquake, road closures shifted network centrality to new corridors where post-disaster amenities concentrated, showing how road-network diagnostics can flag where emergency land take is likely to persist.

title: From delineation to implementation of urban development boundaries: A two-stage game of land development rights
authors: Qilong Wang; Yong Liu; Qiaoran Yang; Qi Yin; Wenze Yue
keywords: Urban development boundary; Territorial spatial planning; Land development right; Principal-agent theory; Evolutionary game theory
abstract: Urban development boundaries (UDBs) have been introduced in China's territorial spatial planning system as a key tool to regulate urban expansion. However, existing research has paid limited attention to how land development rights are negotiated and exercised among multiple stakeholders under UDBs, from delineation to implementation. We develop a two-stage game model to explain the UDB policy, using the Pearl River Delta (PRD) urban agglomeration as a simulation case. In the first stage, a principal–agent model is applied to examine how land development rights are allocated through negotiations between superior and subordinate governments. In the second stage, an evolutionary game model is used to analyze the strategic interactions among governments and developers regarding land development rights under UDBs. Simulation results indicate that during delineation, higher land values and stronger bargaining capacity improve efforts to obtain quotas, whereas greater external volatility and heavier protection tasks reduce these efforts. During implementation, stakeholders' strategies are linked with land quota scarcity in the first stage. In a quota-abundant scenario, the system converges to the optimal evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) of strict supervision, prohibition, and compliance. In a quota-scarce scenario, achieving the optimal ESS becomes more difficult, requiring an effective penalty and strict accountability for subordinate governments. Overall, the proposed two-stage game framework provides a numerical illustration that captures the behavioral dynamics of multiple stakeholders and provides practical insights to strengthen the enforcement of UDBs.
summary: A two-stage principal-agent and evolutionary game model of China's urban development boundaries shows that enforcement converges to strict compliance when land quotas are abundant but needs strong penalties and accountability when quotas are scarce.

title: Exploring the determinants and recursive influences of land degradation and climate change adaptation technologies in Ethiopia: Evidence from a recursive multivariate probit model
authors: Atalel Wubalem; Jan Cools; Zerihun Nigussie; Charlotte Fabri; Amare Sewnet Minale; Sophie Van Schoubroeck; Wubante Fetene Admasu; Bosena Tegegne; Sofie Annys; Tesfaye Shiferaw; Amaury Frankl; Enyew Adgo; Steven Van Passel
keywords: Land degradation; Climate change; Sustainable land management; Adaptation; Recursive multivariate probit; Ethiopia
abstract: Land degradation and climate change remain pressing challenges to agricultural development in Ethiopia, where rural farm households rely heavily on rainfed agriculture amid mounting ecological stress and climate risks. Although Sustainable Land Management (SLM) practices are central to mitigating these risks, intervention outcomes are mixed, and most empirical studies rarely consider the recursive and endogenous nature of farmers' adaptation decisions, failing to distinguish between independent and conditionally interdependent adaptation decisions, leaving a missing link in our understanding of their combined effects. While the standard multivariate probit model accounts for interdependence through correlated error terms, it still overlooks the structural and directional connections among SLM adaptation choices. Recursive specifications explicitly capture how upstream adaptation conditioned the feasibility and effectiveness of downstream adaptation, incorporating both correlation and causal ordering across SLM domains. Using this framework, the study investigates the determinants and interdependencies among structural, agronomic, and ecosystem-based SLM adaptation strategies, employing nationally representative data and a recursive multivariate probit (RMVP) model. Using 15,839 pooled observations from two waves of the Ethiopian Living Standards Measurement Survey (2018/19 and 2021/22), we modeled the recursive relationships among the three adaptation domains. Results demonstrate that the uptake of structural and agronomic measures significantly enhances ecosystem-based adaptation. In contrast, agronomic adaptation is positively influenced by structural adaptation, revealing strong complementarities among SLM technologies. Other exogenous covariates, such as education level, annual expenditure, food security, landholding, and participation in watershed programs, significantly increase the likelihood of adaptation, whereas market distance and plot remoteness constrain adaptation decisions. Viewing decision-making as a recursive process offers a more realistic depiction of how smallholders integrate multiple adaptation pathways amid complex socioeconomic and ecological constraints. Policies that promote integrated SLM practices are more likely to yield resilient, sustainable, and climate-smart land-use outcomes in Ethiopia.
summary: Using Ethiopian LSMS data and a recursive multivariate probit, the study finds strong complementarities among sustainable land management practices, with structural and agronomic measures boosting ecosystem-based adaptation.

title: Heterogeneous climate risks for China's GI products under the China-EU Agreement: Disentangling effects across product categories and protection boundaries?
authors: Yiying Hong; Zhenbang Ma; Sijian Wang; Ruisi Luo; Yipeng Wang; Wenli Qiang; Imanmadi Duman; Ermekov Farabi Kerimbaevich
keywords: Geographical indication; Climate change adaptation; Protection boundaries; Chinese agri-food product; Territorial governance
abstract: Agri-food products with geographical indications (GI products) are territorially embedded agricultural systems whose production and value depend on legally defined protection boundaries, rendering them biophysically vulnerable to climate change. Despite extensive examination of terroir-associated climate risks, the heterogeneous climate-driven potential land-use risks across product categories and protection boundaries remain insufficiently understood. Based on 7260 planting occurrence records, this study employs the MaxEnt model to conduct an exploratory simulation of shifts in the suitable areas for 185 Chinese GI products across seven categories under the China-EU GI Agreement. Consequently, it identifies high-risk GI products/categories, assesses their potential sensitivity and pressures from intra- and extra-zone exposure disparities under future climate scenarios. This study addresses three core questions: (i) identifying key environmental variables; (ii) assessing the potential climate sensitivity of specific categories; and (iii) quantifying potential intra- and extra-zone exposure pressures. Results demonstrate that (1) climatic factors constitute the primary biophysical drivers of GI product suitability, followed by topographic and soil factors; (2) Tea & Coffee products exhibit the highest potential climate sensitivity among all categories, while 35 identified high-sensitivity GI products face significant suitable area change or displacement risks; and (3) under future climate scenarios, the potential legal exposure induced by suitability expansion outside designated GI zones is projected to be approximately twice that of the potential moral hazard to product quality arising from environmental mismatches inside, underscoring a profound spatial mismatch between shifting ecological niches and static institutional boundaries. These findings highlight emerging land-use and institutional governance challenges for GI systems under climate change, offering policy insights for empowering entrepreneurial resilience, implementing category-specific interventions, and dynamically adjusting GI protection boundaries.
summary: Species-distribution modeling of 185 Chinese geographical-indication products shows climate change will shift suitable growing areas, especially for tea and coffee, creating a mismatch with fixed GI protection boundaries.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Heterogeneous effects of weather shocks on firm economic performance
authors: Tarsia, Romano
keywords: Climate change; Firms; Climate damages; Economic performance
abstract: This paper provides novel firm-level estimates of the economic damages caused by temperature shocks to European firms. I rely on a panel data analysis to show wide heterogeneities in the impact of temperature shocks, which depend on firm characteristics. This paper reveals the importance of micro-level data for quantifying climate damage estimates, as the average relationship between temperature and economic outcomes masks firms' different susceptibilities to weather shocks. These create both winners and losers, harming less productive firms, particularly those in warmer regions, while benefiting more productive ones. Compared with the pooled marginal effect, the least-productive firms experience negative effects roughly ten times as large, while the most-productive firms experience positive effects roughly three times as large. Additionally, higher temperatures increase exit probability among the least productive firms in warmer regions. I highlight the distributional effects of climate change, and offer insights for adaptation policies.
summary: Firm-level European data show temperature shocks create winners and losers: the least productive firms, especially in warm regions, suffer damages about ten times the average and exit more, while the most productive firms gain.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Competition between green and blue hydrogen and indirect network effects
authors: Kine Josefine Aurland-Bredesen; Rolf Golombek; Mads Greaker
keywords: Blue hydrogen; Green hydrogen; Carbon capture and storage; Salop circle; Emission allowances; Market imperfections; Network externalities
abstract: Whereas hydrogen is currently a marginal energy carrier, the aim of the EU is to trigger low-carbon hydrogen production that covers around 10 percent of EU's energy needs by 2050. If this comes true, it will be an energy revolution. We study competition between green and blue hydrogen using an extended Salop model that encompasses the value chains for hydrogen and CCS. For blue hydrogen, we distinguish between exports of blue hydrogen—natural gas is converted into hydrogen close to the extraction site of natural gas and hydrogen is then transported over a long distance to the hydrogen consumers—and local production of blue hydrogen—natural gas is exported over a long distance and then converted into hydrogen near the hydrogen consumers. We find that mark-ups are highest in the case of exports of blue hydrogen production, which implies that total production of hydrogen, supply of blue hydrogen, and share of plants investing in carbon capture facilities are lower in the case of exports of blue hydrogen than in the case of local production of blue hydrogen. We provide numerical simulations of the alternative market outcomes and the corresponding first-best outcomes and identify policy instruments that should be used to sustain the first-best social outcomes in the cases of exports of blue hydrogen and local production of blue hydrogen.
summary: An extended Salop model of green versus blue hydrogen shows mark-ups are highest when blue hydrogen is exported, lowering total hydrogen output and carbon-capture investment relative to local blue hydrogen production.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: The environmental justice implications of industry consolidation: Evidence from U.S. landfills
authors: Hui Zhou; Shan Zhang; Matthew D. Gordon
keywords: Environmental justice; Solid waste; Industry consolidation; Regulation
abstract: Over the past three decades, the number of U.S. landfills has fallen by 41%, while average capacity has risen by 130%. This paper studies the distributional consequences of this consolidation. We show these changes coincide with waste disposal shifting toward locations with lower population density and higher shares of low-income, Black, and Hispanic residents. Event studies of landfill openings rule out large effects on migration, though new landfills are sited in places with fast-changing demographics. Using a novel measure of regulation built from large-language-model classifications of state statutes, we show evidence that increased state regulations may contribute to increasing disparities.
summary: Consolidation of U.S. landfills into fewer, larger sites has shifted waste disposal toward less dense areas with more low-income, Black and Hispanic residents, with stricter state regulation possibly widening disparities.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Substituting storage for transmission: Implications for renewable energy
authors: J. Scott Holladay; Ben Meadows; Tim Roberson; Charles Sims
keywords: Energy storage; Electric power; Transmission; Renewable energy
abstract: We analyze the potential for electricity storage to substitute for transmission capacity. We develop a spatial-dynamic model of the grid where a utility manager dispatches generators and batteries to serve load at the lowest possible cost. The addition of storage requires the manager to optimize charging and discharging across the day, making the problem dynamic. We identify general conditions under which transmission and storage can serve as substitutes. When transmission is constrained and the battery is being charged or discharged, storage and transmission are substitutes at that instant. The investment-relevant capacity value depends on the aggregation of these instantaneous scarcity values across all hours of the day: storage substitutes for transmission investment when additional storage capacity reduces the time-averaged shadow value of the transmission constraint. This suggests storage can serve as transmission in markets where transmission is frequently constrained and the battery rarely sits idle. We calibrate our model to the electric grid in Texas and show that transmission and storage are substitutes even when wind generation is curtailed. The ability to substitute storage for transmission enables utilities to forgo costly and contentious grid expansion projects.
summary: A spatial-dynamic grid model calibrated to Texas shows battery storage can substitute for transmission capacity where lines are often constrained, letting utilities avoid costly grid expansion.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Convergent validity in incentive-compatible contingent valuation: Bid-vector and elicitation format effects
authors: Wojciech Zawadzki; Mikołaj Czajkowski; Jens Rommel; Julian Sagebiel; Christoph Schulze
keywords: Non-market valuation; Stated preferences; Biodiversity; Yea-saying; Anchoring; Open-ended; Single binary choice; Payment card; Behavioral anomalies; Fat fails
abstract: This study investigates convergent validity between elicitation formats within contingent valuation methodology, focusing on theory-driven formats designed to align with incentive compatibility. While earlier literature endorsed the single binary choice (SBC) format as the only incentive-compatible option, recent studies outline theoretical conditions under which payment card (PC) and open-ended (OE) formats may also encourage truthful preference revelation. We contribute to this debate by directly comparing these three theory-driven formats and assessing their robustness against bid-vector effects and other biases such as anchoring, yea-saying, and strategic misrepresentation. We conduct a large-scale, multi-country survey with 12,343 respondents across Poland, Sweden, Hungary, Spain, Germany, and the Netherlands, examining consumers' willingness to pay (WTP) for an EU-wide biodiversity-enhancing program. The results indicate limited convergent validity across formats, with substantial discrepancies in WTP estimates. However, analysis of choice frequencies suggests that convergent validity holds for lower bid levels, whereas higher bids introduce differences. We argue that these differences stem from both behavioral biases and methodological factors, including bid vector design and econometric assumptions. Our results underscore the critical influence of bid structure on WTP estimates and highlight the need for further research to refine elicitation formats and econometric methods used in contingent valuation studies.
summary: A six-country contingent valuation survey of 12,343 respondents finds limited convergent validity of WTP across single binary choice, payment card and open-ended formats, with divergence driven by higher bid levels.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: How to rapidly assess the economic consequences of floods with public data sources? Evidence from Northern Italy
authors: Gentili, Elena
keywords: Floods; Economic growth; Nightlights; Housing market; Difference-in-differences
abstract: This paper uses high-frequency public data to provide an ex-post evaluation of two floods that hit the Italian region of Emilia-Romagna in May 2023, just a few weeks after they occurred. Using nightlight data to measure output growth and considering a difference-in-differences empirical framework, we find a decline in nightlight growth in flooded municipalities in the three weeks surrounding the two floods, a rebound effect in the following three weeks, but no effect thereafter. In the most pessimistic scenario, the reduction in GDP growth in flooded municipalities in 2023 is between 0.3% and 0.8%, excluding the agricultural sector. The duration of the impact of the floods is broadly confirmed by the other two proxies for economic activity available at the daily frequence and municipal level, i.e., hiring and road traffic data. We also find temporary effects on the housing market demand, but no effects on the house prices asked by the sellers and the number of posted advertisements for house sales, suggesting that the housing market in flooded municipalities already discounts the risk of such natural events.
summary: High-frequency nightlight, hiring and traffic data show the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna floods caused only a short-lived dip in local activity (0.3–0.8% lower 2023 GDP growth at worst) and no effect on asking house prices.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Minimum energy performance standards and house price capitalization: Evidence from France's rental ban on 'energy sieves'
authors: Alexandre Garel; Eva Cheng
keywords: Climate policy; Energy efficiency; Housing markets; Energy performance certificates; Minimum energy performance standards
abstract: Energy performance disclosure is increasingly paired with minimum energy performance standards to accelerate the capitalization of energy inefficiency into housing prices and strengthen homeowners' incentives to renovate inefficient dwellings. We study the 2021 French policy implementing a progressive rental ban on the least energy-efficient dwellings ("energy sieves") and examine whether it has affected house prices. Using more than 900,000 housing transactions over 2014–2024, we document that energy sieves sell at an additional discount of about 5 percent following the policy announcement. Consistent with expected renovation costs driving the post-ban-announcement discount, the discount is much larger for houses that are costlier to renovate. The increase in the supply of G-rated houses on the sales market is also concentrated among those properties. While the post-ban-announcement discount reduces the gap between expected renovation costs to achieve compliance and expected sale loss due to non-compliance, we find limited evidence of a renovation response.
summary: France's 2021 rental ban on the least energy-efficient homes led such 'energy sieves' to sell at an extra ~5% discount, larger where renovation is costlier, but prompted little renovation.

journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Testing for spillovers in resource conservation: Evidence from a natural field experiment
authors: Lorenz Goette; Zhi Hao Lim
keywords: Spillovers; Field experiment; Resource conservation; Real-time feedback; Social comparisons
abstract: This paper studies whether behavioral interventions designed to promote resource conservation in one domain generate spillovers in another. Using a natural field experiment involving over 2000 residents, we identify the direct and spillover effects of real-time feedback and social comparisons on water and energy consumption. We implement three interventions: two targeting shower use and one targeting air-conditioning use. We find significant reductions in shower use from both water-saving interventions, but no direct effect of the energy-saving intervention on air-conditioning use. For spillovers, we estimate precise null effects of water-saving interventions on air-conditioning use, and of the energy-saving intervention on shower use.
summary: A natural field experiment with over 2,000 residents finds real-time feedback cut shower water use but produced precisely estimated null spillovers between water and air-conditioning energy conservation.

title: Local protectionism in China's government disclosure of food safety information
authors: Jiangyuan Liang; Wen Lin; Shengping Shang; Jiehong Zhou
keywords: Government; Information; Local protectionism; Food safety
abstract: This paper provides new evidence of local protectionism by examining government information disclosure and suggests that public information reporting may serve as a potential channel through which governments favor local firms. Focusing on China's food safety information disclosure, we compare food safety testing results conducted by local and national administrations for the same product within the same manufacturer and year. Our findings reveal a significantly lower probability of failure in food safety tests conducted by the local prefectural administration, holding across model specifications, accounting for different fixed effects, collusions between manufacturers and independent inspection agencies, technical differences in testing between administrations and the impact of the pandemic. Food manufacturing firms with higher registration capital and those strategic to local economies show lower probability of failure reported by local administrations, particularly in regions with aggressive GDP growth targets. This implies competition among regional governments drives a local bias in public information reporting, undermining the accuracy and transparency of food safety disclosure.
summary: Chinese local administrations report significantly lower food-safety test failure rates than national ones for the same products, especially for locally strategic firms in regions with aggressive GDP targets, revealing local protectionism in disclosure.

title: Assessment and valuation of government policies to improve food animal welfare
authors: Richard Bennett; Kelvin Balcombe; Heather Maggs; Siobhan Abeyesinghe; Gareth Arnott; Nick Bell; Andrew Butterworth; Jennifer Duncan; Cathy Dwyer; Marie Haskell; Fritha Langford; Siobhan Mullan; Christine Nicol; Niamh O'Connell; Elizabeth Rowe; Victoria Sandilands; Simon Turner
keywords: Food animal welfare; Policy appraisal; Welfare assessment; Valuation tool
abstract: There is a need to assess the benefits of government policy to improve the welfare of food animals. We present a holistic, animal-centred welfare assessment method using an expert panel of independent animal welfare scientists linked to a survey of food shoppers' willingness to pay (WTP) to improve welfare levels, using a 0–100 animal welfare scale. We apply this method to six food animal types in the UK and 15 different topical policy scenarios. We find that several current production systems have welfare scores below 50 but that some of the policy initiatives analysed could increase welfare scores substantially if implemented. We provide valuation tables of people's WTP to increase welfare scores for each of the six animal types. Marginal WTP was found to diminish as welfare scores increased. WTP values are fully transferable across any policies affecting the animals involved and are not tied to specific production practices or contexts. The UK government has been using the method to evaluate a range of policy options to improve welfare. The method can be applied in other countries. The method enables government policy makers to better make the case for policies to improve the welfare of food animals and its application should lead to an increased likelihood of such policies being implemented. The outputs can also be used to inform consumers regarding the animal welfare provenance of the food they purchase.
summary: Linking expert animal-welfare scores to UK shoppers' willingness to pay, the paper provides transferable valuation tables for improving welfare of six food animal types and appraises 15 policy scenarios, a method used by the UK government.

title: The dual role of crop-livestock diversification in household nutrition security: Evidence from rural Ethiopia
authors: Taye Melese Mekie; Luchen Huang; Yanjun Ren; Tadie Mirie Abate
keywords: Crop-livestock diversification; Micronutrients; Nutrition; Pathways; Trade-off; Rural Ethiopia
abstract: Nutrition insecurity remains a pressing global challenge, and while crop-livestock diversification offers a promising strategy to improve household nutrition, its relationship with micronutrient consumption remains underexplored. Using panel data from the Ethiopian Socio-economic Survey (ESS) from 2018/19 to 2021/22, this study examines the role of crop-livestock diversification in household nutrition security in rural Ethiopia and explores the underlying pathways. Three aspects of farm production diversity are considered: crop-livestock diversification, crop diversification, and livestock diversification. The results indicate that crop-livestock, crop, and livestock diversification are positively associated with total and own-produced nutrient intake but negatively associated with nutrient intake from market-purchased foods. The findings further indicate that the nutritional benefits of diversification are generally stronger among households with better market access, while heterogeneity by shock exposure is more limited and nutrient-specific. The pathway analysis suggests that the relationship between crop-livestock diversification and nutrition outcomes operates through total food consumption, own-produced consumption, market-purchased consumption, farm output, and income channels. Among these channels, total food consumption and own-produced consumption represent the strongest channels, while the income channel appears comparatively weaker. These findings highlight an important nutritional trade-off: diversification is associated with greater nutrient acquisition from household production while reducing nutrient consumption from market-purchased foods. The findings suggest that policies supporting crop-livestock diversification, together with complementary nutrition-sensitive and market-supporting interventions, may contribute to improved household nutrition security while addressing production–market trade-offs.
summary: In rural Ethiopia, crop-livestock diversification raises total and own-produced nutrient intake but lowers nutrients from purchased food, with stronger benefits for households with better market access.

title: Feeding a fifth of the world under land constraints: Agricultural innovation and grain yield growth in China
authors: Gang Wu; Jingru Chen; Sichang Luo; Changyi Jiang; Shiping Mao; Yu Zhong
keywords: Agricultural technological innovation; Grain yield; Field-management innovation; Input-oriented innovation
abstract: Ensuring food security under binding land constraints is a central challenge for many developing economies. Using a county-level panel dataset for China from 2000 to 2022, this study examines how agricultural technological innovation affects grain yield under land scarcity. We construct quality-adjusted patent stocks of grain-related technologies based on patent microdata and distinguish between input-oriented innovation and field-management innovation. By integrating patent data, business registration records, and official agricultural statistics, we empirically examine the effects of agricultural technological innovation on grain yield. The results show that agricultural technological innovation significantly increases grain yield: a doubling of the quality-adjusted stock of grain-related patents is associated with an approximately 1.10% increase in grain yield. However, its effects differ sharply by innovation type. Input-oriented innovation exhibits limited or even negative effects, whereas field-management innovation consistently enhances grain yield. Heterogeneity analyses show stronger yield effects in major grain-producing regions, areas with broader technological coverage and greater patent collaboration, and lower-yield counties. Mechanism analyses indicate that production organization and agricultural socialized services are key channels through which innovation translates into yield gains. Overall, the findings suggest that productivity gains in land-scarce agricultural systems depend less on input intensification than on effective production management and supportive institutional arrangements, with broader implications for other land-constrained developing economies.
summary: County-level Chinese data show doubling grain-related patent stocks raises grain yield about 1.1%, driven by field-management rather than input-oriented innovation.

title: Beyond coordination: responsibility and the crisis of global food governance design
authors: Carolan, Michael
keywords: Governance; Multilateralism; Coordination; Accountability; Governance grammar; Food security; Populism
abstract: Global food governance is increasingly described as being in crisis, as multilateral cooperation weakens amid rising nationalist and populist politics. However, less attention has been paid to how dominant multilateral modes of governance within the broader field of global governance shape the political conditions in which such tensions emerge. This paper examines how contemporary global food governance is organized primarily around coordination as a governing grammar—a mode of governing oriented toward aligning action across fragmented authority. Drawing on an interpretive analysis of a purposively selected body of authoritative global food governance documents produced between 2012 and 2025, the paper examines how coordination structures action, responsibility, evaluation, and contestation across multilateral institutions. The analysis identifies recurring patterns through which coordination diffuses responsibility, manages failure procedurally, and reframes distributive trade-offs as technical problems, enabling sustained engagement and institutional durability in the absence of centralized authority. These features constrain multilateral institutions' capacity to assume responsibility, adjudicate conflicts, or respond politically to uneven consequences. Grievances associated with food system transformation often struggle to gain traction within multilateral arenas; this may contribute to their articulation in other political contexts, including national and subnational arenas where responsibility is more readily attributed. Rather than treating such mobilizations as external threats to multilateralism, these dynamics are interpreted as being consistent with the institutional features of coordination-based governance. The paper concludes by outlining implications for global food governance, emphasizing the need to complement coordination with institutional arrangements that clarify responsibility, link measurement to material response, and enable political contestation over distributive trade-offs.
summary: Global food governance built on coordination diffuses responsibility and recasts distributive trade-offs as technical problems, which may push grievances into national populist arenas.

title: Food traceability systems and the probability of using chemical fertilizers and pesticides − empirical evidence using plot and farm household data from agriculture census
authors: Hung-Hao Chang; Yu-You Liou
keywords: Food traceability system; Chemical fertilizer; Pesticide; Groundwater; Plot data
abstract: In response to rising consumer demand for food safety, many countries have implemented food traceability systems (FTS) to enhance transparency and accountability along agricultural supply chains. While existing research has largely focused on demand side aspects, evidence on supply side responses remains limited. This study addresses this gap by examining the effects of FTS adoption on farm production practices, specifically the probability of using chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and groundwater, as well as farm revenue and marketing channel selection. We use microdata from Taiwan's 2020 agriculture census, which provides both plot-level and farm household-level information covering all registered crop farms. Motivated by a farm profit maximization model, we employ an instrumental variable (IV) approach to identify the local average treatment effect of FTS adoption. At the plot level, FTS adoption reduces the probability of using chemical fertilizer, pesticide, and groundwater by 8.2, 15.4, and 40 percentage points, respectively. At the household level, FTS adoption increases farm revenues and expands sales through direct-to-consumer and distributor channels. These findings suggest that while FTS is primarily designed to ensure food safety and market transparency, its adoption may generate unintended environmental co-benefits through reducing the likelihood of using environmentally sensitive inputs in farm production.
summary: Using Taiwan's 2020 agriculture census, adopting food traceability systems reduces the probability of using chemical fertilizer, pesticides and groundwater by 8–40 percentage points while raising farm revenue.

title: Implications of information presentation mode for internal and external validity in consumer experiments
authors: Christopher R. Gustafson; Antoine Champetier
keywords: Experiment; Methodology; Consumer choice; Information; External validity; Internal validity
abstract: The causal impact of information on consumer decision-making has been a prime area of interest for issues including novel food technologies, nutrition, food safety, and food authenticity. Experiments are oftentimes the only way to estimate causal impacts of information, as secondary data lack details on individual-specific information exposure. Response to information is relevant for many policy questions and has been formally integrated into some policy processes, such as those related to provision of nutrition information. However, the standard approach, which exposes participants to information, may provide inaccurate predictions of real-world outcomes. In the real-world, consumers may choose whether to access information, driven by a variety of motives. Forced exposure in experiments may also unintentionally bias results—threatening the internal validity of the design—by signaling the information's importance to participants. This study investigates how different methods of presenting information impact both the internal and external validity of research designs. Participants were randomized to one of four conditions: information exposure, opt out to bypass information, opt in to access information, and a no-information control. Our findings indicate that the information presentation method has large impacts on external validity, demonstrated by significant differences in results across conditions. Information provision mode also yields significant, though smaller, impacts on internal validity among the subset of participants who accessed the information. In the study, participants are exposed to information about honey fraud, a topic that is both present in general media and of concern for the beekeeping industry globally.
summary: Randomizing whether consumers are forced, opt in, or opt out of information about honey fraud shows the presentation mode substantially changes experimental results, threatening external and, to a lesser degree, internal validity.

title: Eating nature: Revealing the ecological cost of food trade through a global biodiversity-risk footprint
authors: Stella Lauro; Silvana Dalmazzone; Giorgio Vacchiano; Marco M. Bagliani
keywords: Biodiversity footprint; Deforestation; Biodiversity loss; Life-cycle assessment; Land-use change; Agricultural expansion
abstract: International trade in food commodities is a major driver of global biodiversity loss through the conversion of forests to agriculture. Yet existing deforestation metrics often fail to capture the full ecological consequences. We introduce a Biodiversity Risk indicator that weights deforested hectares by species vulnerability and endemism, offering a more nuanced assessment of biodiversity impacts from agricultural expansion into forests. Linking spatially explicit deforestation data with food trade flows, we uncover strong mismatches between countries' Deforestation Footprint and Biodiversity Risk. Indonesia, despite lower deforestation volumes than Brazil, emerges as the most impacted country due to high species vulnerability and specific crop conversion patterns. Commodity-level analysis distinguishes locally consumed crops (e.g., meat, cassava, rice) from globally traded biodiversity-intensive commodities (e.g., palm oil, soy, natural rubber), offering new insights for targeted interventions. Our findings underscore the need to integrate biodiversity metrics into supply-chain governance and deforestation policies to promote more ecologically responsible trade.
summary: A biodiversity-risk footprint weighting deforestation by species vulnerability shows mismatches with plain deforestation footprints, with Indonesia most impacted despite less forest loss than Brazil, driven by traded commodities like palm oil and soy.

title: The UK's middle-income dietary trap: High emissions, low nutrition
authors: Yunhuan Gao; Pablo Piñero; Eduardo Aguilera; Martin Bruckner; Alberto Sanz Cobeña; He He; Christian Reynolds
keywords: Dietary transition; Income disparities; Nutrient Rich Food index; Global warming potential; Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index; Middle-Income Dietary Trap
abstract: Dietary transitions driven by income disparity increasingly impose a dual burden on health and the climate. This study integrates the Nutrient Rich Food (NRF9.3) index and Global Warming Potential (GWP) to evaluate the nutrition‑carbon trade-off in UK household food purchases in 2013. Our analysis reveals a 'middle-income dietary trap'. Across Deciles 4–8, households increase their overall food purchases as income rises, but this expansion is dominated by carbon-intensive, nutrient-poor foods such as meats, dairy, sugars, and vegetable oils. As a consequence, calorie intake peaks while improvements in diet quality lag behind, and carbon emissions reach their highest levels among all income groups. This misalignment reflects a stage in which rising food quantity precedes nutritional gains, generating a dual burden of high‑carbon, low-nutrition diets. In contrast, high-income groups (Deciles 9–10) achieve modest improvements in both nutrition and carbon efficiency, associated with higher consumption of nutrient-dense, low-GWP foods such as vegetables, fruits, and seafood. These findings highlight a non-linear income-emission relationship, consistent with the Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis. Our decomposition analysis identifies two mechanisms shaping dietary carbon efficiency: a static opposition between expenditure and energy density, and a dynamic trade-off between nutrient density and the carbon intensity of nutrients. Policy interventions should adopt stage-specific strategies targeting middle-income households, where the dietary trap is driven by expenditure–structure imbalance, by steering substitution toward nutrient-dense, lower-carbon foods and accelerating structural dietary change.
summary: UK middle-income households (deciles 4–8) expand purchases of carbon-intensive, nutrient-poor foods as income rises, producing the highest dietary emissions without matching nutrition gains, an EKC-like pattern.
