title: Pro-social versus pro-self motivations for green roof adoption: Evidence from a discrete choice experiment
authors: Georges Farina; Peter J. Robinson; W.J. Wouter Botzen; Pieter Van Beukering
keywords: Green roofs; Willingness-to-pay; Discrete choice experiment; Nature-based solutions; Information treatment; Urban adaptation
abstract: Green roofs are a promising Nature-Based Solution (NBS) for urban climate adaptation, yet their adoption remains limited due to multiple factors, including mixed incentives between private and public benefits. This study investigates the impact of information nudges on public preferences and willingness-to-pay (WTP) for green roof co-benefits in the Netherlands. Using a split-sample (n = 2173) Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE), we examine how highlighting private (e.g., indoor cooling, roof lifespan) versus public (e.g., biodiversity, flood risk reduction) benefits influences WTP. The results show that respondents value green roof benefits overall highly. Information nudges significantly affect WTP for specific attributes. In particular, the Pro-self treatment, that communicates the private benefits of green roofs, increases WTP for indoor cooling and flood risk reduction, while the Pro-social treatment, communicating the public benefits, positively influences preferences for biodiversity improvements. Our findings suggest that even when information emphasizes private benefits, it can simultaneously enhance WTP for collective outcomes, likely due to perceived spillover effects. The preferences also display a high level of heterogeneity, indicating diverse valuation patterns within the population. The study further highlights that focusing individuals on their private gains is an effective strategy to increase their support for green roofs. This result is particularly salient for households that rank low on the altruism scale. Additionally, the high demand for biodiversity suggests that cost-benefit analyses should account for non-use values when evaluating green roof policies.
summary: A Dutch discrete choice experiment finds emphasizing private benefits of green roofs raises willingness to pay for cooling and even flood-risk reduction, especially among less altruistic households, while public-benefit framing boosts biodiversity values.

title: Land-use optimization to support cost-effective landscape transformation policies for wildfire mitigation
authors: Rui Serôdio Simões; Paulo Flores Ribeiro; Marta Mesquita; Isabel Martins; João Morais Mourato; José Lima Santos
keywords: Land-use choice models; Fire regime models; Land-use optimization; Cost-effectiveness; Landscape transformation; Non-monetary cost assessment; Integer linear programming
abstract: This study develops and tests an innovative analytical framework integrating a fire regime model and a land-use choice model to maximize the net economic returns from land use while keeping the probability of an extreme fire regime (EFR) below a socially acceptable level. This framework is applied and tested at a nationwide scale, for the whole of mainland Portugal, where an EFR characterized by high cumulative burnt areas and their temporal concentration has been expanding, and a Landscape Transformation Programme has been adopted by Government. By taking into account biophysical and socioeconomic heterogeneity, and thus variation in the relative profitability of different land-use classes across the country, the optimization model yields case-specific land-use solutions that respect the wildfire policy constraint on EFR probability at a minimum cost for each particular landscape area. By running the model for successively lower levels of the EFR probability, we got the required areal extent, intensity, direction (in terms of land-use change) and marginal cost of landscape transformation for each level of policy ambition about the EFR probability reduction. This marginal cost rises with the level of policy ambition, which raises issues about the affordability and optimality of each level of policy ambition. The approach is assessed as useful to promote the cost-effectiveness of the Landscape Transformation Programme in Portugal as well as that of policies in different countries with similar policy goals and fire regimes.
summary: Combining a fire-regime model with a land-use choice model for mainland Portugal, the paper optimizes land use to maximize net returns while keeping extreme-fire-regime probability below set limits, showing marginal costs rise with policy ambition.

title: Hydropower dams, deforestation, and land use change: Evidence from Brazil
authors: Chiara Falco; Valentina Raimondi
keywords: Hydropower dam; Forest loss; Land use change; Institutions
abstract: In Brazil, hydropower generates more than 60% of the national electricity supply, placing the country among the most hydropower-dependent economies worldwide. This study analyses the causal impact of dam construction on forest loss using a new municipality-level panel dataset covering 379 hydropower projects, combined with high-resolution satellite data on forest cover and land use. Applying modern staggered difference-in-differences estimators robust to heterogeneous treatment effects, we find that dam construction and operation reduce municipal forest cover by nearly 10% relative to the mean, with losses accumulating steadily after construction and driven primarily by cropland expansion. Impacts are concentrated in the North and Northeast and are amplified in municipalities with large shares of public land and insecure property rights. Higher pre-construction enforcement intensity reflects prior deforestation pressure under the PPCDAm targeting framework rather than institutional strength. We also document significant spatial spillovers, with dam-induced deforestation extending to neighboring municipalities at roughly 40–50% of the direct effect, implying that administrative boundaries systematically understate the total environmental footprint of hydropower expansion. These findings highlight that while hydropower contributes to energy security, it entails substantial environmental costs requiring stronger land governance and watershed-scale environmental assessment.
summary: Hydropower dams in Brazil cut municipal forest cover by nearly 10%, mainly via cropland expansion and amplified by insecure property rights, with spillover deforestation in neighboring municipalities of 40–50% of the direct effect.

title: Climate change skepticism and farmers' responses to CO2e taxation
authors: Kahsay Haile Zemo; Mette Termansen
keywords: Climate Change Skepticism; Beliefs; Climate Policy; CO2e Tax; Agriculture; Agri-Environment-Climate Measures
abstract: Agriculture is a major contributor to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, yet it has largely been exempt from stricter environmental regulations, partly due to strong resistance from the sector. Across Europe, farmers' widespread opposition has often resulted in the weakening or rollback of ambitious environmental policies. In Denmark, the recent introduction of a CO2e (CO2-equivalent) tax on agricultural emissions, one of the first global attempts to directly target non-fossil fuel-based GHGs, has similarly prompted immediate organized farmer protests. This study examines whether and to what extent climate change skepticism (CCS) is associated with farmers' belief misalignment about the economic impact of the CO2e tax on agriculture, resistance to the tax, and adoption of climate mitigation measures, drawing on a survey of 981 Danish farmers. We find that climate skeptic farmers substantially overestimate the tax's negative impacts while discounting expert assessments. Climate neutral and skeptic farmers show greater opposition to the CO2e tax, with CCS strongly predicting resistance even after accounting for tax design, information, and farm characteristics. Higher CCS is also associated with lower adoption of climate mitigation measures, with participation in subsidized climate initiatives about 25% lower among skeptics compared with non-skeptics. These patterns are more pronounced among livestock producers than crop producers. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of climate-related beliefs in explaining variation in beliefs about policy impacts, policy acceptance, and behavioral responses.
summary: A survey of 981 Danish farmers finds climate-skeptic farmers overestimate the harm of Denmark's agricultural CO2e tax, oppose it more, and are about 25% less likely to join subsidized climate mitigation initiatives.

title: Tax-financed green policies and income inequality in an agent-based model
authors: Lucca Gustafson Rodrigues; Gilberto Tadeu Lima; Pedro Romero Marques
keywords: Decarbonization policies; Carbon tax; Wealth tax; Income inequality; Agent-based modeling
abstract: The interdependent dynamics among economic growth, income inequality, and greenhouse gas emissions have attracted attention in both academic and policy discussions on decarbonization strategies. Notwithstanding this expanding body of work, theoretical and empirical contributions underscore the difficulty of simultaneously achieving favorable outcomes across these three dimensions, suggesting the existence of a structural trilemma involving growth, income distribution, and environmental degradation. This paper develops an agent-based model (ABM) to explore these trade-offs and focuses on the impacts of different tax-financed green policies. Financing and environmental policy instruments produce complex effects on key macroeconomic variables, raising questions about whether—and under what conditions—the trilemma holds. The simulations examine scenarios in which either a carbon tax or a wealth tax finance the following green policies: (i) green price subsidy, (ii) public non-patented green R&D, (iii) subsidy for private green R&D, and (iv) green public procurement. While the carbon tax is both a financing and an environmental policy instrument, the wealth tax is primarily a mechanism of income redistribution. Findings suggest that the policy mix is a key determinant of whether the trilemma might occur. On the one hand, carbon taxation is more effective in reducing emissions but at higher social and macroeconomic costs. On the other hand, despite promoting redistribution, wealth taxation must count on specific complementary policies—such as public-led green innovation—to foster a low-carbon economy.
summary: Agent-based simulations show carbon-tax-financed green policies cut emissions more but at higher social and macro costs, while wealth-tax financing aids redistribution but needs complements like public green R&D to decarbonize.

title: Valuing improvements in native fish populations from river restoration projects: Evidence from a choice experiment in the Murray-Darling Basin in Australia
authors: John Rolfe; Megan Star; Nicole Flint; Rodrigo Zilleruelo; Jeremy De Valck; Darshana Rajapaksa; Azad Rahman; Matthew Gordos; Boyd Blackwell
keywords: Non-market Valuation; Discrete Choice Experiment; River Restoration; Native Fish; Murray-Darling Basin; Value Stability
abstract: There is increasing focus on restoration projects to improve environmental health of native fish, but the high cost of these interventions requires careful assessment of the benefits in project justification. While engineering projects such as fish ladders and fish screening in river systems are expensive, the benefits are more immediate and targeted on native fish than generic conservation approaches. This study reports a discrete choice experiment used to value improvements in native fish populations from river restoration projects in the Murray-Darling Basin in New South Wales. As well as considering improvements to native fish, the choice experiment also framed potential changes in river health to benefit water birds, recreational fishing opportunities and the length of the waterway that was improved. The results add to the small pool of primary valuation studies focused on improvements to native fish populations through river restoration projects, providing one of the first economic analyses of this issue. The choice experiments also tested for differences in values between in-catchment and out-of-catchment populations. The present value of each 1 % improvement in native fish populations is estimated at $5.73 per household. Over an estimated 3,228,000 households in New South Wales, this translates to $18.5 M for each 1 % improvement. The consistency of these value estimates with results of other comparable studies indicates that the values for improving fish populations have remained stable over time as well as being consistent across different management options for river restoration.
summary: A choice experiment values each 1% improvement in Murray-Darling native fish populations at $5.73 per household, about $18.5M across New South Wales, with values stable over time and across restoration options.

title: From scarcity to strategy: Designing hay markets to mitigate feed shortages and income shocks
authors: Julia Kunkel; Jonathan Haag; Robert Finger; Sergei Schaub; Jürgen Groeneveld; Christian Klassert; Birgit Müller
keywords: Drought; Grassland; Hay prices; Forage trading; Network structures; Trading networks; Optimisation
abstract: Grassland-based forages — such as grass, silage, and hay — are a key feed source for dairy cows. In the transition to more sustainable dairy systems, grassland-based production is increasingly valued for its contributions to biodiversity and regional resilience. However, droughts reduce grassland yields and raise feed prices, challenging farmers to secure feed and stable incomes. Existing coping strategies, such as early slaughter or livestock sales, can have long-term consequences beyond the drought event.In this study, we propose hay markets as a short-term buffer for drought-induced feed shortages and income shocks. We compare potential trading networks differing in trading radius and trading partners in terms of effectiveness, efficiency and possible side effects using a stylised network model. For farm units aggregated at the German county level, we simulate cost-minimal trading schedules and derive remaining feed shortages and income shocks. Results show that forage trading can reduce shocks by around two-third during nationwide droughts and fully mitigate localised shocks. Effective mitigation requires either a broad trading radius or sufficient trading partners. However, poorly connected nationwide networks can lead to inefficient transport, while segmentation at state level may lock in shortages and reduce both effectiveness and efficiency. We also observe unintended side effects: trading may shift income shocks to unaffected farm units and increase overall transport distances. Overall, we show that hay markets could enhance dairy farmers’ drought resistance, but must be designed carefully. Policy makers, farmer associations, and agricultural chambers can support this by providing a well-designed market infrastructure.
summary: The paper studies how hay (forage) trading networks and market design can mitigate drought-induced feed shortages and farm income shocks.

title: How managed lake-level fluctuations affect waterfront property values: Evidence from a regulated lake system
authors: Thapa, Ganesh
keywords: Hedonic Valuation; Hydrologic Risk; Lake Levels; Property Markets; Water-Level Management
abstract: Climate change is increasing hydrologic variability and management trade-offs. This study examines how managed lake-level fluctuations are capitalized into waterfront property values within a regulated lake system in Wisconsin, USA. By linking residential property transactions from 2013 to 2024 with high-frequency hydrologic and lake water-quality data, we estimate two-way fixed-effects hedonic models that isolate the economic impacts of deviations from expected seasonal lake levels under existing management rules. The results indicate that seasonal lake-level deviations (in.) reduce waterfront property sale prices by about 2%. Additional functional-form analyses provide limited evidence of strong nonlinear or asymmetric responses. Monte Carlo simulations suggest that stabilizing seasonal lake-level deviations within ±3 in. increase the aggregate value of lakefront housing by approximately $4.6 million (2013 USD), equivalent to an average gain of roughly $16,254 per property. The findings demonstrate how housing markets internalize hydrologic instability in regulated freshwater systems facing increasing climate risk.
summary: In a regulated Wisconsin lake system, deviations from expected seasonal lake levels lower waterfront sale prices by about 2%, and stabilizing levels within ±3 inches would add roughly $4.6 million to lakefront housing value.

title: Welfare implications of no net loss policies with heterogeneous cultural ecosystem services
authors: Hagem, Cathrine
keywords: Cultural ecosystem services; Land loss; No net loss; Offset markets; Offsets; Ambient permits
abstract: No net loss (NNL) targets for nature are increasingly implemented at both national and subnational levels. While these policies are typically framed in terms of area or biophysical equivalence, they may overlook heterogeneity in the cultural ecosystem service (CES) values associated with undeveloped land. This paper develops a parsimonious economic model to analyze the welfare implications of alternative NNL policy designs when CES values differ across municipalities. We distinguish between local CES values, such as recreational and amenity benefits accruing to nearby populations, and a national CES value associated with the existence of undeveloped nature.We compare unilateral and cooperative municipal policies and examine the performance of taxes and subsidies versus offset markets under area-based and CES value-based NNL targets. We show that area-based NNL policies are generally welfare suboptimal in the presence of heterogeneous local CES values, even when implemented cost-effectively through offset markets. By contrast, NNL targets defined in CES value terms can achieve constrained welfare optima using appropriately designed fiscal instruments or ambient permit markets. Although inter-municipal cooperation reduces aggregate costs, distributional effects may prevent mutually beneficial outcomes without side payments. Numerical illustrations based on Norwegian data support the analytical results and highlight implications for subnational and national offset policy design.
summary: A parsimonious economic model analyzes the welfare implications of alternative no-net-loss nature policy designs when local and national cultural ecosystem service values of undeveloped land differ across municipalities.

title: Toward low-carbon diets: Exploring the role of climate perceptions and household mitigation practices in reducing meat consumption
authors: Lan Tran; Ye Su
keywords: Behavioral spillovers; Climate perceptions; Dietary transition; Ecological footprint; Household mitigation; Meat consumption
abstract: Transitioning toward a sustainable food system requires reducing meat consumption, yet global meat demand continues to rise. This study investigates the behavioral mechanisms linking abstract climate perceptions and routine household mitigation practices (e.g., recycling, energy efficiency) to sustainable food choices. Specifically, we examine whether routine pro-environmental behaviors act as a "spillover" mechanism and a behavioral bridge toward lower-carbon dietary changes, such as reducing meat intake or adopting plant-based substitutes. Using a nationwide climate survey of U.S. households (2024–2025), we analyze the drivers of these shifts. The findings reveal that climate change perceptions influence dietary outcomes through both direct and indirect pathways, with household mitigation practices serving as a significant mediating mechanism toward more demanding shifts such as plant-based food adoption. The results further show that climate justice perceptions are significant drivers of high-commitment dietary choices, while specific socio-demographic factors remain persistent barriers to change. By situating food choices within the broader context of household environmental pressure, the study offers a quantified framework for understanding how to align individual consumption with ecological limits. This research also provides actionable insights for policymakers and food marketers in developing integrated strategies to facilitate the transition toward a more sustainable, low-carbon food system.
summary: A U.S. household survey finds climate perceptions reduce meat consumption both directly and via routine household mitigation practices, which act as a bridge to more demanding shifts like plant-based adoption.

title: Biodiversity benefits of the climate adaptation policy: Evidence from millions birdwatching records in China
authors: Hantian Sheng; Canfei He; Wenbo Hu
keywords: Climate adaptation; Biodiversity; Birdwatching records; Ecological conservation; China
abstract: Climate adaptation policies are critical for building urban resilience, yet their ecological consequences remain underexplored. We take China's climate adaptation pilot policy (CACP) as a quasi-natural experiment and employ a difference-in-differences approach to examine the biodiversity effects. By using a unique dataset of over four million birdwatching records from 2012 to 2021, we find that the policy significantly increases biodiversity, raising the Shannon diversity index by 0.25–0.40 units in pilot cities. Mechanism analyses reveal three influencing channels, including improved air quality, enhanced vegetation cover, and stimulated green innovation. Meanwhile, the positive ecological effects are more pronounced in disaster-prone and less economically developed regions, and are conditioned by both public concern and governmental attention. Our findings highlight synergies among climate action, biodiversity conservation, and equitable urban development, and provide empirical evidence that climate policies could create win-win outcomes across these policy domains. We also propose that ecological considerations should be incorporated into adaptation planning both in China and globally.
summary: China's climate adaptation pilot cities saw bird diversity (Shannon index) rise by 0.25–0.40 units, via better air quality, vegetation cover and green innovation, according to four million birdwatching records.

title: Beyond resilience: Domestic and cross-border economic impacts and co-benefits of regional climate change adaptation
authors: Dimitrios Stamopoulos; Petros Dimas; Ioannis Sebos; Dionysis Assimacopoulos
keywords: Climate change adaptation; Climate resilience; Input–output analysis; Adaptation benefits; Regional Adaptation Action Plan; Crete; Multiplier effects
abstract: This paper presents a novel methodology for assessing the economic impacts of climate change (CC) adaptation measures included in the Regional Adaptation Action Plans (RAAPs). To this end, a regional input-output (I-O) model is developed that allocates the required investments in different economic sectors, and quantifies their effects on key socioeconomic indicators. The methodology is then applied on the Greek region of Crete, as a specific case study that analyzes the structural impacts of its RAAP on its regional, domestic, and cross-border economic linkages. We find that the successful implementation of Crete's RAAP has the potential to contribute approximately €200 mil. to national GDP, enhancing production output, employee compensation, and government revenue. Beyond their social and environmental value, CCA actions also generate substantial economic co-benefits, offering a tangible basis for communicating their importance to policymakers and stakeholders.
summary: A regional input-output model for Crete estimates its Regional Adaptation Action Plan could add about €200 million to Greek GDP, showing economic co-benefits of climate adaptation investment.

title: From domestic collapse to global dispersion: Post-Fukushima carbon redistribution
authors: Su, Tong
keywords: Carbon redistribution; Fukushima nuclear crisis; Carbon decoupling; Supply chain reorganization; Trade-embodied carbon; Input–output analysis
abstract: The 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster triggered systemic disruptions to Japan's aquatic sector, yet the long-term redistribution of its carbon footprint through global supply chains remains underexplored. Using multi-regional input–output analysis (2008–2020), this study makes three contributions. First, a decoupling paradox: while production-side emissions declined 21%, consumption-based emissions remained stable through import substitution, with carbon intensity improvements systematically offset by consumption-side lock-in toward carbon-intensive sourcing patterns, a redistribution further evidenced by asymmetric upstream–downstream supply chain adjustments. Second, an asymmetric policy irreversibility: actual import liberalization by the US and UK recovered merely 0.48% production, whereas simulated removal of Chinese restrictions would trigger a 10.6% rebound, revealing that geopolitically differentiated trade governance creates durable carbon lock-in. Third, a market bifurcation: destination market characteristics systematically bifurcate post-disaster carbon decoupling trajectories, with East Asian markets deteriorating while Western markets achieved sustained strong decoupling, evidence that uniform mitigation strategies are insufficient across trading partners. These findings challenge the adequacy of territorial emission accounting and producer-responsibility frameworks for globally traded food commodities. They demonstrate that disaster-induced supply chain disruptions can permanently redistribute global carbon footprints rather than merely causing temporary perturbations, necessitating of consumption-based climate governance, proactive carbon leakage monitoring in food safety trade policy, and coordinated regional environmental standards, offering lessons extending beyond Japan to any economy facing compound trade–environment shocks.
summary: After Fukushima, Japan's aquatic-sector production emissions fell 21% but consumption-based emissions stayed flat through import substitution, showing disasters can permanently redistribute carbon footprints via trade.

title: Undermined by rebounds? assessing the role of energy efficiency in alleviating energy poverty in Italy
authors: Alfonso Carfora; Francesco Maria Chelli; Giuseppe Scandurra
keywords: Energy poverty; Rebound effect; Energy efficiency; Italian household budget survey
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between household energy efficiency, rebound effects, and energy poverty in Italy, using microdata from the 2023 Italian Household Budget Survey. We employ a two-step approach: first, a stochastic frontier energy demand model is estimated to derive household-level measures of energy efficiency and the direct rebound effect; second, these estimates are incorporated into a logistic regression to assess their association with the probability of experiencing energy poverty. Our results indicate that higher energy efficiency significantly lowers energy expenditures and reduces the likelihood of energy poverty. However, these benefits are partly offset by the rebound effect, whereby households increase energy use after efficiency gains. The analysis also shows that current incentive schemes disproportionately benefit wealthier households, while vulnerable groups remain under-supported. By highlighting the dual role of efficiency gains and rebound dynamics, this study underscores the importance of designing equity-oriented policies that combine efficiency improvements with targeted financial support. These findings contribute to ongoing debates on how to make European energy transition strategies more socially inclusive and effective.
summary: Italian household data show higher energy efficiency lowers energy spending and energy-poverty risk, but rebound effects partly offset gains and current incentives mostly benefit wealthier households.

title: Digital infrastructure and territorial heterogeneity in quality-of-life outcomes
authors: Angela Stefania Bergantino; Benedetta Coluccia; Giulio Fusco; Gianluca Monturano
keywords: Digitalization; Broadband infrastructure; Difference-in-differences; QoL; Italy
abstract: Digital infrastructure is widely recognized as a key driver of territorial development, yet its effects on multidimensional quality of life (QoL) remain insufficiently understood. This paper examines the impact of ultra-fast broadband expansion on QoL across Italian provinces over the period 2014–2022. Exploiting the gradual and policy-driven rollout of broadband infrastructure in rural "white areas", we implement a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences framework with fixed effects. We analyze four core dimensions of QoL, income, education, environmental conditions, and health outcomes, and construct a composite index to assess aggregate effects. The results reveal heterogeneous and non-aligned impacts. Broadband expansion improves economic and educational outcomes, but is also associated with a deterioration in environmental conditions, while effects on health remain limited. As a result, the overall impact on Qol is weak or negative, reflecting trade-offs across dimensions. These findings suggest that digital infrastructure does not generate uniform improvements in QoL, but rather reshapes its internal composition. The paper contributes by providing causal evidence on the multidimensional and uneven effects of digitalization across territories.
summary: Ultra-fast broadband rollout in Italy's rural 'white areas' improved income and education outcomes but worsened environmental conditions, leaving overall quality-of-life effects weak or negative.

title: Revitalizing marginal areas: A foundational economy approach
authors: Giuseppe Varavallo; Filippo Barbera; Riccardo Di Clemente
keywords: Marginal areas; Rural territories; Foundational economy; Google maps API; Service provision; Multi-service hubs; Economic service coverage
abstract: This study presents a novel data-driven methodology to assess service provision and territorial fragility in Italy's marginal areas, focusing on the Piedmont region. Based on the foundational economic theory, this research emphasizes the role of essential services in sustaining daily life and territorial cohesion. We develop a Foundational Economy Index (FEI) that maps the availability of key services including healthcare, education, food, transportation, and civic infrastructure at the local level. Leveraging ISTAT data and over 17,000 geolocated service points through the Google Maps API, we identify distinct service configurations across 372 municipalities using hierarchical clustering techniques. We further introduce the concept of multi-service hubs, defined as multi-functional facilities that emerge in response to service scarcity and evaluate their capacity using the Economic Service Coverage (ESC) metric. Results reveal pronounced intraregional disparities, with most municipalities exhibiting critically low levels of foundational service availability. Hierarchical clustering identifies three distinct territorial profiles, with most municipalities concentrated in the low-service group, reflecting widespread structural under-provision. By operationalizing the foundational economy through a spatial analytical framework, this study provides a replicable and scalable approach for monitoring service equity in marginal territories worldwide. It offers actionable insights for policymakers, community leaders, and stakeholders aiming to reverse structural decline and promote sustainable development.
summary: A Foundational Economy Index built from 17,000+ geolocated services across 372 Piedmont municipalities shows most marginal-area municipalities have critically low essential-service availability.

title: Nonlinear effects of the digital economy on urban-rural factor mobility: A hybrid econometric-machine learning approach
authors: Hongbo Li; Zijun Liu
keywords: Digital economy; Urban-rural factor mobility; Space of flows; A hybrid econometric-machine learning approach; Nonlinear transmission mechanisms
abstract: Unprecedented digital economy (DE) penetration disrupts the traditional urban-rural dichotomy, yet the complex nonlinear interactions driving multidimensional urban-rural factor mobility (URFM) remain largely opaque in regional science. While foundational literature extensively explores the interplay of population flows (PF), land flows (LF), and capital flows (CF), the nonlinear mechanisms governing their synergistic evolution within DE-driven spatial restructuring demand deeper exploration. This study introduces the space of flows theory to unpack these synergistic dynamics, conceptualizing DE as the concrete operational form of the space of flows. By integrating econometrics and interpretable machine learning, we examine panel data from Zhejiang, Hubei, and Sichuan spanning 2013-2022, representing distinct developmental stages. Findings reveal that DE reshapes URFM through profound nonlinearity, exhibiting heterogeneous threshold effects across flow types. PF displays diminishing marginal returns as digital networks initially accelerate migration but subsequently enhance rural retention capacity. LF transitions from early land-saving optimization to later demand-reshaping spatial expansion. CF demonstrates exponential growth, primarily driven by expanding digital financial networks. Beyond these nonlinear effects, we identify region-specific dynamic transmission chains elucidating internal factor linkages. In advanced markets (Zhejiang), DE and capital form a bidirectional amplification loop, deepening localized resource accumulation. In transitional economies (Hubei), capital accumulation precurses subsequent digital and land reconfiguration, highlighting strong capital-driven features. Conversely, in geographically constrained regions (Sichuan), DE acts as a pioneering force, bypassing spatial friction to trigger subsequent factor adjustments. These heterogeneous pathways demonstrate that the space of flows, through DE as its operational architecture, fundamentally alters the factor allocation logic within both urban and rural spaces. These findings advance spatial economics by decoding digital-spatial restructuring, illustrating how regional endowments dictate multidimensional URFM mechanisms.
summary: Panel data from Zhejiang, Hubei and Sichuan show the digital economy affects urban-rural population, land and capital flows nonlinearly with threshold effects, via region-specific transmission chains.

title: Gender diversity, institutional weakness, and waste management outcomes in Italian municipalities
authors: Maria Carmela Aprile; Livio Ferrante; Stefania Fontana; Simona Monteleone
keywords: Women; Institutional quality; Waste sorting; WIC indicator; Italy
abstract: This study examines the relationship between female political representation and environmental outcomes, focusing on waste management practices in Italy. Using a panel dataset of over 7000 municipalities (2011–2020), we employ fixed effects regressions complemented with a regression discontinuity design based on close mixed-gender mayoral elections and an instrumental variables strategy exploiting the introduction of gender quotas under Law 215/2012. We find that a higher share of female councilors is associated with higher separate waste collection rates, particularly in areas with weaker institutional integrity, as measured by corruption-related offenses. In contrast, female mayors show weaker or delayed associations with waste management outcomes, suggesting that environmental performance may depend more on the collective oversight and deliberative functions of the city council rather than on individual executive action. Importantly, higher waste sorting rates are not associated with higher public expenditure, pointing to potential efficiency gains. Results are robust to alternative measures of institutional weakness. The findings contribute to the literature on gender and environmental governance by documenting a robust association between gender diversity in local governance and environmental performance, particularly in contexts where institutional integrity is weaker.
summary: Across 7,000+ Italian municipalities, more female councilors are associated with higher separate waste collection rates without higher spending, especially where institutional integrity is weak.

title: The spatiotemporal patterns and driving decomposition of carbon inequality in the Triangle of Central China
authors: Yan Qiao; Limin Jiao; Weiqian Lei; Qiqi Jia; Yajie Zhang; Jia Li; Bingjie Li
keywords: Carbon inequality; Urban agglomeration; City network; Social network analysis; Shapley value decomposition
abstract: Non-evenness of carbon emissions among cities poses a dilemma for equitable access to low-carbon transitions. As cities within clusters are interconnected nodes shaping emission dynamics, carbon inequality emerges not merely from local disparities but from the regional connectivity. Based on urban interaction networks, this study innovatively treats the urban agglomeration as an organic whole to measure the evolution pattern and decompose driving factors of carbon equity in the Triangle of Central China (TOCC) formed by three metropolitan areas. Key findings reveal that: (1) Carbon inequality presents a 'polycentric' spatial pattern, primarily driven by intra-metropolitan disparities (72.4 %), with policy responses of quantitative carbon inequality lagging spatial inequality by 1-2 years. (2) Industrial structure is the most powerful reduction forces for city carbon emissions across the metropolitan areas and urban agglomeration. Dense intra-metropolitan flows inhibit emissions, yet polycentric structures in the TOCC generate positive spillover. (3) Significant emission reduction factors are the main cause of the carbon inequality, mainly including industrial modernization and city interaction capability, while technological innovation and optimization of green infrastructure effectively mitigate metropolitan disparities. This research offers a transformative perspective that bridges isolated urban analyses with collaborative governance frameworks, emphasizing fair environmental responsibility and multi-level governance across 'city-metropolitan-agglomerations'.
summary: Carbon inequality in China's Triangle of Central China urban agglomeration is polycentric and driven mostly (72.4%) by intra-metropolitan disparities, with industrial modernization and city interaction as key drivers.

title: Unveiling the role of eco-certifications as spatial drivers of green tourism in Italian provinces
authors: Riccardo Gianluigi Serio; Maria Michela Dickson; Diego Giuliani; Andrea Mazzitelli; Giuseppe Espa
keywords: Environmental sustainability; Sustainable tourism; Sustainability indicators; GWPCA; SDEM
abstract: The measurement of sustainability in tourism remains a critical challenge for socio-economic planning, as many existing indicators describe environmental conditions or pressures rather than the concrete actions undertaken by destinations and tourism actors. This study develops a spatially explicit composite indicator of certification-based sustainability effort for Italian provinces. The indicator is built from eco-certifications and environmental management schemes adopted by public institutions, accommodation providers, tourism-related services, and environmental management actors. Rather than providing an absolute ranking of destination sustainability, the indicator captures the intensity and local coherence of certified environmental effort in tourism. Methodologically, the indicator is constructed through Geographically Weighted Principal Component Analysis (GWPCA), which allows the relevance of each certification to vary across territories according to local covariance structures. The resulting indicator is then analyzed through a Spatial Durbin Error Model (SDEM), to examine how certification-based sustainability effort is associated with local tourism, socio-economic, and environmental characteristics, as well as with neighboring territorial contexts. The empirical analysis highlights the spatially differentiated and interdependent nature of green tourism effort, showing that sustainability-oriented certification patterns are shaped by both local conditions and broader territorial linkages. The study contributes to the literature by combining an effort-oriented interpretation of tourism sustainability with a spatially sensitive framework for indicator construction and spatial modeling.
summary: A geographically weighted composite indicator of eco-certification effort in Italian provinces shows green tourism effort is spatially differentiated and shaped by both local conditions and neighboring territories.

title: Public-sector decision support for digital-agriculture rollout: Feasibility-constrained provincial sequencing in Vietnam
authors: Thanh Van Do; Enjun Xia; Binh Anh Pham
keywords: Digital agriculture; Public-sector decision support; Socio-economic planning; Portfolio regret; Robustness analysis; Integer programming; Multi-criteria decision analysis; Vietnam
abstract: Digital-agriculture programmes are increasingly central to public-sector modernization, but governments cannot usually roll them out everywhere at once. This article examines Vietnam as a territorially heterogeneous planning case and asks how public agencies can stage provincial rollout when productivity opportunity, equity need, low-greenhouse-gas (low-GHG) baseline advantage, and implementability do not peak in the same places. The study develops an ex-ante decision-support framework that links baseline forecasting, multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), exact 0–1 integer-programming portfolio selection, and regret diagnostics under weight uncertainty. The framework is not an ex-post causal evaluation of concrete policy packages; rather, it provides a transparent sequencing architecture for bounded public allocation. The results show that a neutral Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) baseline produces a territorially mixed priority set rather than a single readiness block, while feasibility-constrained optimization expands the selected frontier from 23 provinces under the narrow B0 envelope to 37 under B1 and 48 under B2. Robustness checks based on Dirichlet weight draws, rank-reversal tests, alternative feasibility proxies, and alternative MCDA methods show that the broad sequencing logic is not driven by one arbitrary weight vector or one isolated readiness proxy. The contribution is a practical public-sector planning framework for converting spatially misaligned objectives into defensible rollout tiers under administrative constraints.
summary: An MCDA and integer-programming framework for sequencing Vietnam's provincial digital-agriculture rollout yields territorially mixed priority sets that are robust to weighting choices.

title: Beyond efficiency: Quality of Government and eco-productivity convergence in the EU
authors: Marc Aliana; Maria Teresa Balaguer-Coll; Diego Prior; Emili Tortosa-Ausina
keywords: Cohesion policy; Eco-productivity convergence; Multilevel governance; Quality of Government
abstract: This paper examines eco-productivity convergence across European Union regions while explicitly incorporating institutional quality within a multilevel governance framework. Using a panel of 216 NUTS-2 regions over the period 2010–2023, we analyse whether regions converge in their ability to generate economic output while limiting environmental pressures, and whether the estimated convergence patterns differ once both national and regional Quality of Government (QoG) are taken into account. Eco-productivity is measured using a nonparametric frontier approach based on Data Envelopment Analysis, with labour and capital as inputs, GDP as a desirable output, and Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions, transformed into an output-oriented 'GHG savings' indicator. The results show that average eco-productivity levels are around 8% higher when QoG is accounted for, cross-regional dispersion is considerably lower, and β-convergence is consistently stronger and statistically significant across all subperiods. Overall, eco-productivity convergence is associated with QoG, suggesting that sustainable regional catch-up is more likely where green investment is matched by improvements in institutional quality.
summary: Across 216 EU NUTS-2 regions (2010–2023), accounting for Quality of Government raises measured eco-productivity by about 8% and strengthens regional convergence, linking sustainable catch-up to institutional quality.

title: Income inequality in Southern Africa: Evidence from interpretable machine learning and panel econometric models
authors: John Mulenga; Lenganji Simwanda; Sergei Pismennyi; Irena Benešová; Wilem Heijman; Anna Tsenteradze
keywords: Income inequality; Gini index; Machine learning; Economic development; Developing countries; Interpretable machine learning; Ensemble learning
abstract: This study analyses the determinants of income inequality in Southern Africa by combining interpretable ensemble machine learning with panel econometric models. The study uses an un-balanced panel dataset covering eleven Southern African countries over the period 1991–2019. The analysis is anchored in an adapted Social Determinants of Health framework, which helps organise the selected variables into structural, institutional, and intermediary socio-economic domains. Four ensemble models, namely Categorical Boosting, Extreme Gradient Boosting, Gradient Boosting Machine, and Adaptive Boosting, are used to capture non-linear relationships and interaction effects, while random effects and two-way fixed effects models provide econometric benchmarks. The machine learning models show strong internal predictive performance, with an out-of-sample R2 ≈ 0.98, although the training and testing design is based on a stratified random split across pooled country-year observations. Therefore, the reported test results are interpreted as internal validation within the observed Southern African panel rather than evidence of full generalisation to new countries or future periods. SHapley Additive exPlanations results show that unemployment is the most influential predictor of income inequality across all four ensemble models, followed by gross domestic product per capita and institutional quality. The comparison with panel econometric models shows partial convergence, particularly for gross domestic product per capita, years of schooling, and natural resource rents, while differences in unemployment and democracy suggest that their effects may be non-linear or interaction-dependent. The findings indicate that inequality in Southern Africa is shaped by labour market exclusion, uneven economic growth, institutional conditions, education-related disparities, and resource dependence. The results support policies that promote inclusive employment, improve the quality and equity of education, strengthen accountable institutions, and ensure transparent management of natural resource revenues. The study contributes by showing that interpretable machine learning can complement, rather than replace, conventional panel econometrics in explaining complex inequality dynamics.
summary: Interpretable machine learning on 11 Southern African countries (1991–2019) identifies unemployment as the strongest predictor of income inequality, followed by GDP per capita and institutional quality.

title: Effective influence on the preferences towards public and active transport following the implementation of pedestrianization
authors: Jing Tang; Muhammet Deveci; Ilgin Gokasar; Dursun Delen; Volkan Yıldız; Weizhong Wang
keywords: Pedestrianization; Multi-criteria decision-making; Consensus-building; Sustainable transport; Urban mobility
abstract: Pedestrianization can be defined as a spatial reconfiguration strategy that reallocates street space from vehicles to people to improve urban livability. As cities pursue a shift away from car dependency, pedestrianization has become an increasingly important component of sustainable mobility agendas. One of the fundamental questions in this transition concerns which governance scale is best suited to lead implementation. To address this, four alternatives (i.e., government (nation), metropolitan (city), local (county), consensus-building (public)) with fifteen criteria under demographic, environmental, transportation, and political aspects are evaluated through a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) method with input from four subject matter experts. According to the proposed framework, the consensus-building alternative obtains the highest utility degree, suggesting that public involvement may improve legitimacy, reduce resistance, and support policy continuity in pedestrianization strategies. These findings can support policymakers in designing pedestrianization strategies that better account for equity, resilience, and public acceptance.
summary: An expert-based multi-criteria evaluation finds public consensus-building ranks highest among governance scales for leading pedestrianization, supporting legitimacy and policy continuity.

title: Impact of integrated transportation on city high-quality development in China
authors: Tao Li; Ruidong Fan; Xiangbin Li; Qianqian Zheng
keywords: Highway; High-speed rail; Air transportation; City high-quality development; Multimodal transportation; Difference-in-differences
abstract: Against the backdrop of rapid urbanization, city high-quality development (CHQD) has become a core goal with integrated transportation (IT) emerging as a critical supporting factor. Based on the panel data from 2007 to 2023 of 287 cities in China, this paper applies a difference-in-difference (DID) model to investigate the impacts and mechanism of highway (HW), high-speed rail (HSR), air transportation (AT), and the coexistence of all three modes on CHQD. The result reveals that HW, HSR and AT operations promote CHQD, and the IT also shows a notably positive impact on CHQD. Because the IT indicator captures the availability of the three modes rather than operational coordination, the findings are interpreted as evidence of potential modal complementarity, not as proof of a super-additive synergistic effect. Furthermore, the impacts of HW, HSR and AT on CHQD display some heterogeneities in terms of geographical location, city scales, and city economic levels. Finally, the mediating effect test reveals that IT and HW can indirectly facilitate CHQD by boosting Per Capita Gross Domestic Product (PCGDP) growth while the mediating effects of HSR and AT are not significant in the short term. Overall, these findings provide critical references for optimizing integrated transportation layout, thus supporting the advancement of CHQD.
summary: Across 287 Chinese cities (2007–2023), highway, high-speed rail and air transport openings, and their coexistence, promote 'high-quality' city development, with highways working partly through per-capita GDP growth.

title: Efficiency evaluation of fishing entities and sustainable fishery policies: Evidence from Japan
authors: Hisashi Ito; Taiga Shimotsuura; Tomoaki Nakaishi; Shigemi Kagawa
abstract: This study evaluates efficiency and its determinants in Japan's coastal fisheries using a Slack-Based Measure (SBM) Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) and a meta-frontier DEA framework. We analyze 250 fishing entities—132 active, 46 passive, and 72 hook-and-line fisheries—across five coastal regions. The SBM results reveal pronounced regional heterogeneity: the average inefficiency in active fisheries ranges from 0.35 in the Northern Sea of Japan Coast to 0.50 in the Seto Inland Sea. The input decomposition shows that fuel costs are the largest contributors to inefficiency (0.67), followed by gross vessel tonnage (0.46), crew size (0.42), and fishing days (0.35). Meta-frontier analysis indicates that inter-regional inefficiency dominates on the Northern Pacific Coast, Southern Sea of Japan Coast, and Seto Inland Sea, whereas intra-regional inefficiency is predominant on the Southern Pacific Coast. These results highlight the need for quantitatively targeted regional- and fishery-specific policy interventions.
summary: DEA of 250 Japanese coastal fishing entities finds large regional inefficiency differences, with fuel costs the largest contributor, calling for region- and fishery-specific policies.

title: Flowers and flames. The determinants of biorefineries location in the EU circular economy: a core–periphery perspective
authors: Giuseppe Celi; Vincenzo D'Atteo; Edgardo Sica
keywords: Circular bioeconomy; Biorefineries; Secondary biomass; Core-periphery; EU green deal
abstract: This study explores the determinants of the Circular Bioeconomy (CBE) within a core–periphery framework, with a particular focus on the factors influencing the localisation of biorefineries across European regions. Drawing on a panel data approach at the NUTS-2 level, the research investigates the socio-economic, techno-territorial, and resource-endowment determinants shaping the spatial distribution and uptake of biorefineries, with particular attention to facilities utilizing secondary biomass and cleaner conversion technologies. The findings reveal marked regional heterogeneity: core regions benefit from well-developed technological infrastructures and strong innovation capacity, whereas semi-peripheral and peripheral regions are constrained by limited resources and technical expertise. The analysis highlights the importance of tailored, place-based policy interventions to address territorial disparities and support equitable CBE implementation. By elucidating these spatial dynamics, the study contributes to the growing literature on regional sustainability transitions and offers actionable insights for EU policymakers seeking to mitigate economic and spatial inequalities while fostering circularity.
summary: NUTS-2 panel evidence shows EU biorefinery location favors core regions with strong technology and innovation capacity, while peripheral regions are held back by limited resources and expertise.

title: Occupational mismatch in European labour markets: A joint analysis of education, skills, and severe mismatch
authors: Sergio Longobardi; Margherita Maria Pagliuca
keywords: Occupational mismatch; Overeducation; Overskilling; Labour market alignment; European countries
abstract: This paper examines occupational mismatch in European labour markets by jointly analysing overeducation, overskilling, and their overlap, defined as severe mismatch. Using recent OECD-PIAAC data for nine European countries, the study compares statistical and subjective measures of mismatch and estimates multinomial logit models to identify its main determinants. The results show that mismatch is widespread but highly heterogeneous across countries and worker groups, and that measurement choices substantially affect estimated patterns. Severe mismatch emerges as a distinct and relevant form of human capital underutilisation, especially among highly educated workers and STEM graduates. Cross-country differences suggest that mismatch reflects not only individual characteristics but also broader institutional and structural conditions. The findings highlight the need for policies that improve both skill formation and the effective use of skills in the workplace.
summary: PIAAC data for nine European countries show occupational mismatch is widespread and heterogeneous, with severe mismatch (overeducation plus overskilling) concentrated among highly educated and STEM workers.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Take it to the streets: Spatial and sociodemographic determinants of e-commerce demand in the Netherlands
authors: Sanne Wolf; Paul Buijs; Dirk Pieter van Donk
keywords: E-commerce; Online shopping; Last-mile delivery; Urban freight; Retail accessibility; Spatial analysis
abstract: E-commerce has transformed freight systems by shifting goods distribution from a limited number of retail locations to millions of individual households. This shift poses challenges for transport policy and practice, because demand for goods is increasingly generated in residential areas not designed for high levels of delivery activity. At the same time, existing research offers no clear consensus on how sociodemographic and spatial characteristics shape e-commerce demand, limiting the ability of transport and land-use planners to anticipate where delivery activity is most likely to arise. Using unique fine-grained e-commerce order data from the Netherlands, combined with fine-grained sociodemographic and spatial characteristics, this study examines how e-commerce demand varies across space. We model non-linear relationships and examine whether these relationships differ across five levels of urbanisation. The results show that demand is highest in areas with larger shares of middle-aged and middle-educated residents and rises with income at a diminishing rate. Demand is also lower in more urbanised areas and highest in rural areas. Beyond urbanisation, demand is higher where many stores are located nearby, but lower where residents have many retail options across the wider surrounding area. By showing that several relationships are non-linear and depend on the spatial scale at which retail access is measured, the results help reconcile mixed evidence and provide a basis for anticipating where freight activity is likely to concentrate. The findings support more targeted transport and land-use planning.
summary: Fine-grained Dutch order data show e-commerce demand is highest in rural areas and among middle-aged, middle-educated residents, rising with income at a diminishing rate and depending non-linearly on the scale of retail access.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Fare-free subway eligibility and older adults' traffic safety: Evidence from Seoul, Korea
authors: Shin, Eun Jin
keywords: Fare-free transit; Traffic safety; Older adults; Regression discontinuity design; Mode shift
abstract: Population aging is reshaping urban mobility and intensifying concerns about older adults' traffic safety in many countries. Although prior studies show that transit fare subsidies can change older adults' travel behavior, it remains unclear whether these changes translate into improved traffic safety. Focusing on Seoul, this study examines changes in age-specific crash rates around the eligibility threshold for South Korea's fare-free subway policy, which grants free subway rides to adults aged 65 and older. Using a regression discontinuity design, the analysis estimates discontinuities in neighborhood-by-age crash rates at the age-65 eligibility cutoff. The results indicate discontinuous declines in both driver-involved and non-motorized-user-involved crash rates at the cutoff. Supplementary travel survey evidence suggests that the decline in driver-involved crashes may reflect a shift from private car use to subway travel, an interpretation also broadly consistent with the comparable reductions observed in at-fault and non-at-fault driver crashes. For crashes involving non-motorized users, the decline at the age-65 cutoff is not accompanied by a reduction in walking or cycling trip frequency and is concentrated in crashes involving drivers younger than 65. Taken together, these findings indicate that fare-free subway eligibility is associated with improved traffic-safety outcomes for older adults both as drivers and as non-motorized users, highlighting the importance of considering traffic safety in evaluations and reforms of age-targeted transit fare policies.
summary: A regression discontinuity at Seoul's age-65 fare-free subway threshold shows discontinuous drops in crash rates for older adults as drivers and as pedestrians/cyclists, consistent with a shift from cars to subway.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: The 15-minute neighbourhood and housing affordability: insights from Los Angeles
authors: Dena Kasraian; Emma Kurihara; Ahmadreza Faghih Imani; Tom Rous; Audrey de Nazelle
keywords: 15-minute neighbourhood; Affordable housing; Point of Interest; Intervention for just urban transition; Los Angeles
abstract: The 15-minute neighbourhood is a planning concept that aims to address urban environmental, health and social challenges by enabling residents to meet their daily needs within a 15-minute walk or cycle. While widely promoted, equity concerns have emerged regarding 15-minute neighbourhood transitions, particularly the tension between livability and accessibility gains and housing affordability protection. This work addresses two gaps in the existing 15-minute city literature. First, it presents empirical evidence on the relationship between local accessibility and housing affordability; second, it provides actionable guidance on how to ensure that interventions balance accessibility gains with affordability protection to promote just transitions that actively address, rather than exacerbate, existing inequalities. To assess the potential for 15-minute neighbourhoods to contribute to just transitions towards sustainable and healthy urban environments, we evaluate linkages between 15-minute neighbourhood status and affordable housing in Los Angeles county which faces a growing unhoused population alongside rising rent and home values. Informed by a literature review, we apply a scoring methodology that accounts for access and choice to different categories of amenities to assess 15-minute neighbourhood status, which we compare against different housing affordability metrics using geospatial analysis. Findings reveal a weak but positive correlation between 15-minute neighbourhood scores and affordable housing availability. Notably, residents of affordable housing in Los Angeles often have relatively high access to amenities traditionally perceived as less accessible to low-income populations, such as green spaces and grocery stores. Our findings suggest that cities may be able to pursue proximity-based planning without inherently exacerbating inequities, provided that affordability is explicitly considered. Beyond our immediate empirical findings, our proposal to jointly evaluate affordability and 15-minute neighbourhood scores, as well as the resulting neighbourhood typology and suggested interventions offer a practical approach to help cities support a just transition to affordable 15-minute neighbourhoods. This approach is especially relevant for other car-dependent metropolitan regions that are promoting proximity-based planning while facing affordability challenges.
summary: In Los Angeles County, 15-minute neighbourhood scores correlate weakly but positively with affordable housing availability, suggesting proximity-based planning need not worsen inequities if affordability is explicitly considered.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Revealing the built environment impacts of idling emissions from electric ride-hailing vehicles through explainable machine learning
authors: Fuqiang Lu; Song Wang; Hualing Bi
keywords: Idling emissions; Electric ride-hailing vehicles; Explainable machine learning; Built environment; Nonlinear threshold effect
abstract: Understanding how built environment characteristics influence electric vehicles (EV) idling emissions is crucial for designing low-carbon transportation systems, yet this stationary emission source remains largely overlooked. This study fills this gap by integrating high-resolution GPS trajectory data, grid carbon intensity, and explainable machine learning to quantify the nonlinear impacts of the built environment on EV idling emissions. We developed a LightGBM-SHAP framework that achieves robust predictive performance (R2 = 0.889) and systematically identified nonlinear thresholds. Three key findings emerged. First, across the seven observation days, lower daily mean temperatures were generally associated with higher estimated daily CO2 emissions under the adopted temperature-dependent emission-accounting framework. Second, road network length, residential land, transportation facilities, and population density collectively accounted for nearly 80% of total SHAP importance, with multiple built environment features exhibiting nonlinear threshold effects. Third, feature significance exhibited spatiotemporal heterogeneity, with identical built environment configurations exerting markedly different impacts across varying time periods and spatial scales. These findings should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal planning standards, offering diagnostic evidence for future policy evaluation.
summary: GPS trajectories and explainable machine learning show road network length, residential land, transport facilities and population density explain nearly 80% of predicted idling emissions from electric ride-hailing vehicles, with nonlinear thresholds.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: A residential e-bicycle parking mismatch? Unpacking a neglected issue in cycling policy
authors: Ugo Lachapelle; Patrick Rérat; Emmanuel Ravalet
keywords: Apartments; Accessible; Cycling; Home; Locked room; Parking; Safety
abstract: To support bicycling, cities have focused on providing infrastructure to ensure safe movement. Much less research assesses the provision of adequate bicycle parking, especially residential parking. Because of their higher weight and costs, e-bicycles especially require safe, sheltered and accessible parking. The paper describes the features of home-based bicycle parking for Swiss individuals with and without e-bicycles and assesses variations and discrepancies in residential bicycle parking availability and e-bicycle ownership across land use and household characteristics. The 2021 Swiss Mobility and Transport Microcensus (MTMC) provides a representative national sample of data on e-bicycle ownership and residential bicycle parking (n = 10,154). Variations in logit-based estimated probabilities of e-bicycle ownership and quality parking access across predictor variables are assessed. The probability of having accessible sheltered and secured bicycle parking in a locked room, the golden standard of safety, protection from the elements and ease of use, is low and below that of e-bicycle ownership probabilities, regardless of socio-demographics and location features. Across group characteristics, specific mismatches between parking access and e-bicycle ownership are identified. The largest mismatches are found for homeowners and residents of areas poorly served by public transit. Current housing stock is ill-equipped for parking of e-bicycles, especially in areas where regular cycling is historically low. While existing standards can help shape new housing stock, retrofitting existing residential buildings is an important policy challenge. On street veloboxes may be more feasible. The variety of observed bicycle parking forms also points to the limits of current survey instruments. Improvements to survey instruments are proposed.
summary: The paper examines whether residential bicycle parking fails to meet the needs of e-bicycle owners, who require safe, sheltered and accessible parking because of their bikes' weight and cost.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: The impact of fuel prices and supply availability on user behavioural change in Australian household travel amidst global turmoil
authors: David A. Hensher; Edward Wei; Wen Liu; John D. Nelson
keywords: Global turmoil; Oil supply; Fuel prices; Supply uncertainty; Car user responses; Behavioural change; Survey of car users; Elasticities
abstract: The global conflict in the Middle East is having a significant impact on the availability of oil to many countries, with Australia feeling the impact more than most countries. Fuel prices escalated during the first three weeks of the war (up to the end of March 2026), typically being 30–50% higher than the retail prices at the pump under normal market conditions. Supply uncertainty has also created problems in distribution, especially for farmers, trucking companies and retail outlets. In response to the escalated fuel prices at the pump, the Federal government announced, on 31 March, a reduction in fuel excise for three months (from 52.6 to 26.3 cents per litre) with state and territory leaders agreeing to pass on the additional goods and services tax windfall to motorists (further reducing the total to 20.6c/litre as well as the removal of the heavy vehicle road user charge for the same period (the latter of 32.4 cents per litre is reduced to zero). This paper explores ways in which users of passenger cars have responded to these price hikes and supply uncertainty. A series of questions incorporated in a survey of 1,024 New South Wales (Australia) residents in the first two weeks of April 2026, up to a temporary ceasefire and US blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, sought evidence on behavioural change responses such as modal switching for work and non-work-related travel, changes in car kilometres, car sharing, working from home, purchase of an electric or hybrid vehicle, and switching car use between petrol/diesel and electric vehicles in the current household fleet. These responses are embedded in several scenarios that vary fuel prices and fuel scarcity (availability and rationing) to assess the likely behavioural response in the short run and in the longer run if a scenario becomes reality. Overall, the key policy takeaway is that fuel pricing is most effective as a short–run signal and selective rationing tool, while long–run resilience depends on structural adaptation, especially vehicle technology, income buffering, and access to substitutes.
summary: A survey of 1,024 NSW residents during the 2026 Middle East oil shock finds fuel prices work mainly as a short-run signal and rationing tool, while long-run resilience hinges on vehicle technology, income buffers and substitutes.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Breaking Down the Barriers: Understanding Consumer Resistance to Zero-Emission Vehicle Purchases
authors: Shoumic Shahid Chowdhury; Md Shahadat Hossain; Mahmudur Fatmi
keywords: Zero-emission vehicle (ZEV); ZEV resistance; Incentives; Policy; Logit model
abstract: Canada has established ambitious goals to reduce transportation emissions, targeting all new vehicle sales to be zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs) by 2040. In this study, ZEVs refer to battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs), consistent with Canadian policy definitions. Despite increasing policy support, a large segment of the population remains resistant to adopting ZEVs. While prior research has primarily focused on factors driving adoption, the reasons underlying non-adoption remain less explored. This study investigates ZEV resistance using data from the British Columbia ZEV Market Research Survey, comprising 3,850 respondents, of which 3,253 individuals who have never owned a ZEV are analyzed. A random parameter multinomial logit model is employed to classify resistance into five categories: cost, charging and range limitations, vehicle unavailability, environmental concerns, and other reasons, while accounting for unobserved heterogeneity. The results reveal that resistance is highly segmented across population groups. Younger and lower-income individuals are primarily constrained by cost, whereas higher-income individuals are more likely to resist due to limited availability of preferred vehicle models. Older adults and residents of multi-unit dwellings are significantly more affected by charging and range-related barriers. These findings demonstrate that ZEV resistance is not uniform but driven by distinct constraints across population segments. The results provide targeted policy insights to support more effective and equitable strategies for accelerating ZEV adoption in Canada.
summary: British Columbia survey data show resistance to zero-emission vehicles is segmented: cost for younger and lower-income people, model unavailability for higher-income people, and charging/range for older adults and apartment dwellers.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Distributional incidence of car feebates with spillovers to the second-hand market
authors: Hoarau, Quentin
keywords: Environmental policy; Distributional effects; Automobile; Second-hand markets; Corporate vehicles
abstract: Feebates applied to new vehicles are widely used to reduce emissions from the automobile sector, yet most vehicles are traded in second-hand markets. This paper studies how interactions between new and used car markets affect the distributional incidence of a car feebate. Using comprehensive French administrative data on vehicle transactions over the period 2008–2019 and detailed information on used car prices, we develop an accounting framework linking the feebate spillover to vehicle depreciation. We find that over half of the initial feebate is redistributed through used car markets within five years, with important consequences for incidence. Corporate buyers, who face the largest direct tax on new cars, recover approximately two-thirds of their burden through resale and end up close to neutral overall. Among private households, the burden shifts further towards high-income groups, who purchase both more new and more recent used cars. Yet the feebate remains progressive: the net burden as a share of income increases with household income, whether accounting for used car markets or not. These results suggest that the distributional effects of vehicle regulations cannot be assessed on the basis of new car markets alone, and that corporate buyers play a key role in transmitting feebate costs across the car lifecycle.
summary: Using French vehicle transaction data (2008–2019), the paper studies how spillovers from new- to used-car markets, via depreciation, shape the distributional incidence of a car feebate.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Latent paths in mode choice models: incorporating street-level environment features for active travel policy
authors: Corin Staves; Qin Zhang; Aruna Sivakumar; Ismail Saadi; SM. Labib; Belen Zapata-Diomedi; James Woodcock
keywords: Active travel; Walking; Cycling; Mode choice; Built environment; MATSim
abstract: There is growing empirical evidence that walking and cycling are influenced by street-level environment features such as greenness and traffic stress. To assess active travel policy, these features are increasingly incorporated into mode choice models through predictors that aggregate spatial information along the route. However, this requires assumptions about which routes decision-makers evaluate. Simple assumptions (e.g., fastest path) can produce unrealistic routes and therefore inaccurate predictors, potentially biasing estimated street-level environment coefficients. We present a practical estimation process to evaluate plausible paths without prior route choice knowledge. In this proof of concept, we introduce a latent path selection mechanism in which routes are optimised together with mode choice. Implementations in Manchester (England) and Melbourne (Australia) produced plausible estimates comparable to existing mode and route choice literature. For example, cycling on high-stress paths was utility-equivalent to travelling 94–177% longer on low-stress paths for males, and this was higher for females (up to 389%) and children (up to 768%). Furthermore, using latent paths improved log-likelihoods and produced larger street-level environment coefficients versus fastest paths. For scenario forecasts, our methodology produced similar mode shifts at the population level, but with substantial variations at the trip-level by evaluating more decision-relevant routes. Latent path estimation could therefore be advantageous for forecasting applications where reliable chosen route data is unavailable. With growing availability of micro-spatial data and policy focus towards sustainable transport, this methodology can enhance how street-level features are represented in empirical literature and forecasting models.
summary: Jointly optimizing latent routes with mode choice in Manchester and Melbourne yields larger street-environment effects than fastest-path assumptions; high-stress cycling equals 94–177% longer low-stress travel for males and far more for women and children.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: No impact without details: Quasi-experimental evidence on carpooling regulations and usage
authors: Yite Sun; Xiaobing Liu; Yu Duan; Yun Wang; Chun Zhang; Xuedong Yan
keywords: Ridesharing; Carpooling; Regulation; Staggered difference-in-differences model; Transportation network companies
abstract: Carpooling is widely regarded as an effective approach to mitigating urban traffic congestion and environmental pollution. However, adoption remains limited, and rigorous causal evidence on carpooling regulatory policies (CRP) is scarce. Using high-resolution order data from 28 cities in three major Chinese urban agglomerations in 2017, this study exploits staggered city-level CRP implementation as a quasi-natural experiment to estimate its effects on carpooling activity. We develop a spatiotemporal feature-based classification algorithm (SFBCA) to distinguish LF-HSC drivers, characterized by lower carpooling frequency or higher spatiotemporal concentration, from HF-LSC drivers, characterized by higher carpooling frequency and lower spatiotemporal concentration. We estimate average effects using a two-way fixed-effects staggered difference-in-differences model and dynamic effects using heterogeneity-robust event-study estimators, supplemented by robustness checks. Under the monthly specification, SFBCA achieves consistency rates of 93.8% for LF-HSC drivers and 73.0% for HF-LSC drivers, yielding a harmonic consistency of 82.1%. CRP reduce total carpooling orders by 10.2% and HF-LSC drivers' orders by 25.0%, while having no statistically significant average effect on LF-HSC drivers' orders. These findings suggest that CRP primarily constrain more intensive and potentially quasi-commercial carpooling activity without producing a detectable average reduction in lower-frequency or more spatiotemporally concentrated carpooling. Heterogeneity analyses reveal variation across urban agglomerations, policy designs, and market environments, with statistically detectable effects concentrated in cities with standalone and detailed regulations. Overall, the findings provide implications for governments and transportation network companies (TNCs) to refine carpooling regulation through targeted and context-sensitive implementation.
summary: Staggered carpooling regulations across 28 Chinese cities cut total carpooling orders by 10.2% and high-frequency (quasi-commercial) drivers' orders by 25%, with effects concentrated where rules were standalone and detailed.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
