Such methods are typically discontinuous, limited in spatio-temporal resolution, costly, and overlook the role of sound in shaping environments. To address these gaps, this study explores the feasibility of using Street View Video (SVV), a novel, promising, yet under-utilized data source, for capturing street-level dynamics. Leveraging widely available crowdsourced city tour videos as a representative form of SVV, we develop an automated and scalable framework for high-precision geo-localization of SVV by extracting textual and depth information. Further, we propose a visual–auditory pipeline that integrates continuous pedestrian activity and sound environments as complementary dimensions that reveal street-level social dynamics. Using Melbourne as a case study, we identified 892 high-quality and geolocatable videos totaling over 542 h and achieved an accuracy of 77% for geo-localization. We generated spatio-temporal maps that not only reproduced well-studied pedestrian volume patterns, but also previously neglected aspects, including human actions (walking, standing, sitting), sound intensity, and sound types (speech, music, vehicle). Correlation and quadrant analyses further explored the relationships among these vitality dimensions, revealing distinctive street characteristics and highlighting the limitations of conventional road classifications. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of SVV as a multimodal and reproducible source of urban vitality indicators, providing a proof-of-concept for future urban sensing applications.
summary: Assesses the potential of street view video for measuring urban vitality.

title: Where to start with urban Digital Twins? Backward-chaining key indicators for cross-sector water, heat, and housing impact analysis
authors: Iván Cárdenas-León; Pirouz Nourian; Mila Koeva; Karin Pfeffer
keywords: Causal reasoning; Digital Twins; Evidence-based planning; Planning support systems; Strategic urban planning
abstract: Digital planning for urban systems can benefit from integrated frameworks that capture cross-sectoral dependencies, impact assessment, support causal reasoning, and adapt to diverse data sources. We present a methodological approach for Digital Twinning that combines backward-chaining analysis with Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to identify, decompose, and interlink key performance indicators across three critical planning domains: drinking water supply, urban heat stress, and housing provision. Building on a comprehensive indicator review, we selected key targets and traced each to its fundamental components using the DPSIR framework (Driving Forces, Pressures, States, Impacts, Responses). We quantified relational dependencies and network centrality metrics to construct sector-specific DAGs, then merged overlapping elements into an integrated cross-sector model, revealing critical causal pathways. This enables scenario testing across diverse drivers, including climate change, demographic shifts, and credit conditions. Our results demonstrate how infrastructural and natural system interventions propagate through water reliability, thermal comfort, and housing affordability. The framework clarifies data requirements and analytic workflows for Digital Planning tools while offering a scalable template for cross-sectoral impact analysis. By structuring complex interactions into a unified causal schema, planners can use this approach to evaluate trade-offs and derive evidence for decision-making.
summary: Proposes backward-chaining key indicators to scope urban digital twins for cross-sector water, heat and housing impact analysis.

title: OptimalStop: Predictability–complexity trade-off for optimising stop detection in human mobility data
authors: Kamil Smolak; Katarzyna Sila-Nowicka
keywords: Entropy; Human mobility; Predictability; Stop detection; Stop location; Trajectory analysis; Urban analytics
abstract: Human mobility analysis increasingly relies on large-scale trajectory data, yet results remain highly sensitive to preprocessing choices that are rarely applied in a consistent or well-documented manner. Stop detection, which transforms raw location traces into sequences of visited places, is a particularly critical and bias-prone step, with parameter choices often guided by dataset-specific conventions. The absence of systematic and transparent parameter-selection practices risks introducing methodological bias and limits the comparability and reproducibility of mobility studies. Here, we introduce OptimalStop, a model-agnostic optimisation framework for stop detection that exploits a predictability–complexity trade-off in human mobility trajectories to guide preprocessing. OptimalStop operates as a higher-level tuning layer applicable to any method that produces symbolic mobility sequences. By framing stop detection as a multi-objective optimisation problem, the framework identifies compact Pareto-optimal sets of parameter configurations that balance predictability and structural complexity, avoiding over-fragmented or over-aggregated representations. We evaluate OptimalStop on both real-world and synthetic mobility datasets using multiple stop detection algorithms, and confirm through controlled synthetic experiments that the predictability–complexity trade-off is structurally grounded in recurrent return-to-place behaviour rather than being a mathematical artefact of discretisation. The results show that OptimalStop consistently retains near-optimal solutions while substantially reducing the effective parameter search space within a reasonable computational time. An optional automatic selection strategy further demonstrates that high-quality stop detection can be obtained without ground truth, outperforming or matching commonly used sensitivity-based tuning approaches. We release OptimalStop under an open licence, providing a transparent and reproducible framework for parameter selection that supports more structured mobility data preprocessing. While demonstrated here for stop detection, the underlying predictability–complexity balance offers a general perspective for mitigating methodological bias in mobility analytics.
summary: Introduces OptimalStop, which optimises stop detection in human mobility data via a predictability–complexity trade-off.

title: Revealing exacerbated socioeconomic stratification of urban mobility: A case study in Beijing, China
authors: Liangkan Chen; Mingxing Chen; Weiyu Li; Mengyao Han; Xiaofei Xu; Shujuan Tang; Huiping Jiang
keywords: Beijing; Mobile signaling data; Social stratification; Socio-spatial relations; Urban mobility
abstract: As the COVID-19 pandemic recedes, urban life, economic activities, and transportation systems appear to have returned to normal. Yet latent post-pandemic impacts on shifts in socioeconomic stratification within human mobility remain under-explored. Using large-scale longitudinal mobile signaling data for nearly 8 million residents in Beijing between 2019 and 2024, weighted using census data and integrated with social attributes and housing price data, this study examines how socioeconomic stratification patterns and mobility behaviors evolve across socioeconomic groups. Here, we show that the potential stratification has intensified in the post-pandemic era. First, the place-level and inter-group contact-based socioeconomic stratification index increased by 34.83% and 32.34%, respectively. Counterfactual simulations reveal that shortened travel distances and homogeneous mobility preferences reduced opportunities for cross-group encounters. Second, residential proximity and shared social attributes significantly explain variations in opportunities for inter-group co-presence. Spatial disparities in urban infrastructure configuration can either mitigate or reinforce mobility-related socioeconomic stratification across locations. Collectively, this study underscores that spatial context, socioeconomic characteristics, and behavioral preferences shape mobility stratification, offering empirical evidence for understanding post-pandemic socioeconomic stratification dynamics.
summary: Documents growing socioeconomic stratification of urban mobility in Beijing.

title: Beyond 2D land consumption: A scaling-law framework for evaluating 3D urban space consumption and population dynamics in fifteen East Asian megacities
authors: Weipeng Lu; Qihao Weng
keywords: Building volume; Dasymetric mapping; East Asia; Land use efficiency; Sustainable development goals; Urban scaling law
abstract: As cities expand both outward and upward, assessing global urbanization requires a three-dimensional perspective that captures the complete picture of urban growth. However, conventional land-consumption metrics fail to capture vertical intensification, while large-scale building-volume data that are consistent across years in data source, method, resolution, and precision remain difficult to obtain. To address this gap, this study asks whether population potential, inferred from remotely sensed physical environments, can serve as a scalable proxy for building volume and reveal urban expansion patterns that remain hidden in 2D assessments. Using fifteen East Asian megacity regions as a comparative sample, we integrate gridded population potential, land consumption rate, height change rate, space consumption rate, and district-level development indicators within an urban scaling framework. The results show that population potential explains building volume more effectively than population count, increasing the mean R2 of the scaling model from 0.4891 to 0.6432 when using population potential. Development-mode analysis further reveals scale-dependent patterns: across megacity regions, vertical growth differentiates national urban systems more clearly than horizontal expansion, whereas within megacity regions, more developed districts generally expand less horizontally and often grow more vertically. Finally, the comparison between LCRPGR and SCRPGR shows that many districts appearing coordinated under the 2D land-consumption assessment still exhibit rapid volumetric growth relative to population growth. These findings suggest that population potential and volumetric diagnostics can complement conventional SDG 11.3.1 indicators by revealing dimensions of urban expansion that are overlooked in two-dimensional land-use assessment.
summary: Develops a scaling-law framework to evaluate 3D urban space consumption relative to population in fifteen East Asian megacities.

title: HyperLayout: A decoupled and planning-oriented framework for parcel-level building layout generation
authors: Ming Jiang; Yimin Chen; Xiaoping Liu; Haifeng Li
keywords: Building layout generation; Controllable generation; Decoupled framework; Multi-agent reinforcement learning; Planning constraints
abstract: Urban development is increasingly shifting from outward expansion toward the renewal and optimization of existing urban areas. This transition has created a growing demand for building layout generation methods that can satisfy complex planning requirements while maintaining sound spatial organization. However, most existing end-to-end approaches jointly model building attributes, morphology, and spatial arrangement. This unified process makes it difficult to trace how planning requirements affect spatial outcomes, inspect intermediate decisions, or adjust generated scenarios. This study proposes HyperLayout, a decoupled and planning-oriented framework for parcel-level building layout generation. Rather than treating layout generation as a single synthesis task, HyperLayout organizes it into three interpretable stages: development-capacity configuration, building form generation, and spatial layout optimization. Through explicit constraint propagation, parcel-level planning objectives are progressively converted into building attributes, geometric conditions, and spatial optimization criteria. This structure makes intermediate decisions and outputs easier to inspect and revise throughout the generation process. Experiments show that HyperLayout improves upon the evaluated baselines in both building form generation and building layout optimization. The framework produces layouts with improved geometric consistency, spatial organization, adaptation to parcel boundaries, and compliance with planning constraints. It also supports the controlled exploration of alternative scenarios under different planning objectives at parcel and community scales. These findings suggest that workflow decomposition and explicit constraint propagation provide a practical framework for developing interpretable and controllable AI-assisted planning tools for urban design and redevelopment.
summary: Presents HyperLayout, a planning-oriented framework for generating parcel-level building layouts.

title: Open-access model for detecting openly dumped dispersed municipal solid waste from crowdsourced UAV imagery in Sub-Saharan Africa
authors: Steffen Knoblauch; Ram Kumar Muthusamy; Luís M.A. Bettencourt; Costas Velis; Pierre Chrzanowski; Edward Charles Anderson; Pete Masters; Innocent Maholi; Antonio Inguane; Levi Szamek; Alexander Zipf
keywords: Computer vision; Crowdsourced UAV imagery; Municipal solid waste; Open dumping; OpenAerialMap; Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Managing municipal solid waste in rapidly urbanizing Sub-Saharan Africa remains challenging due to dispersed informal dumping and limited high-resolution datasets for spatial monitoring. We present an open-access deep learning model for automated detection of openly dumped dispersed MSW (ODD-MSW) via crowdsourced UAV imagery, trained and evaluated across 29 regions in 10 Sub-Saharan African countries, encompassing diverse environmental contexts. A deep learning model trained on manually annotated image tiles achieved an overall accuracy of 92.87% (F1 = 0.927) in detecting ODD-MSW across all study regions. Applied without any site-specific retraining to 25 independent OpenAerialMap scenes from 21 cities in 19 countries on five continents, the frozen model retained an F1 score of 0.867, providing direct evidence of transferability beyond the training domain. Predicted distributions reveal heterogeneous accumulation patterns, ranging from localized hotspots — often along waterways, where waste can exacerbate flood and public health risks — to more dispersed litter across urban areas. Waste accumulation is most strongly associated with population density (Spearman ρ = 0.674, p<0.001) and indicators of lack of local infrastructure access (ρ = 0.700, p<0.001), whereas its relationship with broader measures of regional development is weaker and not statistically significant (ρ = 0.215, p=0.26), highlighting the importance of fine-scale data for understanding localized waste dynamics. By releasing the model, this study provides a ready-to-use tool for UAV imagery collected by municipalities and local mapping communities, enabling ODD-MSW monitoring without extensive technical expertise. This approach empowers local practitioners to convert UAV imagery into actionable insights, supporting targeted interventions and improved municipal solid waste management across Sub-Saharan Africa.
summary: Releases an open-access model that detects openly dumped municipal solid waste in crowdsourced drone imagery from Sub-Saharan Africa.

title: A representation-explanation framework for flow-based border effects on intra-urban commuting using geographically weighted additive gravity model and machine learning
authors: Junyang Zhao; Zhaodong Zhang; Xixiang Wen; Mengwei Xin; Yongxi Gong; Yu Liu
keywords: Border effect; Geographically weighted additive gravity model; Intra-urban commuting; Representation-explanation framework
abstract: Border effects suppress cross-boundary flows of people and goods, and it is precisely this suppression that drives the gradual divergence of built environment and socioeconomic conditions on either side of a boundary. Measuring border effects from flows is therefore more proximate to the border effect itself than inferring them from downstream outcomes such as housing price differentials or service provision gaps. To address the challenge that flow-based border effects are inherently unobservable and thus unable to be systematically characterized, this study proposes a representation-explanation framework. In the representation stage, a flow-based geographically weighted additive gravity model (FB-GWAGM) that treats each border crossing as an additive increment to physical distance is adopted. In the explanation stage, reliability-weighted random forest models with SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis identify the built environment and socioeconomic factors affecting border thickness. On the basis of the modeling results, the spatial heterogeneity of border thickness is identified and quantified in distance-equivalent units, and the contributions of built environment and socioeconomic factors to this heterogeneity are decomposed in the same metric, enabling direct comparison across border types and factor dimensions. These findings demonstrate that the representation-explanation framework provides a replicable and physically interpretable approach to quantifying flow-based border effects, advancing the understanding of how borders shape spatial interaction within cities and revealing the socioeconomically contingent nature of border thickness heterogeneity.
summary: Combines a geographically weighted additive gravity model with machine learning to represent and explain border effects on intra-urban commuting.

title: A novel simulation-based approach to optimizing road networks for disaster evacuation in dense urban informal settlements
authors: Chun Song; Zhijie Zhou; Rui Cao
keywords: Crowd simulation; Disaster response; Informal settlements; Multi-objective optimization; Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG 11); Urban regeneration
abstract: Urban informal settlements in China are often characterized by high building and population densities, narrow alleys, and intricate road networks. These features present significant safety challenges and complicate evacuation planning due to their high vulnerability to disasters and the difficulty of large-scale reconstruction. To address these challenges, we propose a coupled simulation–optimization framework designed to evaluate and enhance the road-network performance in these dense informal settlements, thereby improving their disaster-evacuation resilience. By integrating geographic information system (GIS)-based environmental reconstruction, potential-field navigation, and a Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH)-based crowd density and movement model, the framework models pedestrian dynamics. The movement model is calibrated and validated against empirical corridor-level fundamental-diagram data, while paired multi-seed village-scale simulations and plausibility checks are used to examine the consistency of the resulting evacuation patterns. A multi-objective optimization algorithm is then used to identify nondominated micro-regeneration strategies that balance evacuation efficiency with reconstruction cost. A case study conducted in Shipai Village, a dense informal settlement in Guangzhou, China, demonstrates that this approach effectively pinpoints critical network bottlenecks. The representative intervention yields substantial improvements in evacuation metrics while requiring only localized road widening. Sensitivity analyses of crowd-model and optimization parameters further show the robustness of the evacuation performance and intervention selection. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and the findings offer practical and cost-effective guidance for urban planners seeking to improve the resilience and safety of urban informal settlements. The code is available at https://github.com/rui-research/roadnet-evac-opt.
summary: Proposes a simulation-based method to optimise road networks for disaster evacuation in dense informal settlements.

title: Assessing the significance of intra- and inter-species interactions using probabilistic space-time prisms and agent-based null models
authors: Zachary J. Smith; Mohammad Aslani; Joni Downs
keywords: Agent-based model; Inter-species interaction; Interaction; Probabilistic space-time prisms; Random walk model; Space-time analysis; Time geography
abstract: Probabilistic space-time prisms (PSTPs) are used to measure probabilities of location for individuals over time. Intersecting PSTPs for different individuals enables probabilities of co-location and proximity to be computed for each voxel, or volume element, that represents a time step for a specific location. This paper extends PSTP analysis by developing an approach to test the statistical significance of the calculated co-location and proximity measures. First, PSTPs were generated for 20 individual Mallard and Muscovy ducks tracked simultaneously. Second, the PSTPs were used to calculate probabilities of co-location and proximity for all 190 possible dyads. Third, species-specific agent-based models (ABMs) and a generic random walk model (RWM) were developed as null models to simulate tracking data over the same tracking duration, with 1000 replicates used to generate confidence intervals for each dyad. Finally, 95% confidence intervals for co-location and proximity obtained from the PSTP analysis were compared to 95% confidence intervals for co-location and proximity derived from the 1000 replicates of ABMs and RWM to evaluate if dyads were interacting more than, less than, or as expected under the null models. The results showed differences in co-location and proximity between dyads, but most importantly, the significance of those interactions was highly dependent on the null model used for comparison. The RWM typically predicted fewer co-locations and larger proximities in comparison to the species-specific ABMs, often yielding different conclusions about the direction and strength of interactions. The findings suggest that the significance of intra-and inter-species interactions should be evaluated in the context of the species' habitat and movement preferences through ABMs.
summary: Uses probabilistic space-time prisms and agent-based null models to test the significance of intra- and inter-species interactions.

title: Joint building height estimation and pose optimization using single-view smartphone image
authors: Junting Liu; Pai Wang; Hai Fu; Jianghui Geng
keywords: 3D building model; Building height estimation; Pose optimization; Single image; Smartphone localization
abstract: Building height is a critical but largely underrepresented element of 3D geospatial information. Existing height estimation methods often rely on expensive equipment or labor-intensive data collection, which restricts their scalability and practical deployment in large-scale scenarios. Although abundant sensors such as cameras and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) chips embedded in smartphones offer a low-cost alternative solution for retrieving building height information, these approaches typically require extensive manual intervention. To address these challenges, this article presents a joint building height estimation and pose optimization method using single-view smartphone image, leveraging widely available 2D building footprints. The proposed approach utilizes visual geometric features to identify building corner points and assign associated confidence scores. Building height and smartphone pose are then jointly estimated by minimizing the confidence-weighted reprojection errors between the 3D corner points and their corresponding image observations. Numerous experiments on 50 diverse real-world buildings demonstrate that the proposed method, with fully automated processing, achieves a mean absolute error of 0.70 m and a relative error of 3.47% in height estimation, outperforming both existing smartphone-based methods and street-view image-based methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The joint optimization scheme yields an improvement of 22.7% in absolute building height estimation accuracy over existing pose-only optimization. Furthermore, the average horizontal positioning error is significantly reduced from 10.0 m, based on initial GNSS chip results, to 1.8 m. These results highlight the method's potential as a lightweight and scalable solution for Level-of-Detail 1 3D building modeling and robust smartphone localization in real-world urban environments using only low-cost consumer devices.
summary: Jointly estimates building height and camera pose from a single smartphone image.

title: Census-validated agent-based modeling of immigrant settlement and diversity in Metro Vancouver
authors: Liliana Perez; Maryam Yousefi; Navid Mahdizadeh Gharakhanlou; Sinisa Vukicevic; Suzana Dragicevic
keywords: Agent-based modeling (ABM); Complex systems; Geographic information systems (GIS); Immigrant settlement; Residential segregation; Spatial diversity
abstract: Population growth and economic vitality in Metro Vancouver increasingly depend on immigration, as natural population growth is projected to stagnate by 2035. Residential segregation patterns emerge from complex interactions between individual preferences, socio-demographic characteristics, and urban spatial structure. This study develops a geospatial agent-based model to simulate settlement dynamics of immigrants who arrived between 2016 and 2021 in Metro Vancouver, comparing two classification scenarios: a broad ethnic diversity scheme and a more finely resolved origins diversity scheme. Model performance was evaluated using the Simpson's Diversity Index (SDI) and error metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE), while kernel density analysis (KDA) was primarily applied on an ethnic basis to identify where different ethnic groups concentrated spatially. Results indicated that the origins diversity scenario more accurately reproduces primary settlement hubs, captures population heterogeneity, and aligns with observed Census patterns, outperforming the ethnic diversity scenario with lower errors (MAE = 0.210, MSE = 0.063, RMSE = 0.251). Nonetheless, secondary, dispersed, and minority clusters remain underrepresented, highlighting the challenge of modeling smaller and peripheral populations. Besides, sensitivity analysis and model calibration indicated that settlement outcomes are influenced by both social preferences and spatial accessibility, with social affinity playing the more dominant role. These findings underscore the utility of ABMs for understanding urban settlement dynamics, guiding planning strategies, and supporting policy interventions, while emphasizing the need for methodological refinements to better capture minority populations and fine-scale spatial patterns. The study provides actionable insights to inform equitable, inclusive, and sustainable urban development aligned with Metro 2050.
summary: Builds a census-validated agent-based model of immigrant settlement and neighbourhood diversity in Metro Vancouver.

title: Disentangling nonlinear and context-contingent built environment effects on social encounter opportunities: Evidence from explainable spatial machine learning in 15-min community life circles
authors: Man Zhang; Yuwei Wu; Qianqian Li; Peiqing Cao; Tao Shen
keywords: Built environment; Community life circle; Encounter opportunity; Explainable machine learning; GPS trajectory; Nonlinear effects
abstract: The built environment shapes everyday social encounters, yet existing research often relies on linear effects and overlooks contextual heterogeneity. This study investigates how multi-scale built environment features of 15-min community life circles influence social encounter opportunities in Chengdu, China. We construct an Encounter Opportunity Index (EOI) from anonymized GPS dwell trajectories of 7,480,793 users to quantify potential copresence intensity in open public settings. A total of 18,856 network-constrained life circles are delineated, and 21 built environment and control variables spanning place-level perceptual quality, block-level functional structure, and community-level accessibility are assembled from street view imagery, points of interest, building footprints, remote sensing, and road networks. A Geographical XGBoost model (R2 = 0.862) trained with spatially blocked cross-validation is coupled with SHAP decomposition to reveal nonlinear response patterns. K-means clustering classifies life circles into three socio-spatial types for stratified analysis. Results identify three dominant nonlinear patterns: threshold-plateau responses in pedestrian infrastructure and transit density, persistent negative associations between green coverage and encounter opportunities, and staged escalation effects in spatial overlap and floor area ratio. Stratified SHAP analysis reveals pronounced contextual dependency: peripheral life circles are most sensitive to infrastructure deficit compensation, middle-ring life circles respond to green environment quality and pedestrian safety, and core life circles are shaped by spatial agglomeration and streetscape quality. These findings advance the understanding of nonlinear, context-contingent pathways through which the built environment structures encounter opportunities, offering differentiated planning guidance for community life circle optimization.
summary: Uses explainable spatial machine learning to uncover nonlinear built-environment effects on social encounter opportunities in 15-minute community life circles.

title: Understanding location preferences of firms in the circular economy
authors: Merten Nefs; Maryam Omar
keywords: Circular economy; Firm location; Location choice; Spatial planning; The Netherlands
abstract: Although the transition to the circular economy (CE) is slowly underway, business activities that contribute to the CE struggle to find sufficient space. Land is scarce and contested by multiple societal needs, and not just any place is suitable; CE firms are highly diverse, each with their distinct location requirements. To develop effective policies that secure and create space specific to the CE's needs, in-depth knowledge about these requirements is necessary. This paper contributes to this debate by analyzing the locational preferences of four classes of CE firms in the Netherlands, namely those that contribute towards: the reduction of raw material usage, the substitution of raw materials, product life extension, and high-grade processing. Negative binomial and Poisson models are estimated for a sample of 14,129 neighborhoods, based on business microdata and spatial data on infrastructure, zoning, and agglomeration economies. The models show that infrastructure plays a smaller role than expected in CE firm location in the Netherlands, while the presence of business parks and the concentration of economic sectors in the area, such as the industry and energy sector, are decisive. The analysis confirms that location patterns of CE firms in reduction and extension are quite distinct from substitution and processing, highlighting the need to plan for a diverse network of business parks to stimulate circularity. Some combinations of location qualities are quite scarce, such as business parks in centrally located urban locations, suggesting that conservation and more intensive use of these location types is recommended.
summary: Examines where circular-economy firms prefer to locate and what drives those location choices.

title: Territorial dynamics of wind power expansion in rural Europe: Insights from a wind-leading region
authors: Álvaro García-Riazuelo; Rosa Duarte; Sol María Halleck Vega; Cristina Sarasa
keywords: Agglomeration effects; Spatial planning; Wind energy; Wind farms deployment
abstract: The rapid expansion of wind energy is reshaping many rural regions across Europe. While this growth supports decarbonization objectives, it also raises territorial challenges related to the spatial concentration of infrastructure, uneven distribution of impacts, and growing local conflicts. These dynamics highlight the need to analyse wind energy development as a spatiotemporal territorial process. This paper examines these dynamics through the case of Aragón, a rural region in northeastern Spain that has become one of the Europe's leading wind power producers. Over the last decades, wind capacity has experienced rapid and unplanned expansion, largely in the absence of comprehensive territorial planning. Using a combination of geo-referenced spatial techniques and energy balance analysis, the study highlights the region's role as a net electricity exporter and reveals the persistent spatial agglomeration pattern of wind farms. Beyond the specific case, the paper proposes an analytically transferable framework for assessing the pace, geography and governance of wind deployment. Such an approach can help to anticipate spatial mismatches, institutional coordination challenges and potential conflicts that many rural European regions are likely to face in the energy transition process. Understanding wind energy deployment as a spatiotemporal territorial process is therefore essential for designing more balanced and socially accepted pathways toward a just energy transition in Europe.
summary: Studies the territorial dynamics of wind power expansion in rural Europe using a leading wind region as a case.

title: Below critical mass: Marshallian constraints, Jacobian synergies, and density thresholds for creative ecosystems
authors: Slavomír Ondoš; Oto Hudec
keywords: Creative industries; Critical mass; Jacobian spillovers; Knowledge spillovers; Marshallian externalities
abstract: While the transition toward a knowledge-based economy has established cultural and creative industries as primary drivers of regional innovation, the underlying agglomeration mechanisms may only operate above specific density thresholds. This article examines whether creative industries require a critical mass of co-located talent before self-sustaining agglomeration can emerge, and whether this threshold differs across functionally distinct segments. We address these questions by disaggregating the spatial configurations of digital technology, science, and arts segments within the semi-peripheral, monocentric economy of Slovakia. Using segment-specific location quotients, we examine their nonlinear density dependence and cross-district spillovers, and the role of industrial legacy. Combining a spatial Durbin model with random forest simulation and formally verified density breakpoints via piecewise regression and Davies tests, we present three interrelated findings. First, we document a spatial tension in agglomeration externalities: while the science segment acts as a local Jacobian nexus supporting digital and artistic activities within the district, it simultaneously generates regional backwash effects, absorbing creative capacity from neighbouring areas. Second, contrary to death-of-distance assumptions, the digital segment is more spatially constrained by density than the arts, with a critical mass threshold of approximately 1000 inhabitants/km² identified as a structural precondition for multi-segment cluster formation. The districts below this threshold show no evidence of self-sustaining creative agglomeration regardless of policy investment. Third, manufacturing path-dependency functions as an independent spatial suppressor of digital creative specialization, confirming that industrial legacy and density constitute distinct structural barriers to creative diversification. Our findings challenge place-neutral creative policy frameworks and suggest that regional strategy must shift from broad dispersal to strategic reinforcement of districts already approaching critical density.
summary: Investigates density thresholds for creative ecosystems, weighing Marshallian specialisation constraints against Jacobian diversity synergies.

title: How does digital economy development affect banking competition? Evidence from a spatial spillover perspective
authors: Changjun Zheng; Lei Pu; Yuxin Chen; Chen Liu
keywords: Banking competition; Competitive boundaries; Digital economy; Financial geography; Spatial Durbin error model
abstract: Regional digital economy development lowers the cost of providing banking services across geographical distance, but its effect on local banking concentration is not unidirectional. Using nearly 820,000 commercial bank branch records and a provincial digital economy index for 31 Chinese provinces from 2013 to 2023, this paper applies a spatial Durbin error model to distinguish the absorption of local digital resources, exposure to neighboring digital capacity, and unobserved regional shocks. Local digital economy development is significantly associated with greater banking concentration, suggesting that digital resources may initially reinforce the competitive advantages of incumbent institutions. By contrast, digital economy development in neighboring regions is associated with lower local concentration, reflecting the external competitive pressure created by greater cross-regional service capacity. A three-regime model and bank-type decomposition further show that digital competition follows distinct financial-geographical pathways: local digitalization is more closely associated with the expansion of city commercial banks, whereas neighboring digitalization more often facilitates the cross-regional entry of nationwide joint-stock banks, potentially generating greater openness across bank categories alongside increased concentration within categories. The digital economy therefore reshapes not merely the degree of banking competition, but also the spatial direction from which competition enters and the organizational carriers through which it operates. Provincial banking concentration should consequently be interpreted in the context of cross-regional digital linkages.
summary: Estimates how digital economy development affects banking competition, including spatial spillovers across regions.

title: Spatial disparities in hiring problems: The role of firm characteristics, job features, and search channels
authors: Michaela Fuchs; Annekatrin Niebuhr; Jan Cornelius Peters; Georg Sieglen
keywords: Composition effects; Hiring problems; J63; JEL classifications: R23; Labour shortage; Urban-rural disparities
abstract: Against the backdrop of discussions about growing regional labour shortages, this study investigates spatial disparities in hiring problems using representative micro data on vacancies and establishments in Germany. Our results point to significant disparities that vary between location types along the urban-rural continuum depending on indicator. While establishments in rural areas receive less suitable applications and more often abandon hiring plans, firms in cities more often report problems related to the applicants’ qualification and wage expectations. Prevailing types of establishments and jobs explain an important part, but not all of the disparities. Evidence on concessions suggests, moreover, that employer responses to labour shortages differ depending on the location type. While establishments in urban areas are more likely to compromise on wages, concessions on qualification are more frequent outside big cities. However, rural establishments report problems related to applicants’ insufficient qualifications less often. Heterogenous hiring problems indicate that there is need for place-sensitive policies rather than place-based policies that focus on specific locations.
summary: Explains regional differences in firms' hiring problems through firm characteristics, job features and search channels.

title: Migrant remittances and regional economic disparities
authors: Ubaid Ali; Mazhar Mughal; Oussama Ben Atta; Muhammad Ayaz
keywords: Asset Inequality; Education Inequality; Gender Inequality; Health Inequality; Income Inequality; Instrumental Variable; Regional Inequality; Remittances
abstract: While remittances are known to reduce poverty at the household-level, their broader distributional impacts at the subnational level remain underexplored. Using panel data from 109 districts in Pakistan, drawn from three household surveys combined with remote sensing data, we employ an instrumental variable strategy to examine the role of migrant remittances in shaping regional inequalities in income, assets, education, and healthcare use. We estimate the effects of remittance incidence, income share, and per capita inflows on various economic inequality measures by using three instruments including distance to the nearest international airport alternatively interacted with weighted transaction cost, global oil prices, and weighted GDP of destination countries. Our findings are four-fold. First, remittances increase regional income inequality. A 1 % increase in the share of recipient households increases income Gini by 0.55–0.74 and MLD by 0.44–0.69 percentage points. The effect plateaus beyond the 24% remittance income threshold. Second, remittances widen inequality in home ownership but reduce those in non-farmland assets. No significant effects are observed for farmland or commercial property ownership. These divergent patterns reflect differential market access. Third, remittances boost private schooling enrolment both at primary and secondary levels. A 1 % rise in remittance incidence or income share increases private school enrolment by 3.31–4.91 percentage points. The gender gap in education also widens. Fourth, remittances increase healthcare inequality, but do not affect gender gap in healthcare use. These results are robust to spatial autocorrelation correction, and the use of alternative instruments and remittance indicators.
summary: Examines how migrant remittances relate to regional economic disparities.

title: Divergent futures and structural change: Regional economic scenarios and resilience for trade shocks
authors: Olga Ivanova; Theodoros Chatzivasileiadis; Kristian Bakker; Sacha den Nijs
keywords: Econometric analysis; Regional CGE model; Scenario's; Storylines; Structural change
abstract: This paper develops quantitative regional economic scenarios for Dutch NUTS2 provinces, with varying global structural conditions, over 2020–2060 to assess regional economic resilience. Using panel econometric estimations combined with the EU-EMS recursive-dynamic spatial computable general equilibrium model, we translate scenario narratives, grounded in the SSP1 and SSP3 global pathways, into internally consistent projections of production value, employment, and sectoral specialization. The high-growth scenario assumes continued globalization and knowledge-intensive service expansion, whereas the low-growth scenario assumes deglobalization, reshoring of industrial production, and demographic stagnation. While the Dutch economy grows under both scenarios, growth falls substantially below the historical average and its spatial distribution diverges sharply. The high-growth scenario deepens the urban–peripheral divide by concentrating knowledge-intensive activity in the Randstad whereas the low-growth scenario revitalises industrial production in Noord-Brabant and Limburg through reshoring. The northern peripheral provinces face negative employment growth regardless of scenario, pointing to structural vulnerabilities that persist across both futures. The findings argue for adaptive, geographically differentiated resilience strategies rather than static policy commitments to a single structural future.
summary: Builds regional economic scenarios to assess structural change and resilience to trade shocks.

title: Regional resilience of Ukrainian oblasts in the period of Russian invasion
authors: Jakub Sanojca
keywords: Economic resilience; Oblasts; Regional resilience; Resilience; Ukraine
abstract: In resilience theory, regions can be persistent to the crisis or adapt to a new situation and even change their dependence path. In that, the text author focuses on the regional resilience of Ukrainian oblasts. To measure the resilience of regions, a resilience index was created using the following indicators: 1) GDP per capita, 2) employment diversity, 3) employment rate, 4) number of SMEs per 10.000 people, 5) investment rate by GDP, 6) expenditures on R&D by GDP. That index was created for the years 2012–2021, and for the last year, a typology was created, which divided oblasts into four categories: very low, low, medium, and high. Only Kyiv was in the last type for the whole period. Using the Pearson correlation coefficient, the Resilience index for 2021 was compared with the dynamics (2021 =100%) of the following data: 1) number of active enterprises, 2) number of employed in business enterprises, 3) capital investments, 4) turnover of enterprises for 2022–2024. The result shows no correlation between the index and the data. There is a negative correlation between warfare damage and the data, but it was lower in 2024 than in previous years. Sources of regional resilience are eRobota, foreign aid, businesses' ability to adapt, and the relocation of enterprises, while obstacles include warfare, blackouts, and floods. The best situation was in the western regions of Ukraine: Lvivska, Zakarpatska, Volynska, Chernivetska, and Ternpoliska, which are adapting to new challenges and have a chance to change their dependence path in the future.
summary: Assesses the economic resilience of Ukrainian oblasts during the Russian invasion.

title: The spatiotemporal dynamics of interpersonal income inequality: Empirical evidence from the Greek regions
authors: Leonidas Doukissas; Panagiotis Pantazis; Yannis Psycharis; Konstadinos Politis
keywords: Gini index; income inequality; regional policy
abstract: This paper examines interpersonal income inequality across the Greek regions over the period 2002–2019. Based on individualised household income data, it investigates the geographical pattern and socioeconomic correlates of interpersonal/intraregional inequality. The results show strong evidence of a negative correlation between the Gini index and GDP per capita and a positive correlation between the Gini index and the unemployment rate. Thus, higher regional economic performance is associated with lower, rather than higher, interpersonal inequality, whereas higher unemployment is associated with greater inequality. Unemployment therefore emerges as a persistent factor associated with interpersonal/ intraregional inequality. These findings provide important inputs for the design of policies aimed at more territorially balanced and socially inclusive development.
summary: Traces the spatiotemporal dynamics of interpersonal income inequality across Greek regions.

title: What drives the location and diffusion of biogas units in Western France?
authors: Martin Faulques
abstract: In recent years, biogas plants have become an important part of the energy transition, capable of converting waste and biomass into biogas. However, the efficiency and profitability of these biogas units influence their location. A trend towards co-location of these eco-innovations has been demonstrated, mainly due to the proximity of resources and the exchange of technical knowledge between neighboring units (mimicry effects). However, this proximity can also lead to increased competition for local resources, which can undermine the collective efficiency of facilities. This article aims to understand this trade-off by exploring how geographical proximity between units influences the siting of biogas units in the regions of Brittany, Normandy and Pays de la Loire. Using a spatial Durbin model, we examined the interactions between units and how these dynamics influence the factors affecting the probability of unit installation. Our results show that there are clusters of biogas units extending over a range of 11 to 16 km. However, these effects are spatially limited: when units are too close, competition for resources limits their installations, while when they are too far apart, the effect disappears.
summary: Using a spatial Durbin model for Brittany, Normandy and Pays de la Loire, the paper finds biogas units cluster within 11–16 km, but siting is deterred when units are too close due to competition for local resources.

title: Modelling regional economic resilience to climate disasters: A recovery forecasting framework illustrated by the 2024 Valencia floods
authors: Priscila Espinosa; Maria Teresa Balaguer-Coll; Jose M. Pavía; Emili Tortosa-Ausina
abstract: The floods that struck the Valencian region (Spain) in October 2024 illustrate how climate change is intensifying extreme weather events in Mediterranean flood-prone areas, challenging regional economic resilience. This disaster, which resulted in numerous fatalities and extensive infrastructure damage, disrupted supply chains across a region already vulnerable due to decades of urban and industrial development in the area. Drawing on regional economic resilience theory and recovery curve methodologies, we present a near-real-time (early post-disaster) framework for promptly assessing climate disaster impacts on regional economic growth, based on post-event damage and administrative data and designed to be operational within weeks of the event using readily available information. Our approach combines sectoral recovery dynamics with worker-level impact data to update GDP growth forecasts, addressing a critical gap in disaster response capabilities for increasingly climate-vulnerable regions. Applied to the Valencia floods, our methodology projects differential sectoral resilience patterns: under the assumed sector-specific recovery functions, construction shows rapid recovery due to reconstruction demand, whereas agriculture shows prolonged vulnerability reflecting the sector's exposure to climate risks. Compared to pre-flood forecasts, results indicate economic contractions of up to 0.2 percentage points in 2024 and 2025, followed by a policy-supported rebound adding 0.3 percentage points to growth in 2026. The analysis illustrates how the assumed level of government intervention may shape post-disaster economic trajectories in flood-prone regions. Beyond providing timely impact assessment, this framework could support climate resilience planning in Mediterranean and other climate-vulnerable territories, enabling policymakers to revise economic forecasts within weeks of the disaster, when policy decisions are most critical, as extreme weather events become more frequent and severe under climate change.
summary: A near-real-time recovery forecasting framework applied to the 2024 Valencia floods projects GDP growth losses of up to 0.2 points in 2024–25 and a 0.3-point policy-supported rebound in 2026, with fast construction recovery and prolonged agricultural vulnerability.

title: The unexpected effects of place-based remote work incentives: evidence from the Tulsa Remote Program
authors: Bowei Dong
abstract: Place-based remote work incentives have emerged as a new tool for regional development, aiming to attract talent and stimulate local economies. Tulsa Remote is one of the nation's largest and best-funded programs, offering a $10,000 grant to remote workers relocating to Tulsa, Oklahoma. This study examines the spillover and sometimes unexpected patterns associated with the program's introduction using county-level migration data and individual-level microdata. The analysis documents that the implementation of Tulsa Remote Program coincides with increased interstate in-migration, alongside reduced intrastate inflows and increased intrastate outflows. The program is associated with stronger migration responses among married, middle-aged individuals with moderate incomes originating from high-cost metropolitan areas. The findings highlight both the potential and the trade-offs of well-funded place-based policies in shaping migration dynamics.
summary: The Tulsa Remote relocation grant coincided with higher interstate in-migration to Tulsa but reduced intrastate inflows and increased intrastate outflows, with the strongest responses among married, middle-aged, moderate-income movers from high-cost metros.

title: How does labour force participation respond to unemployment? A regional and gender-based exploration of Italy
authors: Anna Rita Germani; Claudia Nardone; Walter Paternesi Meloni
abstract: This study examines whether, and how, unemployment dynamics shape labour force participation across Italian macro-regions, asking whether added or discouraged worker effects prevail and whether participation responds persistently to unemployment shocks. Using quarterly data for the period 1977–2024, we investigate the dynamic interaction between unemployment and participation by accounting for territorial and gender heterogeneity. We employ a structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) framework to trace the dynamic effects of unemployment shocks on labour force participation while addressing their simultaneity. The results show that unemployment shocks generate a significant and persistent increase in participation at the aggregate level, at odds with long-run independence over the horizons considered. However, this effect is highly heterogeneous across space and gender. Unemployment invariance holds in the North–West area, while added worker effects emerge mainly in Central and southern Italy, driven almost entirely by female participation. Male participation exhibits only transitory discouraged worker effects (especially in the North–East). Overall, the findings highlight the importance of regional labour market structures in shaping long-run adjustment mechanisms, particularly the gendered nature of participation responses to unemployment shocks. The results may have important implications for the design of place-based and gender-sensitive labour market policies.
summary: An SVAR analysis of Italian macro-regions (1977–2024) finds unemployment shocks persistently raise labour force participation, driven by female added-worker effects in Central and Southern Italy, while male participation shows only transitory discouraged-worker effects.

title: Wage inequality when pollution taxation interacts with privatization
authors: Jiancai Pi; Shumin Yu; Ping Xu
abstract: In the real world, pollution taxation often interacts with privatization. This paper incorporates the pollution tax and privatization into a unified general equilibrium framework, and analyzes how the pollution tax and privatization affect skilled–unskilled wage inequality. For the pollution tax, an increase in the pollution tax will reduce wage inequality in most cases. For privatization, the effect of privatization relies on the strength of the pollution tax. Specifically, privatization tends to reduce wage inequality (unless the capital market is open) when there is a high pollution tax, and privatization is likely to increase wage inequality when there is a low pollution tax.
summary: A general equilibrium model shows higher pollution taxes usually reduce skilled–unskilled wage inequality, while privatization reduces inequality under high pollution taxes (unless capital is mobile) but tends to raise it under low taxes.

title: Fiscal stress and divergent fiscal responses by central cities and their suburbs
authors: Annie Yu-Hsin Hsu; Steven G. Craig
abstract: We study how long-run employment decentralization shapes local government responses to adverse economic shocks. Since the 1970s, employment activity has increasingly shifted from central cities toward suburban areas, generating heterogeneous fiscal environments within commuting zones. Using the China trade shock following China's WTO accession as a source of exogenous variation, we show that central cities experience larger revenue losses and reduce infrastructure spending more sharply, consistent with stronger adjustment to longer-lasting fiscal pressures in central cities, while financial reserves represent an additional margin of adjustment among suburban governments. Similar results under a Bartik-style employment-shock specification indicate that the heterogeneous fiscal responses are not unique to the China-specific trade channel. Our findings highlight how employment decentralization generates heterogeneous fiscal responses within the same local labor market.
summary: Exploiting the China trade shock, the paper shows US central cities suffer larger revenue losses and cut infrastructure spending more sharply than their suburbs, which instead draw on financial reserves.

title: Is a smart city greener? A dynamic differential game and empirical research based on regional synergy in China
authors: Mengyu Jia; Xiaoxiao Zhou
abstract: As a new urban mode that considers digitalization and greenization, the smart city provides an efficient way to reduce carbon emissions for green development. By constructing a dynamic differential game model, this study clarifies the optimal strategy selection of smart cities for inhibiting carbon emissions and explains the internal mechanism behind it while adhering to a Technological, Organizational, and Environmental framework. A multi-period difference-in-differences model is taken to evaluated the implementation effects and executive mechanisms of smart city policies (SCP) on carbon emissions with Chinese city data from 2003 to 2019. It can be found that inter-regional smart cities' cooperation provided the optimal strategy to effectively reduce carbon emissions. Mechanism analysis showed that SCP reduce carbon emission through technological progress, resource allocation, energy-saving, information agglomeration, and carbon absorption enhancement. A multidimensional policy system plays a synergistic role in carbon reduction. Heterogeneity analysis showed that SCP's low-carbon effects are more significant in type I large, eastern, western, highly marketable, and cities with high environmental constraints. The spatial effect showed that SCP can reduce carbon emissions of neighboring cities. This study supports the vital role of SCP in carbon reduction and provides relevant policy suggestions for achieving green transition in China.
summary: Combining a differential game model with a multi-period DID on Chinese cities (2003–2019), the study finds smart city pilots cut carbon emissions locally and in neighboring cities, with inter-regional cooperation the optimal strategy.

title: Cleaning up one city, affecting another? zero-waste city pilots and spatial spillovers in China
authors: Xinhai Lu; Shi Liang; Qianchao Li; Wenyan Li
abstract: Against the backdrop of interregional solid-waste flows and tightening land constraints, this paper examines whether the Zero-Waste City pilot policy improves urban land green use efficiency, and whether such effects extend beyond pilot jurisdictions through spatial spillovers. Using panel data for 284 prefecture-level and above cities in China from 2010 to 2024, we treat the policy as a staggered quasi-natural experiment. We identify local policy effects with a multi-period difference-in-differences design, and estimate spillover effects using a spatial exposure test and a two-way fixed-effects spatial Durbin model. We further probe potential channels and supplement the baseline results with an imputation-based modern DID estimator. The results reveal that the Zero-Waste City pilot generates both significant local effects and significant positive spatial spillovers. Urban land green use efficiency rises substantially in pilot cities, while neighboring cities also exhibit a statistically significant positive response. The channel analysis suggests that, within pilot cities, the policy increases the intensity of construction land use and strengthens the capacity to organize land supply and reallocate resources under constraints on existing construction land, providing evidence consistent with the interpretation that these factors may serve as channels. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the local policy effect is more pronounced in cities located southeast of the Hu Huanyong Line, in cities with stronger dependence on land finance, and in cities with a higher initial industrial share. The supplementary imputation-based modern DID estimates yield qualitatively consistent results. A wide range of robustness checks, including parallel-trend tests, permutation placebo tests, lagged-treatment specifications, alternative dependent variables, sample exclusions, and alternative spatial weight matrices, further corroborate the baseline findings. Overall, the evidence indicates that the Zero-Waste City pilot has moved beyond waste management per se and become embedded in broader processes of land allocation and regional interaction.
summary: China's Zero-Waste City pilots raise urban land green use efficiency in pilot cities and generate positive spillovers to neighboring cities, operating partly through more intensive construction land use and land-supply reallocation.

title: Unpacking spatial dependence: a new experimental design for spatial autoregressive simulation
authors: Wei Kang; Levi Wolf
abstract: Simulating spatial patterns with varying levels of spatial autocorrelation is essential for evaluating models, estimators, and diagnostics. The spatial autoregressive (SAR) process is widely used for this purpose, but its main parameter affects both spatial autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity. Only the former is usually acknowledged. Unfortunately, these unintended variance effects can bias Monte Carlo interpretations when ignored. This paper introduces a variance-stabilized SAR (VSSAR) process that decouples spatial autocorrelation from heteroskedasticity. The proposed approach preserves the spatial patterning implied by the SAR process while enforcing constant marginal variance, making it possible to more accurately assess the behavior of models and estimators under spatial autocorrelation. We validate the VSSAR method by replicating three canonical simulation experiments and demonstrate that it should serve as the new default data-generating process for simulation studies in spatial analysis when spatial autocorrelation is the primary object of interest.
summary: The paper proposes a variance-stabilized SAR process that separates spatial autocorrelation from heteroskedasticity, arguing it should become the default data-generating process for spatial simulation studies.

title: Maritime hub-corridors: examining the spatial structure in global maritime networks
authors: Wanhee Kim; Hyun Kim; Paul Jung
keywords: Hub-corridors; Global maritime networks; Spatial structure; Global supply-chain disruptions; Red Sea Crisis; Panama Canal drought
abstract: Global maritime networks are highly complex and dynamic systems, organized around hubs and corridors that form hierarchical structures essential to international trade. Hubs and corridors are conceptually interconnected; however, their identification has often relied on distinct analytical approaches, with hubs typically defined by connectivity-based metrics and corridors by patterns of spatial interaction and flow concentration. Although resilience studies recognize the interdependence of hubs and corridors, existing approaches often rely primarily on hub-centered data, offering limited empirical insight into how corridor-level flow dynamics evolve under external disruptions such as pandemics or economic shocks. To bridge this gap, this study introduces a Maritime Hub–Corridor framework that integrates hubs and their inter-hub linkages into a hierarchical network system, developed through a structured, sequential analytic procedure. Applying this framework to Port-of-Call data, we use three complementary indices—connectivity, freight capacity, and spatial interaction—to capture distinct dimensions of hub functionality. Rather than treating these as isolated computed measures, we use them to screen candidate hubs, evaluate them against a Cumulative Flow Contribution Curve (CFCC) criterion across all dimensions, identify the resulting hub set and hierarchy, and grouped interconnected hubs into corridor clusters. Findings reveal that maritime networks organize as differentiated hub-corridor systems across four spatial types, exhibiting multi-scale hierarchies. Additionally temporal analysis reveals the adaptability and contrasting resilience mechanisms of hub-corridors to socio-economic disruptions: Suez consolidation versus Panama fragmentation. This research contributes a novel analytical approach for identifying hub-corridors structures systematically, characterizing multi-scale maritime network organization, and understanding resilience mechanisms under major disruptions.
summary: A Maritime Hub–Corridor framework applied to port-of-call data shows global shipping organizes into multi-scale hub-corridor systems of four spatial types, with contrasting resilience to disruptions (Suez consolidation versus Panama fragmentation).

title: On the Effectiveness of the Weighted Least Squares Technique for Urban Scaling: Empirical Evidence on the Relationship Between Labor Productivity and City Size in the U.S., Europe, and Latin America
authors: Kemal Dinçer Dingeç; Furkan Börü; Emine Tahsin
keywords: Urban scaling; Agglomeration and scaling; Linear regression; Weighted least squares; Lognormal distribution; Urban economics
abstract: The cities are the places where scale economies are created. Therefore economics of agglomeration is important to understand different aspects of urbanization. The principles of agglomeration economies can be quantified by scaling analysis. The standard statistical method for scaling analysis is simple linear regression (ordinary least squares). However, the special characteristics of city data such as non-normality and non-constant variance (heteroskedasticity) complicate the statistical estimation and make it necessary to use special estimation techniques. In this paper, to overcome these problems, the standard approach of utilizing the classical weighted least square technique is suggested. The novelty of the paper is the derivation of a specific weighting rule starting from a lognormal model of the individual-level metric. We applied the ordinary least squares (OLS) and the weighted least squares (WLS) technique for the investigation and comparison of the scaling behaviors of labor productivities in the cities of three different regions (Latin America, Europe, and the USA). It is revealed that while in the US and Europe OLS and WLS yield similar results, the OLS is incapable of detecting the scaling behavior in Latin America. The WLS is capable of identifying the "increasing return to scale" relationship between city size and labor productivity.
summary: Deriving a lognormal-based weighting rule for urban scaling regressions, the paper shows WLS detects increasing returns between city size and labor productivity in Latin America where OLS fails, while both agree for the US and Europe.

title: Sustainable Transport and Liveability: Emerging Perspectives on Neighbourhood Mobility
authors: Mehrnaz Zargarzadeh; Anabela S. Narciso Ribeiro; Aura Reggiani
summary: Editorial introducing a special issue on sustainable transport, liveability and neighbourhood mobility.

title: Township-Level Framework for Assessing Social Vulnerability in a Multi-Ethnic Area: Evidence from Lushan, Southwest China
authors: Lu Gan; Leqi Zhou; Shan Yang; Xia Liao; Jiangjun Wan
keywords: Multi-ethnic; Social vulnerability; DEMATEL; ISM
abstract: Multi-ethnic areas often involve diverse demographic and social characteristics, which may create additional challenges for disaster vulnerability assessment and governance. However, existing research has paid relatively little attention to the social vulnerability of multi-ethnic areas. Therefore, this study constructs an integrated framework for assessing social vulnerability in multi-ethnic areas. This framework combines the Social Vulnerability Index (SoVI) with the Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) and Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) methods to assess township-level variations in social vulnerability within a multi-ethnic area and the influence relationships among its dimensions. The framework was applied to a case study in Lushan County, southwestern China. The results show that areas with lower social vulnerability are concentrated in the county center - Luyang Subdistrict, while areas with higher social vulnerability are distributed around it. The DEMATEL analysis shows that socioeconomic status has the highest centrality (D + R = 9.644), while its net influence is close to zero (D - R = 0.032). Ethnic composition shows the strongest net influencing tendency (D - R = 1.528), followed by age structure (D - R = 0.946). Emergency and governance capacity has the strongest net influenced position (D - R = -1.732). The ISM analysis further reveals hierarchical relationships among the vulnerability dimensions based on expert judgments. These results indicate that social vulnerability involves interconnected demographic, socioeconomic, service, and governance dimensions. They also provide a context-specific reference for differentiated governance in multi-ethnic areas.
summary: Combining SoVI with DEMATEL and ISM for Lushan County, the study finds social vulnerability lowest in the county center and higher in surrounding townships, with ethnic composition and age structure the strongest net drivers and governance capacity the most influenced dimension.

title: Historical Nodes and Urban Evolution: A GIS-Based Assessment of the Spatial Drivers of Settlement Growth in Bangalore City
authors: Sandipta Das; Dhanaraj K; Sangita Das
keywords: HGIS; Urban evolution; Historic structure; Bangalore history; Spatial statistics
abstract: Bangalore possesses a long and layered historical legacy of the spatial distribution of inscriptions, temples, mosques, churches, historic structures, and other cultural landmarks. Although the exact morphology of earlier urban landscapes cannot always be directly traced due to limited cartographic evidence. The spatial configuration of these historical nodes provides critical proxies for understanding past settlement patterns. Most often, the city's layers are composed of its past superimposed and juxtaposed with new development. Using an HGIS (Historical Geographic Information System) framework, the present study is trying to reconstruct the possible zones of early habitation in Bangalore by analysing the spatial concentration, clustering, and directional trends of historical structures and heritage buildings from 700 CE to 1950 CE (from the ancient Western Ganga Dynasty - Colonial - British modern era). The study used HGIS and statistical techniques such as mean center, standard distance, standard deviational ellipse, Average Nearest Neighbour, Kernel density, and variable buffer model to examine how these nodes were distributed across different historical periods and subsequent expansion corridors. The study demarcates probable settlement areas and interprets how cultural, religious, and administrative anchors structured the continuing urban evolution of Bangalore through spatial statistical techniques. The findings suggest that the colonial period's administrative and infrastructural developments possibly contribute to the increasing concentration of urban growth.
summary: Using historical GIS and spatial statistics on heritage structures from 700 to 1950 CE, the study reconstructs probable early settlement zones in Bangalore and suggests colonial-era administrative and infrastructural development concentrated urban growth.

title: A Spatial Multi-Criteria Decision Framework for Eco-Industrial Park Siting in Syria's Reconstruction: A Case Study in the Coastal Region
authors: Tarek Rahmoun; Sham Mahmoud; Yunyan LI
keywords: Analytic Hierarchy Process AHP; GIS; Eco-industrial Park EIP; Industrial Symbiosis IS; Post-conflict recovery; Site selection
abstract: Eco-industrial parks (EIPs) offer a strategic means to merge industrial symbiosis principles into post-conflict reconstruction; however, their adoption in Syria remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, this research introduces a replicable methodology for EIP site selection in Akkar Plain, located in Syria's southern coastal region, thereby advancing the broader discourse on integrating EIPs into reconstruction policy. This study combines Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and utilises both quantitative and qualitative methods. A literature review and expert focus group identified 12 site selection criteria, which were then classified and weighted through AHP pairwise comparisons, and synthesized using weighted overlay analysis. Following this, the suitability map was divided into five zones, from least to most suitable. Key findings include: (1) geographical and environmental criteria were most significant, accounting for 39% of the total site selection weight; (2) the most influential sub-criteria were proximity to settlements and major roads, as well as slope and elevation, each weighted between 11.5% and 20.5%; (3) the analysis identified 3.83 km² of highly suitable land (suitability index > 80%), with ~ 150 ha concentrated in the northeastern sector, and 34.29 km² classified as suitable, while avoidance zones comprise 66.5% of the effective study area; (4) the optimal site aligns with the Regional Plan 2040 development vision, supporting desired industrial symbiosis. These findings provide planning decision-makers with an evidence-based, defensible tool for EIP site selection in data-limited, post-conflict contexts. Thus, it facilitates the balanced integration of environmental, economic, and social priorities in sustainable industrial development.
summary: A GIS–AHP site-selection analysis for Syria's Akkar Plain identifies 3.83 km² of highly suitable land for an eco-industrial park, with geographic and environmental criteria carrying 39% of the weight and the optimal site consistent with the Regional Plan 2040.

title: Spatial Heterogeneity and Driving Mechanisms of Construction and Demolition Waste Generation Efficiency: Provincial Evidence from China
authors: Zhenshuang Wang; Yufei Wang; Zhikang Bao
keywords: Construction and demolition waste generation efficiency; Dagum gini coefficient; Geographical detector; SBM-DDF model; Spatial heterogeneity; Spatial markov
abstract: Construction and demolition waste generation efficiency (CDWGE) is a critical indicator for assessing the capacity of cities and regions to advance sustainable urban development, circular construction, and zero-waste city transitions. Understanding its spatiotemporal evolution and associated factors can support evidence-based urban governance and differentiated policy design. This study investigates the spatiotemporal heterogeneity, regional disparities, spatial transitions, and driving mechanisms of CDWGE across China from 2005 to 2023. A super-efficient SBM-DDF model is first employed to measure CDWGE, followed by the Dagum Gini coefficient and its decomposition, kernel density estimation, spatial Markov chains, and the geographical detector model to reveal its dynamic evolution and influencing factors. The results show that China’s overall CDWGE improved during the study period, suggesting progress in construction and demolition waste management performance and resource efficiency. However, regional growth rates varied considerably, following the pattern of central > western > northeast > eastern, indicating differentiated pathways toward sustainable construction and demolition waste management. At the provincial level, CDWGE displayed a relatively balanced but clustered spatial distribution, with evidence of club convergence. Regional disparities widened over time, with transvariation density contributing most to the overall inequality. The spatial Markov results further reveal path dependence and neighbourhood effects, suggesting that provincial CDWGE transitions are associated not only with local conditions but also with the states of neighbouring regions. Among the driving factors, technological innovation shows the strongest explanatory power for the spatial differentiation of CDWGE, while factor interactions mainly exhibit two-factor enhancement and nonlinear enhancement effects. These findings contribute to sustainable cities research by providing a spatial decision-support framework for identifying priority regions, strengthening interregional collaboration, and designing differentiated policies to advance the achievement of zero-waste cities and circular urban development in developing countries.
summary: The study examines spatial heterogeneity and drivers of construction and demolition waste generation efficiency across Chinese provinces.

title: Determinants of Homeownership Rates among Migrants: Changes in the Process of Mobility Transition in China
authors: Fan Zhang; Liyue Lin; Tingting Li; Yu Zhu; Wenqian Ke
keywords: China; Housing tenure; Mobility transition; Family migration
abstract: Homeownership rates among migrants in China have grown rapidly in recent years, driven by diversified migration and policy development. However, how homeownership rates change under the ongoing mobility transition remains insufficiently understood. This study addresses this gap using data from the 2011 and 2017 China Migrants Dynamic Survey. Employing the Fairlie non-linear decomposition method, we examine migrants with varied socioeconomic characteristics and migration patterns to identify the factors associated with homeownership rates. Results show that the homeownership rates among migrants in their destination cities more than doubled during this period, increasing from 8.97% to 19.41%. Higher household income and education, longer residence, family-oriented migration, willingness to integrate, nonagricultural hukou, and public sector employment are positively associated with homeownership, while migrants in provincial capitals or municipalities are less likely to own housing. Decomposition results further indicate that family-oriented, long-term migration, and improvements in migrants' socioeconomic status make the largest contributions, highlighting the growing importance of mobility transition. These results will advance our theoretical understanding of the migration-housing nexus in transitional societies, with policy implications for integrating migrants into urban housing markets.
summary: Using the 2011 and 2017 China Migrants Dynamic Survey, the study shows migrant homeownership in destination cities more than doubled (8.97% to 19.41%), with family-oriented long-term migration and rising socioeconomic status contributing most.

title: Road-Closure Stress Testing of Essential-Service Accessibility in Yemen
authors: Dmitry Erokhin
keywords: Yemen; Accessibility; Road-network vulnerability; OpenStreetMap; WorldPop; Service access; Percolation; Spatial disruption
abstract: Road disruption can change access to basic services even when the services themselves remain in place. This study develops a national network stress test for Yemen using OpenStreetMap road extract and WorldPop constrained population surface. Demand is represented by 8,460 population-weighted grid cells covering 41.18 million people and linked to mapped markets, health facilities, and fuel stations.
