The study then evaluates five stylized closure mechanisms at 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of simplified physical road links, including random removal, spatially clustered removal, major-road targeting, access-betweenness targeting, and exact-bridge targeting. At 1% random removal, the mean newly disconnected population share across services is 1.12%, indicating a shallow low-intensity response. The most disruptive mechanism depends on closure intensity. Exact bridges produce the largest disconnection at 1% closure (15.65% across services), access-betweenness targeting at 5% (35.28%), and major-road targeting at 10% and 20% (49.65% and 65.04%). Among people who remain connected, rerouting is highest under major-road targeting at 1% and 5%. At higher intensities, connected-only delay becomes non-monotonic because disconnected users no longer remain in that distribution. Spatial closures look modest in national averages but impose severe local losses. At 1% closure, 2.01% of the national population is newly disconnected, compared with 59.64% of the population within 25 km of the closure center and 93.95% within the realized closure footprint. These findings show that national averages should be complemented by local exposure measures when assessing road-network vulnerability and prioritizing access-sensitive recovery.
summary: A national road-closure stress test for Yemen finds bridge closures most disruptive at low intensity and major-road targeting at high intensity (up to 65% of people cut off from services), while spatially clustered closures cause severe local losses masked by national averages.

title: Quantifying Rural Lifestyle Mobilities in China: A Spatio-temporal Accessibility Perspective on Livelihood Pathways
authors: Rongrong Zhuo; Yanwei Feng; Wenzhong Zhang; Yunxiao Dang; Mark Rosenberg; Yuchen Zhou
keywords: Spatio-temporal accessibility; Everyday life; Urbanization; Rural livelihoods; Household-level analysis; Rural China
abstract: While urbanization has profoundly reshaped rural China, empirical evidence on the nuanced transformation of daily life remains limited by quantification challenges. To address this gap, this study refines the concept of "rural lifestyle mobilities"—the evolving spatio-temporal organization of daily activities in relation to livelihood change—and operationalizes it through a multidimensional accessibility framework. Drawing on survey data from 2,437 households across three counties of the Jianghan Plain, China, we use an observed-variable serial multiple-mediation path analysis implemented in a structural equation model (SEM) to examine whether livelihood capital and livelihood transition are statistically associated with household-level mobility changes and whether the proposed indirect pathways are consistent with the data. Results reveal that housing and consumption have larger average mobility change scores than working and leisure, reflecting a consumption-oriented transition in rural daily life. Livelihood capital has the most consistently positive estimated association with mobility outcomes, whereas livelihood transition shows domain-specific and, in some cases, opposing-sign indirect paths. Because the data are retrospective and observational, these estimates are interpreted as model-based associations rather than causally identified effects. By integrating temporal dimensions into the analysis of rural lifestyle mobilities, this study advances applied spatial research on rural transitions and provides policy-relevant evidence for improving everyday accessibility and living conditions in rapidly urbanizing regions.
summary: A survey of 2,437 Jianghan Plain households finds rural daily-life mobility changes concentrated in housing and consumption rather than work and leisure, with livelihood capital most consistently associated with greater mobility change.

title: Spatiotemporal Evolution of Urban Systems in Artificial Watersheds: Evidence From China's Grand Canal
authors: Zhibao Wang; Nana Zhao; Yujian Pang
keywords: Artificial watershed; China’s grand canal; Urban system; Urban tree
abstract: With the help of relevant historical data, this paper analyzes the characteristics and dominant factors of the spatiotemporal evolution of the urban system in China’s Grand Canal during various historical periods to summarize the unique laws governing the evolution of urban systems in artificial watersheds based on the “UT” theory and the Central Place theory. During China’s feudal period, with the help of convenient canal transport, a “North-South dual-core” urban system formed in China’s Grand Canal, with several “single-center” or “multicenter” urban systems in its subregions. In the 20th century, especially since railway construction in mainland China, the continuous decline in inland river canal transport led to major changes in the urban system but left its main core cities basically unchanged. In the 21st century, the excavation of historical and cultural value has once again revitalized some cities that once flourished along China’s Grand Canal. However, affected by the rapid development of modern transportation, these cities have not recovered their former regional status. The urban system along China’s Grand Canal has not changed much, with only the fine-tuning of regional functional division and the reorientation and transformation of some cities in the urban system of China’s Grand Canal.
summary: The paper traces the spatiotemporal evolution of urban systems along China's Grand Canal as an artificial watershed.

title: Cause-Specific Infant Mortality and Area-Level Deprivation in Russia: Associations and Policy Implications
authors: Anastasia Zelenina
keywords: Deprivation; Infant mortality; Public health; Sex
abstract: To examine the impact of regional socioeconomic and environmental deprivation on cause-specific infant mortality in Russia. Using data from the Russian Fertility and Mortality Database (2015–2022) covering 83 regions, we analyzed cause-specific infant mortality via multivariable negative binomial regressions, with the infant population applied as an offset term. In the primary analysis, models were adjusted for infant sex and place of residence (urban vs. rural) to capture group-specific risks. To evaluate the systemic robustness of deprivation effects against latent geographic processes and healthcare supply, a separate sensitivity analysis was performed on the total population without sex and residence stratification, integrating spatial eigenvector filtering and pediatrician density. In the baseline models adjusted for infant sex and place of residence, mortality rates from poisonings, injuries, and external causes escalated progressively alongside gradient increases in economic deprivation. These findings remained robust and unchanged upon the further integration of spatial eigenvectors and pediatrician density into the regression frameworks. Additionally, the primary stratified analysis revealed significantly elevated infant mortality from neoplasms specifically within environmentally deprived rural pockets. However, in the unstratified sensitivity framework, this highly localized rural hazard signal disappeared due to a classic signal dilution effect caused by aggregating data across the total regional population without urban-rural segmentation. This study provides the first empirical evidence that socioeconomic and environmental deprivation significantly shapes cause-specific infant mortality in Russia, demonstrating robust associations that vary by infant sex and residence, while highlighting the major mediating role of regional healthcare infrastructure.
summary: The paper examines associations between area-level deprivation and cause-specific infant mortality in Russia and their policy implications.

title: Dining Opportunities in Transition: Restaurant Spending-Tier Recomposition in Beijing, 2019–2025
authors: Jinyuan Gu; Yue Sun; Dongfeng Yang
keywords: Beijing; Dining opportunities; Restaurants; Spatial association; Spending tiers; Urban commercial change
abstract: As consumption choices become more cautious and differentiated, urban-scale longitudinal evidence remains limited on how the spending-tier composition of local restaurant supply changes over time. Using Dianping restaurant records from Beijing’s six central districts in 2019 and 2025, this study classifies restaurants with fixed 2019 platform-recorded per-person spending thresholds and examines tier composition, state transitions, and spatial associations within 500 m units. The share of low-tier records rose from 21.3% to 26.7%, while the share of high-tier records fell from 19.6% to 12.8%, indicating an aggregate shift toward lower tiers. Yet local structures were largely continuous: 73.18% of comparable units retained their original dominant tier, and units that changed moved mainly toward middle-tier dominance or mixed-balanced states, suggesting gradual recomposition rather than direct substitution between the low and high ends. Spatial associations show that low-tier provision was more embedded in dense everyday living spaces, whereas high-tier continuity was concentrated in urban nodes able to support experiential, business-oriented, and recognizably higher-quality consumption. By grounding consumption adjustment in the spending-tier composition of local restaurant supply, the study shows how everyday dining opportunities are reconfigured through local structural continuity, middle- and mixed-state recomposition, and spatially differentiated supply outcomes.
summary: The study documents how Beijing's restaurant supply recomposed across spending tiers between 2019 and 2025.

title: How Does Administrative Restructuring Affect Wage Income?
authors: Dongkun Li; Wenxin Xing; Huizhong Lu
keywords: Urbanization; Wage income; “County-to-city” policy
abstract: Wage income constitutes a fundamental benchmark for evaluating the quality of regional development and serves as a crucial indicator for retrospectively assessing the effectiveness of administrative division adjustments. This study utilizes the new round “county-to-city” policy as a quasi-natural experiment, employing a difference-in-differences approach to investigate the impact and mechanisms of administrative division adjustment policies on wage income. The results demonstrate that the implementation of the “county-to-city” policy significantly increases wage income. This policy fosters wage income growth through two primary channels: attracting investment to create jobs, and improving human capital by developing education. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the policy exhibits regional disparities, with more pronounced effects observed in areas adjacent to urban centers and regions experiencing net population inflows. This study highlights how administrative division adjustments reshape public resource allocation, providing valuable insights for advancing county-centered urbanization.
summary: The paper estimates the effect of administrative restructuring on wage income.

title: Urban Housing Speculation Based on Housing Indoor Image Recognition: A Case Study of Kunming, China
authors: Ziheng Guo; Yang Wang; Haolei Zheng
keywords: Housing indoor images; Housing speculation; Housing speculation index; Kunming; Real estate; Visual understanding models
abstract: Housing speculation is an important factor affecting the stability and spatial differentiation of urban real estate markets, yet existing measurement approaches have difficulty capturing speculative differences at the intra-urban micro scale. Based on housing indoor image recognition, this study proposes a method that uses the actual occupancy rate of listed second-hand housing (during the listing period) as an inverse indicator of housing speculation and further constructs a Housing Speculation Index (HSI). Taking Kunming, China as a case study, this method is used to measure housing speculation at the block level and reveal its spatial pattern. The results show that the overall level of housing speculation in Kunming is moderate and exhibits a clear zonal gradient characterized by low speculation in the core area, moderate speculation in the main urban area, and high speculation in the suburban areas, with the suburbs becoming the main concentration of highly speculative housing. The findings demonstrate that the measurement framework based on housing indoor image recognition can effectively overcome the limitations of traditional macro-level indicators at the micro spatial scale, and provide a new perspective for identifying the intra-urban spatial pattern of housing speculation and formulating differentiated regulatory policies.
summary: The study uses image recognition of housing interiors to identify housing speculation in Kunming, China.

title: Do Lower-income Neighborhoods Always Face Higher Waterlogging Risk in Megacities? Evidence From Chengdu, China
authors: Jingyi Xu; Li Peng; Xia Chen
keywords: China; Environmental inequality; Gumbel copula; Housing prices; Spatial mismatch; Urban waterlogging
abstract: Environmental justice theory predicts that lower-income populations bear disproportionate environmental hazards, yet emerging evidence from Chinese megacities suggests the opposite may be true for urban waterlogging. This study examines the spatial relationship between waterlogging risk and income groups in Chengdu, China, using housing prices to represent income. Waterlogging probability maps for 2015 and 2025 were generated using a random forest model. Spatial relationships were assessed via the spatial mismatch index, bivariate LISA, colocation analysis, and the Gumbel copula for upper-tail dependence. Contrary to environmental justice expectations, the high-income group concentrated in the urban core faces elevated waterlogging risk, while the low-income group in peripheral areas experiences lower exposure. The spatial mismatch index reveals greater divergence for the high-income group. Local spatial association identifies significant high-risk–high-income clusters, and the Gumbel copula confirms significant upper-tail dependence between high housing prices and high waterlogging probability. Colocation analysis further reveals that emergency shelters exhibit stronger spatial overlap with high-income core areas than with low-income peripheral areas, creating a paradox: the high-income group is colocated with both higher waterlogging risk and better risk-mitigation facilities, such as emergency shelters, suggesting that such facilities may be capitalized into housing prices to a greater extent than flood risk, while the low-income group faces neither.These findings highlight the complexity of environmental risk justice in megacities.
summary: The paper tests whether lower-income neighborhoods in Chengdu face systematically higher urban waterlogging risk.

title: Dynamics of Airline Network Types using Multiplex Network Model: An Examination of the Alignment between Market Responses and Policy Objectives in China
authors: Yue Hu; Liang Dai; Frank Witlox
keywords: Airline classification; Aviation policy; China; Complex network; Network structures
abstract: Airline networks are highly shaped by regulatory environments, particularly in China where route access, airport capacity, and network development are subject to government intervention. However, existing studies have primarily focused on the network development patterns of major carriers, while the responses of other airlines operating under the same regulatory conditions remain insufficiently understood. Although airlines face similar policy constraints, they may adopt different network strategies due to differences in market positioning, operational capabilities, and competitive priorities. Identifying these network patterns provides a way to evaluate how regulatory environments shape heterogeneous market responses and whether airline behaviors align with policy objectives. Using data from the Official Aviation Guide’s Schedule Analyzer module (2009–2019), this study develops a multiplex network-based framework to classify airlines based on network characteristics and interactions. The temporal stability of these network structures is examined through longitudinal comparisons. The results reveal five relatively stable airline network types in China’s domestic aviation market: Mature, Hub-led, Direct-flight-led, Network-developing, and Fluid. Furthermore, by analyzing changes in market shares among different airline types at slot-controlled airports and on approved routes, we examine how airlines respond to regulatory constraints. The findings reveal a misalignment between airlines’ market responses and the intended regulatory objectives. This study highlights the value of a multiplex network perspective for understanding heterogeneous airline behaviors and provides implications for evaluating aviation policy effectiveness in China.
summary: Using a multiplex network model, the study examines whether the evolution of China's airline network types aligns with policy objectives.

title: Identifying Urban Centers and Modeling Nonlinear Housing Price Gradients in a Polycentric Metropolitan Region: Geographically Weighted Regression and Tree-Based Approaches in the Seoul Metropolitan Area
authors: Changhyo Yi; Seongho Kim; Byung-Hun Yun
keywords: Housing prices; Polycentric urban structure; Seoul metropolitan area; Spatial nonlinearity; Urban centrality
abstract: This study investigates the spatially nonlinear relationship between housing prices and urban centrality within the polycentric structure of the Seoul Metropolitan Area. Employing a hybrid analytical framework, we first identify multiple urban centers using kernel density estimation and spatial clustering techniques. Subsequently, we apply Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) and Tree-Based approaches (DTR/RF) to model the complex, location-specific association between distance to the centers and housing prices. The results reveal significant spatial heterogeneity and nonlinear distance-decay patterns, indicating that proximity to different urban centers is associated with housing prices in varied and complex ways. These findings underscore the limitations of traditional monocentric assumptions and emphasize the importance of considering polycentric urban structures and spatial nonlinearity in urban planning and housing policy development.
summary: The study identifies urban centers and models nonlinear housing price gradients in the polycentric Seoul Metropolitan Area using GWR and tree-based methods.

title: People and place research for people and place based policies: a study of professional well-being of alumni of North Kazakhstan with Generalized Q Analysis
authors: Tomaz Ponce Dentinho; Alnur Valiev; Maira Valieva; Altyn Iskakova; Dinmukhammed Shaikin
abstract: This study aimed to show why people and place-based policies should be grounded on people and place research, using Generalized Q Analysis, and shift the focus of the research from the features of observed entities on the study of entities associated with combined and evident features of people and places. For the present study "people and places" were recent alumni from the University of North Kazakhstan. The "people and place-based policies" were programs of English proficiency and international mobility provided by the University. The literature links regional development with human capital and professional wellbeing, as well as English proficiency and international mobility. First, to test this hypothesis we used a regression relating professional wellbeing of 1250 alumni with their places of origin, gender, marks, sector of employment, English proficiency and international mobility, but no major evidence was achieved. Then, to test people and places that have higher professional wellbeing, following a Generalized Q Analysis 1250 alumni from the University of North Kazakhstan were explained analyzed by 10 profiles. On the one hand, directly related with professional wellbeing and, on the other hand, clustered and related with professional wellbeing using differences and differences regression. Results indicated that people with English proficiency did not have higher professional well-being because English was not useful for existing follow-up studies and for more common employment. Alumni with professional wellbeing were male, self-employed, urban or rural that participated in student mobility activities most probably in a Russian speaking language environment. This clearer evidence justifies more attention to people and place-based approaches for people and place-based policies.
summary: Applying Generalized Q Analysis to 1,250 North Kazakhstan university alumni, the study finds English proficiency did not raise professional well-being, whereas male, self-employed alumni who took part in student mobility (likely in Russian-speaking settings) fared better.

title: Determinants of green production behavior among Bangladeshi farmers in an era of commercial agriculture
authors: Shovan Nasim Haider; Miloslava Chovancova
keywords: Green production behavior; Commercial agriculture; Sustainable agriculture practices; Farmers adoption
abstract: Transitions to sustainable agriculture demand a nuanced understanding of the psychological, normative and contextual factors driving farmer adoption of environmentally responsible practices. This study integrated the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), Value-Belief-Norm (VBN) theory, and Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory to examine the determinants of Green Production Behavior (GPB) among 424 farmers in northwestern Bangladesh, using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with multi-group analysis to account for regional heterogeneity. The findings revealed that Knowledge and Perceived Behavioral Control are the primary drivers of GPB, with Knowledge channeling its influence through Perceived Behavioral Control (PBC) and positive attitudes. Contrary to theoretical expectations, Environmental Beliefs, Personal Norms and Subjective Norm were non-significant predictors, suggesting that moral and social motivations are superseded by pragmatic capability assessments in contexts of economic precarity and rapid commercialization. Commercial Orientation exhibited a dual role: a direct negative effect on GPB, but a positive moderating effect on the intention-behavior relationship, indicating that commercially empowered farmers are more effective at executing sustainable intentions. Measurement Invariance of Composites (MICOM) analysis confirmed full compositional invariance. The Multi-Group Analysis (MGA) revealed regional differences: Knowledge had a stronger effect on Attitude in Rangpur (β = 0.501) than in Rajshahi (β = 0.247), though the difference was not statistically significant. These findings challenge the universal applicability of VBN theory in developing economy contexts and advocate for capacity-building interventions over awareness-raising campaigns. The results contribute to regional science by demonstrating that behavioral determinants of GPB are embedded within spatially structured processes of market integration and infrastructure development.
summary: A PLS-SEM study of 424 farmers in northwestern Bangladesh finds knowledge and perceived behavioral control, not environmental beliefs or norms, drive green production behavior, while commercial orientation lowers it directly but strengthens intention-to-behavior conversion.

title: Livelihood vulnerability of rice-cultivating households under climate variability in the Mekong Delta, Vietnam
authors: Anh Phuong Nguyen; Takeshi Mizunoya
abstract: Climate change has led to reduced yields, land loss and lower incomes among rice-cultivating households in the Mekong Delta (MD). However, large-scale, multi-year studies examining household vulnerability in this region remain limited. This study aimed to determine the vulnerability status of these households to climate stress between 2018 and 2022 and to evaluate the contributing factors. The adjusted livelihood vulnerability index (ALVI), which reflects recent advances in the understanding of climate change vulnerability, was used to assess vulnerability using data from the Vietnam Household Living Standards Survey for 2018, 2020 and 2022. The results showed that the ALVI of rice-cultivating households in the MD ranged from 0.412 to 0.422 between 2018 and 2022, indicating that these households were moderately vulnerable to the negative impacts of climate variability. The most vulnerable component was the natural component in 2018, which shifted to the financial component in 2022. Low crop diversity, substandard housing, low rice profitability, limited educational attainment among household heads, and insufficient institutional support were the main factors influencing the vulnerability of rice households in the MD. Additionally, rice-cultivating households in Ca Mau, Kien Giang and Ben Tre Provinces were the most vulnerable to climate variability, with ALVI ranging from 0.411 to 0.478 during the period 2018 to 2022. These findings provide valuable insights into climate vulnerability in the MD and imply targeted, issue-specific interventions for rice-farming households in the MD, particularly those in coastal areas. Such interventions can reduce vulnerability and provide a reference for policymakers developing effective adaptation strategies in the context of climate change.
summary: Using an adjusted livelihood vulnerability index on 2018–2022 household survey data, the study finds Mekong Delta rice households moderately vulnerable to climate variability, with vulnerability shifting from natural to financial components and highest in Ca Mau, Kien Giang and Ben Tre.

title: Working While Studying and Graduate Migration: New Evidence Accounting for Multinomial Endogenous Treatment
authors: Elena Del Rey; Jorge González Chapela
keywords: Graduate migration; Pre-graduation jobs; Endogenous treatment
abstract: Previous studies have generally found that working while in college reduces the out-migration of graduates, with the extent of this reduction depending on the type of work experience. We evaluate the extent to which these findings are causal by assessing their robustness to controls for individual-specific unobserved heterogeneity. An existing methodology that accommodates multinomial endogenous treatment and exploits a measure of employment potential at the student's place of residence as an instrumental variable is applied to a large sample of graduates from the region of Catalonia, Spain. Our estimates suggest an impact of working while studying that is larger in magnitude, and in one case of the opposite sign, than estimates developed assuming exogeneity of pre-graduation work activities.
summary: Accounting for multinomial endogenous treatment with an instrumental-variable approach on Catalan graduates, the study finds effects of working while studying on graduate out-migration that are larger than, and in one case opposite in sign to, estimates assuming exogeneity.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Zipf's law on international temperatures
authors: Laura Hipólito; Guillermo Peña
keywords: Zipf; Eeckhout; Temperatures; Heating
abstract: Global warming and the increased frequency of high-temperature episodes have not only heightened interest in understanding average temperatures but also reinforced interest in how temperature distributions are changing. This study examines the evolution of global temperature distributions by country from 1960 to 2021, using reference years for each two decades to make various comparisons. A key focus is the adherence to Zipf's law in the upper portion of the distribution: Zipf's law holds true when, upon ordering countries from most to least extreme temperatures, the drop between ranges follows a very regular pattern. The aim is to determine in which ranges Zipf's law appears and how the exponent changes as the sample size increases. Finally, the study tests Eeckhout's hypothesis, which posits a reduction in the coefficient when the sample size is increased under specific conditions. The results are conclusive: the more extreme the weather, the higher productivity, electricity consumption, health, and tourism activity the country will benefit.
summary: Examining country temperature distributions from 1960 to 2021, the study tests where Zipf's law holds in the upper tail and how the exponent changes with sample size, including a test of Eeckhout's hypothesis.

journal: Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences
title: Fractal dimension complexity of gravitational fractals based on hexagonal and square lattices: Christaller and Lösch revisited
authors: Michał Banaszak; Krzysztof Górnisiewicz; Peter Nijkamp; Waldemar Ratajczak
keywords: Christaller; Lösch; Central place theory; Regular hexagonal and square lattices; Fractal dimension; Gravitational modeling; Space resistance; Transport costs; Gravitational attraction basins
abstract: The central place theory (CPT) formulated by Walter Christaller in 1933 and in the same spirit by Lösch was widely introduced into the economic geography literature in the 1950s. CPT has become one of the leading theoretical frameworks describing the spatial order of settlements in the space-economy, and consequently, the geographical differentiation and specialization of economies in various regions and countries. In a geometric sense, CPT is essentially based on a comparative study of three types of regular network configurations that completely cover a plane, i.e., hexagonal, square, and equilateral triangle networks. This paper examines spatial interaction patterns between central places using a dynamic gravitational model applied to square and hexagonal lattices. The study focuses on the formation of attraction basins and their geometric properties, which are analyzed through numerical simulations and visualized as color maps. The model represents spatial interactions as movements of agents in a potential field generated by central places, with transport costs expressed through a spatial resistance parameter. The results show that, for low spatial resistance, the system exhibits irregular and fractal-like structures, reflecting complex and highly sensitive spatial interactions. As spatial resistance increases, these patterns gradually converge toward regular geometric configurations consistent with central place theory. A comparative analysis demonstrates that neither square nor hexagonal lattices exhibit a systematic advantage in terms of attraction basin size. Instead, the spatial structure is primarily determined by the level of transport costs and the relative importance of individual centers. The findings are further illustrated using empirical examples from real-world city networks in the United States. These examples confirm that actual spatial interaction patterns deviate from ideal geometric forms and are shaped by heterogeneous spatial conditions. The study contributes to the understanding of spatial structure by providing a reproducible modeling framework that links geometric theory, dynamic processes, and empirical observations.
summary: A dynamic gravitational model on square and hexagonal lattices shows attraction basins are fractal-like at low spatial resistance and converge to regular central-place patterns as transport costs rise, with neither lattice systematically advantaged.

title: Integrating spatial lag and heterogeneity into double machine learning
authors: Yichuan Tian
keywords: Causal machine learning; Spatial econometrics; Two-stage estimator; Double machine learning
abstract: Micro-level spatial empirical research has long faced the dual challenges of nonlinear confounding and spatial non-stationarity. To address this dilemma, this study innovatively proposes a spatial double machine learning (SDML) framework. The first-stage estimator of this framework employs tree-based models to orthogonalize confounding factors and their spatial lag terms, upon which the second-stage multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) modeling is conducted to obtain local direct effect (LDE) and local spillover effect (LSE). Simulation experiments demonstrate that SDML achieves the best overall performance compared with baseline models, and exhibits strong robustness against interference. Furthermore, applying the framework to a micro-level dataset from Hong Kong's short-term rental market reveals that SDML achieves both superior predictive performance and estimation stability, while further corroborating the role of neighborhood interference mechanisms in property pricing. In conclusion, the present study contributes a fresh perspective on unifying spatial econometrics, causal inference, and machine learning.
summary: A spatial double machine learning framework combining tree-based orthogonalization with MGWR recovers local direct and spillover effects, outperforming baselines in simulations and in an application to Hong Kong short-term rental pricing.

title: Agricultural drone use, pesticide reduction, and biodiversity restoration: evidence from China
authors: Jianjun Tang; Jingru Chen; Jingyang Yan; Fei Li
keywords: Agricultural drones; Precision agriculture; Biodiversity; Environmental sustainability; Technological progress
abstract: Recent advances in smart agriculture offer a promising pathway to reconcile production efficiency with environmental sustainability, yet their ecological effects remain insufficiently understood at large-scale. This paper examines the impact of agricultural drone use on biodiversity in China using a prefecture-level panel from 2018 to 2023. By constructing a rich dataset composed of micro-level subsidy records for drone purchase, remote sensing data, and citizen science bird observations, we find that drone use significantly increases both biological abundance and species richness. A one-standard-deviation increase in agricultural drone density raises biological abundance by 19.7% and species richness by 9.4%. Mechanism analysis shows that drones improve biodiversity through a pesticide-reduction channel, which reduces pesticide use by 1.11 kg/ha (7.6% of the mean). Heterogeneity analyses show that the biodiversity gains are concentrated among bird groups whose habitats and diets are closely tied to farmland ecosystems and are more evident in southeastern China, while the effects remain limited for rare and environmentally sensitive species, like China-endemic birds. We find no evidence of cross-prefecture spillover effects. These findings provide the first macro-level evidence that agricultural drones generate biodiversity restoration effects through pesticide reduction, supporting the role of directed technological change in reconciling agricultural modernization with biodiversity restoration.
summary: A prefecture-level panel for China (2018–2023) shows a one-SD rise in agricultural drone density raises bird abundance by 19.7% and species richness by 9.4%, operating through reduced pesticide use.

title: Continuous multi-facility location problem with inter-facility separation and obstacle-constrained overlapping service coverage
authors: Bikram Parajuli; Xin Feng
keywords: GIS; Spatial optimization; Location analysis; Mobile radar deployment
abstract: Observation-based sensor deployment problems require facility configurations to satisfy geometric, topographic, and redundancy constraints in addition to the coverage objectives that directly influence the quality of the observations. In many real-world monitoring systems, effective service areas are shaped by terrain-constrained visibility, distance-dependent signal attenuation, overlapping coverage requirements, and separation between facilities. These characteristics are not explicitly considered in widely used continuous maximal covering formulations, which commonly assume simplified circular service regions, homogeneous demand distribution, and uniform coverage strength. This study develops the Obstacle- and Geometry-Constrained Continuous Coverage Model (OG-CCM), an extension of the continuous maximal coverage problem that incorporates distance-decay coverage attenuation, obstacle-constrained visibility, redundant coverage requirements, admissible beam intersection geometry, and inter-facility separation constraints within a unified optimization framework. The proposed model is solved using heuristic methods based on swarm and evolutionary intelligence, and we demonstrate the applicability of the proposed model through a case study on optimizing dual-Doppler mobile radar configuration to observe severe weather events in Central Oklahoma. The results demonstrate that the proposed model effectively captures coverage attenuation, redundant coverage requirements, geometric constraints, and topography-dependent service areas within a unified optimization framework. By doing so, it provides a flexible and robust methodology for sensor facility deployment planning where conventional models fall short, enabling more reliable and operationally feasible deployment decisions.
summary: The paper develops an obstacle- and geometry-constrained continuous coverage model with distance decay, redundancy and separation constraints, demonstrated by optimizing dual-Doppler mobile radar deployment for severe weather in Central Oklahoma.

title: Interregional spillovers in European science: a spatial Durbin approach
authors: David Emanuel Andersson; Mofei Jia; Casto Martín Montero Kuscevic
keywords: NUTS2 region; Web of science; Spatial Durbin model; Science output; Geographical proximity; Spatial spillovers
abstract: The science output of a region may depend on various intraregional and interregional factors. A Spatial Durbin Model was used to estimate the impacts of regional factors as well as spillovers from other regions on science output in European NUTS2 regions. Three different weightings of interregional impact were tested to capture geographical proximity: the inverse distance, the inverse distance squared, and a binary distance-threshold specification that excluded distant regions. The main findings are that research and development (R&D) employment in higher education institutions in the region and in surrounding regions has a positive impact on science output, while R&D employment in high-tech industries in the region has a negative impact. There are also intraregional and interregional effects of disciplinary specialization, with less specialized regions exhibiting higher science output. Regions with older universities exhibit higher within-region scientific output, although the total spatial effect of university age is not statistically robust once spillovers are accounted for.
summary: A spatial Durbin model of European NUTS2 regions finds higher-education R&D employment at home and in neighboring regions raises science output, while local high-tech industry R&D employment and disciplinary specialization lower it.

title: Export diversification in agriculture: products, partners, and structural change in developing economies
authors: Abu Bakkar Siddique; J. P. Singh
abstract: This study investigates whether diversification of agricultural products and export partners contributes to the growth of agricultural trade in developing countries. Despite historically facing restrictive trade policies, such as quota-based preferences under the Generalized System of Preferences, many developing economies have experienced substantial growth in agricultural exports over the past five decades. Using a panel dataset of 64 low- and lower-middle-income countries from 1990 to 2018, the study employs two-way fixed-effects models to estimate the relationship between export diversification and agricultural trade. The analysis leverages data from the UN Comtrade and World Integrated Trade Solution databases, using both product-level and partner-level diversification metrics. The findings indicate that a 1% increase in agricultural product lines is associated with a 0.50% increase in exports, while a 1% increase in export partners leads to a 0.29% increase. These results are robust across different model specifications and control for various variables. Case studies from South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa further illustrate the benefits and challenges of diversification strategies. The study concludes that expanding both product and partner diversity, especially through extensive margins, is a critical driver of export growth and offers valuable policy insights for sustainable agricultural development in the Global South.
summary: Across 64 low- and lower-middle-income countries (1990–2018), a 1% rise in agricultural product lines is associated with 0.50% higher agricultural exports and a 1% rise in export partners with 0.29% higher exports.

title: Revealing overlooked strategic sectors in Oman: a network centrality approach beyond Leontief multipliers toward vision 2040 goals
authors: Behnaz Saboori; Ali Faridzad
abstract: Economic diversification remains a major challenge for hydrocarbon-dependent economies, where identifying sectors with systemic influence is essential for achieving sustainable structural transformation. In Oman, existing input–output studies have primarily relied on Leontief multipliers and traditional backward and forward linkage measures, which may overlook sectors that play critical roles within the broader production network. This study advances input–output network analysis by integrating conventional linkage indicators with network centrality approaches to identify structurally influential sectors relevant to Oman Vision 2040 diversification objectives. Using the latest available Oman input–output table, the study applies backward and forward linkage analysis, along with PageRank and random walk centrality algorithms, to evaluate sectoral importance from both multiplier-based and network-based perspectives. The results demonstrate that Oman's economic structure remains strongly hydrocarbon-centered, with oil and gas-related activities consistently ranking among the most influential sectors. However, network centrality analysis reveals that public administration, defense, and construction possess substantial systemic importance despite relatively limited traditional linkage effects, indicating that their strategic roles are underestimated by conventional multiplier approaches. Conversely, several non-oil sectors, including fisheries and social services, exhibit weak network integration, highlighting structural vulnerabilities in the diversification process. Robustness tests confirm the stability of the identified key sectors under alternative model specifications. The findings suggest that effective diversification strategies should consider production network positions and sectoral centrality, rather than relying exclusively on direct and indirect output multipliers, to strengthen economic resilience and support Oman Vision 2040 goals.
summary: Combining input–output linkages with PageRank and random-walk centrality, the study finds Oman's economy remains hydrocarbon-centered but that public administration, defense and construction are systemically important sectors underestimated by Leontief multipliers.

title: Asymmetric decentralization: nature and determinants
authors: Santiago Lago-Peñas; María Cadaval-Sampedro; Jorge Martínez-Vázquez; Ana Herrero-Alcalde
abstract: Over the last five decades, decentralization has been a central feature of governance reforms. However, its implementation rarely follows a symmetrical pattern across subnational units. Instead, asymmetric decentralization has become prevalent in both federal and unitary states. Nevertheless, the empirical determinants of asymmetric decentralization remain insufficiently explored. This paper tries to fill this gap offering a systematic analysis of the nature and determinants of asymmetric decentralization across a large cross section of countries and regions using data from the Regional Authority Index (RAI). The empirical analysis combines cross-country and cross-regional models estimated using ordinary least squares (OLS) and robust least squares (RLS). At the country level, ethnic fragmentation, population size, and territorial characteristics are associated with higher levels of asymmetry. At the regional level, a greater distance from the national capital and the presence of distinct linguistic identities are linked to above-average regional authority. The analysis of changes over time indicates that transitions to democracy act as a catalyst, activating structural conditions and fostering increases in interregional asymmetry.
summary: Using Regional Authority Index data, the paper finds asymmetric decentralization is associated with ethnic fragmentation, population size and territorial features at country level, and with distance from the capital and distinct linguistic identity at regional level, with democratic transitions acting as a catalyst.

title: Functional specialization and upgrading along global value chains in European regions: new insights from FDI data
authors: Andrea Coveri; Elena Paglialunga; Antonello Zanfei
abstract: The geographic dispersion of production activities has led regions to increasingly specialize in distinct value chain functions, giving rise to a finer spatial division of labour. Using georeferenced FDI data on cross-border investments distinguished by value chain function, we provide the first systematic mapping of functional specialization across European NUTS-2 regions over the period 2003–2018. We show that the most intangible-intensive functions at the upper ends of value chains are concentrated in a small number of advanced regions, while lower-income ones are largely and persistently engaged in production operations. We document the strong spatial persistence of functional specialization before and after the 2008 crisis and find that regions trapped in production functions are the least likely to upgrade towards more knowledge-intensive industries. By contrast, only the few regions which experienced functional upgrading trajectories have been able to diversify towards more innovative industries, revealing a close interdependence between functional and inter-sectoral upgrading. Accordingly, regional policies should aim at favouring functional upgrading of laggard regions as a key vehicle for economic and spatial convergence in Europe.
summary: Mapping value-chain functions of FDI across European NUTS-2 regions (2003–2018), the study finds high-value functions concentrated in a few advanced regions, with regions trapped in production functions least likely to upgrade into knowledge-intensive industries.

title: Flood risk information, housing markets, and spatial inequality
authors: Allan Beltran; Karlygash Kuralbayeva; Eileen Tipoe
abstract: This article examines how housing markets respond to nearby floods that do not directly damage properties, and whether these responses differ across more- and less-deprived neighbourhoods in England between 2010 and 2018. Nearby floods increase time-on-market everywhere, but price effects vary systematically by deprivation: in more-deprived areas, prices fall, consistent with risk-related price revaluation and weaker seller bargaining power, while in less-deprived areas prices remain broadly stable. The implied short-run risk-information discounts are about 3.8 per cent in more-deprived neighbourhoods and 1.2 per cent in less-deprived ones, summarizing how flood-related risk information is capitalized jointly into prices and selling times.
summary: Nearby non-damaging floods in England lengthen time-on-market everywhere but cut house prices only in more-deprived neighbourhoods (about 3.8% vs 1.2% discounts), revealing unequal capitalization of flood-risk information.

title: Decentralization, ethnic fractionalization, and public services: evidence from Kenyan healthcare
authors: Camille Hémet; Liam Wren-Lewis; Jessica Mahoney
abstract: This article examines the impact of ethnic fractionalization on public service use by exploiting a major constitutional reform in Kenya. Following an important period of inter-ethnic conflict, responsibility for local health services was decentralized to forty-seven newly created county governments across the country. Crucially, this changed the ethnic composition of the administrative area responsible for healthcare, while leaving the composition of the local population unchanged. Using an event-study design, we find that the use of public clinics for births increased significantly more in counties that were relatively ethnically homogeneous after the reform. We also find a significant increase in the correlation between county ethnic fractionalization and a range of other measures of public health service use. Using within-county variation to investigate mechanisms, we find healthcare use increases were concentrated among individuals of the same ethnicity as members of the new county government executives. Overall, the results suggest that more ethnically homogeneous subnational jurisdictions can lead to more public service use relative to more fractionalized ones.
summary: Exploiting Kenya's health decentralization to new counties, the paper finds public clinic use rose more in ethnically homogeneous counties, concentrated among co-ethnics of county executives.

title: Planetary boundaries as spatial constraints: rethinking regional development under ecological limits
authors: Xuefeng Hu
abstract: Economic geography has increasingly engaged with environmental change, yet ecological limits are rarely treated as binding constraints on regional development. This article argues that planetary boundaries remain underexplored in economic geography and reframes them as spatially differentiated constraints that define region-specific ecological feasibility. This perspective shows how non-linear limits, uneven exposure, and burden shifting reshape development trajectories, challenge assumptions of convergence, and generate new forms of regional inequality and spatial conflict. It also outlines an agenda for research on feasibility and governance in the Anthropocene.
summary: The article reframes planetary boundaries as spatially differentiated constraints on regional development and sets out a research agenda on ecological feasibility, inequality and governance.

title: Trade diversification and food price volatility
summary: The paper develops a framework to study how diversification of international agri-food trade relates to food price volatility, motivated by recent shortages and value-chain vulnerabilities.

title: Breeding delays determine the wavelength of the pork cycle
summary: Using a system dynamics model, the paper argues that breeding delays determine the three-to-six-year wavelength of the pork cycle's price and production oscillations.

title: Design of Mass Transit System and Compact City
authors: Se‐il Mun; Yuma Murakami; Asato Taguchi
abstract: We incorporate the key design variables of mass transit—the number of stations, the length of a transit line, and the number of transit lines—into a monocentric city model of urban land use. We demonstrate that increasing the number of stations (i.e., reducing the spacing between them) promotes higher population density, leading to a more compact urban form. Conversely, extending transit lines further into the suburbs encourages urban dispersion. We examine two approaches to endogenizing transit designs: maximizing profit from transit operations and maximizing social welfare. It is shown that the number of stations chosen under a profit‐maximizing design is smaller than that under a social welfare‐maximizing design. We extend the analysis by modeling the city as a system of corridors, distinguishing between transit corridors and auto corridors. The development of the transit system is represented as the conversion of auto corridors into transit corridors. Using numerical simulations calibrated with parameter values reflecting real‐world Japanese cities, our results indicate that the development of mass transit system can contribute to a more compact urban structure. This effect is driven mainly by the relocation of residents from auto corridors to transit corridors.
summary: In a monocentric city model calibrated to Japanese cities, more closely spaced transit stations densify cities while longer lines promote sprawl, and profit-maximizing operators choose fewer stations than is socially optimal.

title: Peer Effects on Climate Change Beliefs
authors: Xialing Zhao; Linlin Fan; Yilan Xu
abstract: Understanding how climate change beliefs are shaped by peer networks is critical for designing effective climate communication strategies, yet the degree of peer influence across spatial and political contexts remains insufficiently understood. This study examines the influence of peer counties on local climate change beliefs using a generalized spatial autoregressive (GSAR) model. We construct geographic, political, and economic peer networks at the county level and quantify the magnitude of peer effects. Results show that a 10% increase in climate change beliefs among peer counties is associated with a 4.2% to 9.4% increase in average beliefs within the focal county, depending on the network type. The geographic peer network exerts the strongest influence, with estimated effects ranging from 6.7% to 9.4%, followed by the political network, with effects between 4.2% and 7.5%, for different climate beliefs. Counterfactual simulations show that targeting interventions to the most connected counties (MCCs)—those occupying central positions in the network—is more effective than focusing on counties with extreme belief levels or on MCCs with below‐average beliefs. Targeting low‐belief counties yields the largest relative improvements among the most vulnerable groups, whereas targeting top MCCs maximizes aggregate impact without disproportionately disadvantaging low‐belief counties in percentage terms. These findings provide actionable insights for policymakers seeking to promote climate belief formation and encourage climate‐friendly behaviors through network‐informed interventions.
summary: County-level spatial autoregressive estimates show climate beliefs spill over from peer counties (4.2–9.4% per 10% increase), strongest through geographic networks, so targeting the most connected counties maximizes aggregate impact.

title: Graduate Migration and Job Quality: Evidence From Five Cohorts of UK Graduate Outcomes Data
authors: Sean Brophy
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between graduate employment migration and subjective job quality in the UK, using five cohorts of Higher Education Statistics Agency Graduate Outcomes microdata covering the 2018/19 to 2022/23 cohorts. Graduates are classified using a five‐way typology: Stayers (never leave the home region), Late Migrants (study in the home region but migrate for employment), Returners (migrate for study but return home for employment), Migrants (migrate for study and remain in the university city for employment), and Repeat Migrants (migrate at both stages). The primary outcome is a composite job quality index, with log annual salary as a comparison outcome. Estimation uses high‐dimensional institution‐by‐subject fixed effects. Spatial mobility at the employment stage is robustly associated with higher subjective job quality, and this association scales monotonically with the distance traveled, with long‐distance movers reporting larger premia and long‐distance Returners facing larger penalties. Late Migrants and Repeat Migrants report composite scores around 0.14 standard deviations above Stayers and salary premia of 6%–8%. Returners report significantly lower composite job quality than Stayers despite statistically indistinguishable salaries. The pattern is not driven by London and, as Oster (2019) bounds indicate, is unlikely to reflect unobservable selection. Migration premia are systematically larger for men and vary across the four UK nations. The findings are interpreted within a spatial job search framework that distinguishes the price paid for generic graduate human capital and credentials, reflected in wages, from the variety of graduate‐level role matches available locally, reflected in job quality.
summary: UK graduates who move regions for employment report higher job quality (about 0.14 SD) and 6–8% salary premia, rising with distance, while returners to their home region report lower job quality despite similar pay.

title: Infrastructure Shocks and Regional Resilience: Evidence From the 2012 Cologne‐Leverkusen Bridge Closure
authors: Jeffrey P. Cohen; Carolin Hoeltken; Yuchen Huang
abstract: The unexpected 2012 closure of a key bridge on the Rhine River near Cologne, Germany was an exogenous shock to businesses and residents nearby. We exploit this event as a quasi‐experiment to study the impact of this critical infrastructure shock on the region. We propose a basic conceptual framework where the bridge closure significantly reduced accessibility discontinuously for one side of the bridge, raising transportation costs. Local economic agents adapted via different mechanisms: real asset prices fell gradually and proportionally to the loss in accessibility, and firms decided to move‐out in cases where the loss in accessibility outweighed the fixed cost of relocation. We then estimate the implications of this framework empirically. We show that the bridge closure reduced the market potential of locations on the left side of the Rhine by 10%–15%. Relying on a difference‐in‐differences estimation approach, we then find that firm move‐outs rose by over 40% on the left side of the Rhine River after the closure. Move‐outs were directed toward their ideal destination out of the region (many of which ended up in Berlin), rather than moving locally. We further show that commercial rental prices fell by around 13%–15% and home prices fell by 8%–14% after the closure on the left side of the river, with the impact attenuating further from the bridge. Overall, our analysis demonstrates the impact of a shock to critical infrastructure on regional resilience and explores the different mechanisms by which it occurred, shedding light on the magnitude, duration, and continuity of the impacts on different sectors.
summary: The 2012 Leverkusen bridge closure cut market potential on the Rhine's left bank by 10–15%, raising firm move-outs by over 40% and lowering commercial rents by 13–15% and home prices by 8–14%.

title: Herd Effects in United States Internal Migration: Complementary Emulation Mechanisms Across Distance and Educational Attainment
authors: Shih‐Keng Yen; Ernesto F. L. Amaral
abstract: Internal migration in the United States is highly structured, concentrating into persistent corridors that link specific origins and destinations. While earlier studies have focused on social networks and push‐pull factors, less is known about how individuals emulate migration choices across regions. This study decomposes herd effects into two mechanisms: same‐destination emulation, in which people follow a pinpoint signal based on flows from adjacent origins to a specific destination, and nearby‐destination emulation, in which people follow a diffuse regional cue based on flows to the general area around a destination. Using migration data from 996 MIGPUMAs in the 2024 American Community Survey, along with lagged flows from 2016 to 2020, this study estimates spatial interaction models with two‐way fixed effects. The results show a complementary structure: nearby‐destination emulation is stronger in short‐distance moves, while same‐destination emulation becomes more important as distance increases, suggesting migrants rely more on pinpoint signals when uncertainty is greater. The moderating effect of distance on same‐destination emulation is more pronounced for migrants without a university education, but the difference is only marginally significant. Overall, the findings suggest that spatial dependence structures interregional migration, in which geographically embedded information diffusion creates and maintains migration corridors. By separating these emulation mechanisms, this study improves the modeling of interregional mobility and contributes to regional science research.
summary: Using 2024 ACS migration flows, the study finds US migrants emulate diffuse regional cues for short moves but follow specific-destination signals for longer moves, helping sustain persistent migration corridors.

title: Flash Floods, Business Adjustment, and Ripple Effects on Displaced Workers
authors: Pedro Jorge Alves; Philipp Ehrl; Ricardo Carvalho de Andrade Lima
abstract: This paper examines how an extreme weather event affects the establishments and workers in the affected region, using the devastating 2008 Santa Catarina Flash Flood in Brazil as a natural experiment. We combine synthetic‐aperture radar images, which show the exact location of flood spots, with geocoded matched employer‐employee data to estimate the impact of the disaster using a difference‐in‐differences approach. Treatment and control areas are defined using an inner‐and‐outer‐ring approach based on distance from the mapped flood spots. We find that affected establishments are more likely to close, while detecting no statistically significant change in spatial relocation. We then examine the ripple effects of these disaster‐induced closures on displaced workers. We find that displaced workers are less likely to remain formally employed after the shock, with the adverse employment effects concentrated among low‐skilled workers. Both effects persist over the analyzed 5‐ to 9‐ year post‐disaster period.
summary: Brazil's 2008 Santa Catarina flash flood raised establishment closures without inducing relocation, and displaced—especially low-skilled—workers were persistently less likely to stay formally employed.

title: NextGenerationEU Landing: Assessing the Territorial Allocation of Italy's Recovery and Resilience Facility Funding
authors: Francesco Scotti; Carlo Caporali; Davide Luca
abstract: In response to the COVID‐19 crisis, the European Union introduced NextGenerationEU, its largest stimulus package to date. We focus on Italy, the program's largest beneficiary, and analyse the territorial distribution of funds. Although centrally coordinated, most expenditures were awarded through calls and implemented by local governments. Using a sample of approximately 4500 Italian municipalities for which administrative‐efficiency measures can be constructed, we estimate a two‐stage Heckman selection model to distinguish between realized access to funding and award intensity conditional on participation. Results show that funds are disproportionately allocated to Southern, relatively poorer urban municipalities with stronger administrative capacity and prior experience with EU Cohesion Policy. We then test if, across different policy areas, funds were targeted following specialization or convergence logics. We find that, across some of the key policy areas, such as digital, education and healthcare, the allocation is reinforcing existing spatial specialization, as opposed to targeting "lagging behind" territories. Finally, we uncover how administrative efficiency and stronger local governance are significant predictors of reduced project delays, while we do not find a significant North‐South divide here. Taken together, these findings highlight key allocative trade‐offs and the uneven administrative capacity of territories expected to implement the program.
summary: Italy's NextGenerationEU funds flowed disproportionately to poorer Southern urban municipalities with strong administrative capacity, but in digital, education and health they reinforced existing specialization rather than targeting lagging areas.

title: Autonomous Vehicles, Urban Deployment, and Welfare Effects
authors: Zhi‐Chun Li; Wen‐Jing Liu; André de Palma; Yuki Takayama; Takao Dantsuji
abstract: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of the effects of autonomous vehicles (AVs) on the spatial structures of future cities. We consider two types of AVs, private AVs (PAVs) and shared AVs (SAVs). We assume that AVs have a lower marginal travel time cost than human‐driven traditional vehicles (TVs) due to additional utility caused by free activities in AVs, and PAVs have a lower marginal travel time cost than SAVs due to better privacy, convenience, and comfort. Two urban spatial models are presented and compared: one focusing on a city with only TVs and the other on a city with mixed PAVs and SAVs. Both models account for land competition among firm production, household residence, and parking. The optimal residential lot size and the optimal SAV market share are determined, with an objective of maximizing social welfare. The findings show that introducing AVs may lead the city size to expand or shrink, and both the social welfare and the total congestion cost to increase or decrease, depending on the maturity degree of AV technology and the SAV market share.
summary: A spatial urban model with private and shared autonomous vehicles shows AVs can expand or shrink cities and raise or lower welfare and congestion depending on technology maturity and shared-AV market share.

title: Graduate Labor Market Opportunities Across Chinese Cities: Urban Opportunity Regimes and Their Dynamics
authors: Yuanyuan Xie; Baoding Wang
abstract: This study examines how advertised graduate‐oriented entry‐level opportunity sets are unevenly organized across Chinese cities and how urban opportunity regimes evolve over time. Existing research on labor market entry and interurban differentiation rarely conceptualizes entry‐level opportunities as multidimensional city‐level configurations. Using online recruitment data on graduate‐oriented job postings for 200 Chinese cities from 2016 to 2024, this study combines inequality measures, Gaussian mixture models, and Markov‐based transition analysis to examine the scale, quality, and structure of entry‐level opportunities. The results show substantial interurban inequality. Inequality in opportunity scale and structure declined over time, whereas opportunity quality remained the most unequal dimension and displayed the strongest spatial clustering. Four urban opportunity regimes are identified: a Scale‐led regime, an Intermediate regime, a High‐quality, high‐structure regime, and a Moderate‐quality, lower‐structure regime. The Scale‐led regime is the most persistent, whereas the High‐quality, high‐structure regime remains the least persistent in the high‐posterior comparison, although the estimated magnitude of its persistence is sensitive to classification confidence. These findings show that a less concentrated observed distribution of online postings does not by itself imply a comparable equalization in the housing‐cost‐adjusted quality of advertised graduate‐oriented opportunities.
summary: Online graduate job postings across 200 Chinese cities (2016–2024) show declining inequality in opportunity scale and structure but persistent, spatially clustered inequality in housing-cost-adjusted opportunity quality, organized into four urban regimes.

title: Spatiotemporal Evolution and Nonlinear Associations of Digital Enterprise Agglomeration in China: An XGBoost‐SHAP Approach
authors: Yangyang Yang; Yong Zhou
abstract: Based on micro‐level data for nearly five million firms, this study measures the spatial agglomeration of digital firms in 297 Chinese cities from 2000 to 2023 using the DO. GIS‐based spatial analysis and an XGBoost‐SHAP machine learning model are then used to examine its spatiotemporal evolution and associated factors. The results show that digital firm agglomeration in China increased over the study period. The agglomeration scale is 15–35 km. The spatial pattern shifted from point‐based clustering in a few southeastern coastal cities to a multi‐core agglomeration structure. Digital inclusive finance, university supply, and research and development human capital are identified as the core factors associated with digital firm agglomeration. When university supply exceeds 13.51, the interaction effect of digital inclusive finance becomes positive. When the number of research and development personnel exceeds 128,136, its positive effect increases substantially. The heterogeneity results show clear regional differences. Eastern China depends on digital inclusive finance and university supply, whereas central China depends mainly on digital inclusive finance. Western China is more strongly affected by basic urban conditions, such as the level of economic development. Higher‐tier cities depend on innovation resources, whereas lower‐tier cities rely more on digital inclusive finance. Different types of digital firms are influenced by knowledge and talent resources, user bases, and digital inclusive finance, respectively. This study provides empirical evidence for optimizing the spatial layout of digital industries and formulating differentiated policies.
summary: Firm microdata for 297 Chinese cities show digital-firm agglomeration rising and shifting to a multi-core pattern at a 15–35 km scale, driven nonlinearly by digital inclusive finance, university supply and R&D human capital.

title: From University to Work: Graduate Migration Across Urban Hierarchy and the Roles of Economic Opportunities and Urban Amenities
authors: Xiaozhen Qin; Jianfu Shen; Eddie Chi‐Man Hui; Menglan Liu
abstract: Graduate migration plays a key role in the spatial reallocation of human capital, yet little is known about how graduate migration mechanisms differ across directions within a hierarchical urban system. Using LinkedIn resume data, this study classifies intercity graduate migration in China into upward, lateral, and downward modes and examines the economic opportunities and urban amenities associated with each migration trajectory. We show that three migration modes exhibit distinct spatial patterns, with upward migration towards first‐tier and new first‐tier cities dominating national flows and downward migration occurring mainly between higher‐ and lower‐tier cities within regions. Over time, new first‐tier cities have become increasingly important destinations for graduates. Empirical results indicate that graduate migration is jointly associated with economic opportunities and urban amenities in both origin and destination cities. The temporal analysis shows that wages, climatic conditions, and healthcare provision in destination cities have become increasingly important over time. Migration mechanisms also differ across the urban hierarchy: upward migration is primarily associated with destination economic opportunities, whereas downward migration is associated with both push factors from higher‐tier origin cities and pull factors from improving opportunities and living conditions in lower‐tier destinations. These relationships further vary across human capital groups, while talent‐attraction policies are associated with shifts in graduates' responses to destination characteristics. By extending the traditional push‐pull framework to incorporate urban hierarchy, human capital heterogeneity, and institutional context, this study provides a more nuanced understanding of the factors associated with intercity graduate mobility.
summary: LinkedIn resume data show Chinese graduates' upward migration is driven mainly by destination opportunities, while downward moves combine push factors from top-tier cities and improving conditions in lower-tier ones.

title: Social Capital or Financial Burden? Ritual Gift Expenditure and Income Growth in Rural China
authors: Tieqiang Li; Yao Zhang; Qiqi Huang; Yizhu Li
abstract: In rural China, ritual gift expenditure is often viewed as expressive consumption, a ritual obligation, or a financial burden embedded in renqing relations. Its possible role as social‐capital investment, however, remains less understood. Using an unbalanced panel from the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022 waves of the China Family Panel Studies, this paper examines the association between ritual gift expenditure and rural household income. We estimate household and year fixed‐effects models and use mechanism tests to explore possible pathways. The results show a statistically significant positive association. This association remains robust to alternative variable definitions, sample adjustments, and supplementary analyses that partially address endogeneity concerns. Mechanism results provide suggestive evidence for pathways through liquidity buffers, entrepreneurship, non‐farm employment, and productive fixed assets. The association is weaker among households with Internet use, consistent with the possibility that digital access reduces reliance on traditional renqing networks. Subsample analyses indicate broadly stable associations, with somewhat larger point estimates among older, low‐income, and western households. The findings offer policy implications for rural social‐capital governance and income support under China's rural revitalization strategy.
summary: CFPS panel data show ritual gift spending is positively associated with rural Chinese household income, via liquidity, entrepreneurship and non-farm work channels, with weaker links among Internet-using households.

title: AI‐Related Hiring Expansion and Within‐City Occupational Demand Reallocation in China: Evidence From Listed‐Firm Job Postings
authors: Zhaoming Sun; Yawen Zhai; Xianghui Tian
abstract: AI‐related hiring demand is unevenly distributed across urban labor markets. Using online job‐posting data from Chinese listed firms between 2016 and 2024, this study constructs a city–occupation–year panel and examines whether expanding AI‐related hiring demand is associated with differences in the structure of occupational hiring demand within cities. The results show that: (1) higher city‐level AI‐related hiring demand is significantly associated with greater relative hiring demand for occupations that are more closely related to AI. This finding indicates that AI‐related opportunities are not evenly distributed across occupations; instead, hiring demand is selectively concentrated in occupations with stronger links to AI. The result remains robust across a series of robustness checks; (2) AI‐related hiring expansion is associated with stronger hiring demand for digitally complementary occupations and a larger share of AI‐related vacancies within occupations; and (3) these associations are more pronounced in cities with greater higher‐education capacity and more developed innovation ecosystems. This study extends the literature on AI and the structure of urban labor demand and provides recruitment‐based evidence relevant to cities seeking to improve talent‐development systems, strengthen their innovation environments, and address the growing divergence in occupational demand associated with AI.
summary: Job postings from Chinese listed firms show city-level AI hiring expansion shifts demand toward AI-related and digitally complementary occupations, especially in cities with strong higher-education and innovation ecosystems.

title: Ontario and Mexico in North America's Automotive Production Network: A Subnational Test of Stratified Regional Integration
authors: Carlos Eduardo Canfield Rivera; Selene Rocío Gaxiola Laso
abstract: Ontario accounts for the overwhelming majority of Canada's motor vehicle production, yet its exposure to Mexican manufacturing shocks has generally been treated as indirect, transmitted only through Canada's relationship with the United States. This paper tests that assumption using a purpose‐built panel of 10 Canadian provinces and 12 US states, with Mexico's manufacturing cluster growth as a common shock variable (2006Q1–2024Q4). Granger causality tests, the primary evidence, show that Mexico's nearshoring shock predicts Ontario directly ( χ 2 = 15.21, p < 0.001) while the US automotive corridor does not ( χ 2 = 0.83, p = 0.661). A placebo test confirms automotive specificity: motor vehicles respond on impact, aerospace does not. Markov‐switching regression shows Mexico and the US achieve 97.4% regime concordance while Ontario enters recession independently in 16 of 76 quarters, including a rising episode from 2023Q4 without a continental counterpart. Local projections corroborate this response, though differential estimates do not survive wild cluster bootstraps and are treated as directional. These results are consistent with a triangular rather than bilateral network, Mexico as the upstream source, with Ontario and the US Midwest as parallel downstream receivers, with implications for regional‐science models of stratified production geographies and for the USMCA review initiated in July 2026.
summary: Granger and regime-switching evidence suggests Mexican nearshoring shocks reach Ontario's auto sector directly rather than via the US, implying a triangular North American production network relevant to the USMCA review.

title: Same, Same, but Different: Geographical Labor Mobility of Older Workers in Sweden
authors: Sebastian Hanika; Mikhail Martynovich
abstract: Research on migration in later life has predominantly focussed on retirement, amenities, and family‐related relocation, while determinants of work‐related migration has received comparatively little attention. Yet, rising labor force participation among older individuals makes understanding their work‐related mobility increasingly important. Using longitudinal Swedish register data covering 1993–2019, this study examines interregional work‐related migration patterns among workers aged 60–74 and investigates which regional characteristics are associated with higher attraction and retention of older workers. The results show that both employment and work‐related migration among older adults increased substantially during the study period, with the number of older workers changing region of employment doubling between 1993 and 2019. Moreover, the geography of older worker flows became increasingly similar to that of younger workers, as older workers generally relocated to and from the same regions as workers in younger age groups. At the same time, important differences remain. Older workers appear less responsive to aggregate labor market conditions and regional wage levels. Instead, regional age structure plays a stronger role, with regions characterized by older populations attracting more older workers. The findings highlight the need for labor mobility frameworks and regional labor market policies that explicitly account for late‐career mobility and workforce aging.
summary: Swedish register data show work-related interregional moves by workers aged 60–74 doubled from 1993 to 2019, following younger workers' geography but responding less to wages and more to regional age structure.

title: When Administrative Reform Misleads: Reclassification and Artificial Urbanization Signals in Provincial Economic Structure—Evidence From Türkiye
authors: Gamze Çürüksulu Usta; Abdullah Altun; Ahmet Usta
abstract: This paper examines how administrative reclassification can distort empirical inferences regarding the relationship between urbanization and provincial economic structure, using Türkiye's Law No. 6360 as an institutional setting. The reform redefined rural settlements as urban within newly designated metropolitan provinces, introducing a sharp discontinuity in official urbanization statistics without a contemporaneous change in provincial economic structure.
