summary: A spatial analysis of patterns and determinants of regional electricity consumption across Europe.

title: A non-compensatory multidimensional framework for regional attractiveness and peripherality
authors: Salvatore Corrente; Benedetto Torrisi; Gianpiero Torrisi
keywords: islands; peripherality; Regional attractiveness; spatial disparities
abstract: This paper proposes a new way for assessing regional attractiveness using a multidimensional framework, including distance from development poles. It applies the Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis (SMAA)- Preference Ranking Organisation METhod for Enrichment of Evaluations (PROMETHEE) approach, which, departing from common practice, avoids data normalisation, compensatory trade-offs and arbitrary weight assignments. PROMETHEE handles data aggregation without normalisation or compensation, while SMAA eliminates subjective weights. Applied to 238 EU NUTS 2 regions, with a focus on islands as peculiar peripheral regions, it emerges that distance plays a limited role in regional development, as socio-economic factors largely capture its effects. This approach offers insights to enhance policy design regarding peripheral areas.
summary: Proposes a non-compensatory multidimensional method for measuring regional attractiveness and peripherality.

title: Do state borders constrain internal mobility? Evidence from Brazil
authors: Fernando Antonio Ignacio González
keywords: Brazil; commuting; home-state bias; Internal migration; spatial friction
abstract: This paper documents that state borders are a meaningful source of friction in internal labour mobility in Brazil, a large emerging economy with substantial labour-market informality and historically heterogeneous borders. Using geocoded municipality-to-municipality migration and commuting flows from the 2010 Brazilian Census (20.6 million person records, 5565 municipalities), at equivalent distances Brazilians are about 1.8 times as likely to migrate to a same-state municipality as to one across a state border (1.61–1.74 once travel-cost controls are added), and 1.87 times as likely to commute within-state. Three patterns of heterogeneity shed light on the underlying mechanisms: (i) formal-sector workers face a proportionally larger penalty than informal workers (Riemann ratio 2.12 vs. 1.70); compositional reweightings absorb about 45 percent of the raw migration-rate gap but attenuate the formal border-penalty coefficient by only 12–14 percent, leaving a residual consistent with state-scoped institutional channels such as professional licensing, employer concentration and recruitment networks; (ii) colonial-era borders impose larger penalties than recently created ones, a cross-sectional pattern consistent with home-state bias developing gradually; (iii) the penalty is concentrated among individuals living in their birth state (Riemann ratio 12.02) and reverses for interstate migrants (0.45). Fiscal discontinuities in state consumption taxes (ICMS) provide no support for a tax-based mechanism. Headline magnitudes are rate-based Riemann ratios; the conditional Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML) border coefficient implies a smaller penalty (exp(0.289) ≈ 1.34), reflecting conditioning and flow-weighting. The results are robust to controls for physical geography (rivers, elevation, terrain ruggedness), paved-road distance and driving time, their joint inclusion, two-way clustering, PPML gravity estimation with origin- and destination-state fixed effects, distance bandwidths up to 200 km, leave-one-out exclusion of the Tocantins border, population-size matching and a permutation placebo test.
summary: Tests whether state borders act as barriers to internal migration in Brazil.

title: Do place-based capital investment policies influence public safety? Evidence from the Opportunity Zones program
authors: David Mitre-Becerril
keywords: community investments; Place-based interventions; urban crime; urban development
abstract: The Opportunity Zones program, established under the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, is a prominent place-based policy that provides tax benefits for capital investments to foster economic growth and job creation in distressed census tracts. This study examines the relationship between economic conditions and public safety by evaluating the program’s impact in 31 major U.S. cities 7 years after its implementation. Using a propensity score matched difference-in-differences design, the program has had no broad effect on public safety, as evidenced by calls for service, police stops, crime, and arrests. These overall null results do not mask city-specific impacts. However, the safest neighborhoods seem to have driven an increase in construction projects. The results suggest that preexisting public safety conditions are critical to the success of market-driven place-based programs. Public safety is not only an outcome of capital investments but also a requisite that shapes where and when investments occur.
summary: Evaluates whether the US Opportunity Zones place-based investment program affected public safety outcomes.

title: Security through decommodification: Limited equity cooperatives in the gentrifying city
authors: H. Jacob Carlson; Kiara Thomas
keywords: cooperatives; decommodification; gentrification; Housing; policy
abstract: Limited equity cooperatives (LECs) are a form of affordable homeownership, where someone can buy a home below market rate on the condition that they also resell it below market rate. New York City is home to over 95,000 units of LEC housing, most of which has its origins in the union and tenant movements. Yet as the city has changed, the neighborhoods surrounding these working-class homes have changed, too. We document the changing neighborhood contexts of LECs from 1970 to 2020, finding that gentrification rises around them. Additionally, we provide some of the first systematic estimates of the cost differences between these homes. On average, an LEC unit costs 25% less per month than a unit in a comparable building and has a market value that is 30% lower. We suggest that LECs are a viable policy to prevent exclusionary displacement that inhibits low- and middle-income households from moving into gentrifying neighborhoods.
summary: Examines how limited equity housing cooperatives provide residential security through decommodification in gentrifying cities.

title: Regulation from below or domination from above? Reassessing community-bank partnerships from the Austin area of Chicago
authors: Andrew Born
keywords: Community reinvestment; community-bank partnerships; racial capitalism
abstract: Community reinvestment advocates have encouraged banks to invest in redlined neighborhoods through a process known as “regulation from below.” This process has produced community-bank partnerships, institutional arrangements between community development organizations and banks, intended to ensure effective bank reinvestment. However, community-bank partnerships and their political effects remain largely unexamined. Using the generative theoretical lens of racial capitalism, this article analyzes data from an ethnographic study of the Austin area of Chicago, the birthplace of the community reinvestment movement. It finds that two major interest groups in Austin have successfully pursued and formed partnerships with banks since the 1970s: working-class homeowners and community development professionals. While both groups form partnerships with banks that channel investments toward property rehabilitation and neighborhood redevelopment, their partnerships have done little to interrupt the racialization of Austin as Black and risky, nor to protect many of its residents from economic predation and extraction. This article concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for future community development research and practice.
summary: Reassesses community–bank partnerships in Chicago's Austin neighborhood, asking whether they empower communities or entrench bank dominance.

title: Smart without the local? Experimenting with smart grids in India's urban energy transitions
authors: Lucas Barning
keywords: Assemblage Theory; energy governance; India; smart grids; Urban energy transitions
abstract: India’s urban energy systems face significant challenges in modernizing electricity distribution networks while integrating emerging technologies for decarbonization. Smart grids, promoted under the National Smart Grid Mission (NSGM), have been positioned as key instruments to digitalize and reform this sector. Yet their contribution to urban energy transitions remains unclear. This paper examines how smart grid projects were embedded in urban contexts and what forms of governance reconfiguration they produced, drawing on Assemblage Theory and comparative case studies of three NSGM projects in Panipat, Guwahati, and Mysuru. The findings show that while the projects were installed within urban distribution infrastructures, they were only weakly embedded into broader urban governance contexts and local problem constellations, rendering them largely unstable as urban interventions. At the same time, the projects facilitated a subtle functional reorganization of the distribution sector at the urban scale, shifting key responsibilities from public distribution companies to private system integrators through ICT-driven technologies and operational processes. Given the instability of the projects, the findings suggest that sustainable urban energy transitions require deeper urban embedding, strengthened public-sector capacities, and deliberate alignment with localized problem-solving strategies.
summary: Studies smart-grid experiments in India's urban energy transitions and the role of local actors in them.

title: Boundary as a technology of governance: The operation of spatial boundaries and the production of publicness among Guangchangwu groups
authors: Luer Sun; Qiang Feng
keywords: Boundary; Chinese public spaces; political ecology; publicness; urban governance
abstract: Guangchangwu (square dancing) groups have become a prominent feature of public life in urban China, yet little is known about how they shape the production of publicness in everyday public spaces. Drawing upon a comparative multi-sited ethnography of Guangchangwu groups across three Chinese cities, this paper examines how spatial boundaries are established, negotiated, and adjusted through interactions among dancers, state actors, and other space users. The findings show that publicness is produced through the dynamic interplay between institutional regulations and everyday boundary practices, in which formal rules define participation while routine negotiations and symbolic mechanisms continually reshape spatial order. They further reveal that different levels of urban hierarchy generate distinct forms of boundary governance by embedding state power to varying degrees, resulting in differentiated patterns of publicness across cities. Rather than functioning as spontaneously open public spheres, Chinese urban public spaces are characterized by a governance logic of invited coexistence, where participation remains conditional and negotiated. The paper contributes to debates on publicness and urban governance by conceptualizing boundary as a technology of governance and demonstrating how power, space, and everyday practice jointly produce publicness in contemporary China.
summary: Examines how spatial boundaries operate as governance tools shaping publicness among Chinese square-dance (Guangchangwu) groups.

title: Everyday climate adaptation inequality: Weatherization, racial segregation, and health risks in a changing climate
authors: Nathaniel O'Grady
keywords: hazards; Housing; social theory
abstract: Access to infrastructure plays a significant role in shaping our ability to adapt to a changing climate. It also underpins the uneven distribution of climate vulnerability. This article extends debates at the intersection of infrastructure, adaptation, and vulnerability by exploring everyday practices of climate adaptation through people’s attempts to weatherize their houses during climate-related emergencies. Referring to the adjustments people make to their homes to lessen the effects of such events, I frame weatherization as a socio-technical process. This framing matters because it underscores that one’s capability to undertake everyday climate adaptation, and the consequences associated with not being able to do so, is contingent on wider political urban planning processes and decisions that dictate and manage infrastructural provision. The article subsequently elaborates on three types of distinct health risks associated with diminished weatherization capabilities, showing specifically how it can: exacerbate pre-existing health issues, heighten the possibility of “maladaptation” risks, and set pathways for wholly new kinds of health risks to emerge. The article substantiates its argument through research into lived experiences of heat waves in U.S. cities.
summary: Examines inequalities in everyday climate adaptation through home weatherization, linking racial segregation and health risks.

title: Echoes of resilience: Urbicide, wartime memorials, and urban identity in Chongqing
authors: Jie Xiao; Jian Xu
keywords: collective identity; Urban memory; urban resilience; urbicide; wartime memorials
abstract: During World War II, Chongqing endured severe urbicide from sustained aerial bombardment, targeting not only its infrastructure but also the social relations, symbolic meanings, and collective life embedded in urban space. This paper examines how Chongqing’s responses to wartime destruction, through memorials and preserved air-raid shelters, have shaped its contemporary urban identity and collective memory. Employing a qualitative research design, the study draws on semi-structured interviews with residents, urban planners, and historians, complemented by municipal archival materials and site-based observations. Focusing on key commemorative sites, including the Anti-Japanese War Memorial and preserved underground shelters, the analysis explores how urban memory is produced, governed, and recontextualized over time. The findings show that these sites function simultaneously as anchors of collective remembrance and as arenas of memory governance, while also serving as catalysts for urban renewal, heritage tourism, and place branding. Through processes of selective preservation, adaptive reuse, and commodification, wartime memory is actively integrated into Chongqing’s contemporary urban development. By foregrounding a non-Western case, this study challenges Euro-American–centric understandings of urbicide and demonstrates how post-urbicidal recovery unfolds through contested remembrance and everyday urban practice. The findings contribute to broader debates on urban resilience, memory politics, and post-conflict urbanism.
summary: Explores how wartime destruction and memorials shape urban identity and resilience narratives in Chongqing.

title: The faster the better: The impact of public transport speed and transfer pricing on job accessibility
authors: Diego Hernandez; Renzo Massobrio; Antonio Mauttone; Juan Pablo Chavat; Sara Perera
keywords: equity; job accessibility; operational speed; Public transport; transfers
abstract: This paper analyzes how different public transport scenarios in Montevideo, the capital city of Uruguay, impact accessibility to job opportunities. It also assesses whether these changes increase or decrease equity in accessibility. Specifically, we simulate scenarios defined by changes in two characteristics of the public transport system: improvements in the operational speed on specific corridors in the network and fare scheme restrictions on the number of transfers allowed per trip. Our results indicate that both increasing operational speed and allowing passengers to make more transfers result in increasing accessibility to job opportunities by public transport. Nevertheless, the magnitudes of these effects differ: increasing operational speed on specific corridors has a much greater impact compared to allowing for free transfers. We reach the same conclusions regarding the analysis of equity results. From a policy perspective, this paper shows the need to adopt accessibility as a policy goal to shed light on the challenges that Montevideo’s public transport system must address. The fare scheme currently in place in the city, which allows for one transfer, seems to be already successful in assuring basic connectivity to citizens. However, there is room—and need—for improvement regarding operational speed to improve accessibility and equity.
summary: Assesses how public transport speed and transfer fare policies affect job accessibility.

title: Becoming durable–becoming makeshift: An assemblage approach to informal settlement construction
authors: Matthijs van Oostrum; Kim Dovey; Elek Pafka; Tanzil Shafique
keywords: Durability; housing; informal settlement; morphology; upgrading
abstract: Non-durable construction is conventionally used as a criterion for identifying “slum” conditions and a proxy for material well-being. While informal settlements often embody makeshift construction, we seek to disentangle durability from formality to show multiple ways in which durability is formally and informally produced, sustained or diminished over time. Durability in informal settlement is part of a complex adaptive process that incorporates a plurality of types and degrees of both becoming durable and becoming makeshift. This approach enables a better understanding of both the production of “slum” conditions and the “improvement” that is embodied in “improvisation.” Makeshift construction can be a means to durability, and formalized housing can become makeshift. At micro-scales this approach reveals the importance of incremental construction, maintenance and repair. At larger scales it enables a more nuanced understanding of how durability is linked to issues of land tenure, governance, density, land-use mix, political economy, forced eviction and livelihoods. It cuts across binary thinking to show how urban development is always an assemblage of informal and formal upgrading strategies, and how they can work in synergy.
summary: Uses an assemblage approach to analyse how informal settlement buildings become durable or remain makeshift.

title: Cultural mapping for digital data interrogation
authors: Norhan Abdelgawad; Shalini Misra; Thomas Sanchez; Kris Wernstedt; Paroma Wagle
keywords: creative cities; Culture; urban planning
abstract: The abundance of openly accessible datasets, including institutional Open Government Data (OGD) and crowdsourced OpenStreetMap (OSM), presents opportunities and challenges for cultural planning. Recognizing that data are not neutral representations but are shaped by the institutional, social, and political dimensions that produce them, our study presents a methodologically innovative approach to address how and whether community perceptions align with or differ from digital data representations. Using a critical GIS perspective, we conducted a proof-of-concept study leveraging cultural mapping as our method and Kevin Lynch’s concept of imageability as our theoretical lens to develop a systematic multilevel analytical approach to compare digital datasets with community perceptions. At the macro level, we compared spatial patterns from individuals’ cultural maps with digital representations. At the community level, we identified the most salient cultural assets for community members. At the individual level, we identified factors that are often overlooked in digital datasets, including accessibility, meaning, perceptions, and everyday practices. Our findings revealed perceived spatial discrepancies and a lack of conceptual consensus on what constitutes culture between institutional data and community-sourced data. This approach provides opportunities to evaluate planning outcomes and develop community-centered cultural datasets, which can advance just, data-driven cultural planning.
summary: Proposes cultural mapping as a method for critically interrogating digital data in urban contexts.

title: "This is an exposure of all the things that were previously wrong": Renters' experiences with Emergency Rental Assistance
authors: Patricia C. Lewis; Kyra Rost; Penelope Schlesinger; Danya Keene
keywords: COVID-19; Eviction; housing policy; qualitative
abstract: Housing insecurity is a pervasive problem for American renters. This precarity is rooted in a system that privileges ownership rights over occupancy rights, causing an imbalance of power between landlords and renters. While the insecurity of renting in urban America has been a focus of investigation for over a century, the economic fallout of the COVID-19 pandemic reignited public interest in this issue and centered important questions regarding housing affordability and the rights of tenants. In 2020, the federal government launched Emergency Rental Assistance (ERA) programs to prevent mass displacement. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 57 adults in Bridgeport, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio, we examined the ways in which ERA policy intersected with existing housing inequalities. We identified three patterns: (1) ERA provided short-term relief for those whose housing was relatively stable; (2) ERA was a stopgap for those without access to stable affordable housing, doing little to ensure long-term stability; and (3) the most vulnerable renters, particularly without formal leases, were unable to demonstrate eligibility for the program and were excluded entirely. Our findings underscore the limitations of ERA and point to the need for broader, more equitable housing policy reforms.
summary: Documents renters' experiences with Emergency Rental Assistance and what they reveal about pre-existing housing-system problems.

title: Navigating property formalization in post-disaster recovery: An analysis of Puerto Rico's title clearance program in Villa Esperanza, Puerto Rico
authors: Ivis Garcia; Leslie Martínez-Román
keywords: disaster recovery; Hurricane María; Informal communities; property formalization; social vulnerability
abstract: This study examines the implementation of Puerto Rico’s Title Clearance Program in Villa Esperanza, an informal settlement in Toa Alta, following Hurricane María in 2017. Through semi-structured interviews conducted in summer 2022 with 20 participants, including residents, community leaders, government officials, legal advocates, and other stakeholders, this research examines the intersection of property formalization and disaster recovery in marginalized communities. The findings reveal significant barriers to program participation, including complex documentation requirements, limited resources, and historical patterns of exclusion from formal systems. Despite these challenges, residents demonstrate remarkable agency in pursuing title clearance as a pathway to accessing basic services and future disaster assistance. The study contributes to understanding how a land title clearance program in the post-disaster recovery phase interacts within the context of informality. In addition, the study highlights the need for more inclusive approaches to disaster recovery and acknowledges the challenges and realities related to informal land tenure from the perspective of a single case study in Puerto Rico.
summary: Analyses Puerto Rico's post-disaster title clearance program in Villa Esperanza and residents' navigation of property formalization.

title: Wanghong urbanism: Platform aesthetics and urban change in Kennedy Town, Hong Kong
authors: Shizheng Liang
keywords: aesthetics; digital platform; gentrification; Hong Kong; Wanghong urbanism
abstract: This article examines how platform aesthetics shape neighborhood change through the case of wanghong (“internet-famous”) urbanism in Kennedy Town, Hong Kong. Drawing on visual analysis, social media data, surveys, and interviews, it argues that the transformation of Kennedy Town into a wanghong destination demonstrates how digital platforms and the collective practices of their users interact with and amplify preexisting gentrification processes. The article conceptualizes wanghongization as a mode of urban change driven by the production and circulation of specific aesthetics, which reconfigure urban experiences and spatial practices in ways not fully captured by existing theories. To theorize this process, the article introduces the gentrification–wanghongization cycle to describe how platform visibility and algorithmic amplification convert the preexisting aesthetics of gentrification into reproducible wanghong aesthetics, which subsequently intensify commercial restructuring and incremental landscape change. By foregrounding the aesthetic and visual politics, the article contributes to debates on platform urbanism, gentrification, and neighborhood change, offering a conceptual framework for understanding how digital representations and platform logics increasingly mediate and reshape contemporary urban transformation.
summary: Examines how social-media 'wanghong' platform aesthetics drive urban change in Kennedy Town, Hong Kong.

title: Planning formalization and its consequences: The socioeconomic impacts of slum resettlement
authors: Omar Ben Haman
keywords: critical urban theory; impoverishment; informality; resettlement; Urban planning
abstract: This paper explores the socioeconomic consequences of slum resettlement through the resettlement of the Lebrahma slum to Al Marouwa in Casablanca, Morocco. Intended to enhance housing quality and urban order, the Villes Sans Bidonvilles program underestimated the importance of informal economies and social relations that sustained everyday life in Lebrahma. Based on ethnographic fieldwork, the study shows how resettlement disrupted home-based livelihoods, weakened neighborhood solidarities, and constrained residents’ access to informal employment. These changes reveal the limitations of urban planning models that impose formal structures without engaging with the lived practices and adaptive strategies of low-income communities. The paper argues that informality should not be viewed as a problem to be eliminated, but as a dynamic system of survival and innovation that urban policy must recognize and incorporate. By centering residents’ experiences, the study highlights the need for inclusive planning approaches that build on local knowledge and strengthen, rather than displace, the socioeconomic networks that sustain urban life.
summary: Studies the socioeconomic impacts on households of slum resettlement under planning formalization.

title: Planning accessible housing for people with environmental illness: Lessons from three affordable housing projects
authors: Justin D. Stern
keywords: accessible housing; disability; environmental illness; Healthy housing; multiple chemical sensitivity
abstract: This paper explores how to create accessible environments for people with environmental illness, focusing on affordable housing. People with environmental illness can experience severe and often disabling health problems when exposed to even small amounts of everyday chemicals, such as fragrances and pesticides. These reactions can include migraines, asthma attacks, dizziness, seizures, musculoskeletal pain, and anaphylaxis. Recognized as a disability in Canada and many other countries, and accommodated on a case-by-case basis in the United States, environmental illness creates various urban accessibility barriers, one of the most frequently cited being access to healthy housing. Despite this, the condition has been largely overlooked in urban planning and policy scholarship. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing three affordable housing projects designed for people with environmental illness in Canada and the United States: Barrhaven Community Housing for the Environmentally Hypersensitive in Ottawa, Ontario; Ecology House in San Rafael, California; and Old Concho Community Housing in Snowflake, Arizona. From these case studies, the paper derives 10 lessons for creating affordable and accessible housing for people with environmental illness. Finally, it discusses how urban planning and policy can improve urban accessibility for people with environmental illness and related disabilities.
summary: Draws lessons from three affordable housing projects on planning accessible housing for people with environmental illness.

title: Flood Protection and Adaptation Labor in Jakarta, Indonesia
authors: Sophie Webber; Wahyu Kusuma Astuti; Rhino Ariefiansyah; Umar Hamzah; Abyan Madani
abstract: Jakarta is undergoing an infrastructural transformation in response to increasing flood risks, constructing new dams, flood canals, reservoirs and retention ponds, and ongoing normalization of the city’s rivers. However, one crucial element of responding to severe flood risks that has so far been overlooked in Jakarta and other vulnerable cities is the work of building and maintaining this flood protection infrastructure. In this article, we respond to this research gap by analyzing the work of the Blue Troops, a new provincial workforce who construct and maintain Jakarta’s flood protection infrastructure. Drawing from extensive fieldwork interviewing and observing the Blue Troops in Jakarta, we catalog their adaptation labor practices, showing the accumulated health and safety risks of their work. At the same time, we demonstrate that the workers find this to be reliable and meaningful collective work, essential for reproducing cities in a time of climate catastrophe. In short, we show that workers trade precarious labor practices and bodily risks against secure public-sector employment and a sense of contributing to their city. This article, therefore, contributes to a growing scholarly concern with the labor implications of climate change, suggesting that the organization, conditions, and value of this work will be crucial political and analytical terrain.
summary: Examines the labor involved in flood protection and climate adaptation in Jakarta.

title: The Role of Regional Recombination Capacity in Shaping the Technological Space
authors: Diego Ocampo-Corrales; Rosina Moreno
abstract: This article investigates the role of regions’ recombinatorial technological capacity in shaping the technological space. To do so, we identify novel combinations of technologies and track their evolution by tracing all subsequent inventions that incorporate the same combination. Building on the concepts of relatedness and geographic proximity, we focus on the relevance of the technological antecedents of a pair of technologies combined for the first time in determining their success. This is due through the estimation of the likelihood of a new technological combination eventually becoming embedded within the broader knowledge space. Using patent data from 1976 to 2022 in the case of the European regions, we find strong evidence that a higher degree of relatedness between the technological antecedents of the two combined technologies significantly increases the likelihood that the combination will be reused in future inventions. Additionally, we find that the success of a new combination also benefits from the presence of dissimilar knowledge—not directly involved in the combination’s antecedents but accessible within the surrounding technological environment. In these cases, the greater the relatedness between the new invention’s antecedents and the broader regional knowledge base, the more likely it is to generate a high number of follow-on inventions and contribute meaningfully to the formation of the technological space.
summary: Studies how regions' capacity to recombine knowledge shapes their position in the technological space.

title: Population Density and Air Pollution: Should Incentives Be the Same Across U.S. Cities and States?
authors: Yuval Arbel
abstract: Population concentration generates both economic benefits and environmental costs through agglomeration-related spatial externalities. This paper examines how population density shapes fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations across U.S. states over the period 2000–2023, conceptualizing density as a structural driver of nonlinear environmental externalities within regional systems. Using a balanced panel of all fifty states, I estimate fixed-effects models in which logged PM2.5 is modeled as a flexible quadratic function of logged population density, allowing coefficients to evolve over time and across density regimes. The results reveal a convex relationship between population density and PM2.5, indicating that the environmental externalities of agglomeration increase at an accelerating rate over much of the density distribution. However, the strength of this nonlinear effect has weakened over time, consistent with regulatory adaptation and technological diffusion. A split-regime analysis further shows that the curvature of the density–pollution relationship differs systematically between low- and high-density states, suggesting heterogeneity in regional externality structures. These findings contribute to the regional science literature by demonstrating that the environmental consequences of population concentration are nonlinear, heterogeneous, and dynamic within an advanced economy context. More broadly, the results highlight the importance of incorporating spatial externalities and governance scale into density-sensitive regional policy design, particularly in transportation investment, land-use planning, and environmental regulation.
summary: Across U.S. states in 2000–2023, PM2.5 rises convexly with population density, though this nonlinear pollution penalty of agglomeration has weakened over time and differs between low- and high-density states.

title: Urban, Rural, or In-Between? An adapted Territorial Typology for NUTS 2 regions
authors: Tuomas Väisänen; Maija Havusela; Milad Malekzadeh; Olle Järv
abstract: We describe the adapted urban-rural typology at the NUTS 2 regional level, an extension of the official regional urban-rural typology provided by the European Union at the NUTS 3 regional level. We used the Census Grid 2021 data and urban agglomerations data to construct an adapted typology. A typology at the NUTS 2 level enables more opportunities for regional analyses and policymaking, as European regional statistics are primarily provided at this level. The EU's regional policies, such as its Cohesion Policy, are implemented at the NUTS 2 level, and for many countries NUTS 2 levels represent administrative regions with substantial administrative, legislative, and fiscal powers. In this resource description article, we describe our adapted urban-rural typology at the NUTS 2 level and how we produced the dataset using the Census Grid 2021, Joint Research Centre's Urban Agglomerations data, and the NUTS 2 regional polygons provided by Eurostat, the European Union statistical authority. We provide the adapted urban-rural typology layer at the NUTS 2 regional level and the typology production scripts openly to support regional analyses and policymaking in Europe.
summary: The authors build and openly release an urban-rural typology for EU NUTS 2 regions from Census Grid 2021 and JRC urban agglomeration data, extending the official NUTS 3 typology to the level at which Cohesion Policy operates.

journal: Scienze Regionali - Italian Journal of Regional Science
title: Does the Quality of Local Institutions Trigger Improvements in Waste Related Performances?
authors: Alessio D'Amato; Edoardo Fermante; Matteo Mazzarano
keywords: municipalities; waste Kuznets curve; institutional quality
abstract: This paper focuses on the role of institutional quality and income, together with other potential drivers, in determining sorted and unsorted collection. A Spatial Seemingly Unrelated Regression (spatial-SUR) model is estimated based on a municipal-level dataset. Accounting for spatial spillovers and semi-parametric estimations, we examined nonlinearities in the relation between waste performances and institutional quality, finding a previously overlooked asymmetry in waste performances improvements across municipalities, with underperforming ones improving the most as institutional quality improves. On the other hand, and somehow surprisingly, institutional quality improvements yield similar effects between average- and best-performing municipalities in terms of waste collection.
summary: A spatial SUR model of municipal waste collection finds that better local institutional quality improves waste performance most in underperforming municipalities, while effects are similar for average and best performers.

title: How government performance, informational environment, trust, and traditional authority shape local land governance in Africa
authors: Stephen Kehinde Medase; Maxwell Sifuna
keywords: disinformation; government performance; traditional leaders; institutional trust; land allocation
abstract: Land governance in African countries often unfolds at the intersection of formal state institutions and informal traditional authority structures. In many communities, unelected traditional leaders and chiefs continue to wield substantial influence over land allocation and local dispute resolution, operating alongside elected officials. These patterns raise critical questions about how perceived government performance influences who governs key resources, such as land. Does a well-performing state crowd out the influence of traditional authorities, or does it create an environment where formal and informal actors collaborate for better outcomes? Our study investigates these issues, focusing on the role of chiefs in land distribution as a key outcome. We use the Afrobarometer dataset from 2021 to 2023 for 31 African countries in which traditional authorities govern rural and local communities. We conducted moderated mediation analyses using absorbed regression (AREG), logit, and wild-cluster linear regressions, accounting for country and broad regional-level fixed effects. We find that perceived government performance is positively associated with land governance. Traditional authority positively mediates the link between government performance and land governance. Furthermore, while disinformation attenuates the mediation effect, perceived responsiveness of traditional leaders amplifies this effect. Lastly, perceived institutional trust positively strengthens the traditional authority-land governance nexus. We ground our approach in an institutionalist perspective that views governance in Africa as the product of ongoing interactions between formal state structures and informal societal institutions. We further discuss the theoretical and practical findings, as well as major limitations and avenues for future research.
summary: Using Afrobarometer data for 31 African countries, the study finds that perceived government performance is positively associated with land governance, with traditional authorities mediating the link and institutional trust strengthening it while disinformation weakens it.

title: 'Rentierism' at the peri-urban edge: Studentification, speculative land markets, and the uneven geographies of gentrification in Ghana
authors: Frederick Mensah; Stephen B. Liwur; Francisca Agyei; Michael Osei Asibey
keywords: Gentrification; Displacement; Ayeduase; Kumasi; Peri-urbanism; Mixed-use development
abstract: Rapid urbanisation around major educational institutions are increasingly transforming peri-urban settlements in African cities, yet the mechanisms and consequences of these changes remain underexplored. This study examines the processes, drivers, and impacts of gentrification in Ayeduase, a peri-urban community adjacent to the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi, Ghana. Drawing on a mixed-methods case study approach, the study combines household surveys, key informant interviews, field observations, and GIS-based land-use analysis to investigate how university expansion influences land-use change, housing development, and socio-economic transformation. The findings reveal that growing demand for student accommodation has stimulated the conversion of traditional residential properties into hostels, apartments, commercial facilities, and mixed-use developments. Between 2005 and 2025, residential land declined substantially while commercial and mixed-use land uses expanded, accompanied by sharp increases in land values and intensified redevelopment activity. Although these changes have generated employment opportunities, business growth, and higher household incomes for some residents, they have also contributed to rental pressures, exclusionary displacement, socio-cultural change, and the weakening of long-standing community networks. The study argues that the transformation of Ayeduase is best understood as a form of institution-driven gentrification, in which university expansion creates the conditions for market-led redevelopment within a fragmented governance environment characterised by the interaction of customary and statutory land administration systems. The study advances understanding of how gentrification unfolds in rapidly urbanising African contexts, and highlight the need for integrated planning approaches that balance economic development, housing accessibility, and social inclusion in university-adjacent settlements.
summary: Studentification around a Ghanaian university drove conversion of homes into hostels and commercial uses, sharply raising land values between 2005 and 2025 while causing rental pressure and exclusionary displacement, a pattern the authors term institution-driven gentrification.

title: The European No Net Land Take objective: A meta-challenge
authors: Antoine Decoville; Frédéric Durand
keywords: Land take; Spatial planning; Land policies; Urban sprawl; Europe
abstract: The European objective of achieving "No Net Land Take" (NNLT) by 2050 represents an ambitious paradigm shift in the fields of urban planning and architecture. However, the primary obstacles to its implementation are not technical in nature, but rather stem from our society's inability to reform itself in order to attain this fundamental goal. This viewpoint paper reviews the political, economic, and sociocultural barriers that must be overcome to effectively halt the loss of agricultural and natural land.
summary: This viewpoint argues that the main obstacles to the EU's 2050 No Net Land Take goal are political, economic and sociocultural rather than technical, and reviews the barriers to halting the loss of agricultural and natural land.

title: From legitimization to structured legalization: A governance framework from Türkiye's 2018 zoning amnesty
authors: Orhan Ercan; Orhan Mataracı; Ümit Gedik; Erdem Ercan
keywords: Informality; Institutional legitimization; Structured legalization; Land governance; Spatial data integration; Institutional governance
abstract: Informality remains one of the most persistent challenges for land governance, particularly where large-scale legalization policies seek to reconcile existing development with formal planning and regulatory systems. Although zoning amnesties often generate comprehensive administrative records of informal development, they rarely establish institutional mechanisms capable of transforming legitimization into sustainable legalization. This study examines the implementation outcomes of Türkiye's 2018 Zoning Amnesty and evaluates how they provide the foundation for a governance model for structured legalization. An integrated analytical framework combining spatial assessment, institutional analysis, and policy evaluation was applied using national administrative statistics, orthophoto-based spatial analysis, municipal inventories, zoning-amnesty datasets, and evidence from the environmentally sensitive Uzungöl case study. The findings demonstrate that the Building Registration Certificate functioned primarily as an instrument of institutional legitimization rather than complete legalization, creating a nationwide administrative inventory while leaving critical planning, technical, environmental, and legal issues unresolved. Building on these findings, the study proposes a governance model that transforms administrative legitimization into structured legalization through a sequential institutional pathway integrating legal verification, spatial assessment, technical and environmental assessment, and administrative integration. The proposed model offers a transferable approach for more transparent, adaptive, and risk-informed land governance in countries facing similar challenges of large-scale informality.
summary: Evaluating Türkiye's 2018 zoning amnesty, the study finds the Building Registration Certificate legitimized informal buildings administratively without resolving planning, technical, environmental and legal issues, and proposes a sequential governance model for structured legalization.

title: De facto land consolidation leads to exclusion: The role of commodity expansion in Salamina, Colombia
authors: Andres Suarez
keywords: Access; Land concentration; Plantations agriculture; Land use policy; Market-oriented
abstract: Land consolidation (LC) is commonly regarded as a sustainability-oriented strategy designed to enhance agricultural productivity and promote rural development. LC can occur through de jure mechanism (formal, state-led programs, public-private partnerships) or de facto processes that evolve informally. However, there remains a significant gap in understanding the negative implications of de facto LC, particularly within commodity booms in the Global South. This study addresses that gap by examining an ongoing LC process driven by the expansion of Hass avocado plantations in Salamina, Colombia. Grounded in the Theory of Access, the analysis argues that de facto LC fosters exclusionary dynamics within traditional agricultural landscapes. These dynamics manifest through both direct and indirect mechanisms, generating a range of adverse consequences for peasant communities living adjacent to expanding plantations.
summary: Examining Hass avocado expansion in Salamina, Colombia, the study argues that informal (de facto) land consolidation creates direct and indirect exclusion of neighbouring peasant communities.

title: Climate-policy pathways reshape cropland-expansion-driven deforestation and agricultural-carbon trade-off imbalance in the Amazon
authors: Wencang Shen; Zhengfeng Zhang; Walter Timo de Vries; Yuanyuan Yang; He Gao; Lu Niu
keywords: Cropland expansion; Climate policy; Forest carbon sink; Land-use modeling; Agricultural outputs
abstract: Urbanization, population growth and agricultural commodity demand increasingly shift land-use pressure toward distant rural frontiers, intensifying cropland expansion into tropical forests and creating substantial trade-offs between agricultural production and carbon-sink capacity. Yet where regional climate-policy land-demand pathways translate into forest-conversion risk, and how these risks overlap with agricultural-value and carbon-sink outcomes at fine spatial resolution, remains insufficiently quantified. We couple the Global Change Assessment Model (GCAM) with the Future Land Use Simulation (FLUS) model to assess cropland-expansion-driven deforestation in South America from 1992 to 2050, with the Amazon basin as the focal analytical region, under reference and 1.5 °C -consistent (1p5) pathways. We estimate agricultural value using a data-driven approach and quantify carbon impacts as changes in vegetation carbon-sink capacity. From 1992–2020, Amazon cropland increased by 2.12 × 105 km2 while forests declined by 3.51 × 105 km2, accounting for more than 60% of South America forest loss. Under the reference pathway, forest loss reaches 8.23 × 105 km2, including 1.10 × 105 km2 converted to cropland, causing an annual loss of 1.04 × 1010 kg of forest carbon sequestration while generating 4.79 × 108 GK$ in agricultural revenue. Under the 1p5 pathway, Amazon forest-to-cropland conversion declines to 7.00 × 103 km2, a 93.6% reduction relative to the reference pathway, and the net land-conversion effect shifts toward a carbon-sink gain. These results indicate an asymmetric agriculture-carbon trade-off, in which cropland expansion produces relatively limited agricultural-value gains while imposing large carbon-sink costs. The GCAM-FLUS framework identifies where such trade-offs are spatially concentrated and where mitigation-consistent land-demand pathways may reduce conversion risk. These policy implications should be interpreted together with local governance, tenure and supply-chain conditions, which are not directly simulated in the present modelling framework.
summary: Coupling GCAM and FLUS models, the study finds that a 1.5 °C-consistent pathway would cut Amazon forest-to-cropland conversion by 93.6% relative to the reference pathway, revealing an asymmetric trade-off in which cropland expansion yields limited agricultural value at large carbon-sink cost.

title: Urban form under China's politico-economic transition: The role of decentralization, marketization, globalization, and regionalization in the Greater Bay Area
authors: Shiyi Wang; Yangyi Wu; Xianchun Zhang
keywords: Urban form; Politico-economic transition; Decentralization; Marketization; Globalization; Regionalization
abstract: Urban form is undergoing rapid transformation amid global politico-economic transitions, yet the mechanisms shaping these changes in non-Western contexts remain under-theorized. Taking China's transition as an example, we reconceptualize the transition by adding regionalization into the traditional framework of decentralization, marketization, and globalization, highlighting the role of regional cooperation. We delineate the evolution of urban form through morphological analysis in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area (GBA) from 2010 to 2019, and employ regression methods to validate the pathways through which this extended transitional framework influences form outcomes. Empirical results demonstrate that urban form is co-shaped by local governments' fiscal expenditure, land market prices, foreign direct investment, and the intensity of inter-city cooperation. A compound growth model integrating industrial land, transport networks, and real estate is emerging as a significant mechanism forging urban spatial structure. Overall, our study reaffirms the pivotal impact of local government play among the various actors shaping urban development and spatial configuration in China. While regionalization has shown tangible effects in enhancing inter-city collaboration and reducing regional disparities, it has yet to fundamentally transform the entrenched governance logic through which local governments leverage land markets to drive urban growth.
summary: In the Greater Bay Area (2010–2019), urban form is co-shaped by local fiscal spending, land prices, FDI and inter-city cooperation, and regionalization has improved collaboration without displacing local governments' land-market-driven growth logic.

title: A review of collective agri-environmental schemes using a human–AI framework
authors: Robert Huber; Sara Ammann; Claudia Bethwell; Caitriona Carlin; Viviane Fahrni; Andrea Fürholz; Katrin Karner; Raja Imran Hussain; Gesche Kindermann; Monika Suškevičs; Sandra Uthes; Martin Schönhart; Christian Stetter
keywords: Collective agri-environmental schemes; Policy dimensions; Policy design; Agricultural policy; Human-AI interaction
abstract: We systematically review collective agri-environmental schemes that support landscape stewardship in agriculture. We analyze 96 case studies across OECD countries based on 73 peer-reviewed articles. To guide this review, we develop a framework based on policy dimensions, the policy cycle, and micro-level implementation dimensions. This framework provides a basis for defining evaluation criteria and for assessing how these schemes are designed. The review combines the analytical power of artificial intelligence with expert domain knowledge. The synthesis of both enables a comprehensive examination of policy and implementation dimensions, resulting in critical insights into the schemes' designs and functioning, and their broader applicability. Our results describe patterns of design and implementation in the reviewed literature, without establishing a causal link between the design and implementation of schemes and ecological outcomes. We find considerable heterogeneity among schemes indicating flexibility for decision-makers to adapt schemes to specific environmental targets at local scale, but that there is still significant room to enhance the role of farmers as key players in collective agri-environmental schemes. By integrating human expertise with the capabilities of large language models, our approach exemplifies how to balance and mitigate the limitations of each, increasing the transparency of the review process.
summary: A human–AI systematic review of 96 collective agri-environmental scheme cases across OECD countries finds considerable design heterogeneity that allows local targeting but substantial room to strengthen farmers' role in the schemes.

title: Urban agriculture as a land-use policy instrument for protecting peri-urban agricultural land: A grid-based analysis from Erzurum, Türkiye
authors: Selvi Karasungur; Merve Yavaş
keywords: Urban agriculture; Peri-urban areas; Land-use policy; Grid-based analysis; Secondary cities
abstract: Uncontrolled urban expansion places increasing pressure on natural resources and poses a significant threat to agricultural production. The loss of agricultural land negatively affects food security and ecosystem services, while rising carbon emissions further exacerbate environmental challenges. In this context, the protection of fertile agricultural lands surrounding cities is critical for sustainable food production. Urban agriculture has emerged as an alternative approach that supports local food production, economic viability, and environmental sustainability. This study examines the suitability of agricultural lands located on the urban fringe of Erzurum for urban agriculture as a response to urban sprawl. The study area, covering selected neighbourhoods in the western part of Erzurum, was divided into 1 × 1 km grid cells. Spatial analyses were conducted for each grid cell based on seven main parameters and twenty-three sub-criteria. An agricultural suitability synthesis map was generated according to the cumulative impact scores derived from these parameters. Rather than limiting the analysis to suitability identification, the spatial results were translated into eight planning-oriented urban agriculture typologies targeting different user groups by integrating suitability outcomes with existing land-use and functional characteristics. The findings indicate that 848 ha of land in Erzurum's urban periphery exhibit very high suitability for urban agriculture, while 1385 ha demonstrate high suitability. Overall, the study demonstrates that urban agriculture can function as a strategic land-use policy instrument by linking spatial suitability assessment with typology-based planning approaches, thereby supporting peri-urban land protection and guiding statutory planning decisions in secondary cities such as Erzurum.
summary: A grid-based suitability analysis of Erzurum's urban fringe identifies 848 ha of very highly and 1385 ha of highly suitable land for urban agriculture, which the authors frame as a land-use instrument to protect peri-urban farmland from sprawl.

title: Land-use policy architectures for brownfield regeneration: A comparative analysis of Spain and the Netherlands
authors: Albert Lladó-Martínez
keywords: Brownfields; Land-use policy; Urban regeneration; Soil remediation; Planning integration; Value capture; Comparative governance
abstract: Brownfield regeneration is increasingly central to sustainable land-use policy in Europe, as it supports soil protection, compact urban development, urban restructuring, and reduced pressure on greenfield land. Yet redevelopment remains difficult because contaminated land is shaped not only by market conditions, but also by the institutional design of planning, remediation, financing, and intergovernmental coordination. This article compares Spain and the Netherlands to examine how different land-use policy architectures condition brownfield regeneration. Using a qualitative comparative approach that combines doctrinal legal analysis with institutional interpretation, it analyzes four dimensions: risk allocation, planning–environment integration, value-capture mechanisms, and governance modes. The findings identify two contrasting models. Spain operates through a codified and redistributive framework in which liability and value capture are largely predefined by statute, while remediation and planning remain institutionally differentiated. The Netherlands exhibits a more integrated and adaptive model in which environmental regulation is more closely embedded within spatial planning and redevelopment relies more heavily on negotiated coordination and local administrative capacity. The comparison shows that legislative integration alone does not ensure effective regeneration. What matters more is the alignment between liability rules, financial design, and governance capacity. The article concludes that brownfield redevelopment should be understood as a land-use policy problem of institutional coordination, not merely as a technical question of remediation or a market question of land valorization.
summary: Comparing Spain's codified, redistributive regime with the Netherlands' integrated, negotiated model, the article finds that brownfield regeneration depends less on legislative integration than on aligning liability rules, financial design and governance capacity.

title: Assessing the alignment of land consolidation policies with the Sustainable Development Goals: A case study of China
authors: Yasi Tian; Yice Zhang; Yan Zhang
keywords: SDGs; Land consolidation; Alignment evaluation; PMC model; Fit-for-Purpose assessment
abstract: Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) requires mechanisms that translate global objectives into context-sensitive local policies. Land consolidation connects land governance, spatial planning, and sustainable development, yet systematic frameworks for evaluating its alignment with the SDGs remain limited. Guided by Fit-for-Purpose (FFP) principles, this study develops an SDG-oriented framework based on the Policy Modeling Consistency (PMC) index. It first applies content analysis to extract land-consolidation measures from a national policy. It then establishes a multidimensional mapping between policy measures and SDG targets through expert consultation, constructing an indicator system covering social, economic, ecological, spatial, and managerial dimensions. Differentiated weights based on provincial development orientations and indicators of local policy innovation are incorporated to reflect the FFP principles of purpose-driven, fit-to-context, inclusiveness, and flexibility. Using 26 provincial-level administrative units in mainland China as empirical cases, the results reveal significant interprovincial variation in SDG alignment. Spatial and managerial dimensions performed strongly, while the social dimension showed a relatively high mean but considerable variation. Economic alignment was weaker, and the ecological dimension recorded the lowest mean and greatest variation. Cluster analysis identifies three policy types, including institution-led, spatial and social response-dominant, and multi-dimensional synergistic advancement. This study extends FFP from project suitability assessment to SDG-oriented policy text analysis and proposes a transferable evaluation paradigm for land governance and broader spatial planning research.
summary: A PMC-index evaluation of land consolidation policies in 26 Chinese provinces finds strong spatial and managerial alignment with the SDGs but weaker economic alignment and the lowest, most variable ecological alignment.

title: Clarifying overlapping land rights in semi-formal systems: The case of Mailo tenant lands in Uganda
authors: Kate Marple-Cantrell; Heather Huntington; Daniel Ayalew Ali; Thea Hilhorst
keywords: Uganda; Property rights; Impact evaluation; Mailo land; Kinship; Land governance
abstract: This paper examines the effects of clarifying overlapping land rights on Mailo land in Central Uganda, contributing to broader debates on property rights and rural development. The study leverages a quasi-experimental design implemented across three districts, where interventions included systematic demarcation of parcel boundaries and land inventories, dissemination of legal knowledge, conflict mediation services, and facilitation of tenant–landlord agreements. Drawing on a panel of Mailo tenants, a large-N tenant survey, and a survey of landlords, we assess how land rights awareness raising shaped institutional clarity (improved documentation and legal awareness), tenure security (reduced conflict and strengthened perceptions of security), and economic behavior (evidence of land market activity). The findings highlight the central role of annual Busuulu (ground rent) payments—functioning simultaneously as a rent obligation and as formal evidence of tenant rights—as a mechanism linking institutional reforms to greater tenure security and market participation. We further identify heterogeneous effects, with distinct patterns for female-headed households and for tenants with kinship ties to landlords on all three outcomes. Taken together, the results provide new evidence on the mechanisms through which property rights interventions shape security and economic activity in rural Africa.
summary: A quasi-experimental evaluation of rights-clarification interventions on Uganda's Mailo land finds that annual Busuulu ground-rent payments are the key mechanism linking the reforms to greater tenure security and land-market participation, with distinct effects for female-headed and kin-linked tenants.

title: Suburbanisation's impact on local government: New spatial management roles and challenges in the suburbs today
authors: Julia Gorzelany; Katarzyna Cegielska; Barbara Olczak; Renata Różycka-Czas
keywords: Periurban areas; Integrated management; Survey; Conflicts; Spatial analysis; Local authorities
abstract: Suburbanisation is the central force in urban development today. It is particularly impactful in post-socialist countries where its significant momentum and chaotic effects pose challenges to local governance. Although suburbanisation is a well-established field of research, the novelty of this study lies not in reiterating suburban growth itself, but in examining its impact on local governance in suburban municipalities of a post-socialist metropolitan region. The article aims to scrutinise the dynamics of suburbanisation in municipalities adjacent to Kraków and evaluate its effect on governance in the economic, environmental, and societal contexts. The study combines statistical and spatial analyses with surveys conducted among local residents and local authorities, confronting social perceptions with institutional assessments. The results indicate highly dynamic suburbanisation, land cover transformation, pressure towards new infrastructure, and social conflicts, which hinder municipal governance. They also show that the duration of residence significantly differentiates perceptions of suburbanisation-related problems and expectations towards local authorities. By providing evidence from a post-socialist institutional context, the study contributes to international comparative discussions on the diversity of suburbanisation and local governance models. The conclusions emphasise the necessity of implementing integrated and flexible management, reinforcing planning and participatory instruments that support sustainable development, and improving the quality of life.
summary: In municipalities around Kraków, rapid suburbanisation brings land-cover change, infrastructure pressure and social conflicts that hinder local governance, with residents' length of residence shaping their perceptions of problems and expectations of local authorities.

title: Unraveling the spatial dynamics and mechanism heterogeneity of land transfer on carbon emission: Evidence from China's Yangtze River Economic Belt
authors: Chenlu Liu; Chen Zeng; Pengrui Wang; Mingyuan Chang; Xingzi Yu; Ruijing Yu
keywords: Land marketization; Spatial spillover effect; Low-carbon; The Yangtze River Economic Belt
abstract: In the context of greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation, effective land management emerges as a paramount policy priority worldwide for carbon mitigation and low-carbon transitions. Using the Yangtze River Economic Belt (YEB) as a case study, this study systematically explores the mechanisms and heterogeneity of land transfer's impact on carbon emissions, taking spatial spillover effects into account. The findings reveal that: (1) newly allocated built-up land has a markedly stronger effect on carbon emissions compared to the redevelopment of existing land, primarily due to the conversion of agricultural and forest land and the built-up of new infrastructure. (2) In 2015–2022, there is an increase in land transfers for industrial, public service, and transportation purposes at the outskirts, while residential and commercial land allocations have decreased, particularly in the lower reaches of the YEB. (3) Industrial land transfers have the most substantial impact on carbon emissions, while emissions from residential and commercial land can be mitigated through energy-efficient technologies and green building standards. (4) Land transfer area (LTA) is positively correlated with carbon emissions, while land marketization (LM) shows a negative influence. Significant spatial autocorrelation was also observed, underscoring the complex spatial dynamics at play in land use and carbon emissions. Based on the findings, policy recommendations are proposed on differentiated land supply management system, optimizing land marketization process, ecological and environmental standards and guidelines to mitigate carbon emissions through integrated land resource management across regions.
summary: In China's Yangtze River Economic Belt, newly allocated built-up land and especially industrial land transfers raise carbon emissions more than redevelopment, while greater land marketization is associated with lower emissions, with significant spatial spillovers.

title: A land management, biodiversity preservation, and climate change mitigation analysis in Brazil
authors: Gustavo da Silveira Schiavo; Annibal Scavarda; Virginia Bodolica; Shahadat Khan; Luiz Felipe Scavarda
keywords: Biodiversity; Climate action; Life on land; Mitigation hierarchy; Resilience
abstract: This research aimed to evaluate Brazil's performance in achieving the goals and targets related to Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 13 (Climate Change) and SDG 15 (Life on Land), while systematically assessing how governmental actions align with the mitigation hierarchy (avoidance, minimization, restoration, offsetting, and enhancement). Based on a qualitative content analysis of scientific literature and official evaluation reports, this work contributes to the debate on climate change and biodiversity loss. The research identifies areas of progress and areas that still require attention from policymakers in this context. This study was developed with a qualitative approach and was structured in two stages, namely the scoping review and documentary research based on data retrieved the Institute of Applied Economic Research (IPEA), a foundation linked to the Brazilian Ministry of Planning and Budget. Documentary research identified reports evaluating Brazil's progress on SDG 13 and SDG 15, and document analysis revealed that Brazil has action plans with varying levels of achievement (fully achieved, partially achieved, and not achieved targets) related to biodiversity preservation, climate change mitigation, and sustainable development. Based on the Brazilian actions to mitigate impacts, it was possible to observe a hierarchy with a stronger emphasis on preservation (avoidance) compared to restoration actions, particularly in land management and biodiversity preservation. Furthermore, key points of progress and areas requiring attention from policymakers regarding this topic were also identified. In view of the need for progress in public policies focused on land management and on addressing climate change and biodiversity loss, this research advances the understanding of how integrated mitigation strategies can support the joint achievement of SDG 13 and SDG 15, offering a structured analytical framework to evaluate governmental performance and inform policy design.
summary: A scoping review and analysis of official IPEA reports finds that Brazil's progress on SDG 13 and SDG 15 targets is mixed, with government actions emphasizing avoidance (preservation) over restoration within the mitigation hierarchy.

title: Reducing cropland requirement by optimizing provincial grain trade patterns in China
authors: Xin Xuan; Yuping Bai; Xiangzheng Deng; Yecui Hu; Fan Zhang
keywords: Cropland requirement reduction; Grain; Interprovincial grain trade; Virtual cropland trade; National food security
abstract: Optimizing grain trade patterns to conserve cropland is crucial for enhancing the "internal circulation" of grain production. This study characterized the current supply and demand dynamics for China's three primary staple crops—wheat, maize, and rice—encompassing demand for human consumption, animal feed, and food loss and waste across the entire food supply chain. We developed a linear programming-based grain trade simulation and optimization model to determine the interprovincial trade patterns of these three crops and their virtual cropland trade structure, to assess the potential reduction in cropland requirements achieved by optimizing interprovincial grain trade patterns. We found that in profit-driven trade schemes, grain trade largely follows the principle of proximity, and major grain-producing provinces such as Henan, Shandong, and Anhui alleviate cropland resource imbalances to some extent through interprovincial trade. Optimizing trade patterns could reduce national cropland requirements by nearly 15,000 km2. Attention should also be paid to the synergistic benefits of reducing cropland requirements and reducing transport-related carbon emissions. Optimizing the grain trade structure and leveraging the production advantages of major grain-producing regions contribute to reducing cropland requirement, while simultaneously enhancing the role of land resource management in guaranteeing a stable food supply.
summary: A linear-programming model of interprovincial wheat, maize and rice trade in China shows that optimizing trade patterns could cut national cropland requirements by nearly 15,000 km2, with co-benefits for transport emissions.

title: Forecasting territorially differentiated land-use transitions: Behavioural evidence from discrete choice experiments and diffusion modelling in Southern Italy
authors: Ruggiero Sardaro; Piermichele La Sala
keywords: Land-use transitions; Agroecological innovation; Discrete choice experiments; Bass diffusion model; Territorial policy; Southern Italy
abstract: In contexts characterized by agricultural specialization and environmental pressures, varietal choices are not simply agronomic decisions, but shape land management and the transformation of rural landscapes. Therefore, the study aims to assess producers' attitudes toward the use of local varieties and to forecast their rate of diffusion over space and time. This allows an analysis of the temporal dynamics associated with land-use transitions. The research analyses the case of Apulia, i.e. Italy's second-largest region in terms of vineyard area, through a combined approach. On the one hand, discrete choice experiments investigate the attitudes of producers towards landraces for sparkling wine production. On the other, the Bass diffusion model predicts the temporal trend of adoption and distinguishes between innovators and imitators. The Discrete Choice Experiments (DCE) results identify four types of producers with different preferences and Willingness To Accept (WTA) levels, which range from 2500 € ha−1 to 11,400 € ha−1. The Bass model highlights a prevalence of the imitation effect (q = 11.7%) over the innovation effect (p = 2.3%). The adoption curve is characterized by slow initial penetration, acceleration after the tenth year and territorially differentiated diffusion by the thirtieth year (24% of farms). However, the trajectories are rapid in intermediate areas and slow or incomplete in intensive or marginal areas. These trajectories suggest territorially calibrated and time-sensitive land-use policies for land-use transitions, i.e. agricultural zoning and land banks for marginal areas, support for districts and cooperatives in intermediate areas, diversification incentives and supply chain contracts for intensive areas.
summary: Combining discrete choice experiments with a Bass diffusion model for Apulian grape growers, the study finds willingness-to-accept for adopting local grape varieties of 2500–11,400 € per ha and projects slow, imitation-driven adoption reaching 24% of farms by year 30, fastest in intermediate areas.

title: Design principles for result-based, collective and value chain-based environment and climate contract solutions in agriculture and forestry: Learning from 44 case studies across Europe
authors: T. Eichhorn; T. Runge; D. Viaggi; J. Kantelhardt; F. Bartolini; T. Bradfield; P. Dupraz; K.S. Harmanny; A. Iglesias; F. Le Gloux; E. Majewski; A. Malak-Rawlikowska; D. Nikolov; M. Raggi; C.J.E. Schulp; S. Targetti; K. Todorova; E. Tyllianakis; D. Vergamini; E. Viitala; M. Zavalloni; L. Schaller
keywords: Ecosystem services; Voluntary schemes / measures; Novel contract solutions; Result-based payments; Collective implementation; Value-chain-based solutions
abstract: The European Union promotes the provision of agri-environment-climate public goods (AECPGs) from agriculture and forestry through dedicated policies. Nevertheless, despite long-term efforts and earmarking of significant financial resources for voluntary agri-environmental schemes, the provision of AECPGs from Europe's agro-ecosystems is continuing to decline. New governance instruments are urgently required to revert this process. Promising new approaches are seen in novel contract solutions promoting result-based payments, collective implementation, and value-chain-based approaches. However, a deeper understanding of the practical design of these novel schemes is needed to achieve acceptance and successful implementation. We systematically examine real-world examples of contract solutions and their design characteristics by analyzing a dataset of 44 case studies from 13 European countries. Data or information from these case studies was collected using a uniform protocol across countries, and a qualitative content analysis was conducted. Our findings show that result-based approaches differ in their design with regard to measuring environmental performance. Successful result-based approaches enable flexible management, include features for knowledge provision, and are often designed as hybrid solutions to enhance uptake, combining action- and result-based elements. Collective contract solutions are based on a common management agreement of the involved group members, but vary in their degree of formalization, often include a coordinator, and foster meetings and exchanges. Value chain-based solutions differ in terms of the relationship between the production of private goods and the provision of AECPGs, their incentive system, value chain characteristics, and marketing, and often comprise an element of cooperation, also representing a hybrid approach. The findings of this research can help shape the design of such alternative approaches and provide inspiration for promoting the voluntary delivery of AECPGs under the Common Agriculture Policy (CAP) and beyond.
summary: Analysing 44 European case studies, the paper finds that successful result-based, collective and value-chain contract schemes for agri-environment-climate public goods tend to allow flexible management, provide knowledge, and combine action- and result-based elements as hybrids.

title: Institutional configurations and conservation agriculture outcomes: A fuzzy-set analysis of production units in Lishu County, China's black-soil region
authors: Hongwei Yu; Yufeng Hou; Youchao Xing; Huixin Ran; Chuanling Xiang; Mingze Xia; Zijie Liu; Hu Zhou
keywords: Conservation agriculture; Institutional complementarity; Cooperative governance; FsQCA; Black soil protection; China
abstract: Conservation agriculture in China's black-soil region is delivered through service-providing production units operating under shared county policy frameworks, yet implementation outcomes vary substantially across units. This study asks which configurations of governance conditions are associated with high sustainability performance. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis on 26 production units in Lishu County, Jilin Province, we examine four conditions, standard implementation intensity, service-chain coordination, outsourcing, and financial support, against a composite sustainability outcome combining soil protection, grain yield, yield stability, and spillover effects (Cronbach's alpha = 0.76). No single condition approaches necessity for high performance. The baseline solution identifies a high-coverage coordination pathway and a finance-conditioned outsourcing route; under stricter frequency thresholds the solution simplifies to coordination alone, a pathway stable across 100% of threshold-grid specifications and 96% of leave-one-out runs. The analysis identifies a conditional complementarity between outsourcing and financial capacity that generic complementarity theory does not predict for sub-national agricultural governance. We frame the findings as a provisional governance reference point for institutionally and biophysically comparable settings, with policy implications for shifting county instruments from area-based expansion metrics to governance-quality gates.
summary: A fuzzy-set QCA of 26 conservation-agriculture production units in Lishu County finds no single necessary condition for high sustainability performance, with service-chain coordination the most robust pathway and outsourcing effective only when paired with financial support.

title: Massive hidden cropland transitions undermine China's agricultural sustainability
authors: Nufang Fang; Renjie Zong; Qiongdan Liang; Yi Zeng; Wei Dai
keywords: Land use transitions; Agricultural sustainability; Food security; Ecological restoration; Geographically weighted regression model
abstract: Balancing cropland protection and abandonment is a major challenge for sustainable food production. The link between cropland abandonment and reclamation is still unclear, making it hard to assess their combined effects on land use.
