An illustrative calculation suggests potential annual savings of RMB 261.2 billion (US$38.3 billion) in out-of-pocket medical expenditure across the policy-targeted regions. These findings underscore the importance of clean energy accommodation and provide evidence to inform policies aimed at translating renewable electricity into more equitable household welfare gains.
summary: Studies the link between clean energy accommodation and households' health-related defensive expenditure in China.

title: Can a wealth tax reduce CO2 emissions in Europe?
authors: Alexander Guschanski; Rafael Wildauer
keywords: Climate policy; CO2 emissions; Household finance and consumption survey; Wealth inequality; Wealth tax
abstract: We analyse the potential of wealth taxes to reduce CO2 emissions through two transmission channels: the inequality channel, which links reductions in wealth inequality to lower emissions, and the consumption channel, which operates through the effect of wealth taxes on consumption by top wealth holders. We simulate the effects of various wealth tax designs over one- and ten-year horizons using harmonized microdata from 22 European countries. Our analysis accounts for survey non-response bias, heterogeneous rates of returns across households, and behavioural responses to taxation. We find that, through the inequality channel, a recurrent annual progressive wealth tax could reduce annual CO2 emissions by 7.5%–14.7% after 10 years relative to a no-tax scenario, depending on tax progressivity. Through the consumption channel, the average reduction is 1.5%–3.6% after 10 years. In addition, we show that the revenues generated cover the entire investment gap identified by the European Commission's ‘Fit for 55’ emissions reduction programme. These findings highlight the potential of wealth taxes to serve a dual purpose: curbing wealth concentration and contributing meaningfully to climate mitigation and justice, by focusing on high-net-worth households that account for a disproportionate share of emissions.
summary: Assesses whether a wealth tax could reduce CO2 emissions in Europe.

title: Individual adaptation to extreme heat and the interpretation of risk perceptions: Evidence from counterfactual beliefs
authors: Masahide Watanabe
keywords: Adaptation Monitoring; Climate Adaptation; Extreme Heat; Individual Adaptation; Risk Perception
abstract: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, heat-health policies increasingly use alerts, forecasts, and behavioral guidance to encourage individual self-protection. Evaluations of such policies often track survey-based intermediate outcomes, including warning awareness, perceived heat risk or vulnerability, and protective behavior, in addition to health outcomes. Yet routine self-protection can make reported risk perceptions difficult to interpret: perceived risk may motivate prevention, while reported risk may already reflect the protection that respondents have adopted. In a web-based survey of residents of Tokyo's 23 wards, we elicit subjective probabilities of heatstroke under realized and counterfactual prevention scenarios. Respondents are randomly assigned to evaluate either a no-prevention scenario or a full-prevention scenario. Reported risk changes systematically with the assumed level of prevention, suggesting that reported risk perceptions may reflect both perceived susceptibility and behavior-conditioned reappraisal and may be misleading as stand-alone indicators in adaptation monitoring and evaluation. We also find that perceived risk under the no-prevention scenario is positively associated with realized preventive effort, suggesting that this counterfactual belief provides a more interpretable basis than realized-prevention risk for examining how perceived susceptibility relates to preventive effort.
summary: Uses evidence on counterfactual beliefs to study individual adaptation to extreme heat and how stated risk perceptions should be interpreted.

title: Green debt for nature-based solutions: aligning municipal budgeting and banking practices
authors: Axelle Vincent; Tara Op de Beeck; Heleen Van Hecke; Tine Compernolle; Jan Cools; Tom Coppens
keywords: Banks; Climate adaptation; Green debt-financing; Green lending; Municipal finance; Nature-based solutions
abstract: Local governments face growing risks from climate change, which require substantial investments in climate adaptation to safeguard future generations. Nature-based solutions (NBS) have been recognized as a cost-efficient strategy to redevelop public space, to create greener and more climate adaptive urban environments. However, development of NBS is hindered by a lack of financial resources to fully scale up the transformation. To overcome this barrier, literature calls for clear sustainable finance frameworks and business model approaches to include private financing in the development of public NBS. In our research we consider the perceptions of municipalities and banks, as institutional lenders, towards using green debt-financing to finance NBS. We draw on sustainability transitions literature to theorize NBS as a niche innovation within established banking-municipal relations. Using qualitative interviews with Belgian banking experts and urban and financial planners from Flemish cities, we reveal competing financial logics between municipal financing practices and banking requirements, limiting the uptake of green debt for NBS. While NBS are mostly absorbed in traditional municipal deficit financing, this conceals their value and prevents market development. Alternatively, project finance remains difficult due to capacity constraints and differing valuation logics. Emerging sustainable finance frameworks create opportunities but shift administrative burdens onto municipalities. Overall, current practices mainly support NBS to fit and conform, rather than transform established debt-practices. Substantial upscaling of NBS will require changes in both banking practices and municipal financing approaches, including explicit integration of physical climate risk and collective financing mechanisms.
summary: Examines how green debt could finance nature-based solutions by aligning municipal budgeting with banking practices.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: High-speed rail, expressways, and revitalization after the Great East Japan Earthquake
authors: Sunbin Yoo; Junya Kumagai; Longfei Zheng; Sung Hoo Kim; Paul H. Jung; Zheng Chang
keywords: Disaster recovery; MA; High-speed rail (HSR); Expressways; Production networks; Network connectivity
abstract: This paper examines whether restoring connectivity fosters medium-run post-disaster revitalization in Japan's Tohoku region after the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake. We measure connectivity using mode-specific Market Access (MA)–a travel-time–weighted index of how easily places can reach people and markets–separately for high-speed rail (HSR) and expressways, controlling for air connectivity. Using city-year data (2006–2020), we estimate fixed-effects regressions and address endogeneity with 2SLS, instrumenting realized MA with least-cost, terrain-based hypothetical networks built via a spanning-tree algorithm. We find that expressway connectivity delivers larger and more robust gains, particularly for population and manufacturing-related outcomes, while HSR effects are smaller and more localized near major hubs. Buffer-based MA and Sendai-exclusion tests show that HSR gains attenuate quickly with distance, whereas expressway benefits persist. Counterfactual "no-recovery" simulations imply notable 2020 secondary GDP losses without restoration (about 0.13% for HSR and 0.21% for expressways). Overall, the results provide causal evidence that restoring connectivity is central to diffusing revitalization beyond core nodes after large disasters.
summary: Using 2SLS on Tohoku city-year data, restoring expressway market access after the 2011 earthquake produced larger and more persistent population and manufacturing gains than high-speed rail, whose benefits were concentrated near major hubs.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: From announcement to operation: The changing impact of light rail transit on housing prices across implementation phases
authors: Hisham Negm; Rodrigo Victoriano-Habit; Mylene Riva; Ahmed El-Geneidy
keywords: Property values; Transit premiums; Hedonic pricing; Difference-in-differences (DiD); Natural experiment
abstract: New public transit infrastructure can significantly influence housing prices. While most studies examine impacts only after construction or compare a limited number of implementation phases, little is known about how transit-induced property value capitalization evolves dynamically throughout the implementation process. This study investigates the impact of Montreal's new light rail project (the REM) on housing prices across four stages: announcement, construction, testing, and initial operation. The phased implementation of the REM also allows us to examine whether the operation of one branch generates anticipatory price effects along branches that remain under construction. Drawing on panel data of 14,711 residential property transactions over eleven years (from 2013 to 2023), we employ a natural experiment design through a difference-in-differences (DiD) approach to isolate the project's net effect at different stages on housing prices. Our findings show that the four stages of REM implementation affect property values differently across catchment areas along operating and non-operating branches. The project announcement raised housing premiums within 800 m of some parts of the corridor, and this effect persisted throughout the construction period. REM-related premiums around the branch that underwent testing remained positive throughout the construction period. However, during testing and early operation, these gains were largely offset, possibly due to operational impacts such as noise and vibration. While premiums dissipated near the operating branch, properties along unopened branches remained stable or continued to appreciate compared to the rest of the region. By highlighting how home values evolve across different stages of implementation of large-scale transit investments, this study provides insights that can inform the design of Land Value Capture policies to capitalize on property gains while mitigating externalities.
summary: A difference-in-differences analysis of 14,711 Montreal home sales shows the REM light rail raised nearby housing premiums from announcement through construction, but these gains were largely offset during testing and early operation while unopened branches kept appreciating.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Do better street configurations mean higher land prices? Nonlinear and spatial heterogeneity effects revealed by GeoShapley
authors: Quang Cuong Doan; Thi Cam Ngoc Bui
keywords: Nonlinear relationship; Spatial heterogeneity; Land prices; Machine learning; GeoShapley; Vietnam
abstract: Street configuration plays an important role in urban transport systems, influencing accessibility, movement patterns, and spatial interactions. While prior studies have examined the association between spatial accessibility and land prices using linear assumptions, the roles of nonlinearity and spatial heterogeneity in transport networks are underexplored. To address this gap, we investigate how street configuration affects land prices through nonlinear and spatially varying mechanisms, using Hanoi as a case study. We integrate XGBoost with GeoShapley to disentangle the marginal and location-specific effects of multiple street configuration metrics. Results indicate that street configuration is an important predictor of land prices, with notable spatial heterogeneity. In addition, we observe that improved accessibility does not always lead to higher land prices; that is, marginal effects peak within specific connectivity thresholds and decline beyond them. Among the configuration measures examined, local connectivity has the strongest effect, followed by degree centrality and betweenness, highlighting the importance of fine-grained street networks for land prices. GeoShapley analysis reveals that geographic context alone explains 6.8% of land-price variation after accounting for all covariates, emphasizing the limitations of linear and globally averaged models. The marginal effects of features on land prices vary across the study area, underlining the interaction between geographic context and land price determinants. This study provides important implications for transport-oriented land-use planning, especially in designing street hierarchies and accessibility-driven development strategies in rapidly urbanizing cities.
summary: Combining XGBoost with GeoShapley for Hanoi, the study finds street configuration strongly and nonlinearly predicts land prices, with local connectivity mattering most, effects peaking at connectivity thresholds, and geographic context alone explaining 6.8% of price variation.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Transit-induced household migration: A survival analysis of heterogeneous income effects near urban rail corridors
authors: Adam Schmidt; Eleni Bardaka
keywords: Light rail transit; Survival analysis; Household migration; Consumer microdata; Displacement risk; Low-income households
abstract: Urban rail investments can reshape neighborhood demographics, yet the timing and magnitude of any displacement pressures remain poorly documented. This study develops a methodological framework that links annual, household-level consumer microdata with quasi-experimental design to (i) trace in- and out-migration near new light-rail stations, (ii) explore the sociodemographic profile of moving households, and (iii) estimate how proximity, project milestones, and household income interact to change the risk of households migrating out of their neighborhoods. Our econometric analysis includes survival models with two alternative timescales, two control areas, and estimation of heterogeneous impacts by household income level. We illustrate the method with a case study of Charlotte's LYNX Original and Extension of the Blue Line, drawing on a 16-year panel of 437,606 geocoded households. For the Original line, our results show a 4-5% increase in the probability of low- and medium-income households exiting from their neighborhood 5–9 years after the light rail began operating but no long-term effect. On the newer Extension, low- and middle-income households were 6-10% less likely to move out in the first four years after the light rail began operating. However, the share of low-income residents living near stations still declined, mainly due to medium-income household in-migration. Our findings highlight important lessons for policymakers. First, displacement pressure can surface years after opening; second, net demographic shifts often arise from selective in-migration rather than disproportionate exits; and third, equity measures must combine long-term anti-displacement policies with tools that preserve affordability and social mix in new development near transit.
summary: Survival models on a 16-year panel of 437,606 Charlotte households show light rail raised low- and medium-income out-migration by 4-5% only 5-9 years after opening on the original line, while falling low-income shares near stations mainly reflected selective in-migration rather than exits.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Distributional welfare impacts and compensatory transit strategies under NYC congestion pricing
authors: Xiyuan Ren; Zhenglei Ji; Joseph Y.J. Chow
keywords: Congestion pricing; Mode and destination choice; Public transit; Welfare analysis; Synthetic data; New York City
abstract: Early evaluations of NYC's congestion pricing program indicate overall improvements in vehicle speed and transit ridership. However, its distributional impacts remain understudied, as does the design of compensatory transit strategies needed to mitigate potential welfare losses. This study identifies population segments and regions most affected by congestion pricing, and evaluates how those welfare losses can be compensated through transit improvements funded by the toll revenues. We estimate joint mode and destination models using aggregated synthetic trips in the NY–NJ–CT–PA Combined Statistical Area (CSA) and calibrate toll-related parameters using post-toll changes reported by MTA. Welfare impacts of congestion tolls are measured as changes in consumer surplus (CS) before and after program implementation. Compensatory transit strategies are evaluated by quantifying the reductions in transit wait time and fare discounts required to offset the CS losses. The results show that the program leads to an accessibility-related CS loss of $397.23 million per year, while generating net passenger toll revenue of $523.44 million per year estimated based on the MTA's report—indicating a net welfare gain. However, these gains in benefits conceal significant disparities. CS losses are concentrated in upper Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and Hudson County, particularly among travelers less able to shift to transit or alternative destinations. Achieving a general compensation requires modest investment—a 0.63-minute (13%) reduction in wait time or $165.15 million in annual fare subsidies for NYC residents, and a 2.12-minute (28%) reduction or $171.42 million for New Jersey residents. However, ensuring that no population group and county unit is made worse off is substantially more costly and infeasible through transit improvements alone. These findings underscore the need for differentiated compensation strategies: uniform fare discounts lead to overcompensation for some groups, whereas segment-specific discounts, origin-based fare reductions, or commuter pass bundles can achieve equitable accessibility restoration at lower fiscal cost.
summary: NYC congestion pricing yields a net welfare gain ($523M in toll revenue against a $397M annual consumer-surplus loss), but losses concentrate in upper Manhattan, outer boroughs and Hudson County, and targeted rather than uniform transit fare compensation restores accessibility more cheaply.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Public transit funding and transit use: a panel study of U.S. urbanized areas 2010–2019
authors: Pengyu Zhu; Zining Wang; Xuan Zhang; Kailai Wang
keywords: Transit funding; Transit ridership; Urbanized area (UZA); Unlinked passenger trips; Vehicle revenue miles; Capital investment
abstract: Despite the potentially crucial role of public transit in addressing climate change, reducing traffic congestion, and providing affordable transportation options, it remains underutilized in the United States. Policymakers regard increasing investments in public transit as a crucial means to encourage public transit ridership and alleviate the negative consequences of auto dependence. In recent years, a tremendous amount of government funds has been allocated to transit agencies to make transit an appealing mobility alternative. However, transit use has been declining overall. This study investigates this disconnect by assessing the effects of federal, state, and local funding on transit ridership (unlinked passenger trips, UPT) and supply (vehicle revenue miles, VRM, and vehicle revenue hours, VRH). Using a comprehensive panel of over 400 Urbanized Areas (UZAs) from 2010 to 2019, we employ fixed effects, random effects, and instrumental variable models—leveraging political competition metrics (Swing County Population Share and Election Margin) as instruments for federal funding to address endogeneity—to isolate the impacts of distinct funding sources. The results reveal that federal funding serves as the strongest driver of transit metrics, primarily by fueling capital accumulation and asset expansion—a mechanism confirmed through our analysis of fleet capacity. However, the impact of funding is not uniform. We uncover a divergence in efficiency: while transit legacy cities maintain structurally higher baseline ridership, funding exhibits diminishing marginal returns in these large metropolitan areas compared to smaller, developing transit markets. These findings suggest that while federal capital grants are effective, maximizing national ridership requires tailoring allocation strategies to the maturity and scale of urban transit systems.
summary: Instrumenting federal funding with political-competition measures across 400+ U.S. urbanized areas (2010-2019), the study finds federal capital funding is the strongest driver of transit ridership and supply, with diminishing marginal returns in large legacy transit cities.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Less parking, more life? Promises and challenges of urban parking-space repurposing. Evidence from a controlled before-after quasi-experimental study in Berlin
authors: Katja Salomo
keywords: Parking-space reduction; Car use reduction; Transport intervention; Urban transition experiment; Controlled before-after experiment; Climate mitigation; Germany
abstract: Private cars generate substantial urban health, environmental, and social costs. Despite their continued dominance and extensive subsidization, cities are increasingly experimenting with measures to reduce private car use. In 2023, a residential neighborhood in Berlin repurposed approximately 350 on–street parking spaces – about 13% of the area's total – by converting them into green spaces, outdoor classrooms, shared–mobility stations for e–bikes and e–scooters, and designated zones for deliveries and local businesses. The intervention was evaluated using a controlled before–after quasi–experimental design, based on surveys conducted shortly before implementation and six months afterward. The research design distinguishes between a main and a secondary treatment area, two demographically and socioeconomically comparable control areas, and two adjacent neighborhoods potentially affected by traffic and parking displacement. More than 11,000 residents were invited to participate in each survey wave. Treatment areas were fully sampled, while residents in control areas were selected through area–based random sampling, yielding effective sample sizes of 2,027 respondents before and 1,770 after the intervention. Difference–in–differences analyses show no significant reduction in private car use among respondents. However, the intervention was associated with improvements in perceived road safety and outdoor physical activity, as well as small reductions in noise annoyance and traffic–related quality–of–life impacts. At the same time, parking search times increased, noise annoyances from visitors and restaurants increased slightly, and adjacent neighborhoods experienced very modest parking displacement. Policy acceptance declined somewhat after implementation but remained positive among a majority of respondents in the wider treatment area, while opinions were more evenly divided among residents living in the main treatment area that was most affected by the intervention. Overall, this study – one of the few quasi–experimental evaluations of parking–space repurposing – highlights both the potential benefits and the trade–offs of neighborhood–level parking-space repurposing.
summary: Uses a controlled before-after quasi-experiment to evaluate the promises and challenges of a 2023 Berlin intervention that repurposed about 350 on-street parking spaces (13% of the neighborhood total) into green space, outdoor classrooms, shared-mobility stations and delivery/business zones.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: New public transit accessibility metrics: system and system-facilitated accessibility measures
authors: Manish Yadav; Gopal R. Patil; Rakhi Manohar Mepparambath
keywords: Public transit system; System accessibility; System-facilitated accessibility; 20-minute town and 45-minute city; Singapore
abstract: This study proposes a public transit accessibility measure that integrates intrazonal system accessibility, the ease of reaching transit stops, for system-facilitated accessibility, the ability to access opportunities using the transit network. The proposed accessibility measure addresses key limitations of traditional metrics, which often rely solely on gross travel times and overlook intrazonal variations in walking and waiting times. By calculating Public Transport Accessibility Levels (PTAL) at a fine spatial resolution of 400 m square grids and integrating them with zone-to-zone travel times, a modified impedance function is developed to create a more comprehensive system-facilitated accessibility index. Results from multiple linear regression show that the proposed measure outperforms traditional methods in explaining public transit mode share. A non-linear relationship is identified, indicating diminishing returns on transit mode share as accessibility improves beyond a threshold. Using the proposed accessibility measure, the study further evaluates Singapore's alignment with the "20-Minute Town and 45-Minute City (20T-45C)" framework. Access to fourteen essential services categorised into four groups: (i) education, (ii) healthcare, (iii) commerce, and (iv) entertainment and community facilities, analysed within the town with a 20-minute travel time threshold. The analysis of job opportunities is conducted at the city level with a of 45 min threshold. The results reveal spatial disparities, with subzones in the Central, East, and Northeast Regions are well served, while many subzones in the North and West Regions remain underserved. A decision-making framework based on the cross-classification of PTAL and service accessibility is proposed to guide urban planners toward sustainable transit planning.
summary: A new transit accessibility index combining fine-grained stop access (PTAL) with zone-to-zone travel times better explains transit mode share in Singapore and reveals that North and West subzones fall short of the 20-Minute Town/45-Minute City goals.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Metro prosperity and bus decline: A causal relationship? A quasi-experimental study of 17 key cities in China
authors: Meng Liu; Sheng Jin; Chunqin Zhang; Kun Gao; Chengcheng Yang; Congcong Bai; Xi Gao; Wenzhu Xu
keywords: Public transport; Dynamic network data envelopment analysis; Propensity score matching; Differences in Differences
abstract: Understanding the dynamics of competition and cooperation between metro and bus systems is essential for optimizing urban public transport networks. Using data from 281 Chinese cities from 2010 to 2022, this study employs a quasi-natural experiment to analyze the relationship between metro and bus systems from a macro-network perspective. A dynamic network data envelopment analysis model quantifies the operational benefit of both transit modes in 17 developed cities. Propensity score matching evaluates the impact of network densities on operational benefit, serving as a heterogeneity analysis for developed cities. Finally, the difference in differences method is applied to a large sample to analyze the impact of metro network expansion on bus ridership and obtain generalized conclusions. The analysis shows that a 1 % increase in metro network density results in a 2.3 % decrease in bus ridership and a 1.4 % increase in total public transport ridership. In developed cities, the difference in bus operational benefit between cities with high and low metro network density is not significant. The average metro operational benefit in cities with high bus network density is 0.217 lower than in cities with low density. These findings highlight the importance of metro expansion in developed cities and suggest that redundancy within the bus network may detract from the effectiveness of metro and broader public transport systems. Coordinated metro expansion alongside strategic optimization of bus networks is recommended, highlighting the necessity for integrated multimodal public transport planning to promote sustainable urban transport development, particularly in cities where urban rail density has not yet reached a critical threshold. These insights provide valuable guidance for policymakers seeking to better understand the interactions between urban metro and bus systems in Chinese cities, supporting the development of optimized public transport priority policies.
summary: Across 281 Chinese cities (2010-2022), a 1% increase in metro network density cuts bus ridership by 2.3% but raises total public transport ridership by 1.4%, suggesting coordinated metro expansion with bus-network rationalization.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Will high-speed rail compete for long-distance travel in a car-dependent society? Insights from a Canadian high-speed rail survey
authors: Yu (Billie) Zhang; Ahmed El-Geneidy
keywords: High-speed Rail; Long-distance Mode Choice; Discrete Choice Modelling; Canada; Transport Policy
abstract: High-speed rail (HSR) represents a significant transport investment designed to drive economic growth and enhance long-distance regional connectivity. While HSR has demonstrated strong competitive performance against road and short-haul air travel in European and East Asian corridors, the behavioural parameters governing how HSR competes against the private vehicle in automobile-oriented North American markets, where car travel accounts for over 80% of intercity trips, remain comparatively underexamined. It is therefore less clear how travellers in such markets weigh travel time, cost, and service quality when a mature HSR alternative is introduced into a car-dominated mode share structure. The goal of this paper is to evaluate the potential for modal shift to HSR within the structural constraints of a car-dependent society. Unlike studies in transit-integrated European or Asian contexts, this study isolates the group travel penalty and car-habituation effects that characterize North American intercity travel. The study uses the Toronto-Québec City corridor in Canada, which was announced as an HSR project in 2025, to better understand if such investment can achieve its intended ridership and sustainability targets. The study analyzes data from an online bilingual long-distance travel behaviour survey (N = 6,813) conducted in October 2025. We develop a two-stage sequential weighted multinomial logit model capturing current travel behaviour and stated HSR adoption intentions. The analysis reveals that travellers are most sensitive to travel cost and travel time, with an implied value of travel time of approximately $31.5 per hour. Under a medium-adoption scenario, HSR is projected to capture 26% of corridor trips, with the largest substitution from private car and conventional rail. These findings provide an evidence-based demand projection that is essential for investment decisions while avoiding the common pitfall of ridership overestimation in large HSR projects. Practitioners can use these insights to prioritize fare-based incentives and target specific trip purposes such as business and student travel, to maximize the operational success of future HSR projects.
summary: A survey of 6,813 travellers in Canada's Toronto-Québec City corridor implies a value of travel time of about $31.5/hour and projects that high-speed rail could capture 26% of corridor trips under medium adoption, drawing mostly from car and conventional rail.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: On the policy relevance of modeling choice: Causal evidence from GPS-tracked diaries regarding the effect of telework on travel in Switzerland
authors: Daniel Heimgartner; Kay W. Axhausen
keywords: Telework; Kilometres travelled; Treatment effect; Ordered probit switching regression; Endogenous switching regression; Selection bias
abstract: The net effect of telework on transport demand remains actively debated. This study estimates causal treatment effects on weekly kilometres travelled using ordered probit switching regression (OPSR) applied to the TimeUse+ GPS-tracked diary data from Switzerland. OPSR corrects for selection bias that arises when unobserved factors jointly influence telework adoption and travel outcomes. The results reinforce the narrative that telework reduces travel distance and that rebound effects are too small to offset foregone commutes by a wide margin. Relative to a no-telework reference scenario, the estimated travel reduction attributable to the current telework situation is −16%. Unit treatment effects correspond approximately to the two-way commute distance. Crucially, these causal estimates are substantially larger than those obtained from simple group comparisons, underscoring that failing to account for self-selection leads to considerable underestimation of the true treatment effects — a methodological lesson with policy relevance well beyond this study's scope.
summary: Correcting for self-selection with ordered probit switching regression on Swiss GPS-tracked diaries, telework cuts weekly kilometres travelled by about 16%, with rebound effects far too small to offset foregone commutes and naive comparisons understating the effect.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Are telework and teleservices the solution for reducing traffic congestion and emissions? Findings from a comprehensive activity-based modeling analysis
authors: Qinhua Jiang; Brian Yueshuai He; Qiao Yu; Yifang Zhu; Jiaqi Ma
keywords: Telework; Teleservices; Travel behavior; Activity-based Modeling; Emissions and Environment
abstract: The telework and teleservices (Tele-X) are becoming increasingly popular with the development of Information and Communications Technologies, and the COVID-19 pandemic significantly changed the trend. As post-pandemic society increasingly embraces Tele-X and conducts more activities online, Tele-X's potential to alleviate congestion and reduce traffic-related emissions remains unclear. This study investigates the impacts of Tele-X adoption on travel behaviors and evaluates the potential to decrease Vehicle-Miles-Traveled (VMT) and emissions. We developed an integrated modeling framework that includes a hybrid survey, discrete choice models, dynamic travel demand and supply models, and environmental analysis. A case study focusing on Los Angeles (LA) County revealed that about 45% of workers telework at least once a week. However, the reduction in commuting trips is counterbalanced by an increase in non-work trips induced by the flexible schedules of telework, resulting in minor changes total daily activity numbers (+0.2%). The VMT decreases by 3.9% after the pandemic, accompanied by similar reductions in emissions: NOx by 2.1%, PM2.5 by 3.1%, and greenhouse gases by 3.1%. This indicates that Tele-X can be an effective mitigation strategy. Furthermore, a community-level analysis of the Westwood region in LA County shows that while further promotion of Tele-X could reduce local travel, it may induce more passing-by traffic, leading to higher emissions in sub-region.
summary: An activity-based modeling study of Los Angeles County finds that telework and teleservices, adopted weekly by about 45% of workers, lower VMT by 3.9% and greenhouse gases by 3.1% despite induced non-work trips, though local promotion can shift through-traffic and emissions to sub-regions.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: A tale of two perspectives: the mileage-based user fee conundrum
authors: Hyunjun Hwang; Irfan Batur; Dale Robbennolt; Angela J. Haddad; Miguel G. Rodriguez Ocana; Ram M. Pendyala; Chandra R. Bhat
keywords: Mileage-based user fee; Pricing policy fairness; Mobility management; Multivariate econometric model; Individual attitudes; Transportation funding
abstract: The limitations of the current transportation funding system based on federal and state gas taxes have resulted in steep shortfalls in the Highway Trust Fund in the U.S., especially given the growing adoption of high fuel-efficient gasoline vehicles and electric vehicles. While the notion of mileage-based user fees (MBUF) has received attention as an alternative to the current gas tax, public support for MBUF is still low. In this study, we unravel the potential reasons for such low public support by examining the perceived fairness of the MBUF system through the conceptualization of fairness from two perspectives: the perspective that MBUF is fair because everyone pays equally for using the infrastructure, and the perspective that MBUF is less fair because those who adopt cleaner vehicles are not rewarded. Using a bivariate ordered model with attitudinal variables, and employing data from the first wave of the Transportation Heartbeat of America (THA) Survey conducted from October 2024 through January 2025, the effects of socio-economic, demographic, and attitudinal factors on each of the two perspectives of MBUF fairness are examined. The findings suggest substantial heterogeneity in fairness perceptions based on these factors, as well as based on the specific perspective of fairness considered, underscoring the importance of positioning MBUF-based policies with care and sensitivity to different groups of individuals to garner broad support.
summary: Using a bivariate ordered model on the Transportation Heartbeat of America survey, the study shows U.S. perceptions of mileage-based user fee fairness vary substantially across socio-economic, demographic and attitudinal groups depending on whether fairness is framed as equal payment or as rewarding cleaner vehicles.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: On the theoretical distribution of cost overruns: A lognormal baseline
authors: Jeppe Rich
keywords: Cost overruns; Optimism bias; Reference class forecasting; Infrastructure planning; Project appraisal
abstract: Empirical cost overruns in large infrastructure projects are often right-skewed, yet the probabilistic mechanisms underlying this pattern remain poorly understood. This paper develops a stochastic framework distinguishing within-project uncertainty from across-project aggregation. Within individual projects, costs evolve through sequential compounding of proportional shocks, e.g., via price changes, design modifications, delays, making the cost ratio between actual and estimated costs (R=Ca/Ce) approximately lognormal. This compounding generates right-skewed outcomes even when individual shocks are unbiased. Across projects, correlation preserves right-skewness by maintaining a lognormal structure at the portfolio level, whereas probabilistic independence implies convergence toward symmetry. The key lesson: "optimism bias" partly reflects the mathematics of compounding risk within projects and correlation across projects, not just forecaster psychology. Drawing on reported results from well-known project datasets, the empirical illustration interprets observed patterns through this lens, showing how dispersion changes from early planning (high uncertainty) to later project stages (reduced but persistent variability). The results support log-space cost modeling, quantile-based budgeting, and grouping projects by shared risk exposure rather than superficial similarity.
summary: A stochastic framework shows that compounding proportional cost shocks within infrastructure projects and correlation across projects naturally produce right-skewed, roughly lognormal cost overruns, so apparent optimism bias partly reflects risk mathematics rather than forecaster psychology.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Impact of infrastructure investment on Chinese railway efficiency
authors: Wanting Wu; Hongchang Li; Jianda Wang; Kun Wang
keywords: Railway efficiency; Infrastructure investment; Three-stage DEA model; Regional heterogeneity; LightGBM regression model
abstract: Since 2000, China has significantly increased investment in railway infrastructure, particularly following the 2009 financial crisis. However, the effectiveness of such investment in improving railway efficiency has not been thoroughly assessed. To this end, this study uses a three-stage DEA model to evaluate the PFP and TFP of 18 railway bureaus from 2009 to 2020, analyzing the impact of infrastructure investment on railway efficiency across regions of China. Furthermore, a LightGBM regression model is employed to identify the key infrastructure factors influencing railway efficiency. We find that infrastructure investment significantly alleviates environmental heterogeneity and reduces efficiency disadvantages across regions. Efficiency improvements are primarily driven by network scale effects, as infrastructure expansion enhances network connectivity and enables railway operations to approach more efficient production scales. Moreover, the marginal efficiency gains from infrastructure investment are markedly stronger in low-efficiency regions, where infrastructure constraints are more binding. Feature importance analysis also reveals heterogeneous effects across different types of infrastructure inputs. Basic infrastructure components, including bridges, tunnels, and stations, play a dominant role in improving efficiency in low-efficiency regions, whereas infrastructure upgrading, particularly electrification and seamless tracks, has a greater impact in high-efficiency regions. These findings highlight the importance of differentiated infrastructure investment strategies, prioritizing network connectivity improvements in lagging regions while emphasizing infrastructure upgrading in more developed areas to promote balanced efficiency development within the railway sector.
summary: A three-stage DEA of 18 Chinese railway bureaus (2009-2020) finds infrastructure investment narrows regional efficiency gaps via network scale effects, with basic infrastructure paying off most in lagging regions and upgrading (electrification, seamless track) in advanced ones.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: How do subsidiary low-cost carriers affect Chinese airline market? Route entry pattern and competitive impacts
authors: Wenliang Ma; Yuankai Zhang; Weichen Peng; Xiaowen Fu; Kun Wang
keywords: Low-cost carriers; Full-service carriers; Airline-within-airline; High-speed rail; China
abstract: In recent years, Chinese full-service carriers (FSCs) have increasingly adopted the "airline-within-airline" (AinA) strategy by establishing low-cost carrier (LCC) subsidiaries. This study examines the impact of these established subsidiary LCCs in China, focusing on their route-entry patterns and competitive effects on the Big Four FSCs and the overall aviation market equilibrium. We first use descriptive statistics to provide an overview of China's LCC sector, with particular emphasis on the evolution of subsidiary LCCs. We then apply econometric models to empirically examine both the route entry patterns and the competitive effects of these subsidiary LCCs. The results reveal that Chinese subsidiary LCCs exhibit distinct features that differ from their international counterparts. (1) With respect to route-entry patterns, contrary to the patterns documented in many international markets, most subsidiary LCCs are inclined to enter routes with high-speed rail (HSR) competition and dense traffic. At the same time, they tend to avoid routes involving highly concentrated airports. There is no evidence to suggest that subsidiary LCCs support market expansion for their parent airlines in China. (2) With respect to competitive impacts, contrary to practices observed in other countries, Chinese subsidiary LCCs are not deployed as a strategic tool to compete against rival LCCs mainly because they exhibit only limited overlap in their route networks. Earlier-formed subsidiary LCCs do not appear to exert statistically significant downward pressure on their parent airlines' yields, whereas later entrant (Lucky Air) is associated with more noticeable yield reductions for the parent airlines. (3) At the route level, subsidiary LCCs are effective in stimulating passenger demand and reducing market fares, although the magnitude of these effects is substantially smaller compared to their international counterparts. Overall, this empirical study provides valuable insights and policy implications for sustainable AinA development in China and offers useful references for other emerging airline markets.
summary: Chinese full-service carriers' low-cost subsidiaries tend to enter dense routes facing high-speed rail competition rather than target rival LCCs, and they raise route demand and lower fares by much less than LCCs abroad.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Longitudinal evaluations of the coverage and pricing differences between transportation network companies and traditional taxis: A case study of New York city
authors: Hanyong Xu; Jinhua Zhao
keywords: Service accessibility; Surge pricing; Ride-hailing; Taxi services; Transportation network companies
abstract: App-based ride-hailing has expanded and operated alongside traditional street-hail taxi services for the past decade, both competing with and complementing one another. This evolution raises questions about how the two systems compare longitudinally in pricing and coverage. This study provides an empirical analysis of seven years of trip records from New York City, examining spatial and temporal differences between Transportation Network Companies (TNCs) and traditional taxis. It highlights how their comparative dynamics have evolved, particularly during major shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic and congestion pricing policy. First, the study applies trip count Log Ratios, Shannon's Entropy, the Gini Index, and counterfactual fare estimation to show that TNCs offered wider, more consistent coverage and a more pronounced price surge than taxis during the pandemic. Second, it introduces a composite typology based on fare differences and relative coverage, revealing a gradual shift toward a TNC-dominated market. Third, a spatial lag panel model with random effects, controlling for trip attributes and built environment, uncovers associations between neighborhood characteristics and the service differences between TNCs and taxis. In general, comparing before and after the pandemic, neighborhoods with more car-less households experience fare gaps reversing and TNC trips surpassing taxis, while neighborhoods with more minorities saw lower TNC fares and growing TNC share. These findings underscore the need to establish ongoing monitoring frameworks, foster competitive markets, move beyond simplistic trade-offs, address spatial disparities in algorithmic pricing, and recognize systematic change in behaviors for long-term planning.
summary: Seven years of New York City trip records show ride-hailing companies offered wider, steadier coverage but sharper pandemic surge pricing than taxis, with the market shifting toward TNC dominance, especially in car-less and minority neighborhoods.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Induced e-bike adoption from income-conditioned rebates in British Columbia: who are the marginal purchasers?
authors: Polina Polikakhina; Amir Hassanpour; Meghan Winters; Alexander Bigazzi
keywords: Electric bicycles; E-bikes; Rebates; Price incentives
abstract: Electric-assist bicycle (e-bike) purchase incentive programs have gained popularity worldwide, yet evidence on their effectiveness in generating new (marginal) e-bike purchases remains limited. The objective of this research is to examine the marginality of e-bike purchases incentivized by income-conditioned rebates (i.e., the likelihood an e-bike would not have been purchased without the rebate), and to determine whether rebate value, household income, and other factors moderate this marginality. We use survey data from 1,110 participants in two e-bike rebate programs in British Columbia, Canada. Rebate values ranged from CA$350 to CA$1,600, with higher rebate values only available to lower-income recipients. A latent class model of purchase motivations identified five types of purchasers, including Cost Minimizers (27%), Mode Substituters (17%), and Effort Minimizers (7%), along with two mixed categories of Cost Secondary (34%) and Cost Indifferent (15%) purchasers. The average likelihood of a marginal purchase was 56%, ranging from 21% to 75% with increasing rebate value. Besides the strong effect of rebate value, rebates were more effective (i.e., likely to generate a marginal purchase) when recipients were from lower-income households, commuted regularly, and were not cycling prior to the purchase. More marginal e-bike purchases were also associated with lower-priced e-bikes and rebate recipients who were younger, had a post-secondary degree, and were Cost Minimizers. The findings are promising for potential mode shift stimulated by e-bike rebate programs and support income-conditioning of e-bike rebates to improve effectiveness and equity.
summary: Among 1,110 British Columbia e-bike rebate recipients, 56% of purchases were marginal (would not have happened without the rebate), rising from 21% to 75% with rebate value and higher for lower-income, commuting, previously non-cycling recipients, supporting income-conditioned rebates.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Accelerating electric vehicle adoption in India: A System Dynamics approach considering purchase and charging infrastructure subsidies
authors: Mahavadi Dhanshyam; Ashish Srivastava; Alok Raj; Prateek Bansal
keywords: Electric vehicles; System dynamics modeling; Charging Infrastructure; Purchase subsidy; EV diffusion; Government subsidy; India
abstract: Policymakers worldwide increasingly view faster adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) as an important pathway to reducing transport-related greenhouse gas emissions. However, EV adoption is shaped by interactions among various stakeholders and by a range of economic, technological, infrastructural, and perceptual factors. To examine this dynamic process, we develop a System Dynamics (SD) model comprising five interlinked modules—the Vehicle Adoption Dynamics Module, EV Utility and Market Share Module, Cost and Market Evolution Module, Charging Infrastructure Module, and subsidy module that considers two policy levers: a purchase subsidy and a charging infrastructure subsidy. Using India's EV market as the empirical setting, we examine the relative effectiveness of these two policy instruments under 14 scenarios. Our results show that under the Business-as-Usual scenario, adoption is initially driven by affordability and later by convenience, especially through reduced range anxiety and improved service support. While purchase subsidies generate stronger short-run gains by overcoming the early affordability barrier, their marginal impact declines over time, and they impose a higher fiscal burden. In contrast, charging infrastructure subsidies are more cost-efficient, producing stronger long-run adoption gains by improving charging availability, reducing range anxiety, and supporting ecosystem development. Overall, a phased composite policy mix performs better than both standalone interventions and extreme front-loaded support, indicating that early affordability support combined with sustained infrastructure investment is the most effective and fiscally prudent strategy for accelerating EV adoption. These findings offer practical guidance for policymakers designing EV-promotion strategies that are both effective and fiscally prudent.
summary: A System Dynamics model of India's EV market shows purchase subsidies deliver faster early gains but charging-infrastructure subsidies are more cost-efficient in the long run, with a phased policy mix outperforming either alone.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Quality or convenience? Behavioral evidence on how facility grade influences urban destination choice
authors: Yang Zhou; Sicheng Wang; Chaofan Wang; Quan Yuan; Tianren Yang
keywords: Travel behavior; Destination choice modeling; Facility-grade heterogeneity; Nested logit model; Non-work activity
abstract: Modeling non-work activity destination choices is essential for urban transportation planning, as these activities involve greater flexibility and more complex behavioral decision-making than mandatory activities. However, existing studies often treat all facilities within the same activity category as homogeneous and have rarely examined how facility-grade heterogeneity shapes individuals' destination preferences. To address this gap, this study develops a hierarchical location choice modeling framework that explicitly incorporates facility-grade distinctions into the destination choice process. Four common non-work activity categories—shopping, dining-out, recreation, and medical care—are analyzed, with urban facilities classified into high-grade and low-grade types. Destination choice sets are generated using fuzzy logic inference and stratified importance sampling that account for both travel distance and facility grade. Conditional logit (CL) and nested logit (NL) models are then estimated to capture alternative-specific utilities and within-grade correlations. Results show that (i) destination choices exhibit distinct decision-making logic across facility grades, with high-grade facilities usually planned for quality-seeking purposes and low-grade facilities primarily serving convenience-oriented needs; (ii) facility-grade heterogeneity significantly shapes destination choice behavior, with preferences varying across activity purposes and population groups; (iii) the nested logit results reveal correlated destination choices within facility-grade categories, highlighting the importance of accounting for within-grade substitution patterns when modeling non-work destination choices; and (iv) the effects of accessibility improvements vary across activity types, with stronger impacts observed for shopping and recreation and comparatively limited impacts for dining-out and medical-care. These findings highlight the critical role of facility-grade heterogeneity in shaping non-work travel behavior and offer new insights for demand analysis and facility planning.
summary: Nested logit models of shopping, dining, recreation and medical trips show that people choose high-grade facilities for quality and low-grade ones for convenience, and that accessibility improvements shift destination choice more for shopping and recreation than for dining or medical care.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: The reverse side of online shopping: examining sociodemographic and built-environment determinants of delivery returns
authors: Angela J. Haddad; Chandra R. Bhat
keywords: E-commerce returns; Online shopping behavior; Transportation planning; Reverse logistics; Consumer behavior; Built environment
abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce has created new transportation challenges through increased product returns, yet the behavioral determinants of delivery return patterns remain understudied from a consumer-centric perspective. This research develops a comprehensive econometric framework to analyze online shopping frequency, delivery return rates, and the realized distribution of returns across channels using data from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey (NHTS). We employ a multivariate modeling approach integrating probit ordered-response and probit fractional response models to examine three interconnected outcomes: (1) frequency of online goods purchases, (2) proportion of online purchases returned, and (3) distribution of returns across four channels (home pickup, post office, Amazon drop-off, and physical store). The modeling framework accounts for causal relationships between outcomes while controlling for unobserved factors that lead to correlations across the three dimensions just listed. Results reveal significant sociodemographic heterogeneity in online purchasing and return behavior. Women, teleworkers, individuals with higher formal education, and those with higher incomes tend to exhibit increased e-commerce engagement. Older adults and zero-vehicle households, in contrast, have lower online purchase participation and return accessibility. Built environment factors significantly influence return behaviors, with rural residents showing reduced return rates and limited access to Amazon drop-off locations, while individuals residing in areas with high retail density exhibit increased use of Amazon drop-off and physical store returns. The analysis reveals causal relationships where higher online shopping frequency is associated with increased return rates, and both shopping frequency and return rates jointly influence return channel choices. These findings have important implications for transportation planning and urban logistics, highlighting the need for policies that ensure equitable return access and the importance of integrating e-commerce return trips into travel demand models.
summary: Joint models of 2022 NHTS data show online shopping and return behavior vary strongly by sociodemographics and built environment, with rural residents returning less and having poorer drop-off access while high-retail-density residents use drop-off and in-store returns more.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Evaluating urban rail transit vulnerability: A link-centric framework integrating network connectivity and passenger accessibility
authors: Yun Wang; Rufan Yang; Yunqiao Xiang; Mingfang Yuan; Yu Zhou; Xuedong Yan; Xing Chen
keywords: Urban rail transit; Link disruption; Network vulnerability; Accessibility assessment; Passenger assignment
abstract: Understanding how disruptions reshape network structure and generate heterogeneous accessibility losses is essential for vulnerability assessment in urban rail transit (URT) systems. This study develops a unified link-centric framework that jointly examines disruption-induced structural changes and passenger accessibility consequences under multi-scenario settings. Disruption scenarios are constructed using an interval-based representation that captures structural dependencies under turn-back constraints, ensuring realistic propagation patterns. Passenger impacts are evaluated through an OD-level accessibility classification based on feasible paths and detour thresholds, distinguishing unaffected, partially affected, and fully affected OD pairs. These components are integrated through a composite link-importance indicator that couples network topology with demand distribution, enabling identification of structurally critical and functionally consequential links. The framework links structural fragility with passenger outcomes, supporting more realistic identification of critical links based on structural dependency and accessibility loss. Application to the Beijing URT network shows that vulnerability is concentrated in the southwestern corridor, particularly along the Fangshan Line and southern Line 9, where disruptions cause significant accessibility losses. Targeted structural interventions effectively mitigate impacts, as adding a connection in the vulnerable corridor reduces fully affected OD pairs from 10,565 to 2,470. Sensitivity analysis confirms the stability of identified vulnerable regions under different penalty factors, while validation in Shenzhen and Nanchang demonstrates the framework's transferability across systems with varying sizes, topologies, and demand patterns. This study provides a unified, demand-sensitive framework linking structural disruptions with accessibility outcomes, offering practical guidance for resilience-oriented URT planning and emergency management.
summary: A link-centric vulnerability framework coupling network topology with passenger accessibility identifies Beijing's southwestern rail corridor as most vulnerable, where adding one connection would cut fully affected OD pairs from 10,565 to 2,470.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Context-sensitive effects of the built environment on HelloRide e-bike sharing demand
authors: Xiang Liu; Yijia Hu; Ailing Yin; Yang Huang; Yongping Zhang
keywords: E-bike; Micromobility; Built environment; Context-sensitive planning; Suburban
abstract: E-bike sharing is an emerging micromobility service that offers a higher travel speed and greater riding comfort than other micromobility modes. Although the deployment of e-bike sharing services has expanded rapidly worldwide, the relationship between e-bike sharing demand and the built environment remains insufficiently understood, particularly across different urban contexts. Using five weekdays of trip data from the HelloRide in Kunming (China), and employing Spatial Lag Models, this study examines how built environment characteristics are associated with e-bike sharing demand in urban, suburban, and rural areas. The results indicate that population density, land-use mix, and public transport accessibility are positively associated with e-bike sharing demand across most contexts, while the effects of street-network characteristics, housing prices, and distance to the city centre vary considerably across space. These findings support capacity allocation decisions for service providers and highlight the need for context-sensitive shared e-bike governance strategies for planners and policy-makers.
summary: Spatial lag models of HelloRide trips in Kunming show population density, land-use mix and transit access raise shared e-bike demand across urban, suburban and rural areas, while street-network, housing-price and centrality effects vary by context.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Does ride-hailing moderate the relationship between public transit preference and transit use?
authors: Ruijia Sun; Kunbo Shi; Frank Witlox; Tianren Yang
keywords: Travel attitudes; Pro-transit users; Sustainable mobility; Public transit; Ride-hailing; China
abstract: It has been widely accepted that people who have a strong preference for public transit tend to use public transit more frequently. However, the growing popularity of ride-hailing systems, by offering door-to-door mobility services, may be correlated with a decline in people's reliance on public transit. Therefore, a critical question arises: Does ride-hailing moderate the positive relationship between public transit preference and transit use? To empirically investigate this question, this study uses data from an online questionnaire survey covering 81 Chinese cities, yielding a total of 7,205 valid participants. The results indicate that a high preference for public transit is strongly correlated with frequent public transit trips (including both bus and metro). However, with ride-hailing frequency increasing, this positive association becomes significantly less pronounced. These findings reshape the traditional understanding of the relationship between public transit preference and public transit use, indicating that the popularization of ride-hailing is potentially linked to lower loyalty among pro-transit users. This poses a new challenge to the sustainability transition of urban transportation systems and calls for strategic policies to address it.
summary: A survey of 7,205 residents in 81 Chinese cities finds that strong transit preference predicts frequent bus and metro use, but this link weakens significantly as ride-hailing use rises, signaling eroding loyalty among pro-transit travelers.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Modelling the effects of travel time use on mode choice and the value of travel time savings: tackling self-selection and endogeneity bias
authors: Ana Luiza S. de Sá; Patrícia S. Lavieri; Jacek Pawlak; Charisma F. Choudhury
keywords: Travel time use; Travel-based multitasking; Integrated Choice Latent Variable model; Value of travel time; Mode choice
abstract: Travel time use (i.e., conducting activities while travelling) can have substantial impacts on crucial transport dimensions: mode choice and the value of travel time savings (VTTS). Preferences for travel-based activities may lead individuals to choose travel modes that best accommodate activity needs. In theory, "passengerised" modes, such as public transport and automated vehicles (AVs), could become the preferred options, as they enable a wider range of activities. This potential to use in-vehicle time could, in turn, decrease VTTS, thereby reducing resistance to longer journeys. However, previous research has faced challenges in disentangling these effects due to self-selection and endogeneity bias. This study aims to investigate the effects of travel time use on mode choice and VTTS while addressing these challenges. To achieve this, it employs an attitude-based approach to capture mode choice self-selection and control endogeneity in VTTS estimates by considering traveller- and travel-related characteristics that influence travel time use and accounting for value of time heterogeneity. Results suggest that the construct capturing the causal effect of travel time use on mode choice increases the probability of choosing rail modes in journeys over 5 km and car driving in journeys shorter than 5 km, confirming the presence of self-selection. Regarding VTTS, accounting for traveller and travel context characteristics yielded non-significant effects of travel-based activities on VTTS, suggesting that this approach may effectively control for endogeneity bias. These findings have implications for road safety, residential location choice, and potential AV-related behavioural changes, all of which have consequences for transport planning, policy, and appraisal. Overall, this study highlights the importance of accounting for travel time use to achieve a more realistic representation of activity-travel behaviour.
summary: An integrated choice and latent variable model shows that valuing in-vehicle activities raises the likelihood of choosing rail for trips over 5 km (and driving for shorter trips), while travel-based activities have no significant effect on the value of travel time savings once endogeneity is controlled.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: A New Approach to collinearity and elasticity problems in value of travel time savings estimation with multinomial logit models
authors: Louis de Grange; Matthieu Marechal; Raúl Pezoa; Felipe González; Rodrigo Troncoso
keywords: Value of travel time savings; Collinearity; Elasticity; Multinomial logit models; Constrained estimation; Hausman test
abstract: The value of travel time savings (VTTS) is a central parameter in transport-project appraisal. When estimated from a multinomial logit (MNL) model of mode choice, the VTTS can become imprecise under two structural conditions of the data: strong collinearity between travel time and travel cost, common in revealed-preference samples where cost is imputed at a fixed rate per kilometer; and low absolute price-elasticity of demand, which makes the estimated cost coefficient close to zero and inflates the variance of the VTTS estimator, formed as a ratio with that coefficient in the denominator. Both conditions share a common cause: the cost coefficient is not well identified by the data. This paper diagnoses both conditions analytically and through simulation, and proposes an elasticity-constrained estimator that addresses this common cause by tying the cost coefficient to a value consistent with external price-elasticity evidence. The estimator is compared through simulations to maximum likelihood and ridge estimation. The results show that under adverse collinearity and demand elasticity conditions, maximum likelihood estimates exhibit high variance and errors, even with large samples, while ridge estimates display less variance and improved stability but also significant levels of bias. By contrast, the proposed method, although it introduces bias if the actual demand elasticity is distant from that of the applied restriction, achieves lower values for mean squared error. The three methods are also compared in an application to the Swissmetro mode choice dataset. The results in this case show that although multinomial logit can, in theory, be consistent, the elasticity-constrained method again obtains the lowest mean squared error by reducing the variance of the VTTS estimates. The ridge estimator, meanwhile, proved to be less competitive. Complementing these comparative findings are the results of the Hausman test. The proposed estimator is recommended for VTTS estimation in revealed-preference contexts where strong collinearity and inelastic demand jointly compromise identification, and we provide guidance on the contexts in which it is most useful and on its relationship with alternatives such as willingness-to-pay-space estimation.
summary: An elasticity-constrained multinomial logit estimator that anchors the cost coefficient to external price-elasticity evidence yields lower mean squared error for value-of-travel-time-savings estimates than maximum likelihood or ridge estimation when time and cost are collinear and demand is inelastic.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: When air meets ground: Modeling the congestion externalities of urban air mobility in integrated air-ground transportation networks
authors: Zhenwei Gong; Zhuoye Zhang; Fangni Zhang
keywords: Urban air mobility; Air-ground integrated system; Network equilibrium; Macroscopic fundamental diagram
abstract: This study develops an integrated modeling framework to analyze the network equilibrium and congestion externalities of Urban Air Mobility (UAM) within a low-altitude air-ground transportation system. The model couples a ground transportation network with a low-altitude airspace network via vertiports, incorporating elastic traveler demand with cross-price effects and employing Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams to capture traffic dynamics in both layers. We investigate how system controls (perimeter boundary and vertiport operations), UAM network design, and pricing strategies influence overall system performance. Analytical findings reveal significant paradoxes: well-intentioned perimeter and vertiport controls can exacerbate congestion (control paradox), airspace capacity expansion may worsen system-wide conditions (capacity paradox), and fare adjustments can produce counterproductive demand shifts (pricing paradox). These paradoxes are fundamentally driven by the interplay between demand elasticities and the coupling strength between air and ground networks. Numerical experiments based on Hong Kong Island demonstrate that the impact of UAM is highly sensitive to network design: while UAM services with very few routes have limited system-wide effects, a complex, highly connected network acts as a powerful network reconfiguration tool, redistributing demand and fostering a more polycentric and resilient urban structure. Sensitivity analyses further show that the control paradox is amplified by low own-price sensitivity and high cross-price sensitivity for ground controls, whereas airspace and vertiport controls exhibit opposite patterns. The study underscores that the primary value of UAM lies not merely in point-to-point speed but in its potential as a strategic lever for reshaping city-wide mobility. Our framework provides critical insights for policymakers and operators to navigate these complexities and design integrated management strategies that harness the benefits of UAM while mitigating unintended congestion spillovers.
summary: A coupled air-ground network equilibrium model with elastic demand reveals control, capacity and pricing paradoxes in urban air mobility, and Hong Kong Island simulations show that only highly connected UAM networks meaningfully redistribute demand toward a more polycentric urban structure.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Incentive-driven evolutionary game for maritime decarbonization: Evidence from Shanghai Port
authors: Le Hong; Lang Xu; Ran Yan
keywords: Maritime decarbonization; Evolutionary game theory; Multi-stakeholder coordination; Policy incentives; Policy coherence; LNG retrofitting
abstract: Maritime transport underpins global trade, but remains a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, posing challenges for coordinated decarbonization. This paper develops a four-stakeholder evolutionary game model (4S-EGM) to analyze strategic interactions among the International Maritime Organization (IMO), port states, terminal operators, and shipowners, with the port state as the central decision-maker. The model integrates regulatory enforcement, financial incentives, and infrastructure investment and is contextualized through liquefied natural gas (LNG) retrofitting, with parameters referenced to Shanghai Port. Replicator dynamics, stability analysis, and sensitivity analysis are used to identify conditions supporting cooperation. The model evaluates the joint effects of green subsidies, carbon-related market benefits, initial conditions, and profit-sharing arrangements. The results show that cooperation depends on coordinated incentives, initial-condition path dependence, and contractual alignment through profit-sharing. Conditional parameter-sensitivity analysis further indicates that, under a supportive incentive configuration, full cooperation remains unchanged under moderate variations in most examined parameters except the subsidy and carbon-related market benefit. However, cooperation is not unconditional: the system does not reach full cooperation when these incentives are removed, while excessive subsidy costs may disrupt it. The findings emphasize combining sufficiently strong incentives with fiscally sustainable subsidy arrangements and provide scenario-based policy implications for coordinating stakeholder actions in transitional-fuel adoption and maritime decarbonization.
summary: A four-stakeholder evolutionary game calibrated to Shanghai Port shows that cooperation on LNG retrofitting for maritime decarbonization requires coordinated subsidies, carbon-market benefits and profit-sharing, collapsing without incentives and destabilizing when subsidy costs become excessive.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Identification of emission characteristics under global shipping decarbonization pathways
authors: Lang Xu; Lele Li; Jihong Chen; Ran Yan; Yang Zhang
keywords: Emission characteristics; Generative model; Global shipping; Mitigation target; Shipping decarbonization
abstract: Maritime shipping is central to global trade and climate mitigation. We propose an interpretable generative modeling framework to characterize shipping carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and analyze shipping decarbonization pathways via 1,202 scenarios from the IPCC AR6 database. Climate categories are consolidated into three mitigation groups, and 50 shipping-related variables are converted into cumulative-change features. We then train three generative models to produce synthetic mitigation scenarios and evaluate their performance through bidirectional random-forest (RF) label-transfer tests, distributional realism and structural consistency checks. The results suggest that shipping CO2 emissions are associated with the joint variation in demand heterogeneity, energy-system conditions, policy stringency, and fuel substitution. The synthetic scenarios further demonstrate that higher carbon prices, greater power electrification, and lower oil-based fuel dependence are consistently associated with lower-emission shipping pathways. These findings offer a data-driven basis for identifying CO2 emission characteristics and supporting long-term shipping decarbonization strategies.
summary: Generative models trained on 1,202 IPCC AR6 scenarios indicate that higher carbon prices, greater power electrification and lower oil-based fuel dependence are consistently associated with lower-emission global shipping pathways.

journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
title: Substitution and user heterogeneity in electric moped and bike sharing for first- and last-mile transit in Taiwan
authors: Hui-Chieh Li; Jyun-Kai Liang; Yu-Shyun Chien
keywords: Shared mobility; Market segmentation; First- and last-mile; Integrated choice and latent variable model
abstract: In Taiwan, where motorcycle ownership is widespread, the rapid growth of electric moped sharing (EMS) and bike-sharing services for first- and last-mile connectivity has intensified competition among micromobility modes and public transport. Understanding the substitution dynamics between these modes is critical for cities pursuing sustainable mobility transitions while curbing private vehicle dependency. This study applies a hybrid ICLV-MIMIC-LCL modeling framework to analyze stated preference data from 547 Taipei metro users, integrating observed travel behavior with latent psychological factors. Three distinct user segments were identified: time- and cost-sensitive bike-sharing users, convenience-oriented bus users, and flexible micromobility users. Results indicate that dedicated EMS parking primarily draws demand from buses (−5.37 %) rather than bike-sharing (−3.89 %). Dedicated EMS parking emerges as a key driver of adoption, enabling a meaningful modal shift from private motorcycles to shared micromobility. This shift offers greater sustainability benefits than policies that merely redistribute demand among public transport modes. The findings provide segment-specific policy insights for EMS and bike-sharing positioning, targeted parking infrastructure investment, and cost-sensitive subsidy design, supporting enhanced first- and last-mile connectivity and Net Zero Emissions goals in moped-dominant Asian cities.
summary: Stated-preference models of 547 Taipei metro users identify three first/last-mile user segments and show dedicated electric-moped-sharing parking draws demand mainly from buses (-5.37%) and bike sharing (-3.89%) while also shifting riders away from private motorcycles.

title: How do firm circular economy practices affect supply chain resilience from a sustainable development perspective?
authors: Xueya Xu; Vincent Charles; Tatiana Gherman; Wanzhen Li; Xin Zhao
keywords: Circular economy; Supply chain resilience; Resource effect; Structural effect; Collaboration effect; Machine learning
abstract: Under increasing external uncertainty, promoting sustainable transformation and building data-driven supply chain resilience (SCR) supported by frontier technologies has become an important issue. This study uses Chinese A-share listed companies from 2005 to 2024 as the sample. From the perspective of frontier technologies, it employs text analysis and machine learning to identify large-scale unstructured annual report texts and quantify firm circular economy (CE) practices. SCR is measured using an entropy-weighted indicator system, and the relationship between CE practices and SCR is examined using panel regression models. The results show that CE practices significantly improve SCR, and the findings remain robust across multiple robustness and endogeneity tests.
