Mechanism analysis indicates that CE practices enhance SCR through three channels: resource effects, structural effects, and collaboration effects. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the positive effect is more pronounced in non-state-owned firms, firms in non-heavy-polluting industries, high factor-intensive firms, and firms with active environmental information disclosure, as well as in regions with higher economic development and stronger governmental attention to green development, and in the period following the signing of the Paris Agreement in 2015. Further analysis shows that CE practices significantly improve the resistance dimension of SCR, while their effect on recovery is insignificant. Economic consequence analysis indicates that SCR enhancement driven by CE practices helps reduce operational risk and increase firm value. This study provides new empirical evidence on how CE practices strengthen SCR, and offers theoretical and practical implications for enabling sustainable supply chain development through frontier technologies and data-driven analytics.
summary: Text-mining annual reports of Chinese listed firms (2005-2024), the study finds circular economy practices strengthen supply chain resilience, mainly its resistance dimension, via resource, structural and collaboration channels, lowering operational risk and raising firm value.

title: E-commerce supply chain planning with Space-as-a-Service: Two-stage stochastic programming approach
authors: Seungchae Na; Sangjun Yoon; Junhyeok Lee; Youngchul Shin
keywords: E-commerce supply chain planning; Space-as-a-Service; Two-stage stochastic programming; Benders decomposition algorithm
abstract: Digital technologies have transformed the retail industry, shifting it from traditional offline markets to online sales. In response, many companies have adopted micro-fulfillment centers in urban areas. However, high initial investments, expensive rents, and limited storage space make it difficult to handle peak demand. Recently, Space-as-a-Service providers have emerged, offering idle logistics spaces that retailers can use to supplement insufficient capacity. Despite the growing adoption of such services, most existing studies have not fully considered practical issues such as demand uncertainty, flexible rental sizes, and the handling of residual stock when leases expire. To address this gap, we consider a supply chain network design problem in an e-commerce environment that incorporates these practical concerns. We formulate the problem as a two-stage stochastic program to incorporate the demand uncertainty and solve it by combining the sample average approximation method with an accelerated Benders decomposition algorithm. Computational results demonstrate that the proposed approach efficiently provides high-quality solutions.
summary: A two-stage stochastic program solved with sample average approximation and accelerated Benders decomposition designs e-commerce supply chain networks that rent idle urban logistics space on demand (Space-as-a-Service) under demand uncertainty.

title: How should workers be prepared for Industry 4.0? Antecedents of employee readiness for digital transformation
authors: Carla Diniz S. Silva; Lino Guimarães Marujo; Pedro Senna
keywords: Change management; Digital transformation; Employee readiness; Human factors; Industry 4.0; Systematic literature review
abstract: This study develops a conceptual framework to identify the antecedents of employee readiness for digital transformation within the context of Industry 4.0. Drawing on theories of Change Management and Information Systems, it addresses a critical conceptual gap by shifting the analytical focus from organizational readiness and technological maturity to individual-level preparedness. A systematic literature review was conducted using the Web of Science and Scopus databases, resulting in the analysis of 434 studies published between 2017 and 2023. The review reveals that employee readiness remains underexplored, with existing models predominantly emphasizing technological, structural, and organizational dimensions while neglecting human and social factors. Five antecedents of employee readiness were identified: new business models and processes, awareness, supportive leadership, digital inclusion, and digital skills. Each construct was mapped to observable variables, yielding a testable conceptual framework with research propositions. This study represents the first integrative attempt to conceptualize employee readiness for Industry 4.0 at the individual level, offering a theoretical foundation for future empirical research. From a practical and socio-economic planning perspective, the framework guides organizations and policymakers seeking to foster workforce preparedness and mitigate digital transformation-related labor-market risks.
summary: A systematic review of 434 studies (2017-2023) identifies five antecedents of individual employee readiness for Industry 4.0 (new business models and processes, awareness, supportive leadership, digital inclusion and digital skills) and builds them into a testable framework.

title: Balancing human and digital aspects in the retailers' loyalty measurement
authors: Sandro Castaldo; Andrea Ciacci; Lara Penco; Ginevra Testa
keywords: Customer loyalty; Measurement; Human-to-human relationship; Digital touchpoint; Relational governance; Retail; Gioia method
abstract: In the contemporary retail sector, characterized by high dynamism and frequent customer switching behaviors, customer loyalty represents a strategic cornerstone. The multidimensional nature of loyalty, fierce competition between alternative formats, and evolving company-customer interactions in digital and physical contexts are leading retailers to reassess their customer loyalty measurement strategies. In this evolving scenario, loyalty increasingly emerges not only as a transactional outcome but as a relational construct grounded in trust and continuous human interaction. This research aims to investigate how retailers measure and manage customer loyalty and how retailers plan to improve customer loyalty measurements in the future, considering the relevance of human-to-human and human-to-technology relationships. To address these objectives, the study applies a qualitative exploratory methodology, following the Gioia approach, based on in-depth interviews with Italian grocery retailers. The findings reveal key issues crucial for the innovation of loyalty measurement strategies. Five aggregate dimensions emerge from the analysis, namely: 1) Overemphasis on behavioral/transactional loyalty measurements; 2) Phygital touchpoints; 3) Loyalty measurement governance; 4) New loyalty perspectives; and 5) Trust-based relationship with customers as a crucial loyalty strategy to preserve relationships. Across these dimensions, the research highlights how achieving trust-based loyalty represents a journey in which organizations tend to continuously improve their measurements to capture not only purchase behavior but also emotional attachment, commitment, and long-term relational value. The study contributes to the literature by emphasizing the centrality of trust and relational dynamics in loyalty measurement systems and offers practical implications for professionals seeking to develop a more human-centered and customer-centered KPI framework.
summary: Interviews with Italian grocery retailers, analysed with the Gioia method, reveal an overemphasis on transactional loyalty metrics and a shift toward phygital touchpoints and trust-based relational measures of customer loyalty.

title: Multi-country analysis of healthy life expectancy gap
authors: Emilia Di Lorenzo; Gabriella Piscopo; Alba Roviello; Marilena Sibillo
keywords: Healthy life expectancy; HALE gap ratio; Functional data clustering; Health inequality; Quality of life
abstract: Life expectancy (LE) at birth is one of the most used indicator to quantify possible future lifespan and quality of life of populations. However, critical challenges are associated with health conditions in later life, during which the need for appropriate healthcare facilities and long-term care systems is intensified. In this context, switching to indexes that consider future life expectancy in good health results to be more informative. In this paper we focus on the Healthy-Adjusted Life Expectancy (HALE) and construct the Healthy Life Expectancy Gap Ratio (HGR). HALE measures the average number of years that an individual will spend in good health while HGR provides a normalized measure of the inequality in health between countries. Taking into account HALE at birth of the global population over the period 1999–2023, made available by the Global Burden of Disease (GBD), and considering High-Income countries as a benchmark, a functional data clustering procedure is applied to global HGR with the aim of providing a multi-country perspective and to assess for similarities among different areas. Our findings shows that distinct clusters can be observed, suggesting a heterogeneous pattern of convergence toward high-income health standards. These results emphasize the need for a strong intervention to improve health system quality and public health policy in order to mitigate factors shaping HGR different dynamics.
summary: Functional data clustering of a new Healthy Life Expectancy Gap Ratio built from GBD data (1999-2023) reveals distinct country clusters and heterogeneous convergence toward high-income healthy life expectancy standards.

title: Risk-averse placement optimization in refugee resettlement
authors: Fatemeh Farajzadeh; Narges Ahani; Osman Y. Özaltın; Andrew C. Trapp
keywords: Refugee resettlement; Optimization under uncertainty; Risk; Fairness
abstract: Operational decision-making for refugee resettlement is an emerging area of research in humanitarian operations and public-sector planning. These decisions are irreversible, with substantial consequences for refugee integration outcomes and host communities. Previous studies have relied on employment likelihood as a key measure of refugee integration, and used it as a quality score to guide optimal placement decisions of refugees into communities. Motivated by the inherent uncertainty in these point estimates, we propose risk-averse placement optimization models and examine the extent to which uncertainty can be appropriately incorporated in light of the risk preferences of the decision-makers. The varying levels of risk reduction observed across families provide further motivation to pursue fairness in allocation, so that particularly vulnerable refugees with the lowest employment likelihoods are not disproportionally disadvantaged. We developed three formulations that progressively model risk: in the aggregate, at the family level, and by adding fairness considerations for families. The proposed models aim to achieve stronger risk reduction while maintaining expected outcomes. Computational experiments on real refugee data show that, at comparable expected employment levels, mean family-level risk decreases from 73% to 53% when moving from aggregate to family-level risk, while adding fairness reduces outcome variability by approximately 50% on average for families with lower employment likelihoods. Our research offers several planning insights into operational improvements in refugee resettlement. We demonstrate the value of risk-aware approaches that empower decision makers to optimize placement decisions while mitigating outcome uncertainties for refugees.
summary: Risk-averse refugee placement models tested on real resettlement data cut mean family-level employment risk from 73% to 53% at comparable expected employment, and adding fairness halves outcome variability for families with the lowest employment prospects.

title: Closed-loop pharmaceutical supply chains: State of the art, emerging trends, and future research needs
authors: Fatemeh Shekoohi; Payam Afkhami; Bokang Li; Mohsen Khabir; Nasrin Malekpoor Joneghani; Maxim A. Dulebenets
keywords: Pharmaceutical supply chains; Closed-loop supply chains; Reverse logistics; Circular economy; Waste management; Sustainability; Resilience
abstract: The growing complexity of pharmaceutical logistics, combined with increasing medication use and frequent global health emergencies, emphasizes the need for closed-loop pharmaceutical supply chains that improve sustainability, resilience, and public health consequences. This study presents a systematic and comprehensive review of closed-loop pharmaceutical supply chains, which integrate forward and reverse logistics to assist product recovery, reuse, and recycling during the pharmaceutical lifespan. Over seventy relevant peer-reviewed studies published during the past two decades are investigated, involving applications in closed-loop pharmaceutical supply chains, waste management, closed-loop vaccine supply chains, and other healthcare contexts. Each study is evaluated according to its closed-loop features, sustainability dimensions, resilience attributes, methodological approaches, modeling characteristics, and case study settings. The analysis depicts that current research concentrates greatly on reverse logistics operations, economic-environmental trade-offs, and exact optimization approaches, while often neglecting essential factors, including social sustainability considerations, circular economy principles, and supply chain resilience against disruptions. Several key knowledge gaps have been identified: the lack of holistic multi-stage models that address complete product lifetime, poor incorporation of social sustainability measures in strategic decisions, minimal use of advanced analytical methodologies, and insufficient empirical validation across diverse regulatory frameworks. This review provides comprehensive strategies for establishing closed-loop pharmaceutical supply chains that are socially inclusive, environmentally responsible, logistically practical, and resilient to systemic disturbances by identifying the existing weaknesses and presenting the current state of the field. The results provide useful insights for researchers, supply chain planners, and policymakers aiming to boost the sustainability, adaptability, and efficiency of pharmaceutical supply networks.
summary: A systematic review of over seventy studies on closed-loop pharmaceutical supply chains finds research concentrated on reverse logistics and economic-environmental trade-offs while neglecting social sustainability, circular economy principles and disruption resilience.

title: Evaluating synthetic population approaches for Italian municipal-level microdata
authors: Silvia Scarpa; Massimo Baldini; Andrea Barigazzi; Giovanni Gallo; Marcello Morciano
keywords: Synthetic population; Spatial microsimulation; Reweighting algorithm; Policy evaluation
abstract: The growing demand for fine-scale microdata to support ex-ante and ex-post small area public policy evaluation is often hampered by a familiar trade-off: socio-economic surveys offer rich individual and household information but only at coarse geographic levels, while administrative sources provide detailed local counts with limited variable depth. This paper addresses this challenge by systematically implementing and evaluating deterministic (Iterative Proportional Fitting, Generalized Regression) and probabilistic (Simulated Annealing) reweighting algorithms to align survey weights with known population benchmarks. As a practical application, we construct a spatially disaggregated synthetic population representing the residents of the municipalities in the Emilia-Romagna region (NUTS 2 level) from the Italian EU-SILC data. Our comparative analysis highlights the trade-offs between the computational efficiency of deterministic methods and the precision of probabilistic approaches. By providing a robust foundation for spatial microsimulation models, this work offers practical guidance for researchers navigating the constraints of method fidelity, computational resources, and statistical accuracy.
summary: Comparing deterministic (IPF, GREG) and probabilistic (simulated annealing) reweighting to build a municipal-level synthetic population for Emilia-Romagna from EU-SILC, the study shows a trade-off between computational efficiency and precision for spatial microsimulation of local policy.

title: Scheduling working shifts of train dispatchers considering workers' preferences
authors: David Canca; Francisco A. Ortega; Ramón Piedra-de-la-Cuadra
keywords: Schedule design; Shift scheduling; Railway dispatching; Evolutionary algorithms
abstract: Railway dispatchers are responsible for monitoring the train locations, communicating with train crews, and supervising the train movements to prevent accidents and ensuring service punctuality. This research proposes a new mathematical formulation based on feasible working and rest block patterns that integrates mandatory surveillance requirements with dispatcher preferences. The computational complexity of this problem for large real-life scenarios suggests the need to develop heuristic procedures to obtain good solutions in short computation times. We developed an Evolutionary Algorithm and a suite of eight specialized metrics to assess solution quality across 105 experimental configurations, including scenarios with isolated and time-bound surveillance zones. Our results reveal a significant finding: the algorithm maintains absolute adherence (100%) to structural and legal shift requirements while successfully navigating the complex search space of individual zone and hour preferences. Validated against the Madrid commuter rail network, the proposed approach achieves near-optimal global scores, providing a scalable solution for managing the complex interplay between operational safety and workforce satisfaction.
summary: An evolutionary algorithm for train-dispatcher shift scheduling fully satisfies legal and structural shift rules while accommodating workers' zone and hour preferences, achieving near-optimal results on the Madrid commuter rail network.

title: Digital transformation, price discrimination, and equity in medical tourism trade: A North–South framework
authors: Tonmoy Chatterjee
keywords: Medical tourism; International trade; Quality of life; Digitally enabled quality innovation; Income redistribution; Monte Carlo simulation; Dynamic game; North–South framework
abstract: The current study examines how digital transformation reshapes the economics of medical tourism within a North–South framework, focusing on its effects on inequality and quality of life. This model features a dynamic setup in which a Southern-based Multinational Medical Tourism Service Provider (MMTSP) engages in price differentiation and digitally enabled quality innovation amid income disparities and cross-border market integration. Unlike typical trade models, this analysis places medical tourism within a rapidly digitalizing ecosystem characterized by platform intermediation, algorithmic pricing, and AI-enabled diagnostics. This shift from physically mediated exchange to digitally coordinated healthcare markets reflects a larger move from Homo Sapiens to Homo Digitalis, raising important concerns about access, quality of life, and the distribution of welfare benefits. The model includes state-led income redistribution in the South to explore how domestic equity policies interact with international competitiveness. Additionally, Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess how changes in spending capacity, patient mobility, and regional cost differences influence quality of life, equilibrium prices, and market reach. The results show that digital mobility and improved domestic health access strengthen incentives for digitally enabled quality innovation and enhance trade viability. However, without redistributive and regulatory safeguards, digital transformation might worsen inequality by expanding health access gaps and concentrating market power. Overall, the findings suggest that the advantages of digital medical tourism rely on inclusive policies that promote equitable healthcare access and support sustainable improvements in quality of life.
summary: A North-South dynamic trade model with Monte Carlo simulations shows digital transformation strengthens quality innovation and trade viability in medical tourism, but without redistributive and regulatory safeguards it can widen health-access gaps and concentrate market power.

title: Digital twin use-case prioritisation for sustainability in smart manufacturing: A multi-criteria decision analytics approach
authors: Adel Ben Youssef; Adelina Zeqiri; Sama Mbang
keywords: Digital twin; Supply chain resilience; Sustainable manufacturing; Multi-criteria decision analysis; TOPSIS; VIKOR; SMAA; Industry 4.0
abstract: Manufacturers face growing pressure to invest in digital twins for sustainability and supply chain resilience. Yet, no systematic framework exists to guide the prioritisation of use cases amid competing objectives and practical resource constraints. Digital twins, which integrate real-time sensing, simulation, big data analytics, and artificial intelligence, are among the frontier technologies reshaping industrial production, and their prioritisation is a core socio-economic planning problem of the Industry 4.0 transition. This study addresses this gap by developing an interview-informed multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) that prioritises seven recurring digital twin use cases based on sustainability and operational benefits, as well as implementation and scaling burdens. The decision model scores sustainability benefits and feasibility burdens directly. At the same time, implications for supply chain resilience are interpreted ex post through the comparative positioning of the use cases rather than being scored as a separate family of criteria. Drawing on 50 semi-structured expert interviews conducted across 27 countries, the analysis combines qualitative content analysis with a pipeline comprising TOPSIS, VIKOR, and Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis (SMAA). Criteria weights derived from interview salience reveal that data readiness, legacy integration, and interoperability effort dominate the prioritisation. The energy and facilities twin ranks first in TOPSIS. In contrast, the supply chain and scenario twin emerge as the VIKOR compromise solution and the most robust first-rank option under interview-centred weight uncertainty (85.6% probability). Sensitivity analysis shows that product passport and circularity twins rise to the top when sustainability benefits are privileged over feasibility burdens. The results yield a prioritisation framework for digital twin investment applicable to manufacturers, industry consortia, and policymakers designing Industry 4.0 roadmaps. Prescriptive implications address both private-sector technology prioritisation and staged implementation, and public policy on digital infrastructure, interoperability standards, and sustainability regulation, with attention to emerging economies.
summary: An interview-informed MCDA (TOPSIS, VIKOR, SMAA) drawing on 50 experts in 27 countries ranks seven digital twin use cases for sustainable manufacturing, with data readiness and interoperability dominating and the supply chain and scenario twin the most robust top choice.

title: Blockchain-driven cooperative decision-making for low-carbon supply chain under multi-source heterogeneous decision information
authors: Jiafu Su; Baojian Xu; Di Shen; Na Zhang; Junjun Li
keywords: Low-carbon supply chains; Blockchain-driven; Multi-source heterogeneous decision information; GRA-DEMATEL
abstract: The benefits of blockchain-driven cooperation in low-carbon supply chains (LCSCs) are becoming increasingly evident, as it facilitates product traceability and carbon footprint tracking, thereby effectively addressing consumer trust issues regarding eco-friendly, low-carbon products. However, this cooperation also introduces the challenge of multi-source heterogeneous decision information (MSHDI) in collaborative decision-making. Decision information originating from diverse sources, such as blockchain systems, suppliers, and consumers, often takes various forms, including real numbers, interval numbers, and triangular fuzzy numbers. To address this challenge, this paper constructs a hybrid hesitant fuzzy set (HHFS) by integrating hesitant fuzzy sets, interval-valued hesitant fuzzy sets, and hesitant triangular fuzzy sets to represent MSHDI. Furthermore, four distance measurement methods for HHFSs are proposed to enable effective fusion of MSHDI. Based on this, we improve the ORESTE and GRA-DEMATEL methods and propose a novel multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) framework for LCSC applications. Specifically, the GRA-DEMATEL approach is enhanced by incorporating HHFS properties, and the proposed distance measurement methods are integrated into ORESTE to improve the global preference scoring function. The proposed method is validated through a case study, sensitivity analysis, and comparative analysis. The results demonstrate that HHFSs can effectively represent MSHDI in decision-making processes, and the improved MCDM method exhibits superior performance in multi-criteria group decision-making scenarios.
summary: A hybrid hesitant fuzzy set representation with new distance measures, embedded in improved ORESTE and GRA-DEMATEL methods, fuses heterogeneous blockchain, supplier and consumer information for cooperative decision-making in low-carbon supply chains.

title: Forecasting the success of megaprojects with judgmental methods: the role of expertise, stakeholder perspectives, and implications for socio-economic planning
authors: Konstantia Litsiou; Yiannis Polychronakis; Stelios Sapountzis; Konstantinos Nikolopoulos
keywords: Megaprojects; Judgemental forecasting; Expertise; Stakeholders; Socio-economic planning
abstract: Forecasting the success of megaprojects is a very difficult task because of the complexity of such projects. Some scholars argue that forecasting is not really needed in this context: the master Gantt chart with tasks and allocated person-hours, and the respective Bill of Materials, should suffice for an accurate estimation of the duration and cost of a project. If that was however the case, then projects would finish on time and budget – but this is far from true, as the numerous examples attest: HS2, Channel Tunnel, IT public projects in NHS, to name a few. In this research, we employ judgmental forecasting methods to predict the success of a megaproject ('constructing a major recreational facility in the city centre of a metropolis'). We evaluate separately the forecasted excesses in the budget and the duration of the project. Furthermore, the participants forecast the extent to which the socio-economic benefits are realised. We do analyse three different stakeholder perspectives: that of the a) project manager, b) funder(s), and c) the public. We do also examine two levels of expertise – novices, and semi-experts. Finally, we discuss the implications for socio-economic planning and the potential integration with data driven methodologies while considering wider megaproject settings and contexts.
summary: Applies judgmental forecasting by novices and semi-experts, taking project-manager, funder and public perspectives, to predict budget overruns, delays and realised socio-economic benefits of a city-centre recreational megaproject.

title: Balancing the scales: Fair and efficient resource allocation for student success
authors: Mohammadsina Almasi; Hadis Anahideh; Denisa Gandara; Abolfazl Asudeh
keywords: Resource allocation; Fairness; Integer programming; LP relaxation; Financial aid allocation; Randomized rounding
abstract: Equitable access to higher education remains a pressing challenge, particularly for underrepresented and marginalized groups. Financial aid is one of the most important policy tools for addressing these disparities, yet allocation decisions are often guided by ad hoc rules that neither systematically enforce fairness nor optimize the use of limited institutional resources. This can undermine both the effectiveness and the equity of financial aid policies. In this paper, we study financial aid allocation as a fairness-aware resource allocation problem for continuing higher education students. We formulate the problem as an Integer Programming (IP) model that maximizes aggregate predicted student success subject to unique-allocation, limited-budget, Per-Capita Fairness (PCF), and Equal Opportunity Fairness (EOF) constraints. Student success probabilities are estimated from historical data using a Random Forest classifier. Because solving the exact IP formulation can be computationally expensive, we develop an LP relaxation coupled with a randomized rounding based on permutation selection . The proposed rounding framework first expands the LP solution into a column-stochastic matrix and then pads it to obtain a doubly stochastic matrix. It subsequently applies the Birkhoff algorithm to sample a permutation-based integer allocation. We provide theoretical analysis for the proposed LP-relaxation approach. In particular, we prove that the permutation-selection-based rounding is unbiased with respect to the expanded LP solution, show that the padded matrix used by the rounding procedure is doubly stochastic, prove that the EO and PC fairness constraints are satisfied in expectation after rounding, and characterize the overall computational complexity of the LP-relaxation framework. We evaluate the framework on a real educational dataset under two budget scenarios and multiple fairness-aware optimization settings. The results show that the LP-based approach achieves near-optimal objective values relative to the IP model while substantially reducing computational burden. The experiments also demonstrate that activating fairness constraints markedly improves fairness scores across demographic groups, with only a limited reduction in the objective value. These findings highlight the practical potential of fairness-aware predictive and prescriptive analytics for designing transparent, resource-efficient, and equity-conscious financial aid policies.
summary: Develops integer-programming methods (with LP relaxation and randomized rounding) for allocating higher-education financial aid in ways that are both fair to underrepresented groups and efficient in using limited institutional resources.

title: Robust location of collection facilities for waste management
authors: Massimiliano Caramia; Maria Sole Gatta; Diego Maria Pinto; Giuseppe Stecca
keywords: Waste management; Location problems; Robust optimization; Transshipment
abstract: This paper presents a robust optimization model for the location of collection facilities in municipal waste management under uncertain demand. A two-tier collection system is considered where waste generated by households and businesses is aggregated in local transshipment facilities and then transported by mother vehicles to final treatment sites. The problem is modeled as a capacitated facility location problem and extended using the Bertsimas–Sim robust optimization framework to hedge against fluctuations in waste demand explicitly. A deterministic mixed-integer linear programming model is first formulated and next its robust counterpart is derived by introducing a budget-of-uncertainty parameter that controls the trade-off between cost and protection level. The model is applied to a real case study in Latina (Italy), using detailed geo-referenced data on users, candidate transshipment points, and available vehicles. Computational experiments show that the robust model can reduce worst-case total costs by up to several tens of percent compared to a purely deterministic design, at the price of a moderate increase in nominal operating costs. The results demonstrate that robust facility configuration tends to open a slightly larger number of strategically located transshipment points, resulting in shorter average collection distances and improved resilience to demand surges. Managerial implications for local authorities and waste management companies are discussed, and promising directions for extending the model to multi-period and multi-waste-stream planning are identified.
summary: A Bertsimas-Sim robust facility location model for municipal waste collection in Latina, Italy, cuts worst-case total costs by up to several tens of percent versus deterministic designs by opening slightly more, better-placed transshipment points at a modest nominal cost increase.

title: Socio-economic determinants of health literacy among blood donors: A cross-sectional study in Italy
authors: Pietro Renzi; Alberto Franci
keywords: Health literacy; Blood donors; HLS-EU-Q16; Public health; Italy; Socioeconomic determinants; Health behaviours
abstract: Blood donation is a crucial service for healthcare systems and contributes to saving and improving lives. As a humanitarian act, it also symbolises social solidarity and individual responsibility. Health literacy (HL) is the ability to access, understand and use health information. This study aimed to assess HL levels among blood donors and compare them with those of the general population, thereby establishing whether individuals with higher HL are more likely to donate blood. It focused on 471 donors aged 18 or older and affiliated with AVIS (Italian Blood Donors Association) within a local health authority in the Marche Region. The HLS-EU-Q16 tool was administered via a web-based interview method, and its 16 items were aggregated into a General HL Index standardised on a scale from 0 to 50. Statistical analysis, including independent t-tests and multinomial logistic regression, was conducted to explore associations with sociodemographic factors. The results revealed a mean HL score for blood donors of 30.29 ± 7.11. Notably, 38% of donors demonstrated adequate HL, significantly higher than the 25% observed in the general Italian population. Higher HL levels were significantly associated with higher education, economic status, and better self-perceived health, while inadequate HL was more prevalent among those with chronic diseases. The potential reasons for this latter situation were explored. That HL scores for blood donors were higher than those for the general Italian population suggests that improving HL could serve as a strategic lever to enhance the donor base and the impact of increased blood donations.
summary: Among 471 blood donors in Italy's Marche Region, 38% had adequate health literacy versus 25% of the general Italian population, with higher literacy linked to education, economic status and self-perceived health.

title: Mapping policy priorities and family needs in regional official documents of Northeast Italy using generative text analysis
authors: Simone Di Zio; Yuri Calleo; Manuela Scioni; Marco Marozzi; Mario Bolzan
keywords: Family needs; Official documents; Northeast Italy; Generative text analysis; Policies; Statistics
abstract: Family well-being is a cornerstone of social and economic stability, influencing both individual development and broader societal dynamics. Recently, declining birth rates, population aging, and economic instability have significantly reshaped family structures in Italy. Regional administrations, particularly in Northeast Italy (Friuli Venezia Giulia, Trentino-Alto Adige, Veneto, and Emilia-Romagna), hold considerable autonomy in family policy development. However, the extent to which these policies align with actual family needs remains unclear. This study evaluates whether regional policies reflect principles of anticipatory governance, which emphasize proactive, adaptive approaches to emerging societal challenges. Specifically, the paper aims to identify family-related policies and needs articulated in official documents from 2018 to 2022 and assess the alignment and potential gaps between them. We applied generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs), to analyze unstructured legislative texts retrieved from official regional websites. The method integrated topic modeling, structured policy, and needed extraction using tailored prompts, and inter-regional comparisons via the Jaccard similarity metric. Findings reveal diverse regional priorities but common challenges, including mental health support, childcare accessibility, economic vulnerability, and fragmented service delivery. This study demonstrates the value of GPT-based text analysis in assessing policy effectiveness, enhancing the responsiveness and inclusivity of family-oriented policies in a rapidly changing social landscape.
summary: GPT-based text analysis of 2018-2022 official documents from four Northeast Italian regions finds diverse regional family-policy priorities but shared gaps in mental health support, childcare access, economic vulnerability and fragmented services.

title: Measuring gender equality in quality of life satisfaction: A composite index for Italian regions
authors: Margherita Maria Pagliuca; Daniela Fusco; Paola Giordano; Maria Antonietta Liguori
keywords: Quality of life satisfaction; Gender equality; AMPI; Composite index; Regional disparities; Italy
abstract: Gender disparities in quality of life satisfaction have been widely investigated, yet empirical evidence remains mixed. This paper aims to measure gender equality in quality of life satisfaction by developing a composite and partially compensatory index specifically designed to capture balanced gender outcomes across multiple life indicators. Using data from the Italian National Institute of Statistics (Istat) multipurpose survey Aspects of Daily Life, this study builds a Gender Equality Index of Quality of Life Satisfaction, based on women-to-men ratios and the Adjusted Mazziotta–Pareto Index (AMPI) methodology. The analysis is conducted at the regional level in Italy over the period 2018–2022, allowing for spatial and temporal comparisons before and after the COVID-19 pandemic. The composite index integrates satisfaction-based indicators related to: Positive judgement of future perspectives, Leisure time satisfaction, Life satisfaction, Satisfaction with friends' relationships and Satisfaction with family relationships. The results reveal substantial territorial heterogeneity in gender equality with persistent and structurally rooted disadvantages for women in several regions. While disparities appear limited when individual indicators are considered separately, the composite index highlights pronounced and enduring inequities, particularly in indicators related to time use and future expectations. The COVID-19 pandemic further amplified these disparities in several regional contexts.
summary: A composite AMPI-based gender equality index of quality-of-life satisfaction for Italian regions (2018-2022) reveals persistent, territorially uneven disadvantages for women, especially in time use and future expectations, amplified by COVID-19 in several regions.

title: Energy-conscious dynamic electric vehicle routing for urban cold-chain delivery: A K-means-ALNS approach
authors: Jiarui Zhou; Jianxin Wang; Hui Jia; Yijiao Huang
keywords: Urban logistics; Instant fresh produce delivery; Cold-chain logistics
abstract: With the rapid growth of instant fresh-produce delivery and the increasing adoption of EVs (Electric Vehicles, EVs), urban cold-chain routing has become increasingly challenging due to dynamic customer orders, battery-capacity limitations, refrigeration requirements, and time-varying traffic conditions. This study investigates the EC-DEVRPTW (Energy-Conscious Dynamic Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows, EC-DEVRPTW) for urban cold-chain delivery under a periodic re-optimisation framework. The problem jointly considers dynamic order updates, period-dependent vehicle speeds, charging decisions, and both driving and refrigeration energy consumption. A MILP (Mixed-Integer Linear Programming, MILP) model is formulated to minimise total cost. To improve computational efficiency, a hybrid solution framework integrating K-means clustering and ALNS (Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search, ALNS) is developed to adjust delivery routes at each periodic re-optimisation cycle. Benchmark experiments show that the proposed ALNS algorithm can generate feasible and competitive solutions in dynamic scenarios and achieves a good balance between solution quality and computational time. A real-world case study in Taiyuan further verifies the applicability of the proposed framework. The results indicate that refrigeration energy consumption is non-negligible, and that time-window penalties, electricity prices, vehicle speeds, re-optimisation frequency, and service-region partitioning all have important impacts on total cost.
summary: A K-means plus adaptive large neighborhood search framework for dynamic electric-vehicle routing of urban fresh-produce cold-chain deliveries, tested in Taiyuan, shows refrigeration energy is non-negligible and that time windows, electricity prices, speeds and re-optimisation frequency drive total cost.

title: Robust optimization for bioethanol supply chain networks: Balancing sustainability, resilience, and responsiveness
authors: Seyed Vahid Ahmadi; Seyed Hossein Iranmanesh; Aliyeh Kazemi
keywords: Bioethanol supply chain; Sustainability; Resilience; Responsiveness; Uncertainty modeling; Robust optimization
abstract: The rising global demand for sustainable energy has increased attention on bioethanol as a renewable resource. This study presents a multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming model to design and optimize a sustainable, resilient, and responsive bioethanol supply chain network. The model supports strategic and tactical decision-making, including supplier selection, facility location, capacity expansion, production planning, and distribution flows. To account for uncertainties in supply chain parameters, a multi-objective robust interval stochastic possibilistic programming approach is introduced. Additionally, a modified meta-goal programming method, based on the Torabi–Hassini approach, is used to improve computational efficiency. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through a real-world case study, with results indicating that the proposed approach outperforms deterministic and multi-choice models across various performance metrics. The findings affirm that robust optimization techniques can effectively manage uncertainties in bioethanol supply chains. This research contributes to the literature by integrating sustainability, resilience, and responsiveness into a comprehensive optimization framework, thereby enhancing decision-making under uncertainty and more effectively capturing the complexities of real-world problems.
summary: A multi-objective robust interval stochastic possibilistic programming model for bioethanol supply chain design outperforms deterministic and multi-choice models in a real-world case while balancing sustainability, resilience and responsiveness.

title: A hybrid approach for the dynamic routing of police patrols
authors: Moacir Almeida Simões; Denis Borenstein
keywords: Police patrol; Hotspot; Simulation; Ant colony optimization; Crime analytics
abstract: Efficient allocation of police resources is critical to public safety, particularly in urban environments with limited resources and high crime rates. This study proposes a dynamic approach to police patrolling that integrates predictive analytics, Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), and discrete-event simulation to optimize hotspot coverage and incident response times. The method combines historical Calls for service data and urban structures to predict high-risk areas (hotspots) and guide patrol deployment. The model dynamically adjusts patrol routes based on real-time hotspot conditions and incident priorities, employing Bayesian decision-making and a dynamic pheromone mechanism. A case study in Porto Alegre, Brazil, demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in reducing idle time at crime hotspots and improving incident response times across priority levels. The results highlight the potential of data-driven policing to enhance operational efficiency and balance resource allocation and public safety.
summary: Combining hotspot prediction, ant colony optimization and discrete-event simulation, a dynamic police patrol routing method reduces hotspot idle time and improves incident response times across priority levels in Porto Alegre, Brazil.

title: Pharmacy on-duty planning in urban environments: A gradual covering approach with workload equity
authors: Elifcan Yaşa; İsmail Kayahan; Seda Baş Güre
keywords: Pharmacy on-duty; Gradual covering; Workload equity; Demand aggregation; Hierarchical clustering; Healthcare service management
abstract: This study addresses the pharmacy on-duty problem in areas with high demand density and diverse pharmacy distribution, utilizing a case study conducted in Istanbul's Kadıköy district. The primary objective is to identify the optimal groups of pharmacies that maximize coverage while ensuring balanced workload distribution among the on-duty pharmacy groups with a gradual covering workload equity mathematical model. The proposed model is validated through extensive tests on large-scale random datasets involving both homogeneous and heterogeneous demand and pharmacy spatial distributions where performance metrics are analyzed across various instances. To provide a comprehensive evaluation, the current pharmacy on-duty system in Kadıköy is analyzed and optimized, serving as a baseline for performance improvements with an improvement of coverage efficiency by over 10%. We combine spatial decomposition with hierarchical clustering to aggregate demand to overcome the computational challenges of high-density areas like Kadıköy. The results show that achievable coverage is strongly influenced by the spatial distribution of pharmacies and demand points; highly crowded areas tend to create workload imbalances between on-duty groups. Tightening workload equity constraints reduces coverage-variance between on-duty groups but decreases overall coverage in heterogeneous areas. Conversely, relaxing the workload equity constraint has no statistically significant impact on proximity between on-duty pharmacies within groups on both homogeneous and heterogeneous areas. Therefore, the proposed framework allows planners to tune the balance between maximizing coverage and workload equity. Overall, the proposed approach delivers significant improvements in coverage and workload balance, ensuring both demand point accessibility and pharmacy workload equity.
summary: A gradual covering model with workload-equity constraints for on-duty pharmacy grouping in Istanbul's Kadıköy district improves coverage efficiency by over 10% relative to the current system, with tighter equity constraints trading off overall coverage in heterogeneous areas.

title: Design of a sustainable closed-loop supply chain under supply-side disruption: A quantity discount strategy
authors: Shahab Rahiminia; Saman Hassanzadeh Amin; Liping Fang; Victor Shi
keywords: Closed-Loop Supply Chain; Circular economy; Quantity discount; Disruption; Multi-objective optimization; Uncertain programming
abstract: Reusing the components of commercial merchandise considerably reduces the adverse ecological effects while enhancing firms' profitability. In this paper, a multi-objective optimization model is presented for designing a Closed-Loop Supply Chain (CLSC) network. The proposed model strategically determines the optimal locations for the key facilities and the flows of the products/components among different echelons. In procurement operations, the suppliers are assumed to leverage quantity discounts to offer diverse price levels to the manufacturer. Despite signing the supplier-manufacturer contract, in many real-life cases, suppliers might face partial/complete disruption in their service operations. To navigate such disruption risks, a Two-Stage Stochastic Programming (TSSP) approach is proposed to help achieve comprehensive decisions. Furthermore, uncertainty in demand, return, and cost parameters is addressed with a Possibilistic Chance-Constraint Programming (PCCP) approach, hedging the network against inherent uncertainty. The application of the model is shown by a real-life home appliance CLSC network in Canada. Through statistical measures, the model demonstrates to be uncertainty-resilient and also benefits from employing the TSSP model.
summary: A multi-objective closed-loop supply chain design model combining two-stage stochastic and possibilistic chance-constrained programming, applied to a Canadian home-appliance network, handles supplier disruptions and quantity discounts while remaining resilient to demand, return and cost uncertainty.

title: Optimal social distancing policy incorporating compliance of individuals
authors: Hyelim Shin; Taesik Lee
keywords: Epidemics; Game theory; Optimal control; Social distancing
abstract: We develop a novel optimization model for designing optimal social distancing policies by explicitly incorporating individuals' compliance behavior, a factor often neglected in existing studies. Building on prior work that characterizes equilibrium compliance in a social distancing game, we integrate such equilibrium behavior into a policy optimization framework. The proposed framework captures individuals' decisions on social activity levels as strategic responses to social distancing policies within a game-theoretic setting. However, directly embedding equilibrium compliance as a constraint renders the resulting optimization problem highly intractable due to its implicit and nonlinear structure. To address the computational challenges, we exploit structural properties of the equilibrium conditions and reformulate the problem as a tractable optimal control model. This enables the computation of optimal policy trajectories while endogenously accounting for individuals' behavioral responses. Through numerical experiments, we examine how optimal policies vary with disease characteristics and behavioral factors. Our results reveal that the effectiveness of social distancing policies depends critically on perceived infection risk, sensitivity to individual utility to social activity, and the transmission rate of the epidemic. Notably, we find that it may be optimal to maintain or even strengthen social distancing measures even as the epidemic subsides. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating behavioral responses into policy design and provide actionable insights for effective epidemic control.
summary: An optimal control model embedding game-theoretic equilibrium compliance shows social distancing effectiveness hinges on perceived infection risk, utility from social activity and transmission rates, and that it can be optimal to maintain or tighten measures as an epidemic subsides.

title: Centralized resource allocations with adjustment costs and a nonconvex production technology
authors: Giovanni Cesaroni; Gabriel Villa; Sebastián Lozano
keywords: Centralized resource allocation; Free disposal hull (FDH); Adjustment costs; Short-run rigidities
abstract: This paper aims to extend the Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) literature on Centralized Resource Allocation (CRA) by introducing a new model for a nonconvex technology, where the organizational units face adjustment costs to adapt inputs and outputs to those of their reference operating points. These costs imply that the optimal CRA allocation obtained from the aggregate model, which describes a long-run position, may not be optimal or even feasible in the short-run. An empirical application involving bank branches is presented and a sensitivity analysis regarding unit adjustment costs and input and output change bounds is conducted to illustrate how monetary penalties and structural rigidities constrain the optimal reallocation strategy. The results suggest that, within a CRA framework, these frictions can limit the practical reach of the efficient frontier for individual units, as the marginal cost of adjustment may outweigh the potential systemic efficiency gains. By reconciling non-convexity with adjustment frictions, this approach addresses the limitations of standard convex models in representing indivisibilities, demonstrating that neglecting these factors leads to unfeasible strategic targets in real-world centralized planning.
summary: A nonconvex (FDH) centralized resource allocation DEA model with adjustment costs, applied to bank branches, shows that adjustment frictions and rigidities can make long-run efficient reallocations infeasible or not worthwhile in the short run.

title: Artificial intelligence-enabled green innovation: Evidence from patent data
authors: Tiziano Volpentesta; Roberto Urbani; Valerio Deriu
keywords: Artificial intelligence; Green innovation; Technology transfer; Patent quality; Innovation; Sustainability
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how knowledge is created and combined, yet raising a sustainability paradox. While AI systems are resource-intensive, they may indirectly contribute to climate mitigation by supporting the development and diffusion of sustainability-oriented technologies. We examine this second-order channel by assessing whether green patents incorporating AI are more technologically influential than those that do not. Drawing on OECD REGPAT patent data from 1977 to 2024, we assemble a large dataset of climate-mitigation inventions, flag AI-enabled patents, and link them to standardized quality indicators and applicant information. We operationalize technological quality using three complementary indicators: originality, radicalness, and forward citations within five and seven-year windows. We estimate Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood models with high-dimensional fixed effects for citation outcomes and fractional logit models for originality and radicalness, including extensive patent, team, and applicant-level controls. We further implement propensity score matching and reweighting strategies. Across specifications, AI-enabled green patents are consistently associated with higher forward citations and higher radicalness, while no association emerges for originality. We further show that the citation premium is strongest for narrower-scope inventions, declining as patent scope increases, suggesting that the influence of AI-enabled green inventions is contingent upon technological breadth. Overall, AI-enabled green inventions appear to diffuse more widely and to be more radical, but not because they draw on a broader knowledge base. These findings inform debates on AI's sustainability implications beyond its immediate environmental footprint.
summary: Using OECD REGPAT climate-mitigation patents (1977-2024), AI-enabled green inventions receive more forward citations and are more radical but not more original, with the citation premium strongest for narrow-scope patents.

title: Designing cost-effective and environmentally responsible saffron supply chains: A two-stage data-driven approach for public and service sector decision-making
authors: Sajjad Kaheni; Mohammad Saeed Jabalameli; Ehsan Dehghani; Peiman Ghasemi
keywords: Saffron supply chain; Multi-objective optimization model; Data envelopment analysis; Long short-term memory; Autoencoder; Environmental responsibility
abstract: Modern agricultural supply chains face increasing complexity due to escalating environmental pressures and growing demand for affordable, high-quality food products. These challenges underscore the critical need for strategic, quantitative decision-making frameworks that enhance operational efficiency and sustainability, particularly within socio-economic sectors. Saffron, as a unique agricultural product with specific biological and production characteristics, requires a specialized and well-structured supply chain network to address these demands. This study develops an advanced data-driven decision-support framework designed to assist managers in public and service sectors in effectively designing and managing saffron supply chains that balance efficiency with environmental responsibility. This framework uniquely integrates supplier evaluation, environmental impact, demand prediction, and network design, including spoilage considerations, addressing gaps in the literature. The framework consists of two integrated phases. The first phase employs a hybrid supplier evaluation model that combines data envelopment analysis with autoencoder-based neural networks to assess supplier performance in terms of operational efficiency and environmental stewardship, even when faced with incomplete or uncertain information. In the second phase, selected suppliers are incorporated into a multi-objective optimization model that guides strategic network design by simultaneously minimizing costs and environmental impacts. A life cycle assessment using the ReCiPe methodology evaluates environmental effects comprehensively across the supply chain. Additionally, long short-term memory neural networks provide accurate demand forecasting to align supply strategies with market fluctuations. The results indicate that the model identifies efficient facility locations, demonstrates how modest cost adjustments can enhance environmental performance, and supports managerial decision-making by balancing cost efficiency with sustainability objectives.
summary: A two-stage framework combining DEA-autoencoder supplier evaluation, LSTM demand forecasting, life-cycle assessment and multi-objective network design for saffron supply chains identifies efficient facility locations and shows how modest cost adjustments can improve environmental performance.

title: Planning for equitable public health: A framework for interpretable causal policy learning
authors: Kushal Anjaria
keywords: Causal policy learning; Quantile optimization; Instrumental variables; Explainable AI; Public health interventions
abstract: Designing public health interventions that are both effective and equitable is a central challenge in socio-economic planning, particularly when observational data are affected by hidden socio-economic biases. This paper proposes a quantitative framework for evidence-based public-health policy planning under unmeasured confounding. Rather than focusing only on population-average outcomes, the framework adopts a quantile-oriented objective so that policy learning can emphasize selected segments of the health-outcome distribution, including vulnerable or disadvantaged groups. The proposed approach combines instrumental-variable-based structural quantile identification, minimax estimation, conservative policy learning, and surrogate-based local explanation. This allows policy recommendations to be estimated under maintained causal assumptions while also making the reasoning behind individual recommendations more transparent. We illustrate the framework using the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) dataset to derive educational-support policy recommendations linked to health outcomes. The empirical analysis highlights a key planning trade-off: linear models provide simpler and more interpretable policy boundaries, whereas neural-network specifications can capture more flexible and heterogeneous recommendation patterns. The explanation component further shows how observed demographic and socio-economic covariates contribute to individual policy recommendations through an interpretable surrogate model. Overall, the study provides a causally informed, distribution-sensitive, and explainable framework for supporting equitable public-health policy design using observational data.
summary: An instrumental-variable, quantile-oriented causal policy learning framework with interpretable surrogate explanations, illustrated on BRFSS data, targets equitable public-health interventions under unmeasured confounding and exposes an interpretability-flexibility trade-off between linear and neural models.

title: Coupling coordination of digital economy vitality and real economy green development efficiency: Spatiotemporal dynamic evolution and nonlinear driving mechanisms
authors: Jialiang Xie; Zhicai Wu
keywords: green development efficiency; Digital-real integration; Spatiotemporal dynamics; Nonlinear interaction effects; Machine learning
abstract: Despite widespread scrutiny of the environmental externalities stemming from digital-real integration—a dominant trend in today's global economy—the critical questions of how to evaluate and foster its sustainable development remain largely overlooked in the literature. Addressing this gap is imperative for the attainment of the sustainable development goals (SDGs). In this research, a pioneering theoretical framework for understanding the coupling coordination of digital economy vitality and real economy green development efficiency (CCDR) is constructed. Methodologically, we begin by applying exploratory spatiotemporal data analysis to examine the spatiotemporal dynamic evolution of the CCDR in the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration. We then innovatively integrate the TOE framework with an XGBoost-SHAP model to investigate nonlinear driving mechanisms. The findings indicate that (1) CCDR levels demonstrate an upward trajectory, forming a gradient hierarchical pattern characterized by "core area > central area > peripheral area." (2) CCDR exhibits notable path dependency, yet its dynamics intensify over time, with this strengthening trend being most pronounced in core regions. (3) Drivers at the technological and organizational levels have a significantly stronger influence than environmental factors do; industrial structure emerges as the pivotal determinant and presents complex nonlinear interactions with artificial intelligence, green technology, and human capital. This study offers policymakers and businesses fresh theoretical and empirical insights to drive sustainable digital-real economy integration and the achievement of the SDGs.
summary: In the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration, coupling coordination between digital economy vitality and green development efficiency is rising along a core-central-periphery gradient, with industrial structure the pivotal nonlinear driver per XGBoost-SHAP analysis.

title: Tied to home? Emotional attachment, family life cycles and migrants' return intention to counties in China
authors: Sainan Lin; Kaidi Liu
keywords: China; County; Family life cycle; Migrant; Place attachment; Return intention
abstract: Counties have increasingly become pivotal arenas in China's new-type urbanization, with return migration playing a critical role in reshaping rural–urban relations. However, existing studies often emphasize macro spatial patterns or economic rationality while overlooking the interaction between emotional embeddedness and family-based decision-making in shaping return intentions. Drawing on survey data from 881 county out-migrants in two major migrant-sending counties in central China, this study develops an integrated analytical framework that combines hometown attachment and family life cycle to examine the formation and stage-specific variation of return intention. The results show that 66.36% of county out-migrants express return intention, while overall hometown attachment remains moderate and the family life cycle is dominated by the Full Nest II stage. Hometown attachment is the strongest and most stable correlate of return intention, whereas only Full Nest I and Full Nest II show significant positive effects. Limited local employment opportunities further reveal a mismatch between emotional attachment and livelihood feasibility. Rather than operating independently, hometown attachment interacts with stage-specific family demands and is linked to intra-household resource allocation. Return intention among Single migrants reflects development selectivity; in Full Nest I it aligns with childcare reorganization; in Full Nest II it prioritizes children's educational security; and in the Empty Nest/Living Alone stage it is more strongly associated withroot-oriented motivations. This study contributes to the literature by highlighting the stage-specific emotional mechanisms of return migration and provides empirical evidence for promoting sustainable county-level urbanization in developing countries.
summary: Examines how emotional attachment to home and family life-cycle stages shape Chinese migrants' intentions to return to county-level areas.

title: Landed elites in Latin America: A systematic literature review of elites, wealth and land from colonial times until today
authors: Josué García Veiga; Olaf Kaltmeier; Andres Jiménez Corrales; Carolina Hormaza; Roberto Cassaglia; Afonso Henrique de Menezes Fernandes; Esteban Vladimir López Andrade; Melina Teubner; Christian Büschges; Jorge Carlos Dias de Sousa Júnior; Carlos Alexis Flores Cancino; Letícia Londres Fernandes; María Fernanda López-Sandoval; Carlos Manuel Olano Paredes; Valter Lúcio de Oliveira; Jean Lucas Ramos Veloso; Ana Carolina Ribeiro Cardoso; Ricardo Martín Sinchigalo Martínez; Karen Souza da Silva; Gabriel Tenesaca Guzmán; Mariano Torres; Nataly Torres Guzmán; Adrián Gustavo Zarrilli; Emmanuel David Cicirello; Fernando Darío Pintos
abstract: A defining feature of Latin American history is the long-term concentration of land among elite groups, a key factor in explaining the region's persistent wealth inequalities. Scholars and civil society organizations have conceptualized the relationship between elites, wealth, and land (EWL nexus) through a range of terms and approaches that reflect historical configurations of this articulation in specific contexts. Examining how these terms have been employed over time can therefore provide a means of comparing continuities and changes in the main actors, strategies and mechanisms of this nexus in Latin America history. This is of particular relevance to understand the agency of the 1-10% of the richest in the (re-)production of extreme social inequality. This article presents a systematic literature review (SLR) as a methodological tool to examine the EWL nexus. The protocol combined PRISMA Guidelines based reporting, framework-based extraction through a semi-inductive code system and a historical narrative synthesis approach. This SLR is based on 45 journal articles in a multilingual database spanning over 70 years. The results are presented in four major historical phases to facilitate a historical comparison of changes and continuities in the EWL nexus. Our findings highlight the complex role that land plays in the (re-)production of elite wealth, the moving entanglements of multiple actors, strategies and mechanisms in the region. Our results show how the emic and etic terms to denote landed elites and the EWL nexus are historically contingent and conceptually situated. Recent terms increasingly capture the variety of corporate forms and mechanisms of land control. Meanwhile, colonial and “feudal” terms persist or acquire new meanings, revealing structural continuities within contemporary EWL realities. This SLR reveals that important gaps suggest that the EWL nexus provides a fertile ground for developing a distinct field of study in order to contribute to a historical grounded analysis of the landed elite in Latin America.
summary: Systematically reviews research on Latin America's landed elites, tracing the links between elites, wealth and land ownership from colonial times to the present.

title: How does rural governance adaptively address multiple rural development objectives? - The case of Qingshan Village, China
authors: Xinxin Wang; Yijing Peng; Kevin Z. Chen; Wei Zhang; Ryan Nehring; Praveen Kumar
keywords: Adaptive governance; China; Embedded enabling; Net-mapping; Social network analysis
abstract: Adaptive governance offers a promising theoretical lens for addressing the trade-offs between ecological conservation and economic development in sustainable rural development. Yet much of the existing literature remains largely conceptual, offering high-level principles but limited insight into how adaptive governance is operationalized within real administrative systems. This study addresses this implementation gap by synthesizing a mechanism-based analytical framework and applying it to the case of Qingshan Village in China. Using Social Network Analysis combined with participatory Net-Mapping, the study traces the structural evolution of local governance across four distinct phases. The analysis shows that the shift from hierarchical to polycentric governance was propelled by the sequential activation of three mechanisms: shared problem recognition triggered by external shocks, institutionalized collaboration platforms that bridged top-down resources with bottom-up agency, and boundary-setting that redistributed enabling capacities across stakeholders. Network analysis further shows a gradual redistribution of coordination functions from governmental actors to community-based platforms, while the state retained strategic authority and enabling capacities. These findings suggest that adaptive governance in state-embedded rural contexts may emerge sequentially through cumulative processes of problem reframing, cross-sector coordination, and institutional stabilization.
summary: Uses the case of Qingshan Village, China, to examine how rural governance adapts in order to pursue multiple rural development objectives at once.

title: "It is a matter of educating people": Exploring farmers' approaches to in-person engagement with non-farming people through a social licence to farm lens'
authors: Catherine Broomfield; Matt Lobley
keywords: Farming-nonfarming disconnect; Interpersonal communication; Red meat debate; Ruminant livestock farming; Social licence to farm
abstract: The last agricultural transition to productivist farming presaged disconnection between farming and non-farming people. This paper draws on social licence to operate (SLO) and community engagement literatures to draw attention to the role of in-person engagement between farmers and the public to bridging the disconnect which, despite its importance to the farmer's social licence, has not attracted research attention nor critical review of the farming industry's settled conception of engagement as reconnection with the consumer in the marketplace. Taking the ruminant livestock region of the south-west of England as its geographic area, we address this lack of critical review and empirical research. We present findings from in-depth interviews with beef and/or sheep farmers and senior representatives of regional and national organisations working in the ruminant sector. Findings align with research in other European and North American context which finds a deficit model approach dominates farmers' engagement practices despite being unconducive to achieving a resilient social licence to farm (SLF). We add nuance by emphasizing a range of secondary purposes and practices to farmers' engagement. This suggests accessible pathways towards a broader more relational approach to in-person engagement with the farmer qua person-in-community with fellow non-farming people. We offer a novel engagement-as-integration framework as a starting point for the farming industry to support farmers transition towards in-person engagement with non-farming people that is more conducive to overcoming the disconnect and to building relationships between farmer and non-farming people that is the bedrock of the farmer's resilient SLF.
summary: Explores, through a social-licence-to-farm lens, how farmers approach face-to-face engagement with non-farming members of the public.

title: Self-determination and empowerment in rural women-led innovation: A relational perspective from Slovenia
authors: Sara Mikolič; Darja Kobal Grum; Barbara Lampič; Irma Potočnik Slavič; Eva Boštjančič; Hana Hawlina
keywords: Empowerment; Mentorship; Rural development; Rural innovation; Self-determination theory (SDT); Slovenia; Women-led innovation
abstract: This study examines how women-led innovations in rural Slovenia are experienced through the fulfilment and interaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness, the three basic psychological needs identified in Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using a qualitative, exploratory design, the study draws on semi-structured interviews with 20 women innovators from the FLIARA (Female-Led Innovation in Agriculture and Rural Areas) project. The interview material was analysed through thematic content analysis supported by ATLAS.ti, combining deductive coding based on SDT dimensions with inductive identification of empirically grounded subthemes. The revised ATLAS.ti-based analysis also enabled a more transparent assessment of how broadly key subthemes were represented across participants. Findings show that women-led innovation supported autonomy through self-initiation, boundary-setting, temporal control, resistance to restrictive norms, and value-driven purpose; competence through experiential learning, novelty-related experimentation, adaptive problem-solving, recognition, and growing self-efficacy; and relatedness through emotional support, professional collaboration, community contribution, and intergenerational and gendered solidarity. Mentorship emerged as a context-specific mechanism linking competence support with relational involvement and, in some cases, autonomy support. The study contributes by applying SDT to women-led rural innovation and showing how established SDT concepts can illuminate the motivational, relational, and place-based conditions under which rural women initiate, sustain, and give meaning to innovation. The findings suggest that rural development policies and support programmes may benefit from strengthening psychosocial and relational conditions, including autonomy-supportive environments, competence development opportunities, mentorship, peer learning, and participatory networks. These implications should be interpreted in light of the qualitative and context-specific nature of the study.
summary: Examines self-determination and empowerment in innovation led by rural women in Slovenia from a relational perspective.

title: Can rural schools save declining villages? rethinking schools, social capital, and the (Re)construction of socio-cultural resilience in rural China
authors: Zhenjie Yuan; Yuting Wu; Xinhui Wu
keywords: China; Rural decline; Rural school; Social capital; Social infrastructure; Socio-cultural resilience
abstract: The closure of rural schools has become a pressing global issue. In China, rural schools have declined by over 80 percent since the early 2000s, and they are increasingly viewed as casualties of rural decline, despite their historical roles as centres of education, culture, and social cohesion. While existing research often links school closure to village decline, this study offers a different perspective. Drawing on a comparative case study of three villages in a Hakka region of Guangdong, China, this paper examines how rural schools function as socio-cultural infrastructures under conditions of rural shrinkage. The findings show that rural schools can operate as multi-scalar hubs of social capital accumulation through a tri-layered interactive mechanism linking personal networks, institutional partnerships, and village-level relations. However, this capacity is contingent upon the degree of integration across these relational layers, as revealed by contrasting village trajectories. Building on these findings, the paper develops a context-sensitive analytical framework that highlights the interplay between cultural specificity, institutional environment, and resilience pathways in shaping how rural schools contribute to socio-cultural resilience. The study provides a direct but nuanced answer to its central question: rural schools alone cannot reverse structural rural decline, but when embedded within supportive relational, cultural, and institutional contexts, they can function as critical infrastructures that help sustain social cohesion, reactivate local networks, and support pathways of rural revitalisation. This study contributes to debates on rural resilience and educational geographies and offers insights for policy approaches in non-Western contexts.
summary: Asks whether rural schools can help declining Chinese villages by rebuilding social capital and socio-cultural resilience.

title: Infrastructuring short food supply chains: how intermediaries bind rules, norms and values
authors: Francisco Garrido-Garza; Allison Loconto; Douglas K.R. Robinson
keywords: Alternative food networks; Certification; Digitalisation; Intermediaries; Market infrastructures; Short food supply chains; Transformative potential
abstract: Food supply chains are crucial for food security and socio-economic development, yet their length concentrates value away from producers and consumers disproportionate resources. As the COVID-19 pandemic and the wars in Ukraine and Iran exposed, overreliance on long chains produces global interdependencies that exacerbate food insecurity. In reaction, alternative agri-food networks (AFNs) and short food supply chains (SFSCs) have proliferated. Addressing gaps in recent reviews, this article asks whether SFSCs organise markets distinctly and, if so, where their transformative potential lies. We argue that this potential lies not in any single market device but in the interaction between two that the literature has treated separately: certification and digitalisation. Drawing on transformative social innovation and the ‘infrastructure’ turn in economic sociology, we propose that certification and digital tools cannot be filed as either rules or norms. Each is a material site in which what actors are allowed to, ought to, and want to do are bundled together; it is the ongoing infrastructuring work of intermediaries that binds these registers and thereby creates value. We examine 156 SFSC initiatives self-described online across the 27 European Union member states. Wherever a certificate appears, it is made actionable through a digital interface: certification no longer travels without digitalisation. We identify two modes through which the devices work as one hybrid infrastructure: transmission, where a digital channel conveys a certification claim; and substitution, where digital transparency and feedback perform the assurance a certificate would otherwise do. These findings reposition intermediaries as the core actors of SFSC markets-in-the-making.
summary: Analyses how intermediaries in short food supply chains build the infrastructure that binds together their rules, norms and values.

title: Beyond the factor-driven paradigm: Spatiotemporal dynamics and system coupling of agricultural transition in Henan Province, China
authors: Xuhong Li; Yuanzhi Guo
keywords: Agricultural transition; GTWR model; Social-ecological-technological systems; XGBoost-SHAP model; “Element coupling–external manifestation” framework
abstract: The core of agricultural transition lies in changes to the various components of the agricultural systems and their interactions. Drawing on the social-ecological-technological systems (SETS) framework, this study developed an “element coupling–external manifestation” analytical framework and a corresponding evaluation index system for agricultural transition.
