Using county-level data from Henan Province spanning 1990 to 2020, this study further examined the spatiotemporal patterns of agricultural transition in Henan Province and identified its key influencing factors through the XGBoost-SHAP and GTWR models. The results show that the average agricultural transition index rose steadily from 0.280 in 1990 to 0.565 in 2020, while regional disparities narrowed. During the study period, the spatial pattern of agricultural transition has shifted from a “higher in the north and lower in the south” model to one featured by multi-point diffusion and cluster-based development, with hypervariable density emerging as the primary source of overall inequality. Government macro-control capability and economic development level are the two factors most strongly associated with agricultural transition, collectively accounting for 63.3% of the total contribution. Both exhibited a U-shaped relationship, and all factors demonstrated significant nonlinearity and spatiotemporal non-stationarity, with government macro-control capability being particularly prominent. By establishing a SETS-based analytical paradigm, this study redefines agricultural transition as a coupling process within the SETS framework and provides theoretical and empirical insights into the diversity of its pathway as well as the nonlinearity and spatiotemporal heterogeneity of its influencing factors.
summary: Traces the spatiotemporal dynamics and system coupling of agricultural transition in Henan Province, China, going beyond a purely factor-driven explanation.

title: Following and untangling multiple metabolisms of Chinese beekeeping
authors: Haohui Cai
keywords: Care; Honey; Honeybees; Metabolic justice; Metabolic labour; Pesticides
abstract: This paper traces the multiple metabolisms in Chinese apiculture through three ethnographic stories, adopting the orienting practices of following material flows and untangling metabolic knots. The first story analyses the Langstroth beehive as an animal infrastructure that renders honeybees as metabolic labour. The second follows the flow of honey back to nectar – a metabolic output of flowers – to examine the intimate metabolic relations among insects, flowers and weather. The last story addresses the metabolic disruptions caused by pesticides used on lychee trees, reflecting the complex interactions between lives and materials, as well as lychee growers and nomadic beekeepers. Acknowledging the profound and universal interconnectedness of these metabolisms, the paper argues that achieving metabolic justice requires developing careful attentiveness to metabolic multiplicity while confronting the situated conflicts over diverse metabolic care practices and the hidden structural challenges of Chinese smallholder farmers’ precarious livelihood. Ultimately, metabolic justice must confront the uneven material-social politics affecting both human and more-than-human actants marginalised in contemporary food regimes.
summary: Follows and untangles the multiple (social and material) metabolisms at work in beekeeping in China.

title: Market outlet choice, crop diversification and household welfare: Empirical evidence from Ghana
authors: Ebenezer Kondo; Freda Elikplim Asem; Yaw Bonsu Osei-Asare; Akwasi Mensah-Bonsu
keywords: Crop diversification; Food consumption score; Food security; Market outlet choice; Multinomial endogenous switching regression; per capita household consumption expenditure
abstract: Market outlet choice is a critical strategy adopted by farm households to enhance their welfare through improved crop revenue, food security, and overall living standards. This study leverages the wave 3 cross-sectional data of the Ghana Socioeconomic Panel Survey to examine the impact of market outlet choice on crop diversification, per capita household consumption expenditure, and food consumption score. To account for endogeneity and address the potential problem of self-selection bias associated with the random participation in a given market outlet, the multinomial endogenous switching regression (MESR) model was used for the estimation. The results indicate that participation in the consumer-based, institutional and contract-based, and intermediary and wholesale-based market outlets increases the count of diversified crops by 22%, 13%, and 34%, respectively. Food consumption score and per capita household consumption expenditure are higher among participants in all market outlets relative to non-participants, with participation in the intermediary and wholesale-based market outlets resulting in the largest welfare gains. Gender disaggregated findings show that female-headed farm households benefit more from market outlet participation, with increased crop diversification and food consumption score. Policy efforts should prioritise reducing transaction costs through investments in rural infrastructure, strengthening farmer organisations and promoting gender-sensitive market interventions.
summary: Estimates how farm households' choice of market outlet and their crop diversification relate to household welfare in Ghana.

title: Attracting, recruiting and retaining residents and staff – a systematic literature review of studies in northern Sweden, Finland and Norway
authors: Karolina Parding; Emma Lundholm; Birgit Abelsen; Grete Overvåg
keywords: Arctic; Incentives; Remote; Rural; Skills-supply; Strategies
abstract: This paper is based on a systematic literature review, with the aim of identifying and discussing what previous research says regarding strategies local, regional and national actors have, to attract, recruit and retain residents and staff to the north of Sweden, Finland and Norway. Being geographically peripheral, grappling with a demographic challenge; with an aging and declining population, at the same time as there are increased work force needs due to the green transition and the changed military presence in the area, this is a clear case of a region with severe skills-supply issues. A main finding is that the literature is rather limited, only 21 publications of relevance were identified. Three key themes emerged: attracting, recruiting and retaining staff (and residents) in the healthcare sector, immigration as strategy for attracting, recruiting, and retaining residents and staff, and regional and municipal development strategies. Rather few studies examine specific strategies, and even fewer their outcomes. One exception is research on the healthcare sector specifically, where it is found that connecting individuals as early as possible, via initiatives such as internship and decentralized education and training, along with offering good conditions for learning and professional development are key aspects in sustainable strategies for attracting, recruiting and retaining medical staff and residents to work and live in the rural north. Still, more studies are needed, on different levels, where the outcomes of specific strategies are examined. Such studies would contribute with much needed basis for policy makers in making evidence-based decisions regarding staff recruitment and retention.
summary: Systematically reviews studies on attracting, recruiting and retaining residents and staff in northern Sweden, Finland and Norway.

title: Burnout among female farmers and farm workers in Germany - Results of an online cross-sectional survey
authors: Christine Niens; Susanne Padel; Zazie v. Davier
keywords: Agriculture; Copenhagen Burnout Inventory; Gender; Mental health; Occupational roles on farms
abstract: The mental health of farmers has been receiving increasing attention in recent years. While studies are available in many European and non-European countries, there is a lack of corresponding data in Germany. This study therefore examines the prevalence of burnout among women on farms in Germany and the relationship to various, partly gender-specific, risk factors. The study uses data of an online survey of 7345 women that was conducted in 2021. The risk of burnout was measured using the “Personal Burnout Scale” of the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI). The results show that 21.5% of women on farms in Germany represented in this sample suffer from burnout, with non-family employees without management functions showing a particularly high burnout rate of 27%. The strongest associations with the CBI Burnout Score were observed for self-rated general health status, stress related to household and farm work, lack of free time, and family and generational conflicts. However, the comparability of the present results with previous studies is unclear due to the potential influence of the COVID-19 pandemic at the time of data collection. It cannot be ruled out that the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, such as isolation, fear of illness, and financial uncertainty, may have biased the data. Nevertheless, the study is the first Germany-wide survey of the prevalence of burnout among women in agriculture, and therefore offers initial important insights into a previously under-researched topic.
summary: Reports an online cross-sectional survey of burnout among female farmers and farm workers in Germany.

title: Bridging intuition and digitalization: Decision-making in regenerative agriculture
authors: Joni Kukkamäki; Laura Rosenberg; Jenni Valorinta; Emma Salminen; Iivari Kunttu
abstract: Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) and regenerative farming have emerged as complementary approaches to addressing the environmental, economic, and social challenges posed by climate change. While CSA emphasizes productivity, resilience, and emissions reduction, regenerative agriculture focuses on ecological restoration, particularly soil health. This study investigates how regenerative farmers integrate intuitive reasoning with data-driven methods in their decision-making and identifies the key drivers and barriers to adopting digital tools. Drawing on in-depth interviews, the research reveals that intuitive decision-making—rooted in experiential knowledge, situational awareness, and ecological sensitivity—remains central to farm management in regenerative systems. Although digital technologies offer valuable support, their adoption is shaped by usability, interoperability, and alignment with farmers' values and regulatory requirements. The findings challenge the assumption that data-driven approaches replace traditional intuition, instead highlighting how digital tools can complement and refine intuitive strategies. Moreover, the study underscores the importance of designing decision-support systems that respect the epistemological foundations of regenerative farming, including indigenous and traditional knowledge systems. By bridging intuitive and analytical reasoning, digitalisation can enhance adaptive capacity and environmental outcomes without undermining farmers’ experiential expertise. This research contributes to the broader discourse on sustainable agriculture by offering nuanced insights into the interplay between intuition and technology in farm-level decision-making.
summary: Studies how decision-making in regenerative agriculture combines farmers' intuition with digital tools.

title: Piloting Nordic connectivity: Examining perspectives on the potential of electric aviation to enhance accessibility and socio-economic development in Nordic remote rural regions
authors: Jonas Kačkus Tybjerg; Nicola Wendt-Lucas; Tove Lundberg; Rebecca Cavicchia; Hilma Salonen; Maja Brynteson; Sæunn Gísladóttir; Hjalti Jóhannesson; Linnea Löfving
keywords: Electric aviation; Nordic countries; Regional development; Remote rural regions; Sustainable transport
abstract: Lack of accessibility is both a defining characteristic and a key obstacle for the development of remote rural areas. In the Nordic context, challenging travel conditions have reinforced the need for new, sustainable transport solutions. This article explores the perceived potential of electric aviation as an environmentally low-impact and innovative way to improve accessibility and thereby strengthen the socio-economic development of remote regions. The study applies an analytical framework on accessibility components to explore how electric aviation could strengthen remote rural areas in the Nordic countries. The study adopts a qualitative approach exploring five case studies, selected through a pre-study to identify which routes in the Nordic region would benefit the most from the introduction of electric aviation. These case studies draw on focus group discussions with local stakeholders and aviation experts from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden. The study offers an analytical contribution by suggesting an additional dimension to Geurs and van Wee's accessibility component model highlighting the importance of energy infrastructure to better understand and support the green shift in the transport sector. Stakeholders perceived electric aviation as a possible contributor to regional development, but only under restrictive conditions relating to affordability, service frequency, integration with local transport, public trust, and energy infrastructure. The study highlights both the promises and challenges of electric aviation and its perceived potential impact on regional development trajectories in sectors including tourism and healthcare as well as the design of sustainable and context-sensitive transport policies.
summary: Examines perspectives on whether electric aviation could improve accessibility and socio-economic development in remote rural regions of the Nordic countries.

title: Beyond the forest: Land-use transitions and the futures of cocoa in post-forest Côte d'Ivoire
authors: Sarah Belalia; Hadrien Di Roberto
abstract: Côte d’Ivoire offers an emblematic case of post-forest transition: the world's leading cocoa producer is facing the exhaustion of forest resources that historically supported its agricultural development, raising questions about its economic resilience and the broader risks of frontier displacement. This turning point is particularly significant, as concerns about imported deforestation have prompted the development of traceability schemes whose impacts remain modest. In this context, Côte d’Ivoire's capacity to shift from a “plantation economy” to a “replantation economy” becomes critical not only for its own development, but for the future of truly zero-deforestation cocoa. Combining qualitative and quantitative data from 279 farms and 1163 agricultural plots, this study reconstructs land-use transitions across three illustrative sites in Côte d’Ivoire's main cocoa regions, based on farmer-reported plot histories and triangulated with field observations. This bottom-up approach allows a fine-grained analysis of crop succession dynamics that remain largely invisible to remote sensing. Our findings show that, contrary to expectations, cocoa has not collapsed following forest exhaustion, but is instead undergoing contrasting reconfigurations, shaped by local and global drivers. These differentiated adaptation pathways challenge simple Malthusian–Boserupian narratives and highlight contrasting longer-term outcomes for cocoa renewal, agricultural landscapes, and rural resilience. This calls for a reorientation of current approaches to cocoa sustainability, toward greater attention to context-specific transitions and dynamic farm-level strategies, rather than short-term plot productivity. Drawing on the illustrative case of cocoa, our analysis also contributes to the broader understanding of agrarian transitions following the end of pioneer phase in plantation economies.
summary: Explores land-use transitions and the possible futures of cocoa farming in post-forest Côte d'Ivoire.

title: Cultivating social innovation for agri-food sustainability transformations: a literature review
authors: Machteld Catharina Simoens; Caroline Hélène Dabard; Jonathan Friedrich; Juan Garzon; Felix Zoll
keywords: Agri-food system; Alternative food networks; Rural development; Social enterprise; Sustainability Transition; Transformative change
abstract: This scoping literature review focuses on the operation and orientation of social innovations (SI) in agri-food systems, in order to understand their role in sustainability transformations. Its main objective is to analyze and synthesize the types of cases studied in SI literature, with a specific focus on what is reported regarding their characteristics, how they form relations, the societal problems they respond to and their contributions to transformation processes. The review is based on 86 empirical English articles published in Scopus and Web of Science between 2013 and 2023, covering 168 empirical SI cases. The data reveal limited geographical variation and a Eurocentric focus in the study of SI, but diverse spatial and operational foci of SI cases. We identify seven SI types: community food networks, food equity initiatives, capacity-building programs, agri-cooperatives, social agri-enterprises, agri-environmental initiatives, and tech-driven agri-services. These often-localized solutions address different internal and external relations, aim to respond to a variety of societal needs and problems, and are rhetorically linked to transformations of various kinds. In addition to providing insights into key trends in the operation and orientation of SI, this analysis contributes to the discussion on the transformative potential of SI, including the ambivalent role of strong ties between SI and the state. Furthermore, this study identifies potential research avenues for the study of SI in agriculture and food with a particular focus on rural places. In particular, we call for reflexivity in researchers' normative assumptions, more rigorous reporting of relations and transformative contributions, and more systematic approaches to better integrate findings across SI cases as well as with adjacent concepts.
summary: Reviews the literature on how social innovation can be cultivated to drive sustainability transformations in agri-food systems.

title: Public perception and segmentation of agricultural protests in Germany
authors: Marius Michels; Thore-Maximilian Biß; Sven Grüner; Oliver Musshoff
keywords: Agrarian populism; European agricultural policy; Farmer movements; Legitimacy theory; Public segmentation; Socio-ecological transformation
abstract: Using Germany as a case study, this paper examines public perceptions of agricultural protests across different societal segments. Based on quota-representative survey data from 637 adults collected in 2024, we employ factor and cluster analyses to identify distinct attitude patterns. Our findings reveal four population segments: Agricultural Distance Critics, Pro-Reform Agricultural Supporters, Politically Concerned Agricultural Supporters, and Protest-Affirming Agricultural Supporters. While farmers' protests were attributed comparatively high legitimacy relative to the other protest movements included in the comparison, acceptance varies statistically significantly with protest tactics. Support patterns are primarily shaped by proximity to agriculture and political orientation rather than traditional socio-demographic factors.
summary: Examines how the German public perceives agricultural protests and segments the population by its views of them.

title: From tea monoculture to rural tourism: Variegated ruralities in Çamlıhemşin, Turkey
authors: Ali Mert Ipek
keywords: Neoliberal agrarian transformation; Rural tourism; Ruralisation; Rural–urban relationality; Translocal livelihoods
abstract: This article examines how rural tourism transforms livelihoods, attachments, and land claims in the Çamlıhemşin district of Turkey's Eastern Black Sea region. Building on recent ruralisation scholarship, it integrates tourism, overlooked in these debates despite its growing role in rural landscapes, into the analytical framework, and extends discussions developed primarily through Southeast Asian cases to a setting where tourism intersects with a longstanding tea economy and decades of rural–urban migration. Drawing on participant observation and open-ended interviews conducted during fieldwork in 2025, the findings show that tea cultivation produced variegated ruralities: coastal villages sustained livelihoods through tea, while settlements deeper in the valley combined small-scale cultivation with circular urban migration. These mobility patterns preserved village properties, kinship networks, and land attachments across distance, laying the material groundwork for tourism's emergence. As tea income declined and regional development shifted towards tourism, inherited assets became activatable through three mechanisms: converting mansions and highland cottages into rental properties (spatial value-activation), generating local employment beyond agriculture (labour market formation), and symbolically revaluing rural residence. Tourism, however, does not produce uniform outcomes: its interaction with pre-existing resource configurations yields divergent trajectories, from mass, construction-intensive development where agriculture persists to more eco-sensitive tourism where it has almost ceased. The article concludes that tourism constitutes a distinct form of ruralisation in which rural life persists not despite deagrarianisation but through the re-functioning of inherited rural assets into visitor economies.
summary: Examines the shift from tea monoculture to rural tourism and the variegated ruralities it produces in Çamlıhemşin, Turkey.

title: An identification framework for urban-rural relations based on rural endogenous drivers: A perspective of population mobility
authors: Wenbo Zhang; Hongbo Li; Xiaoliang Hu; Xiaolin Zhang; Bohao Wei; Libang Ma; Yu Chen
keywords: China; Four quadrant; Population migration; Rural decline; Urban shrinkage; Urban-rural relationship
abstract: Distinguishing itself from existing studies that conduct parallel analyses of urban and rural systems, this paper starts from the internal symbiosis status of “rural settlement-cropland-industry” in rural areas and constructs an identification framework for urban-rural relations driven by rural endogenous processes. Scientifically identifying the typologies of these urban-rural relations and their underlying drivers is critical for formulating differentiated integration strategies. Bridging rural endogenous dynamics with urban demographic shifts, this study constructs a unified analytical framework based on urban-rural population mobility. We developed a “rural settlement-cropland-industry” symbiosis index (S) and an urban shrinkage index (SK), utilizing a “ΔS-ΔSK” four-quadrant matrix to classify urban-rural relations across Chinese prefecture-level cities. Mechanisms driving these patterns were further explored using data from the China Migrants Dynamic Survey (CMDS). Results indicate that China's urban-rural landscape is dominated by “rural revitalization & urban population growth” (RR-UG, 51%) and “rural decline & urban population growth” (RD-UG, 33%). However, approximately 10% of cities, predominantly in the Northeast, face the dual crisis of “rural decline & urban population shrinkage” (RD-US). The primary drivers of population out-migration include rural industrial scarcity, constraints on realizing cropland value, and diminishing agricultural returns. by integrating symbiosis theory into rural geography, this study quantifies the interaction mechanisms among internal rural elements and elucidates the transmission pathway: “rural endogenous processes → urban-rural population mobility → urban exogenous outcomes”. We provide an operational framework for diagnosing regional differentiation in urban-rural relations, offering a theoretical basis and policy implications for promoting integrated development through zonal and categorical interventions.
summary: Proposes a framework for identifying urban-rural relations from rural endogenous drivers, viewed through population mobility.

title: "I live here to escape things": Mobilities and access for older people on smaller islands
authors: Gustav López-Svensson; Vanessa Stjernborg; Lena Winslott Hiselius; Lena Levin
keywords: Accessibility; Aging; Digital service solutions; Island studies; Mobility
abstract: The conditions for service access differs distinctly between the north and south of Sweden, and older residents of islands face different challenges of aging in place. As islands are a specific form of geography that place restrictions on mobility in different ways, service provision is sometimes hindered, or absent. This study aims to understand the conditions of accessibility and mobility for older people living on smaller islands in Sweden. With the perspective of rural mobilities, the study investigates two islands located in the north and south of Sweden, respectively. The purpose is to discern how the islanders perceive their need for mobility and accessibility as they age, and what they deem to be desirable future developments of services in their local contexts. For this purpose, 18 island residents aged 65-85 from two different islands were interviewed via telephone. The study finds that the community on the islands act as a safeguard against declining service provision, and that the residents are vigilant against solutions that threaten to erode the social cohesion of the community.
summary: Explores the mobilities of older people living on smaller islands and their access to services and activities.

title: From planned space to a place to stay: Community capital networks and the formation mechanism of rural residents' intention to stay
authors: Dan-Ni Mei; Lei Xiong; Bo-Wei Zhu; Gwo-Hshiung Tzeng
keywords: Community capitals; Intention to stay; Rural revitalization; Theory of planned behavior
abstract: This study integrates the Community Capitals Framework with the extended Theory of Planned Behavior to examine how community capitals reconfigured through rural revitalization shape residents' psychological evaluations of staying. Based on survey data from 364 residents in six villages in Guangdong, China, this study employs a multi-method approach combining the Fuzzy Delphi Method, PLS-SEM, DEMATEL, and fsQCA to jointly analyze both net effects and configurational pathways. Research findings indicate that social capital is the primary source-side driver within the community capital network and the only capital that significantly influences attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control. Perceived behavioral control is the strongest direct predictor of intention to stay and a key psychological condition underpinning high intention to stay. Higher human capital may undermine perceived control over staying where local opportunities are scarce. Although political, built, and natural capital do not directly shape the TPB psychological variables, they play an important role within specific capital configurations. This study advances research on rural residents’ intention to stay by moving beyond a static resource-accumulation view of community capitals to integrate capital interactions, psychological mechanisms, and configurational logic, thereby clarifying how planned rural spaces may become places where residents are willing to stay.
summary: Investigates how community capital networks shape the formation of rural residents' intention to stay in planned rural settlements.

title: Dairy farmers' preferences for reducing pesticide use: does workload matter? Evidence from a discrete choice experiment among dairy farmers in Brittany, France
authors: Julia Denantes; Aude Ridier; Carole Ropars-Collet; Anne-Lise Jacquot; Matthieu Carof
keywords: Discrete choice experiment; Mental workload; Skills and knowledge; Work organization
abstract: Specialized dairy farms have a high workload, with most of their labor resources devoted to livestock-related tasks. The feasibility of reducing pesticide use is influenced by work dimensions. Using a discrete choice experiment, we assessed trade-offs among determinants that can hinder reducing pesticide use on dairy farms, particularly workload. The attributes of the experiment were the reduction in pesticide use, change in gross operating surplus, risk of yield loss, number of labor peaks during the year, skills and knowledge, and mental workload. 94 dairy farmers in Brittany (western France) were interviewed face-to-face. Three classes were identified: (1) 20 farmers expressed negative preferences for reducing pesticide use, and this class exhibited a higher workload, (2) for 21 farmers, reduction in pesticide use had no significant effect on preferences and those farms had the most intensive milk-production systems, and (3) 53 farmers were willing to reduce pesticide use, most of the farmers in this group were already involved in a pesticide-reduction program. An increase in the number of labor peaks without outsourcing and an increase in mental workload had a significant negative effect on all of the three classes. Public policies should address the work dimension of reducing pesticide use on particularly labor-intensive farms such as dairy farms.
summary: Uses a discrete choice experiment with dairy farmers in Brittany, France, to measure their preferences for reducing pesticide use and whether workload shapes them.

title: How does the construction of national demonstration parks for rural industrial integration development affect county economic resilience ——evidence from China
authors: Dong Guo; Guoguang Pang; Li Cao
keywords: Agricultural “Three New” economy; County economic resilience; Financing constraints; Industrial agglomeration; Rural industrial integration
abstract: Against the global backdrop of frequent supply chain disruptions, climate shocks and rural economic recessions, improving county economic resilience (CER) has become a core consensus of global rural governance research. As a crucial node connecting urban and rural areas, CER directly influences national economic security and rural revitalization. Rural industrial integration, as an inevitable choice for driving the economic transformation of county economies, is also an essential impetus for enhancing CER. However, whether and how it effectively enhances CER remains insufficiently explored. Based on data from Chinese counties spanning 2012 to 2023, this paper regards the pilot policy of constructing national demonstration parks for rural industrial integration development (CRIID) as a quasi-natural experiment and employs the staggered DID model to empirically examine the impact and mechanism of CRIID on CER. The findings are as follows: (1) The eastern counties exhibit high levels of CER with contiguous distribution; the central region is at a medium level, showing transitional characteristics; and the western region is generally weak but features distinctive high-value areas. The “pole scattering” effect of CER within urban agglomerations in the eastern region is pronounced, and overall, the CER of southern counties outperforms that of northern counties. (2) CRIID can enhance CER, and the enhancement effect is more pronounced in major grain-producing counties, labor-importing counties, and industrial counties. (3) CRIID can enhance CER through channels such as improving the level of industrial agglomeration, increasing the output of the agricultural “Three New” economy, and alleviating financing constraints. (4) CRIID exerts a significant positive spatial spillover effect on CER and can significantly improve the economic resilience of neighboring counties. The above research conclusions imply that promoting rural industrial integration with counties as the carrier is a critical path for improving CER, providing generalizable empirical references for other emerging economies to stabilize rural economies and respond to global systemic risks.
summary: Evaluates how China's national demonstration parks for rural industrial integration affect county-level economic resilience.

title: Understanding the pathways for scaling rural innovations: Insights from 34 rural revitalization cases in Asia
authors: Mingmin Emily Pan; Wai-Fung Lam; Winnie W.Y. Law; Theresa M. Lorenzo
keywords: Asia; Rural innovations; Rural revitalization; Scaling
abstract: Despite a growing number of innovative rural revitalization practices in Asia, the patterns and mechanisms through which such innovations are scaled have not been thoroughly explored. This study distinguishes three forms of rural innovation scaling, namely expansion, replication, and translation, and examines 34 rural revitalization efforts across eight Asian jurisdictions to identify robust pathways associated with each scaling form. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) and in-depth case analysis, our results suggest that each scaling form requires the support of different configurations of enabling conditions. While recognized leadership, strong extra-local networks, and effective knowledge aggregation and circulation form a shared backbone of successful scaling, replication proves more demanding than expansion. Translation requires a further convergence of demonstrated wider relevance, windows of opportunity, authoritative legitimation, and active advocacy for formal adoption. Our analysis highlights the importance of strengthening the backbone of scaling by encouraging civil society and other extra-local actors to take the lead in coordinating, codifying, and disseminating rural innovation practices. It also enriches our understanding of the multiple roles that governments can play in fostering the scaling of rural innovations across Asian contexts.
summary: Draws on 34 rural revitalization cases in Asia to identify the pathways through which rural innovations are scaled up.

title: Origin-linked quality and local development: A case study of artisanal furniture in Santa Cruz de Minas, Brazil
authors: E.F.M.N. Moreira; F.M. de Mendonça; E.M. Guerra
keywords: Artisanal production; Brazil; Creative economy; Geographical indications; Rural development; Territorial governance
abstract: Geographical Indications (GIs) have gained prominence as institutional tools that link product differentiation to territorial identity, contributing to rural development and value creation. While widely applied in agri-food systems, their use in artisanal and manufacturing-based rural economies remains limited, particularly in developing countries. This study assesses the potential for GI recognition of artisanal demolition-wood furniture produced in Santa Cruz de Minas (MG), Brazil. A qualitative case study approach was adopted, applying the Virtuous Circle of Quality Linked to Origin (VCQLO) framework, supported by field observations, documentary analysis, and institutional data. The findings reveal a consistent product–territory nexus, evidenced by the high concentration of approximately 180 active artisanal workshops within a small territorial area (3.56 km2), shared know-how, intergenerational knowledge transmission, and regional market reputation. However, structural constraints, such as incipient collective organization, heterogeneity of technical standards, and governance weaknesses, coexist with challenges in translating this symbolic value into direct economic returns for local artisans. The results suggest that GI recognition as an Indication of Source is feasible, provided that institutional coordination, technical standardization, and collective action mechanisms are strengthened. The study contributes to expanding the analytical scope of GIs beyond agri-food systems and highlights their role in promoting diversified and sustainable rural development.
summary: Uses a case study of artisanal furniture in Santa Cruz de Minas, Brazil, to examine how origin-linked quality relates to local development.

title: Gentrifying the rural heritage site: the co-production of heritage by gentrifiers and local communities in China
authors: Jun Lu; Wei Tao; Shaoxu Wang
keywords: Baisha village; Gentrifiers; Heritagization; Rural gentrification; Rural heritage site
abstract: Heritagization refers to the process of transforming historic artifacts and places into objects of commemoration, exhibition, and conservation that influence the present. It is increasingly intertwined with gentrification strategies worldwide and is now spreading to rural areas alongside urban-to-rural migration. The urban middle class’s definition of rural heritage involves a process of heritagization that is largely subjective and imaginative, rather than reflective of rural realities. However, the instrumental role of heritage in rural gentrification has not received sufficient attention in academic circles, particularly with regard to how the privileges associated with heritagization shape rural transformation. Using Baisha Village in Lijiang as a case study, this research provides a comprehensive analysis of the dynamic process of rural gentrification through the lens of heritagization. First, relocated urban newcomers, leveraging their access to land and housing in rural heritage sites, reshape heritage into an abstract object with specific aesthetic and economic values and (re)invest in it, thereby triggering the initial stages of rural gentrification. Consequently, a new mechanism of capital accumulation emerges, generating symbolic and economic value through rural heritage and increasing the appeal of rural areas to cross-regional investment. Meanwhile, local government management strategies, while restricting construction by local communities, render heritage sites more favorable to investment and capital accumulation by gentrifiers. As a result, the social life of local residents becomes increasingly alienated from the gentrifying heritage sites, culminating in the gradual loss of villagers’ effective access to and control over rural heritage assets. This paper demonstrates how privileged access to land and housing in rural heritage sites, combined with the assembly of heritagization practices into exclusive lifestyle and commercial experiences, contributes to social differentiation and reinforces the dynamics of rural gentrification.
summary: Examines how gentrifiers and local communities co-produce heritage at a gentrifying rural heritage site in China.

title: From spillovers to recursive coupling: The development of rural entrepreneurial ecosystems over time
authors: Tore Frimanslund
keywords: Ecosystem development; Institutional adaptation; Rural entrepreneurial ecosystems; Spillovers
abstract: How do entrepreneurial ecosystems develop in thin rural contexts? This article addresses this question through a qualitative longitudinal multiple-case study of two rural entrepreneurial ecosystems in Western Norway, based on 37 interviews conducted across repeated fieldwork waves between 2017 and 2026. Using a process-oriented analysis combining within-case temporal bracketing and cross-case comparison, the study traces how entrepreneurial activity, resource flows, and institutional responses became connected over time. The findings show that ecosystem development depended not simply on the accumulation of favourable conditions, but on whether initially isolated spillovers became recursively coupled across actors, organisations, and successive entrepreneurial events. Knowledge, legitimacy, competence, capital, and organisational initiative were carried forward, recombined, and recycled into subsequent entrepreneurial activity, while support actors adapted increasingly toward brokerage and ecosystem-level enabling. At the same time, fragmentation, missing brokerage, declining interaction, and resource leakage could weaken or interrupt these dynamics. The article contributes to entrepreneurial ecosystem research by conceptualising recursively coupled spillovers as a micro-to-macro mechanism through which dispersed entrepreneurial actions may generate contingent ecosystem-level self-reinforcement over time.
summary: Traces how rural entrepreneurial ecosystems develop over time, from spillovers to recursive coupling.

title: Rural youth seeing community through photovoice
authors: Jaelyn Sewell; Colin C. Caso; Audrey E.H. King; J. Shane Robinson; Linnea Harvey
keywords: Agricultural education; Photovoice; Rural; Youth perceptions
abstract: Youth are an integral part of rural communities. However, scholars and policymakers frequently exclude them from discussions on rural life, which can limit the feasibility of community development and renewal efforts. This study examines how 15 school-based agricultural education (SBAE) students in an Oklahoma community perceive their rural community using the photovoice methodology. Students used photos, captions, and group dialogue to document their community's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and challenges. Guided by the Critical Consciousness Theory (CCT) and the Community Capitals Framework (CCF), findings demonstrate rural youth possess a broad understanding of community life. Participants identified agriculture, social support networks, and local businesses as core strengths of their community, while pointing to significant infrastructure decline, economic fragility, and population loss as threats. Despite challenges, SBAE students remained optimistic, seeing a future of stronger rural communities through civic engagement, jobs, and investment.
summary: Uses photovoice to explore how rural youth see and represent their communities.

title: The role of the third sector in China's agri-food transitions: Integrating transformative social innovation and the state–society paradigm
authors: Junyu Zhang
keywords: Agri-food system; China; State–society relations; Sustainability transitions; Third sector
abstract: The third sector is increasingly recognised as a key driver of transformative change in the agri-food system, though its potential depends largely on the institutional context. This study integrates transformative social innovation theory with a state–society framework to examine the extent to which the third sector can support a society-driven transition pathway alternative to the state-led one. Combining a narrative literature review with case studies of 24 third sector organisations, it identifies and compares the two pathways through their guiding agendas and the social relations that characterise each. This study employs a deductive qualitative content analysis of organisations' activities, drawing primarily on public materials such as statements and reports available on the organisations' websites and social media. The findings reveal a nuanced interplay: while the third sector and the state share many agendas for transitions, particularly in recognising challenges and setting goals, their underlying motivations diverge. The state pursues transitions as a national strategy for food security, whereas third sector initiatives are grounded in community demands. State-led transitions intensify the concentration of power among large-scale operators while displacing smallholders. In contrast, the third sector reconnects farmers with the land and producers with consumers through alternative food networks. In only three cases, the third sector fosters social relations that remain compatible with the state's agendas. The study concludes that the third sector holds significant transformative potential, and that Chinese agri-food transitions could benefit from collaborative engagement between the two pathways.
summary: Examines the role of the third sector in China's agri-food transitions by combining transformative social innovation theory with the state–society paradigm.

title: Impact of reverse rural-urban migration on the utilization and conservation of cultivated land: A case study of Xiantao in the Jianghan Plain of China
authors: Qianlong Yang; Yuanyuan Zhu; Cheng Chen; Qi Wen
keywords: Cultivated land conservation; Cultivated land utilization; Key agricultural areas; Reverse rural-urban migration; Xiantao City
abstract: Reverse rural-urban migration (RRUM) plays a crucial role in optimizing the territorial system of human-environment interaction in rural areas. This phenomenon introduces diverse resource elements crucial for rural development while simultaneously exerting significant impacts on the level of cultivated land utilization (LCLU) and the level of cultivated land conservation (LCLC). However, the mechanisms underlying the RRUM’s influence on cultivated land utilization and conservation remain underexplored. In this paper, we evaluated the changes in the RRUM and the level of cultivated land utilization and conservation in Xiantao City, China, from 2012 to 2021. The results showed that the RRUM in Xiantao City fluctuated along a “W” trajectory. Concurrently, the LCLU and LCLC in Xiantao City demonstrated an upward trend during the study period. In addition to revealing the evolutionary laws, we also examined the driving factors, mechanisms of action, and characteristics of spatiotemporal heterogeneity using the fixed-effect and mediation-effect models. The model results show that RRUM promotes LCLU but exerts a negative effect on LCLC, with these effects operating through differentiated transmission pathways across regions and over time. Overall, industrial promotion and technological progress exhibit heterogeneous mediating effects across spatial and temporal contexts. Moving forward, we contend that moderate RRUM could contribute to the accumulation of human capital in the countryside, benefiting the reverse trend of rural decline and agricultural modernization globally.
summary: Uses a case study of Xiantao in China's Jianghan Plain to examine how reverse rural-urban (return) migration affects the use and conservation of cultivated land.

title: Geographies and changes in homeownership in the United States, 1970–2020
authors: Kanglin Chen; Bora Ju; Cenqi Zhu; Rockli Kim; S.V. Subramanian
keywords: Affordability; County-level analysis; Housing stock; Housing tenure; Inequality; Population
abstract: Homeownership has long been an important component of housing policy initiatives. U.S. national homeownership has remained relatively stagnant at around 65% from the establishment of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) in 1965 through the 2020s, prompting discussion about the effectiveness of related policies. Given the limited understanding of long-term housing trajectories, this study examines the trends and geographies of the number of owner-occupied housing units (the Number), homeownership (the percentage of owner-occupied units among all occupied units), population, and households from 1970 to 2020. Nationally, both the Number (39.8 million to 80.1 million) and households (63 million to 126.8 million) roughly doubled, while homeownership remained relatively stable (63.0% to 63.1%). This suggests that sizable expansions in housing stock do not translate into higher homeownership, whereas declines are more likely when housing growth lags behind increases in households. The Number, households, and population were closely related, although population grew more slowly, increasing by about 1.6 times compared with 2 times for the former two measures. Disparities in the Number widened across the country and within states despite stable national homeownership rates. Meanwhile, homeownership exhibited reduced spatial clustering and declines particularly in regions experiencing rapid housing and population growth. Overall, the expansion of the U.S. housing supply broadly kept pace with household growth and accommodated declining household sizes nationally, although regional divergences in homeownership outcomes remained. This study identifies where and when housing divergences emerged and highlights the need to better align housing development with regional and demographic dynamics to support homeownership attainment.
summary: Maps the geography of homeownership across the United States and how it changed between 1970 and 2020.

title: Does urbanization formalize the economy? The role of local governance in Vietnam
authors: Cong Minh Huynh; Nam Hoai Tran
keywords: Formal job creation; Local governance quality; Shadow economy; Urbanization
abstract: This study investigates how urbanization affects the shadow economy in a transitional context, emphasizing the roles of formal firm expansion and local governance quality. Using a panel dataset of 63 Vietnamese provinces over 2006–2021, we employ fixed-effects and System GMM estimators to examine direct, mediating, and moderating effects. The results reveal that urbanization significantly reduces the shadow economy, primarily by stimulating formal firm expansion and registered employment opportunities. Higher local governance quality - particularly stronger corruption control, simplified administrative procedures, greater transparency, and enhanced vertical accountability - also directly constrains informality. Moreover, local governance quality strengthens the formalizing effect of urbanization, indicating that provinces with stronger institutions derive greater benefits from urban growth. These findings suggest that the formalizing impact of urbanization depends critically on institutional capacity and governance quality. By developing a moderated mediation framework linking urbanization, governance quality, and formal firm expansion, this study contributes to the literature on structural transformation, informality, and decentralization, while offering policy implications for managing informality through coordinated urban and institutional reforms in developing economies.
summary: Tests whether urbanization formalizes the economy in Vietnam and how local governance shapes that relationship.

title: Spatial governance under polycrisis: Reconfiguring agglomeration policy
authors: Sofia Borushkina; Anton Gorodnichev
keywords: Polycrisis; Russia; Spatial governance; Territorial resilience; Urban agglomeration
abstract: Agglomeration policy has long been a dominant paradigm in spatial development, premised on the assumption that large, integrated city-regions drive national economic growth through productivity, innovation, and global integration. This paper examines how this paradigm is reworked under conditions of polycrisis, a durable state in which economic, geopolitical, and institutional shocks interact and reinforce one another. We argue that, while a crisis is often addressed through recalibrating policy tools and objectives, polycrisis reshapes the underlying rationalities of spatial planning. Focusing on Russia, the study analyses how national spatial priorities shift from growth and competitiveness toward territorial stabilisation, population retention, and the management of systemic vulnerability. It compares the 2019 and 2024 Spatial Development Strategies, drawing on policy documents, implementation materials, and expert discussions, and applies a process-tracing approach to reconstruct changes across two planning cycles. The findings show that agglomeration policy is not a universally stable development model but a contingent framework dependent on growth, openness, and functional integration. As these conditions erode under polycrisis, agglomeration policy is reworked from a governance technology of growth into a mechanism of territorial anchoring and control, signalling a broader shift from development to stabilisation in spatial planning.
summary: Examines how agglomeration policy and spatial governance are being reconfigured under conditions of polycrisis.

title: The gender dimension of homeownership: Evidence from China
authors: Daphne Wing Chan; Natalie Xiaoqi Liu; Helen X.H. Bao
keywords: Education; Gender gap; Homeownership; Housing asset
abstract: This paper presents findings on the relationship between gender and three key housing asset indicators in China: homeownership, second homeownership, and housing asset value. The analysis also considers whether having a son modifies the relationship between gender of the household head and the housing asset indicators. The empirical analysis found that male household heads are more likely to have homeownership, female household heads are more likely to own a second home, and female homeowners tend to own more expensive homes than male homeowners. These findings are robust across alternative functional forms and variable definitions. The results highlight the importance of exploring the differential likelihood of homeownership and second homeownership as well as disparities in housing asset values from a gender perspective.
summary: Examines the gender dimension of homeownership in China.

title: Materialism and subjective well-being among rural migrant women in China: The mediating role of residential conditions
authors: Moli Gu; Shuangshuang Tang
keywords: Materialism; Residential conditions; Rural migrant women; Social comparison; Subjective well-being
abstract: Rural migrant women in urban China commonly face insufficient economic resources and limited opportunities for self-development, which may hinder improvements in subjective well-being (SWB) and foster materialistic orientations. Residential conditions may serve as behavioral and consumption-related manifestations of materialistic pursuits and, in turn, affect SWB. Grounded in the Model of Goal-Directed Behavior (MGB) and based on questionnaire survey data collected in Nanjing, China, this study employs linear regression and mediation analyses to examine how materialism affects SWB among rural migrant women and to test the direct and mediating effects of residential conditions. Social comparison is incorporated as a moderating variable, and moderation analysis is used to assess its role within these pathways. The results show that materialism is significantly negatively correlated with SWB. Regarding residential conditions, both housing tenure and household amenities exert direct effects on SWB, while community type and household amenities mediate the relationship between materialism and SWB. Furthermore, social comparison moderates both the direct and indirect effects of materialism on SWB. The findings suggest that rural migrant women's material pursuits reflect motives of psychological compensation and the pursuit of social recognition, and that constrained gender and institutional identities, together with individual capital, may underlie the adverse consequences of materialism, with residential choices embodying these mechanisms.
summary: Studies how materialism relates to subjective well-being among rural migrant women in China, with residential conditions as a mediator.

title: Housing developers' resilience in a crisis-prone region: An analysis for Turkey-Istanbul
authors: Seyma Oztas; Sevkiye Sence Turk
keywords: Crises; Housing Developers; Istanbul; Resilience; Turkey
abstract: Some countries are more prone to crises not only due to their location in a highly volatile region or their macroeconomic weaknesses, but also because of their inherent natural attributes (such as climate conditions, seismic activity, and the presence of wetlands, etc.). The housing sector is highly vulnerable due to its immense size, capital requirements, long investment cycles and sensitivity to external shocks, making it even more fragile in these crisis-prone environments. In building resilience against crises, the role of housing developers -especially within a market-driven residential sub-sector supported by hybrid state interventions- is critical. The aim of this study is to explore how housing developers in a crisis-prone region, such as Istanbul, can strategically adapt to and manage crises through practical urban resilience strategies. Using a methodological approach centered on Structural Equation Modelling (SEM), a survey was conducted with 140 housing developers in Istanbul, Turkey. The sample was selected using a stratified design taking into consideration operational longevity, spatial footprint, and development volume. The model uses 10 latent and 36 observed variables, including internal (scope of activity, structure, brand, working model, network) and external factors (political climate, imbalances, global developments, and social balances) that shape housing developers' resilience. The findings show that resilience depends on internal and external factors, with internal capabilities exerting a higher impact. This reveals that resilience is largely related to organizational capacity, decision-making processes, and corporate strategy. This helps explain corporate responses to crises and the private sector's role in urban resilience.
summary: Analyses the resilience of housing developers operating in crisis-prone Istanbul, Turkey.

title: State entrepreneurialism and the growth-equity trade-off: Dipiao and public rental housing in Chongqing, China
authors: Weijie Hu; Renhao Yang; Jing Zhou
keywords: Central-local mediation; Debt-financed urbanisation; Dipiao; EAD interlock; Public rental housing; State entrepreneurialism
abstract: This paper examines Chongqing's state-entrepreneurial governance through two flagship urbanisation policies: Dipiao, or land tickets, and Public Rental Housing (PRH). It defines the Equity through Assetization and Debt (EAD) interlock as a Chongqing-specific mechanism that combines Dipiao-based assetization, debt-backed PRH provision, and central-local mediation within the broader logic of state entrepreneurialism. By the end of 2022, Dipiao transactions had reached 369,000 mu and 72.442 billion CNY, with redistribution mechanisms supporting rural migrants. Since 2010, Chongqing's PRH programme had delivered more than 40 million square metres of affordable housing. The public record supports institutional co-articulation through temporal sequencing and a shared fiscal-land regime, without establishing a dedicated revenue chain from Dipiao receipts to PRH construction. Reliance on volatile land markets and debt financing creates fiscal vulnerabilities, while peripheral PRH siting imposes heavy commuting burdens and sustains socio-spatial inequalities. Using directed thematic analysis of policy documents, audited statistics, and peer-reviewed studies, the paper traces how the three EAD components were assembled, examines their economic and social consequences, and identifies the governance tensions created by land-market volatility, debt service, peripheral siting, and uneven service provision. It offers a mechanism-based refinement of state entrepreneurialism and evidence from an inland Chinese municipality facing growth pressure, fiscal constraints, and equity commitments.
summary: Examines how state entrepreneurialism in Chongqing, China, through the dipiao (land ticket) system and public rental housing, trades off growth against equity.

title: Determinants of the spatial relationship between morphological and functional centers across different stages of economic development: Evidence from 338 ASEAN cities
authors: Guanfeng Li; Yutian Liang
keywords: ASEAN; Functional centers; Morphological centers; Spatial relationship; Stages of economic development
abstract: The spatial relationship between morphological and functional centers influences the efficiency of resource allocation and the coordination of spatial structure. However, existing studies predominantly focus on macro-level trend analysis, lacking not only typological examinations based on their spatial relationships but also investigations into the factors influencing these spatial relationships. Using ASEAN as a case study, this paper identifies its morphological and functional centers, conducts a comparative analysis across different economic development stages, and examines their spatial relationships, typologies, and underlying drivers. The results reveal three key findings: (1) Morphological centers in ASEAN cities generally display polycentric and dispersed patterns, while functional centers tend to be monocentric and concentrated. (2) The spatial linkage between morphological and functional centers is heterogeneous and closely tied to economic development stages. Among these factors, Fragmentation, Transportation, and History remain consistently influential across all stages. In contrast, the influence of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and industrial parks exhibits a growing trend during the middle and later stages of economic development. (3) While the number, scale, and spatial relationships of morphological and functional centers vary distinctly across different economic development stages, their spatial distribution characteristics exhibit notable commonalities.
summary: Analyses 338 ASEAN cities to identify what determines the spatial relationship between their morphological and functional centers at different stages of economic development.

title: The spatiality of informal settlement displacement: Insights from Mumbai, Ho Chi Minh City and Manila
authors: Matthijs van Oostrum
keywords: Asia; Displacement; Eviction; Informal settlement; Mapping; Neoliberal urban development
abstract: While internationally condemned, residents of informal settlements around the world continue to face the threat of eviction and displacement. In Asian cities, neoliberal urban development policy has been identified as a key driver of development-inducted displacement. Through the mapping of informal settlement displacement in three megacities in Asia, this paper investigates the spatial and temporal patterns of such displacement in a comparative way. Complemented by policy analysis, the displacement of informal settlements is analysed through trends in the annual distribution of displacement, the spatial concentration around central business areas and waterfronts, their post-demolition land-use, and the scale of individual demolitions. While practices of slum clearance and urban renewal in the three case study cities are all informed by neoliberal urban planning policy, this paper finds that the governance and finance arrangements characterizing each city have a clear impact on the spatiality of informal settlement displacement.
summary: Compares the spatial patterns of informal settlement displacement in Mumbai, Ho Chi Minh City and Manila.

title: The knowledge complementary potential of cities: Opportunities for technological diversification in multilocational firms
authors: Hongji Chen; Pengxin Chen; Nina Zhu; Yi Guo; Gang Zeng
keywords: Cities; Complementary knowledge; Knowledge relatedness density; Multilocational firms; Technological diversification
abstract: We develop an analytical framework of knowledge complementary potential of cities for firms and its innovation effects, and conduct empirical analysis based on 998 listed firms in China. We find that the complementary knowledge (CK) significantly increases the likelihood of technological diversification, and this effect does not exist in isolation but forms a complementary relationship with the firm's knowledge relatedness density. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the innovation effects of CK vary substantially across different types of firms. In high-tech industries and private firms, the effect relies more heavily on the support of firms' internal knowledge structures; whereas in non-high-tech industries and state-owned firms, CK also exerts a direct promoting effect.
summary: Examines how complementary knowledge across cities creates opportunities for multilocational firms to diversify technologically.

title: Do local politicians share their constituents' attitudes on housing policy?
authors: Alex B. Rivard; Jack Lucas
keywords: Housing; Municipal politics; Public opinion; Substantive representation
abstract: In this paper, we combine a nationally representative survey of Canadians with a survey of more than 700 mayors and councillors in municipalities across Canada to explore (a) the extent to which politicians align with their constituents in their housing policy attitudes and (b) the extent to which politicians' views are more representative of more privileged local residents, such as homeowners. We find strong evidence of macrolevel attitudinal congruence: when local communities are more supportive of a housing policy proposals, local politicians tend to be more supportive as well. We also find that politicians' attitudes on housing are not more aligned with privileged local residents; instead, elite-mass alignment is primarily shaped by ideological congruence.
summary: Tests whether local politicians' attitudes on housing policy match those of their constituents.

title: Evaluating the differential impacts of formal and informal environmental regulation on urban wellbeing
authors: Congyu Zhao; Xiucheng Dong; Farhad Taghizadeh-Hesary
keywords: China; Environmental regulation; Income group; Wellbeing
abstract: Environmental regulation is key to sustainable development, yet its impact on societal wellbeing remains underexplored. This study uses prefecture-level panel data from China (2000−2022) to examine how environmental regulations, both formal and informal, affect wellbeing across cities with varying economic development. Our findings show: (1) formal regulation does not typically enhance wellbeing, while informal regulation positively affects all cities. (2) The impact of formal regulation depends on a city's per capita GDP, supporting the “Porter Hypothesis” in wealthier cities, where formal regulations improve wellbeing, while the opposite occurs in poorer cities. (3) The moderating roles of industrial structure upgrading and employment are identified: they amplify the positive effect of formal regulation in wealthier cities but exacerbate its negative effect in poorer cities. For informal regulation, these two factors consistently serve as positive moderators across all city groups, reinforcing its beneficial effect on wellbeing. This study sheds light on the nuanced role of environmental regulation in promoting sustainable wellbeing in urban contexts.
summary: Evaluates how formal and informal environmental regulation differ in their effects on urban wellbeing.

title: How culture shapes cities' economic resilience: Global evidence on individualism-collectivism
authors: Lei Chen; Fenjie Long; Lei Li; Jianing Liu; Longfei Zheng
keywords: Collectivism; Economic resilience; Global; Individualism; National culture
abstract: As global shocks become more frequent, strengthening the economic resilience of cities has become a central concern for sustainable urban development and governance. While economic and institutional conditions are widely acknowledged, the role of cultural factors in shaping cities' economic resilience remains underexplored in urban studies and policy debates. This study develops a global city-level gross domestic product (GDP) dataset for 7652 cities across 177 countries by combining monthly nighttime light data with a two-stage machine learning approach. Random forest is first employed in response to the post-2020 shock period, followed by XGBoost to generate high-frequency GDP estimates. Using these data, we evaluate cities' economic resistance, recoverability, and overall resilience to a series of shocks after 2020. Leveraging Hofstede's individualism index and applying OLS regressions with instrumental variable techniques, our results show that individualism has a significant negative effect on all three resilience dimensions. The negative association is more pronounced for recoverability than for resistance. Importantly, strong government regulation and robust infrastructure help to offset this adverse effect. These findings suggest that cultural orientation matters not only for how cities absorb shocks, but also for how effectively they coordinate recovery. By bringing culture into the analysis of global cities' economic resilience, this study extends existing research beyond material and institutional explanations and highlights the importance of governance capacity and infrastructure in culturally diverse contexts.
summary: Uses global evidence to examine how individualist versus collectivist culture shapes cities' economic resilience.

title: Urban vertical equity under the Matthew Effect: A case study of spatial differentiation of housing prices in Nanjing
authors: Xiqian Wang; Jingxuan Hu; Zhijie Yang
keywords: Housing prices; Matthew Effect; Multiscale geographically weighted regression; Spatial differentiation; Time-based accessibility; Vertical equity
abstract: Amid soaring housing prices and increasing social stratification, issues of housing equity in Chinese cities have become progressively prominent. Previous studies have mostly focused on the formal equity of spatial balance, while neglecting substantial disparities in urban facility accessibility and time costs across social groups. From the perspective of vertical equity, this study introduces the Matthew Effect to examine how the accumulation of socioeconomic advantages intensifies spatial differentiation and the unequal distribution of housing resources, revealing structural inequality among income groups in urban space. Using Nanjing as a case study, this research establishes a time-based evaluation system of urban facility accessibility and applies the multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) model to analyze the spatial heterogeneity of housing prices. Integrating the Theil index with spatial match analysis, it further assesses the vertical equity of facility resource accessibility across different income levels. The results reveal a distinct concentric spatial structure of housing prices: high-income groups cluster in core areas with convenient transportation and abundant educational and environmental resources, while low-income groups are marginalized to peripheral zones with higher commuting costs and limited facilities. Differences in time accessibility to urban facilities further amplify price spillover effects in core areas, aggravating vertical inequity in the housing market. By integrating temporal accessibility analysis with multi-scale spatial modeling, this study advances the theoretical and methodological framework of housing equity and proposes a vertical-equity-oriented housing resource optimization strategy to promote balanced urban facility allocation, prevent resource over-concentration, and foster socially integrated urban development.
summary: Uses Nanjing as a case study of spatial differentiation in housing prices to examine urban vertical equity under a Matthew effect.

title: Toward inclusive city-regions: How inter-city cooperation shapes cultural-symbolic mobility
authors: Xuelian Li; Tianlan Xia; Yuanshuo Xu
keywords: Cultural-symbolic mobility; Inclusive city-regions; Inter-city cooperation; Natural language processing (NLP)
abstract: Inter-city cooperation has become a central institutional framework for city-regional development, yet its implications for cultural-symbolic connectivity remain underexplored. Drawing on insights from the policy mobilities literature, this study conceptualizes inter-city cooperation as an institutionalized relational infrastructure that shapes cultural-symbolic mobility within an uneven urban hierarchy. Using data from 41 cities in China's Yangtze River Delta (YRD), we measure cultural-symbolic flows with 250,616 place-name POIs and cooperation intensity with 247,035 government-reported cooperation events identified through natural language processing (NLP). The results show that stronger cooperation is positively associated with greater cultural-symbolic connectivity, operating through strengthened investment linkages, population mobility, and collaborative knowledge innovation. This association is more pronounced among non-adjacent cities, across metropolitan boundaries, and in relationships involving peripheral and non-metropolitan cities. These findings suggest that cultural-symbolic mobility within city-regions is shaped not merely by proximity or market forces but also by formal cooperation arrangements, which foster more inclusive regional integration.
summary: Examines how inter-city cooperation shapes cultural-symbolic mobility and the inclusiveness of city-regions.

title: Measuring overlapping suburbanization and peri-urbanization processes in Warsaw Metropolitan Area
authors: Dorota Mantey
keywords: Peri-urbanization; Rural-to-urban transformation; Suburbanization; Urban sprawl; Warsaw Metropolitan Area
abstract: While suburbanization remains one of the most extensively studied spatial processes, peri-urbanization has only recently gained comparable scholarly attention. It is conceptualized as a multidimensional and dynamic process capturing rural-to-urban transformations, differing from suburbanization in terms of density, land use, migration patterns, employment structure, and a more dispersed form of urbanization. Peri-urbanization can be understood as an umbrella concept encompassing diverse processes at urban peripheries, including suburbanization, and extending beyond the suburban zone. Although these processes overlap, this article proposes a method for measuring both, enabling the analysis of their spatial relationships using the Warsaw Metropolitan Area (WMA) as a case study and public statistics as a data source. Suburbanization is measured as the inflow of urban residents into the city's outskirts relative to the outflow, while peri-urbanization is assessed using a synthetic indicator – the unweighted mean of normalized variables describing demography, entrepreneurship, employment in agriculture, and infrastructure development. The results show no clear link between peri-urbanization intensity and distance from the city. Three trajectories of urban-to-rural transformation are identified, reflecting different combinations of economic, infrastructural, and demographic transformations. In contrast, suburbanization is more strongly associated with city-centered gravitational forces, with generally increasing intensity with distance from the core, although not in a strictly linear manner. A comparison of both indicators shows that, although they intensify in similar sectors of the WMA, municipalities with the highest and lowest values often do not coincide. The proposed operationalization and analytical framework may be applied to other cities with similar development contexts.
summary: Measures how suburbanization and peri-urbanization processes overlap in the Warsaw Metropolitan Area.

title: Investigating data center site planning of major ICT companies in the U.S.: A spatial and methodological framework
authors: Seung Jun Choi; Kijin Seong; Junfeng Jiao
keywords: Data center; Digital infrastructure; ICT enterprises; Site selection
abstract: As AI becomes more embedded in urban systems, the demand for data centers continues to rise. This study analyzes 212 data centers in the U.S., focusing on those operated by major ICT enterprises. We examined key site-selection factors using clustering, suitability scoring, graph-based network analysis, and conditional logistic regression. K-means was selected for clustering. Variables were grouped into environmental and locational site-level factors to generate separate suitability indices. To identify siting determinants, we then estimated conditional logistic regression models, comparing each data center against spatially comparable control locations. The results highlight the complexity of selecting a site for a data center. In general, data centers exhibit spatial agglomeration and gain operational advantages from economies of scale. Clustering analysis grouped sites into six categories, each reflecting distinct locational and environmental patterns. The graph-based network analysis further illustrates the trade-offs companies must make between environmental suitability and operational site-level advantages. Regression results revealed that land use structure, particularly land use diversity and was the most powerful determinant of data center siting. Infrastructural factors, including substation density and proximity to primary roads, as well as the concentration of IT workers, also exhibited strong positive effects. Among environmental factors, lower wind speeds and PM2.5 concentrations positively influenced data center siting, while state-level policy incentives remained statistically insignificant. Our findings highlight the distinctive infrastructural characteristics of these facilities. Acknowledging their widespread operational footprint across diverse urban landscapes, planners must proactively engage with the physical and spatial dimensions of digital infrastructure.
summary: Develops a spatial and methodological framework for analysing where major ICT companies site their data centers in the U.S.

title: Unravelling the dual displacement risks of urban renewal: A causal inference framework integrating double machine learning and XAI
authors: Guang Li; Wei Li; Chuan Lin; Chuanzhun Sun; Yinxin Su; Jingna Liang; Yilun Liu
keywords: Displacement risk; Double machine learning; Gentrification; Shenzhen; Urban renewal; XAI
abstract: With urban renewal advancing globally, intensified gentrification and rising living costs are exacerbating displacement risk. However, existing research has rarely examined how renewal-induced cost pressures vary across fine spatial units, where their spatial spillover boundaries emerge, and how housing and consumption costs jointly shape displacement risk. We construct a novel analytical framework integrating Double Machine Learning (DML) for causal inference, sliding-window threshold detection for boundary analysis, and eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). Our analysis in Shenzhen reveals that urban renewal significantly increases displacement risks by raising the relative market standing of housing rents and catering consumption costs. Specifically, the model estimates that renewal causally elevates the inflation-adjusted relative market standing of housing rents by 5.46% and catering consumption costs by 9.69% within the city-wide distribution. Crucially, the spatial analysis uncovers asymmetric patterns: while rental increases exhibit a clear spillover range of approximately 1103.6 m, no significant spatial boundary was detected for consumption cost changes. Further examination identifies three displacement-risk pathways shaped by renewal's differentiated impacts, highlighting how functional replacement and the relative dominance of the “housing-cost crowding-out effect” versus the “consumption-demand substitution effect” shape displacement risk. These findings not only deepen the understanding of the fundamental processes driving direct and indirect displacement but also bridge a critical gap in conventional theory regarding spatial responsiveness to renewal, providing policymakers with spatially-grounded quantitative evidence to advance the complementary objectives of social equity and inclusive development.
summary: Combines double machine learning with explainable AI in a causal framework to assess the dual displacement risks created by urban renewal.

title: State-led flexibility through temporary land use: Governing time-bounded land rights in urban China
authors: Jie Guo; Zhiwei Du
keywords: Asymmetric assetization; State-led flexibility; Temporary land use; Time-bounded land rights; Urban China
abstract: Temporary land use is commonly understood as an informal, experimental, or bottom-up response to planning rigidity and market uncertainty. This article develops a different perspective by examining how public authorities can actively institutionalize temporariness through the temporal organization of property rights.
