Drawing on the redevelopment of the Jianyuzhou industrial heritage site in Dongguan, China, it shows how differentiated and time-bounded rights can enable present land activation while preserving public control over future redevelopment. Rather than transferring a coherent bundle of property rights, the arrangement selectively distributes rights to use, operate, generate income, and exit across public authorities, developers, and tenants. This produces a form of state-led flexibility in which operational adaptability is combined with institutional reversibility, allowing the state to retain strategic control over land disposition and redevelopment. At the same time, risks and value-capture opportunities are unevenly distributed, generating what we term asymmetric assetization. The article therefore reframes temporary land use as a mode of urban land governance based on the temporalization and differentiation of property rights. It contributes to debates on temporary urbanism by showing that temporariness can be deliberately designed as a governing arrangement for reconciling short-term activation with long-term redevelopment control.
summary: Examines how the Chinese state uses temporary land use and time-bounded land rights to build flexibility into urban land governance.

title: The threshold effect of green space-urban expansion allometric growth on healthy cities: A multi-city panel analysis
authors: Jing Bai; Xiaoke Sun; Jiaying Liu; Yunyun Shi; Ying An; Xi Wang; Yan Yan
keywords: Allometric growth; Green space; Healthy cities; Panel threshold model; Threshold effect; Urban expansion
abstract: While global urbanization drives economic development, it imposes significant pressures on urban ecological security and public health, with the expansion imbalance between “gray” built-up areas and “green” ecological spaces being a common challenge. Understanding the coordination of their expansion dynamics is key to sustainable urban health. This study examines four Chinese cities, analyzing the allometric growth relationship between built-up areas and green spaces over three decades, and employs a panel threshold regression model to identify the critical threshold of the green-urban allometric growth coefficient ( b ) that causes a threshold effect on the composite healthy city index. Results show: 1) All four cities exhibit a phased evolution from “scale-priority expansion” to “quality-oriented transformation”. 2) Significant regional heterogeneity exists in allometric growth patterns: Shanghai is “green space expansion-dominated”, Beijing and Haikou are “built-up area expansion-dominated”, and Chongqing is undergoing a “transition-improvement” type toward a more coordinated mode. 3) The panel threshold model reveals a nonlinear marginal diminishing return relationship between b and the healthy city index, with a critical threshold γ = 1.130. Beyond this threshold, the promoting effect remains significant but weakened. 4) The key to regulating the health threshold lies in coordinating ecological endowment, policy interventions, and development stage suitability, with planning foresight and regulatory flexibility being central. This study provides a new analytical framework and quantitative evidence for understanding urban green-built-up expansion dynamics across different development stages, and offers a quantitative benchmark for healthy city policymakers facing similar ecological-development trade-offs to optimize spatial planning and cross the health threshold.
summary: Uses a multi-city panel to test for threshold effects of the allometric growth of green space relative to urban expansion on healthy-city outcomes.

title: Institutions, inclusive innovation, and the post-industrial city: Why equitable development will fail without attention to local politics
authors: Allison Bramwell
keywords: Collaborative planning; Equitable economic development; Inclusive innovation; Post-industrial economic development; Urban policymaking
abstract: Aspirational demands to improve equity have gained some traction alongside the growth imperative on post-industrial urban policy agendas, but the pressing question of how to expand economic opportunity to people and places ‘left out’ of technology-driven growth remains a pressing puzzle. Adding granularity about the actors involved, the power dynamics that ensue, and the consequences for urban policymaking, comparative institutional research over the past decade suggests that equitable post-industrial development will fail without attention to local politics. The institutional capacity required to implement these types of agendas requires cross sector coalitions that are difficult to build and even more difficult to sustain. Illustrative cases of unsuccessful inclusive innovation in two mid-sized restructuring cities, one in the United States and one in France, indicate that these initiatives failed due to weak engagement from local politicians and the business community, suggesting the need for meaningful participatory incentives. Regardless of differences in national policy context, size and specialization matter: these types of cities must work especially hard for economic reinvention while juggling equity imperatives that vie for attention on local policy agendas.
summary: Argues that equitable development through inclusive innovation in post-industrial cities will fail without attention to local politics and institutions.

title: The gap between inclusionary urban visions and exclusionary housing practices: Converting progressive support and electoral wins into practical authority
authors: Walter Nicholls; Jeannine Pearce
keywords: Bureaucratic field; Code enforcement; Discourse analysis; Immigrant marginality; Inclusionary housing; Long Beach
abstract: Sustained mobilization can transform how a city talks about housing without changing how it governs. We ask why progressive discourse and electoral majorities so often fail to reshape administrative practice, using Long Beach, California, where an equity-voicing electorate and council adopted inclusionary language even as code enforcement against immigrant neighborhoods rose twelvefold. Drawing on Bourdieu's bureaucratic field, we theorize the local state as a relatively autonomous field stratified into right-hand (public safety), left-hand (provision), and hybrid (development) positions. That stratification, fixed in place by a council-manager charter and an owner-weighted electorate, generates three mechanisms by which transformations stall at implementation: capture of the discretionary budget, performative layering of inclusionary text atop an exclusionary enforcement core, and buffered autonomy among provision agencies. The framework explains the discourse-implementation gap institutionally.
summary: Examines the gap between inclusionary urban visions and exclusionary housing practices, and how progressive support and electoral wins can be converted into practical authority.

title: Unraveling post-socialist urban expansion: Long-term built-up dynamics in Polish and Romanian urban regions
authors: Oliver-Valentin Dinter; Abdelillah Hamdouch; Corneliu Iațu
keywords: Land restitution; Peri-urbanisation; Post-socialist urban regions; Time-series clustering; Urban sprawl
abstract: Post-socialist urbanisation in Central and Eastern Europe is often described through common processes of decentralisation, land-market formation and suburban expansion, yet the spatial outcomes of transition have diverged substantially across countries. This study examines how contrasting land-ownership reforms and planning instruments shaped long-term built-up dynamics in six second-tier Polish and Romanian urban regions. Using fine-grained Global Human Settlement Layer data from 1975 to 2020, the study applies time-series clustering to identify recurrent trajectories of built-up expansion and compares their spatial distribution, built-up intensity and population-adjusted land consumption. The results show that both countries experienced dispersed peri-urban growth, but in different forms. Romanian urban regions display faster, more fragmented and more land-intensive post-2000 expansion, especially in the newest and lowest-density classes. Polish urban regions also show dispersed development and weak coordination, but their observed spatial signatures are relatively less atomised and more frequently associated with existing settlement structures. These differences are interpreted as the cumulative outcome of ownership reform, parcel structure and development-right allocation within a broader post-2000 context of housing demand, credit expansion, mobility and infrastructure constraints. The paper contributes to comparative post-socialist urban studies by showing that shared socialist legacies did not produce a single urban-regional trajectory and by linking institutional divergence to micro-spatial, multi-decadal evidence beyond capital-city cases.
summary: Traces long-term built-up dynamics to unravel post-socialist urban expansion in Polish and Romanian urban regions.

title: Social infrastructures for the marginalized: The case of subdivided-unit tenants in Hong Kong
authors: Xiao Lu Wang; Ze Tao Lin; Wing Ka Ho
keywords: Hierarchical cluster analysis; High-rise high-density cities; Marginalized group; Participatory mapping; Social infrastructure; Spatial cluster analysis
abstract: This study examines the production and typology of social infrastructure among subdivided-unit (SDU) tenants in Hong Kong, a population marked by housing precarity and spatial poverty. Drawing on participatory mapping and ethnographic diary methods, 101 residents living in Sham Shui Po (a district of Hong Kong) logged 5092 outings over a three-week period, tagging places visited and evaluating them across four dimensions: publicness, biophysical environment, affordance for socialities, and social surplus. Spatial cluster analysis (DBSCAN) revealed five high-frequency clusters concentrated near tenants' homes, while hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) identified five distinct place typologies. Findings show that informal gathering spaces and commercial spaces in Sham Shui Po—such as fruits shops, traditional herbal tea shops, and other street-level eateries—often outperform formally designated community facilities in generating social surplus and fostering social connection, care, and emotional support for SDU tenants. The study highlights the agency of marginalized residents in co-producing social infrastructure through everyday spatial practices and underscores the limitations of planning paradigms that rely solely on “stated” infrastructure. By foregrounding gendered routines and embedded spatial rhythms, this research contributes to a more context-sensitive understanding of social infrastructure and offers insights for inclusive urban design in high-density cities.
summary: Examines the social infrastructures available to marginalized subdivided-unit tenants in Hong Kong.

title: Unveiling inequalities in forgotten enclaves: A geospatial–streetscape integrated framework for assessing urban village livability
authors: Zhijie Zhou; Chun Song; Rui Cao
keywords: Informal settlements; Livability; Street view images; Sustainable Development Goals (SDG); Urban upgrading; Vision-language models (VLM)
abstract: Urban villages (UVs), widespread informal settlements across Chinese cities, play a vital role in providing affordable housing; however, their livability remains underexamined. This gap hinders progress toward sustainable and equitable urban development. To bridge the gap, we propose a dual-scale livability assessment framework that integrates macro-level geospatial indicators with micro-level human perceptions of streetscapes. At the macro scale, we evaluate UV livability from four key dimensions: safety, health, convenience, and comfort, with indicators derived from multi-source geospatial data. At the micro scale, we incorporate human-centered visual assessments through a vision-language-model-based multi-agent framework, in which multiple agents interpret street-view images, generate rubric-based scores, and arbitrate scoring discrepancies to quantify perceived environmental quality. We choose Shenzhen, a megacity with diverse UV typologies, as the empirical case. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in capturing diverse aspects of livability. The findings reveal a pronounced center–periphery gradient and location-specific trade-offs: centrally located UVs generally have higher convenience but lower comfort, whereas peripheral and mountainous UVs show the opposite pattern. Within the sampled UVs, exploratory evidence further suggests broad perceptual deficiencies in alley-dominated interiors, modest improvements in daylighting and openness associated with greater open-space shares, and broader but moderate advantages associated with commercial streets. The proposed framework provides a cross-sectional diagnostic tool for identifying spatial inequalities in UV livability and offers baseline evidence for differentiated urban renewal. It also holds promise for broader urban applications and contributes to the advancement of United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 11.
summary: Proposes a framework integrating geospatial and streetscape data to assess livability and inequalities in urban villages.

title: Organizing against organized crime: The entanglement of drug trafficking, housing financialization, and urban renewal in Barcelona
authors: Guillaume Dumont
keywords: Community organizing; Ethnography; Housing financialization; Organized crime; Resistance strategies; Urban renewal
abstract: Current analysis of organized crime in the urban space focuses either on its social or spatial embeddedness. As an alternative, this article develops a socio-spatial perspective that recognizes and situates the lived experience of organized crime within urban transformation processes. I developed this perspective by building on ethnographic data about drug trafficking in Barcelona's El Raval, which I examine through the lens of the residents. I focus specifically on the interpretative framework of the “narco-especulació” which links the expansion of the narcopisos phenomenon to rampant speculative practices of real-estate-investors and city-led urban regeneration processes. I argue that this framework articulates a critique of urban governance, underscoring the dispossession of residents' social control, a weakened sense of place, and the fragmentation of community relationships. I also show how this framework can foster collective resistance strategies that express community agency against organized crime while disrupting the ongoing process of urban transformation and public management.
summary: Examines how drug trafficking, housing financialization and urban renewal are entangled in Barcelona, and how communities organize against organized crime.

title: Buffering structural decline with place-based fiscal transfers in South Korea
authors: Ji Eun Lee; Seung Kyum Kim
keywords: Fiscal transfers; Housing vacancy; Local governance; Place-based policy; South Korea; Urban shrinkage
abstract: Population decline and rapid aging are placing growing pressure on local governance, yet evidence remains limited on whether targeted fiscal transfers are associated with slower deterioration in shrinking regions. South Korea's 2021 Depopulation Area program provides a nationwide setting to examine this question. Using a district-level panel covering 2012–2024, this study estimates event-study and dose–response models linking local outcomes to designation timing and per-capita fund intensity. Because designation and funding intensity reflect targeted allocation, the estimates are interpreted as diagnostic evidence on relative post-designation trajectories rather than causal treatment effects. Population growth and youth net migration show no statistically detectable association with observed funding intensity over the short post-funding period, consistent with demographic inertia. The most stable pattern concerns housing vacancy: higher funding intensity is associated with lower vacancy rates within districts, a result that persists across exposure-timing, treated-only, baseline-vulnerability, and pre-allocation vacancy-change diagnostics. Associations for housing-stock aging and fiscal self-reliance are more specification-sensitive. Heterogeneity analyses suggest stronger vacancy-related adjustment in structurally vulnerable districts, although these subgroup patterns warrant cautious interpretation. Taken together, the results are consistent with selective functional buffering under structural demographic decline, most clearly in vacancy outcomes, while providing no evidence of short-run population reversal.
summary: Assesses whether place-based fiscal transfers in South Korea buffer localities against structural decline.

title: Income-specific mobility networks reveal persistent socioeconomic representations of metropolitan functional structure
authors: Yuri Perez
keywords: Functional polycentricity; Longitudinal analysis; Socioeconomic inequality; São Paulo; Urban mobility networks
abstract: Metropolitan functional structure is commonly inferred from population-wide mobility flows, but the extent to which this representation is shared by different socioeconomic groups remains unclear. We address this question using harmonized Origin-Destination household travel surveys for the São Paulo Metropolitan Region in 2007, 2017 and 2023. Weighted directed networks were constructed for five income quintiles and the aggregate population and evaluated using complementary network indicators, permutation tests, bootstrap intervals and equal-person rarefaction. Lower-income networks were consistently sparser, more compartmentalized and characterized by lower duration-based reachability, whereas higher-income networks contained more direct interzonal connections and weaker community separation. The functional-center sets of the poorest and richest quintiles overlapped by less than 10%, and none of their ten highest-PageRank zones coincided in 2023. These differences were persistent but not static: community compartmentalization was the most durable socioeconomic distinction, while connectivity gaps narrowed and centrality concentration changed more substantially. Aggregate networks also represented income groups unevenly, exhibiting consistently lower center-set similarity with the poorest quintile than with upper-income groups. The findings reveal a socially differentiated polycentricity in which multiple centers exist but do not constitute the same functional metropolitan system for all populations. Income-disaggregated networks therefore complement aggregate representations and provide a planning-relevant basis for evaluating metropolitan integration beyond population-wide averages.
summary: Uses income-specific mobility networks to show persistent socioeconomic differences in how metropolitan functional structure is represented.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution of ecological resilience, catch-up dynamics, and carbon-carrying constraints in the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration (2000–2023)
authors: Chen Xu; Anqi Wang; Suling Zhou; Honglin He; Liang Shi; Rui Xiao; Shuxian Miao; Hua Qin; Zihao Guo; Xi Zhang; Yuchuan Fan
keywords: Carbon carrying capacity; Ecological resilience decomposition; Forest carbon storage; Structural equation modelling; Urban agglomeration
abstract: High-density urban agglomerations face increasing ecological risks from rapid development and carbon pressure. However, ecological resilience is often assessed as a single index, with limited attention to its internal components and carbon-related constraints. We evaluated ecological resilience in 27 cities of the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration from 2000 to 2023 by decomposing it into ecological potential, stability, and elasticity. Multi-source spatial and socioeconomic data were analyzed using correlation analysis, random forest–SHAP interpretation, and structural equation modelling. Ecological resilience increased overall but showed substantial spatial heterogeneity. Changes in resilience were strongly and negatively related to baseline conditions in 2000 (R2 = 0.972), indicating a pronounced catch-up pattern in which initially less resilient cities generally achieved greater improvements. Resilience was more closely associated with vegetation-based carbon capacity than with population or total carbon emissions. Forest carbon storage was positively correlated with resilience in both 2000 ( r = 0.70, p < 0.001) and 2023 ( r = 0.64, p < 0.001), whereas population and carbon emissions showed weak overall correlations. Predictor importance nevertheless shifted over time. Per-capita carbon carrying capacity was the leading predictor in 2000, while carbon emissions became the dominant predictor by 2023 and exerted increasingly negative effects at high emission levels. Structural equation modelling showed that forest carbon storage strongly enhanced ecological elasticity in both years ( β = 0.90–0.91, p < 0.001), which remained the principal pathway supporting resilience. These results indicate a transition from vegetation-driven ecological asset building toward carbon-constrained resilience management. Future improvement will require structural decarbonization, ecological corridor protection, and differentiated governance tailored to city-specific resilience conditions.
summary: Tracks the spatiotemporal evolution of ecological resilience, catch-up dynamics and carbon-carrying constraints in the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration from 2000 to 2023.

title: A race without rules: Industrial transfer, competition, and the coordination dilemmas in the Shanxi-Shaanxi-Henan Region
authors: Yuanfang Zhang; Shuying Wang
keywords: Coordination dilemmas; Industrial transfer; Multi-layer policy network; Regional coopetition; Shanxi-Shaanxi-Henan Region
abstract: As core recipient regions for industrial transfer in the middle reaches of the Yellow River in China, Shanxi, Shaanxi, and Henan face not only inter-provincial competition but also deeper structural imbalances and coordination dilemmas, highlighting the need to construct a balanced and highly interactive collaborative network. To systematically characterize the regional industrial coordination pattern, this study uses industrial policy text data from 2012 to 2024 to construct a three-layer policy network consisting of policy issuance, policy implementation, and governance-chain layers. Furthermore, competition and complementarity matrices are introduced to examine the evolutionary structure of industrial transfer competition among the three provinces. The findings reveal that while the macro-level policy network exhibits a trend toward cross-provincial coordinated evolution, the micro-level implementation chains remain deeply fragmented. Meanwhile, homogeneous competition exhibits a significant distance-threshold effect, suggesting that geographical distance constrains industrial isomorphism only within certain spatial ranges. Consequently, inter-provincial competition is characterized by parallel competition across multiple industrial channels and structural congestion in key sectors. Additionally, intense external competition in core industrial sectors triggers multi-agency overlapping responses and internal attrition within local implementation systems. In light of these findings, this study proposes mitigating institutional friction by establishing a dedicated intergovernmental consultation mechanism, promoting Smart Specialization in industrial positioning, and implementing a lead-department accountability system.
summary: Examines industrial transfer and inter-jurisdictional competition in the Shanxi-Shaanxi-Henan region and the coordination dilemmas they create.

title: How multi-sensory experience shapes place-based human sentiments: A hyperlocal analysis using environmental sensing and social media data in the Bronx, New York City
authors: Xiaotong Zhang; Yuhao Kang; Simone Mora; Fábio Duarte; Carlo Ratti; An Wang
keywords: Mobile sensing; Multi-sensory sentiments; Social media; Urban physical environments
abstract: People experience cities through their senses of sight, hearing, smell, touch, and taste. However, most research focuses only on visual stimuli. In this study, we develop a straightforward multi-sensory, data-based linear regression model to explain human sentiment in cities through visual, acoustic, olfactory, and tactile explanatory features. We use social media to reflect people's sentiments, and concurrent urban environmental data ranging from street view imagery to air quality, collected in the Bronx, New York. We observe correlations between non-visual features and urban experience, where noise and thermal comfort are identified as significant impact factors. The adjusted coefficients of determination for the simple linear models can reach 0.80 and 0.60 for positive and negative sentiments, respectively, indicating moderate to strong interactions between multi-sensory urban features and human sentiments.
summary: Combines environmental sensing with social media data in a hyperlocal analysis of the Bronx, New York City, to study how multi-sensory experience shapes place-based sentiment.

title: A global structural typology of cities from urban centers
authors: Shuai Pang; Lei Dong
keywords: Center networks; Scaling laws; Urban structure
abstract: Cities are most often categorized by population size, a continuous indicator that captures scale but does not distinguish internal structural organization. Yet structural typologies require discrete representations of how urban components are arranged and connected. Here, we construct directed networks of dominant interactions among intra-urban centers for more than 9400 cities worldwide, transforming internal organization into comparable topological configurations. We show that urban center-to-center networks occupy a highly restricted subset of theoretically possible configurations. As the number of centers increases, cities do not reorganize arbitrarily but expand through nested, incremental extensions of smaller network configurations. This structural regularity gives rise to a small repertoire of recurrent configurations, enabling a discrete classification of cities based on their internal organization. Beyond typology, we show that structural properties of center networks, including size, breadth, and depth, scale sublinearly with urban population, establishing a quantitative link between internal organization and city size. By shifting the focus from aggregate size to structural configuration, this framework offers a globally consistent and interpretable basis for comparing cities across regions.
summary: Builds a global typology of urban spatial structure derived from the configuration of cities' urban centers.

title: An interpretable hybrid multiscale geographically weighted XGBoost (HMGWX) model with an empirical application to urban transport systems
authors: Fan Gao; Sylvia Y. He
keywords: Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI); Interpretability; Non-linearity; Spatial heterogeneity; Spatially explicit machine learning
abstract: Spatially explicit machine learning (SEML) models have recently been developed to address spatial heterogeneity and non-linearity. However, many existing SEMLs require post-hoc interpretability methods to extract the functional relationships between independent and dependent variables. Essentially, this type of SEMLs remain approximations derived from prediction outputs rather than from direct estimation of variable contributions, propagating prediction errors and potentially leading to biased interpretations of spatially varying processes. Additionally, SEMLs often face a trade-off between capturing non-linearity and spatial heterogeneity, meaning that a greater focus on non-linearity may reduce the capability of capturing spatial heterogeneity, and vice versa. These limitations constrain their ability to interpret geographical phenomenon. This study proposes a hybrid multiscale geographically weighted XGBoost (HMGWX), which integrates geographically weighted XGBoost (GWXGB) and geographically XGBoost (GXGB) within a semi-parametric additive model framework. The model assigns the most appropriate local estimator (GWXGB or GXGB) for each response-predictor relationship, balancing the ability to address non-linearity and spatial heterogeneity. HMGWX directly estimates the marginal contribution of each variable, thereby avoiding post-hoc errors propagated from prediction outputs. We validate HMGWX using both a synthetic dataset with known parameter surfaces and non-linear relationships, and a real-world ride-hailing waiting time dataset. Results show that HMGWX outperforms traditional spatially varying coefficient models (e.g., multiscale geographically weighted regression, Geographical Gaussian Process Generalized Additive Model) and existing SEMLs (e.g., XGBoost, Geographical-XGBoost, GWXGB, and GXGB) in both interpretability and predictive accuracy when spatial heterogeneity and non-linearity coexist. Compared with the baseline models, HMGWX reduces root mean square error by at least 8%. Furthermore, by introducing spatial clustering, early stopping, and dynamic bandwidth shrinking, we improve the computational efficiency of the calibration procedures for GWXGB, GXGB, and HMGWX, reducing total training time by over 76%. Finally, we propose an evaluation route map to guide appropriate model selection in practice.
summary: Proposes an interpretable hybrid multiscale geographically weighted XGBoost (HMGWX) model and demonstrates it on urban transport systems.

title: GeoPandas: Fundamental data structures for vector spatial data in Python
authors: Martin Fleischmann; Joris Van den Bossche; Kelsey Jordahl; Matthew John Richards; James McBride; Jacob Wasserman; Brendan Ward; Levi John Wolf
keywords: Data structures; GIS; python; Software; Spatial analysis; Vector geometry
abstract: Spatial analysis depends upon accessible, flexible tools. As a leading language for data science, Python requires reliable packages to handle complex geospatial tasks effectively. This article presents GeoPandas, a package providing a high-level, user-friendly API that extends standard pandas data structures to support vector geometries, simplifying spatial data handling for a broad scientific audience. The package is built around three core data structures (GeometryArray, GeoSeries, and GeoDataFrame) that unify geometric operations and tabular data management. It achieves performance and scalability by wrapping fast, compiled libraries—handling geometry operations, coordinate transformations, and file reading and writing—behind a Pythonic interface. Over its ten-year history, GeoPandas has evolved from a single package to a cornerstone of geospatial analysis in Python, anchoring a broader ecosystem of tools. Thousands of downstream projects rely upon GeoPandas, spanning scientific fields from Earth observation and climate modelling to urban analytics and epidemiology. This article provides an overview of the package's history, design, social and technical infrastructure, and future plans. By making spatial analysis more accessible with a standard open-source toolset, GeoPandas democratises access to spatial analysis, facilitates reproducibility, and accelerates scientific discovery.
summary: Describes GeoPandas, the Python library providing the fundamental data structures for vector spatial data.

title: Interpretable mapping of fine-grained urban building functions from street-view images using foundation models
authors: Jiaming Sun; Wei Yang; Tingting Xu; Zongshun Tian; Yongchuan Zhang; Mengjia Yin
keywords: Building function; CLIP; Foundation models; Street view image; Zero-shot
abstract: Accurate building function mapping is vital for urban analytics, yet existing methods often rely on costly labels and struggle with mixed-function complexity. This study develops an integrated framework that combines street view images (SVIs) with foundation models to achieve scalable and fine-grained building function analysis. Specifically, the GroundingDINO+SAM method detects and segments building facades, and the CLIP model identifies fine-grained building function via zero-shot prompting. A façade segmentation method then quantifies mixed-function intensity, and a cognitive alignment module evaluates the consistency between model attention and human reasoning. We validated the framework using a large corpus of SVIs from Shenzhen, China, covering diverse building types and functions. Results show that our framework achieves an overall classification accuracy of 74.25%. It also captures mixed-function patterns and intra-building functional diversity, offering insights beyond conventional methods. Human-model cognitive alignment shows both consistency and divergence, with visual, semantic, and overall scores of 0.14, 0.48, and 0.63. Interpretability analysis indicates that humans focus on symbolic cues, whereas foundation models emphasize textures, geometry, and context. These findings provide methodological and practical insights for future urban analytics and city management.
summary: Uses foundation models on street-view images to map fine-grained urban building functions in an interpretable way.

title: Deep learning reveals cross-platform consistency in street view imagery for urban perception mapping
authors: Tingting Bai; Dong Xu; Feng Gao; Jiawei Liu; Yongze Song
keywords: ADE20k; Baidu; Google; MIT place pulse 2.0; Street view image; VGG-16
abstract: Street view imagery (SVI) is now widely used to assess urban living environments, yet cross-platform differences in sensors, viewing geometry, and image quality continue to limit data integration. Using paired Baidu Street View (BSV) and Google Street View (GSV) images from Hong Kong, we propose a dual-scale framework to test whether physical streetscape structure and model-derived perception remain comparable across platforms. The framework combines stacking ensemble learning, SHAP-based interpretation, and Mantel correlation analysis at both sampling-point and pixel scales. At the sampling-point scale, vegetation, buildings, and sky show strong BSV-GSV agreement, with correlations of 0.753, 0.756, and 0.720, respectively. Perceptual dimensions also show moderate-to-high consistency, ranging from 0.591 for “Depressing” to 0.672 for “Safe.” At the pixel scale, simulated vegetation distributions are highly consistent, with an average correlation of 0.84 and more than 98% of the study area significant at p < 0.001; “Beauty” also maintains a positive correlation of 0.645. Further structural and causal analyses suggest that natural elements tend to enhance perceived beauty, whereas artificial and traffic-related features are generally linked to negative perceptual effects. Robustness tests using SegFormer and DeepLabv3+ under ADE20K and Cityscapes, together with perception-backbone tests using ResNet50 and CLIP, indicate that the main structural consistency findings are stable across segmentation pipelines, while perceptual consistency remains more sensitive to the selected backbone. Overall, this study offers a robust methodological foundation for urban design and sustainable city assessment by improving spatial prediction accuracy and interpretability.
summary: Uses deep learning to test whether street view imagery from different platforms gives consistent results for urban perception mapping.

title: Identifying micro-scale risk zones for climate-driven emergency medical demand: A spatiotemporal machine learning study in Beijing
authors: Yuxiao Wang; Yongming Zhang; Zanmei Wei; Junyu He; Huaxiong Jiang; Zhenbiao Tian; Zitong Zheng; Yuming Guo; Luxia Zhang; Wenyi Zhang
keywords: Cold waves; Emergency medical services (EMS); Heatwaves; Machine learning; Megacity resilience; Spatiotemporal heterogeneity
abstract: Driven by the synergistic intensification of global climate change and rapid urbanization, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) demand in megacities is increasingly sensitive to environmental fluctuations. However, existing studies often rely on aggregated data at coarse spatial scales, masking intra-urban heterogeneity and micro-scale risk patterns. This study developed a high-resolution spatiotemporal analysis framework by integrating 379,382 EMS dispatch records from Beijing (2017–2018) into a 1 km * 1 km grid. We employed a Tweedie-distribution-based XGBoost machine learning model combined with SHAP framework to quantify non-linear effects, time-lag dynamics, and spatial heterogeneity of environmental drivers. The model effectively explained over 82% of spatiotemporal variation in EMS demand (R2 = 0.8211). Mean temperature exhibited a U-shaped association with EMS demand, with high temperatures (>25 °C) exerting stronger effects than low temperatures (<0 °C). Both cold waves and heatwaves exhibited significant time-lag effects, with risk intensity peaking at lag week 2. Spatially, heatwaves and cold waves present distinct risk zones across different lag periods, with the most severely impacted areas concentrated primarily in the urban core and the central districts of suburban areas. These findings underscore the necessity of micro-scale risk identification for building climate-resilient EMS systems. We recommend implementing 1 km grid-based early warning systems and maintaining 2-week enhanced monitoring windows following extreme weather events, alongside targeted interventions for vulnerable populations within the identified “risk patches.”
summary: Applies spatiotemporal machine learning in Beijing to pinpoint micro-scale zones at risk of climate-driven emergency medical demand.

title: City2Graph: A Python library for Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks and spatial analysis in urban systems
authors: Yuta Sato; Elisabetta Pietrostefani; Ron Mahabir; Daniel Arribas-Bel
keywords: 15-minute accessibility; Geospatial artificial intelligence; Graph representation learning; Multimodal transportation; Open source software; Overture Maps; Urban morphology
abstract: City2Graph is an open-source Python library that streamlines workflows for heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in urban systems. Cities are complex systems of diverse spatial relations long modelled as graphs in network science, and recent advances in GNNs have further enabled the identification of non-linear patterns of urban complexity. Unlike homogeneous graphs with a single node and edge type, heterogeneous graphs with multiple types are receiving growing attention to accommodate richer information in GNNs. However, their diffusion remains constrained by fragmented graph construction processes across different data domains, and by the lack of a unified framework for converting constructed graphs into GNN-ready tensors. City2Graph standardises graph construction across domains of morphology, transportation, mobility, and proximity. The library supports conversions between spatial geometries, network topologies, and tensors for spatial analysis with visualisation, network analysis, and GNN training, respectively. City2Graph also supports metapath construction, capturing higher-order connections across node and edge types (e.g., areas linked via multimodal transit). The library's efficacy was demonstrated through a case study on clustering urban functions in Liverpool, UK, using Graph Autoencoder models with three relation types: spatial contiguity, walk-based accessibility, and multimodal accessibility between census units. Compared with the homogeneous model, heterogeneous models identified spatially coherent clusters that aligned more closely with defined accessibility patterns. City2Graph enables reproducible workflows for heterogeneous GNNs and model interpretation, fostering comprehensive understanding of urban systems across disciplines. The library is released under the BSD 3-Clause License on GitHub.
summary: Introduces City2Graph, a Python library for heterogeneous graph neural networks and spatial analysis of urban systems.

title: FloodLang and FloodLoc-Four: A bilingual dataset and fine-grained multilevel framework for flood-related geospatial information understanding
authors: Changyan Xie; Wenying Du; Zeqiang Chen; Lei Xu; Xiang Zhang; Yingbing Liu; Nengcheng Chen
keywords: Benchmarking framework; Disaster dataset; Flood disaster; Geoinformation extraction; Large language models
abstract: Social media offers vital near real-time data for flood response, yet extracting accurate geospatial information from unstructured texts remains a significant challenge. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) presents new opportunities to address this task. This study systematically evaluates the spatial reasoning capabilities of LLMs within disaster contexts. We introduce FloodLoc-Four, a hierarchical framework comprising four tasks: disaster-related information validity classification, location span extraction, spatial semantic classification, and standardized address generation. Additionally, a bilingual benchmark dataset, FloodLang, was developed covering Chinese and English flood social media texts. Experiments indicate that Gemini 2.5-Pro and GPT-5 achieve the best overall performance, showing clear advantages in English across all tasks, particularly in location span extraction and standardized address generation. In contrast, the DeepSeek series exhibits more balanced performance between Chinese and English, with relatively small cross-lingual gaps across task levels. While Qwen and Llama exhibit limited cross-lingual stability. These results delineate the practical capability boundaries of current LLMs and offer guidance for selecting models in multilingual flood emergency applications.
summary: Presents a bilingual dataset (FloodLang) and a fine-grained multilevel framework (FloodLoc-Four) for understanding flood-related geospatial information.

title: Function over morphology: Understanding street environment and pedestrian flow in urban villages through UAV-based tracking
authors: Chenfan Cai; Wenlin Zhao; Zixuan Hu; Jin Rui
keywords: Deep learning; Pedestrian flow; Street typology; UAV remote sensing; Urban villages
abstract: Urban villages (UVs) are distinctive informal settlements formed during China's rapid urbanization. These settlements are characterized by high-density buildings, mixed functions, and complex street layouts, currently accommodating nearly one-quarter of the urban population in cities across developing regions. While the influence of street environmental characteristics on residents' walking behavior has been well documented, their application in microscale environments of informal settlements has been rarely explored. Moreover, previous studies have primarily relied on traditional methods such as questionnaire surveys and GPS tracking, neglecting high-frequency real-time pedestrian trajectory tracking, which may lead to incomplete understanding of environment-behavior relationships. To address these research gaps, we employed Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) remote sensing technology combined with deep learning algorithms to trace pedestrian spatiotemporal behavior patterns across four street typologies in a Shenzhen UV. We extracted functional features and human-scale visual features from street view imagery, then employed machine learning models to analyze their influence mechanisms on pedestrian flow. Our findings suggest that, in the observed daytime UV settings, functional accessibility variables showed stronger predictive associations with pedestrian flow than objective visual/morphological variables, and this influence mechanism exhibits strong spatial dependency across street types. Moreover, certain functional attributes demonstrate consistent dominant effects, while spatial interventions show contrasting impacts depending on street width and capacity. Cross-regional analysis across 43 UVs suggests that the visual-feature extraction framework is scalable across diverse UV contexts, while full functional-behavioral validation remains future work. These insights question current regeneration practices focused on appearance-oriented physical upgrading and suggest prioritizing functional accessibility enhancements, offering evidence-based guidance for informal settlement upgrading across broader geographic scopes in cities within emerging economies.
summary: Uses UAV-based pedestrian tracking in urban villages to examine how street environment, especially street function rather than morphology, relates to pedestrian flow.

title: Evaluating the digital divide in public transport services: A natural language processing analysis of user experiences in Birmingham
authors: Lu Huafeng; Lei Zhang; Silvia Gullino; Miguel Hincapié Triviño
keywords: Artificial intelligence; Digital divide; Inclusive planning; Natural language processing; Public transport; Smart City
abstract: Digitalisation has transformed public transport services worldwide, yet disparities in access, skills, and outcomes continue to reinforce a digital divide in how citizens engage with these services. While previous studies have examined the digital divide in internet use and smart technologies, few have explored how these inequalities manifest in everyday interactions with digital public transport platforms, extending to citizen participation in government-provided digital services. To this end, we investigated user experiences of public transport applications in Birmingham, whose digital inclusion is disproportionate to its status as a major urban and economic hub in the UK, by analysing 4275 user reviews on public transport services collected from the Apple App Store and Google Play Store between 2016 and 2025. Using a mixed natural language processing (NLP) approach combining topic modelling and sentiment analysis, we identified key themes and emotional tones in user feedback. Results revealed three dominant topics: App Performance, Usability, and Service Satisfaction, each conceptually aligned with the access, ability, and motivation dimensions of the digital divide theory. Sentiment analysis showed generally negative evaluations, particularly around technical access barriers and satisfaction issues. By integrating user-generated data with digital divide theory, these results provide novel empirical evidence of how inequalities in digital engagement persist within digital twin planning and smart city transport systems and highlight the importance of inclusive digital design for equitable and sustainable mobility access.
summary: Applies natural language processing to user experiences of public transport services in Birmingham to evaluate the digital divide.

title: Urban regeneration and health: Quasi-natural experimental evidence from China
authors: Haiyang Lu; Fengling Chen; Weiliang Hu
keywords: urban regeneration; health status; difference-in-differences; health inequality
abstract: With rapid urbanization, many countries have adopted urban regeneration initiatives to address urban decline and promote sustainable development. Yet limited evidence exists on the health effects of large-scale urban regeneration. This study focuses on an early urban regeneration policy in China, the Urban Double Repairs (UDRs) initiative, which aims to promote ecological restoration and urban repair in selected cities. Using nationally representative data from the Chinese General Social Survey and a difference-in-differences approach, this study examines the impact of the UDR policy on residents' health. The results show that, following implementation, self-reported health improved and obesity declined, with more pronounced effects observed in large cities and in cities with higher levels of population aging. Mechanism analysis indicates that increased social participation and improved perceived environmental quality play important roles in linking the UDR policy to better health. Further analysis based on quantile regression shows that the benefits are stronger among individuals with poorer initial health, indicating a reduction in health disparities.
summary: China's Urban Double Repairs regeneration policy improved residents' self-reported health and cut obesity—more so in large, older cities and among the initially less healthy—via greater social participation and better perceived environmental quality.

title: Cape Town's community kitchens as healing commons: The politics of care in a fractured city
authors: Nicole Paganini; Vanessa Farr
keywords: urban food commons; community kitchens; trauma; Cape Town; social justice; feminist resistance; feminist communing
abstract: This paper explores how community kitchens in Cape Town, predominantly led by women from low-income areas, function as everyday infrastructures of solidarity and resistance. Drawing on participatory action research conducted between 2020 and 2024, we apply a feminist perspective on community kitchens as urban food commons. In a city marked by extreme and racialised spatial inequalities, these women-led initiatives respond to chronic food insecurity, gender-based violence (GBV) and persistent gang violence, through care and organising. Drawing on commoning as a transformative social paradigm, and on healing justice, we argue that community kitchens in Cape Town serve both as pragmatic responses to chronic food insecurity and as sites of embodied healing, addressing intergenerational trauma, systemic neglect and violence. These spaces nourish more than bodies: They offer emotional and physical safety, (gender-based) violence prevention and moments of dignity amid structural abandonment. As such, these spaces serve as temporary safety nets and embody feminist commoning practices that recall traditions of caring while challenging extractive, colonial-capitalist urban systems. We also attend to the contradictions these spaces embody: the feminisation and extraction of care labour, the risk of state co-optation, and tensions between invisibility as protection and recognition as a political demand.
summary: Women-led community kitchens in Cape Town work as feminist urban food commons that tackle chronic food insecurity and serve as sites of healing from violence and trauma, while risking extraction of care labour and state co-optation.

title: Water, ritual, and the spectral urban commons
authors: Ulises Moreno-Tabarez
keywords: spectrality; hydrosocial relations; uneven urbanisation; Afro-Indigenous urbanisms; Guerrero; Mexico
abstract: This article theorises the spectral urban commons through Participatory Action Research with Afro-Indigenous and Afrodescendant groups in the Costa Chica of Guerrero, Mexico. It locates the urban in these small coastal municipalities in an uneven regional process through which roads, pipes, administrative concentration, development promises and extractive projects reorganise water, territory and collective life. From this starting point, the article examines water rituals, rain petitions and shared narrative practices across Xochistlahuaca, Ometepec, Cuajinicuilapa and Azoyú to show how commoning persists through interruption, absence and return. The commons appears through ritual labour, memory, translation and refusal, which sustain relations that exceed state legibility while retaining material force. In doing so, the article contributes to debates on the urban commons by showing how commoning in small-city and regional contexts is shaped by infrastructural unevenness, ecological strain and colonial histories of erasure. I offer the spectral urban commons as a sensitising concept for commoning held in interruption, materially organised through ritual labour, distributed custodianship and contested return, yet never fully secured as property or institution.
summary: Participatory research with Afro-Indigenous and Afrodescendant groups in Guerrero's Costa Chica shows how water rituals, memory and refusal sustain a 'spectral urban commons' amid uneven infrastructure, ecological strain and colonial erasure in small coastal municipalities.

title: Negotiated urbanism: Informal adaptations of Thai townhouses for mixed residential and commercial use
authors: Sunaree Lawanyawatna; Martin Schoch
keywords: architecture; development; governance; policy; informality
abstract: This research examines the widespread informal modifications of townhouses (also known as row houses) in Thailand, particularly in urban and peri-urban districts. These adaptations reflect systemic disjunctions between formal planning frameworks and the emerging spatial economies of urban and residential–commercial hybridity. With the rise of small-scale entrepreneurship and flexible workspaces, townhouses are increasingly being repurposed for mixed-use, often outside the scope of legal and planning oversight. Through fieldwork, interviews, and architectural analysis, this study identifies types of modifications and examines their relationship to property characteristics, socio-economic drivers, and spatial needs. Findings reveal systemic shortcomings between policy intent and lived practice, underscoring the need for a more inclusive, adaptive, regulatory approach that aligns with grassroots spatial agency and urban resilience. This study contributes to discussions on informality, everyday urbanism, and housing governance in rapidly transforming Southeast Asian cities.
summary: Fieldwork and architectural analysis show Thai townhouses are widely and informally modified for mixed residential–commercial use outside planning oversight, exposing a gap between policy intent and practice that calls for more adaptive, inclusive regulation.

title: Governing the just transition: The reach and limits of anchor-led place-based governance
authors: Christina Wolf; Hulya Dagdeviren
keywords: just transition; multiscalar governance; anchor institutions; local authorities; London
abstract: This article examines what forms of governance can enable a just and scalable green transition at the local level. While place-based approaches centred on anchor institutions are often promoted as vehicles for equitable and community-led transitions, their effectiveness is shaped by broader multiscalar governance relations. The article develops a conceptual framework that integrates distributive, procedural, and restorative dimensions of climate justice within a multiscalar governance perspective, highlighting how transition governance unfolds across scale and time. Drawing on 26 interviews with officials from London local authorities, the article shows that while local authorities have emerged as key anchor institutions in transition governance – leading by example, influencing public and private sector behaviour, and fostering community buy-in – their ability to advance just transitions beyond their immediate locality is limited by higher-level governance processes. Austerity-driven reductions in public sector capacity, competitive funding structures, and the lack of clear national policy guidance have created a fragmented and uneven landscape of climate action, reinforcing spatial disparities across localities. It concludes that anchor-led place-based governance requires procedural, redistributive and restorative mechanisms embedded across scales of governance. The findings advance debates on transition governance, the "local trap," and climate justice by clarifying how place-based transitions depend on multiscalar, redistributive governance architectures.
summary: Interviews with 26 London local-authority officials show councils act as key anchor institutions for a just green transition, but austerity, competitive funding and weak national guidance limit their reach and deepen spatial disparities in climate action.

title: The lifecycle of platform-mediated urban desirability: Digital nomadism and the temporal politics of visibility
authors: Brigitte de Boef
keywords: digital nomadism; platform capitalism; urban desirability; algorithmic visibility; temporal extraction
abstract: Through comparative content analysis of 600 high-engagement social media posts (2021–2024) across Rio de Janeiro, Barcelona and Chiang Mai, this article develops a lifecycle framework for understanding how cities move through platform-mediated attention economies. Three representational stages are identified, namely speculative emergence, infrastructural saturation and platform obsolescence, through which digital nomad urbanism operates primarily through aestheticisation. This aesthetic work may precede and participate in conditioning material transformation, whilst its representational traces can persist after algorithmic attention recedes. Cities enter representational obsolescence when their narratives cease generating algorithmic momentum, a process that reveals digital nomadism as extractive visibility: appropriating urban difference for affective circulation whilst obscuring its consequences for long-term and less-mobile residents. The analysis extends postcolonial critique to account for temporal extraction, showing how digital colonialism operates through cycles of discovery, commodification and abandonment that intensify existing global inequalities.
summary: Content analysis of 600 social media posts on Rio de Janeiro, Barcelona and Chiang Mai yields a three-stage lifecycle (speculative emergence, infrastructural saturation, platform obsolescence) through which digital nomadism extracts urban visibility while obscuring costs for less-mobile residents.

title: Placemaking in an almost post-authoritarian Myanmar: Questioning "best practice" in Yangon's back drainage spaces
authors: Jayde Lin Roberts
keywords: placemaking; best practice; Yangon; Myanmar; global South
abstract: This article critiques the promotion of placemaking as "best practice" in global South cities by analyzing the short-lived beautification of back drainage spaces into back-alley gardens in Yangon, Myanmar. The rise and fall of the Alley Garden Project (AGP) show how decontextualized and depoliticized "participation" can entrench power hierarchies and enable the state to disregard its responsibilities. In global peripheries where state-society relations are not founded on a history of liberal democratic governance, global North models of urban development, even supposed grassroots methods such as placemaking, become "out-of-place" urban ideas that perpetuate the coloniality of globalized urban knowledge and design. Yangon's AGP serves as a cautionary tale of responsibilization, not under conditions of state and capital withdrawal as seen in neoliberal urbanism, but under increasing state engagement as a new government tried to overcome decades of authoritarian rule. As shown in this article, international placemakers as non-state actors can exert disproportionate influence on urban design and policy in global South cities and this globalized practice requires critical attention.
summary: The rise and fall of Yangon's Alley Garden Project shows how placemaking exported as global 'best practice' can depoliticise participation, entrench power hierarchies and let the state offload its responsibilities in global South cities.

title: Proximity to green spaces: An analysis of neighborhood income distribution in French urban areas
authors: Mathilde Stoltz; Elizaveta Golovanova
keywords: green space; income; environmental justice; distributive justice
abstract: In a context where research on distributive justice is receiving increasing attention, this study aims to identify the existence of inequalities in access to green spaces in French urban areas. To this end, using 200 m grid data combined with the spatial location of green spaces, we estimate several conditional quantile regressions that successively account for the type of green space, their size, and the intensity of their presence in the vicinity of neighborhoods. The results suggest the existence of inequalities in access to certain types of green spaces, which vary according to both the size and the intensity of green spaces.
summary: Conditional quantile regressions on 200 m grid data for French urban areas reveal income-related inequalities in neighbourhood access to certain types of green space, varying with green-space size and intensity.

title: The military–urban nexus in the Chinese context: The case of Lvshun, Dalian
authors: Chen Li; Di Wu
keywords: the military–urban nexus; militarisation and militarised cities; peaceful, non-conflict setting; Lvshun, Dalian, China
abstract: In the context of intensifying arms competition among major powers worldwide, this research examines how militarisation encroaches on urban development and governance. It also analyses the political, institutional, social, economic and spatial dynamics of militarised cities. Such analysis sheds light on the mechanisms and outcomes of militarisation and deepens our understanding of the military–urban nexus – namely, the evolving interactions between the process of militarisation, the economy, society and space within neoliberal urban development. China presents a distinctive case for advancing research on militarisation in cities and the military–urban nexus. This research focuses on Lvshun in the city of Dalian, a historically contested battleground and a key military hub today. It aims to uncover how militarisation has fundamentally shaped Lvshun's socioeconomic evolution, critically influencing its economic and industrial development as well as the production of space. By tracing how militarisation changes over time and examining how local governments respond across different periods, the research identifies a place-specific military–urban nexus. The research primarily addresses three critical aspects: (1) the military in Lvshun: its roles, interventions and interaction with local authorities; (2) economic and industrial development and production of space in Lvshun: the impacts of militarisation; and (3) the exploratory utilisation of military properties in Lvshun: adaptive development strategies under militarisation. Through the Lvshun case, the research highlights the dynamic, multi-scalar character of the military–urban nexus in China within a peaceful, non-conflict setting, extending beyond traditional Euro-American frameworks while capturing the core dimensions of militarisation in an urban area in the Global South.
summary: Tracing Lvshun (Dalian) over time, the study shows how militarisation has shaped the district's economic and industrial development, production of space and local-government strategies, revealing a place-specific military–urban nexus in a peaceful, non-conflict setting.

title: Impacts of new light rail investment on accessibility and housing markets: A difference-in-differences hedonic analysis in Amsterdam
authors: Jip Claassens; Jan Rouwendal; Eric Koomen; Maureen Lankhuizen
keywords: metro expansion; difference-in-differences analysis; house price changes; infrastructure investments
abstract: In 2018, Amsterdam introduced the North-South Line (NZL), a metro connecting the city's north and south via its historic centre. Using a spatially adjusted difference-in-differences approach, combined with hedonic modelling for the relevant submarkets, this study estimates the effects of accessibility improvements, measured as the change in the number of jobs reachable within a 30-minute trip, on housing prices, rents, social housing queues and housing density. Unlike most studies in this literature, which focus exclusively on transaction prices, we examine this broader set of outcomes, an approach of particular relevance in Amsterdam, where owner-occupied housing represents only around 30% of the total stock. We find modest housing market responses to the NZL around specific stations. Effects are strongest where accessibility improvements were most pronounced, but often small or statistically insignificant. While house prices show small capitalisation effects in some locations, private rents, social housing and housing density exhibit weak or largely insignificant changes.
summary: Amsterdam's 2018 North-South metro line produced only modest housing-market responses—small house-price capitalisation near stations with the largest job-accessibility gains and weak or insignificant effects on private rents, social-housing queues and density.

title: The effect of working from home on commuting duration: Evidence for Lisbon metropolitan area
authors: Anthony Macedo; João de Abreu e Silva; Patricia C. Melo
keywords: COVID-19; Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood; propensity score matching; telework; travel patterns
abstract: According to the Portuguese Labour Force Survey (PLFS), in the first quarter of 2024, 17.9% of the total workforce in Portugal and 32.1% in Lisbon Metropolitan Area (LMA) worked from home at least once per week. We use longitudinal microdata for residents in the LMA from the PLFS to study the relation between working from home (WFH) and one-way commuting duration. Worker-level regressions for the period between the second quarter of 2022 and the first quarter of 2024, controlling for demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, suggest that compared with non-WFH workers, working from home 1 day per week is associated with a 4.9% increase in commuting duration. The estimated effect rises to 8.8% for 2 days per week and is around 6% for 3 and 4 days per week. These findings hold even after carrying out different robustness checks.
summary: Longitudinal Labour Force Survey microdata for the Lisbon Metropolitan Area show working from home is associated with longer one-way commutes—about 4.9% longer at one WFH day a week, 8.8% at two, and around 6% at three or four.

title: Cities and regions in transformation: subnational frontiers of transformative innovation policy
authors: Iryna Fil Kristensen; Lasse Bundgaard; Mart Laatsit; Björn Asheim; Mireille Matt
keywords: coordination; governance; legitimacy; regions; Transformative innovation policy
abstract: Transformative innovation policy (TIP) reframes innovation agendas around societal challenges such as sustainability and inclusion. Its rapid uptake in policy discourse contrasts with limited evidence on how it is enacted in regions and cities. This special issue examines how local and regional actors interpret and implement TIP in practice. The contributions reveal uneven public-sector capacities, persistent tensions in mission-oriented approaches and the strong influence of place-based conditions on policy outcomes. They also highlight challenges of legitimacy and coordination across governance levels, where direction-setting meets fragmented institutions and competing priorities.
summary: Introductory article to Regional Studies' collection of the same name, examining cities and regions as subnational frontiers of transformative innovation policy.

title: Natural resources in entrepreneurial ecosystem evolution: leadership challenges in peripheries
authors: Gianni Romaní; Miguel Atienza; Colin Mason
keywords: Chile; Entrepreneurial ecosystem; entrepreneurship; natural resources; peripheral regions; regional development
abstract: Resource-based regions have been overlooked in the analysis of the evolution of entrepreneurial ecosystems (EEs). This article extends Stam and van de Ven’s framework by incorporating natural resources as a structural component of EE dynamics to study the role of the sector in leadership formation in resource-based peripheral regions. Using a qualitative case study of Antofagasta, Chile’s main mining region, between 2007 and 2023, the analysis draws on interviews, documentary sources and participant observation. Although natural resources have promoted significant growth of the EE, the dominance of external actors has led to fragmented leadership and structural constraints that limit resource mobilisation and entrepreneurial transformation.
summary: Examines the role of natural resources in how entrepreneurial ecosystems evolve in peripheral regions and the leadership challenges involved.

title: The uneven distribution of risks and rewards in multi-level mission-oriented green industrial policies
authors: Viktor Skyrman; Karl Wennberg; Brita Hermelin; Simon Haikola
keywords: EV batteries; green steel; local statecraft; Mission-based industrial policies; multi-level governance; place-based policies
abstract: Given the dearth of multi-level approaches in mission studies, we investigate the interplay between supranational mission-oriented industrial policies and local-level mission implementation. Interviewing local stakeholders involved in two gigafactory projects, we show how municipalities position themselves as attractive sites for mission-aligned investment, tailoring public investment, land use policies and public-private partnerships accordingly. Although mission-led policies have catalysed gigafactory investments, lacking state coordination has led to strained municipal finances. The capacity of municipalities to engage with mission-oriented industrial policies depends heavily on their legal autonomy, fiscal resources and administrative capacity – factors that vary significantly across multi-level governance systems.
summary: Analyses how the risks and rewards of multi-level, mission-oriented green industrial policies are unevenly distributed.

title: The cost of regional bank–firm mismatch: capital misallocation and lost productivity in China
authors: Zhanhao Wang; Weina Yu; Xiaoqi Feng; Xin Xie
keywords: Banking structure; capital allocation; corporate financialisation; financial constraints; zombification
abstract: Small banks are better suited for financing small firms, implying that regions with more small firms should have a greater number of small banks. We find mismatches between the size structure of bank sector and that of firm sector lead to capital misallocation: in regions with greater structural mismatch, large firms hold more financial assets and exhibit higher zombie prevalence, while small firms show greater cash-flow sensitivity. And reducing this mismatch by one standard deviation could boost total factor productivity growth by 7%. Additionally, small banks in mismatched regions show greater asset growth and branch expansion, suggesting market correction.
summary: Studies the cost of mismatches between regional banks and firms in China in terms of capital misallocation and lost productivity.

title: Digital platforms and regional development
authors: Han Chu; Robert Hassink; Martin Kenney
keywords: artificial intelligence; Digital platforms; economic geography; platform economy; platformisation; regional development; regional governance
abstract: Online digital platforms have rapidly become central infrastructures shaping contemporary economic, social and political life. Their growing role has important implications for regional development and economic geography. However, so far research on digital platforms remains only partially integrated into debates on regional development and spatial economic change. This special collection aims at improving our knowledge and understanding of the interrelations between digital platforms and regional development. We both discuss the contributions to the collection and, on the basis of that, we provide avenues for future research on the interrelations between digital platforms and regional development.
summary: Introductory article to Regional Studies' collection of the same name, examining how digital platforms relate to regional development.

title: Short term rental regulations in Vienna – enforcement versus deterrence?
authors: Selim Banabak; Franziska Sielker
keywords: housing crisis; housing supply; rental market; rental regulation; Short-term rental
abstract: Cities worldwide are introducing regulations for short-term rentals (STRs). Vienna, an early adopter, revised its rules in July 2024 to restrict professional STR operations while permitting home-sharing. Using a mixed-method approach, utilising difference-in-difference methods and semi-structured Interviews with suppliers and regulators, we assess the reform’s effects. Although we find a slight decline in STR listings, it cannot be clearly attributed to the reform, nor do we observe increased long-term rental supply. Limited effects appear likely due to enforcement challenges and insufficient administrative resources. Nonetheless, that regulatory uncertainty may deter STR supply but risks discouraging compliance among otherwise lawful operators.
summary: Examines whether Vienna's short-term rental regulations work through enforcement or through deterrence.

title: The regional effects of UNESCO heritage on property values: a synthetic control approach
authors: Rainer Andergassen; Alice Guerra
keywords: economic impact; heritage; property values; real estate; synthetic control method; UNESCO world heritage
abstract: This paper estimates the effect of UNESCO World Heritage Site designation on local property values by examining the 2009 inscription of the Dolomites. Using municipality–semester panel data for the period 2005:2–2022:2 and a synthetic control design, we estimate the impact on ordinary dwellings, luxury dwellings and commercial properties. We find a persistent increase in residential property values that grows steadily for more than a decade after inscription. The average estimated effect is €317.29/m2 for ordinary dwellings and €283.48/m2 for luxury dwellings (≈17.4% and ≈13.4% above the counterfactual, respectively). We find no statistically significant effect for commercial properties.
summary: Uses a synthetic control approach to estimate the regional effects of UNESCO heritage status on property values.

title: Towards an evolutionary perspective on institutions in economic geography
authors: Ron Boschma
keywords: institutional change; Institutional complementarities; institutional relatedness; institutional space; policy space; regional diversification
abstract: A long-standing body of literature has investigated the role of institutions for regional development. There is a tendency in the economic geography literature on institutional change to look at institutions as if they operate in isolation from each other. This paper proposes a systemic, evolutionary framework on institutional change that accounts for institutional complementarities. It presents an analytical framework that identifies revealed (instead of pre-defined) complementarities between institutions (institutional space), as well as between policies (policy space). This allows us to take up questions in economic geography that have not yet been fully addressed: (1) how institutional relatedness affects the ability of regions to diversify into new activities; (2) how such a framework on institutional complementarities sheds light on the directionality and feasibility of institutional change in territorial contexts; and (3) how this may contribute to a better understanding of how changes in regional innovation or mission-oriented policies may, or may not, become effective. Doing so, the paper aims to contribute to the further integration of institutions and policy in Evolutionary Economic Geography.
summary: Develops an evolutionary perspective on institutions within economic geography.

title: "Shelter in place": Early COVID-19 TV news reporting at the intersection of housing and health policy
authors: H. Shellae Versey; Kenton Card; Colleen Bogucki; Laura M. Baum; Erika Franklin Fowler
keywords: COVID-19 pandemic; health equity; housing; Media
abstract: How do local media report on housing and health during major crises? The current study examines how housing and policy issues were discussed in the local television (TV) media during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, when policy measures were first introduced and communicated to the public. Drawing from a sample of housing-related news stories between March 2020 and June 2020 (N = 87), we explore how local TV news covered housing policy and health equity, using New York City as a case study. Results suggest that communication about housing and health policy was framed in three ways: (1) issue bifurcation, meaning that housing and health were discussed separately; (2) crisis-oriented reporting, with a short-sighted view of symptoms of a broken system, rather than structural dynamics; and (3) a top-down set of viewpoints and perspectives in which policymakers and advocates received the most attention, often overlooking residents experiencing COVID-related housing hardships. Our findings suggest that mainstream evening TV news does not question the long-term implications of certain public policy areas, despite rigorous local political debate surrounding housing and a centennial health crisis, both of which warrant broader analysis. Implications for future research, policy, and integrated health equity agendas are discussed.
summary: Analyses early COVID-19 television news reporting on 'shelter in place' where housing and health policy intersect.

title: Planning for the sake of the plan: An exploration of the implementability of sustainable, smart, and resilient city models in Monterrey, Mexico
authors: Natalia García-Cervantes; Ryan Anders Whitney; Darío Luna Barrios
keywords: Monterrey; resilient cities; smart cities; sustainable cities; Urban policy
abstract: This article analyzes the integration of the sustainable, smart, and resilient city models into Monterrey, Mexico’s metropolitan and municipal urban policy covering the period from 2000 to 2040. Drawing on a review of four urban development plans and one urban resilience plan, the article traces how these models have become increasingly embedded in official urban policy without engaging with institutional and governance conditions necessary for their implementation. Using the concept of planning for the sake of the plan, we argue that metropolitan and municipal planning in Monterrey reflects a broader performative logic, in which the production of plans serves as a symbolic demonstration of alignment with international urban models rather than a driver of concrete local change, making the plan an end in itself. The persistency of limited implementability across successive plans is interpreted as a consistent pattern over time. To conclude, we call for a shift from planning for the sake of the plan to planning for measurable urban transformation.
summary: Explores how implementable sustainable, smart and resilient city planning models are in Monterrey, Mexico.

title: Tribal consultation in environmental and land-use planning: Lessons from planners and tribal leaders
authors: Michelle E. Zúñiga; Michael Méndez; Clint Carroll; Karla Monroy
keywords: Consultation; environmental stewardship; land-use planning
abstract: California’s Senate Bill 18 (2004) and Assembly Bill 52 (2014) were enacted to enhance tribal consultation in land-use and environmental planning. The state was the first in the nation to adopt such laws, highlighting the need to integrate Indigenous knowledge into local land-use decisions, especially for cultural and ecological sustainability. This study offers the first statewide evaluation of these laws in the context of general land-use planning. Our qualitative approach involved an analysis of general land-use plans, 40 interviews with planners and tribal leaders, and an online listening session attended by over 70 planners. Results show some positive outcomes, including adoption of agency-level tribal liaisons and planning advisory boards with tribal representation.
