We also identify constraints: tight timelines, limited capacity, misunderstandings of Indigenous sovereignty, and misaligned objectives between tribal communities and planners. We conclude by providing practice-based recommendations to assist stakeholders across the nation to improve tribal consultations.
summary: Draws lessons from planners and tribal leaders on tribal consultation in environmental and land-use planning.

title: What is killing the multifamily condominium? Testing the liability-law hypothesis in California and New Jersey
authors: Nicholas J. Marantz
keywords: homeownership; Housing; urban planning; zoning
abstract: The condominium share of new multifamily housing in the United States declined precipitously after the Great Recession and has remained low, despite a recovery in multifamily rental construction. Commentators have suggested two principal reasons for the decline of multifamily condominiums: changes in federal financing and state construction defect liability regimes. This article focuses on the second explanation, providing the first statistically controlled comparison of multifamily condominium development across states with divergent liability regimes. Using parcel-level assessment data from California and New Jersey, I analyze multifamily completions from 2013 through 2019 to identify the correlates of developers’ decisions to build condominiums versus rental projects. New Jersey has a relatively pro-developer liability regime, and the New Jersey study area shows a 52% higher proportion of condominium units compared to the California study area. But multivariate regression reveals that the probability of a new multifamily project being a condominium is no higher in the New Jersey study area than the California study area after controlling for neighborhood median household income. These findings suggest that the availability of sites in high-income neighborhoods, rather than construction defect liability regimes, may be driving geographic divergence in rates of multifamily condominium development.
summary: Tests the hypothesis that liability law is behind the decline of multifamily condominium development, comparing California and New Jersey.

title: Geopolitical Rivalry and the New Global Economic Geography: Dynamics, Networks, and Territories of Global Disorder
authors: Steve Rolf; Seth Schindler; Kean Fan Lim; Jeffrey Henderson
summary: Examines how geopolitical rivalry is reshaping the global economic geography through the dynamics, networks and territories of global disorder.

title: The Spatial Limits to Weaponizing Interdependence: TSMC in the US–China Chip War
authors: Joseph Baines; Steve Rolf; Julian Germann
abstract: The US–China rivalry is focusing attention on how geoeconomics impacts corporate operations and global production networks. States are seeking to weaponize interdependence through policies like sanctions and export controls, and through instrumentalizing corporations as tools to secure relative gains over geopolitical rivals. This article examines how firms’ territorial embeddedness complicates states’ weaponization efforts. To illustrate this phenomenon, we investigate Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). TSMC has played an important role in the development of China’s chip ecosystem and is also critical to securing the competitive advantage of US chip and AI firms. The US government has sought to pressurize TSMC to limit commercial relations with Chinese firms in a bid to impede China’s semiconductor industry. However, TSMC itself is deeply embedded in a cross-strait manufacturing ecosystem, integrating Taiwan and mainland China. We find that the potential compliance costs of TSMC fully discontinuing its commercial links with China and the collateral damage that would be experienced by the US and its firms have enhanced TSMC’s bargaining power. This has enabled the company, in turn, to further expand its China operations. Operationalizing the concept of embeddedness can significantly enhance understanding of how corporate geographies relate to geoeconomic dynamics.
summary: Uses the case of TSMC in the US–China chip war to examine the spatial limits to weaponizing economic interdependence.

title: Economic Statecraft of the Hinge State: Industrialization Paths for the Electric Vehicle (EV) and Battery Industry in Hungary, Mexico, and Thailand
authors: Yuko Aoyama; Luis F. Alvarez León; Shan-yu Wang
abstract: In responding to the calls to better incorporate the role of the state in economic geographic research, in this article we propose an expanded conceptualization of economic statecraft and explore the role of state capacity that forges industrialization paths. We focus on the rise of hinge states as a particular—and we argue, increasingly prevalent—form of economic statecraft under multipolarity that actively develops state capacity to address power asymmetries between states. By taking the case of the electric vehicle and battery industry, we demonstrate how Hungary, Mexico, and Thailand are hedging alliances, leveraging geoeconomics positionality for market access, and territorializing industrialization paths at multiple scales. As such, hinge states play a pivotal role in the global value chains/global production networks, and navigate the US–China geoeconomic competition by exercising supply chain diplomacy to enhance its own strategic autonomy. By engaging with the interdisciplinary debates on economic statecraft and state capacity, our goal is to develop an analytical framework for economic geography that incorporates the role of the state under multipolarity.
summary: Compares the economic statecraft and industrialization paths of Hungary, Mexico and Thailand, framed as 'hinge states', in the electric vehicle and battery industry.

title: Universities' Offshore Campuses as a Geopolitical Strategy Under the Knowledge-Based Economy
authors: Tim Rottleb; Marc P. Schulze; Jana M. Kleibert
abstract: Past years have seen increasing global geopolitical tension, prompting debates in economic geography on ongoing processes of de-globalization, and questions on changing geopolitical and geoeconomic strategies. Within this context and as part of renewed considerations of sovereignty, governments have identified science and higher education as an important field for international relations. While universities have long been shown to be permeated by geopolitical dynamics and international power structures, they now become increasingly active as geopolitical instruments and actors. One particular transnational form of higher education is the development of offshore campuses (or OCs) by universities, which some governments seek to attract. In this article, we conceptualize offshore campus development as a geopolitical strategy under the knowledge-based economy, unfolding across three dimensions: global reputational hierarchies and power asymmetries, global competitiveness and positionality, and territorial logics of power and security. Based on an analysis of qualitative interviews with offshore campus executive managers, as well as with senior administrators from government institutions in the Arab Gulf region and Southeast Asia, we show how governments’ strategies to attract offshore campuses weave transnational higher education into geopolitical considerations that are informed by rationales of the knowledge-based economy. Our analysis shows not only that the lens of geopolitics can help to better understand the logics of offshore campus development but that these campuses also get mobilized in geopolitical strategies of governments directly. As a geopolitical strategy, offshore campuses blend economic and political objectives, fuse coercive and consensual foreign policy strategies, and reterritorialize flows involving state and nonstate actors.
summary: Examines universities' offshore campuses as a geopolitical strategy in the knowledge-based economy.

title: The socioeconomic impacts of energy transition: a macroeconomic energy-input–output model
authors: Kurt Kratena
keywords: energy input-output model; Energy transition; macroeconomic input-output model
abstract: This paper presents important model features for covering the socioeconomic impacts and the energy system dynamics of energy transition. For that, the standard IO model is extended to an energy system-IO model by linking to partial bottom-up energy models. The treatment of energy demand deviates from standard energy/environment CGE models by including energy (E) as a capital-stock specific demand. The IO core of the model identifies energy and non-energy industry linkages. Investments can shift the output shares across different energy-related technologies (e.g. from blast-furnace to electric-arc steel). This mechanism is consistently linked to the IO structure by applying a two-layered framework, i.e. energy flows are measured in both monetary and physical units. The impacts of energy transition on income distribution across households can be modelled by introducing ten different household/labour types.
summary: Presents a macroeconomic energy input–output model to assess the socioeconomic impacts of the energy transition.

title: Input-output micro-macro twins
authors: Umed Temursho; Matthias Weitzel
keywords: distributional analysis; Household expenditure model; intra-budget coefficients; micro-macro modeling; micro-macro twins
abstract: This paper contributes to the literature on demand estimation from survey data and the integration of consumer demand with macro-models. We estimate and analyze EU-wide and country-specific results of (modified) Taylor's [The Internal Structure of U.S. Consumption Expenditures. Springer.] intra-budget regressions, providing insights into the internal structure and interdependencies of European households' consumption expenditures. We propose a modified Taylor consumer demand system by properly incorporating the household budget constraint into the Taylor micro-model and derive closed-form expressions for price and income elasticities. We then integrate the modified Taylor micro-model with an open input-output (IO) quantity setting, analyzing both the non-linear and linearized IO micro-macro systems. The linearized framework enables the integration of any demand system into an IO model, supporting the analysis of consumer price impacts. Finally, we introduce and empirically examine novel multiplier matrices that capture the impacts of price changes on consumption, income, and production, and analyze the effects of consumer price increases in the EU.
summary: Introduces 'micro-macro twins' for input–output analysis, linking micro- and macro-level perspectives in input–output modelling.

title: From financialization to financial reproduction: Territorialized care and life insurance in retirement communities
authors: Xuanyi Nie
keywords: retirement community; life insurance; financialization; spatial bundling; territorialized care
abstract: This paper examines how China's life insurance industry reshapes the built environment and infrastructures of care to achieve financial reproduction. Focusing on Taikang Life's Continuing Care Retirement Communities (CCRCs), the study explores how life insurance capital is not simply invested in real estate to absorb surplus but spatially bundled with territorialized infrastructures of care to reproduce life insurance per se. Drawing on multi-year fieldwork at Taikang Home Yan Garden in Beijing, the paper investigates how life insurance products are spatially bundled with retirement communities, which serve both as long-horizon investment vehicles and as socio-spatial instruments that embed care into territorially bounded built environments. Through this case, the paper develops the concept of "territorialized care" to describe how built environments are engineered not only to provide social reproduction but to structure the spatial fixity and financial durability required by life insurance capital. It argues that these developments represent a shift from traditional financialization of surplus absorption or assetization to financial reproduction, where the built environment is not just a container of capital but a platform for its circulation, extension, and control. In doing so, the paper contributes to debates in financial geography and critical care studies by reframing infrastructures of care as a strategic site of accumulation, negotiation, and spatial control under financialized regimes of aging.
summary: Fieldwork at Taikang Life's retirement community in Beijing shows Chinese life insurers spatially bundling insurance products with 'territorialized care' infrastructures, marking a shift from financialization as surplus absorption to financial reproduction.

title: From regions to neighborhoods: Algorithmic lending and the rescaling of racial inequality in U.S. mortgage markets
authors: Tyler Haupert
keywords: algorithmic governance; rescaling; mortgage lending; racial inequality; fintech
abstract: Over the past decade, mortgage lending in the United States has increasingly shifted from locally embedded underwriting practices to algorithmically mediated risk assessment systems deployed most prominently by financial technology (fintech) lenders. While existing research evaluates whether these systems expand credit access or alter average racial disparities, far less attention has been paid to how they reshape the spatial organization of inequality. Drawing on loan-level data from the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (2018–2020), this study examines whether fintech lending is associated with changes in the geographic distribution of Black-White disparities in mortgage approval and pricing across and within metropolitan areas. Multilevel models reveal substantial compression in cross-metropolitan variation in racial disparities under fintech lending, with reductions of approximately two-thirds in approval disparities and three-quarters in pricing disparities relative to traditional lenders. At the same time, within-metropolitan patterns diverge by outcome: pricing disparities exhibit similar tract-level dispersion across lending regimes, while approval disparities display greater neighborhood-level heterogeneity under fintech lending. These findings are consistent with a rescaling of racial inequality from regionally differentiated patterns toward more localized intra-metropolitan variation. By foregrounding scale as an analytic dimension of financial governance, this study illustrates how algorithmic lending infrastructures may reorganize the spatial levels at which racial inequality is produced and observed in contemporary housing markets.
summary: HMDA loan data (2018–2020) show fintech lending cuts cross-metro variation in Black–White mortgage approval and pricing disparities by about two-thirds and three-quarters, while approval gaps become more uneven across neighbourhoods—rescaling racial inequality from regions to neighbourhoods.

title: The unlawful rent gap: How landlords close rent gaps despite rent regulation
authors: Justin Kadi
keywords: private renting; rent regulation; rent gap; Vienna; landlord compliance
abstract: A common view in the literature is that rent regulation inhibits the operation of the rent gap. This paper argues for a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between rent regulation and the rent gap. I contend that, under specific circumstances, landlords may not comply with rent regulation and close rent gaps nonetheless. This unlawful rent gap closure, whereby landlords charge higher rents than legally permitted, is facilitated by complex and opaque rent regulation, limited sanctions for landlords, as well as demographic and economic conditions that stimulate housing demand and attract capital into the property market. I demonstrate the relevance of the unlawful rent gap for current rent gap dynamics based on a case study of Vienna, Austria. Drawing on a unique data set of more than 2900 court decisions against landlords, I provide a fine-grained analysis of its scale and geography. I examine which social groups are most affected, estimate the size of the gap, and calculate a spatially-differentiated risk index for future exploitation. I argue that, in contrast to the classic rent gap, the unlawful rent gap is inherently unstable, as tenants can challenge high rents in court. This gives the legal system a central role in shaping rent gap dynamics. I end by specifying the wider relevance of my argument for rent gap scholarship beyond the case considered.
summary: Drawing on 2,900+ court decisions against Vienna landlords, the paper shows landlords close rent gaps despite regulation by charging unlawfully high rents—enabled by opaque rules, weak sanctions and strong demand—an 'unlawful rent gap' that stays unstable because tenants can sue.

title: Border region economies: The role of proximity
authors: Tobias Chilla; Hannah Paul; Carola Sommer
keywords: border regions; cross-border integration; proximity; agri-food sectors; regional economies
abstract: While borders have traditionally been understood as barriers that increase transaction costs and divide economic space, processes of liberalization and integration also create opportunities for cross-border interaction. Building on relational economic geography, this paper examines how different forms of proximity shape cross-border economic integration in European border regions. Empirically, the study analyzes three agri-food sectors in European Union border regions: beer in the German–Czech border region, pork in the German–Dutch border region, and soy in the German–Austrian border region. Using a mixed-methods mapping approach, the paper investigates economic flows and governance relations along the entire value chain from cultivation to consumption. The results show that proximity can enable and constrain cross-border interaction. Institutional differences may create opportunities through regulatory or price differentials, while excessive institutional distance hinders exchange. Organizational proximity can foster cooperation through shared infrastructure and expertise; however, competition may reinforce barriers. Cognitive and social proximity facilitate interaction when products and actors are perceived as culturally "regional enough," whereas strong domestic embeddedness limits integration. While spatial proximity supports integration when infrastructure and accessibility reduce transaction costs, geographical closeness alone is insufficient. Borders can function as assets and barriers. Moreover, the degree of cross-border integration depends on the interaction between different forms of proximity, transaction costs, and broader structural conditions.
summary: Mapping beer, pork and soy value chains in German–Czech, German–Dutch and German–Austrian border regions shows institutional, organizational, cognitive/social and spatial proximity can each enable or constrain cross-border integration, making borders both assets and barriers.

title: Taking maps seriously in economic geography
authors: Dariusz Wójcik; Matthew Sim
keywords: economic geography; maps; cartography; visualisation
abstract: The article revisits the debate on the use of maps in economic geography. Using data on articles published in Economic Geography, Regional Studies, and EPA going back to 1974, we show that the evidence of decline is mixed, and that use of maps varies significantly by geographical affiliation of authors as well as by journal. We discuss the changing geographic foci of maps in economic geography, and finish with examples highlighting opportunities for more mapping in the future.
summary: Data on articles in Economic Geography, Regional Studies and EPA since 1974 show mixed evidence of a decline in map use, with usage varying markedly by journal and by authors' geographic affiliation.

title: Regional Disparities and Mobility in the European Space (2000–2024): A Spatial Markov Analysis
authors: Leonidas Doukissas; Panayotis Pantazis
keywords: Spatial inequality; Spatial Markov chains; LISA Markov; Regional mobility; Territorial cohesion; Development traps
abstract: This paper examines the spatio-temporal dynamics of regional income disparities in the European Union over the period 2000–2024 at the NUTS-3 level. Using GDP per capita expressed relative to the EU27 average, the analysis combines unconditional Markov chains, Spatial Markov chains, and LISA Markov methods to assess regional income-state persistence, neighbourhood-conditioned mobility, and the durability of local spatial regimes. The results reveal strong persistence across the regional income distribution, with particularly limited upward mobility among low-income regions embedded in disadvantaged neighbourhood environments. Spatial Markov evidence shows that transition probabilities vary systematically across neighbourhood income regimes, consistent with spatially conditioned mobility barriers. The LISA Markov results provide especially strong evidence of structurally embedded spatial inequality, revealing persistent Low-Low and High-High local spatial-association regimes over time. Robustness checks across alternative state partitions, spatial weights matrices, and policy-relevant subperiods confirm that the main patterns are not driven by a single discretization, neighbourhood specification, or pooled time window. The findings highlight the importance of place-sensitive and spatially coordinated cohesion policies, while preserving a diagnostic rather than causal interpretation of the results.
summary: Spatial and LISA Markov analysis of EU NUTS-3 GDP per capita (2000–2024) finds strong persistence in regional income states—especially little upward mobility for poor regions with poor neighbours—and durable Low-Low and High-High clusters.

title: The Impact of Urban Renewal on Neighborhood Housing Prices: A Spatial Effects and Differential Analysis in Nanjing City, China
authors: Lifang Zhang; Jiajia Liao; Ying Li; Pinhua Jin; Shuqi Li; Yeting Fan
keywords: Urban renewal; Housing price; Difference-in-difference model; Hedonic price model; Geographically weighted regression; Spatial heterogeneity
abstract: Urban renewal generates significant externalities and serves as a vital strategic instrument for sustainable urban development. Its impact on neighborhood housing prices is directly linked to the attributes of a specific region and influences the local residential market. This study employed a difference-in-difference model combined with the Hedonic price framework and geographically weighted regression model to explore the impact of urban renewal on housing prices, by investigating 60 urban renewal projects initiated in Nanjing City between 2014 and 2022. The study explores the heterogeneous effects of different types of urban renewal projects on housing prices and investigates the spatial scope of their influence. The results showed that urban renewal projects have significantly driven up housing prices within a 1.5 km radius. This impact varies depending on the types of urban renewal, the specific locations, and the distance from urban renewal projects. Specifically, commercial-type urban renewal projects yield the greatest increase in housing prices, compared with industrial and residential projects. Projects in the central urban districts exert a stronger influence on neighborhood housing prices than those in suburban districts, which significantly boost housing prices by 28.57% within 1.5 km. Urban renewal effects on housing prices vary by distance, with stronger impacts closer to projects. Both residential and commercial renewal exert positive price effects on surrounding housing across all distance bands; however, commercial projects demonstrate the most pronounced impact within 500 m. Residential and industrial renewals show statistically significant price effects within 500-1,000 m. A deeper insight into how urban renewal intricately influences housing prices would enable more effective policy development for managing renewal initiatives within dynamic housing market contexts.
summary: Across 60 Nanjing urban renewal projects (2014–2022), DID-hedonic and GWR models show renewal significantly raised housing prices within 1.5 km, with the largest effects for commercial and central-district projects and for homes closest to projects.

title: Effect of Public Infrastructure on Interregional Agricultural Trade in Burkina Faso
authors: Ladioum Bienvenue Drabo; Tibi Didier Zoungrana
keywords: Burkina Faso; Gravity; HDFE-PPML; Infrastructure; Agricultural trade
abstract: This research examines the impact of public infrastructure on interregional agricultural trade in Burkina Faso using panel data for the country's 13 regions over the period 2011–2020. Because observed interregional trade flow data are unavailable, trade flows are reconstructed using a spatial equilibrium approach before being estimated within a gravity framework using Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood with high-dimensional fixed effects (HDFE-PPML). The results reveal substantial heterogeneity in infrastructure effects. Road infrastructure in origin regions significantly promotes agricultural trade, whereas road infrastructure in destination regions exerts a negative effect, suggesting that infrastructure impacts depend on its spatial location within the trade network. Information and communication technologies stimulate trade in destination regions but reduce it in origin regions, while electricity infrastructure mainly benefits importing regions. Overall, the findings highlight that interregional agricultural trade depends not only on infrastructure availability but also on how transport, communication, and energy infrastructures interact across regions. These findings suggest that infrastructure policies should account for the heterogeneous effects of transport, communication, and electricity infrastructure across origin and destination regions to better promote interregional agricultural trade.
summary: A gravity model (HDFE-PPML) of reconstructed trade flows among Burkina Faso's 13 regions (2011–2020) finds roads boost agricultural trade from origin regions but not into destinations, ICT raises destination-side trade, and electricity mainly benefits importing regions.

title: Urban AI Adoption and the Settlement Intentions of High-Skilled Workers: Evidence from China
authors: Siyu Meng; Xuan Zou
keywords: Artificial Intelligence; High-Skilled Workers; Settlement Intentions; Cities
abstract: Enhancing talent retention has become a critical pathway for cities to strengthen their core competitiveness and achieve sustainable development. Using data from the China Migrants Dynamic Survey (CMDS), this study examines how urban artificial intelligence (AI) adoption influences the long-term settlement intentions of high-skilled workers. The findings suggest that AI adoption is likely to enhance the settlement intentions of high-skilled workers. The mechanism analysis suggests that AI may influence settlement intentions through three channels—the income effect, the livability effect, and the career development effect. The positive effect is more pronounced among long-term migrants, interprovincial migrants, and those employed in state-owned enterprises. At the city level, the effect is stronger in large cities, in cities outside urban agglomerations, and in cities with higher administrative status. These findings provide useful insights for cities seeking to develop differentiated AI strategies and more targeted talent policies.
summary: China Migrants Dynamic Survey data suggest urban AI adoption raises high-skilled migrants' long-term settlement intentions via income, livability and career-development channels, especially in large, higher-status cities outside urban agglomerations.

title: China's Ecological Conservation Redline and Regional Ecosystem Service Value: Based on Machine Learning and the Quasi-Natural Experimental Evidence of Staggered DID
authors: Guangcheng Ma; Junhong Bai; Yiru Chen
keywords: Ecosystem service value measurement; Staggered policy evaluation; Ecological conservation redline; Machine learning index construction; Quasi-natural experiment
abstract: Quantifying the causal effect of place-based ecological policies on ecosystem service value remains challenging due to the multidimensional nature of ecological benefits and the endogeneity of policy adoption. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a two-stage analytical framework. In the first stage, a machine-learning-based aggregation approach is applied to panel data covering 280 Chinese prefecture-level cities over the period 2000–2024, generating a composite ecosystem service value index that jointly reflects provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting functions. In the second stage, a staggered Difference-in-Differences design exploits the phased rollout of the ecological conservation redline policy across regions to identify its causal effect on the composite index. The results show that the policy generates a statistically significant and progressively increasing improvement in regional ecosystem service value. Mechanism analysis indicates that this effect operates through three partial mediation channels: green technology innovation, ecological spatial reconstruction, and ecological fiscal transfer incentives. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the policy effect is stronger in cities with higher local governmental environmental attention and in regions with greater ecosystem vulnerability. Moderating effect tests further reveal that policy coordination across administrative departments and local governance capacity both amplify the baseline treatment effect. This study contributes to the literature by linking a machine-learning-driven measurement framework with quasi-experimental causal inference, offering actionable evidence for the refinement of national land spatial planning and ecological governance in China.
summary: A staggered DID across 280 Chinese cities (2000–2024) shows the ecological conservation redline policy progressively raised a machine-learning-built ecosystem service value index, via green innovation, ecological spatial reconstruction and ecological fiscal transfers.

title: Occupational Structure Change in a Chinese Metropolitan Region: Case Study of the Pearl River Delta
authors: Zeyu Zhang; Guangzhong Cao
keywords: Occupational Structure; Spatial Temporal Pattern; Polarization; Pearl River Delta; Center-periphery structure
abstract: This research looks into the pattern and mechanism of occupational structure change of the Pearl River Delta, China, from 2000 to 2020, testing the polarization and professionalization hypothesis of western cities in a developing country on a regional scale. It is found that the region had a polarizing trend and its cities followed a trajectory from industrialization, proletarianization to polarization. Centers of the region tended to polarize with faster growth in the high-skilled, while the sub-centers polarized with faster growth in the low-skilled occupations, and the peripheries displayed industrialization and proletarianization in early years and shifted to polarization in the recent decade. Industrial policies promoting advanced manufacturing and services enhanced growth of the high-skilled occupations. Large-scale domestic migration to the region fueled the growth of low-skilled occupations, but also acted as important sources of talents. Functional division and difference in development stage between the centers, sub-centers and peripheries led to the heterogeneity in occupational restructuring patterns in the region. This research complements to the debate on occupational structural changes by providing evidence from the "Global South", proposing differences between central and peripheral cities and a trajectory of occupational change covering different stages of development, and further interpreting how localized factors shaped the occupational restructuring process.
summary: Between 2000 and 2020 the Pearl River Delta's occupational structure polarized—high-skilled growth in centres, low-skilled growth in sub-centres, and peripheries moving from industrialization and proletarianization to polarization—shaped by industrial policy and mass domestic migration.

title: Does Healthy City Pilot Improve Urban Ecological Resilience? Evidence from Quasi-Natural Experiments
authors: Li Chen; Yuezhang Jiang; Zihan Song; Yixiang Zhang; Youyu Luo
keywords: Healthy City Pilot; Ecological Resilience; Difference-in-Differences Model; Spatial Spillovers; Policy Synergy
abstract: Urban ecological resilience (ER) is essential for coping with environmental risks and achieving sustainable urban development. As an important governance initiative integrating public health and environmental management, the Healthy City Pilot (HCP) policy may generate positive ecological externalities. Using panel data of Chinese prefecture-level cities, this study treats the implementation of the HCP policy as a quasi-natural experiment and employs a difference-in-differences (DID) model to examine its impact on urban ER. The results show that the HCP policy significantly improves ER, and this conclusion remains robust after a series of robustness tests. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the policy effect is more pronounced in eastern region, in cities with higher administrative status, and in resource-based cities. Mechanism analysis further reveals that the HCP policy enhances ER primarily through promoting green technological innovation, strengthening public environmental concern, and reducing urban electricity intensity. Spatial econometric analysis demonstrates that the HCP policy generates significant positive spatial spillover effects, facilitating improvements in ER in neighboring cities. In addition, further analysis shows that the HCP policy exhibits a significant synergistic effect with Green Finance policy, and their joint implementation further strengthens the improvement of ER. These findings highlight the ecological co-benefits of health-oriented governance and underscore the importance of policy coordination in addressing urban sustainability challenges, offering valuable insights for enhancing ER and fostering sustainable and resilient cities.
summary: A DID on Chinese prefecture-level cities finds the Healthy City Pilot significantly improved urban ecological resilience—via green innovation, public environmental concern and lower electricity intensity—with positive spillovers to neighbours and synergy with green finance policy.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Carbon-Constrained Energy Efficiency: Direct Effects, Digital Infrastructure Thresholds, and Spatial Effects
authors: Bo Xu; Ruifa Li; Gang Zou; Yingde Hu
keywords: Artificial intelligence; Carbon-constrained energy efficiency; Digital infrastructure threshold; Mediation analysis; Spatial spillovers; Regional heterogeneity
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping urban energy systems at an unprecedented pace, yet its net contribution to carbon-constrained energy efficiency remains an unsettled empirical question. The mechanisms of impact, the role of digital infrastructure, and the spatial patterns of energy savings constitute a critical but underexamined research frontier. Drawing on panel data from 297 Chinese prefecture-level cities over 2011–2024, we employ a parallel multiple mediation model, a panel threshold model, and a spatial Durbin model within a unified framework. We present our main findings as follows. First, AI development exerts a positive effect on carbon-constrained energy efficiency. Raising AI_level by one standard deviation improves carbon-constrained energy efficiency by roughly 10.3% of the sample mean. Second, industrial upgrading and green innovation together explain 38.2% of the total effect, with the remaining 61.8% attributed to the direct effect of AI. Third, digital infrastructure exerts a single threshold effect. The positive association between AI and energy efficiency is stronger in cities with more developed digital infrastructure. Fourth, AI development contributes to energy efficiency gains in neighboring cities via spatial spillovers, yet the size of these indirect effects is modest. The spatial distribution of AI exhibits high persistence, with annual transition probabilities below 4%. Fifth, the positive association is heterogeneous across regions, policy environments, and socioeconomic conditions. This study advances the literature by quantifying the relative importance of direct versus indirect pathways, identifying the threshold role of digital infrastructure, and documenting the spatial persistence and limited spillovers of AI development. These findings offer implications for differentiated regional strategies and infrastructure investment priorities.
summary: Across 297 Chinese cities (2011–2024), a one-standard-deviation rise in AI development lifts carbon-constrained energy efficiency by about 10.3% of the mean—62% directly and 38% via industrial upgrading and green innovation—more so where digital infrastructure is developed, with modest spillovers.

title: Measurement, Spatio-Temporal Pattern and Regional Differences of the Evolution Level in Digital Industry Innovation Ecosystem
authors: Yabing Ma; Yongheng Fang
keywords: Digital industry innovation ecosystem; System evolution; Indicator system; Spatio-temporal pattern; Regional differences
abstract: The digital industry is not only an important carrier and platform for developing new quality productive forces, but also a significant engine for driving economic growth. The development of the digital industry has also shifted from traditional linear innovation to a new paradigm of the digital industry innovation ecosystem (DIIE). Scientifically measuring the evolution level of the DIIE is of great significance for assessing the development status of the system, identifying regional collaboration paths, and optimizing policy supply. This study focuses on the evolution of the DIIE. By using the Meta-analysis method, a measurement model for the evolution level of the DIIE is constructed. The CRITIC- entropy weight method is adopted to calculate the evolution level of the DIIE in 30 provinces across the country from 2010 to 2022. Furthermore, methods such as the standard deviation ellipse, kernel density estimation, Markov chain, Dagum Gini coefficient and its decomposition are employed to reveal the spatiotemporal pattern, dynamic evolution and regional differences of the system evolution level. The research results show that: (1) From 2010 to 2022, the evolution level of the national DIIE continued to rise and the regional gap tended to narrow. The increase rates in each dimension were as follows: factors, environment, functions and structure. The increase rates in each region were as follows: eastern region, central region, western region and northeastern region. (2) There is a significant spatial imbalance in the evolution level of the national DIIE. The standard deviation ellipse shows a "northeast-southwest" trend, and the area continues to shrink, with the center moving towards the southwest. (3) The evolution level of the national DIIE tends to be concentrated, but the internal morphology of each region is clearly differentiated. The eastern region shows a single peak convergence, the central region shows a single or double peak alternation, and the northeastern region shows a double peak fixation. There are significant "club convergence" and asymmetric spatial spillover effects. (4) The overall difference first decreased and then increased, but the overall decline occurred. The contribution rate of regional differences remained dominant. Among them, the difference between the eastern and northeastern regions was the largest, and the difference within the eastern region showed an upward trend.
summary: Measuring the digital industry innovation ecosystem across 30 Chinese provinces (2010–2022), the study finds a steadily rising evolution level with narrowing but persistent spatial imbalance—largest between the east and northeast—plus club convergence and asymmetric spillovers.

title: Spatial Decision Support for Controlled Environment Agriculture in Cold Regions: Evidence from Alberta, Canada
authors: Tingsheng Xie; Ali Hamidoğlu; Hao Wang
keywords: Controlled environment agriculture; Spatial planning; Suitability analysis; Land-use policy; Cold-region food systems; Alberta
abstract: Cold-region food systems face spatial planning constraints arising from long winters, short frost-free periods, seasonal variability, uneven infrastructure access, and land-use restrictions. Controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) can support year-round production, but its expansion depends on the alignment of suitable land, infrastructure, terrain, environmental conditions, and regional connectivity. This study develops a provincial-scale geographic information system (GIS)-based screening and planning-priority framework to delineate eligible land, compare relative suitability, and identify candidate areas for further CEA planning and investigation in Alberta, Canada. The framework applies exclusionary land-use and physical-constraint masks, followed by a multi-criteria assessment integrating infrastructure accessibility, environmental conditions, terrain limitations, and regional connectivity. Results show that development potential is highly uneven. Only 36.64% is eligible; under the baseline five-class equal-interval classification, High and Very High planning-priority areas cover 5.99% of Alberta. These areas are concentrated mainly in central and southern Alberta, with the South Saskatchewan, North Saskatchewan, and Red Deer planning regions containing 88.60% of all High and Very High priority land. The framework identifies areas warranting further planning review; it does not determine final facility locations, development allocations, or project approvals. Benchmark facilities generally scored higher than random eligible points, suggesting that infrastructure and accessibility are associated with their spatial distribution. Robustness analyses show that class-specific area totals vary across classification methods, while broad regional patterns remain stable across methods and weighting configurations. The findings show that effective CEA expansion requires a coordinated regional planning approach that aligns infrastructure investment with land-use policy and broader food-system adaptation goals.
summary: A GIS screening and multi-criteria framework for Alberta finds only 36.64% of land eligible for controlled-environment agriculture and 5.99% in high or very-high planning priority, 88.60% of it in the South Saskatchewan, North Saskatchewan and Red Deer regions.

title: Investigating Spatially Heterogeneous and Nonlinear Associations Between Urban Context and Taxi Related Emissions
authors: Yu Gong; Wei Yang; Yingpeng Li; Jiaming Sun
keywords: Taxi trajectory data; Carbon emissions; GW-RF; SHAP model; Nonlinear associations
abstract: Taxi carbon emissions (TCE) contribute significantly to air pollution and climate change. However, the nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous relationships between environmental factors and TCE remain insufficiently understood. Therefore, this study investigates the spatially heterogeneous and nonlinear associations between environmental factors and TCE using taxi GPS trajectories and multisource urban data. Specifically, a Geographically Weighted Random Forest (GW-RF) model is employed to capture nonlinear relationships while accounting for spatial non-stationarity, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) mode is used to interpret feature importance and nonlinear marginal effect patterns. Using Chongqing, China, as a case study, this study yields the following key findings: (1) Neighborhood-level built environment factors dominated TCE, accounting for 64.5% of total explanatory importance, with transit accessibility, population density, and intersection density emerging as the most influential factors. (2) All examined factors exhibit significant nonlinear marginal effect, revealing complex environment-emission association patterns. (3) The importance and marginal effects of key factors such as bus station density, street enclosure, varied markedly across temporal periods and occupancy statuses. (4) Spatial heterogeneity was evident in both variable importance and local effects, particularly for population density, transit accessibility, and street visual characteristics. The findings provide valuable evidence to inform spatially differentiated, nonlinear-sensitive urban and transport planning policies aimed at sustainable mobility and emissions reduction.
summary: Using Chongqing taxi GPS trajectories with a geographically weighted random forest and SHAP, the study finds neighbourhood built-environment factors—led by transit accessibility, population density and intersection density—explain 64.5% of taxi carbon emissions, with nonlinear and spatially varying effects.

title: Nonlinear and Interaction Effects of the Built Environment on Bus Travel Behavior among People with Disabilities: Evidence from Wuhan, China
authors: Shanzhu Liu; Chengxi Wu; Weiming Zhang; Xuexin Yan
keywords: People with disabilities; Bus travel behavior; Built environment; XGBoost-SHAP; Nonlinear relationship; Interaction effect
abstract: People with disabilities (PWDs) may exhibit distinctive spatiotemporal patterns of bus travel because of their specific physical conditions and travel preferences, which may in turn lead to different associations with the built environment compared with people without disabilities. However, these differences have received limited scholarly attention. This study addresses this gap by comparing the bus travel behaviors of people with and without disabilities in Wuhan, China. The results show that PWDs have significantly higher bus travel frequencies than people without disabilities on both weekdays (3.58 vs. 2.86 trips) and weekends (3.32 vs. 2.63 trips). In terms of spatial distribution, bus trips made by PWDs are more concentrated in central urban areas, whereas those made by people without disabilities are more clustered around transport hubs and employment centers. Further analysis using XGBoost and SHAP reveals significant heterogeneity in the effects of the built environment on bus ridership between the two groups. For PWDs, the three most important factors influencing bus ridership on weekday are road density (14.71%), plot ratio (12.13%), and distance to the city center (8.98%); while the importance of distance to the city center increases to 11.63% on weekends. In addition, all built environment variables exhibit nonlinear relationships with bus ridership and significant threshold effects. For example, road density shows a significantly positive effect on bus ridership among PWDs only when it exceeds 7.5 km/km2 within the station catchment area. Moreover, significant interaction effects are observed. For instance, a plot ratio above 3.0 combined with less than 10 km from the sub-city center produces a positive interaction effect on weekday bus use among PWDs. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the spatiotemporal travel behaviors of PWDs and provide valuable insights for the development of more inclusive and accessible transportation policies.
summary: In Wuhan, people with disabilities make more bus trips than others (3.58 vs 2.86 on weekdays), concentrated in central areas, and XGBoost-SHAP shows their ridership responds nonlinearly to road density, plot ratio and distance to the centre, with clear threshold and interaction effects.

title: Spatial Evidence for Armed-Violence Policy: Concentration, Spatiotemporal Dependence, and Local Network Structure in Metropolitan Rio de Janeiro
authors: Valdecy Pereira; Marcio Pereira Basilio; Fatih Yigit; Elaine Aparecida Araujo
keywords: Applied spatial analysis; Spatial policy; Evidence-based policing; Crime concentration; Spatiotemporal dependence; Hawkes process
abstract: This article asks what event-level spatial analysis adds after the concentration of urban violence is already known. Using 2,800 geolocated and timestamped armed-violence events recorded by Crossfire (Fogo Cruzado) app across 21 municipalities in metropolitan Rio de Janeiro between December 2024 and March 2026, we separate four decision-relevant objects, persistent place burden, short-window event co-occurrence, excess space–time dependence, and model-based self-excitation. The design combines hotspot persistence screening, a 5 km/72 h event graph, shuffled-time and location-permutation benchmarks, and Hawkes point-process models. Linked pairs exceed the shuffled-time null by 27.5% (z=17.57, empirical p=0.0033), but visually strong graph fragmentation is not unusual under the spatially grounded null and attenuates sharply as thresholds widen. Persistent hotspots and temporary event communities therefore represent different policy layers rather than interchangeable maps. The former support sustained place-based prioritization; the latter can support short-run coordination only when their threshold sensitivity and provisional status are displayed. Crossfire app records are produced through a verified multi-source civic-monitoring workflow rather than passive app-location traces, although geographically uneven ascertainment remains possible and low counts in peripheral municipalities must be treated as lower bounds. The study does not identify the causal effect of any policy implemented during the observation period. Its contribution is a transferable framework for matching spatial evidence, uncertainty, and policy time horizons without reifying temporary clusters as fixed territories.
summary: Analysing 2,800 geolocated armed-violence events across metropolitan Rio de Janeiro (Dec 2024–Mar 2026), the study finds linked event pairs exceed a shuffled-time null by 27.5% and argues persistent hotspots and short-lived event clusters should guide different policy layers.

title: Beyond Provincial Averages: A Spatial Diagnostic Framework for Educational Inequality in Vietnam's National Upper Secondary Graduation Examination
authors: Anh Ton Pham
abstract: Provincial average scores are widely used to monitor educational performance, but they may obscure how inequality is distributed within and across administrative units. Using annual data for all 63 provinces in Vietnam's national upper secondary graduation examination from 2017 to 2024, this paper develops a sequential spatial diagnostic framework for three compulsory subjects: Mathematics, Literature, and Foreign Language. The framework first evaluates the adequacy of provincial averages and then examines the spatial structure, persistence, and neighborhood-conditioned mobility of the between-province signal that remains visible at the administrative scale. Theil decomposition indicates that provincial mean scores capture only 6–18% of total examination-score inequality; the dominant 82–94% lies within provinces. This finding establishes the limits of average-based monitoring while motivating a more precise diagnosis of the provincial signal that policymakers observe and compare. The subsequent diagnostics show a clear subject-specific gradient. Mathematics displays the strongest rank stability, spatial clustering, and regime persistence; Literature is more mobile but increasingly spatially differentiated; and Foreign Language occupies an intermediate position. A 3 × 3 Spatial Markov analysis shows differences in observed transition profiles across neighborhood contexts, although estimates based on small conditional origin counts remain imprecise. The findings suggest that province-level educational monitoring would benefit from supplementary spatial diagnostics that track within-province dispersion, persistent low-performing clusters, and subject-specific mobility profiles.
summary: Using 2017–2024 graduation-exam data for all 63 Vietnamese provinces, a Theil decomposition shows provincial means capture only 6–18% of score inequality, and spatial diagnostics reveal Mathematics as the most spatially clustered and persistent subject.

title: How does the Spatial Distribution of Three-Dimensional Green Volume Evolve in Urbanization? Evidence from Nanjing, China
authors: Shining Zhang; Yuan Zong; Ziqi Xu; Zeyang Li; Conghui Zhou
keywords: Green space; Three-dimensional green volume (3DGV); Machine learning; Spatial regression model; Urbanization; Ecosystem services
abstract: Conventional assessments of urban green space usually rely on planar indicators, which cannot fully capture changes in vegetation height, canopy volume, and layered structure during urbanization. To address this limitation, this study estimated three-dimensional green volume (3DGV) and compared its spatiotemporal evolution with two-dimensional green space (2DGS) in the main city of Nanjing from 1990 to 2020. Field-based reference samples, Landsat-derived vegetation indices, and machine-learning regression were integrated to reconstruct decadal-scale 3DGV, while 2DGS was extracted from high-resolution remote-sensing images using support vector machine classification. Spatial autocorrelation analysis and spatial regression models were then used to examine temporal changes, clustering patterns, and associations with socioeconomic, land-use, and natural-environment variables. The results show that both 3DGV and 2DGS experienced a decline–recovery trajectory and exhibited significant positive spatial autocorrelation, but their recovery magnitudes and local clustering patterns differed across phases. The two indicators shared several associated variables, yet differed in coefficient direction, statistical significance, and phase-specific patterns. Land-use variables were more closely associated with changes in 2DGS, whereas socioeconomic and natural-environment variables showed more frequent or indicator-specific associations with 3DGV in several phases. These findings indicate that 3DGV adds a structural dimension to planar green-space assessment by revealing spatially uneven changes in vegetation volume, canopy development, and layered planting structure. The combined 2DGS–3DGV framework provides an additional and complementary basis for diagnosing urban green-space change and supporting structure-oriented greening strategies in high-density cities.
summary: Reconstructing three-dimensional green volume for central Nanjing (1990–2020), the study finds both 3D green volume and planar green space followed a decline–recovery path but with different clustering and drivers, showing 3D measures add structural information to green-space assessment.

title: How Capability of Physical Activity Moderates the Non-linear Association between Greenspace and Subjective Wellbeing: Evidence Based on COPD Patients in Beijing
authors: Mi Yao; Ziqiang Liu; Yuehan Sun; Hongjing Pei; Yujing Su; Guanning Jing; Jiapei Xu; Jianhua Chen; Qiaoli Su; Jiao Xu; Xue Jin; Jingyu Hao; Xueying Li; Jing Ma; Ying Wang; Changrui Ren; Shi Wei; Aimei Dong; Longfeng Wu
keywords: Residential greenspace; Physical activity capacity; EQ-5D; Moderated nonlinearity; COPD patient
abstract: The health impacts of urban greenspace are increasingly acknowledged, yet their relationship with subjective wellbeing may be nonlinear and conditioned by individual capacity. This study examines how capability of physical activity moderates the non-linear association between residential greenspace and health-related quality of life among 331 clinically diagnosed COPD patients in Beijing. Using objective geospatial indicators—tree canopy, total vegetation coverage, and park proximity—and validated wellbeing scores (EQ-5D), we estimated nonlinear and moderated quadratic models. Results reveal a robust U-shaped association between tree canopy and wellbeing, with the association reversing in sign beyond moderate coverage levels. In contrast, vegetation coverage showed no consistent pattern, and park distance displayed a weaker nonlinear relationship. Crucially, physical activity capacity, measured via the 1-minute sit-to-stand and 6-minute walk tests, significantly moderated both the shape and direction of the canopy–wellbeing curve. Higher activity levels flattened or inverted the curve, suggesting that wellbeing gains depend on an individual's ability to engage with their environment. These findings highlight the importance of integrating ecological design with patient mobility needs, offering implications for precision greening in dense urban settings. Urban health strategies for vulnerable populations may benefit from tailoring greenspace interventions to match physical capacity thresholds.
summary: Among 331 COPD patients in Beijing, tree canopy shows a U-shaped association with health-related quality of life, and patients' physical-activity capacity significantly reshapes—flattening or inverting—that canopy–wellbeing curve.

title: Polycentric Morphology and Urban Resilience: AI-Based Assessment of Infrastructure Vulnerabilities in Colombo, Sri Lanka
authors: Jude Nilantha Randeniya; Amila Jayasinghe
abstract: Polycentric urban development is increasingly promoted as inherently resilient spatial strategy for rapidly urbanising Global South megacities. However, limited empirical evidence demonstrates how distributed morphology actually shapes disaster vulnerability, particularly regarding infrastructure interdependencies within polycentric configurations. This research develops and tests the "Polycentric Vulnerability Paradox" framework, examining how distributed urban form simultaneously creates resilience advantages through redundancy and resilience challenges through coordination complexity and inter-centre dependencies. The study provides first systematic AI-based infrastructure vulnerability assessment of polycentric configuration in South Asian context. An AI-based Urban Morphological Quantification Framework integrating K-nearest neighbour algorithms, neural networks, and XGBoost ensemble methods analyzes Colombo's 551.52 km² metropolitan area (9,414 grid cells, 400 m resolution) using OpenStreetMap data. Network analysis identifies polycentric centres, inter-centre connectivity patterns, and critical vulnerability nodes. Processing time: 30 min versus 8–10 h for traditional methods. Analysis identified six distinct polycentric centers spanning 18 km, with 847 critical corridor segments (12.3% of road network) whose failure would disrupt inter-centre connectivity. Vulnerability concentrates at inter-centre connection points rather than centre cores, supporting theoretical proposition. Model accuracy: 73% overall, 78% spatial concordance with historical flood events. Population exposure distributes across multiple centres (68% within/adjacent to six centres) creating paradoxical patterns where single-centre disasters impact maximum 18% of population yet city-wide hazards affect majority despite spatial distribution. Polycentric morphology generates neither uniform resilience nor uniform vulnerability but paradoxical patterns where advantages and challenges coexist, with net effects contingent on infrastructure quality and governance capacity. Distributed urban form requires distributed coordination capacity; otherwise morphological complexity amplifies rather than reduces disaster vulnerability.
summary: AI-based analysis of Colombo's metropolitan area finds six polycentric centres and 847 critical corridor segments (12.3% of roads), with disaster vulnerability concentrated at inter-centre connections—a 'polycentric vulnerability paradox' where redundancy and coordination complexity coexist.

title: Spatiotemporal Analysis of Emotional Trajectories With Electrodermal Activity and Audio: A Case Study in Fanta Oriental Heritage Theme Park
authors: Wei Jiang; Jing Mao; Zongxin Quan; Jingjing Zhao; Dongsong Xu; Yi Long; Xiaoqing Song
abstract: Exploring the spatial variation of emotion has attracted increasing attention in recent years. However, few scholarly attempts have focused on the spatiotemporal process of emotional dynamics. This study aimed to depict continuous and fine-grained human emotions and investigate the patterns of emotional changes from a spatiotemporal perspective. Electrodermal activity (EDA), audio and GPS data were collected from 256 volunteers in the Fanta Oriental Heritage theme park. We developed an integrated framework that combines multimodal emotion recognition, emotional trajectory construction, and pattern mining to examine affective dynamics in a theme park environment. The emotional trajectories were constructed by matching emotional status and GPS. With the support of the hierarchical clustering, the similarities among the emotional trajectories were investigated. Compared with relying solely on single-modal data, our recognition method exhibited significant improvement by fusing EDA and audio, achieving a four-class classification accuracy of more than 0.68. Our results demonstrated that the trajectory model can represent the continuous spatiotemporal changes of minute-by-minute emotional statuses effectively. Further, we have discovered three patterns from emotional trajectories within the theme park. The "Peak-decrease" pattern is sensitive to the exciting experiences and includes most young individuals and females. All tourism projects can stimulate the emotion of individuals belong to the "High-low" pattern significantly. The "Stable-fluctuation" pattern showed the stable emotional dynamic and contained half of the individuals older than 40. This work provides new insights into the fine-grained human emotional changes to enrich the spatiotemporal theories of human emotions, and highlights the potential applications of our findings in urban planning and experience monitoring.
summary: Fusing electrodermal activity, audio and GPS data from 256 theme-park visitors yields minute-by-minute emotional trajectories (four-class accuracy above 0.68) and three emotion patterns—'Peak-decrease', 'High-low' and 'Stable-fluctuation'.

title: Spatial Analysis Approaches and Necessary Policy Interventions in India for Sustainable Cancer Healthcare: A State-of-the-Art Systematic Review
authors: Rahul Dev; Manohar Yadav; Akhil Kapoor
keywords: Cancer; Geographic Information System (GIS); Geospatial; Healthcare; SDG 3.4
abstract: Cancer pose a serious public health issue with more than 1.4 million cases diagnosed annually in India. The country also inhabits the biggest young population globally, whose health and prosperity can definitively impact the progress of United Nations’ (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). As studies have appraised concerns in the achievement of SDG 3.4 by 2030, it is recommended to apply Geographic Information System (GIS) towards disease monitoring, management, prevention and control even by the apex institutions like UN to uncover the complexity of cancer epidemiology vis-à-vis its socio-economic or environmental determinants. This work reviews the state of the art and trends in GIS spatial approaches used for cancer analysis in India, which is absent in the literature yet. Adhering to the PRISMA guidelines, the review found 68 citations in this field of study. While, exposure assessment was found to be the most common approach, there was a lack of studies regarding important topic of cancer screening. Not a single spatial study was found for the head and neck cancer which is highly prevalent in the country. Common challenges in this research field comes out to be data access, human and GIS infrastructure resource constrains and lack of global standard procedure for geocoding. The paper finally discusses several major developments that are crucially required in the field like institutional collaboration, formation of Spatial Interest Groups in GIS, incorporation of clinical utility and outcomes in GIS investigations and data availability and its multi-model integration among others.
summary: Systematically reviews spatial analysis approaches applied to cancer healthcare in India and the policy interventions needed for sustainable cancer care.

title: Urban Green Space and the Transition to Environmental Sustainability in Urban Tourism: An Analytical Review
authors: Raoof Mostafazadeh; Javad Madani; Marzieh Moradi
keywords: Green tourism; Non‑park green spaces; Spatial justice; Sustainable development; Urban green space; Urban tourism
abstract: Urban tourism has experienced rapid growth over recent decades. However, its dual nature is often overlooked: while it stimulates local economies, it simultaneously imposes significant environmental pressures and exacerbates social inequalities. This analytical review examines the transition toward environmental sustainability in urban tourism, focusing on urban green spaces. Using a PRISMA-informed systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar (1993–2025), 24 key sources were selected as the core of the review. Qualitative content analysis was organised around key themes: economic, environmental and socio‑cultural impacts, the sustainability paradox, green tourism and urban ecotourism, climate change adaptation, spatial justice, hierarchy of green spaces and stakeholder perceptions. Urban tourism creates jobs and infrastructure but pressures nature, pollution, congestion, land-use change, and unequal green space access. The sustainability paradox (growth vs. carrying capacity) is acute here. Green tourism and urban ecotourism reduce footprints and boost participation, but face high costs and low awareness. Extreme weather from climate change threatens urban destinations. Non‑park green spaces (roadside strips, community gardens, vacant lots) can, under certain conditions (adequate size, connectivity, formal protection, and community stewardship), reduce inequality, ease tourist pressure, and build climate resilience, but are systematically overlooked. Local resident support is also crucial. The paper calls for integrated action based on spatial justice, community participation, and climate adaptation. Six practical suggestions are proposed: carrying‑capacity‑based planning, equitable resource allocation for NPGS, integration of climate adaptation strategies, local community empowerment, promoting green tourism as a norm, and continuous adaptive monitoring using GIS.
summary: Reviews the role of urban green space in the transition toward environmental sustainability in urban tourism.

title: Spatio-Temporal Coupling Mechanism of Nighttime Vitality in High-Density Cities: A CCM-BiGRU Approach to Transport-Land Use Interaction in Shanghai (2024)
authors: Yuchen Wu; Min'an Yang; Muhai Liang; Yongsheng Qian; Xu Wei
keywords: Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit; Integrated transport network; Nighttime vitality; Shanghai; Spatio-temporal heterogeneity
abstract: Understanding policy-relevant dynamic coupling between nighttime vitality and its drivers is key to evidence-based planning in high-density megacities, particularly amid global efforts to advance sustainable nighttime economies. Existing research lacks targeted quantification and fails to clarify how transport-land use interactions shape nighttime vitality post-public transport curtailment—a gap limiting utility for time-sensitive urban policies. This study focuses on Shanghai’s Inner Ring, using high-resolution mobile signaling data (April 2024), OpenStreetMap (OSM) road networks, and Point of Interest (POI) data to develop a Coupling Coordination Model (CCM)-Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) framework. Key findings: Nighttime vitality shows significant spatial heterogeneity, with high-vitality zones concentrated in commercial areas; transport accessibility has a critical 23:00 threshold, with transport-vitality links extending beyond one-way promotion; transport-land use coupling coordination reflects uneven spatial allocation of nighttime infrastructure.Tailored to Shanghai’s 2024 High-Quality Development Plan for the Nighttime Economy, policy recommendations are: extending metro hours in core commercial districts to fill post-23:00 mobility gaps; upgrading slow traffic facilities (e.g., illuminated walkways) in suburbs to improve nighttime accessibility. This study addresses the gap in dynamic nighttime vitality analysis, delivers actionable policy tools for Chinese megacities, and supports balancing nighttime economic growth with sustainable urban mobility.
summary: Uses a CCM-BiGRU approach to examine how transport–land use interaction shapes the spatio-temporal coupling of nighttime vitality in Shanghai.

title: An Integrated Geovisualization-Driven Spatial Association and Network-Based Multi-Criteria Decision-Making Approach for Urban Fire-Risk Mapping and Mitigation
authors: Atefeh Nasrollahi Aghdam; Bakhtiar Feizizadeh; Sajjad Moshiri; Murat Yakar
keywords: Fire risk mapping; Fire-station accessibility; Geovisualization; GIS spatial analysis; Multi-criteria decision analysis; Uncertainty analysis
abstract: Urban fire-risk management requires both the identification of high-risk areas and an assessment of whether emergency services can reach them efficiently. This study developed an uncertainty-aware GIS-based decision-support framework to map urban fire-risk susceptibility and evaluate the operational performance of fire safety stations (FSS) in Tabriz, Iran. Twelve spatial criteria were weighted using the Analytic Network Process (ANP), and robustness to weight uncertainty was assessed through Monte Carlo simulation and Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA), producing an ANP reference surface and an ANP-GSA sensitivity-adjusted surface. Network-based six-minute service areas were used to evaluate FSS accessibility, while Lee’s local bivariate spatial association, bivariate geovisualization, and local spatial cross-correlation were used to assess spatial consistency with residential and commercial-industrial exposure. Independent event-based validation was performed using ROC/AUC analysis with 60 fire and 60 non-fire/background points. Both models showed strong discrimination, with AUC increasing only marginally from 0.945 for ANP to 0.951 for ANP-GSA. Spatial analyses identified persistent high-risk concentrations in central Tabriz and underserved peripheral and industrial sectors. Overlaying FSS locations further showed that several residential clusters assigned lower relative priority by the ANP-GSA model already coincided with dense station coverage, whereas exposed peripheral and industrial zones remained prominent. The framework therefore provides a transparent basis for uncertainty-aware fire-risk prioritization and targeted FSS planning without overstating the predictive gain from sensitivity-informed reweighting.
summary: Proposes an integrated geovisualization, spatial-association and network-based multi-criteria decision-making approach for mapping and mitigating urban fire risk.

title: Does Social Housing Promote Social Mix? A Systematic Review of Spatial Scales and Housing System Contexts
authors: Juan Yan; Shujie Yang; Xiaoxiao Feng; Tao Wu; Zhiqiang Wu
keywords: Housing system; Social housing; Socio-spatial segregation; Spatial scale; Systematic review
abstract: Social mix has become a prominent objective of contemporary housing policy, yet the international literature offers no consistent answer as to whether social housing actually promotes it. This article addresses that question through a systematic review of 143 English-language studies published between 2000 and 2025. Rather than seeking a simple yes-or-no answer, it examines how findings vary across spatial scales, housing system contexts, and different types of outcomes. The review shows that social mix is not a stable or uniformly defined concept, and that the meaning and effects of social housing vary across institutional settings. Across the reviewed evidence, social housing is most consistently associated with compositional change, including altered residential distribution, greater tenure or social diversity, and, in some contexts, reduced concentrations of disadvantage. Evidence on spatial-structural outcomes is more qualified, while evidence on relational outcomes such as sustained interaction, trust, belonging, or reduced stigma is weaker and more conditional. The article argues that social housing can promote social mix, but only in a limited and uneven sense. Much of the apparent contradiction in the literature reflects differences in spatial scale, housing system context, and outcome type rather than simple empirical disagreement.
summary: Systematically reviews evidence on whether social housing promotes social mix, across spatial scales and housing-system contexts.

title: From Individuals to Industries: Mobile Signal Data Reveals Guangzhou's Offline Market Resilience during the COVID-19 Pandemic
authors: Shan Li; Wanjun Lu; Jintang Chen; Jiarong Zeng; Luyao Yang; Minsheng Li; Fengdeng Wan; Yongheng Feng; Feng Gao
keywords: COVID-19; Individuals-industries; Intra-urban space; Market resilience; Mobile signal data; Space-industry heterogeneity
abstract: Resilience research is a critical component in achieving Sustainable Development Goals, and its importance has become increasingly evident against the backdrop of complex and volatile external shocks. The existing literature predominantly focuses on the resilience of specific regions and industries, while market resilience, which connects the production and consumption sides, receives relatively insufficient attention. The “Wholesale and Retail Industries”, encompassing both corporate manufacturing and individual consumption, constitute a critical window for observing market resilience. Under the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, individual offline visitation can effectively reflect market resilience in specific spaces. Therefore, this study develops an analytical framework based on Mobile Signaling Data to observe market resilience at a fine-grained scale through individual activity. Focusing on Guangzhou, we decode the spatiotemporal patterns of market resilience in the “Wholesale and Retail Industries” under the impact of the COVID-19 shock. Key findings include: (1) The “retail industry” outperforms the “wholesale industry” in both market resistance (− 0.37 vs. −0.41) and market recovery (66% vs. 61%), with “supermarkets” and “shopping centers” showing the highest adaptability. Within the “wholesale industry”, “food and beverages” and “construction materials” are robust. (2) The market resilience of “Wholesale and Retail Industries” exhibits a progressive increase from the urban core to peripheral areas. (3) Government policies, market dynamics, and individual behaviors jointly influence the differentiation of “Wholesale and Retail Industries” market resilience. This study advances a data-driven understanding of market resilience, informing sector-differentiated industrial policies and sustainable revitalization of offline economic ecosystems.
summary: Uses mobile signal data to assess the resilience of Guangzhou's offline markets, from individuals to industries, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Beyond Single Level Explanations: a Spatial Multilevel Regression Approach to Uncovering the Determinants of Urban Running
authors: Qian Wang
keywords: Built environment; Land use mix; Socioeconomic status; Spatial planning; Urban running
abstract: Urban planning and public health policies are increasingly recognizing urban running as a key activity that reflects and shapes the livability and health of cities. Urban running is not merely an individual behavior but a spatially embedded practice influenced by both built environment characteristics and social context. To inform effective spatial planning, it is essential to move beyond single-level explanations and account for the nested social-spatial processes shaping activity patterns. This study introduces a spatial multilevel regression approach that integrates multi-source data to examine urban running across multiple spatial scales. Using running trajectory big data from the Hangzhou central districts, I construct grid level indicators to capture local activity contexts and district level measures to reflect broader structural conditions. The multilevel model explicitly tests cross-scale interactions between built environment features and sociodemographic factors, revealing that urban running patterns emerge from the interplay of local environments and broader social structures. These findings provide actionable insights for planners and policymakers, highlighting areas where interventions can promote equitable, healthy, and sustainable urban environments. More broadly, the study offers a generalizable analytical framework for understanding health-related mobility in rapidly transforming cities, demonstrating the value of moving beyond single-level approaches in spatial analysis and policy design.
summary: Applies a spatial multilevel regression approach to uncover the determinants of urban running.

title: Building a Digital Smart City Index System for Urban Planning and Governance
authors: Zhichang Cai; Guangyu Wu; Ying Li; ChengHe Guan
keywords: Digital algorithms; Digital smart city; Index system; Planning policy; Urban scenario
abstract: Smart city index systems are widely used to guide and evaluate urban digital transformation, yet many remain constrained by static indicators, sectoral silos, and weak ties to real-world governance needs. This paper examines how a smart city index system can be designed to connect data, analytics, institutions, and users to support timely, coordinated, and context-sensitive urban decision-making. We present the Digital Smart City (DISC) Index System, a modular framework developed through a design-oriented, application-based process rooted in municipal digital initiatives in China. The system consists of three interlinked components: a Data Resource System for multi-source integration; a City Algorithm System that generates spatially and temporally grounded indicators; and an Interactive City Dashboard that facilitates scenario-based analysis for different user groups. We demonstrate the system’s application through three cases in mobility, safety, and livability that illustrate how it can organize data flows and decision support in practice. By aligning digital infrastructure with the operational priorities of urban governance, the paper advances a transferable design logic for integrated and responsive smart city planning. We further outline a tiered implementation model, citizen participation mechanisms, and an evaluation agenda through which the DISC design logic can be adapted to lower-resource and institutionally fragmented urban contexts.
summary: Builds a digital smart city index system to support urban planning and governance.

title: All Roads Lead to Rome in Shrinking Cities? Evidence from Northeast China
authors: Xinyu Li; Hao Yuan; Wuxu Tong; Yuanjing Zhang; Guoqiang Shen
keywords: AutoEncoder; DPSIR-SBM framework; Mechanism backbone; SHapley Additive exPlanations; Transition efficiency; Urban shrinkage
abstract: Urban shrinkage threatens fiscal stability, public-service provision, and spatial equity. Existing studies have advanced the understanding of shrinkage drivers, but many still treat these drivers as additive or separately observed factors, leaving limited evidence on recurrent mechanism cores beneath heterogeneous city trajectories. This paper develops a multi-path diagnostic framework for 34 shrinking cities in Northeast China from 2010 to 2021.
