title: Resisting gentrification: Density of belonging in strangled kampung of BSD City, Indonesia
authors: Eka Permanasari; Gita Rama Mahardhika; Muhammad Dimas Prasetya Witono Putra; Melia Dinata
abstract: As Southeast Asia urbanizes, urban expansion repeatedly displaces low-income communities, changes land use, and erodes cultural heritage. In Indonesia, the enclosure of low-income kampung settlements within master-planned private cities was not an organic market outcome but a deliberate product of the Suharto government’s location permit system. This article explores the contradictory pathways of densification through the lens of strangled kampungs, small, irregular settlements trapped within the expansive growth of exclusive, highly regulated private cities. Drawing on historical urban morphological mapping, semi-structured interviews with kampung residents, and field observation across eight strangled kampungs in BSD City, the study analyses four cross-cutting dimensions of this resilience: deliberate cartographic erasure by developers; border-making through enclosing walls, restricted access routes, and engineered flooding; religio-cultural anchoring through mosques, ancestral tombs, and active pilgrimage sites; and adaptive economic practices within the private city itself. The article introduces density of belonging where the concentration of shared memory, emotional attachment, cultural meaning, and religious practice embedded in place function as a critical and underexplored dimension of urban resilience.

title: Predicting U.S. migration flows with online search data
authors: Jaeyong Yoo; Patryk Babiarz
abstract: Residential mobility shapes labor markets, housing demand, infrastructure needs, and regional development in the United States. Policymakers rely on official migration data to monitor population movements, but these data are often released after the underlying moves have occurred. Because many households search online for jobs, housing, cost of living, schools, climate, and other destination-specific information before moving, online search activity may provide early signals of migration interest. This study examines whether Google Trends data improve the prediction of U.S. interstate migration flows. Using Internal Revenue Service state-to-state migration records and Google Trends data for all 50 states and the District of Columbia from 2004 to 2018, the study estimates gravity-based panel models of unilateral out-migration and bilateral origin-destination flows. The results show that migration-related search intensity is associated with subsequent migration flows and improves predictive performance beyond conventional gravity-model covariates and fixed effects. These findings suggest that Google Trends data can serve as a timely complement to administrative migration records. Search data do not replace official statistics, but they can help identify emerging migration patterns before administrative data become available.

title: The politics of calculative tools in practice: Climate budgeting in Edmonton
authors: Taylor Davey
abstract: Climate budgeting aims to integrate carbon accounting into municipal financial budgeting, promising to align annual spending decisions with long-term emissions targets. Yet limited attention has been given to how this calculative framework operates within existing administrative practices and contested political contexts. This article examines the City of Edmonton’s 2022 Carbon Budget, the first municipal climate budget implemented in North America. Drawing on interviews, policy documents, and observations of public budget deliberations, it traces how carbon metrics were developed, applied to budget profiles, and interpreted by administrators and councillors. The analysis finds that efforts to translate climate impacts into conventional fiscal formats encountered substantial methodological limits. Most investments could not be quantified, indirect and longer-term effects remained excluded, and aggregated results suggested proposed climate investments would have little effect on Edmonton’s emissions pathway. Rather than increasing transparency or building consensus, the project intensified disagreements over municipal responsibilities, public support, and the justification of climate spending. Comparison with Oslo demonstrates that climate budgeting’s effects may depend less on technical design than on the political authority, administrative capacity, and institutional relationships within which it operates. Climate budgeting should be understood not as a transferable accounting solution, but as a situated deliberative framework that makes some climate impacts visible while reorganizing, rather than resolving, political contestation.

title: Winning the double war: Urbicide, informality, and reconstruction in Syrian cities after 2011
authors: Munqeth Othman Agha
abstract: Syrian cities experienced extensive destruction during the 2011–2024 conflict, much of it inflicted by the Assad regime. Yet destruction did not end with the cessation of local hostilities; it persisted in formerly opposition-controlled enclaves through organized looting and mass municipal demolitions. This article asks why destruction was disproportionately concentrated in informal and formerly opposition-controlled areas, and especially at their intersection. It argues that these patterns were intentional, serving the regime’s double war: a military war to defeat the armed opposition, and an urban-economic war to incorporate undesirable urban forms into real-estate accumulation. Combining spatial autocorrelation analysis with Bayesian negative binomial and penalized logistic models across Damascus, Aleppo, and Homs, the study shows that destruction was spatially structured, concentrating where informality and opposition-control intersect, which jointly predict destruction beyond military necessity. This logic persisted across wartime, post-capture, and post-conflict periods. Urbicide thus operates as a dual-purpose modality for authoritarian urbanism: a wartime tactic and a mechanism of post-conflict socioeconomic reordering.

title: Commute duration, out-of-home discretionary activities and social inclusion as a multifaceted experience: Evidence from Beijing
authors: Sui Tao; Jing Ma
abstract: The current study seeks to contribute to the understanding of the importance of commute duration in shaping social inclusion at the individual level. Focusing on Beijing, China, a series of analyses has been carried out to probe the inter-relationships among commute duration, discretionary activities, and perceived social inclusion as a multifaceted experience. Empirical findings indicate that prolonged commutes can directly and indirectly compromise one’s social inclusion experience due to both their isolating effect and the constraints exerted on out-of-home discretionary activities. The probability and time use of discretionary activity participation also exert varied impacts on the different dimensions of social inclusion. Particularly, more time spent on recreational and physical activities is associated with enhanced social support and a stronger sense of belonging, respectively. These findings suggest the importance of planning strategies that strive for local job-housing balance. Moreover, it is recommended that higher priorities be placed on certain public facilities (e.g. recreational and sports facilities) in establishing X-minute communities. Making better use of micro public space and promoting transit accessibility should also be considered in urban policies aimed at increasing social inclusiveness.

title: Towards a neurodiverse planning theory and practice
authors: Mohammad Sarraf; Sonya Girdler; Sven Bölte
abstract: Since the emergence of the neurodiversity movement a few decades ago and its emphasis on neurocognitive differences rather than ‘deficits’, the impact of the living environment on the everyday lives of neurodivergent individuals has been central to the community’s pursuit of inclusion and participation. The built environment, as the physical setting in which these experiences unfold, is therefore of particular relevance to these pursuits. As such, urban planning, alongside related disciplines concerned with the material and spatial organisation of the built environment, has an important role to play in advancing this agenda. Despite this, urban planning theory and practice have largely failed to engage with neurodiversity and its call for the recognition of difference within shared urban environments. Drawing on scholarship on the urban politics of difference, this commentary calls for the integration of neurodiversity into urban planning theory and practice, initiating a debate for a neurodiverse planning theory and practice with the aim of informing future theoretical development and empirical research.

title: A bench is just a bench: A spatial justice analysis of older adults’ needs based on municipal hotline data
authors: Rinat Ben Noon; Liat Ayalon
abstract: Population ageing and the expansion of age-friendly cities have increased attention to the built environment, yet small-scale infrastructure remains underexamined. This study frames the equitable distribution of public benches as an issue of spatial justice and investigates how benches may support older adults’ autonomy, mobility, and social connection. We analysed 855 requests concerning benches submitted to municipal call centres in three large Israeli cities and conducted an in-depth thematic analysis of 108 requests that explicitly concerned older adults. Requests frequently identified the immediate area outside the home as a critical location for seating. The findings support a refinement of the Life-Space Mobility framework by conceptualising the home-threshold belt as a link between private and community space. They also indicate that benches may reduce the effort associated with walking and provide opportunities for passive and active social engagement. The absence of seating near homes or along walking routes may restrict life-space mobility. We, therefore, propose bench continuity as a planning principle for age-friendly cities: connected, visible, and appropriately spaced seating that enables older adults to remain present in the public realm.

title: Informal elite urbanism and Pentecostal city-making: Rethinking ‘religious gentrification’ in Lagos (Nigeria)
authors: David Garbin; Taibat Lawanson; Gareth Millington
abstract: This article examines the transformation of Onike, a central Lagos neighbourhood, through the presence and expansion of the Pentecostal mega-church Mountain of Fire and Miracles Ministries (MFM). The paper engages with the concept of ‘religious gentrification’ to describe how MFM religious actors, operating as ‘informal elites’, reshape urban space through moral authority, political patronage and selective compliance with planning regulations. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork and interviews with local residents and urban stakeholders, the study traces how MFM’s territorial and moral projects reconfigure local space and affect everyday life in a context of (relative) religious plurality. By connecting theorisations of informal urbanism with debates on gentrification and religious urbanisation, the paper suggests that Pentecostal city-making in Lagos is both spiritual and entrepreneurial, producing new moralised urban orders without necessarily transforming entrenched urban inequalities. The article contributes to global urban theory by showing how non-state religious elites drive urban change in the Global South through hybrid moral–economic logics. It argues for a rethinking of urban informality and elite power beyond secular and neoliberal paradigms, situating African Pentecostal urbanism within wider debates on governance, spatial inequality and the moral politics of urban transformation.

title: Towards inclusive age-friendly communities: A scoping review of diversity and representation in global initiatives
authors: Fatima Salomoni; Preetha Joseph; Kieran Walsh; Matthias Drilling
abstract: While calls for meaningful inclusion of diverse and socially excluded older populations in age-friendly urban planning initiatives have increased, little is known about how these groups are actually involved in shaping such programmes, and what mechanisms are effective in enabling their inclusion. The aim of this article is to present the findings of a scoping review on how effectively age-friendly urban planning includes socially excluded older populations, including the key strategies employed and the challenges and enablers encountered. Searches yielded 10,857 records, and, together with grey literature screening, resulted in Eight studies meeting the inclusion criteria. The review documents a range of participatory approaches, such as co-design workshops, graphic facilitation, advisory panels, peer research and intergenerational collaboration, that aim to involve older adults in meaningful ways. These approaches target promoting trust and empowerment and offer more equitable representation in age-friendly planning. However, despite promising practices, most efforts were limited in scale, short-term in nature and lacked integration into decision-making systems. These initiatives point to the potential of inclusive planning, but with current impacts remaining uneven and limited. We call for more sustained and embedded forms of participation that support rethinking how inclusion is defined, operationalised and structurally supported in age-friendly planning processes.

title: Embedding urban food policies into commons thinking: A framework analysis of policies and initiatives
authors: Cinzia Tegoni; Elisa Carloni; Gianluca Di Fiore; Matteo Brambilla; Claudia Giordano
abstract: Cities have been at the forefront of transforming the urban food system to address the pressing challenge of providing “good food for all.” In light of the ongoing global urbanization trends, which continue despite major global disruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic, and the progressive dismantling of policy frameworks supporting sustainable food systems in favor of competitiveness-driven agendas, urban food policies (UFPs) represent increasingly relevant governance tools for promoting sustainability-oriented transformations. UFPs are frequently described as a collective and equitable approach to food system governance that could align with principles of common-pool resource management. However, systematic and empirical assessments of whether UFPs’ institutional arrangements actually reflect commons governance remain limited. This study addresses this gap by analyzing 17 UFPs through the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework, assessing the degree to which they create conditions for commons-oriented governance. Results show substantial variation, with only a minority of the analyzed UFPs demonstrating institutional arrangements substantially aligned with commons principles, while most exhibit either centralized municipal control or hybrid arrangements where participation remains consultative rather than transformative.

title: Naming an industry as heritage: Industrial retention and commercial rents in Seongsu, South Korea
authors: Minju Kim; Jung-Eun Lee; Seul Lee; Kang-Bok Lee; Yunmi Park
abstract: In industrial neighborhoods that survive into a city’s expansion phase, a weakened production base and a rising land market are present at the same time. Regeneration plans for such places increasingly name that base as local heritage and commit to retaining it, and evidence on what those commitments deliver, and to whom, remains limited. This study investigates an urban regeneration project in the Seongsu of Seoul, South Korea, which identified the neighborhood’s existing leather and shoemaking industry as an asset to be preserved. Commercial rents from 2014 to 2019 are analyzed using difference-in-differences models, with a supplementary analysis of business entry and establishment counts. The findings revealed a statistically significant positive effect on commercial rents across all business sectors, with the most pronounced effect for the leather and shoemaking industry, which sustained higher entry rates and recorded net growth in establishment counts in treatment areas. Its rents did not follow the prevailing visibility and land value gradients, which points to activity still organized around production. While the results imply that the balance falls toward retention, case studies from the same period leave open the possibility that retention could be the form that displacement takes. As urban expansion continues to reach post-industrial districts, Seongsu is instructive for what made retention possible. For planners who seek to preserve the industrial base, the case points to the need to align the occupants a plan aims to reach with those its instruments protect.

title: Renters, mortgagors and landowners. Social composition and the political economy of urban land supply in Spain
authors: José María Tubío-Sánchez; Santiago Lago-Peñas; Patricio Sanchez-Fernandez
abstract: This article examines how land supply is affected by differing resident interests in urban development. The Spanish housing bubble (1999–2007) offers a relevant context for this study. With the massive influx of credit into the housing sector, it is likely that these conflicting interests intensified, influencing local planning decisions. Drawing on the homevoter and growth machine hypotheses, we explore how resident composition (from renters in urban areas to landowners in rural ones) affects land supply dynamics, with particular focus on mortgagors who predominantly moved into suburban areas during this period. As significant investors in housing, mortgagors are likely more concerned with land planning decisions that might affect their primary investment. Using data from the Spanish housing bubble period, we show that mortgaged housing is negatively associated with land supply expansion, while the percentage of landowners correlates positively with increased land availability. The electoral effects of these land supply decisions vary: a 10% increase in mortgaged housing decreases the incumbent party’s vote share by 0.76 percentage points, whereas a 10% increase in landowners results in a 0.12 percentage point increase in the vote share. Furthermore, municipalities with higher proportions of mortgaged housing and greater increases in property values tend to experience more negative electoral consequences from land supply expansion, whereas areas with a larger amount of landowners and lower increases in property value show the opposite trend.

title: Finding a ‘place’ in public food matters: Gendered urban food initiatives shaping women’s right to the city
authors: Chiara Bergonzini
abstract: This article investigates the potential of urban food initiatives in providing an opportunity for the advancement of women’s right to the city. It does so by retracing the historically rooted patriarchal division of care labour, which includes the so-called ‘foodwork’, that has long confined women to peripheries and private spaces by tying their ‘place’ in cities and societies to private care practices. Yet, in recent years food matters have ‘gone public’ and become recognised as urban issues that should be tackled collectively in a public way. Through interviews with three alternative food networks in Milan, this article shows that the feminisation of care and foodwork has not been disrupted when these matters have become considered as public and collective urban issues. Still, the persistence of these gendered roles in some cases provides women with a chance to advance their right to the city, by facilitating appropriation of urban space and participation in decision-making through urban food initiatives. The article discusses the tensions between the opportunity to ‘find a place’ in public food matters for women facing social fragility and the persistence of patriarchal understandings of gender roles that grant such place.

title: Transit-oriented built environment, accessibility and the intra-urban geography of innovation in Hong Kong
authors: Yuting Hou; Xiaohang Ruan; Yuk Tai Lau; Sylvia Y. He
abstract: This study examines the relationship between transit-oriented development (TOD) and innovation outcomes at the intra-urban scale, using Hong Kong as an example. Patent data are applied to measure the level of innovation activities at the neighbourhood scale and further differentiated into high-tech/medium-to-high-tech manufacturing, knowledge-intensive service and other traditional sectors. Both a zero-inflated negative binomial regression and a spatial econometric framework are applied to explore the innovation impacts of rail-based transit accessibility and a full set of transit-orient built environment features, while accounting for the potential endogeneity of transit accessibility using an instrumental variable approach. The results indicate that neighbourhoods with higher rail-based transit network accessibility measured at the regional scale are observed with higher innovation outputs of all sectors except the traditional sectors. Local intensity of science and technology infrastructure and other TOD built environment features, including higher density in manufacturing sector, mixed land use development, better street connectivity and local access to cooked food centres, are associated with higher neighbourhood innovation outputs of all sectors. The results provide useful suggestions on future transport and land use planning in Hong Kong to improve the spatial allocation of resources, service and amenities in the context of TOD to facilitate the city’ transformation into an innovation hub.

title: Schooling as urban asset: Education, capital and governance in entrepreneurial Chinese city
authors: Zhenjie Yuan; Yulin Xie; Junwanguo Guo; Xinhui Wu
abstract: This paper examines how schooling is being reconstituted as a strategic urban asset in contemporary China. Moving beyond its conventional role as a public good, elite education is increasingly mobilised within a model of education-led entrepreneurial governance. Drawing on an in-depth case study of a public–private school partnership in a peripheral Chinese city, the paper develops an analytical framework at the intersection of educational neoliberalism, entrepreneurial urbanism and the geographies of urban infrastructure, centred on the strategic coupling of three actors: elite educational institutions possessing mobile brand capital, real estate developers seeking symbolic anchors for value creation, and a local state acting as critical facilitator, operating through mobility, hybrid partnership and institutional mediation. The analysis shows how the symbolic capital of schooling is assembled with private investment and state coordination, and converted into property premiums and social-symbolic legitimacy for the project, while political-regulatory legitimacy remains a state monopoly the developer can neither produce nor purchase; the two are hierarchically ordered, and the alliance generates new forms of socio-spatial inequality. We conceptualise this process as the assetisation of schooling, in which value rests on the capitalisation of expected future advantage rather than direct sale. The study draws on polymorphous statehood to show how state entrepreneurialism in peripheral contexts operates through delegated coordination and policy ambiguity, and how such alliances remain inherently fragile, advancing a relational account of how public goods are reworked into value-bearing urban assets and offering a critical lens on urban governance in China and beyond.

title: ParAge: A pilot study using participatory methods to assess outdoor environmental fall risks in older adults
authors: Antoine Langeard; Adéla Kola; Evrim Gökçe; Emma Milot; Valentine Erne-Heintz; Zakaria N. Doueiri; Abby C. King
abstract: Population aging and urbanization have made age-friendly urban design a global priority. While the WHO’s Age-Friendly Cities and Communities framework identifies outdoor spaces as a critical domain, fall prevention remains under-addressed. Falls are a leading cause of injury and loss of autonomy, with approximately 73% of outdoor falls triggered by modifiable environmental factors. This study developed and evaluated a participatory, geolocated method based on the Our Voice citizen science framework to identify environmental fall risks and generate consensus-based solutions. Twenty-eight participants engaged in a workshop, using a mobile app to record 314 geotagged environmental features during diagnostic walks. These data were then reviewed in facilitated sessions where participants co-analyzed findings and rated potential solutions. The research specifically examined whether outputs diverged based on participant profiles, such as age, fall history, or fear of falling. Results highlighted seven categories of risk factors, most frequently involving poor surface conditions, lack of maintenance, and obstacles. Notably, participants with a history of falls or a greater fear of falling reported different risks, suggesting varied perceptions of the urban environment. However, no significant differences were observed in proposed solutions, such as infrastructure maintenance and improved signage, indicating a strong consensus on feasible interventions. Qualitative feedback confirmed the method’s acceptability and feasibility, praising its inclusive, field-based nature. This participatory approach complements existing walkability indices by capturing overlooked hazards. By integrating diverse lived experiences into environmental assessments, this method can contribute to safer pedestrian mobility and the development of truly inclusive cities for all ages.

title: Neo-royal urbanisms: Royal agency in contemporary city building in Southeast Asia
authors: Jane M. Jacobs; Ofita Purwani
abstract: Monarchies in Southeast Asia are neither residual nor archaic institutions. This editorial introduction to the special issue argues that royal entities in the region – across Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia and Thailand – remain adaptive and active forces that shape contemporary urbanisation in significant ways. Drawing on a critical comparative framework, it introduces the concept of neo-royal urbanisms to describe how royal institutions routinely use urban development to realise and express power, while non-royal interests in turn leverage royal endorsement to secure development objectives. The article situates Southeast Asian monarchies within a broader global resurgence of personalistic, quasi-royal political authority, arguing that the region offers a distinctive and theoretically generative vantage point from which to examine these trends. The article also addresses the methodological challenges of researching élite royal power, including restricted access, explicit and implicit censorship and the opacity of networks that blur royal, commercial and military interests. It argues that the built environment itself constitutes a critical field of evidence for tracing royal agency. Together, the articles in this special issue demonstrate that the city is not merely a backdrop to neo-royalism but the primary medium through which symbolic, political and economic royal power is assembled and contested.

title: ‘Going out’ and ‘going on’: Teleology, polyphony and temporal encounters of a Chinese plantation in Tanzania
authors: Wen Lei
abstract: While China’s overseas engagements are frequently scrutinised as spatial enclaves, their temporal constitution remains largely unexamined. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork at a Chinese state-owned sisal plantation in Tanzania, this article identifies a fundamental disjuncture: what I term ‘teleological going out’, the state’s mandate as a teleological projection towards distant futures, collides with ‘polyphonic going on’, the everyday unfolding of divergent lived temporalities. Through dual perspectives examining state temporal governmentality from above and lived experiences from below, the article reveals how this tension permeates the enclave both internally, where state timelines collide with lived temporalities, and externally, at its interface with local communities, generating moments of friction and alignment. Rather than a static container, the enclave emerges as a dynamic site where ‘polyphonic going on’ continuously renegotiates ‘teleological going out’.

title: Planning for place-based circularity in mid-sized industrial cities: Accommodating industrial-scale and vernacular food waste trajectories
authors: Nicole Cook; Elyse Stanes; Chris Gibson; Gordon Waitt; Tim Wall; Sam Quirk; Elloise Ames; Anna Smith; Kaitlyn Rankin; Jessica Holland
abstract: There is growing recognition of the tension between industrial/top-down and vernacular/bottom-up circular economies, as well as the need for place-based approaches to sustainable transitions policy. Yet how to reconcile place-based policy with divergent forms of circularity remains unclear. Rather than viewing such tensions as requiring resolution, we examine the place-based conditions under which industrial-scale and vernacular food waste trajectories can productively coexist, and the conditions under which they cannot. Mid-sized industrial cities (MSICs) are a favourable setting for coexisting forms of place-based circularity, yet they are often overlooked in circular economy research, despite being tasked with managing the heavy, polluting, and industrial metabolic functions upon which larger metropolitan regions depend. Drawing upon longitudinal research over a 15-year period in an exemplary MSIC – Wollongong, NSW, Australia – this article develops a framework of intersecting circularities foregrounding the co-constitution of place-based circularity and city context. Applying this framework reveals the sociomaterial qualities of circularities, the spatial reconfigurations that enable them, and the co-presence of industrial, top-down and smaller-scale vernacular approaches. From multiple qualitative research projects, we outline three drivers of place-based circularity: diverse and flexible land-use planning and zoning; logistical infrastructures that support proximity of actors; and innovative and resourced consumer engagement with food waste’s visceralities. We argue that MSICs offer distinctive sociomaterialities for hybrid circularities, that are not captured by centralised governance and planning models, nor grassroots sufficiency. Realising the potential for place-based approaches in MSICs demands acknowledgement of the regulatory, material and cultural pre-conditions that make circularity possible.

title: The state as democratic growth coalition: Embeddedness within state planning
authors: Kevin Keenan
abstract: This paper answers the following questions: How does the state itself offer embeddedness for a growth coalition, and where exactly does the coalition locate and embed within the state? To answer this question, the author draws on insider experience leading the impact assessment of a state plan in the USA. Through this position, the author had unprecedented access to the highest levels of state government as the state updated its state plan, which had not been done in more than two decades. The investigator positions this access as qualitative data to form a case study, including observations of a variety of policymakers and other actors at the highest levels of state planning. By applying urban geography literature on growth coalitions within a Deleuzian framework of entwined capitalist expansion, I analyze the data to offer three advances. First, while growth coalitions have been theorized at the local level and at the regional level, they have not been theorized as completely embedded within the state itself. This paper reveals that government workers themselves can be the coalition—often clandestinely and without any of the actors commonly theorized present. Second, theory is needed to understand the interface of multiple growth coalitions operating at different scales as well as how government serves as the space where they sometimes meet, and third, that state growth coalitions have the power to dramatically influence local planning, despite what planners’ professional training may require and the existence of local coalitions.

title: Confronting housing and health inequities: Wanted—critical transdisciplinary inquiry
authors: Roderick J. Lawrence
abstract: This critical commentary requests creative, critical, and inclusive dialogue about the persistence of inequitable housing and health inequalities. It complements numerous publications in housing and urban studies about environmental, ethnic, socio-economic, and residential inequalities in an era of growing neoliberal politics and policies that influence housing and health inequities. The main aim is to propose conceptual and methodological reforms in housing and urban studies. I posit that critical transdisciplinary inquiry enables innovative contributions to bridge the gap between persistent housing and health inequities and ineffective responses to them. Critical transdisciplinary inquiry includes ethical and moral values that acknowledge and confront housing and health inequities worldwide. The common actor/institutional framework used by academic researchers in housing and urban studies that devalues dominant power imbalances of private investors and property owners in housing markets is contested; the authority of local and national governing institutions to support alternative approaches is revalued. Given the ineffectiveness of private enterprises and public authorities in reducing housing and health inequities since the 1980s, community consortia should be supported to mainstream cooperative housing and expand their effective responses. Lessons from 19th-century housing and urban history, and coordinated responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, support this way forward.

title:
Cities
                    of care? Towards more ‘scalar-attuned’ perspectives in urban care research
authors: Krisztina Varró; Bárbara Oliveira Soares
abstract: The expanding scholarship on ‘caring’ or ‘care-full’ cities has usefully reconceptualised cities as spaces of care and, by exposing real-world local initiatives, compellingly argued in favour centring care in urban governance and planning. Arguably, however, the insufficiently nuanced understanding and use of the concept of scale has weakened the analytical grip of this body of work on how and which practices and relations of care emerge, with which impact and for whom. Relatedly, the subtle but persisting tendency to foreground the urban as the primary site of caring has undercut the possibility to problematise and repoliticise care as a multiscalar field of praxis and intervention. This intervention develops a sympathetic critique of research on urban care, calling for more ‘scalar-attuned’ perspectives that explicitly and reflexively engage with the concept of scale. To illustrate the relevance of our argument, we call for the (re)insertion of the national scale into scholarship on urban caring and highlight three intertwined modalities in which the national co-constitutes care in the city. We do so not to demand top-down state intervention to care, but to invite scholars working on urban caring to consider, discuss and contest the full spectrum of scales-as-relations that constitute the practices and politics of (un)caring.

title: Neighbourhood linguistic accessibility for older people in Singapore: Spatial mismatch and linguistic gentrification
authors: Xinyi Wang; Gaoyuan Wang; Zhuoxu Qi
abstract: Linguistic accessibility, the availability of services and information in languages familiar to residents, remains largely absent from environmental gerontology and age-friendly city assessment frameworks, despite its growing significance for older adults in multilingual cities undergoing rapid language policy transitions. This study develops a framework of neighbourhood linguistic accessibility for older people and applies it to 10 planning areas with high older-adult concentrations in Singapore. Using 3922 points of interest and 31,275 online reviews collected from Google Maps, it constructs dual supply-side (D1) and demand-side (D2) linguistic diversity indices, refined through sentiment analysis to better reflect the linguistic experiences of everyday service use, and analysed through spatial clustering to identify distributional patterns across the urban environment. The results reveal a systematic spatial mismatch: linguistic diversity hotspots concentrate in the Central Business District, while mature estates where more than 25% of residents are aged 65 and above display no comparable linguistic accessibility. Within Singapore’s planning structure, which designates town centres as mixed-use daily service hubs for older residents, linguistic accessibility varies markedly, with only a minority showing meaningful multilingual diversity. These mismatches suggest two mechanisms of linguistic gentrification: globalisation-driven concentration of multilingual environments, and community-renewal-driven displacement of historically inclusive spaces. Identifying four spatial configurations and four differentiated policy categories, the study challenges the assumption that signage diversity equates to accessibility and calls for embedding language–competence alignment within age-friendly assessment frameworks, offering a transferable approach to achieving linguistic equity in multilingual urban governance.

title: From fragmentation to coordination? Governing urban heat risks in Greater Sydney
authors: Nicky Morrison; Vanita Yadav; Judith Bruinsma; Kelly Gee; Patrick Harris
abstract: Climate-related events such as heatwaves and their impacts on health and wellbeing pose an increasing threat to the future livability of cities. However, in Australia, governance for heat risk management remains less developed than for other climate-related hazards, such as bushfires and floods, and is characterised by fragmented institutional arrangements. This paper examines the formation of the Greater Sydney Heat Taskforce and the co-design of Greater Sydney’s inaugural Heat Smart City Plan as a case through which to interrogate broader challenges in urban climate governance. Drawing on a participatory action research approach, the study analyses how multi-stakeholder governance arrangements emerge in contexts with limited legislative mandate, and how coordination, legitimacy, and shared ownership are constructed across diverse actors. The findings show that while the Taskforce generated progress—improving cross-sectoral understanding, clarifying roles, and building collaborative momentum—significant challenges remain. In particular, unresolved issues relating to resourcing, institutional capacity, and the evolving clarification of governance responsibilities continue to constrain implementation. The paper argues that governance for emerging risks such as extreme heat is shaped not only by formal institutional frameworks, but also by processes of co-design, negotiation, and knowledge co-production, which both enable coordination and challenge existing institutional capabilities. These insights have broader relevance for cities developing coordinated responses to complex climate risks.

title: Urban development as a polyrhythmic project: Reimagining multiple urban futures in the era of slow growth
authors: Shenjing He; Qiong He; Bin Jiang; Rui Ji; Peng Gong
abstract: Temporal imagination of urban transformation in Asian cities is predominantly occupied with spectacular rapidity and high density. This singular representation neglects its messy but generative polyrhythmic assembling process and how previous patterns and recurring growth shape imaginations of multiple futures, which inhibits appreciation of the emerging slow growth. This paper employs a rhythmanalytical lens—particularly its repetition-with-difference and polyrhythmic elements—with a focus on density/densification, to examine the shifting development paradigms in Rushan, a small coastal Chinese city struggling to reconfigure its polyrhythms in the slow-growth era. Rushan once witnessed annual repetition of urban growth through selective housing densification capitalising on trans-local investors’ desire for lower-density coastal living, driven by the housing capital rhythm and a pro-growth coalition. Shrinking housing demand and national strategies promoting compact development, however, ushered in a (different) slow-growth period. The rhythms of seasonal investor-residents and tourists, and the transient density they entailed, became key sites for accumulation. Yet their seasonal and fragmented urban engagement produced incomplete and slow(er) development. Two contested futures emerged polyrhythmically: one seeking to fix the slowness through resuscitating housing capital, the other embracing it and the associated transient density, alongside new manufacturing industries’ remedial temporalities of consistency and stability. In so doing, we extend rhythmanalysis beyond repetition, patterning, and everydayness to emphasise difference, impermanence, and emergence, unravelling its co-constitutive relationship with the density-making process. We also call for foregrounding a polyrhythmic logic in dissecting post-growth urban development and re/imagining urban futures through heterogeneous spatio-temporal modality and innovative polyrhythmic reassembling in China and across Asian cities.

title: Thinking beyond from within the urban PhD
authors: Horizons 2024 Collective; Anwyn Hocking; Tanya Burdett; Ricardo Camacho; Lu Rita Yan; Ana Luiza S. de Sá; Belinda Davis; Anh Van Rosie Pham; Imogen Howe; Amal Alghazo; Jasjit Singh Banga; Ravi Bhushan; Anna Louise Durkin; Abdullah Evan; Bethany Kiss; Damilola Olalekan; Sara Pishgahi; Ngoc Thao Linh Dang; Alexei Trundle; Ash Alam
abstract: This commentary offers reflections and provocations on some of the contradictions we have encountered between our urban research and universities as an interdisciplinary and international group of doctoral students. Based within universities across Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung and Bunurong lands in Melbourne, Australia, these reflections emerge from a settler colonial context in a moment of rising far-right white nationalism and militarism. In drawing on the well-established debates of the possibilities of the university as a site of liberation, we consider our own experiences as PhD students to identify three frictions between our orientation to care-fully just urban futures and the colonial-neoliberal university. In so doing, we join a growing dialogue of critical reflection between international urban early-career researchers.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
GOVERNING OR MANIPULATING LEVERAGE TO BUILD MORE CITIES?
                    Borrowing in the Shadows by Local Governments and Real Estate Developers in China
authors: Ang Liu
abstract: Amid growing interest in how states manage urban development through public finance, this article examines the institutional logics of leverage manipulation as a mode of contemporary urban governance. Focusing on China's evolving political economy, it investigates how local governments and real estate developers co‐produce a shadow financial architecture that enables continued investment and (hidden) debt‐driven urbanization. Mechanisms such as off‐balance‐sheet borrowing through Local Government Financing Vehicles (LGFVs), on‐balance‐sheet hidden debt structures like fake equity used by developers, and informal regulatory signaling (e.g. window guidance) are not peripheral irregularities, but routinized tools embedded within a broader regime of state entrepreneurialism. This article asks how China sustains urban development through hidden and quasi‐fiscal borrowing despite formal regulatory constraints. It argues that urban financial governance operates through pragmatic, state‐led discretion, with regulations and financial instruments deployed flexibly to accommodate shifting policy priorities. Financial innovation becomes a routine instrument of governance, allowing the state to move between public and private roles while managing urban development across blurred lines of formal and informal authority. These findings show that hidden borrowing has become part of urban governance as state‐led development increasingly relies on blurred boundaries between public authority and financial practice.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
TWO CONCEPTS OF POLARIZATION
                    : Urban–National Tension and its Effects on the Liberal Trajectory of Cities
authors: Harel Nachmany; Tal Alster; Nufar Avni
abstract: This study examines how urban–national polarization shapes how progressive cities exercise local autonomy. It introduces a new framework for assessing polarization within specific policy domains, distinguishing between ideological and pragmatic polarization. The analysis focuses on five liberal‐oriented policy domains: gender equality, environmental sustainability, LGBTQ+ rights, immigration, and religion–state relations through the case of Tel Aviv–Jaffa, Israel. For each domain, it evaluates both the degree of polarization between central and local governments and the municipal strategies and mechanisms used for policy implementation. The research findings indicate that higher levels of urban–national polarization are associated with fragmented organizational structures, symbolic or tactical policymaking, and strong fiscal independence, whereas lower levels correspond to comprehensive strategic planning and institutional stability. These patterns, we suggest, affect the legitimacy, sustainability, and accountability of liberal autonomous local policies. As urban–national polarization intensifies worldwide, these insights contribute to broader theoretical debates on local autonomy, municipal activism, and urban progressivism.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
LIVING ARCHIVES
                    : Tracing
                    Territorio–Cuerpo–Tierra
                    and
                    Re‐existencia
                    in Moravia, Medellín
authors: Catalina Ortiz; Natalia Villamizar Duarte
abstract: Territorio–cuerpo–tierra has emerged in Latin American decolonial feminist scholarship as an ontological, epistemic, and political formulation grounded in struggles against violence, extraction, and dispossession. Yet its development has remained largely outside urban debates, despite cities increasingly concentrating displacement, environmental degradation, and contested forms of belonging. Drawing on collaborative research in Moravia, Medellín, this article examines how territorio–cuerpo–tierra is enacted in urban contexts through practices of re‐existencia that sustain collective life amid dispossessions. We approach living archives as a methodological orientation emerging through co‐created practices around tenure insecurity, migration, and ecological harm. Mobilizing decolonial feminist debates alongside community‐based urban epistemologies, we argue that living archives trace and sustain forms of territorial reclamation through practices such as staying put, homing, and ecological repair. Living archives operate as situated and relational processes through which communities maintain belonging and defend urban life.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
PUTTING SOCIAL FINANCE IN PLACE
                    : Geographies and Strategies of Philanthropic Impact Investment in Housing
authors: Yinnon Geva; Matti Siemiatycki
abstract: This article examines the rise of impact investment in social housing in an age of entrenched financialization and enduring public underinvestment through the case of philanthropic investors in Southern Ontario, Canada. Social finance scholarship has highlighted tensions between financial and social returns, while overlooking the role of place embeddedness in mediating investing practices as identified in critical studies of property development. The study draws on a dataset of philanthropic impact investment portfolios and 16 stakeholder interviews, focusing on community foundations, which have local granting and investment mandates. We argue that community foundations operate as distinctive place‐based investors who challenge the financialized logics of impact investment. Their localized mandates produce alternative spatial and financial strategies: downscaling investment to match local organizational capacities, mobilizing regional and local philanthropic networks to field and de‐risk deals, and deploying patient, flexible capital in early‐stage development and acquisition. These practices generate social value by repositioning risk and strengthening non‐profit actors’ capacity to compete in real estate markets. The findings demonstrate the potential of place‐based investment to negotiate the prevailing alignment of risk, return, and impact underpinning housing assetization.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
GOVERNING INFORMALITY
                    : Eviction, Recognition, and Legal Ambiguity in Kampung Akuarium, Jakarta
authors: EKA PERMANASARI; DIAN NOSTIKASARI; AMAL BARRE
abstract: Informal settlements in Jakarta have long been governed through cycles of tolerance, eviction, and selective recognition. Rather than resulting from the absence of planning, informality is often produced through spatial regulations, legal ambiguity, and political intervention. This article examines Kampung Akuarium, a settlement in North Jakarta, to explore how informality is governed through planning instruments and political change. The study combines an overlay analysis of Jakarta's spatial planning documents from 2005, 2014, and 2022 with satellite imagery and a review of news media and policy archives. The findings trace how Kampung Akuarium was alternately erased from planning maps, criminalized through redevelopment agendas, and later partially recognized through state intervention. Eviction under the Basuki Purnama administration functioned as a political assertion of legality rather than a resolution of land‐use conflict. The subsequent shift toward in‐situ redevelopment under the Anies Baswedan administration reconfigured informality into a negotiated condition. Spatial planning documents played a central role in institutionalizing legal ambiguity, enabling flexible governance while sustaining residents’ precarity. The article argues that conflicts over informal settlements are central to remaking urban citizenship, exposing colonial and postcolonial logics of dispossession while opening spaces to renegotiate tenure, design, and belonging through fragile, contested forms of co‐production.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
THE URBANISM OF EXCEPTION
                    : Scalar Rivalry and Political Loyalty in the Making of the Panorama Tbilisi Megaproject
authors: David Gogishvili
abstract: In flawed democracies, such as the Republic of Georgia, legal exceptions for urban megaprojects are becoming a standard mode of governance. While frequently analyzed as singular, top‐down sovereign acts, I argue that the imposition of such exceptions is a complex and dispersed process. Drawing on the case of the Panorama Tbilisi megaproject introduced in 2014 in Tbilisi, Georgia, this article reconceptualizes the urbanism of exception as a governance strategy engineered through intergovernmental rivalry and institutionalized political loyalty. Through a qualitative analysis, I show how rivalry between national and local governments controlled by opposing political parties led to the strategic rewriting of national law to bypass local opposition. Furthermore, I demonstrate how political loyalty functions as a governance tool, blurring public‐private boundaries and ultimately culminating in the promotion of project executives to high‐level state positions. The article contributes to critical urban theory by revealing the contested nature of state power in megaproject implementation and proposes the concept of the commodification of exception: the centralization of the right to bypass rules as a tradable asset available exclusively to political and economic elites.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
TRANSNATIONAL GENTRIFICATION IN NISEKO
                    ,
                    JAPAN
                    : A Model of Displacement Led by Linked Migration
authors: Ni Yan; Keisuke Sakamoto; Shizhen Huang; David Matarrita‐Cascante; Noriko Akita; Song Han; Zhengxu Zhou; Takahiro Yamazaki; Makoto Yokohari
abstract: Transnational gentrification scholarship has provided insights into how transnational migration reshapes urban areas, yet its analytical lens has rarely extended to peripheral rural contexts outside Euro‐American settings, where distinct actors and mechanisms may emerge. This study examines Niseko, a rural area experiencing Japan's highest land price increases alongside significant demographic shifts. Grounded in gentrification scholarship and employing a displacement‐centered approach, this research combines socio‐economic data analysis with 33 semi‐structured interviews conducted in 2023 to trace the actors and mechanisms driving displacement. Our study reveals a ‘linked migration’ pattern: affluent transnational migrants initiate transformation, establishing English‐speaking business environments that, combined with local labor shortages, structurally attract transnational labor migrants. This pattern generates multi‐layered displacement through distinct pathways, with the affluent group driving displacement through capital investment and transformation of the built environment, and the labor force producing displacement pressure through housing competition and socio‐cultural disruption. This research theorizes a dual‐agent displacement model driven by linked migration, identifying the transnational labor force as a gentrifying agent, a role largely overlooked in existing scholarship, and demonstrates that the intersection of transnationality and rurality intensifies these dynamics. These findings offer theoretical and empirical insights for understanding amenity‐led transformations in peripheral communities worldwide.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
THE TRANSCALAR POLITICS AND SPATIAL IMPLICATIONS OF INVESTMENTS IN SHOPPING MALLS IN AFRICAN CITIES
                    : A Study of Accra's West Hills Mall, Ghana
authors: Rosina Sheburah Essien; George Owusu; Kofi Kekeli Amedzro; Musah Aziba Issah; Jennifer Robinson; John Spyropoulos
abstract: A surge in the number of shopping malls across many African cities reflects capital's responses to the continent's growing middle class and deepening neoliberal globalization. This article develops an analysis of the transcalar nature of these urban investments using the case of the West Hills Mall (WHM) in the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area (GAMA). It explores how multiple actors, with their respective calculations, policies and financial resources, are mobilized from across diverse scales to make such an investment possible. Our findings have implications for theorizing urban development politics. First, we consider the ‘circuits’ of transnational financial investments topologically, as embedded within and generated by particular urban contexts: investibility and investment flows are produced through the distinctive histories of urban territories. Second, this focuses attention on the transcalar networks that make urban development possible, in this case involving tightly networked South African and Ghanaian developers, backed by financialized South African private capital and a Ghanaian state pension fund. Third, we interrogate the outcomes and analytical meaning of the development, tracing its territorial impacts, shaped by a wide array of actors and distinctive forms of land governance. The article contributes African‐based starting points for theorizing the actors and outcomes of urban development politics and urban development financing.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
ACCOUNTING FOR BIODIVERSITY
                    : Periphery Urbanization, Environmental Conflict, and Spatial Inequality in Monetizing the Value of Nature
authors: Ihnji Jon
abstract: In terms of mainstream sustainability economics, market‐led initiatives aimed at biodiversity restoration represent a productive, morally conscientious choice. Under this view, efforts in areas such as biodiversity offsetting, net gain, or finance are considered effective tools for preventing or managing environmental degradation. In this article I problematize such optimistic, largely economistic claims by taking readers to specific urban locations where these tools are being deployed or proposed. My case studies of Bristol and Copenhagen illustrate that such tools, under the realities of rent gap‐driven urbanization processes, selectively render certain ecologies and places fungible, thereby advancing inequality by disproportionately burdening lower‐income and peripheral communities. At the same time, we may equally witness how compelling counterarguments are made by local residents and environmental activists in response, particularly regarding the impact of land development on water quality and urban stormwater management. Thereby I show how cities are not just sites on and in which these tools act; they mediate debates over the value of nature and biodiversity, and whose conception of value counts. In this article I therefore make a case for why an ‘urban lens’ is essential in contemporary analyses of biodiversity tools, governance, and their politics.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
THE CITY AS CODE
                    : Assemblage, Surveillance, and Algorithmic Rule in London
authors: Huaxiong Jiang
abstract: This article theorizes London as an illustrative ‘Subjugating City’, where urban governance has evolved over four decades into a distributed surveillance assemblage. Moving beyond fragmented critiques of individual technologies, it examines how algorithmic statecraft produces ‘resilient control’, a mode of governance that preserves its core logic by absorbing and reorganizing democratic contestation. Specifically, the London example operates through three key parameters: a dual policy logic balancing pro‐innovation narratives with intrusive legal data extraction mandates; a hybrid public‐private infrastructure integrating national databases with corporate analytics; and an adaptive governance design that internalizes legal and social friction. Through analysis of London's layered surveillance infrastructure—from the ‘Ring of Steel’ and national Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) systems to the privatization of state functions through partnerships such as National Health Service (NHS)–Palantir—the article demonstrates how governance power is stabilized through technological path dependency and corporate secrecy. Rather than positing an easily transferable or universally reproducible model, the article treats London as a rich empirical example that highlights how liberal democratic institutions normalize expansive surveillance while maintaining the appearance of accountability and public consent across neoliberal urban spaces.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
CONTESTED METABOLIC NODES
                    : Shareholding Cooperatives and Planetary Ruralization in China
authors: Yong Zhang
abstract: China's recent shareholding cooperative (SC) reform heralds a shift from expropriation‐led rural change to a post‐expropriation regime in which the countryside is reconstituted through circulation, capitalization, and new forms of collective governance. Existing interpretations, whether framed as market‐driven de‐collectivization, state‐led re‐collectivization, or pragmatic neo‐collectivization, struggle to grasp the planetary and relational dynamics through which these reforms actually unfold. Drawing on multi‐scalar fieldwork in Jiyuan, an inland municipality that institutionalized SCs across 525 villages, the article advances a framework that conceptualizes SCs as contested metabolic nodes where state directives, capital flows, and local aspirations are continuously translated and reworked. Through comparative analysis of three villages located across an expanded urban–rural interface, the study shows how economic restructuring and territorial remaking materialize through differentiated practices of defensive stabilization, augmentative experimentation, and performative visibility. Relational autonomy emerges as a capacity generated through circulations: villages negotiate actively within and across the state and market logics. By foregrounding the metabolic processes where rural commons recompose collective assets, risks, and identities, the article repositions corporatized villages as active sites of planetary ruralization and laboratories of contemporary rural transformation.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title:
STRATIFIED ADAPTATION
                    : Infrastructure, Elevation, and Cascading Floods in the Urban Mekong Delta
authors: Lizzie Yarina; Vuong Kha Tu; Tran Kim Bao; Ly Quoc Dang
abstract: Flood‐prone cities in the global South are increasingly the target of infrastructure projects aimed at building climate ‘resilience’. At the same time, residents of these cities take adaptation to flooding into their own hands. In this article we examine the interrelationship between household‐scale and urban‐scale flood mitigation projects in Cần Thơ, Vietnam. We use spatial‐ethnographic methods that examine multiscalar flood processes to show how this flood risk plays out through micro‐topographic variations across the city to create a condition of stratified adaptation. This case extends existing scholarship on the political ecology of climate adaptation by demonstrating how flood mitigation projects can exacerbate inequality not only due to the horizontal (space‐claiming) impacts of infrastructure projects but also due to the vertical displacement of water through a shifting ground plane. Flood risk cascades, re‐emerging in new places. As flood levels rise due to compounding factors of subsidence, development, and climate change, interventions at various scales displace water to sites with the lowest elevation, stratifying risks and benefits. This cyclical process displaces adaptation labor from the state to the household, in turn undermining the state's techno‐fixes as flows of water shift once again. The resulting ‘vicious cycle of water’ places the urban poor at increasing rather than decreasing flood risk.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: WORKING THE GREY AREA: Street‑Level Refugee Housing Governance in Sweden
authors: Nicolina Ewards Öberg
abstract: This article explores how refugee housing provision under the Swedish dispersal programme produces uneven pathways to housing stability. Although residence‐permit‐holding refugees assigned to the municipalities are granted the right to housing, there are no stipulations regarding housing type, quality, or duration, resulting in significant local variation. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews with street‐level bureaucrats working with settlement and housing provision for refugees in three major refugee‐receiving municipalities, the article shows how legality is enacted on the ground through everyday administrative practices under conditions of ambiguity. It conceptualizes refugee housing provision as a grey‐area governance landscape and identifies ‘paralegality’ and ‘time politics’ as key mechanisms through which a formally universal system produces conditional, temporary and uneven access to housing. By tracing the logics underpinning different local strategies, the article shows how racialized welfare dualism is produced in practice without a formal dualist policy.

journal: International Journal of Urban and Regional Research
title: ORGANIZING AND SHELTER DECOMMODIFICATION: Lessons and Directions
authors: Alejandra Reyes; Pedro Daher
abstract: Critical urban scholarship is bringing attention to issues of accumulation and their role in hindering housing access globally. By reviewing relevant literature, we advance our understanding of the potential of grassroots organizing for influencing housing policy and outcomes. Beyond promoting housing decommodification, we underscore the broader sociopolitical significance and transformative potential of mobilizing around the housing question, which societies are increasingly returning to.
