title: When Hotspots Disagree: Reconciling Cluster Detection and Relative Risk Surface Estimation in Applied Spatial Analysis
authors: Tilman M. Davies
abstract: Hotspot analysis is central to many point‐referenced geospatial applications, but the term “hotspot” is often used to describe different kinds of evidence: a statistically significant cluster, a region of high estimated intensity, or an elevated relative risk surface. As a result, outputs produced by different methods are often compared within a common visual and practical language, even when they support different spatial claims. We examine this problem through a focused comparison of scan‐statistic cluster detection and kernel‐smoothed relative risk estimation for case‐control point patterns. We develop an agreement‐profile framework that separates four dimensions of comparison: Detection state, Location, Scale, and Morphology. Across repeated simulations and three real‐data examples, we show that similar overall overlap can conceal different containment, extent, and component relationships; that agreement between fitted regions is distinct from recovery of a prespecified spatial target; and that interpretation can change under alternative analytical specifications and reference measures. Rather than ranking methods, it provides a reproducible vocabulary for interpreting and communicating how hotspot outputs relate across analyses.

title: Rethinking the Discrete‐Continuous Choice Problem by Uncovering Asymmetry in High‐Resolution Urban Modeling
authors: Jiaxin Zhang; Eric J. Miller
abstract: A primary bottleneck in integrated urban simulation is the Discrete‐Continuous Choice problem within Land Use Supply modeling, specifically, the challenge of simultaneously determining building type and floorspace capacity. This study develops a high‐resolution, parcel‐level, multi‐stage econometric framework in which the bidirectional interactions between these decisions can be estimated rather than assumed. Using a large‐scale dataset assembled for the Greater Toronto‐Hamilton Area from 2015 to 2023, the framework incorporates real‐world zoning constraints to simulate market behavior. This granular approach also uncovers the behavioral heterogeneity across retail, office, industrial, and mixed‐use developers through their unique spatial preferences and patterns of inter‐sectoral competition. The results reveal an asymmetric relationship between the two decisions. Expected floorspace significantly affects the choice of development type, but only when specified with alternative‐specific parameters. In contrast, the reverse effect is not statistically significant in the floorspace models. Although this asymmetry may be specific to the sectors, region, and period examined, it suggests that bidirectional dependence should not be assumed by default. When the Discrete‐to‐Continuous relationship is weak or not statistically supported, a simpler sequential specification may offer lower modeling complexity. The proposed framework provides a direct way to examine which structure is more appropriate for a given application.

title: Evaluating Spatially Varying Coefficient Models Across Structural Patterns of Spatial Heterogeneity
authors: Musang Yoo; Hyeongmo Koo
abstract: Spatial heterogeneity refers to spatial variation in relationships between dependent and independent variables across geographic locations, conceptualized differently depending on the analytical perspective, each highlighting distinct patterns of variation. Spatially varying coefficient (SVC) models are commonly employed to explore spatial heterogeneity. Because each SVC model utilizes a fundamentally distinct estimation approach, performance is anticipated to vary across patterns. However, prior comparative evaluations have remained fragmented within single structural perspectives. This study systematically evaluates SVC model performance across diverse structural patterns of spatial heterogeneity, conceptualized through continuity, directionality, and scale. Using a controlled simulation framework, 12 patterns are generated and evaluated for multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR), spatial generalized additive models (SGAM), geographical Gaussian process GAM (GGP‐GAM), and Moran eigenvector spatial filter‐based SVC (MESF‐SVC). The findings demonstrate that GAM‐based models consistently excel in capturing smooth, continuous spatial gradients at the global scale. In contrast, MESF‐SVC proves robust in resolving localized and discontinuous spatial fragmentation. Meanwhile, MGWR exhibits instability under high frequency local variations, frequently over‐smoothing abrupt boundaries due to its localized kernel weighting. An empirical analysis of Seoul metropolitan election data shows these distinctions persist under multivariate conditions. Based on these outcomes, this study provides practical guidelines for SVC model selection.

title: The Geographic Moran Effect: Theory, Methods, and Interpretation
authors: Zhenzhi Jiao; X. Angela Yao; Jean‐Claude Thill
abstract: The Moran effect traditionally refers to the synchronization of population dynamics driven by shared environmental forcing rather than direct interactions among populations. Although extensively studied in population ecology, the Moran effect has received limited attention in geography, and its applicability remains insufficiently explored. In this study, we build upon the classical Moran effect in population ecology as a conceptual foundation, developing a more comprehensive conceptual framework in a geographic context. We introduce the new concept geographic Moran effect (GME), defined as temporally coherent and synchronized variation across geographic entities induced by common external forcing, with the magnitude and potentially the direction of local responses varying according to a spatially varying sensitivity field. A two‐step spatiotemporal factor framework is developed to identify and interpret the GME. The framework first tests for the possible presence of GME‐type synchrony in spatiotemporal data and then examines the GME and its spatiotemporal evolution by investigating its structure through spatial and temporal dimensions separately. A synthetic experiment validates the framework's reliability, while an application to US county‐level presidential election data (2008–2024) demonstrates its ability to identify the GME and its spatial and temporal components. By redefining the Moran effect as a geographic theory and a distinct object of inference, this work provides a mechanism‐oriented perspective on spatiotemporal analysis with broad applicability in geography, ecology, and public health, where explicitly identifying and interpreting GME‐type synchrony is essential for understanding system‐level dynamics.

title: A New Method for Detecting and Explaining Local Irregularities in Spatial Synthetic Data
authors: Hadrien Salat; Kimon Krenz
abstract: Spatial synthetic populations are increasingly used in agent‐based models, spatial microsimulation, and other forms of place‐based analysis. Their usefulness, however, depends not only on reproducing aggregate patterns but also on maintaining plausible local distributions. This creates a difficult validation problem when independent benchmarks are limited and validation cannot proceed beyond checking the technical implementation of model constraints. We develop a moment‐based validation framework for detecting and interpreting local irregularities in spatial synthetic data. Local distributions are characterized through their first four moments and we combine hierarchical clustering with SHapley Additive exPlanations to identify and explain areas whose modeled distributions depart from expected local patterns and contextual variables. The framework is demonstrated using modeled salary distributions from the Synthetic Population Catalyst in West Yorkshire, a setting in which fine‐scale synthetic populations are assembled from sources observed at coarser spatial and substantive resolutions. The application identifies locally unusual areas, shows how these can be interpreted against contextual characteristics and local knowledge, and illustrates how the framework can support judgments about whether synthetic data are fit for intended use. More broadly, the article argues that local coherence should be treated as a central criterion in the validation of spatial synthetic populations.

title: On the Distribution of Spatial Polarization Indices
authors: Sergio J. Rey
abstract: This paper develops a statistical framework for inference on recently developed spatial polarization indices and clarifies their relationship to spatial inequality and dependence. The framework builds on a graph‐theoretic decomposition of polarization into global, meso, and local components and accommodates an asymmetry common in regional economic data: low‐income areas often form cohesive clusters, whereas high‐income areas are more spatially fragmented. The principal contributions are a graph‐preserving randomization procedure and asymptotic results for the spatial polarization index. These methods permit assessment of the significance and robustness of observed polarization patterns while connecting spatial statistics, inequality decomposition, and graph theory. A series of Monte Carlo experiments examines the properties of the inferential methods. Two case studies focusing on polarization in Mexico and the United States provide empirical illustrations.

title: A Spatially Weighted Relative Deprivation Index: Incorporating Spatial Structure Into Regional Inequality Measurement
authors: Kyungjae Lee
abstract: Regional inequality is conventionally assessed based on the distribution of economic outcomes across regions. However, regional disparities are spatially structured because regional economic outcomes are interdependent across space. Existing approaches generally capture either the spatial dimension of inequality at an aggregate level or unit‐specific disadvantage without incorporating spatial relevance. This study proposes a Spatially Weighted Relative Deprivation (SWRD) index that combines the one‐sided upward‐gap rule of relative deprivation (RD) with an empirically calibrated spatial weighting structure. Using real gross regional domestic product (GRDP) for 229 Korean districts from 2015 to 2021, the study estimates the distance decay of spatial dependence and constructs annual SWRD values. The empirical comparison shows that SWRD produces spatial patterns and regional rankings that differ from conventional RD. Spatial permutation tests indicate that high SWRD values are unlikely under random spatial reassignment. Monte Carlo simulations on a uniform lattice further show that the divergence between RD and SWRD increases with stronger spatial dependence, steeper distance decay, and greater dispersion and right skewness. These findings show that incorporating spatial structure can change assessments of regional disadvantage under varying spatial and distributional conditions.

title:
ML
                    ‐
                    SAS
                    : A Machine‐Learning‐Based Spatial Autocorrelation Statistic for Mixed‐Type Data
authors: Woohyung Kim; Sang‐Il Lee
abstract: Existing measures of multivariate spatial autocorrelation often rely on covariance structures or fixed distances that are difficult to apply to nonlinear and mixed‐type attributes. This paper proposes the Machine‐Learning‐Based Spatial Autocorrelation Statistic (ML‐SAS), which combines a spatial weights matrix with an attribute‐similarity matrix learned from unsupervised random‐forest path proximities. Global and local statistics are defined within a generalized matrix‐correlation framework, with analytical randomization moments as theoretical references and rank‐based permutation tests for inference. Simulations assess correspondence with classical statistics, sensitivity to forest specifications and proximity definitions, null calibration, and local detection under continuous and nonlinear mixed‐type processes. Path‐based ML‐SAS was stable across the tested forest settings and less sensitive than terminal‐node proximity. Under the spatial null, the empirical probability of any rejection was 0.040. In a continuous multivariate design, ML‐SAS was more selective than Multivariate Local Geary. In a nonlinear mixed‐type design, adding a nominal attribute substantially increased recall and F1 relative to continuous‐only ML‐SAS, and leave‐one‐variable‐out analysis identified that attribute as the largest contributor to changes in the local similarity surface. In Dutch municipalities, adding ordered urbanity changed 23 local classifications. ML‐SAS provides a complementary framework for jointly analyzing continuous and categorical spatial attributes.

title: Scale‐Conditioned Geometry: How Measurement Resolution Induces Distance, Proximity, and Spatial Dependence
authors: Eric Vaz
abstract: Scale is central to inference in natural and social systems, and geography and ecology have treated it as an explicit object of theory for decades. This paper builds on that work with a formal view in which scale is a degree of freedom of description, parameterizing both the mappings between representations and the metric defining distance and neighborhood. Distance is induced by the representation and can change with resolution even when the underlying system is unchanged. In simulated autocorrelated fields aggregated across seven block sizes (30 Monte Carlo replications), Moran's I declines by a factor of 3.4 while a correlation‐threshold range proxy remains comparatively stable. An explicit metric on the family of representations (Fused Gromov–Wasserstein) shows that scale and zoning are distinct, measurable directions. A change‐of‐support null describes the change expected from information loss under a single correlation structure; a mixed‐scale scenario departs from it at six of seven scales, which rejects that null without by itself establishing a change in coupling. Two observational datasets, each analyzed at a single support, show that the induced metric changes global and local dependence. These results motivate a scale‐explicit workflow that treats proximity and dependence as conditional on representation.

title: Capturing Non‐Linear Neighborhood Structure: An Autoencoder Approach to Census‐Based Dimensionality Reduction for Residential Differentiation
authors: Alex Singleton; Owen Goodwin; Stef De Sabbata
abstract: Dimensionality reduction is fundamental to applied spatial data analysis, condensing high‐dimensional indicators into parsimonious representations for mapping and modeling. Principal component analysis (PCA) remains a dominant approach, yet its linearity assumptions constrain its capacity to capture the complex, non‐linear dependencies characteristic of spatial socio‐economic data. We evaluate the effectiveness of autoencoders as a flexible, parametric alternative for constructing composite measures of neighborhood structure. Through encoder‐decoder architectures, AEs learn non‐linear representations that better reflect underlying data complexity, enable projection of new observations without refitting, and provide reconstruction‐based diagnostics that enhance transparency. We demonstrate the approach using small‐area data from the 2021 Census of England and Wales, evaluating how effectively AEs summarize spatial variability and recover composite dimensions of residential differentiation compared with PCA.

title:
M‐
                    SGWR
                    : Multiscale Attribute‐Similarity and Geographically Weighted Regression
authors: M. Naser Lessani; Zhenlong Li; Manzhu Yu; Helen Greatrex; Chan Shen
abstract: The first law of geography is a cornerstone of spatial analysis, emphasizing that nearby locations tend to be more strongly related and similar. However, defining what constitutes “near” and “related” remains challenging because different phenomena operate across distinct spatial dimensions, including physical, social, and network‐based spaces. Conventional local regression models, such as GWR and MGWR, represent nearness and relatedness primarily through geographic proximity. In an era of globalization and digital connectivity, however, geographic proximity alone may not adequately characterize relationships among locations, as many phenomena are shaped by connections that extend beyond physical distance. To address this limitation, we propose a new model, termed M‐SGWR, that characterizes relationships among locations in two dimensions: geographic space and predictor‐specific attribute space. For each predictor, geographic and attribute‐similarity weight matrices are constructed separately and combined using an optimized parameter, , which determines their relative contributions to local model estimation. Analogous to the predictor‐specific bandwidths used in MGWR, the optimal varies across predictors, allowing M‐SGWR to identify geographically dominant, mixed, or attribute‐dominant relationships, including similarities among geographically distant locations. Results from two simulation experiments and one empirical application demonstrate that M‐SGWR consistently outperforms GWR, SGWR, and MGWR across the evaluated goodness‐of‐fit measures.

title: Graph-based machine learning in urban form characterization: a critical methodological review with structured taxonomy and methodological framework
authors: Mansoor Ali; Abdulrazzaq Shaamala; Junyan Yang; Tan Yigitcanlar
abstract: Graph-based machine learning (graph-based ML) offers a structurally well-suited paradigm for encoding the relational properties of urban form, yet its application to urban morphological characterization remains fragmented across disciplinary boundaries. This study presents a critical methodological review of graph-based ML for intrinsic urban form characterization, synthesizing 24 studies through a transparent, reproducible search, screening, and extraction process. The review develops a four-axis taxonomy covering urban form elements, graph construction strategies, learning paradigms, and morphological applications, alongside a reproducible seven-stage methodological framework. Grounded in established principles of representation learning, the review advances the argument that upstream representational choices are a consequential and insufficiently examined source of variation in graph-based urban morphology, with the abstraction of cities into nodes and edges shaping which morphological patterns become computationally accessible. Across the 24 reviewed studies, within-study comparisons show that graph construction strategy and morphometric attribute selection can substantially alter analytical outcomes, a pattern recurring across unsupervised, supervised, and semi-supervised paradigms; the corpus does not, however, contain studies that vary representation and architecture systematically enough to establish which factor contributes more to outcome variation overall. The review further identifies graph construction strategy selection as following from three jointly operating determinants (analytical scale, theoretical conception of meaningful adjacency, and task type), a mechanism explaining representational diversity without reducing it to arbitrary methodological preference. A critical gap is identified: current construction strategies provide limited explicit encoding of spatial discontinuity — its causes, permeability, temporal status, and morphological meaning — constraining analysis of fragmented urban conditions. Three tractable future directions are proposed to address this limitation; these extend beyond the reviewed evidence rather than emerging from the corpus as findings of equivalent standing.

title: Individual Resilience as Human Capital Stock: Neighborhood Social Capital, Environmental Perceptions, and Dynamic Pathways Across COVID-19 Phases
authors: Rui Sun; Yiming Wang
abstract: This study, grounded in the social ecological theories, investigates how the pathways linking neighborhood relationships, perceived environmental quality (PEQ), and individual resilience (IR) differed between the COVID-19 pandemic and the post-pandemic period. The empirical focus is on Chinese international students (CIS) in the UK, who experienced a unique form of “double exclusion” during the pandemic. Multi-phase data collection was conducted through questionnaire survey using a pre-then-post design ( n = 146). Specifically, exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted to validate the dimensions of resilience as a contextual and dynamic construct, followed by a higher-order mediation model using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to explore relationships between main latent constructs both during the pandemic and its aftermath. EFA confirmed sample adequacy (KMO > 0.9, Bartlett’s test p < 0.001) and validated the identification of first-order latent constructs for IR. Findings from PLS-SEM analysis revealed that during the pandemic, both structural and functional dimensions of neighborhood relationship were associated with IR through distinct mediation effects of PEQ. In the post-pandemic period, however, the pattern of associations differed: the mediation effect of PEQ on the relationship between structural neighborhood ties and IR was no longer significant, while PEQ remained a full mediator in the relationship between functional dimensions of neighborhood relationship and IR. These findings highlight the dynamic nature of IR as a stock of human capital. Neighborhood-based social capital functions as the primary investment, while perceived environmental quality acts as the efficiency channel through which this investment is translated into resilience outcomes. This interpretation offers an account of how resilience protection and accumulation may differ between crisis and post-crisis contexts.

title: Panel Spatial Autoregression with an Unknown Transformation of the Weight Matrix
authors: Robert Daniel
abstract: We introduce nonlinearities in analyzing spatial panel data by allowing for an unknown matrix analytic transformation of the spatial weights matrix. The proposed model can be estimated using only O ( n ) parameters which is a vast reduction in parameters when compared to $$O(n^2)$$ parameters as seen in the literature for spatial weight matrix estimation. Analyzing the quasi-maximum likelihood estimator, we show consistency and asymptotic normality. In simulations, this estimator can accurately estimate the transformed spatial weights matrix. The procedure is applied to the estimation of unemployment in New Hampshire with county based spatial dependence.

title: Spatial Heterogeneity And Equilibrium Selection in Urban Mobility
authors: Oliviero A. Carboni; Paolo Russu
abstract: This paper studies how spatial accessibility shapes long-run equilibrium selection in urban mobility systems. The central mechanism is dynamic: accessibility affects not only individual travel incentives and equilibrium conditions, but also the geometry of the evolutionary state space by shifting basin boundaries and changing which long-run mobility outcomes are attainable from different initial conditions. We develop an evolutionary model in which heterogeneous accessibility is generated by generalized commuting distance and value of time, while congestion is distinguished from aggregate private-car usage. We identify structural accessibility thresholds at which the basin configuration changes qualitatively. Poorer accessibility can generate a basin of attraction of positive measure for persistent commuter car use even under maximum public intervention. Pricing can eliminate the fully inefficient equilibrium, but need not induce convergence to the socially optimal outcome because other dynamically attainable configurations may remain. The analysis therefore identifies a channel that static equilibrium comparisons cannot capture: spatial structure affects urban mobility through basin-based equilibrium selection and path dependence, not only through equilibrium travel costs.

title: Bifurcation Patterns in A Remote Work Economy: Intercity Impacts of Remote Work on Spatial Distribution of Workers and Firms
authors: Hiroki Aizawa; Takuhiro Saka
abstract: In this paper, we examine how the introduction of remote work affects the spatial distribution of workers and firms in cities, social welfare, and their utilities. Developing a New Economic Geography model that incorporates remote work, we explore how transportation costs affect these distributions and the utility levels in equilibrium. We conduct a bifurcation analysis of an equilibrium where all mobile workers concentrate in the central location of a long narrow economy where an odd number of locations are evenly distributed along a line segment. The bifurcation mechanism, which represents the emergence of remote workers, is elucidated. Results show that remote work can shift the equilibrium toward two types of equilibria. In one equilibrium, remote workers reside away from the central location, while firms operate in the center. In the other, remote workers reside in the central location, while firms that employ them operate outside the center. In the latter case, even the utility of remote workers declines due to the introduction of remote work.

title: Effectiveness of experiential practice on environmental awareness and pro-environmental behavior: evidence from junior high school students in Toride City, Japan
authors: Shingo Fujii; Kiyokazu Ujiie; Takeshi Mizunoya
abstract: This study verified the effects of “experiential practice” and “visualizing” carbon dioxide reduction on the transformation of junior high school students' environmental awareness and pro-environmental behavior (PEB). We sought to propose measures for sustaining high environmental awareness and choice of appropriate actions. Based on a specific case study from the “Toride City Sustainable Learning Project” in Toride City, Ibaraki Prefecture, the following 2 hypotheses were tested: (1) combining knowledge acquisition with experiential practice effectively sustains PEB, and (2) enhancing responsibility yields the greatest outcomes. A comparative analysis was conducted between School B (knowledge-focused classes) and School A (4 -week decarbonization training program with carbon dioxide [CO₂] calculations). Results showed that School A had action implementation rates that were 2.0–3.4 times higher than those of School B for electricity conservation, water conservation and food waste reduction. Regression analysis revealed that “awareness of responsibility” was a statistically significant factor in sustaining PEB. Text mining indicated that School A students linked daily actions to quantifiable CO₂ reductions, enabling them to perceive global challenges as “personal issues” and recognize their roles. These findings suggest that behavioral change in lower secondary students occurs when they move beyond knowledge acquisition by gaining fresh insights through “visualizing decarbonization” and developing a sense of ownership and responsibility. We propose environmental education programs that guide students from “knowledge” to “behavioral reinforcement” through continuous experiential practice, thereby fostering ownership and responsibility.

title: Regional growth, convergence, and spatial spillovers in India
authors: Carlos Mendez; Sujana Kabiraj; Jiaqi Li
abstract: Using satellite nighttime light data as a proxy for economic activity, Chanda and Kabiraj (2020, World Development) studied regional growth and convergence across 520 districts in India. Adopting a reproducible open-science approach, this article builds on their work by extending their main findings on three empirical fronts. First, we illustrate regional convergence patterns using an interactive tool for satellite imagery visualization. Second, we assess the degree of spatial dependence in their main econometric specification. Third, we employ a spatial Durbin model to measure the role of spatial spillovers in the convergence process. Our results indicate that spatial spillovers increase the estimated speed of regional convergence. In our fully specified model, spillovers raise the convergence speed from about 3.0% to about 5.2% per year, which shortens the half-life of regional disparities from roughly 23 to 13 years. We close by illustrating how the same reproducible workflow extends beyond economic output, with an exploratory analysis of how luminosity relates to cultural participation across Indian states.

title: Digital Innovation in Italian Museums:
authors: Assia Liberatore; Ana Elisa De Sousa; Paula Cardoso
abstract: This paper examines the adoption of immersive technologies -- Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) -- in Italian museums, focusing on how digital tools shape visitor experiences across different regional contexts. Building on earlier exploratory work conducted through online surveys and preliminary field research in winter 2024--25, the study draws on survey data collected in September 2025 from visitors across museums located in diverse territorial and institutional settings. The analysis combines descriptive statistics, regression models, and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) to investigate the relationships between immersive technologies, visitor satisfaction, emotional engagement, post-visit understanding, and future behavioural intentions. The findings indicate that AR/VR experiences are positively and consistently associated with visitor satisfaction, emotional engagement, and cognitive outcomes across the sampled institutions. Emotional engagement and post-visit understanding emerge as the strongest predictors of positive evaluations and future intentions, while pre-visit expectations and familiarity with immersive technologies play secondary but significant roles. The results also indicate territorial variation in the adoption and perceived quality of immersive technologies, with patterns varying across regional and institutional contexts. Rather than suggesting uniform patterns of digital transformation, the study highlights how immersive experiences are associated with specific regional and institutional conditions that warrant further investigation. By combining experiential and territorial perspectives, the paper contributes to current debates on digital transformation in cultural heritage and smart cultural tourism. The findings suggest that the perceived value of immersive technologies is associated not only with technological availability, but also with the quality of narrative design and the broader contextual conditions of each institution. Future research may extend this work through longitudinal approaches and simulation models exploring the diffusion of AR/VR under different policy and funding scenarios.

title: Mapping Linguistic Innovation, Cultural Continuity, and Socio-Economic Disparity Across Indian States – A Culture Based Development Application
authors: J. D. Prabhakar; Annie Tubadji
abstract: This study explores how language evolution and social reality meet in India's varied states. Adopting the Culture Based Development lens, we quantify local culture as two sub-types, cultural heritage (CH) and living culture (LC), and the balance between them (cultural entropy– CE), where the latter is theoretically expected to explain socio economic inequality between cultural groups in a place. Thus, theresearch explores how a culturally different balance across India is associated with socio-economic inequality across space. To achieve this, we use language as a proxy for cultural attitudes. Namely, by comparing the frequency of traditional cultural markers (`"Krishna") (approximating cultural heritage) to current linguistic innovations ("Influencer") (approximating living culture) we check the statistical association of these linguistic variables with measures for English language dominance and caste-wise unemployment. The findings indicate that, while living-culture-related terms increase their frequency over time, theyhave not yet superseded traditional cultural moorings, i.e., the cultural entropy in Indian places is still dominated by the cultural heritage component. Hence, we still observe local inefficiencies and inequalitiesin terms of structural unemployment especially among Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST).The findings are explained from socio-linguistic and Myrdalian point of view.

title: Measuring Market Accessibility of Insular Areas based on Network Distance and Shipment Cost
authors: Theodore Tsekeris; Vassilis Lychnaras; Costas Passas; Georgia Skintzi
abstract: In this paper, we calculate the two-sided (consumer and producer) market accessibility of the Greek islands, based on different measures of transport cost, namely, the actual network distance and the freight shipment cost from/to mainland regions and between them. For this purpose, we employ a unique micro-dataset of 1,026,469 shipments for the year 2021 originated from the platform of Islands’ Transport Equivalent for firms. The shipment cost refers to the receipts of payments made by firms for outsourcing transport services to companies with public-use truck vehicles. The findings show the importance of the population size, geographical proximity to large markets and network connectivity, and underscore the severe imbalances among consumers’ (importers’) and producers’ (exporters’) accessibility to and from the Greek islands. Moreover, the use of shipment cost significantly alters the accessibility hierarchy and trade imbalance inequalities among islands, as it incorporates inherent characteristics of the logistics and product markets. Relevant policy implications are made to support the design of more effective island policies aimed at supporting the competitiveness of local businesses, the living standards of inhabitants and the territorial cohesion of the country.

title: Entrepreneurship and Employment: The Simultaneous Impacts of Establishment Births versus Deaths on Regional Employment across the United States
authors: Eunsuk Hong; In-Hyeock (Ian) Lee
abstract: This study investigates the non-linear effects of establishment births versus deaths on regional employment, which show asymmetric pathways between intra-regional versus inter-regional spillovers. Using state-year data on establishment births, deaths, and employment for service sectors in the 48 contiguous U.S. states from 1980 to 2014, the study implements three-stage least squares (3SLS) regressions to test competing forces of multiplier versus competition effects, with endogeneity and spatial and temporal dependencies addressed. Empirical results support the following ‘four’ non-linear, asymmetric relationships as hypothesized: (i) establishment births initially increase total employment within a focal U.S. state, but decrease it with excessive establishment births within the state (i.e., inverted U-shaped); (ii) establishment births in the neighboring states of a focal U.S. state initially decrease total employment in the focal state, but increase it with excessive establishment births in the neighboring states (i.e., U-shaped); (iii) establishment deaths initially decrease total employment within a focal U.S. state, but increase it with excessive establishment deaths within the state (i.e., U-shaped); and (iv) establishment deaths in the neighboring states of a focal U.S. state initially increase total employment in the focal state, but decrease it with excessive establishment deaths in the neighboring states (i.e., inverted U-shaped). These findings also hold at the fine-grained geographic level of metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) and under diverse contextual conditions. The study contributes to the literature by testing the theoretical thresholds at which the dominance between multiplier and competition effects can be reversed in non-linear pathways, and by empirically estimating the asymmetric interdependences of regional employment between intra-regional versus inter-regional spillovers of establishment births and deaths.

title: The population dynamics in China: understanding the role of spread and backwash effect
authors: Wuqia Liu; Nanxin Deng; Baijun Wu
abstract: Considering the declining population growth and increasing intra-provincial migration in China, the population issue becomes crucial for the sustainable development of the Chinese economy. We utilize data of 2010 and 2020 China Census to study the impact of the “spread-backwash” effects of large cities on county-level population dynamics over the past decade and investigate the potential mechanisms. We find that the spillover effects generated by cities have significantly increased the population of neighboring counties. Regarding the mechanism, the “spread-backwash” effects of large cities facilitate the integration of county-level secondary industries into urban industrial chains, leading to new enterprise investments and job creation. In counties where spillover effects are significant, the number of new enterprises in the tertiary industry is higher, positively impacting local population growth.

title: Do Agriculture and Infrastructure Development Improve Life Satisfaction? Evidence from Rural Tanzania
authors: Victoria Greta Luxen; Moses January Ndunguru; Peter Dannenberg
abstract: Rural development in Sub-Saharan Africa is mostly measured by economic indicators, despite growing calls to broaden this narrow focus. Although wellbeing is used in discourse, it often repackages economic goals rather than capturing people’s subjective wellbeing. We address this gap by analysing how and why agricultural intensification, commercialisation and infrastructure interventions affect life satisfaction, a central component of subjective wellbeing, among Tanzanian smallholder farmers within the Southern Agricultural Growth Corridor of Tanzania (SAGCOT). Using longitudinal survey data from 2019 and 2023 ( N = 871) and focus groups, we show that life satisfaction has increased on average. Among the variables analysed in this study, access to electricity combined with Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) use is associated with higher life satisfaction. Despite development narratives, we do not find statistically significant evidence that agricultural intensification is associated with higher life satisfaction. Commercialisation is negatively associated with life satisfaction, which our qualitative findings link to perceived structural and market barriers. Infrastructure effects are heterogeneous and depend on household access: road improvements are associated with lower satisfaction among households without transport, while electricity is associated with higher satisfaction when used for ICT. These findings show that life satisfaction provides a valuable lens for understanding the intended and unintended impacts of development and can inform policies and practices by highlighting that these impacts are heterogeneous and vary across different groups.

title: Extending unit structure analysis to global value network approach: the case of the Japanese automobile industry
authors: Jun Omata
abstract: As economies become increasingly globalized and production processes are increasingly offshored, it has become essential to clarify the global supply chains to which each country’s industries belong. This study examines countries’ participation in global supply chains by analyzing how domestic industrial groups form networks that connect with global production systems. The approach of this paper consists of two steps. First, while Johnson and Noguera (2012) and Timmer et al. (2013) provided foundational frameworks for global value chain (GVC) analysis, this study introduces a new theoretical approach based on Ozaki’s (1980) unit structure analysis. Earlier studies estimate value added by defining destination countries as final consumers or producers, whereas Kuroiwa (2021) integrated unit structure analysis to present an alternative estimation of total value‑added flows to destination countries. Extending this framework, the present study identifies destination countries as importers involved in subsequent production stages and represents the upstream value‑added structure as a network. Second, using this framework and following Kagawa et al. (2015), this study employs network diagrams to analyze Japan’s automobile industry and its bilateral relationships with the U.S. and China from 2002 to 2022. The results highlight China’s development of domestic industrial networks that enable active participation in GVCs.

title: Urbanização e Endividamento das Famílias: Evidência Empírica para Portugal
authors: Carolina Gonçalves; Maria Basílio; Carlos Borralho
abstract: O presente estudo analisa os determinantes do endividamento das famílias em Portugal, com especial foco nas diferenças territoriais associadas ao grau de urbanização. Para tal, distingue-se entre a probabilidade de contrair dívida e a respetiva intensidade, medida através da taxa de esforço, procurando compreender de que forma o contexto territorial e os fatores socioeconómicos influenciam o comportamento financeiro dos agregados familiares. Com base nos dados do Inquérito à Situação Financeira das Famílias de 2020, é estimado um modelo em duas partes, permitindo analisar separadamente a decisão de recorrer ao crédito e o grau de endividamento entre os agregados endividados. Os resultados indicam que o endividamento constitui um fenómeno multidimensional, influenciado por fatores sociodemográficos, económicos e comportamentais, bem como pelo enquadramento territorial. Verifica-se que os agregados localizados em áreas mais urbanizadas apresentam maior probabilidade de deter dívida e níveis mais elevados de endividamento. Variáveis como o género, a idade, o número de filhos, o rendimento líquido, a escolaridade e a situação perante o emprego revelam-se igualmente estatisticamente significativas, embora alguns dos seus efeitos difiram entre as duas dimensões analisadas e consoante o grau de urbanização. Estes resultados evidenciam a importância de incorporar a dimensão territorial na análise da vulnerabilidade financeira das famílias e na definição de políticas públicas orientadas para a prevenção do sobre-endividamento.

title: Political Literacy and Social Inequalities Among Young People: Evidence from an Outermost Region
authors: Ana Rita Matias; Fernando Diogo
abstract: This article analyses the political literacy of young people in the Azores, aged between 12 and 30, based on an empirical study conducted in this outermost region of Portugal. It aims to contribute to the debate on youth political literacy in peripheral and insular contexts, which remains largely overlooked in national and European surveys. Drawing on a measure of political literacy based on factual knowledge of key political actors and democratic institutions, a Political Literacy Index was constructed using a representative sample of Azorean youth. The findings reveal marked inequalities in political literacy associated with social class, educational attainment, and age, as well as differences in the type and intensity of political participation, mediated by levels of political literacy. By showing that political literacy operates as a socially differentiated form of civic capital, the article advances sociological debates on social inequalities and democratic participation in insular contexts.

title: Mapeamento Multidimensional das Desigualdades Regionais em Angola
authors: Waldemar Sérgio Tavares; Tiago Loiola; Maria da Conceição Peixe Rego; Leonida Tomás Correia
abstract: Angola, classificada pelas Nações Unidas como um país de desenvolvimento humano médio, apresenta marcadas assimetrias sociais e regionais. As desigualdades socioespaciais manifestam-se por meio de fortes disparidades nos indicadores de bem-estar e progresso social entre as províncias. Este artigo tem como objetivo mapear as desigualdades multidimensionais nas províncias angolanas, a partir de dimensões associadas à educação, saúde e economia. Os dados foram extraídos de vários relatórios do Instituto Nacional de Estatística de Angola e de diferentes ministérios, tratados e analisados por meio de técnicas de econometria espacial, com o apoio do software GeoDa, visando identificar padrões espaciais de concentração das variáveis estudadas. Os resultados evidenciam amplas e persistentes desigualdades em todas as dimensões analisadas. As regiões Leste, Norte e Sul e, em menor grau, o Centro apresentam elevados níveis de carências multidimensionais. Destaca-se o caso das Lundas, ricas em recursos naturais, mas marcadas por desigualdades de género, desemprego, escassez de recursos humanos especializados e elevadas taxas de fecundidade. A província de Luanda, apesar do seu dinamismo económico, revela disparidades críticas em indicadores sociais, como baixas taxas de escolarização, elevada mortalidade materno-infantil, elevado desemprego e baixo PIB per capita, sugerindo a presença de uma possível armadilha do desenvolvimento.

title: Industrial Heritage and Tourism Development Through Luso-Spanish Cross-Border Cooperation
authors: Elaine Scalabrini; Roberto Vaz; Joaquín García; João Paulo Teixeira; Paula Odete Fernandes
abstract: Industrial tourism and heritage have become essential instruments for promoting cultural preservation and regional sustainable development, particularly in low-density and post-industrial territories. Within the Duero-Douro cross-border region, industrial heritage represents a joint cultural asset that can strengthen cooperation and foster innovative tourism strategies between Portugal and Spain. In this context, this study focused on mapping and analysing industrial and pre-industrial heritage across 22 Portuguese and 80 Spanish municipalities, resulting in a database of 1,075 catalogued assets. The methodology combined data collection, validation, and analysis through active collaboration among cross-border institutions, involving 9 entities and 21 researchers. The results reveal a predominance of transport infrastructure, wineries, and food industries, reflecting the historical and cultural interdependence between the two territories. The findings focus on the potential of cross-border cooperation to promote the valorisation and sustainable use of industrial heritage, contributing to territorial cohesion, tourism diversification, and the construction of a shared Iberian identity related to industrial tourism.

title: Desigualdades Regionais no Emprego em Portugal: Uma abordagem baseada no Quociente de Localização e no Índice de Hirschman-Herfindahl
authors: Laudelina Alves Ribeiro; Jefferson Andronio Ramundo Staduto; Rui Manuel de Sousa Fragoso; Maria Conceição Peixe Rego
abstract: Este estudo analisa o comportamento locativo e a concentração do emprego nos setores de atividade económica, ao nível das NUTS III, em Portugal e nos seus principais municípios, em 2011 e 2021. A metodologia utilizada baseou-se no Quociente de Localização (QL) e no Índice de Hirschman-Herfindahl (IHH). Os resultados evidenciam a prevalência do setor terciário nas NUTS III e nos municípios analisados, o que significa a especialização e concentração do emprego nas atividades económicas deste sector. A concentração do emprego em atividades do setor terciário, muitas das quais de baixo valor acrescentado, torna os municípios e as regiões mais expostas a crises de natureza económica e social, diminuindo a resiliência e originando maiores disparidades regionais. quedado que a terciarização da economia portuguesa está baseada em bens e serviços de baixo valor, muito dos quais de natureza não transacionável, sugere-se que a política pública deva privilegiar a reindustrialização e o desenvolvimento de serviços geradores de elevado valor acrescentado.

title: Como os Incentivos dos Governos Promovem o Desenvolvimento dos Territórios? Uma Revisão Sistemática e Bibliométrica da Literatura
authors: José Rafael; Rui Silva
abstract: O estudo do uso de políticas de incentivos para promover o desenvolvimento das regiões tem demonstrado um apreciável crescimento, nomeadamente a partir de 2011, sendo amplamente estudado, quer na vertente de incentivos fiscais, quer não fiscais. Os objetivos deste estudo são: mapear a produção científica, identificar os estudos, respetivos autores e fontes, com contribuições mais relevantes, perceber quais são as principais áreas temáticas de investigação, bem como conduzir a linhas de investigação futura. Para o efeito, desenvolvemos uma análise sistemática e bibliométrica da literatura, composta por uma amostra final de 136 artigos, publicados entre 1995 e 2024. A análise bibliométrica realizada evidência a existência de quatro agrupamentos temáticos principais: (1) os objetivos dos governos e das empresas condicionam o resultado dos incentivos, (2)o impacto dos incentivos em zonas empresariais apresenta resultados inconclusivos, (3) oimpacto dos incentivos é multidimensionalmente condicionado e (4) o impacto dos incentivosapresenta resultados limitados no desenvolvimento dos territórios.O estudo dos incentivos como instrumento de política de desenvolvimento demonstra ser um campo de investigação consolidado, no entanto conseguimos identificar ainda áreas de estudo promissoras e de grande interesse público com contributo relevante para a diminuição das assimetrias regionais e desenvolvimento dos territórios.

title: When Carbs Cross the Border: The Impact of Tariffs on the Price of Pasta and Frozen Chips
authors: Lawrence Edwards; Godfrey Kamutando; Matthew Stern; Fouche Venter; Simbarashe Mambara; Zaakirah Ismail
abstract: This paper uses unique data on monthly product prices at the retail outlet level from 2010 to 2022 to study the implications of rising tariff protection in South Africa on consumer prices of frozen chips and pasta. Imports of these products have faced a combination of different trade restrictions, including normal customs duties, safeguards and anti‐dumping ( AD ) duties. Econometric estimates reveal higher retail prices of frozen chips following the imposition of AD duties and higher pasta prices following the increases in MFN tariffs and AD duties on pasta imports. Price increases are stronger in metropolitan compared with other urban areas, corroborating international evidence of higher pass‐through of tariffs to urban centres. On average, frozen chip prices are estimated to have increased by 4.7%, and pasta by 9% over the periods in which AD duties and higher MFN tariffs were applied. The overall effect is a reduction in household welfare equivalent to 0.03% of annual food expenditure, with wealthier households affected more compared with poorer households.

title: Does the Inclusion of Foreign‐Based Players Influence the Performance of National Teams at AFCON Tournaments?
authors: Ernest Yeboah Acheampong; Ellis Kofi Akwaa‐Sekyi; Michel Raspaud
abstract: Team composition in sports rarely considers the significant mix of players in a national team's tournament performance. This study theorises that the mere inclusion of foreign‐based nationals is not enough to guarantee team success, especially in the African Cup of Nations (AFCON) tournaments. Using panel data on AFCON records of participating national teams from 1990 to 2025 in an ordinal logit regression, we reveal that an over‐reliance on either foreign‐based nationals or local players decreases the odds of finishing in the top four and subsequently winning the tournament. Drawing on social capital, modernisation, dependency, performance and systems theories, the study reveals that there is more to team composition and success at tournaments than the mere inclusion of foreign‐based nationals. The study finds a positive relationship between team experience, measured by the number of appearances made in previous tournaments, and team performance. The study provides useful information for coaches, managers, federations and scouts to have a good mix of team composition. Perhaps the playing time or activeness of foreign‐based nationals should be considered before their inclusion in the squad. This makes room for future team composition research to consider the skill sets, experience, techniques and knowledge acquired as a recipe for team performance.

title: A Tribute to ESSA Presidents Serving From 1988 to 2025
authors: Jannie Rossouw; Le Roux Burrows
abstract: The Economic Society of South Africa (ESSA) was established in 1925 and celebrated its centenary in 2025. This is a remarkable milestone for a voluntary society comprising members from all walks of life. To date, three articles have been published on past presidents of ESSA, covering the period up to 1987. This article presents the biographies of the 19 ESSA past presidents who served from 1988 to 2025.

title: Basel III Capital Requirements and the Growth of Non‐Bank Financial Institutions in South Africa
authors: Chimwemwe Chipeta; Lerato Mapela
abstract: We examine the relationship between the implementation of the Basel III accord and the growth of non‐bank financial institutions and fintech platforms in South Africa. Using difference‐in‐differences estimation procedures, we find evidence consistent with regulatory arbitrage . In particular, the imposition of minimum capital requirements is associated with stronger growth among constrained non‐bank financial institutions relative to their unconstrained peers. Similarly, country‐level estimations show that tighter minimum capital restrictions are associated with the growth of fintech platforms in South Africa, whereas innovation appears to be an important factor associated with the growth of fintech ventures in selected African economies. Our results highlight the need for targeted policies that enable and sustain a vibrant fintech ecosystem.
